Welcome - How to Use This Flutter Guide

0.1 How this guide is organised0.2 The right mindset0.3 Tools and setup0.4 Code conventions used here

This guide assumes you already know the basics of Flutter: widgets, build methods, stateless and stateful widgets, and a simple app. It picks up from there and goes deep on everything that matters for production.

Flutter is a declarative UI framework with its own rendering engine. The framework is only half of it: the engine draws with Skia (or Impeller on iOS) and composites the tree itself, which is why a Flutter app looks identical on every platform and why the performance characteristics are different from a web app in a browser.

0.1 How this guide is organised

The five parts of the guide, and which chapters to read for which job.

  • Part I (Ch. 1-6) - the engine and the UI: the three trees, layout and constraints, slivers, custom painting and shaders, animation and physics, and gestures. This is the part that most Flutter developers are weak in, and it is where the framework's real power is.
  • Part II (Ch. 7-8) - architecture: state management in depth - setState, InheritedWidget, Provider, Riverpod, Bloc and signals - and routing with go_router, including deep links and nested navigation.
  • Part III (Ch. 9-12) - product concerns: theming and design systems, accessibility and internationalisation, local storage and offline sync, and networking with generated serialisation.
  • Part IV (Ch. 13-14) - the platform: platform channels, FFI, writing your own plugin, and background work with notifications.
  • Part V (Ch. 15-19) - shipping: testing including golden tests, performance and profiling, desktop and web, security, and release engineering for all six platforms.

0.2 The right mindset

Six beliefs that separate a Flutter developer who ships from one who fights the framework.

  1. Widgets are configuration, and most of them should be small. A widget is an immutable description of what to build. If your build method is long, extract a widget. This is not style advice: it is how Flutter gets the reuse and the performance for free.
  2. 16.7 milliseconds is the budget, and the frame is not negotiable. Everything in the UI thread competes for it. When something is slow, find out whether it is layout, paint or raster - the tool tells you, and the fix is different for each.
  3. Never do work in build. build runs many times per second during animation and scroll. Network calls, JSON parsing, database reads and heavy computation belong in an init method, an isolate or a Future outside the tree.
  4. Const constructors are not an optimisation, they are a contract. const lets Flutter skip rebuilding an entire subtree, and it is how the framework knows a widget can be reused. It costs nothing to add.
  5. State belongs as low in the tree as possible. A setState high in the tree rebuilds everything below it. The fix for "my app is slow when I type" is nearly always to move the state down or make the list lazy.
  6. Measure on a real device, in profile mode. Debug mode is dramatically slower and lies about jank. A Pixel 3 or an iPhone SE from 2018 is a more useful target than a simulator on a modern laptop.

0.3 Tools and setup

What each tool is for, and when to install it

A Flutter development environment is small and each tool in it exists for one job, which is worth knowing because installing the wrong set is the common cause of a project that will not build. The SDK is the framework, the engine and the command-line tool in one download; it contains the flutter command that every other tool is used through, and its channel — stable, beta or dev — determines what features exist and how quickly they change. The Dart SDK ships inside it and is used for analysis and for the formatter, so there is nothing separate to install. An editor with the Dart and Flutter extensions provides analysis, refactoring and the widget inspector, and its value is the analysis server rather than the editor itself: the same analysis runs in continuous integration, which is what makes the tool's advice consistent with what the build will accept. The Android toolchain — a JDK, the Android SDK, and an emulator — is needed to build for Android; the emulator is optional if you test on a physical device, and a physical device is faster and more representative. Xcode is required for iOS and can only be built on macOS. The Flutter SDK's own doctor checks all of this and reports what is missing, which is the first thing to run when a build fails for an environmental reason. Then the four things worth installing deliberately, and each is optional in a way that matters. A code generator — the one that turns your annotations into the typed models and serialisation code the chapters describe — and it must be run after every change to an annotated class, which is a step people forget and the cause of a build that fails with "part of" errors. A linter set, because the analysis that catches the mistakes this guide warns about is opt-in and the strictest useful set is not the default. A state-management package, which is a project decision rather than a tooling one and which the state chapter's argument should decide rather than habit. And a dependency-injection or routing package, for the same reason. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Having two Flutter installations, from a package manager and from a manual download, which produces a build that uses one version and a command that resolves to the other; the diagnostic is to print the version and to have exactly one on the path. Not running the generator, which produces a build error mentioning a generated file that does not exist, and which is resolved by running the generator rather than by creating the file. And developing on a desktop target by default, which is convenient and hides platform issues — the safe-area handling, the keyboard, the back gesture — and which means the first test on a phone finds several defects at once. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Pin the SDK version in the project, because a project that builds on a developer's channel and not on the pinned one is a project that builds for one person. And run the doctor and the analysis before writing code, because both take a minute and both remove a class of problem that is expensive to diagnose later from the symptom.

flutter doctor is the first thing to run on any new machine, and the first thing to check when a build fails on someone else's machine. It validates the SDK, the toolchain, the connected devices and every plugin you have, and it names the exact fix for anything it finds.

The toolchain, and the three tools you will use daily that are not the editor.

// the SDK
flutter --version
flutter doctor              # check everything, and what is missing
flutter devices            # what you can run on
flutter config --enable-web
flutter config --enable-desktop

// the daily loop
flutter create my_app
cd my_app
flutter pub get
flutter run
flutter run --profile            # for performance work: real speed
flutter run --release            # real speed, no debugger
flutter run -d chrome            # web
flutter run -d macos             # desktop

// the quality tools
flutter analyze
dart fix --apply
dart format .
flutter test
flutter test --coverage
flutter test --update-goldens

// the profiling tools
flutter run --profile
# then, in a browser: the VM service URL it prints
# DevTools -> Performance, or the timeline in the IDE

// build_runner, for code generation
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dart run build_runner watch --delete-conflicting-outputs

// what to install alongside Flutter
Android Studio  (Android SDK, emulator)
Xcode 15+       (iOS and macOS, macOS only)
VS Code with the Dart + Flutter extensions

0.4 Code conventions used here

The conventions this guide assumes, and why each one is here

The samples in this guide follow a small set of conventions, and they are worth stating because each one exists to prevent a specific mistake that is easy to make and hard to find. Named constructors everywhere. A widget with many parameters is unreadable as a positional call and impossible to read at a glance, so every widget in this guide takes named parameters and the argument names say what the values are — which matters because a widget call with three positional booleans is a call nobody can review. A widget that can be const is written const. Not as an optimisation habit but as a statement: a const widget tells the reader that nothing in it varies with anything outside the frame, which is a claim that is worth making and is checked by the compiler. Disposal is shown where it applies, rather than omitted for brevity, because the disposal rule is the one that is invisible until it is violated and then produces a leak or a crash. Business logic is kept out of build methods, because a build method should describe structure and anything else in it is untestable — so the samples show the logic in a plain function or a controller and the build method calling it. Errors are handled where the decision can be made, which means a repository returns a result and a screen decides what to do with it, rather than the repository choosing a message. And asynchronous work is awaited or cancelled explicitly, because the alternative is a callback that runs after the widget is gone. Then the three conventions that are about reading, and each is a choice this guide makes deliberately. Samples show the shape, not the tutorial. A sample in this guide is correct and complete in isolation and is meant to be read; the surrounding prose is the explanation, and a sample is not the place for a step-by-step. Comments explain why, not what. A comment restating the code is noise; a comment explaining why a value is a specific number, or why an unusual construct was chosen, is the thing a reader cannot derive. And abbreviated names are used only where the full name would obscure the shape, so a sample reads like an example rather than like an identifier dump. Then the two things worth knowing about reading a guide like this, and both are about what you will not find. There is no production code here, because the value of a sample is that it shows one thing clearly and production code shows ten things imperfectly; the surrounding prose is where the caveats live. And there is no single right architecture, because the chapters give criteria rather than prescriptions and applying them to a specific application is the work; a chapter that told you what to build would be wrong for half the applications it was read by.

The strict lint set is worth the initial cleanup. A codebase that passes flutter analyze --fatal-infos has no accidental setState in a widget that cannot, no missing const, and no unawaited future. Those three classes of warning are the ones that become real bugs.

The style this guide assumes, so the code reads consistently.

// 1. const wherever the compiler allows it
//    the IDE offers this automatically
const SizedBox.shrink()
final text = Text('static');

final dynamic = Text('may change');    // final, not const

// 2. private members with _
// 3. constructors first, then fields, then methods
// 4. build method small: one widget per line where possible
// 5. keys on list items - see chapter 3
// 6. no setState in a StatelessWidget, obviously
// 7. the three trees are respected: build creates Elements and
//    RenderObjects only when they differ

// the analysis options this guide assumes
// analysis_options.yaml
include: package:very_good_analysis/analysis_options.6.0.0.yaml

analyzer:
  exclude:
    - "**/*.g.dart"
    - "**/*.freezed.dart"
  errors:
    # make these fatal, not just warnings
    missing_required_param: error
    missing_return: error

linter:
  rules:
    - always_declare_return_types
    - avoid_print
    - prefer_final_locals
    - prefer_const_constructors
    - prefer_const_declarations
    - require_trailing_commas
    - unawaited_futures

Exercises 1

  1. Run flutter doctor and fix everything it reports. Write down what it checked, because that list is your build environment.
  2. Create a project, add very_good_analysis to analysis_options.yaml, and fix every warning it produces.
  3. Run the same screen in debug, profile and release, and record the frame timings. The difference is the whole reason chapter 16 exists.
  4. Write a widget with a build method over 100 lines, then break it into five widgets. Note the readability difference.
  5. Find three places in your own code where you could add const, and add it.

1 · Architecture and the Widget Tree

1.1 The three trees1.2 Elements and lifecycle1.3 When a widget rebuilds1.4 Keys and element reuse1.5 InheritedWidget and context1.6 Composition, slots and custom widgets1.7 Project structure that scales1.8 initState, dispose and the rest

The mental model that makes the rest of Flutter make sense. If you understand the three trees and when a widget rebuilds, most performance problems and most "why did my state reset" bugs become obvious.

1.1 The three trees

What each tree is responsible for, and which one you debug in

The three trees exist because three different jobs have three different lifetimes, and one object cannot have three lifetimes. The widget tree is a description and has no lifetime at all. A widget is an immutable value: it is constructed, passed down, possibly rebuilt, and thrown away. Two widget instances that are structurally equal are interchangeable, and the framework is free to create a new one on every frame of an animation at no meaningful cost. This is why widgets are cheap and why the guidance is that a widget should be a description and nothing else — no logic, no fields that mutate, no identity. The element tree is identity, and it is the tree you debug in. One element exists per widget position in the tree, it outlives any number of widget instances, and it holds the link between a widget and the thing that widget produces. An element's job is to decide, on every rebuild, whether the widget it is being handed is the same widget it had before — and the answer is the one that produces every bug in this area. The render object tree is layout and painting, and it is the tree that costs memory. A render object holds a size, a position, constraints, a paint, hit-test information, and a possibly-layer. It is created lazily — only when something needs geometry — and it is retained across rebuilds, which is why rebuilding is cheap but creating render objects is not, and why a widget tree that changes shape every frame allocates in a way an otherwise identical one does not.

Then the consequence that makes the three-tree model worth the trouble, because it is the answer to most Flutter performance questions. Rebuilding a widget is cheap; rebuilding a render object is expensive; creating a render object is more expensive still. So the design goal for any Flutter application is that a state change should reach the smallest subtree that needs to know about it, and the three trees give you three different levers for that. A narrower widget means a smaller subtree to rebuild. A const widget means the element can skip the update entirely, because it compares the incoming widget with the previous one structurally and finds them equal — which is why const is a compile-time guarantee rather than an optimisation hint, and why it does nothing at all if the widget contains a non-const child. A repaint boundary means the change does not repaint the parent's paint. And a state change placed in the correct element means the element subtree above it never rebuilds at all. When a Flutter performance problem is described as "rebuilds", the useful first question is almost always which of the three trees is doing the work, because "rebuild" is used loosely to mean all three and the three have completely different costs and completely different fixes.

/* The three trees, by job. */
const TREES = [
  { tree: 'WIDGET', job: 'a DESCRIPTION', lifetime: 'NONE AT ALL',
    facts: ['it is CONSTRUCTED, PASSED DOWN, possibly REBUILT, and THROWN AWAY',
      'TWO WIDGET INSTANCES THAT ARE STRUCTURALLY EQUAL ARE INTERCHANGEABLE',
      'the framework is FREE TO CREATE A NEW ONE on every frame of an animation at NO MEANINGFUL COST'],
    therefore: 'why widgets are CHEAP',
    rule: 'a widget is a DESCRIPTION and NOTHING ELSE - no logic, no fields that mutate, no identity' },
  { tree: 'ELEMENT', job: 'IDENTITY', debugThisOne: true,
    fact: 'ONE ELEMENT EXISTS PER WIDGET POSITION in the tree',
    outlives: 'any number of WIDGET INSTANCES',
    holds: 'the LINK between a widget and THE THING THAT WIDGET PRODUCES',
    job2: 'to DECIDE, on every rebuild, WHETHER THE WIDGET it is being handed IS THE SAME WIDGET it had before',
    produces: 'every BUG in this area' },
  { tree: 'RENDER OBJECT', job: 'LAYOUT and PAINTING', costsMemory: true,
    holds: ['a SIZE', 'a POSITION', 'CONSTRAINTS', 'a PAINT', 'HIT-TEST information', 'and a POSSIBLY-LAYER'],
    createdLazily: 'only when SOMETHING NEEDS GEOMETRY',
    retained: 'ACROSS REBUILDS',
    therefore: 'why REBUILDING IS CHEAP but CREATING RENDER OBJECTS IS NOT',
    and: 'why a widget tree that changes SHAPE every frame ALLOCATES in a way an otherwise IDENTICAL one does not' },
];

/* The consequence. */
const COST = [
  { o: 'REBUILDING A WIDGET', c: 'CHEAP' },
  { o: 'REBUILDING A RENDER OBJECT', c: 'EXPENSIVE' },
  { o: 'CREATING A RENDER OBJECT', c: 'MORE EXPENSIVE STILL' },
];
const GOAL = 'a state change should REACH THE SMALLEST SUBTREE THAT NEEDS TO KNOW ABOUT IT';
const LEVERS = [
  { l: 'a NARROWER WIDGET', gives: 'a SMALLER SUBTREE TO REBUILD' },
  { l: 'a const WIDGET', gives: 'the ELEMENT CAN SKIP THE UPDATE ENTIRELY',
    mechanism: 'it COMPARES the incoming widget with the PREVIOUS ONE structurally and FINDS THEM EQUAL',
    whyCompileTime: 'it is a COMPILE-TIME GUARANTEE rather than an OPTIMISATION HINT',
    caveat: 'and it DOES NOTHING AT ALL if the widget CONTAINS A NON-CONST CHILD' },
  { l: 'a REPAINT BOUNDARY', gives: 'the change does not REPAINT THE PARENTS PAINT' },
  { l: 'a STATE CHANGE in the CORRECT ELEMENT', gives: 'the ELEMENT SUBTREE ABOVE IT NEVER REBUILDS AT ALL' },
];
const FIRST_QUESTION = 'when a performance problem is described as rebuilds, WHICH OF THE THREE TREES IS DOING THE WORK - because rebuild is used LOOSELY to mean all three and the three have COMPLETELY DIFFERENT COSTS and COMPLETELY DIFFERENT FIXES';

The distinction between the element tree and the render object tree is worth internalising because it explains a whole family of Flutter questions: why a const widget is free, why a GlobalKey is expensive, why a Container is several widgets, and why a widget that rebuilds can still be visually identical.

Widget, Element and RenderObject, and the job each one does.

//  1. WIDGET TREE  - the immutable configuration, rebuilt freely
//     - a description: "put a red container here, 10x10"
//     - cheap to create, thrown away on every rebuild
//     - it is what you write
//
//  2. ELEMENT TREE  - the identity, lives for the widget's lifetime
//     - holds a reference to the widget and the build context
//     - manages lifecycle: initState, didUpdateWidget, dispose
//     - one per widget INSTANCE position in the tree
//
//  3. RENDEROBJECT TREE - the layout, paint and compositing data
//     - the actual geometry: Size, constraints, offsets
//     - the expensive part: layout, paint, compositing
//     - created lazily, only when the widget needs a render object
//     - e.g. a Text widget produces a RenderParagraph
// the flow, for a single rebuild
//
//   setState(() => _count++)
//        |
//        v
//   the Element marks itself dirty
//        |
//        v
//   build() is called on that State -> a NEW Widget instance
//        |
//        v
//   the framework diffs the new widget against the old one
//        |
//        +-- same runtimeType and key -> update the existing Element,
//        |   call didUpdateWidget, keep the State
//        |
//        +-- different type or key -> deactivate the old Element,
//            create a new one, and mount the subtree
//        |
//        v
//   RenderObjects are updated: layout, then paint, then composite
//
// THE CONSEQUENCE: a rebuild does NOT recreate the State, unless the
// widget type or key changed. That is why state survives a rebuild
// and why it does NOT survive a page change.
// what is created and when
class CounterPage extends StatelessWidget {
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Column(children: [
      Text('$_count'),        // RenderParagraph: created on first mount,
      ElevatedButton(...),     // updated on every rebuild
    ]);
  }
}

// a RenderObject is created only for render-object widgets.
// these produce no RenderObject: the work is in the Element or in
// nothing at all
//   Container   - a convenience wrapper, not a RenderObject
//   Padding     - a convenience wrapper (a Padding is a property of
//                 the child's RenderObject, not its own object)
//   StatelessWidget subclasses that just return other widgets
//
// these DO produce a RenderObject
//   Row, Column, Stack, SizedBox, Positioned, Align, CustomPaint,
//   Text, Image, DecoratedBox, Transform, Opacity, ...

1.2 Elements and lifecycle

The five callbacks, and what each one guarantees

An element's lifecycle is five calls, and the order is guaranteed and the meaning of each is not obvious from the names. createState and mount — the element is created, then mounted into the tree. Mounting is when the element is told where it is: the widget property is populated and, for a stateful widget, the State object is created and its context becomes usable. Nothing may depend on an ancestor at this point beyond what the constructor received, because the element has not yet inflated its own child. initState runs once, when the State is first attached. It is the correct place to subscribe to a stream, start an animation controller, and read a value from an inherited widget that will not change for the lifetime of this state — and it is the wrong place to do anything that needs layout, because layout has not happened and will not happen until after the first frame. Reading an inherited widget in initState works and is specifically why didChangeDependencies exists: initState is not called again when the dependency changes, but didChangeDependencies is. didChangeDependencies runs when an inherited widget this element depends on changes, which makes it the correct place to respond to a theme or a locale or a media query change — and the trap is that it also runs once, immediately after initState, so anything placed in both places runs twice. rebuild is the one that matters and the one nobody thinks about. When an element is rebuilt, it is not asked to build a new subtree from scratch: it calls update on the new widget, and if the new widget says it is the same type, the existing element is reused and updated in place, which is why the child elements are preserved and their state survives. That preservation is conditional on the widget type being identical, which is the whole basis of the keys discussion in the next section.

/* The five calls, in order. */
const LIFECYCLE = [
  { call: 'createState, then mount', happens: 'the ELEMENT IS CREATED, then MOUNTED INTO THE TREE',
    mounting: 'when the element is TOLD WHERE IT IS - the WIDGET property is POPULATED and, for a stateful widget, the STATE OBJECT IS CREATED and its CONTEXT BECOMES USABLE',
    rule: 'NOTHING MAY DEPEND ON AN ANCESTOR at this point beyond what the CONSTRUCTOR RECEIVED, because the ELEMENT HAS NOT YET INFLATED ITS OWN CHILD' },
  { call: 'initState', runs: 'ONCE, WHEN THE STATE IS FIRST ATTACHED',
    correctFor: ['SUBSCRIBE to a stream', 'START an animation controller',
      'READ A VALUE from an inherited widget that WILL NOT CHANGE for the lifetime of this state'],
    wrongFor: 'anything that NEEDS LAYOUT',
    whyWrong: 'because LAYOUT HAS NOT HAPPENED and WILL NOT HAPPEN until AFTER THE FIRST FRAME',
    trap: 'reading an INHERITED WIDGET in initState WORKS, and that is SPECIFICALLY WHY didChangeDependencies EXISTS - initState is NOT CALLED AGAIN when the dependency changes, but didChangeDependencies IS' },
  { call: 'didChangeDependencies', runs: 'WHEN AN INHERITED WIDGET this element DEPENDS ON CHANGES',
    correctFor: ['a THEME change', 'a LOCALE change', 'a MEDIA QUERY change'],
    trap: 'it ALSO RUNS ONCE, IMMEDIATELY AFTER initState, so anything placed in BOTH PLACES RUNS TWICE' },
  { call: 'rebuild', mattersMost: true,
    isNot: 'it is NOT asked to BUILD A NEW SUBTREE FROM SCRATCH',
    instead: 'it calls UPDATE on the new widget',
    andThen: 'if the new widget SAYS IT IS THE SAME TYPE, the EXISTING ELEMENT IS REUSED AND UPDATED IN PLACE',
    consequence: 'which is why the CHILD ELEMENTS ARE PRESERVED and their STATE SURVIVES',
    conditional: 'that preservation is CONDITIONAL ON THE WIDGET TYPE BEING IDENTICAL',
    connects: 'which is the WHOLE BASIS of the keys discussion in the next section' },
];

The exact order of the lifecycle calls, because the order is what surprises people.

// MOUNTING, in order
//  1. Widget instance created
//  2. Element created, widget attached
//  3. Element.mount() -> State created, state._element set
//  4. State.initState()                 ONCE
//  5. didChangeDependencies()            ONCE
//  6. build()                            called
//  7. framework does layout, paint, composite
//  8. Element mounts its child Elements
//
// UPDATING
//  9. parent rebuilds -> new widget instance
// 10. Element.update() -> State.didUpdateWidget(oldWidget)
// 11. build() again
//
// UNMOUNTING, in order
// 12. Element.deactivate()    (the subtree is leaving)
// 13. Element.unmount()
// 14. State.dispose()         ONCE
// 15. then: deactivate() -> unmount() for the descendants
// deactivate vs dispose: the distinction that matters
//
// deactivate(): the element may come BACK. It is still in the tree
//   in an inactive state - this happens with GlobalKey reparenting,
//   and when an IndexedStack shows a different child
//   YOU DO NOT dispose here.
//
// dispose(): it is gone. Controllers, subscriptions, timers go here.
//
// THE RULE: release resources in dispose, and ONLY in dispose.
// Releasing in deactivate breaks when the widget is reactivated.

1.3 When a widget rebuilds

The complete set of triggers, and the two that are usually forgotten.

// a widget rebuilds when:
//  1. setState is called on its State
//  2. its parent rebuilds and produced a new widget instance
//  3. an InheritedWidget it depends on changed
//  4. a State object it depends on changed (Provider, Riverpod, ...)
//  5. a MediaQuery, Theme, Directionality or other inherited
//     widget it reads changed
//  6. it is inside a widget that was rebuilt
//
// 7. and the two people forget:
//    - Theme.of(context) in build: a theme change rebuilds you
//    - MediaQuery.of(context) in build: a keyboard opening, or a
//      rotation, rebuilds EVERY widget that reads it
// the classic performance bug: reading MediaQuery in build
class BadForm extends StatelessWidget {
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // this rebuilds the ENTIRE form when the keyboard opens
    final keyboardHeight = MediaQuery.of(context).viewInsets.bottom;

    return Column(children: [
      TextField(),   // 50ms of widget construction, on every keystroke
      TextField(),
      TextField(),
    ]);
  }
}

// the fix: read only what you need, as low in the tree as possible
class GoodForm extends StatelessWidget {
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // .paddingOf / .viewInsetsOf read only the sub-values you use
    return Padding(
      padding: EdgeInsets.only(
        bottom: MediaQuery.viewInsetsOf(context).bottom,
      ),
      child: const Column(children: [
        TextField(),
        TextField(),
        TextField(),
      ]),
    );
  }
}

// and for the general rule: the further down a dependency is read,
// the smaller the rebuild scope
Widget build(BuildContext context) {
  // GOOD: only the leaf depends on it
  return Column(children: [
    const ExpensiveHeader(),
    ValueListenableBuilder(
      valueListenable: _counter,
      builder: (context, value, _) => Text('$value'),
    ),
  ]);
}

The two mechanisms, and how the subtree is marked

There are exactly two ways a rebuild starts, and knowing which one you are dealing with explains most of the confusing behaviour. setState marks this element dirty and rebuilds this element and everything below it. The element calls markNeedsBuild on itself, which walks down the tree marking each descendant as needing build, and then the framework rebuilds exactly those. markNeedsBuild on an element marks that element and everything above it. This is the mechanism an inherited widget uses: it marks itself dirty, which forces every element that depends on it to rebuild — and it walks up, because the dependency direction is from dependent to dependency. The asymmetry is the thing to internalise: a state change propagates down from where you called it, and a notification propagates up to the dependents. A consequence worth knowing is that markNeedsBuild is idempotent within a frame — an element already marked is not marked again, and the whole chain rebuilds once — so a hundred calls to setState in one frame produce one rebuild, not a hundred. The second consequence is that a rebuild is scheduled for the next frame rather than happening synchronously, so if you call setState and immediately read a value you have not read it yet, and if you call it inside a build method the framework asserts rather than allowing it.

Then the three levers, in the order to try them, and the order is not by effect but by cost of doing. Make the widget const first. If the widget is const and its children are, then a rebuild of the parent produces an equal widget, the element's update short-circuits, and nothing below is touched at all — this is a compile-time guarantee, not an optimisation, and it costs one keyword. Move the state down as far as it can go. A state object should live in the smallest widget that actually uses the value, and the practical technique is to extract a child widget whose constructor takes the value it needs rather than reading it from an inherited widget higher up — because a child widget's rebuild does not require its parent's rebuild, whereas a dependency on an inherited widget does. Use a selector where the source is a large object. If a state object holds a hundred fields and one widget reads one of them, a naive dependency rebuilds on every change to any of them; a selector-style dependency watches one field and rebuilds only on that one, which is the entire reason that class of package exists and why it is worth understanding rather than reaching for by default. And then the measurement discipline, because every one of these claims is measurable and the profile mode chapter's argument applies: measure a rebuild in profile mode, not debug, since debug builds have their own overhead that distorts what you are trying to observe, and look at the count of rebuilt widgets rather than at frame time — a frame that rebuilds three widgets and one that rebuilds three thousand can both miss sixteen milliseconds, and the widget count is the thing that scales badly.

/* Two mechanisms. */
const MECHANISMS = [
  { m: 'setState', marks: 'THIS ELEMENT and EVERYTHING BELOW IT',
    walk: 'DOWN', why: 'because the ELEMENT CALLS markNeedsBuild ON ITSELF, which WALKS DOWN marking each DESCENDANT as needing build' },
  { m: 'markNeedsBuild on an element', marks: 'THAT ELEMENT and EVERYTHING ABOVE IT',
    walk: 'UP',
    usedBy: 'an INHERITED WIDGET',
    why: 'it marks ITSELF DIRTY, which forces EVERY ELEMENT THAT DEPENDS ON IT to REBUILD',
    andThat: 'the DEPENDENCY DIRECTION is from DEPENDENT TO DEPENDENCY' },
];
const ASYMMETRY = 'a STATE CHANGE propagates DOWN from where you CALLED IT, and a NOTIFICATION propagates UP to the DEPENDENTS';
const CONSEQUENCES = [
  { c: 'markNeedsBuild is IDEMPOTENT WITHIN A FRAME', detail: 'an element ALREADY MARKED is not MARKED AGAIN, and the whole chain REBUILDS ONCE',
    so: 'a HUNDRED CALLS to setState in one frame produce ONE REBUILD, not a hundred' },
  { c: 'a REBUILD IS SCHEDULED FOR THE NEXT FRAME rather than HAPPENING SYNCHRONOUSLY',
    consequences: ['if you CALL setState and IMMEDIATELY READ a value you HAVE NOT READ IT YET',
      'if you CALL IT INSIDE A BUILD METHOD the framework ASSERTS rather than ALLOWING IT'] },
];

/* Three levers, in the order to try them. */
const LEVERS = [
  { n: 1, l: 'make the WIDGET const FIRST',
    mechanism: 'if the widget IS const AND ITS CHILDREN ARE, then a REBUILD OF THE PARENT produces an EQUAL WIDGET, the elements UPDATE SHORT-CIRCUITS, and NOTHING BELOW IS TOUCHED AT ALL',
    kind: 'a COMPILE-TIME GUARANTEE, not an OPTIMISATION',
    cost: 'ONE KEYWORD' },
  { n: 2, l: 'move the STATE DOWN as far as it CAN GO',
    technique: 'EXTRACT A CHILD WIDGET whose constructor TAKES THE VALUE IT NEEDS rather than READING IT from an inherited widget higher up',
    why: 'a CHILD WIDGETS REBUILD does not REQUIRE its parents REBUILD, whereas a DEPENDENCY ON AN INHERITED WIDGET DOES' },
  { n: 3, l: 'use a SELECTOR where the SOURCE IS A LARGE OBJECT',
    problem: 'if a state object HOLDS A HUNDRED FIELDS and one widget READS ONE of them, a NAIVE DEPENDENCY REBUILDS on every change to ANY of them',
    fix: 'a SELECTOR-STYLE DEPENDENCY WATCHES ONE FIELD and REBUILDS ONLY ON THAT ONE',
    and: 'which is the ENTIRE REASON that CLASS OF PACKAGE EXISTS' },
];

/* The measurement discipline. */
const MEASURE = [
  { m: 'MEASURE A REBUILD IN PROFILE MODE, not debug',
    why: 'DEBUG BUILDS HAVE THEIR OWN OVERHEAD that DISTORTS what you are trying to OBSERVE' },
  { m: 'look at the COUNT OF REBUILT WIDGETS rather than at FRAME TIME',
    why: 'a FRAME THAT REBUILDS THREE WIDGETS and one that REBUILDS THREE THOUSAND can BOTH MISS SIXTEEN MILLISECONDS',
    and: 'the WIDGET COUNT is the THING THAT SCALES BADLY' },
];

Reach for const first. A const widget is a compile-time constant, so when the parent rebuilds and produces an identical widget, the framework can skip the entire subtree - it does not even call didUpdateWidget. It is the cheapest performance win in Flutter, and it costs one keyword.

1.4 Keys and element reuse

How Flutter matches old elements to new widgets, and what a key changes.

// HOW MATCHING WORKS
//
// for each child position in the new list, the framework looks for
// an existing element with:
//   - the same runtimeType
//   - and, if a key is present, the SAME key
//
// no key        -> match by position
// ValueKey       -> match by value
// ObjectKey      -> match by identity
// UniqueKey      -> never match: a new element every time
// GlobalKey      -> unique across the whole app, and lets the
//                   element move between trees
// WHEN A KEY MATTERS: a conditional child
// NO KEY: the state attaches to the POSITION, not the item
final items = ['a', 'b', 'c'];
// now remove the first item
final filtered = ['b', 'c'];

Column(children: [
  for (final item in filtered) ItemWidget(label: item),
])
// position 0 had ItemWidget('a'), now it has ItemWidget('b')
// -> same type, same position: the State is REUSED
// -> ItemWidget('b') now has 'a'\'s state, and initState never ran

// WITH A KEY
Column(children: [
  for (final item in filtered)
    ItemWidget(key: ValueKey(item), label: item),
])
// -> the element for 'a' is removed, 'b' keeps its own state
// -> the correct behaviour
// REORDERABLE LISTS ALWAYS NEED KEYS
ReorderableListView.builder(
  itemCount: items.length,
  onReorder: (oldIndex, newIndex) { ... },
  itemBuilder: (context, index) {
    return Card(
      key: ValueKey(items[index].id),   // required: without it the
      child: ListTile(title: Text(items[index].name)),  // state scrambles
    );
  },
)

// SO DOES ANY LIST WITH STATEFUL CHILDREN THAT CAN MOVE
// OR BE INSERTED IN THE MIDDLE.

// WHICH KEY
ValueKey(id)      for a stable id from your data. the default choice.
ObjectKey(obj)    when the object itself is the identity
UniqueKey()       force a rebuild: almost never right
GlobalKey         ONLY for moving a stateful widget between routes
                  (a Hero flight, a Draggable) - it is expensive

GlobalKey, and what it costs

A GlobalKey is a key that is unique across the whole application, and that uniqueness is exactly what makes it expensive. A local key only has to be unique among its siblings, so the framework can find it by walking one list. A global key has to be unique in the entire widget tree, so finding it requires the framework to maintain a map from global key to element — and it does, inserting on mount and removing on unmount. That map is the cost, and it shows up in three places. It forces the framework to consider whether the new widget's subtree could be moving somewhere else in the tree, which means it cannot take the local fast path of reusing the element in place, and it makes the affected part of the tree a candidate for re-parenting — which is the same machinery that lets you reparent a widget across the tree and is worth paying for only when you are actually reparenting. It makes the element's identity survive a move, which is genuinely useful and the reason it exists. And the map itself grows with every global key in the app, so an app that creates global keys in a list is doing the one thing global keys are not for.

Then the decision, and it is short enough to remember. Use a local key — a ValueKey of the item's identity — whenever the list can reorder, insert, remove or filter. That is the entire purpose of keys and the case where getting them wrong produces a visible, reproducible bug: the framework reuses elements by position, so an item that moved keeps the state of whatever is now in its place, and the symptom is a checkbox that ticks the wrong row or a text field containing one item's text in another item's row. Use a ObjectKey when the identity is the object rather than a property of it, which is the same decision with the identity expressed directly. Use a UniqueKey when the item genuinely has no identity and must be treated as new every time — and be suspicious of that answer, because it is correct for a widget whose state is genuinely per-occurrence and wrong for a widget representing a thing in a list, where it makes the framework destroy and recreate rather than move. Do not use a GlobalKey for a list item. It is correct — the state follows the item — and it is measurably slower, and it is not needed because a local key achieves the same result for a list. Reserve GlobalKey for the three cases that genuinely need application-wide identity: moving a stateful widget between trees or between routes while keeping its state; preserving a widget's position and size across a change in the tree's structure, as in a reorderable layout; and reaching into the tree to obtain a context or a state object from an ancestor, such as a Form that needs to validate from a sibling. The third is the one people reach for most and it is the one most often unnecessary, because passing the object down through a constructor is cheaper and clearer than the framework maintaining a global map for you.

/* Local versus global. */
const LOCAL = {
  uniqueWithin: 'its SIBLINGS',
  lookup: 'the framework can FIND IT by WALKING ONE LIST',
};
const GLOBAL = {
  uniqueWithin: 'the ENTIRE APPLICATION',
  thatIsTheCost: true,
  mechanism: 'finding it REQUIRES the framework to MAINTAIN A MAP from global key to element, inserting ON MOUNT and REMOVING ON UNMOUNT',
  showsUpAs: [
    { c: 'it FORCES THE FRAMEWORK TO CONSIDER whether the new widgets SUBTREE COULD BE MOVING SOMEWHERE ELSE in the tree',
      consequence: 'it CANNOT TAKE THE LOCAL FAST PATH of REUSING THE ELEMENT IN PLACE',
      and: 'it makes the AFFECTED PART of the tree a CANDIDATE FOR RE-PARENTING',
      sameAs: 'the SAME MACHINERY that LETS YOU REPARENT a widget across the tree, and is WORTH PAYING FOR ONLY WHEN YOU ARE ACTUALLY REPARENTING' },
    { c: 'it MAKES THE ELEMENTS IDENTITY SURVIVE A MOVE', genuinelyUseful: true, and: 'which is THE REASON IT EXISTS' },
    { c: 'the MAP ITSELF GROWS with EVERY GLOBAL KEY in the app',
      so: 'an app that CREATES GLOBAL KEYS IN A LIST is doing THE ONE THING global keys are NOT for' },
  ],
};

/* The decision. */
const DECIDE = [
  { case: 'the LIST CAN REORDER, INSERT, REMOVE or FILTER', then: 'a LOCAL KEY - a ValueKey of the items identity',
    ifWrong: 'the framework REUSES ELEMENTS BY POSITION, so an item that MOVED KEEPS THE STATE of whatever is NOW in its place',
    symptom: ['a CHECKBOX THAT TICKS THE WRONG ROW', 'a TEXT FIELD containing ONE ITEMS TEXT in ANOTHER ITEMS ROW'] },
  { case: 'the IDENTITY IS THE OBJECT rather than a PROPERTY of it', then: 'an ObjectKey', same: 'the SAME DECISION with the IDENTITY EXPRESSED DIRECTLY' },
  { case: 'the item GENUINELY HAS NO IDENTITY and must be treated as NEW EVERY TIME', then: 'a UniqueKey',
    beSuspicious: 'because it is CORRECT for a widget whose state is GENUINELY PER-OCCURRENCE',
    and: 'WRONG for a widget REPRESENTING A THING in a list, where it makes the framework DESTROY AND RECREATE rather than MOVE' },
  { case: 'a LIST ITEM', then: 'do NOT USE A GlobalKey',
    but: 'it is CORRECT - the STATE FOLLOWS THE ITEM - and it is MEASURABLY SLOWER',
    and: 'it is NOT NEEDED because a LOCAL KEY ACHIEVES THE SAME RESULT for a list' },
];

/* The three cases that genuinely need it. */
const GLOBAL_IS_FOR = [
  { c: 'MOVING A STATEFUL WIDGET between trees or between ROUTES while KEEPING ITS STATE' },
  { c: 'PRESERVING A WIDGETS POSITION and SIZE across a CHANGE IN THE TREES STRUCTURE, as in a REORDERABLE LAYOUT' },
  { c: 'REACHING INTO THE TREE to OBTAIN A CONTEXT or a STATE OBJECT from an ANCESTOR, such as a Form that needs to VALIDATE FROM A SIBLING',
    note: 'this is the one people REACH FOR MOST and it is the one MOST OFTEN UNNECESSARY' },
];
const BETTER_THAN_THE_THIRD = 'PASSING THE OBJECT DOWN through a CONSTRUCTOR is CHEAPER and CLEARER than the framework MAINTAINING A GLOBAL MAP for you';

A GlobalKey is not "a better ValueKey". It registers the element in a global map on every mount, which is measurably slower, and using two of them in the same subtree is an error. Use a GlobalKey for exactly one thing: moving a stateful subtree between routes, such as a Hero or a Draggable. Everything else gets a ValueKey.

// the GlobalKey case that is legitimate: reparenting
class Avatar extends StatelessWidget {
  Avatar({super.key, required this.userId});
  final String userId;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // this GlobalKey moves the Element (and its State) from the
    // header to the sheet, so the widget is not rebuilt from scratch
    return Hero(tag: 'avatar-$userId', child: CircleAvatar(...));
  }
}

// and the case people abuse it for
final _controllerKey = GlobalKey<TextEditingController>();

// this works, but a plain final field is simpler and faster
final _controller = TextEditingController();
final _controllerAlt = GlobalKey<TextEditingController>();   // unnecessary

1.5 InheritedWidget and context

How dependency actually works, and why dependOnInheritedWidget exists

The mechanism underneath InheritedWidget is worth understanding precisely, because the intuition that it "notifies listeners" is wrong in a way that produces the wrong fix. An inherited widget is not a subscription. There is no list of dependents and no callback to remove. What exists is a single immutable instance placed in the widget tree, and the thing that makes it inherited is that when an element mounts, it looks up the tree and registers a dependency on the nearest instance of the requested type. That registration is one entry in a field on the element — nothing more. When the inherited widget's data changes, the framework walks down the tree and marks every element that registered a dependency dirty, using the registration rather than the tree shape, which is why an inherited widget can notify a deeply nested widget without knowing anything about it. The consequence is that you cannot unsubscribe, because there is nothing to unsubscribe from — and this is precisely why dependOnInheritedWidget exists as a separate method from getInheritedWidgetOfExactType. The first both finds and registers; the second only finds. So a widget that will need to rebuild when the value changes uses the first, and a widget that reads a value once and never wants to rebuild uses the second. Using the wrong one is the mechanism behind a whole family of performance bugs: a widget that reads a theme inside a build method it runs on every frame has registered a dependency on the whole theme and will rebuild whenever anything in it changes, when all it wanted was the text style once.

Then the three design points, each of which has a specific failure it prevents. What the updateShouldNotify method is for. An inherited widget is immutable; when the data changes, a new instance is placed in the tree with a new value, and the framework asks the old instance whether dependents should be notified by calling updateShouldNotify on it with the new one. Returning true notifies every dependent; returning false notifies nobody. The idiomatic implementation compares the field that matters, and it is worth knowing that the most common mistake here is returning true unconditionally, which converts the mechanism into "everything below rebuilds whenever anything changes" — and that the second most common is comparing the wrong field, so a change to one part of a theme does not notify the widgets that depended on that part. Why the data should be narrow. Because the notification is not selective: a dependent of an inherited widget rebuilds whenever that widget notifies, regardless of which field it read. So an inherited widget carrying a whole application state object forces every dependent to rebuild on any change to any of it, which is why the selector-style approach — putting one field in its own inherited widget — exists and why it trades a proliferation of small widgets for rebuild granularity. And that context above a widget is not allowed to read it. An element may not depend on an inherited widget that is below it, because the dependency has to be established before the subtree exists; this produces a confusing compile-time error at exactly the point a beginner reaches for it, and the fix is always to move the reader down into the subtree rather than to move the provider up.

/* The mechanism. */
const MECHANISM = {
  notA: 'a SUBSCRIPTION', thereIsNo: 'no LIST OF DEPENDENTS and NO CALLBACK TO REMOVE',
  whatExists: 'a SINGLE IMMUTABLE INSTANCE placed in the widget tree',
  howItIsInherited: 'when an ELEMENT MOUNTS, it LOOKS UP the tree and REGISTERS A DEPENDENCY on the NEAREST INSTANCE of the requested type',
  theRegistration: 'ONE ENTRY IN A FIELD ON THE ELEMENT - nothing more',
  onChange: 'when the INHERITED WIDGETS DATA CHANGES, the framework WALKS DOWN the tree and MARKS EVERY ELEMENT THAT REGISTERED A DEPENDENCY DIRTY',
  using: 'the REGISTRATION rather than the TREE SHAPE',
  andThat: 'which is WHY an inherited widget can NOTIFY A DEEPLY NESTED WIDGET without KNOWING ANYTHING about it',
  consequence: 'YOU CANNOT UNSUBSCRIBE, because there is NOTHING TO UNSUBSCRIBE FROM',
};

/* Why dependOnInheritedWidget exists. */
const TWO_METHODS = [
  { m: 'dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType', does: 'BOTH FINDS and REGISTERS',
    useWhen: 'a widget that WILL NEED TO REBUILD when the value CHANGES' },
  { m: 'getInheritedWidgetOfExactType', does: 'ONLY FINDS', registers: false,
    useWhen: 'a widget that READS A VALUE ONCE and NEVER WANTS TO REBUILD' },
];
const WRONG_ONE = 'using the WRONG ONE is the MECHANISM BEHIND a whole FAMILY of performance bugs';
const BUG = 'a widget that READS A THEME inside a build method IT RUNS ON EVERY FRAME has REGISTERED A DEPENDENCY on the whole theme and WILL REBUILD whenever ANYTHING in it changes, when all it WANTED WAS the text style once';

/* Three design points. */
const DESIGN = [
  { d: 'what updateShouldNotify is FOR',
    because: 'an inherited widget is IMMUTABLE - when the data CHANGES, a NEW INSTANCE is PLACED with a NEW VALUE',
    and: 'the framework ASKS THE OLD INSTANCE whether DEPENDENTS SHOULD BE NOTIFIED by CALLING updateShouldNotify ON IT with the new one',
    semantics: ['returning TRUE notifies EVERY DEPENDENT', 'returning FALSE notifies NOBODY'],
    idiomatic: 'COMPARES THE FIELD THAT MATTERS',
    mistake1: 'returning TRUE UNCONDITIONALLY, which converts the mechanism into everything below rebuilds whenever anything changes',
    mistake2: 'COMPARING THE WRONG FIELD, so a CHANGE TO ONE PART of a theme DOES NOT notify the widgets that DEPENDED ON THAT PART' },
  { d: 'why the DATA SHOULD BE NARROW',
    because: 'the NOTIFICATION IS NOT SELECTIVE - a DEPENDENT rebuilds whenever that widget NOTIFIES, REGARDLESS OF WHICH FIELD it read',
    consequence: 'an INHERITED WIDGET CARRYING A WHOLE APPLICATION STATE OBJECT forces EVERY DEPENDENT to REBUILD on ANY CHANGE to ANY of it',
    and: 'which is WHY the SELECTOR-STYLE APPROACH - PUTTING ONE FIELD IN ITS OWN INHERITED WIDGET - EXISTS',
    trade: 'it TRADES A PROLIFERATION OF SMALL WIDGETS for REBUILD GRANULARITY' },
  { d: 'why context ABOVE A WIDGET MAY NOT READ IT',
    rule: 'an ELEMENT MAY NOT DEPEND on an inherited widget that is BELOW IT',
    because: 'the DEPENDENCY HAS TO BE ESTABLISHED BEFORE THE SUBTREE EXISTS',
    symptom: 'a CONFUSING COMPILE-TIME ERROR at exactly the point a BEGINNER REACHES for it',
    fix: 'always MOVE THE READER DOWN into the subtree rather than MOVE THE PROVIDER UP' },
];

The dependency mechanism, and why context.read in build is a bug.

// InheritedWidget is how data flows down the tree without
// passing it through constructors
class ThemeController extends InheritedWidget {
  const ThemeController({
    required this.mode,
    required super.child,
    super.key,
  });

  final ThemeMode mode;

  // the read helper: returns the nearest instance
  static ThemeController of(BuildContext context) {
    final result =
        context.dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType<ThemeController>();
    assert(result != null, 'No ThemeController found in context');
    return result!;
  }

  // the NO-LISTENER variant: read without subscribing
  static ThemeController read(BuildContext context) {
    final element =
        context.getElementForInheritedWidgetOfExactType<ThemeController>();
    final widget = element?.widget as ThemeController?;
    assert(widget != null, 'No ThemeController found in context');
    return widget!;
  }

  @override
  bool updateShouldNotify(ThemeController oldWidget) {
    return mode != oldWidget.mode;   // only notify on a real change
  }
}
// of() SUBSCRIBES: the calling widget rebuilds when it changes
// read() DOES NOT: safe only where you do not need to react
class Header extends StatelessWidget {
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // BUG: the header rebuilds whenever the theme changes, even though
    // it only needs the value in a callback
    final theme = ThemeController.of(context);

    return TextButton(
      onPressed: () => setState(() => theme.toggle()),
      child: const Text('Toggle'),
    );
  }
}

// the correct version: read in the callback, subscribe nowhere
class Header2 extends StatelessWidget {
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return TextButton(
      onPressed: () {
        // read() inside the callback: no subscription, no rebuild
        ThemeController.read(context).toggle();
      },
      child: const Text('Toggle'),
    );
  }
}

// THE RULE: use of() (subscribe) only if the widget VISUALLY changes
// when the value changes. Use read() for callbacks and event handlers.
// the list of built-in inherited widgets, and what depends on them
// Theme            Theme.of(context)
// MediaQuery       MediaQuery.of(context)
// Directionality   Directionality.of(context)
// Localizations    Localizations.of(context)
// Navigator        Navigator.of(context)
// ScaffoldMessenger ScaffoldMessenger.of(context)
// DefaultTextStyle TextStyle.of(context)
// CupertinoTheme   CupertinoTheme.of(context)

// every one of these is a rebuild trigger when it changes
// which is why MediaQuery in a big build method is expensive:
// opening the keyboard changes viewInsets, and every widget that
// read MediaQuery rebuilds.

1.6 Composition, slots and custom widgets

Slots, and why a widget is a function rather than a class hierarchy

Flutter's answer to widget reuse is not a base class with overridable methods; it is the plain Dart pattern of passing children in. The mechanism is worth being precise about because it is what makes Flutter composable rather than merely configurable. A widget that accepts children takes them as a parameter, not by inheriting from a parent. The composition looks like nesting in the source because the nesting happens in the caller's build method, and that is the whole trick: the parent's build method produces the child's widget and supplies it, so the child never needs to know what produced it, and the same child can be composed with different parents by different code in different places. The multi-child slot pattern is the general form of this, and every framework widget that takes a variable number of children is an instance of it: the widget declares named slots, the caller fills them, and the widget decides how to lay them out. This is why Scaffold has appBar, body and floatingActionButton as parameters rather than as subclasses, and why adding a slot to a framework widget is a breaking change for anyone who subclassed it. The distinction that matters is between a slot and a configuration. A slot takes a widget — arbitrary behaviour, arbitrary layout, arbitrary children. A configuration takes a value — a colour, a duration, an alignment. Framework widgets that expose everything as configuration can only do what the framework anticipated; framework widgets that expose slots let callers do things the framework never thought of. Both are legitimate and a well-designed widget library has both, but a widget with fifty configuration parameters and no slots is a widget nobody can extend, and that is a design smell worth recognising.

Then the two patterns that make composition pay off, and the rule that decides between them. Composition: a widget holds other widgets and delegates. A Card that holds a Padding that holds a Container is composition, and it works because each widget does exactly one thing and does not need to know what is inside it. Slots: a widget exposes named positions and lets the caller fill them. A ListTile with leading, title, subtitle and trailing is slots, and it works because the widget decides the arrangement and the caller decides the content. The rule between them: if the outer widget needs to know something about what it contains — to size itself, to tint a border around it, to pass it an inherited value — it needs composition or a Builder-style callback; if it merely needs to place it, it needs a slot. And the failure to watch for is an accidental deep tree: a hierarchy thirty levels deep where each level is a one-line wrapper, which costs a render object per level in some cases and makes every debugging tool's output unreadable. The discipline that prevents it is to notice a level that exists only to add a property, and to fold it into a parameter instead.

/* The mechanism. */
const MECHANISM = {
  notA: 'a BASE CLASS WITH OVERRIDABLE METHODS',
  is: 'the PLAIN DART PATTERN of PASSING CHILDREN IN',
  rule: 'a WIDGET THAT ACCEPTS CHILDREN TAKES THEM AS A PARAMETER, not by INHERITING FROM A PARENT',
  whereTheNestingHappens: 'IN THE CALLERS BUILD METHOD',
  andThatIsTheTrick: 'the PARENTS BUILD METHOD PRODUCES THE CHILDS WIDGET AND SUPPLIES IT, so the CHILD NEVER NEEDS TO KNOW WHAT PRODUCED IT',
  gain: 'the SAME CHILD can be COMPOSED with DIFFERENT PARENTS by DIFFERENT CODE in DIFFERENT PLACES',
};

/* Slots. */
const SLOTS = {
  is: 'the GENERAL FORM of the multi-child pattern',
  and: 'every framework widget that TAKES A VARIABLE NUMBER OF CHILDREN IS AN INSTANCE of it',
  declares: 'NAMED SLOTS', theCaller: 'FILLS THEM', theWidget: 'DECIDES HOW TO LAY THEM OUT',
  instance: 'Scaffold has appBar, body and floatingActionButton as PARAMETERS rather than as SUBCLASSES',
  consequence: 'adding a SLOT to a framework widget is A BREAKING CHANGE for anyone who SUBCLASSED IT',
};

/* Slot versus configuration. */
const SLOT_VS_CONFIG = {
  slot: 'TAKES A WIDGET - ARBITRARY BEHAVIOUR, ARBITRARY LAYOUT, ARBITRARY CHILDREN',
  configuration: 'TAKES A VALUE - A COLOUR, A DURATION, AN ALIGNMENT',
  frameworksWithOnlyConfiguration: 'can ONLY DO WHAT THE FRAMEWORK ANTICIPATED',
  frameworksWithSlots: 'let CALLERS DO THINGS THE FRAMEWORK NEVER THOUGHT OF',
  both: 'LEGITIMATE, and a WELL-DESIGNED WIDGET LIBRARY HAS BOTH',
  smell: 'a WIDGET WITH FIFTY CONFIGURATION PARAMETERS and NO SLOTS is a WIDGET NOBODY CAN EXTEND',
};

/* Two patterns that make composition pay. */
const PATTERNS = [
  { p: 'COMPOSITION', means: 'a WIDGET HOLDS OTHER WIDGETS and DELEGATES',
    instance: 'a Card that holds a Padding that holds a Container',
    worksBecause: 'each widget does EXACTLY ONE THING and DOES NOT NEED TO KNOW WHAT IS INSIDE it' },
  { p: 'SLOTS', means: 'a WIDGET EXPOSES NAMED POSITIONS and LETS THE CALLER FILL THEM',
    instance: 'a ListTile with leading, title, subtitle and trailing',
    worksBecause: 'the WIDGET DECIDES THE ARRANGEMENT and the CALLER DECIDES THE CONTENT' },
];
const RULE = 'if the OUTER WIDGET NEEDS TO KNOW SOMETHING about WHAT IT CONTAINS - to SIZE ITSELF, to TINT A BORDER around it, to PASS IT AN INHERITED VALUE - it needs COMPOSITION or a Builder-STYLE CALLBACK; if it MERELY NEEDS TO PLACE IT, it needs A SLOT';
const WATCH_FOR = {
  failure: 'an ACCIDENTAL DEEP TREE',
  detail: 'a HIERARCHY THIRTY LEVELS DEEP where EACH LEVEL IS A ONE-LINE WRAPPER',
  costs: ['a RENDER OBJECT PER LEVEL in SOME CASES', 'EVERY DEBUGGING TOOLS OUTPUT UNREADABLE'],
  discipline: 'NOTICE A LEVEL THAT EXISTS ONLY TO ADD A PROPERTY, and FOLD IT INTO A PARAMETER instead',
};

The patterns for reusable widgets, and why inheritance of widgets is not idiomatic.

// COMPOSITION over INHERITANCE for widgets
// a widget takes its content as constructor parameters, not by
// subclassing

// a wrapper: takes a child
class Card2 extends StatelessWidget {
  const Card2({
    required this.child,
    this.onTap,
    this.padding = const EdgeInsets.all(16),
    super.key,
  });

  final Widget child;
  final VoidCallback? onTap;
  final EdgeInsets padding;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final content = Padding(padding: padding, child: child);
    if (onTap == null) return _decorated(content);
    return InkWell(onTap: onTap, child: _decorated(content));
  }

  Widget _decorated(Widget child) {
    return DecoratedBox(
      decoration: BoxDecoration(
        color: Theme.of(context).colorScheme.surfaceContainer,
        borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(12),
        border: Border.all(color: Theme.of(context).dividerColor),
      ),
      child: child,
    );
  }
}

// a layout widget: takes named slots
class Section extends StatelessWidget {
  const Section({
    required this.title,
    this.subtitle,
    this.trailing,
    required this.child,
    super.key,
  });

  final String title;
  final String? subtitle;
  final Widget? trailing;
  final Widget child;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final theme = Theme.of(context);
    return Column(
      crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
      children: [
        Row(children: [
          Expanded(
            child: Column(
              crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
              children: [
                Text(title, style: theme.textTheme.titleMedium),
                if (subtitle != null)
                  Text(subtitle!, style: theme.textTheme.bodySmall),
              ],
            ),
          ),
          if (trailing != null) trailing!,
        ]),
        const SizedBox(height: 8),
        child,
      ],
    );
  }
}

// WHEN A STATELESS WIDGET IS TOO LIMITED: a RenderObjectWidget
// this is for layout behaviour, not content
class Spacing extends SingleChildRenderObjectWidget {
  const Spacing({required this.axis, this.amount, super.key, super.child});

  final Axis axis;
  final double amount;

  @override
  RenderSpacing createRenderObject(BuildContext context) {
    return RenderSpacing(axis: axis, amount: amount);
  }

  @override
  void updateRenderObject(BuildContext context, RenderSpacing renderObject) {
    renderObject
      ..axis = axis
      ..amount = amount;
  }
}

1.7 Project structure that scales

Layering, and the one rule that makes it testable

Project structure in Flutter is usually argued about in terms of folders, and the useful version of the argument is about dependencies. A feature-first layout groups code by what it does rather than by what kind of thing it is — a features/checkout/ directory rather than a models/ directory containing every model in the app — and the reason it wins is that a feature folder can be deleted in one move and its dependencies go with it, whereas a type folder means a change to a model touches directories named after types and the dependency graph is invisible. The reason it loses is that genuinely shared things — a design system, a network client, a router — have no feature, and a feature-first layout forces you to invent one. Layered by technical role — data/, domain/, presentation/ — makes the dependency direction explicit and enforceable, and it is the right choice for an application with real domain logic. The rule worth having is a single sentence: nothing in domain/ may import Flutter. That is not an aesthetic preference; it is the property that makes the domain logic testable with a plain unit test in milliseconds, and it is the difference between a codebase where business rules are exercised by a hundred fast tests and one where every business-rule test needs a widget pump. The corollary is that the domain layer takes plain Dart types — its own value objects, its own failures, no BuildContext, no Widget, no Color — and the presentation layer translates. A barrel file is a boundary statement. One export line per feature means callers import the feature, not its internals, and it is what makes an internal rename a single-file change; the cost is that a barrel that exports everything becomes a place where circular imports hide.

/* The two layouts. */
const FEATURE_FIRST = {
  groups: 'code by WHAT IT DOES rather than by WHAT KIND OF THING IT IS',
  instance: 'a features/checkout/ directory rather than a models/ directory containing EVERY MODEL in the app',
  wins: ['a FEATURE FOLDER CAN BE DELETED IN ONE MOVE and its DEPENDENCIES GO WITH IT',
  'whereas a TYPE FOLDER means a CHANGE TO A MODEL TOUCHES DIRECTORIES NAMED AFTER TYPES and the DEPENDENCY GRAPH IS INVISIBLE'],
  loses: 'GENUINELY SHARED THINGS - a DESIGN SYSTEM, a NETWORK CLIENT, a ROUTER - have NO FEATURE, and a FEATURE-FIRST LAYOUT FORCES YOU TO INVENT ONE',
};
const BY_ROLE = {
  folders: 'data/, domain/, presentation/',
  wins: 'it makes THE DEPENDENCY DIRECTION EXPLICIT AND ENFORCEABLE',
  rightWhen: 'an APPLICATION WITH REAL DOMAIN LOGIC',
};

/* The one rule. */
const RULE = {
  statement: 'NOTHING IN domain/ MAY IMPORT FLUTTER',
  notThis: 'an AESTHETIC PREFERENCE',
  property: 'it is THE PROPERTY THAT MAKES THE DOMAIN LOGIC TESTABLE WITH A PLAIN UNIT TEST IN MILLISECONDS',
  difference: 'the DIFFERENCE between a CODEBASE WHERE BUSINESS RULES ARE EXERCISED by a hundred fast tests and one WHERE EVERY BUSINESS-RULE TEST NEEDS A WIDGET PUMP',
  corollary: 'the DOMAIN LAYER TAKES PLAIN DART TYPES - its OWN VALUE OBJECTS, its OWN FAILURES, no BuildContext, no Widget, no Color',
  and: 'the PRESENTATION LAYER TRANSLATES',
};

/* Barrels. */
const BARREL = {
  is: 'A BOUNDARY STATEMENT',
  rule: 'ONE export LINE PER FEATURE means CALLERS IMPORT THE FEATURE, not its INTERNALS',
  gain: 'it is WHAT MAKES AN INTERNAL RENAME A SINGLE-FILE CHANGE',
  cost: 'a BARREL THAT EXPORTS EVERYTHING becomes A PLACE WHERE CIRCULAR IMPORTS HIDE',
};

A layered structure with a real dependency direction, and the feature-first alternative.

// LAYERED, by technical role. good for a large team, because the
// boundaries are obvious and enforceable by import.
lib/
  main.dart                      composition root: runApp + ProviderScope
  app.dart                       MaterialApp.router, theming, routing
  core/
    theme/                       the design system: colours, type, spacing
    error/                       failure classes, error widgets
    network/                     the configured client, interceptors
    storage/                     the database, the secure store
    utils/                       pure functions, extensions
  features/
    auth/
      data/                       repository, datasource, DTOs
      domain/                     models, use cases (no Flutter imports)
      presentation/              screens, widgets, view models
    entries/
      data/
      domain/
      presentation/
  routing/
    router.dart
    routes.dart                  route table and guards
// FEATURE-FIRST. better for a medium team, because everything
// about a feature lives in one folder.
lib/
  main.dart
  app/
    app.dart
    router.dart
    theme.dart
  core/
    result.dart                  a sealed Result type
    failure.dart
    network/
      api_client.dart
      interceptors.dart
    storage/
      key_value.dart             the interface
      hive_impl.dart
    widgets/
      error_view.dart
      loading_view.dart
      empty_view.dart
  features/
    auth/
      data/
        auth_repository.dart
        auth_api.dart
      domain/
        auth_state.dart
      ui/
        login_screen.dart
        signup_screen.dart
        auth_controller.dart
      auth.dart                  a barrel: exports the public API
    entries/
      data/
      domain/
      ui/
      entries.dart
// THE DEPENDENCY DIRECTION, which is the whole point
//
//   presentation (ui/)   ->  domain  ->  data
//         |                   |          |
//         +--> core <---------+----------+
//
// a presentation file may import core and its own domain and data.
// a domain file imports core ONLY: never Flutter, never data.
// a data file imports core and domain.
//
// WHY domain must not import Flutter:
//   - it becomes plain Dart, so it is fast to test
//   - it cannot accidentally call setState
//   - it can be reused in a CLI tool or a server
//
// ENFORCE IT, because a codebase drifts:
//   a lint rule, or a test that greps the imports.
//   the pragmatic version: a CI check.

// the barrel file: the public API of a feature
// features/entries/ui/entries.dart
export 'entries_screen.dart';
export 'entry_card.dart';
// and the consumer imports only this
import 'package:app/features/entries/entries.dart';
// so an internal rename does not touch a hundred files

1.8 initState, dispose and the rest

Every leak in a Flutter app is one of four things: a controller, a subscription, a timer, or an animation controller that was never disposed. They all follow the same pattern and all have the same fix. If you get one rule from this section, make it that every one of them has a dispose.

The state lifecycle in practice, and the four mistakes everyone makes.

class EntryScreen extends StatefulWidget {
  const EntryScreen({required this.entryId, super.key});
  final String entryId;

  @override
  State<EntryScreen> createState() => _EntryScreenState();
}

class _EntryScreenState extends State<EntryScreen> {
  // 1. controllers, streams, timers, animation controllers
  late final TextEditingController _controller;
  late final ScrollController _scroll;
  late final AnimationController _anim;
  StreamSubscription<String>? _sub;

  // 2. data loaded in initState
  late Entry _entry;
  bool _loading = true;
  Object? _error;

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();

    // _controller used directly in build is a bug:
    //   1. the TextField is a child, not created here
    //   2. it should be created in initState and disposed in dispose
    //   3. if you need it in initState, create it HERE
    _controller = TextEditingController();
    _scroll = ScrollController();
    _anim = AnimationController(vsync: this, duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 300));

    // 3. start the async work
    _load();
  }

  @override
  void didUpdateWidget(EntryScreen oldWidget) {
    super.didUpdateWidget(oldWidget);
    // the parent gave us different data: reload
    if (oldWidget.entryId != widget.entryId) {
      _load();
    }
  }

  @override
  void didChangeDependencies() {
    super.didChangeDependencies();
    // runs after initState, and again if an inherited widget changes
    // do NOT put a provider read here and store it: use build
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    // 4. EVERYTHING is released here, in reverse order
    _sub?.cancel();
    _anim.dispose();
    _scroll.dispose();
    _controller.dispose();
    super.dispose();       // always last
  }

  Future<void> _load() async {
    try {
      final entry = await repository.byId(widget.entryId);
      if (!mounted) return;              // see mistake 1
      setState(() {
        _entry = entry;
        _loading = false;
      });
    } catch (e) {
      if (!mounted) return;
      setState(() => _error = e);
    }
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) { ... }
}
// THE FOUR MISTAKES

// 1. setState after dispose
//    the State is gone; setState throws "setState() called after
//    dispose()". Guard every async continuation with `if (!mounted)`,
//    or use a library that does it for you (Riverpod, Bloc).
Future<void> _load() async {
  final data = await fetch();
  if (!mounted) return;
  setState(() => _data = data);
}

// 2. a controller used in a child's build
// MISTAKE
Text('x', style: TextStyle(color: _controller.textColor));
// RESULT: the parent rebuilds on every keystroke, and the Text
//         rebuilds for nothing
// FIX: make the child a StatefulWidget that owns the controller,
//      or use a value-listenable builder
AnimatedBuilder(
  animation: _controller,
  builder: (context, child) =>
      TextField(controller: _controller, style: _style),
)

// 3. work in build
// BAD
Widget build(BuildContext context) {
  final data = repository.entries;      // if this hits the DB, the
  return ListView(...);                 // UI thread stalls
}
// GOOD: load in initState, or in a Riverpod/Bloc provider

// 4. not disposing
// EVERY controller, subscription, timer, focus node, animation
// controller, ScrollController, TextEditingController, and every
// ChangeNotifier you created must be disposed.
// the leak shows up as memory growth in a long session, and it is
// very hard to find later

If you take one thing from this chapter: put your state as low in the tree as it can go. A setState in a screen-level State rebuilds the whole screen, including a thousand-item list. A setState in the list item's State rebuilds one row. Moving state down is the most common fix for a slow Flutter screen, and it costs nothing.

Exercises 2

  1. Open DevTools and inspect the element tree of a screen. Find the RenderObjects for the widgets you expected not to have any.
  2. Build a list of 50 stateful items, remove the first one, and watch the state scramble. Add ValueKey and watch it fix itself.
  3. Write a screen that reads MediaQuery.of(context) in build, open the keyboard, and count the rebuilds with a debugPrint. Then use viewInsetsOf and compare.
  4. Write a StatelessWidget that calls InheritedWidget.of and one that calls read, and prove the difference by changing the inherited value.
  5. Create a stateful widget, navigate away, and assert in dispose that a timer was cancelled. Then deliberately forget and watch the leak.
  6. Restructure a small app into the feature-first layout, and move domain/ to have zero Flutter imports.

2 · Layout and Constraints

2.1 Constraints: the whole system2.2 Flex in depth2.3 Stack and Positioned2.4 SizedBox, Expanded and the zero-size trap2.5 Intrinsic sizing and its cost2.6 Custom layout with MultiChildLayout2.7 Writing a RenderObject2.8 The layout gotchas

Flutter's layout is unlike every other UI framework. Once you understand constraints as a negotiation, layout stops being mysterious and every layout bug becomes solvable.

2.1 Constraints: the whole system

Constraints go down, sizes go up, and what that means for every widget.

// THE MODEL
//
//  1. the parent gives the child CONSTRAINTS:
//     a minimum size, a maximum size, and a preferred size
//     (min = smallest allowed, max = largest allowed)
//
//  2. the child CHOOSES its size, within those constraints
//     (a container with a colour has no preferred size, so it
//      takes the biggest the constraints allow: it EXPANDS)
//
//  3. the parent positions the child, according to its own
//     alignment
//
// 4. then the same thing happens for the child's children
//
// CONSTRAINTS COME FROM ABOVE, GO DOWN. SIZES COME FROM BELOW,
// GO UP. They are negotiated in the middle.
// A BoxConstraints has: minWidth, maxWidth, minHeight, maxHeight
// and the "tight" case is a special one:

// TIGHT:    min == max. the child MUST be exactly that size.
//           a SizedBox, an Expanded, a full-screen Container
//           there is no choice, so there is nothing to negotiate.

// BOUNDED:  min < max. a range. the child picks.

// UNBOUNDED: max == infinity. "take what you need"
//           a Row or Column inside a vertical scroll view, for
//           the cross axis

// the common surprise, and its explanation
ListView(
  children: [
    Row(children: [          // ERROR: "RenderFlex children have
      Text('a'),             //   non-zero flex but incoming height
    ]),                      //   constraints are unbounded"
  ],
)
// WHY: a ListView gives its children unbounded height (it does
// not know how tall the list is). A Row with Expanded or
// Flexible needs a bounded cross-axis extent, because flex means
// "divide the remaining SPACE" - and there is no space if the
// extent is infinite.
//
// THE FIXES, in order of preference
ListView(children: [
  SizedBox(                            // give it a height
    height: 48,
    child: Row(children: [Expanded(child: Text('a'))]),
  ),
])
// or
IntrinsicHeight(                       // size to the tallest child
  child: Row(children: [Text('a'), ...]),
)
// or
Row(children: [                        // do not use flex at all
  Expanded(child: Text('a')),
])  // inside a Column with mainAxisSize.min
// or
ListView(
  shrinkWrap: true,                    // WRONG for performance, but
  children: [Row(...)],                // it does fix the error
)

The negotiation, and how to read the four numbers

Layout in Flutter is a negotiation in which a widget is offered a set of constraints and responds with a size, and every layout behaviour in the framework follows from that single idea. Constraints are four numbers: minimum width, maximum width, minimum height, maximum height. They are always ranges, never single values, because a parent that says "take whatever size you want" expresses that as zero-to-infinity and a parent that says "be exactly this wide" expresses it as a range whose minimum equals its maximum. There are two phases and the order is not negotiable. In the first, top-down, each parent passes constraints to its children; in the second, bottom-up, each child reports its size and the parent positions what it got. This is why a child cannot depend on its own final position and why a parent cannot assume its children's sizes before laying them out. Three of the four combinations matter and the fourth is the trap. Both axes bounded is the ordinary case. Main axis bounded, cross axis unbounded, is what a horizontal Row inside a vertical scroll view gets, and it is legal — the row can choose its own height. Main axis unbounded is the case that throws: a Column inside a vertical SingleChildScrollView has no upper bound on its height, so it cannot lay out its children, and the error message names the specific widget. Cross axis unbounded with main bounded is the case where a widget is free in one dimension and constrained in the other, which is why Expanded works on one axis and not the other. And then the constraint algebra that makes the whole thing predictable, which is worth memorising because it explains every "why is my widget zero-sized" question. A tight constraint forces a size: minimum equals maximum, so the child has no choice. A bounded constraint is a range, so the child picks within it and its own preference wins. An unbounded constraint is zero-to-infinity, so the child's own preferred size wins and it can grow. And aligning a child inside a tight parent makes it exactly that size, which is the source of the single most common surprise in the framework: putting a child in a Center does not shrink the child, because a centred widget is handed tight constraints and a tight widget is that size.

/* Constraints are four numbers, always a range. */
const CONSTRAINTS = {
  minWidth: 0, maxWidth: double.infinity, minHeight: 0, maxHeight: double.infinity,
  areAlways: 'RANGES, never single values',
  why: ['a parent that says TAKE WHATEVER SIZE YOU WANT expresses that as ZERO-TO-INFINITY',
    'a parent that says BE EXACTLY THIS WIDE expresses it as a RANGE WHOSE MINIMUM EQUALS ITS MAXIMUM'],
};

/* Two phases, order not negotiable. */
const PHASES = [
  { n: 1, name: 'TOP-DOWN', does: 'each PARENT PASSES CONSTRAINTS to its children' },
  { n: 2, name: 'BOTTOM-UP', does: 'each CHILD REPORTS ITS SIZE and the parent POSITIONS WHAT IT GOT' },
];
const ORDER_CONSEQUENCE = ['a CHILD CANNOT DEPEND ON ITS OWN FINAL POSITION',
  'a PARENT CANNOT ASSUME ITS CHILDREN SIZES BEFORE LAYING THEM OUT'];

/* Four combinations. */
const COMBINATIONS = [
  { case: 'BOTH AXES BOUNDED', kind: 'the ORDINARY CASE' },
  { case: 'MAIN BOUNDED, CROSS UNBOUNDED', kind: 'a horizontal Row inside a VERTICAL SCROLL VIEW', legal: true,
    and: 'the row CAN CHOOSE ITS OWN HEIGHT' },
  { case: 'MAIN AXIS UNBOUNDED', kind: 'the case that THROWS',
    instance: 'a Column inside a VERTICAL SingleChildScrollView has NO UPPER BOUND on its height, so it CANNOT LAY OUT ITS CHILDREN',
    note: 'and the ERROR MESSAGE NAMES the specific widget' },
  { case: 'CROSS UNBOUNDED WITH MAIN BOUNDED', kind: 'the widget is FREE in ONE DIMENSION and CONSTRAINED in the OTHER',
    and: 'which is WHY Expanded WORKS ON ONE AXIS and NOT the other' },
];

/* The algebra. */
const ALGEBRA = [
  { c: 'a TIGHT CONSTRAINT FORCES A SIZE', detail: 'minimum EQUALS maximum, so the CHILD HAS NO CHOICE' },
  { c: 'a BOUNDED CONSTRAINT IS A RANGE', detail: 'so the CHILD PICKS WITHIN IT and ITS OWN PREFERENCE WINS' },
  { c: 'an UNBOUNDED CONSTRAINT IS ZERO-TO-INFINITY', detail: 'so the CHILDS OWN PREFERRED SIZE WINS and it CAN GROW' },
  { c: 'ALIGNING A CHILD INSIDE A TIGHT PARENT MAKES IT EXACTLY THAT SIZE',
