    detail: 'a CENTRED WIDGET IS HANDED TIGHT CONSTRAINTS and a TIGHT WIDGET IS THAT SIZE',
    and: 'which is the SOURCE OF THE SINGLE MOST COMMON SURPRISE in the framework' },
];
const SURPRISE = 'putting a CHILD IN A Center DOES NOT SHRINK THE CHILD, because A CENTRED WIDGET IS HANDED TIGHT CONSTRAINTS and A TIGHT WIDGET IS THAT SIZE';

The unbounded-cross-axis error from a flex widget inside a scroll view is the single most common Flutter layout error. The reason it is confusing is that the error is reported on the inner flex widget while the cause is the outer scroll view. When you see it, look two or three levels up for a ListView or Column that is providing unbounded constraints.

2.2 Flex in depth

The properties, and the order they are applied in

A flex widget is two widgets — Row and Column — whose behaviour is described by six properties, and the reason understanding them precisely matters is that two of them are routinely confused for each other and both of them are routinely set without knowing which one is needed. The axis properties come first, because everything else is expressed in terms of them. mainAxisSize decides how much room the flex takes along its main axis: max fills what it is given, min takes only what its children need. textDirection fixes which way is "start" and which is "end", which matters for right-to-left and which is why alignment properties use start/end rather than left/right unless you specifically want physical directions. Then the three alignments, and the distinction between the two that are confused. mainAxisAlignment distributes children along the main axis: start, end, centre, spaceBetween (the first child at the start and the last at the end, gaps between), spaceAround (each child gets equal space around it, so the outer gaps are half the inner ones), spaceEvenly (equal gaps between and around). crossAxisAlignment positions each child across the main axis — start, end, centre, stretch, baseline — and stretch is the one that surprises, because it makes each child fill the cross axis, and a child with no intrinsic height in a Column with crossAxisAlignment: stretch becomes full height or throws. Baseline alignment is the third and the one with a specific purpose: it aligns children by the baseline of their text rather than by their box, which is what makes a row of mixed text sizes look correct, and it requires the children to have text and requires a direction in which a baseline exists. Then the properties people reach for and should not. A Row with mainAxisAlignment: spaceBetween and two children has one gap in the middle, which is usually not what "spread them out" was meant to mean; a Column with mainAxisAlignment: spaceEvenly and one child puts that child in the middle, which is almost never intended. In both cases the fix is Spacer with a flex value, or mainAxisSize: min with a plain start, and knowing which of the two you want is most of the decision.

/* Two widgets, six properties, applied in this order. */
const FLEX = {
  axisFirst: ['mainAxisSize', 'textDirection'],
  whyAxisFirst: 'EVERYTHING ELSE IS EXPRESSED IN TERMS OF THEM',
  mainAxisSize: { values: ['max', 'min'], max: 'FILLS WHAT IT IS GIVEN', min: 'TAKES ONLY WHAT ITS CHILDREN NEED' },
  textDirection: { fixes: 'WHICH WAY IS start AND WHICH IS end',
    mattersFor: 'RIGHT-TO-LEFT',
    and: 'which is WHY ALIGNMENT PROPERTIES USE start/end rather than left/right UNLESS YOU SPECIFICALLY WANT PHYSICAL DIRECTIONS' },
};

/* Three alignments; the two that are confused. */
const ALIGNMENTS = [
  { a: 'mainAxisAlignment', distributes: 'ALONG the MAIN AXIS',
    values: ['start', 'end', 'centre', 'spaceBetween', 'spaceAround', 'spaceEvenly'],
    detail: ['spaceBetween: the FIRST CHILD AT THE START and the LAST AT THE END, gaps BETWEEN',
      'spaceAround: EACH CHILD GETS EQUAL SPACE AROUND IT, so the OUTER GAPS ARE HALF the inner ones',
      'spaceEvenly: EQUAL GAPS BETWEEN and AROUND'] },
  { a: 'crossAxisAlignment', positions: 'EACH CHILD ACROSS the MAIN AXIS',
    values: ['start', 'end', 'centre', 'stretch', 'baseline'],
    surprising: 'stretch',
    why: 'it MAKES EACH CHILD FILL the cross axis, and a CHILD WITH NO INTRINSIC HEIGHT in a Column with crossAxisAlignment: stretch BECOMES FULL HEIGHT or THROWS' },
  { a: 'baseline', is: 'the THIRD and the ONE WITH A SPECIFIC PURPOSE',
    does: 'ALIGNS CHILDREN BY THE BASELINE of their TEXT rather than by their BOX',
    gain: 'which is WHAT MAKES A ROW OF MIXED TEXT SIZES LOOK CORRECT',
    requires: ['the CHILDREN TO HAVE TEXT', 'a DIRECTION in which a BASELINE EXISTS'] },
];

/* What people reach for and should not. */
const REACH_FOR = [
  { mistake: 'a Row with mainAxisAlignment: spaceBetween and TWO CHILDREN',
    actual: 'ONE GAP IN THE MIDDLE',
    usuallyMeant: 'something else',
    fix: ['a Spacer WITH A FLEX VALUE', 'or mainAxisSize: min with a PLAIN start'] },
  { mistake: 'a Column with mainAxisAlignment: spaceEvenly and ONE CHILD',
    actual: 'that CHILD IN THE MIDDLE',
    intended: 'ALMOST NEVER',
    fix: ['a Spacer WITH A FLEX VALUE', 'or mainAxisSize: min with a PLAIN start'] },
];
const DECISION = 'KNOWING WHICH OF THE TWO YOU WANT is MOST OF THE DECISION';

mainAxisSize, crossAxisAlignment, Expanded, Flexible and the three flex fits.

// mainAxisSize: how much of the MAIN axis to occupy
Row(
  mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.max,        // the default: fill the width
  children: [Text('short')],
)   // the Row is as wide as its parent, Text is left-aligned in it

Row(
  mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,       // wrap the children
  children: [Text('short')],
)   // the Row is exactly as wide as the Text

// THE RULE: MainAxisSize.min is what you want inside a
// scroll view, or when the parent would otherwise stretch you.

// crossAxisAlignment: how children sit on the CROSS axis
Column(
  crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,   // the default is center
  children: [Text('a'), Text('b')],
)
//   .start     .left for Row, .top for Column
//   .center    the default
//   .end
//   .stretch   force the cross axis to fill: the child must accept it
//   .baseline  align text baselines - rarely what you want

// the stretch surprise
Row(
  crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.stretch,
  children: [
    Text('a'),              // ERROR: Text cannot be stretched
    SizedBox(width: 10, height: 20),   // fine: it accepts a tight height
  ],
)
// the fix: wrap in IntrinsicHeight, or use a fixed cross-axis size
// THE THREE FLEX FITS
Row(children: [
  // 1. Expanded - flex: 1, always takes the remaining space
  //    the child is given TIGHT constraints
  Expanded(flex: 1, child: Container(color: Colors.red)),

  // 2. Flexible - fit: FlexFit.loose (the default)
  //    the child gets the remaining space as a MAXIMUM, and may
  //    be smaller
  Flexible(child: Container(color: Colors.green)),

  // 3. Flexible - fit: FlexFit.tight
  //    same as Expanded, but with a flex factor
  Flexible(flex: 2, fit: FlexFit.tight, child: Container(color: Colors.blue)),
]);

// Expanded == Flexible(flex: 1, fit: FlexFit.tight)
// Expanded is literally a subclass of Flexible, named for clarity

// the classic: two thirds and one third
Row(children: [
  Expanded(flex: 2, child: Left()),
  Expanded(flex: 1, child: Right()),
]);

// text that must not overflow
Row(children: [
  Expanded(
    child: Text('a very long title that would overflow if it were not in an Expanded'),
  ),
  const Icon(Icons.chevron_right),
]);
// WITHOUT the Expanded, the Row throws a layout overflow
// warning: "A RenderFlex overflowed by 42 pixels on the right"
// THE MAIN-AXIS-SIZE-AND-FLEX INTERACTION, which is subtle
// if mainAxisSize is .min, the children get UNBOUNDED main-axis
// constraints, so flex has nothing to divide

// BROKEN: flex does nothing
Row(
  mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
  children: [
    Expanded(child: Container(color: Colors.red)),   // takes everything
    Text('hello'),                                   // gets 0 width
  ],
)

// WHY: .min means the Row will be as small as its children.
// Expanded asks for the remaining space - but the Row is being
// sized BY the children, so there is no "remaining".

// the correct patterns
// 1. let it fill (the default), and use flex
Row(children: [
  Expanded(flex: 3, child: Sidebar()),
  Expanded(flex: 7, child: Content()),
]);

// 2. a fixed portion plus a flexible remainder
Row(children: [
  const SizedBox(width: 120, child: Sidebar()),  // fixed
  Expanded(child: Content()),                   // the rest
]);

// 3. fixed, flexible, fixed
Row(children: [
  const SizedBox(width: 40),
  const Expanded(child: Content()),
  const SizedBox(width: 40),
]);

// 4. for a button row: size to the children, no flex
Row(
  mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
  children: [
    ElevatedButton(onPressed: f, child: const Text('Cancel')),
    const SizedBox(width: 8),
    ElevatedButton(onPressed: f, child: const Text('Save')),
  ],
);

2.3 Stack and Positioned

Alignment, fit, and how positioning actually works

Stack is a box that gives its non-positioned children the loosest constraints it can, and then optionally places positioned children at explicit coordinates. That single sentence explains most of its behaviour. A non-positioned child of a Stack is sized by itself, which means it gets zero-to-infinity constraints and picks its own size — and that is why an unconstrained child of a Stack does not fill the stack, which surprises people who expect it to. alignment moves the stack itself inside its own constraints, not the children inside the stack, and this is the single most common misreading of the widget: Stack(alignment: Alignment.bottomRight) does not move its children to the bottom right, it moves the whole stack box to the bottom right of the space the parent gave it. To move a child you either use Positioned or put the child in an Align. Positioned has three modes and only three, and which one you are in determines what it means. With both a horizontal and a vertical coordinate, it positions absolutely and the child is handed tight constraints in the specified axes and loose in the others. With only one coordinate, it is still positioned, but only along that axis and unsized on the other. With no coordinates at all, it is not positioned at all — it is simply aligned according to the stack's alignment, which is the case that catches people who expect a Positioned with no arguments to do something. Then the three sizing properties and why they interact badly. fit: loose (the default) lets the stack be larger than its non-positioned children, so it fills what it is given. fit: expand makes the stack take the largest possible size, which combined with a non-positioned child that has an unbounded child is a common source of overflow. fit: shrinkWrap makes the stack exactly as large as its largest non-positioned child — and it is the correct choice for a stack wrapping a single content-sized child, where the default loose fit makes the stack fill its parent and any background decoration stretch. And the last interaction worth knowing: the stack's size comes from its non-positioned children only. A stack containing three Positioned children and nothing else has no size of its own and will collapse, which is the single most common cause of "my positioned child is not appearing where I put it".

/* The one sentence. */
const STACK = 'a BOX THAT GIVES ITS NON-POSITIONED CHILDREN THE LOOSEST CONSTRAINTS IT CAN, and then OPTIONALLY PLACES POSITIONED CHILDREN at explicit coordinates';
const CONSEQUENCE_1 = 'a NON-POSITIONED CHILD of a Stack IS SIZED BY ITSELF';
const DETAIL_1 = 'it gets ZERO-TO-INFINITY CONSTRAINTS and PICKS ITS OWN SIZE';
const SURPRISE_1 = 'which is WHY AN UNCONSTRAINED CHILD OF A Stack DOES NOT FILL THE STACK - something people EXPECT it to';

const ALIGNMENT = {
  moves: 'THE STACK ITSELF INSIDE ITS OWN CONSTRAINTS',
  notChildren: 'NOT THE CHILDREN INSIDE THE STACK',
  theMisreading: 'Stack(alignment: Alignment.bottomRight) does NOT move ITS CHILDREN to the bottom right',
  itActually: 'moves THE WHOLE STACK BOX to the bottom right of the SPACE THE PARENT GAVE IT',
  toMoveAChild: ['use Positioned', 'or put the CHILD IN AN Align'],
};

/* Three modes. */
const POSITIONED = [
  { mode: 'BOTH a HORIZONTAL and a VERTICAL COORDINATE',
    means: 'POSITIONED ABSOLUTELY', childGets: 'TIGHT CONSTRAINTS in the SPECIFIED AXES and LOOSE in the others' },
  { mode: 'ONLY ONE COORDINATE', means: 'STILL POSITIONED, but ONLY ALONG THAT AXIS and UNSIZED on the other' },
  { mode: 'NO COORDINATES AT ALL', means: 'NOT POSITIONED AT ALL',
    behaviour: 'it is simply ALIGNED ACCORDING to the STACKS alignment',
    catches: 'the case that CATCHES PEOPLE who expect a Positioned WITH NO ARGUMENTS to DO SOMETHING' },
];

/* Three sizing properties. */
const FIT = [
  { f: 'loose', isTheDefault: true,
    behaviour: 'lets the STACK BE LARGER than its non-positioned children, so it FILLS WHAT IT IS GIVEN' },
  { f: 'expand', behaviour: 'makes the STACK TAKE THE LARGEST POSSIBLE SIZE',
    badWith: 'a NON-POSITIONED CHILD THAT HAS AN UNBOUNDED CHILD',
    and: 'is a COMMON SOURCE OF OVERFLOW' },
  { f: 'shrinkWrap', behaviour: 'makes the STACK EXACTLY AS LARGE as its LARGEST NON-POSITIONED CHILD',
    rightFor: 'a STACK WRAPPING A SINGLE CONTENT-SIZED CHILD',
    why: 'where the DEFAULT LOOSE FIT makes the stack FILL ITS PARENT and ANY BACKGROUND DECORATION STRETCH' },
];
const INTERACTION = 'the STACKS SIZE COMES FROM ITS NON-POSITIONED CHILDREN ONLY';
const COLLAPSE = 'a STACK CONTAINING THREE Positioned CHILDREN and NOTHING ELSE HAS NO SIZE OF ITS OWN and WILL COLLAPSE';
const COLLAPSE_SYMPTOM = 'which is THE SINGLE MOST COMMON CAUSE OF my positioned child is not appearing where I put it';

Overlay layout, and the two properties that make it or break it.

// Stack: children painted in order, the LAST one on top
Stack(
  alignment: Alignment.center,     // how non-positioned children align
  children: [
    const ColoredBox(color: Colors.grey, child: SizedBox(width: 200, height: 200)),
    const Icon(Icons.play_arrow, size: 64),      // on top
    Positioned(
      right: 8,
      top: 8,
      child: IconButton(onPressed: close, icon: const Icon(Icons.close)),
    ),
  ],
)

// the Stack SIZES to its largest non-positioned child
// a Positioned child does NOT contribute to the Stack's size
// so a Stack with ONLY positioned children collapses to zero

// fit: how non-positioned children are sized
Stack(
  fit: StackFit.loose,       // the default: each child gets loose
                             // constraints, so it can be small
  children: [...],
)
Stack(
  fit: StackFit.expand,      // force every non-positioned child to
  children: [...],           // fill: this is what you want for
)                            // a background image or a gradient
Stack(
  fit: StackFit.passthrough, // children get the Stack's constraints
  children: [...],           // unchanged
)
// Positioned: a subset of a real widget
Positioned(
  left: 0, top: 0, right: 0, bottom: 0,   // all four = fill the stack
  // or two of them: one axis is tight, the other is loose
  child: const ColoredBox(color: Colors.black12),
)

// THE RULE: with Positioned, specify at most TWO of the four
//   left+top     -> the child is loose on both axes
//   left+right   -> tight horizontally, loose vertically
//   left+top+right+bottom -> tight on both: it fills
//   left+top+right+bottom+width -> ERROR: over-constrained

// the pattern for a full-bleed background behind content
Stack(
  fit: StackFit.expand,
  children: [
    Image.asset('hero.jpg', fit: BoxFit.cover),
    DecoratedBox(
      decoration: BoxDecoration(
        gradient: LinearGradient(
          begin: Alignment.topCenter,
          end: Alignment.bottomCenter,
          colors: [Colors.transparent, Colors.black54],
        ),
      ),
    ),
    Padding(
      padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
      child: Text(title, style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.headlineSmall),
    ),
  ],
);

// and for a bottom bar over content
Stack(
  children: [
    ListView.builder(itemCount: 100, itemBuilder: (_, i) => ListTile(title: Text('Item $i'))),
    Align(
      alignment: Alignment.bottomCenter,
      child: SafeArea(child: FloatingActionButton(onPressed: add, child: const Icon(Icons.add))),
    ),
  ],
)

2.4 SizedBox, Expanded and the zero-size trap

Choosing how to express a size

There are four ways to say how big something is and they are not interchangeable, and picking the wrong one is the source of both a large fraction of layout bugs and a meaningful fraction of unnecessary render objects. SizedBox gives a child a tight constraint of an exact size. It is the right answer whenever you know the size: a fixed-height header, a fixed-width icon slot, a spacer of known dimensions. ConstrainedBox adds a constraint without changing the child's type, and it is the right answer when you want to permit a range rather than fix a value, or when you want to add a minimum or a maximum to whatever the child would otherwise choose. Container is a convenience widget that expands to whichever of the four it needs — padding, alignment, decoration, constraints, size, transform — and the cost is that Container with a decoration is not one widget; it is a padding, then a decorated box, then a transform, and with a colour it is more, so a hot path full of Container is a hot path full of render objects that do nothing. UnconstrainedBox escapes the constraints and is the only correct use of which is letting a child be larger than the space it was given. Then the three properties that people confuse with each other in Container specifically, and the confusion is genuinely easy to fall into. width and height are tight constraints. constraints is a complete BoxConstraints that overrides them, and if both are given the constraints wins — so a Container with both is a bug, not a conflict to be resolved by precedence intuition. And child interacts with all of them: if the child is flexible — a Column, a Expanded, anything that wants loose constraints — then a tight parent constraint makes the child fill, and the child is being asked to do something impossible if it also wants to choose its own size. The practical rule: a Container with a child, a colour and nothing else should be a SizedBox wrapped around a DecoratedBox if it is in a hot path, and a Container if it is not. That is not premature optimisation in the usual sense; it is noticing that Container is a convenience for readability and a cost for render objects, and choosing per site.

/* Four ways to express a size, not interchangeable. */
const WAYS = [
  { w: 'SizedBox', gives: 'a CHILD a TIGHT CONSTRAINT of an EXACT SIZE',
    rightFor: 'you KNOW the SIZE',
    instances: ['a FIXED-HEIGHT header', 'a FIXED-WIDTH icon slot', 'a SPACER of known dimensions'] },
  { w: 'ConstrainedBox', gives: 'A CONSTRAINT without CHANGING THE CHILDS TYPE',
    rightFor: 'you want to PERMIT A RANGE rather than FIX A VALUE, or to add a MINIMUM or a MAXIMUM to whatever the child would otherwise choose' },
  { w: 'Container', is: 'A CONVENIENCE WIDGET that expands to whichever of the four it needs',
    canBe: ['padding', 'alignment', 'decoration', 'constraints', 'size', 'transform'],
    cost: 'Container WITH A DECORATION IS NOT ONE WIDGET - it is a PADDING, then a DECORATED BOX, then a TRANSFORM, and WITH A COLOUR it is MORE',
    so: 'a HOT PATH FULL OF Container IS A HOT PATH FULL OF RENDER OBJECTS THAT DO NOTHING' },
  { w: 'UnconstrainedBox', escapes: 'THE CONSTRAINTS',
    onlyCorrectUse: 'LETTING A CHILD BE LARGER than the SPACE IT WAS GIVEN' },
];

/* Three properties that are confused inside Container. */
const CONFUSED = [
  { p: 'width and height', are: 'TIGHT CONSTRAINTS' },
  { p: 'constraints', is: 'a COMPLETE BoxConstraints that OVERRIDES THEM',
    rule: 'if BOTH ARE GIVEN the constraints WINS',
    and: 'so a Container WITH BOTH IS A BUG, not a CONFLICT TO BE RESOLVED BY PRECEDENCE INTUITION' },
  { p: 'child', interacts: 'with ALL OF THEM',
    detail: ['if the CHILD IS FLEXIBLE - a Column, an Expanded, ANYTHING THAT WANTS LOOSE CONSTRAINTS - then a TIGHT PARENT CONSTRAINT MAKES THE CHILD FILL',
      'and the CHILD IS BEING ASKED TO DO SOMETHING IMPOSSIBLE if it also wants to CHOOSE ITS OWN SIZE'] },
];
const RULE = 'a Container WITH A CHILD, A COLOUR and NOTHING ELSE should be a SizedBox WRAPPED AROUND a DecoratedBox if it is in a HOT PATH, and a Container if it is NOT';
const REFRAME = 'this is NOT PREMATURE OPTIMISATION in the usual sense - it is NOTICING THAT Container IS A CONVENIENCE FOR READABILITY and A COST FOR RENDER OBJECTS, and CHOOSING PER SITE';

How to make something exactly this big, and the two widgets that surprise you.

// SIZEDBOX: force a size. the workhorse of layout.
SizedBox(
  width: 100,
  height: 40,
  child: Text('fixed'),
)

// with a child, the child's constraints are TIGHT, so a
// Container with a colour fills the SizedBox
SizedBox(
  width: 100, height: 40,
  child: DecoratedBox(decoration: BoxDecoration(color: Colors.blue)),
)

// one dimension only
const SizedBox(height: 16)          // a vertical gap
const SizedBox(width: 8)            // a horizontal gap
SizedBox.shrink()                   // width: 0, height: 0
SizedBox.expand()                   // the largest the parent allows

// SPACERS, which are just SizedBoxes
const Spacer()                      // Expanded(child: SizedBox.shrink())
// inside a Flex: takes ALL the remaining space
Row(children: [
  const Text('left'),
  const Spacer(),                   // pushes 'right' to the edge
  const Text('right'),
])

Row(children: [
  const Spacer(flex: 1),            // 1/3 of the free space
  const Spacer(flex: 2),            // 2/3
  const Text('right'),
])
// CONTAINER: the convenience wrapper, and its two surprises
Container(
  width: 100,        // -> wraps in a ConstrainedBox
  padding: EdgeInsets.all(8),   // -> wraps in a Padding
  margin: EdgeInsets.all(8),    // -> wraps in a Padding
  decoration: BoxDecoration(...),      // -> a DecoratedBox
  color: Colors.blue,                  // -> a DecoratedBox
  alignment: Alignment.center,         // -> an Align
  child: Text('x'),                    // -> a ConstrainedBox
)

// SURPRISE 1: padding and decoration together
Container(
  padding: EdgeInsets.all(8),
  color: Colors.red,
)
// the colour goes BEHIND the padding: a red box with 8px of
// transparent padding inside it. The colour does not "fill" the
// padding unless the padding is zero.

// SURPRISE 2: width + alignment
Container(
  width: 100,
  alignment: Alignment.center,
  child: Text('x'),
)
// the child is aligned within the 100-wide box, not the box
// centred within the child. This is a common confusion.

// prefer the specific widgets in a hot path: Container composes
// several widgets, each of which is a node in the tree
Container(width: 100, height: 40)   // -> 2-3 layers
const SizedBox(width: 100, height: 40)   // -> 1 layer

2.5 Intrinsic sizing and its cost

What an intrinsic dimension is, and the double layout it forces

An intrinsic dimension is a size a widget computes from its content rather than from the constraints it was given, and the mechanism behind it is the one thing in Flutter layout that is genuinely expensive. To compute an intrinsic size, the framework must lay the widget out before it knows how much space to give it — so it lays it out once with unconstrained dimensions, asks what size it came out, and then lays it out again for real. Two layouts, always. That is not an implementation detail that might be optimised away; it is what the protocol requires, because a child's intrinsic width genuinely depends on how much width it is given (text wraps, so a narrower width is a taller text) and there is no way to answer the question without trying. The widgets that provide it are the *IntrinsicWidth and *IntrinsicHeight family — IntrinsicWidth, IntrinsicHeight, IntrinsicSize for an IntrinsicWidth and IntrinsicHeight pair, and the same applied to rows, columns, tabs and stacks. The cost therefore scales with the size of the subtree being measured. If an intrinsic widget wraps a subtree of two hundred widgets with images, that subtree is laid out twice, and the measure pass runs every frame in which the intrinsic widget is rebuilt. And the common failure is nesting them, which multiplies: an intrinsic widget inside an intrinsic widget lays out the inner one twice for each of the outer one's two passes, so three levels of nesting is eight layouts. The second common failure is using an intrinsic widget to solve an alignment problem — wanting two children the same height, reaching for IntrinsicHeight, and paying a double layout per frame for a result that a different structure achieves for free.

Then the honest answer to "what instead", and it is a structure rather than a widget. For equal-height siblings, put them in the same Row and let the row's cross-axis alignment do it, because the row lays out both children once and positions them relative to the taller one; crossAxisAlignment: stretch makes them equal by construction. For equal-width siblings in a Column, the column has no such mechanism, which is why a GridView or a Row of Expanded children is the standard answer — the grid computes the column width once and hands it to every cell. For a child that must be as wide as its text but no wider than the parent, use a ConstrainedBox with an explicit maximum and let the text wrap, because a maximum constraint plus intrinsic content is the ordinary case and does not need the intrinsic protocol. And for the case intrinsic sizing genuinely exists for — a button whose width matches its label, a chip in a wrapping row, a text field sized to its content — accept the double layout, because those are small subtrees and the alternative is hard-coding a width that breaks when the label or the language or the text scale changes. The judgement in one sentence: intrinsic sizing is a measurement, not a layout, and any subtree you would not want measured twice on every frame should not be inside one.

/* The mechanism. */
const MECHANISM = {
  is: 'a SIZE A WIDGET COMPUTES FROM ITS CONTENT rather than from the CONSTRAINTS IT WAS GIVEN',
  toComputeIt: 'the FRAMEWORK MUST LAY THE WIDGET OUT BEFORE IT KNOWS HOW MUCH SPACE TO GIVE IT',
  so: 'it LAYS IT OUT ONCE WITH UNCONSTRAINED DIMENSIONS, ASKS WHAT SIZE IT CAME OUT, and THEN LAYS IT OUT AGAIN FOR REAL',
  count: 'TWO LAYOUTS, ALWAYS',
  notAnImplementationDetail: 'it is WHAT THE PROTOCOL REQUIRES',
  why: 'because a CHILDS INTRINSIC WIDTH genuinely DEPENDS ON HOW MUCH WIDTH IT IS GIVEN - TEXT WRAPS, so a NARROWER WIDTH IS A TALLER TEXT - and there is NO WAY TO ANSWER THE QUESTION without TRYING',
};

/* Who provides it. */
const PROVIDERS = ['IntrinsicWidth', 'IntrinsicHeight', 'IntrinsicSize for an IntrinsicWidth and IntrinsicHeight pair',
  'and the same APPLIED TO ROWS, COLUMNS, TABS and STACKS'];
const COST = {
  scalesWith: 'the SIZE OF THE SUBTREE BEING MEASURED',
  detail: 'if an INTRINSIC WIDGET WRAPS a SUBTREE of two hundred widgets with images, that SUBTREE IS LAID OUT TWICE',
  and: 'the MEASURE PASS RUNS EVERY FRAME in which the intrinsic widget IS REBUILT',
};
const FAILURES = [
  { f: 'NESTING THEM', effect: 'MULTIPLIES',
    detail: 'an INTRINSIC WIDGET INSIDE AN INTRINSIC WIDGET LAYS OUT the INNER ONE TWICE for EACH of the OUTER ONES TWO PASSES',
    so: 'THREE LEVELS OF NESTING IS EIGHT LAYOUTS' },
  { f: 'using an INTRINSIC WIDGET to solve an ALIGNMENT PROBLEM',
    detail: 'wanting TWO CHILDREN THE SAME HEIGHT, REACHING FOR IntrinsicHeight, and PAYING A DOUBLE LAYOUT PER FRAME for a RESULT that a DIFFERENT STRUCTURE ACHIEVES FOR FREE' },
];

/* The alternatives - a structure, not a widget. */
const INSTEAD = [
  { want: 'EQUAL-HEIGHT SIBLINGS', then: 'PUT THEM IN THE SAME Row and LET THE ROWS CROSS-AXIS ALIGNMENT DO IT',
    why: 'the ROW LAYS OUT BOTH CHILDREN ONCE and POSITIONS THEM RELATIVE TO THE TALLER ONE',
    and: 'crossAxisAlignment: stretch MAKES THEM EQUAL BY CONSTRUCTION' },
  { want: 'EQUAL-WIDTH SIBLINGS in a Column', note: 'the COLUMN HAS NO SUCH MECHANISM',
    then: 'a GridView or a Row of Expanded CHILDREN',
    why: 'the GRID COMPUTES THE COLUMN WIDTH ONCE and HANDS IT TO EVERY CELL' },
  { want: 'a CHILD AS WIDE AS ITS TEXT but NO WIDER THAN THE PARENT',
    then: 'a ConstrainedBox WITH AN EXPLICIT MAXIMUM and LET THE TEXT WRAP',
    why: 'a MAXIMUM CONSTRAINT plus INTRINSIC CONTENT is THE ORDINARY CASE and DOES NOT NEED the intrinsic protocol' },
  { want: 'a BUTTON WHOSE WIDTH MATCHES ITS LABEL, a CHIP in a WRAPPING ROW, a TEXT FIELD SIZED TO ITS CONTENT',
    then: 'ACCEPT THE DOUBLE LAYOUT',
    why: 'those ARE SMALL SUBTREES and the ALTERNATIVE IS HARD-CODING A WIDTH that BREAKS WHEN THE LABEL or THE LANGUAGE or THE TEXT SCALE changes' },
];
const JUDGEMENT = 'intrinsic sizing is A MEASUREMENT, not a LAYOUT, and ANY SUBTREE YOU WOULD NOT WANT MEASURED TWICE ON EVERY FRAME SHOULD NOT BE INSIDE ONE';

Intrinsic sizing inside a long list is a performance cliff. Each intrinsic measurement forces two or three extra layout passes over that subtree, and a list of a hundred rows with an IntrinsicWidth each is three hundred extra passes per scroll. If two buttons must be the same width, measure the labels with a TextPainter instead.

Asking a widget how big it wants to be, and why it is expensive.

// INTRINSIC SIZING: "how big would you like to be?"
// three separate questions, each requiring a full layout pass
IntrinsicWidth    // how wide would you be?
IntrinsicHeight   // how tall would you be?
// the combined version
Center(child: IntrinsicWidth(child: Text('hello')))

// HOW IT WORKS: the framework lays the child out TWICE, or three
// times: once for the intrinsic dimension, then again for the
// real layout. For a deep tree that is a real cost.
//
// THE COST RULE: intrinsic sizing is O(depth x passes). It is
// fine for a small subtree and terrible for a large one.

// THE COMMON USES, all small
// 1. a button row where the buttons should be the same width
Row(
  mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
  children: [
    IntrinsicWidth(
      child: ElevatedButton(onPressed: f, child: const Text('Save')),
    ),
    const SizedBox(width: 8),
    IntrinsicWidth(
      child: ElevatedButton(onPressed: f, child: const Text('Delete all')),
    ),
  ],
)

// 2. an icon next to text of unknown width
IntrinsicHeight(
  child: Row(children: [
    const Icon(Icons.info),
    Expanded(child: Text(longDescription)),
  ]),
)

// 3. aligning a Table or a Wrap
IntrinsicWidth(child: DataTable(...))

// NEVER: on a list, on a long text, or anywhere in a hot path

2.6 Custom layout with MultiChildLayout

The contract, and why it is two methods

Custom layout is more approachable than it looks, because the contract is small and the framework does the hard parts. You implement a delegate that answers one question: given the layout identifier, what is the size this child should have? Then you implement one method that positions and sizes the children according to that decision. That is the whole protocol. The reason it is two methods rather than one is a genuine necessity rather than an API convenience: the parent must know every child's size before it can decide anything, because a custom layout almost always places children relative to each other — the second child below the first, the third in a column beside them — and a layout that could read a child's size while placing it would have to lay children out in order and would be unable to place a later child relative to an earlier one without re-laying the earlier one. So the size pass runs first for every child, then the layout pass runs for every child. That ordering is why the size pass must not touch anything a child owns, and why a delegate that caches state between the two passes must key that state on the layout identifier rather than on "the child I am currently laying out" — the identifier is the only stable thing available, and a delegate that assumes the calls arrive in a particular order is the most common source of a custom layout that works for one child and breaks for two.

Then the three decisions, each of which has a specific failure. How the size is chosen. The delegate receives the constraints and returns a size, and it must respect any tight constraint it is given — a child asked for exactly two hundred pixels cannot return a different size, and returning one produces the overflow stripe rather than an exception, which is why a layout that ignores constraints fails quietly. Whether to honour the constraints or the intrinsic size. A custom layout that ignores its incoming constraints and uses the children's preferred sizes instead will be correct in a loose context and broken the moment it is placed tightly, which is the same trap as intrinsic sizing and for the same reason. And how children are keyed. Each child needs a layout identifier, and reusing an identifier across different children makes the framework treat two children as one, which produces a layout that is correct for the first child and wrong for every subsequent one — the identifier is not a debug label, it is the key the framework uses to match the delegate's answer to a specific child. And then when to stop using it, which is the practical discipline. Reach for CustomMultiChildLayout when the arrangement is genuinely positional and no combination of the standard widgets expresses it — a layout where children overlap in a specific way, where they are placed against each other in a way that depends on measured sizes, or where the arrangement is computed. Do not reach for it to avoid learning the standard widgets: a custom layout delegate is plain Dart and it is testable, but it is also code you own, and the standard widgets have properties — text scaling, directionality, semantics, hit testing — that a delegate must reproduce or consciously omit. A RenderObject subclass is a further step: it is where you go when the widget layer's representation of layout cannot express what you need at all, and it costs you hit testing, semantics and accessibility unless you implement them.

/* The contract is two methods. */
const CONTRACT = {
  youImplement: ['a DELEGATE that answers ONE QUESTION: GIVEN THE LAYOUT IDENTIFIER, WHAT IS THE SIZE THIS CHILD SHOULD HAVE',
    'ONE METHOD that POSITIONS and SIZES the CHILDREN according to THAT DECISION'],
  isTheWholeProtocol: true,
  whyTwo: 'a GENUINE NECESSITY rather than an API CONVENIENCE',
  reason: 'the PARENT MUST KNOW EVERY CHILDS SIZE BEFORE IT CAN DECIDE ANYTHING',
  because: 'a CUSTOM LAYOUT ALMOST ALWAYS PLACES CHILDREN RELATIVE TO EACH OTHER - the SECOND CHILD BELOW THE FIRST, the THIRD in a column beside them',
  and: 'a LAYOUT THAT COULD READ A CHILDS SIZE WHILE PLACING IT would have to LAY CHILDREN OUT IN ORDER and would be UNABLE TO PLACE A LATER CHILD RELATIVE TO AN EARLIER ONE without RE-LAYING the earlier one',
  ordering: ['the SIZE PASS RUNS FIRST for every child', 'then the LAYOUT PASS RUNS for every child'],
  consequences: ['the SIZE PASS MUST NOT TOUCH anything a CHILD OWNS',
    'a DELEGATE THAT CACHES STATE between the TWO PASSES MUST KEY THAT STATE ON THE LAYOUT IDENTIFIER rather than on the child I am currently laying out',
    'the IDENTIFIER IS THE ONLY STABLE THING AVAILABLE',
    'and a DELEGATE THAT ASSUMES THE CALLS ARRIVE IN A PARTICULAR ORDER is THE MOST COMMON SOURCE of a custom layout that WORKS FOR ONE CHILD and BREAKS FOR TWO'],
};

/* Three decisions. */
const DECISIONS = [
  { d: 'HOW THE SIZE IS CHOSEN',
    fact: 'the DELEGATE RECEIVES THE CONSTRAINTS and RETURNS A SIZE',
    rule: 'it MUST RESPECT ANY TIGHT CONSTRAINT it is given',
    failure: 'a CHILD ASKED FOR EXACTLY TWO HUNDRED PIXELS CANNOT RETURN A DIFFERENT SIZE, and RETURNING ONE PRODUCES THE OVERFLOW STRIPE rather than an EXCEPTION',
    and: 'which is WHY A LAYOUT THAT IGNORES CONSTRAINTS FAILS QUIETLY' },
  { d: 'WHETHER TO HONOUR THE CONSTRAINTS or the INTRINSIC SIZE',
    failure: 'a CUSTOM LAYOUT THAT IGNORES ITS INCOMING CONSTRAINTS and USES THE CHILDREN PREFERRED SIZES instead WILL BE CORRECT IN A LOOSE CONTEXT and BROKEN THE MOMENT IT IS PLACED TIGHTLY',
    and: 'which is THE SAME TRAP as INTRINSIC SIZING and for THE SAME REASON' },
  { d: 'HOW CHILDREN ARE KEYED',
    rule: 'EACH CHILD NEEDS A LAYOUT IDENTIFIER',
    failure: 'REUSING AN IDENTIFIER ACROSS DIFFERENT CHILDREN MAKES THE FRAMEWORK TREAT TWO CHILDREN AS ONE',
    symptom: 'a LAYOUT THAT IS CORRECT FOR THE FIRST CHILD and WRONG FOR EVERY SUBSEQUENT ONE',
    and: 'the IDENTIFIER IS NOT A DEBUG LABEL - it is THE KEY THE FRAMEWORK USES to MATCH the delegates ANSWER TO A SPECIFIC CHILD' },
];

/* When to stop using it. */
const REACH_FOR = {
  when: 'the ARRANGEMENT IS GENUINELY POSITIONAL and NO COMBINATION of the standard widgets EXPRESSES IT',
  instances: ['a LAYOUT WHERE CHILDREN OVERLAP IN A SPECIFIC WAY',
    'where THEY ARE PLACED AGAINST EACH OTHER in a way that DEPENDS ON MEASURED SIZES',
    'or where THE ARRANGEMENT IS COMPUTED'],
};
const NOT_FOR = 'DO NOT REACH FOR IT TO AVOID LEARNING THE STANDARD WIDGETS';
const WHY_NOT = 'a CUSTOM LAYOUT DELEGATE is PLAIN DART and it is TESTABLE, but it is ALSO CODE YOU OWN, and the STANDARD WIDGETS HAVE PROPERTIES - TEXT SCALING, DIRECTIONALITY, SEMANTICS, HIT TESTING - that A DELEGATE MUST REPRODUCE or CONSCIOUSLY OMIT';
const RENDER_OBJECT = 'a RenderObject SUBCLASS is A FURTHER STEP - it is WHERE YOU GO WHEN THE WIDGET LAYERS REPRESENTATION OF LAYOUT CANNOT EXPRESS WHAT YOU NEED AT ALL, and it COSTS YOU HIT TESTING, SEMANTICS and ACCESSIBILITY UNLESS YOU IMPLEMENT THEM';

Declarative custom layout, and when to reach for a RenderObject instead.

// MultiChildLayoutWidget: position children yourself, declaratively
class BadgeLayout extends MultiChildLayoutWidget {
  const BadgeLayout({
    required this.label,
    required this.child,
    super.key,
  });

  final Widget label;
  final Widget child;

  @override
  void performLayout(Size size) {
    // 1. size the non-positioned child
    final childSize = layoutChild(getId('child'), BoxConstraints.loose(size));
    positionChild(getId('child'), Offset.zero);

    // 2. size and place the badge in the top-right corner
    const badgeSize = Size(18, 18);
    final badgeConstraints = BoxConstraints.tight(badgeSize);
    final child = getChildById('child');
    if (child != null) {
      child.layout(badgeConstraints, parentUsesSize: true);
      positionChild(getId('label'), Offset(childSize.width - 18, 0));
    }
  }

  @override
  bool shouldRelayout(BadgeLayout old) {
    return old.label != label || old.child != child;
  }
}

// usage
BadgeLayout(
  label: Container(
    padding: const EdgeInsets.all(2),
    decoration: const BoxDecoration(color: Colors.red, shape: BoxShape.circle),
    child: Text('$count', style: const TextStyle(color: Colors.white, fontSize: 10)),
  ),
  child: const Icon(Icons.notifications, size: 32),
)
// CustomMultiChildLayoutDelegate: the same thing, with the
// logic separated from the widget. Easier to test, easier to reuse.
class _RingLayout extends MultiChildLayoutDelegate {
  _RingLayout(this.count);

  final int count;

  @override
  void performLayout(Size size) {
    if (!hasChild('ring')) return;
    final ring = layoutChild('ring', BoxConstraints.loose(size));
    positionChild('ring', Offset.zero);
    if (!hasChild('dot')) return;

    // a badge at the top-right, offset by a fixed margin
    const dotSize = 16.0;
    layoutChild('dot', BoxConstraints.tight(const Size(dotSize, dotSize)));
    positionChild(
      'dot',
      Offset(ring.width - dotSize + 4, -4),
    );
  }

  // called when a child changes: do the layout again
  @override
  bool shouldRelayout(_RingLayout old) => count != old.count;
}

class Ring extends StatelessWidget {
  const Ring({required this.count, super.key});
  final int count;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return CustomMultiChildLayout(
      delegate: _RingLayout(count),
      children: [
        LayoutId(id: 'ring', child: const CircleAvatar(radius: 24)),
        LayoutId(
          id: 'dot',
          child: Container(
            width: 16, height: 16,
            decoration: const BoxDecoration(color: Colors.red, shape: BoxShape.circle),
            alignment: Alignment.center,
            child: Text('$count', style: const TextStyle(fontSize: 9, color: Colors.white)),
          ),
        ),
      ],
    );
  }
}

2.7 Writing a RenderObject

The three methods, and the contract between them

A render object is a node in the tree that holds geometry, and writing one is far more tractable than it first appears because there are only three methods you must implement and the framework provides everything else. performLayout decides the size. It receives the incoming constraints and either chooses a size satisfying them or calls size on itself — and it must then position and size its children, which is the part people forget: a render object that sets its own size and does nothing with its children produces an empty box with correct dimensions. paint draws, and must do nothing else. It receives an OffsetPair and a PaintingContext, translates the canvas if this node is offset, and paints. The rules that make paint tractable are worth stating because violating them produces the two characteristic bugs. Do not modify anything outside the canvas — no fields, no cached geometry — inside paint, because paint may be called without layout and any state you derive there will be stale or absent. Never call markNeedsPaint from inside paint, because that schedules another paint and produces a frame that never ends. And hitTest answers "was I touched, and by how far", and its contract is unusual enough to be worth stating precisely: it returns true only if this node or a descendant was hit, and if a child was hit but the hit is outside the child's bounds — a tap on an overflow region — you must return a distance-to-translate ratio, which is what makes the framework scroll or dismiss correctly rather than swallowing the event.

Then the four things that decide whether it works, and each is a specific bug. Always call markNeedsLayout when geometry changes. Changing a field without marking anything produces a node that lays out correctly once and then lies forever, and the symptom is a change that appears on one rebuild and not the next. Call it in the setter, not in the caller, for the same reason: the setter is the only place guaranteed to run, and marking at the call site means every caller has to remember. Repaint without relayout when only paint changed, because a colour change that triggers a layout re-runs the whole subtree's layout for no reason, and on a large tree that is the difference between a smooth animation and a dropped frame. And implement describeSemanticsConfiguration if your render object paints anything meaningful, because a custom render object that paints a control and does not report semantics is invisible to a screen reader — which is not an accessibility nicety but the framework treating it as decorative. And the final discipline, which is the one that keeps this from becoming a maintenance problem: a RenderProxyBox that adds a single behaviour is almost always the right thing to write, because it inherits layout, painting and hit testing from its child and lets you override only what you need; a from-scratch render object re-implements all three and every one you get slightly wrong is a bug that appears only in the case you did not test.

/* Three methods. */
const METHODS = [
  { m: 'performLayout', decides: 'THE SIZE',
    receives: 'the INCOMING CONSTRAINTS',
    must: ['either CHOOSE A SIZE satisfying them', 'or CALL size ON ITSELF'],
    andThen: 'it MUST THEN POSITION and SIZE ITS CHILDREN',
    forgotten: 'the part PEOPLE FORGET',
    failure: 'a RENDER OBJECT THAT SETS ITS OWN SIZE and DOES NOTHING WITH ITS CHILDREN PRODUCES AN EMPTY BOX WITH CORRECT DIMENSIONS' },
  { m: 'paint', doesOneThing: 'DRAWS',
    receives: ['an OffsetPair', 'a PaintingContext'],
    does: ['TRANSLATE THE CANVAS if this node IS OFFSET', 'and PAINT'],
    rules: [
      { r: 'do NOT MODIFY anything OUTSIDE THE CANVAS - no fields, no cached geometry - inside paint',
        why: 'paint MAY BE CALLED WITHOUT LAYOUT and ANY STATE YOU DERIVE THERE WILL BE STALE or ABSENT' },
      { r: 'NEVER CALL markNeedsPaint from INSIDE paint',
        why: 'that SCHEDULES ANOTHER PAINT and PRODUCES A FRAME THAT NEVER ENDS' },
    ] },
  { m: 'hitTest', answers: 'WAS I TOUCHED, AND BY HOW FAR',
    contract: ['it RETURNS TRUE ONLY IF this node OR A DESCENDANT was hit',
      'and if a CHILD WAS HIT BUT THE HIT IS OUTSIDE THE CHILDS BOUNDS - a TAP ON AN OVERFLOW REGION - you MUST RETURN A DISTANCE-TO-TRANSLATE RATIO'],
    whyTheRatio: 'which is WHAT MAKES THE FRAMEWORK SCROLL or DISMISS CORRECTLY rather than SWALLOWING THE EVENT' },
];

/* Four things that decide whether it works. */
const WORKING = [
  { w: 'ALWAYS CALL markNeedsLayout WHEN GEOMETRY CHANGES',
    failure: 'CHANGING A FIELD WITHOUT MARKING ANYTHING PRODUCES A NODE THAT LAYS OUT CORRECTLY ONCE and THEN LIES FOREVER',
    symptom: 'a CHANGE THAT APPEARS ON ONE REBUILD and NOT the next' },
  { w: 'CALL IT IN THE SETTER, not in the caller',
    why: 'the SETTER IS THE ONLY PLACE GUARANTEED TO RUN, and MARKING AT THE CALL SITE MEANS EVERY CALLER HAS TO REMEMBER' },
  { w: 'REPAINT WITHOUT RELAYOUT WHEN ONLY PAINT CHANGED',
    because: 'a COLOUR CHANGE THAT TRIGGERS A LAYOUT RE-RUNS THE WHOLE SUBTREES LAYOUT FOR NO REASON',
    cost: 'and on a LARGE TREE that is THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN a SMOOTH ANIMATION and A DROPPED FRAME' },
  { w: 'IMPLEMENT describeSemanticsConfiguration if your render object PAINTS ANYTHING MEANINGFUL',
    why: 'a CUSTOM RENDER OBJECT THAT PAINTS A CONTROL and DOES NOT REPORT SEMANTICS is INVISIBLE to a SCREEN READER',
    reframe: 'which is NOT AN ACCESSIBILITY NICETY but the FRAMEWORK TREATING IT AS DECORATIVE' },
];
const DISCIPLINE = 'a RenderProxyBox THAT ADDS A SINGLE BEHAVIOUR is ALMOST ALWAYS THE RIGHT THING TO WRITE';
const BECAUSE = 'it INHERITS LAYOUT, PAINTING and HIT TESTING FROM ITS CHILD and LETS YOU OVERRIDE ONLY WHAT YOU NEED';
const WARNING = 'a FROM-SCRATCH RENDER OBJECT RE-IMPLEMENTS ALL THREE and EVERY ONE YOU GET SLIGHTLY WRONG IS A BUG THAT APPEARS ONLY IN THE CASE YOU DID NOT TEST';

The lowest level of layout, and the three methods you must implement.

// when you need a RenderObject: a layout behaviour that no
// existing widget provides. NOT for styling or content.

class RenderPaddingBetween extends RenderProxyBox {
  RenderPaddingBetween({required this.spacing, EdgeInsets? padding})
      : super(padding);

  final double spacing;

  @override
  void performLayout() {
    // 1. give the child the constraints minus the padding
    var childConstraints = constraints;
    if (child != null) {
      child!.layout(constraints.deflate(padding), parentUsesSize: true);

      // 2. set YOUR size: as large as the constraints allow,
      //    because we have no intrinsic preference
      size = constraints.constrain(child!.size + padding.horizontal);
    } else {
      size = constraints.constrain(Size.zero);
    }
  }

  @override
  void paint(PaintingContext context, Offset offset) {
    if (child != null) context.paintChild(child!, offset + padding.topLeft);
  }

  // 3. hit testing: expand to include the padding
  @override
  bool hitTest(BoxHitTestResult result, {required Offset position}) {
    if (child != null) {
      return result.addWithPaintOffset(
        offset: offset,
        position: position,
        hitTest: (result, transformed) =>
            child!.hitTest(result, position: transformed - padding.topLeft),
      );
    }
    return false;
  }

  @override
  void applyPaintTransform(RenderObject child, Matrix4 transform) {
    transform.translate(padding.left, padding.top);
  }
}
// THE FOUR METHODS, and what each is for
//  performLayout()   - REQUIRED. call layout() on children, set size
//  paint()           - draw yourself, or delegate to the child
//  hitTest()         - where clicks land
//  applyPaintTransform() - so transforms and hit tests work
//
// THE SIZING RULES IN performLayout
//   size = constraints.constrain(desiredSize)
//   ALWAYS use constraints.constrain(), never assign size directly
//   it clamps to the constraints and it asserts if you exceed them

// the debugging that makes RenderObject work bearable
void performLayout() {
  assert(() {
    debugPrint('layout: constraints=$constraints');
    return true;
  }());
  // ...
  assert(() {
    debugPrint('layout: size=$size');
    return true;
  }());
}

// and the flag that makes mistakes visible
void main() {
  runApp(const MyApp());
  // in debug, Flutter asserts on constraint violations
  // and paints a red-and-yellow overflow stripe for you
}

2.8 The layout gotchas

The gotchas that survive experience, and how to check for them

Most layout bugs fall into a small set of shapes, and the ones below are the ones that keep appearing in code written by people who have shipped Flutter for years — which is the argument for having a checklist rather than relying on recall. The unbounded-axis pair. A Column in a vertical scroll view, a Row in a horizontal one, a ListView inside a Column without a fixed height, a GridView inside another Scrollable: in every case the inner widget is given an infinite main-axis constraint and cannot choose a size. The two correct answers are shrink-wrap the inner widget when it is genuinely small, or give the inner one a bounded height when it should fill, and choosing between those two is the actual decision. The unbounded Row inside a horizontal scroll view is the same problem on the other axis and is fixed the same way. The tight-constraint surprise: Center, Align and Positioned.fill hand their child tight constraints, so a child that wanted loose constraints fills or throws — which is why Align around a Column produces a full-height column and why the fix is Align(alignment: ..., child: ...) with the column inside something that shrinks, or IntrinsicSize, or simply putting the column in the stack directly. The Expanded outside a flex. Expanded must be a direct child of a Row, Column or Flex; wrapping it in a Container or an Align makes it a grandchild and produces a runtime error that reads as a null assertion rather than a hint about flex. The nested-shrink-wrap explosion. An IntrinsicHeight around a subtree that itself contains an IntrinsicHeight around a long list is a measurable frame cost and the reason a list inside a shrink-wrapped column must become a ListView with a bounded height or a Column of a fixed number of items. And the two that are about text rather than geometry: text scales with the user's accessibility setting and every fixed height that contains text is a bug for somebody; and a Row of text of mixed sizes is misaligned at the top rather than on the baseline unless crossAxisAlignment is set to use the baseline.

/* The shapes that keep appearing. */
const GOTCHAS = [
  { g: 'THE UNBOUNDED-AXIS PAIR',
    instances: ['a Column IN A VERTICAL SCROLL VIEW', 'a Row IN A HORIZONTAL ONE',
      'a ListView INSIDE A Column WITHOUT A FIXED HEIGHT', 'a GridView INSIDE another Scrollable'],
    why: 'the INNER WIDGET IS GIVEN AN INFINITE MAIN-AXIS CONSTRAINT and CANNOT CHOOSE A SIZE',
    answers: ['SHRINK-WRAP the INNER WIDGET WHEN IT IS GENUINELY SMALL',
      'or GIVE THE INNER ONE A BOUNDED HEIGHT WHEN IT SHOULD FILL'],
    and: 'choosing BETWEEN THOSE TWO is THE ACTUAL DECISION',
    also: 'the UNBOUNDED Row INSIDE A HORIZONTAL SCROLL VIEW is THE SAME PROBLEM on THE OTHER AXIS and is FIXED THE SAME WAY' },
  { g: 'THE TIGHT-CONSTRAINT SURPRISE',
    fact: 'Center, Align and Positioned.fill HAND THEIR CHILD TIGHT CONSTRAINTS',
    so: 'a CHILD THAT WANTED LOOSE CONSTRAINTS FILLS or THROWS',
    instance: 'which is WHY Align AROUND A Column PRODUCES A FULL-HEIGHT COLUMN',
    fixes: ['put the COLUMN IN THE STACK DIRECTLY', 'or wrap it in IntrinsicSize'] },
  { g: 'THE Expanded OUTSIDE A FLEX',
    rule: 'Expanded MUST BE A DIRECT CHILD of a Row, Column or Flex',
    failure: 'WRAPPING IT in a Container or an Align MAKES IT A GRANDCHILD',
    symptom: 'a RUNTIME ERROR THAT READS AS A NULL ASSERTION rather than a HINT ABOUT FLEX' },
  { g: 'THE NESTED-SHRINK-WRAP EXPLOSION',
    instance: 'an IntrinsicHeight AROUND a SUBTREE THAT ITSELF CONTAINS an IntrinsicHeight AROUND A LONG LIST',
    cost: 'a MEASURABLE FRAME COST',
    and: 'the REASON A LIST INSIDE A SHRINK-WRAPPED COLUMN MUST BECOME a ListView WITH A BOUNDED HEIGHT or a Column OF A FIXED NUMBER OF ITEMS' },
  { g: 'THE TWO THAT ARE ABOUT TEXT rather than GEOMETRY',
    items: ['TEXT SCALES WITH THE USERS ACCESSIBILITY SETTING and EVERY FIXED HEIGHT THAT CONTAINS TEXT IS A BUG FOR SOMEBODY',
      'a Row OF TEXT OF MIXED SIZES is MISALIGNED AT THE TOP rather than ON THE BASELINE unless crossAxisAlignment IS SET TO USE THE BASELINE'] },
];

/* The checklist, in the order it is worth running. */
const CHECKLIST = [
  { step: 1, check: 'EVERY SCROLLABLE HAS A BOUNDED CROSS-AXIS SIZE', how: 'check the PARENT, because the scroll view itself cannot know' },
  { step: 2, check: 'NO INTRINSIC WIDGET WRAPS A LIST OR A LONG SUBTREE',
    how: 'search for IntrinsicHeight and IntrinsicWidth and LOOK AT WHAT IS INSIDE EACH' },
  { step: 3, check: 'EVERY ALIGNMENT WIDGET HAS A CHILD THAT WANTS TIGHT CONSTRAINTS',
    how: 'if the child is a Column, it will FILL - and that is usually not what was meant' },
  { step: 4, check: 'EVERY Expanded, Flexible and Spacer IS A DIRECT CHILD of a Flex',
    how: 'one grep' },
  { step: 5, check: 'NO FIXED HEIGHT CONTAINS TEXT', how: 'check with the platform text-scale setting raised' },
  { step: 6, check: 'THE OVERFLOW STRIPE IS A SYMPTOM, not a WARNING',
    how: 'it means a CHILD WAS GIVEN A SIZE IT CANNOT USE; find WHICH ONE by reading the stripes coloured boundaries' },
];

Every error in this section has the same shape: something asked for space that nobody could tell it was available. When a layout error appears, the fix is almost never in the widget named in the message - it is in the ancestor that supplies the constraints.

The six layout bugs everyone hits, with the diagnosis and the fix.

// 1. OVERFLOW: the yellow-and-black stripe
// "A RenderFlex overflowed by N pixels on the right"
// CAUSE: the children want more than the parent offers
// DIAGNOSE: which axis, and by how much
Row(children: [                       // right / bottom
  Column(children: [...]),            // the INNER widget overflowed
])
// FIXES, in order
Expanded(child: Text('long text'))   // let it shrink
Flexible(child: Text('long text'))   // looser
FittedBox(child: ...)                // scale it down
SingleChildScrollView(               // scroll it
  scrollDirection: Axis.horizontal,
  child: Text('very long'),
)
OverflowBox(                          // let it overflow visibly
  maxWidth: double.infinity,
  child: Text('clipped'),
)

// 2. UNBOUNDED CONSTRAINTS: "incoming height constraints are unbounded"
// CAUSE: a flex widget inside a scroll view, on the cross axis
// FIX: SizedBox, IntrinsicHeight, or mainAxisSize.min

// 3. INFINITE HEIGHT: "RenderFlex children have non-zero flex"
// inside a Column inside a SingleChildScrollView
Column(
  children: [                        // the Column's height is infinite
    Expanded(child: ...),            // so it cannot divide anything
  ],
)
// FIX 1: mainAxisSize.min on the outer Column
SingleChildScrollView(
  child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [...]),
)
// FIX 2: shrinkWrap on the ListView
// FIX 3: use CustomScrollView with slivers, which is the right
//        answer for a long scrollable page with a header
// 4. THE INVISIBLE WIDGET
Expanded(child: Column())            // a Column with no children
// a Column EXPANDS to fill, so it demands all the space
// and then there is none left for its siblings
// FIX: give it content, or use mainAxisSize.min

// 5. THE UNCONSTRAINED TEXT
Row(children: [
  Text('a very long title...'),       // EXPANDS to fill the row
  Icon(Icons.star),                   // so the icon is pushed off
])
// FIX: the text goes in Expanded
Row(children: [
  Expanded(child: Text('a very long title...')),
  const Icon(Icons.star),
])

// 6. THE UNBOUNDED TEXT
SingleChildScrollView(
  child: Text('very long'),          // a Text in a vertical scroll
)
// this is fine, because Text takes the width it is offered

// 7. THE DOUBLE-TAP-GESTURE BUG: a full-screen GestureDetector
// over a scrollable eats the scroll
Stack(children: [
  ListView(...),                     // the scroll view
  Positioned.fill(child: GestureDetector(...)),   // swallows the drag
])
// FIX: put the gesture detector BEHIND, or use
//      HitTestBehavior.translucent, or add a RawGestureDetector
//      with a custom arena

Exercises 3

  1. Recreate the "unbounded constraints" error, then fix it three different ways and note the trade-offs.
  2. Write a screen with a scrollable Column containing an Expanded and fix the infinite-height error.
  3. Build a Stack with a gradient overlay and a text label, and get the overlay sizing right without a Positioned hack.
  4. Write a MultiChildLayoutWidget for a notification icon with a count badge in the corner.
  5. Use IntrinsicWidth to make two buttons the same width. Then measure the layout passes with debugPrint and see the cost.
  6. Write a RenderProxyBox that adds a gap between a row of children, and test the hit testing by tapping exactly in the gap.

3 · Slivers and Long Lists

3.1 Why slivers exist3.2 CustomScrollView and the sliver list3.3 Sliver layouts and the geometry3.4 Pinned and floating headers3.5 Keys, item extent and reordering3.6 Infinite and paginated lists3.7 Images in a list3.8 Making a list fast3.9 The list antipatterns

A scrolling list is the most common thing in a mobile app, and the place where Flutter's performance is most often lost. Slivers are how it is done properly.

3.1 Why slivers exist

The two problems, and why each needs a different mechanism

A sliver exists to solve two separate problems that a Column inside a scroll view solves badly, and understanding them separately is what makes the API make sense rather than looking arbitrary. The first problem is that a Column builds every child before it can paint anything. A Column with ten thousand children is fully constructed, laid out and — because a widget that is never visible still has an element and possibly a render object — accounted for in memory. The list is scrollable in the sense that the user can move it, but every row was built. Slivers invert that. The scroll view tells its sliver "you have this much viewport, here is what is visible", and the sliver builds only what it needs plus a margin. Nothing off-screen exists. That is the whole idea and it is why a sliver list of ten thousand rows costs about as much as one of thirty. The second problem is that a Column inside a scroll view gives the framework no way to know how far the content extends. The scrollable needs the total scroll extent to size its scrollbar, to decide whether it is at the top, and to compute the scroll physics; and the Column can only tell it after everything is laid out. A sliver answers incrementally: it is asked "lay out as far as you need to", it produces geometry as it goes, and it reports how much scroll extent it consumed as it does. So the two properties are: only build what is needed, and know the extent without building it all. Everything else about the sliver API is a consequence of the two-phase interaction the framework has with a sliver: first scroll layout, in which the sliver is told how much of the viewport is available and how far it is scrolled, and it reports its geometry; then paint, in which the sliver is told which part of its output is actually visible and draws only that. A sliver is not a widget in the ordinary sense — it has no build method, no size, and no place in the element tree in the way a box does; it is a participant in a protocol with the scroll view, and a widget that wraps it converts sliver constraints into the geometry a normal widget needs.

/* Two separate problems. */
const COLUMN_PROBLEMS = {
  p1: 'a Column BUILDS EVERY CHILD BEFORE IT CAN PAINT ANYTHING',
    detail: 'a Column WITH TEN THOUSAND CHILDREN is fully CONSTRUCTED, LAID OUT and - because a WIDGET THAT IS NEVER VISIBLE STILL HAS AN ELEMENT and POSSIBLY A RENDER OBJECT - ACCOUNTED FOR IN MEMORY',
    reframe: 'the list is SCROLLABLE in the sense that the USER CAN MOVE IT, but EVERY ROW WAS BUILT',
  p2: 'a Column INSIDE A SCROLL VIEW GIVES THE FRAMEWORK NO WAY TO KNOW HOW FAR THE CONTENT EXTENDS',
    whyItMatters: 'the SCROLLABLE NEEDS the TOTAL SCROLL EXTENT to size its scrollbar, to DECIDE WHETHER IT IS AT THE TOP, and to COMPUTE the SCROLL PHYSICS',
    and: 'the Column CAN ONLY TELL IT AFTER EVERYTHING IS LAID OUT',
    sliverAnswer: 'it IS ASKED lay out as far as you need to, PRODUCES GEOMETRY AS IT GOES, and REPORTS HOW MUCH SCROLL EXTENT it CONSUMED AS IT DOES',
};

/* The two properties, and everything else follows. */
const PROPERTIES = ['ONLY BUILD WHAT IS NEEDED', 'and KNOW THE EXTENT WITHOUT BUILDING IT ALL'];

/* Two phases. */
const PHASES = [
  { n: 1, name: 'SCROLL LAYOUT', told: 'HOW MUCH OF THE VIEWPORT IS AVAILABLE and HOW FAR IT IS SCROLLED', reports: 'ITS GEOMETRY' },
  { n: 2, name: 'PAINT', told: 'WHICH PART OF ITS OUTPUT IS ACTUALLY VISIBLE', does: 'DRAWS ONLY THAT' },
];
const NOT_A_WIDGET = 'a SLIVER IS NOT A WIDGET in the ordinary sense - it has NO BUILD METHOD, NO SIZE, and NO PLACE in the element tree IN THE WAY A BOX DOES';
const WHAT_IT_IS = 'it IS A PARTICIPANT IN A PROTOCOL with the scroll view';
const WRAPPER = 'a WIDGET THAT WRAPS IT CONVERTS SLIVER CONSTRAINTS INTO THE GEOMETRY A NORMAL WIDGET NEEDS';

Before you build anything clever with slivers, check whether itemExtent alone fixes it. The majority of "my list is slow" reports are a list without a known item height, and adding one constant is a single line. Custom slivers are for headers that pin, not for faster lists.

What ListView does, what it costs, and the insight behind slivers.

// ListView: the easy path. It is a SLIVER underneath.
ListView(
  itemCount: 10000,
  itemBuilder: (context, index) => Card(child: Text('Item $index')),
)
// how it works:
//  - the ListView is a viewport
//  - it creates a SliverFixedExtentList or SliverList
//  - it builds only the items in the viewport, plus a cacheExtent
//    margin on either side (default 250px)
//  - as you scroll, it builds the incoming items and destroys
//    the outgoing ones
//
// SO: it is already lazy, and it is fine for most lists.
//
// THE TWO THINGS ListView DOES NOT DO
//  1. it cannot pin a header, shrink a header, or overlap content
//     - a SliverAppBar that collapses as you scroll needs slivers
//  2. it cannot build from a custom geometry
//     - a grid with a different column count per row, a
//       masonry layout, a staggered grid
//
// THAT is what CustomScrollView with slivers is for.
// THE SLIVER MENTAL MODEL
//
// a sliver describes a piece of scrollable content in terms of
// GEOMETRY relative to the scroll position:
//
//   scrollOffset  -> how far the viewport has scrolled
//   remainingPaintExtent  -> how much space is left to paint
//   overlap        -> how much this sliver overlaps the NEXT one
//
// the three standard configurations
//
// 1. BoxScrollView (ListView, GridView)
//    children have a fixed extent in the scroll direction
//    geometry is simple: layoutOffset and paintExtent
//
// 2. SliverFixedExtentList
//    a box scroll view with a KNOWN item height
//    ListView with itemExtent set uses this
//    FASTER than a plain ListView, because it can skip the layout
//    pass for offscreen items entirely
//
// 3. SliverList / SliverGrid
//    a box scroll view, but the child decides its own extent
//    SliverList is what a plain ListView uses: it lays out each
//    child, measures it, and builds the next one

3.2 CustomScrollView and the sliver list

Cache extent, item extent, and the two knobs that decide everything

Three properties of a sliver list govern whether it is fast, and understanding what each one actually controls explains most of the performance advice about long lists. cacheExtent is how much beyond the visible area is built. The default is a small margin, which is correct for a list the user scrolls slowly but produces visible blank space during a fast fling, because the sliver cannot build a row that was not already built when the scroll offset arrived. Raising it makes flicks smooth and costs memory and build work; the trade is worth making for any list that is fast to scroll and not worth making for a list the user reads. And it is a distance, not a number of items, which is the detail that matters: a cache extent of two hundred pixels is ten rows on a dense list and one on a sparse one, so a fixed pixel value behaves differently on different screens and at different text scales, and a value chosen on a small phone can be enormous on a tablet. itemExtent is the fixed height of every row, and supplying it — or itemExtentBuilder for a height computed from the item — is the single highest-leverage optimisation available for a long list, because it lets the sliver compute any row's position without having laid out the rows before it, and therefore know the scroll extent from the item count alone. Without it, the sliver must build a row to discover its height, and that is the difference between a list whose scroll extent is known before painting and one that is not. prototypeItem is the other half of the same idea, and it is the one that works when rows are not uniformly sized: a sample row that the sliver lays out once to learn the average height, so that its extent estimate is roughly right before it has built anything, which is a heuristic and produces a small scrollbar jump when the estimate is wrong. Then the two ways to build and the reason they are not interchangeable. SliverList with a list of already-constructed widgets has the whole list in memory before the sliver is asked for anything, so it defeats the point of slivers for a large list and is appropriate only when the list is small, bounded and known. SliverList.builder and SliverChildBuilderDelegate build on demand, taking an item count and a builder, which is what makes a list of a million records possible; the delegate also carries the finding predicate and the child count, and the finding predicate is what lets a lazy list avoid materialising the whole sequence. The practical guidance: builder for anything unbounded, delegate with a finding predicate for anything lazy, and if a list still feels slow, check itemExtent before anything else.

/* Three properties. */
const PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'cacheExtent', is: 'HOW MUCH BEYOND THE VISIBLE AREA IS BUILT',
    default: 'a SMALL MARGIN',
    rightForDefault: 'a LIST THE USER SCROLLS SLOWLY',
    failureOfDefault: 'produces VISIBLE BLANK SPACE DURING A FAST FLING, because the SLIVER CANNOT BUILD A ROW THAT WAS NOT ALREADY BUILT when the scroll offset ARRIVED',
    gainOfRaising: 'makes FLICKS SMOOTH', costs: ['MEMORY', 'BUILD WORK'],
    rule: 'worth making FOR ANY LIST THAT IS FAST TO SCROLL and NOT worth making for a list the user READS',
    criticalDetail: 'it IS A DISTANCE, not a NUMBER OF ITEMS',
    why: 'a CACHE EXTENT OF TWO HUNDRED PIXELS is TEN ROWS on a DENSE LIST and ONE on a SPARSE ONE',
    consequence: 'so a FIXED PIXEL VALUE BEHAVES DIFFERENTLY ON DIFFERENT SCREENS and AT DIFFERENT TEXT SCALES, and a VALUE CHOSEN ON A SMALL PHONE can be ENORMOUS on a TABLET' },
  { p: 'itemExtent', is: 'THE FIXED HEIGHT OF EVERY ROW',
    supplyAlso: 'itemExtentBuilder for a HEIGHT COMPUTED FROM THE ITEM',
    rank: 'the SINGLE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE OPTIMISATION available for a long list',
    why: 'it LETS THE SLIVER COMPUTE ANY ROWS POSITION without having LAID OUT THE ROWS BEFORE IT, and therefore KNOW THE SCROLL EXTENT FROM THE ITEM COUNT ALONE',
    difference: 'WITHOUT IT, the SLIVER MUST BUILD A ROW TO DISCOVER ITS HEIGHT',
    and: 'that is THE DIFFERENCE between a list whose SCROLL EXTENT IS KNOWN BEFORE PAINTING and one that is NOT' },
  { p: 'prototypeItem', is: 'THE OTHER HALF OF THE SAME IDEA',
    worksWhen: 'ROWS ARE NOT UNIFORMLY SIZED',
    does: 'a SAMPLE ROW that the SLIVER LAYS OUT ONCE to LEARN THE AVERAGE HEIGHT',
    so: 'its EXTENT ESTIMATE is ROUGHLY RIGHT BEFORE IT HAS BUILT ANYTHING',
    honest: 'it is A HEURISTIC and PRODUCES A SMALL SCROLLBAR JUMP when the ESTIMATE IS WRONG' },
];

/* Two ways to build. */
const WAYS = [
  { w: 'SliverList WITH A LIST OF ALREADY-CONSTRUCTED WIDGETS',
    problem: 'HAS THE WHOLE LIST IN MEMORY BEFORE the sliver IS ASKED FOR ANYTHING',
    consequence: 'so it DEFEATS THE POINT OF SLIVERS for a LARGE LIST',
    rightFor: 'a LIST THAT IS SMALL, BOUNDED and KNOWN' },
  { w: 'SliverList.builder and SliverChildBuilderDelegate',
    does: 'BUILD ON DEMAND',
    shape: 'AN ITEM COUNT and a BUILDER',
    and: 'which is WHAT MAKES A LIST OF A MILLION RECORDS POSSIBLE',
    delegateAlsoCarries: ['the FINDING PREDICATE', 'the CHILD COUNT'],
    and: 'the FINDING PREDICATE is WHAT LETS A LAZY LIST AVOID MATERIALISING the WHOLE SEQUENCE' },
];
const GUIDANCE = ['BUILDER for anything UNBOUNDED',
  'DELEGATE WITH A FINDING PREDICATE for anything LAZY',
  'and if a LIST STILL FEELS SLOW, CHECK itemExtent BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE'];

The correct structure for a screen with a header and a list.

CustomScrollView(
  slivers: [
    // 1. a collapsing app bar
    const SliverAppBar(
      pinned: true,
      expandedHeight: 200,
      flexibleSpace: FlexibleSpaceBar(
        title: Text('Field Notes'),
        background: Image(image: AssetImage('hero.jpg'), fit: BoxFit.cover),
      ),
      actions: [IconButton(onPressed: search, icon: const Icon(Icons.search))],
    ),

    // 2. any widget can be a sliver
    const SliverToBoxAdapter(
      child: Padding(
        padding: EdgeInsets.all(16),
        child: Text('Your notes, sorted by date'),
      ),
    ),

    // 3. the list
    SliverList.builder(
      itemCount: entries.length,
      itemBuilder: (context, index) {
        final entry = entries[index];
        return EntryCard(
          key: ValueKey(entry.id),     // essential
          entry: entry,
        );
      },
    ),

    // 4. a loading footer
    const SliverToBoxAdapter(child: SizedBox(height: 80, child: CircularProgressIndicator())),
  ],
);
// THE SLIVER WIDGETS
// SliverToBoxAdapter   - one child, normal layout rules
// SliverList           - a variable-extent list
// SliverFixedExtentList - a fixed-height list, faster
// SliverGrid            - a grid
// SliverPadding         - adds padding, and it SLICES geometry
//                       so the first and last children can
//                       extend under the padding
// SliverAppBar          - a toolbar that can pin, float, snap
// SliverPersistentHeader - pinToBox, a custom pinned header
// SliverFillRemaining   - fills whatever space is left
// SliverCrossAxisGroup  - two slivers side by side
// SliverMainAxisGroup   - two slivers sharing the main axis extent
// SliverAnimatedPaintBox - a custom-painted sliver
// THE MOST IMPORTANT OPTIMISATION: itemExtent
// if every row is the same height, TELL FLUTTER.
//
// WITHOUT itemExtent: Flutter must build and layout each item as
// it scrolls, because it does not know how tall they are.
// WITH itemExtent: it can compute the offset of item 5000 without
// building items 0 through 4999.

ListView.builder(
  itemExtent: 72,                    // a constant
  itemCount: 10000,
  itemBuilder: (context, index) => const SizedBox(height: 72, child: ListTile(title: Text('x'))),
)

// or a builder for a computed extent, for variable heights
ListView.builder(
  itemExtentBuilder: (index, dimensions) {
    return entries[index].body.length > 80 ? 120.0 : 72.0;
  },
  itemCount: entries.length,
  itemBuilder: (context, index) => EntryTile(entry: entries[index]),
)

// THE MEASUREMENT: add --profile, then look at the build count
// in the DevTools Performance panel. With itemExtent on a
// 10,000-row list, the build count drops to roughly the number
// of rows actually on screen plus the cache extent, regardless
// of scroll position.

3.3 Sliver layouts and the geometry

Sliver geometry, and why custom slivers are rare

A custom sliver is a class that extends one of the framework's sliver bases and participates in the two-phase protocol, and it is worth being clear that this is a genuinely advanced technique — there are very few reasons to write one. The base classes exist so that you implement one method. RenderSliverSingleBoxAdapter handles a single child and requires you to compute the child's extent in performLayout; RenderSliverFixedExtentBoxAdapter handles a list of equally-sized children and computes everything from the count and the extent; RenderSliverList handles variable extents and does the difficult incremental work of building and discarding children as the viewport moves. If one of those fits, the whole sliver is a constructor and a builder. The three numbers a sliver produces. paintExtent is how much of the sliver is visible, cacheExtent is the region including the off-screen margin, and scrollExtent is the total extent of the content, and the geometry is expressed in the sliver's own coordinate space with the scroll offset applied — which is why a sliver that reports its paint origin incorrectly produces content drawn in the wrong place rather than an error. And the one rule about invalidation. A sliver that caches anything derived from its children must invalidate that cache in performLayout, and must not assume that paint follows performLayout — because a repaint can happen without a layout, and a sliver whose paint depends on a cached layout value will draw the previous frame's geometry. That single rule accounts for most of the custom slivers that appear correct and are subtly wrong.

Then the four places a custom sliver is genuinely the right answer, so that the judgement is not "never". A header that must be measured rather than assumed. A collapsing app bar whose height depends on content: you need to lay out the child during scroll layout and report its extent, which the adapters do for you but the composition of several children does not. A sticky or floating group header that spans a run of items, because that is a sliver that is not a child of the list sliver — it is a separate sliver placed between two list slivers in the same CustomScrollView, which is the actual mechanism and requires no custom code at all. A list whose items have genuinely variable and unknown heights, where prototypeItem gives an estimate and the sliver must correct it as it builds — which the framework's list sliver already does. And a rendering technique with no widget equivalent — a custom-painted effect that must be computed during scroll rather than during paint. And then the honest alternative, which should be the default: build the effect out of several standard slivers in a CustomScrollView, which is what the second and third cases above actually are, and which costs nothing to maintain and has none of the invalidation hazards. The rule of thumb: try to express the effect as a composition of standard slivers first; reach for a subclass only when the effect must be measured during scroll layout rather than composed from pieces.

/* Base classes exist so you implement one method. */
const BASES = [
  { b: 'RenderSliverSingleBoxAdapter', handles: 'a SINGLE CHILD', implement: 'compute the CHILDS EXTENT in performLayout' },
  { b: 'RenderSliverFixedExtentBoxAdapter', handles: 'a LIST OF EQUALLY-SIZED CHILDREN', computes: 'EVERYTHING FROM THE COUNT and the EXTENT' },
  { b: 'RenderSliverList', handles: 'VARIABLE EXTENTS', does: 'the DIFFICULT INCREMENTAL WORK of BUILDING and DISCARDING CHILDREN as the VIEWPORT MOVES' },
];
const FITS = 'if one of those FITS, the WHOLE SLIVER IS A CONSTRUCTOR and a BUILDER';

/* The three numbers. */
const NUMBERS = [
  { n: 'paintExtent', is: 'HOW MUCH OF THE SLIVER IS VISIBLE' },
  { n: 'cacheExtent', is: 'THE REGION INCLUDING THE OFF-SCREEN MARGIN' },
  { n: 'scrollExtent', is: 'THE TOTAL EXTENT OF THE CONTENT' },
];
const COORDINATE_SPACE = 'the GEOMETRY IS EXPRESSED IN THE SLIVERS OWN COORDINATE SPACE with the SCROLL OFFSET APPLIED';
const GEOMETRY_BUG = 'which is WHY A SLIVER THAT REPORTS ITS PAINT ORIGIN INCORRECTLY PRODUCES CONTENT DRAWN IN THE WRONG PLACE rather than an ERROR';

/* The invalidation rule. */
const INVALIDATION = 'a SLIVER THAT CACHES ANYTHING DERIVED FROM ITS CHILDREN MUST INVALIDATE THAT CACHE in performLayout';
const PAINT_ASSUMPTION = 'and MUST NOT ASSUME THAT paint FOLLOWS performLayout - because A REPAINT CAN HAPPEN WITHOUT A LAYOUT';
const CONSEQUENCE = 'a SLIVER WHOSE PAINT DEPENDS ON A CACHED LAYOUT VALUE WILL DRAW THE PREVIOUS FRAMES GEOMETRY';
const ATTRIBUTION = 'that SINGLE RULE ACCOUNTS FOR MOST of the CUSTOM SLIVERS that APPEAR CORRECT and ARE SUBTLY WRONG';

/* The four cases a custom sliver is right. */
const RIGHT_WHEN = [
  { c: 'a HEADER THAT MUST BE MEASURED rather than ASSUMED',
    instance: 'a COLLAPSING APP BAR whose HEIGHT DEPENDS ON CONTENT',
    why: 'you NEED TO LAY OUT THE CHILD DURING SCROLL LAYOUT and REPORT ITS EXTENT, which the adapters DO FOR YOU but the COMPOSITION of SEVERAL CHILDREN DOES NOT' },
  { c: 'a STICKY or FLOATING GROUP HEADER that SPANS A RUN OF ITEMS',
    mechanism: 'it IS A SEPARATE SLIVER PLACED BETWEEN TWO LIST SLIVERS in the same CustomScrollView',
    and: 'which is THE ACTUAL MECHANISM and REQUIRES NO CUSTOM CODE AT ALL' },
  { c: 'a LIST WHOSE ITEMS have GENUINELY VARIABLE and UNKNOWN HEIGHTS',
    and: 'where prototypeItem GIVES AN ESTIMATE and the SLIVER MUST CORRECT IT AS IT BUILDS - which the FRAMEWORKS LIST SLIVER ALREADY DOES' },
  { c: 'a RENDERING TECHNIQUE WITH NO WIDGET EQUIVALENT',
    instance: 'a CUSTOM-PAINTED EFFECT that MUST BE COMPUTED DURING SCROLL rather than DURING PAINT' },
];

/* The honest alternative. */
const ALTERNATIVE = 'BUILD THE EFFECT OUT OF SEVERAL STANDARD SLIVERS in a CustomScrollView';
const BECAUSE = 'which is WHAT THE SECOND and THIRD CASES ABOVE ACTUALLY ARE, and which COSTS NOTHING TO MAINTAIN and HAS NONE of the INVALIDATION HAZARDS';
const RULE_OF_THUMB = 'try to EXPRESS THE EFFECT AS A COMPOSITION of standard slivers FIRST; reach for a SUBCLASS ONLY WHEN the effect MUST BE MEASURED DURING SCROLL LAYOUT rather than COMPOSED FROM PIECES';

The numbers, so custom slivers stop being magic.

// THE ARGUMENTS performLayout RECEIVES
//
//   constraints
//     .scrollOffset      how far the viewport has scrolled
//     .remainingPaintExtent  how much of THIS sliver is still
//                        visible and needs painting
//     .overlap           how far this sliver runs under the NEXT
//                        one, so you can compensate
//     .cacheExtent       a little beyond the visible area
//     .userScrollDirection
//
// WHAT YOU MUST SET
//   geometry!.scrollExtent    the total scrollable length of this
//                             sliver: everything, visible or not
//   geometry!.maxScrollExtent the maximum extent, if you need to
//                             reserve space (e.g. for a footer)
