//   geometry!.paintExtent     how much to paint NOW
//   geometry!.hitTestExtent    where clicks land: paintExtent is
//                             often too small
//   geometry!.cacheExtent     the cached extent, for perf
//
// THE RULE: paintExtent <= remainingPaintExtent. If you paint
// more than is left, the framework clips it and you get overflow
// stripes. If you paint less, you get gaps.
// A MINIMAL CUSTOM SLIVER: a divider every N pixels
class TickerSliver extends SliverPersistentHeaderDelegate {
  TickerSliver({required this.price, required this.onTap});

  final double price;
  final VoidCallback onTap;

  @override
  double get minExtent => 32;
  @override
  double get maxExtent => 32;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context, double shrinkOffset, bool overlaps) {
    return GestureDetector(
      onTap: onTap,
      child: Container(
        alignment: Alignment.centerRight,
        padding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 16),
        color: Colors.amber.shade100,
        child: Text('\$$price', style: const TextStyle(fontWeight: FontWeight.bold)),
      ),
    );
  }

  // a NEW delegate means the content changed: rebuild it
  @override
  bool shouldRebuild(TickerSliver old) => old.price != price;
}

// usage
CustomScrollView(slivers: [
  SliverPersistentHeader(pinned: true, delegate: TickerSliver(price: price, onTap: buy)),
  const SliverToBoxAdapter(child: Text('Chart goes here')),
  SliverList.builder(itemCount: 50, itemBuilder: (_, i) => ListTile(title: Text('Row $i'))),
]);
// SliverPersistentHeaderDelegate: a header that can pin and
// shrink. minExtent is the pinned height, maxExtent is the
// expanded height.

class SectionHeader extends SliverPersistentHeaderDelegate {
  const SectionHeader({required this.title, required this.color, super.key});

  final String title;
  final Color color;

  @override
  double get minExtent => 44;              // the pinned height

  @override
  double get maxExtent => 44;              // same: it does not expand

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context, double shrinkOffset, bool overlapsContent) {
    // shrinkOffset goes 0 (expanded) to maxExtent-minExtent (pinned)
    final progress = (shrinkOffset / (maxExtent - minExtent)).clamp(0.0, 1.0);
    return Container(
      height: maxExtent,
      padding: EdgeInsets.only(left: 16 * (1 - progress) + 8, top: 16 * (1 - progress)),
      color: color.withValues(alpha: 1 - progress * 0.2),
      child: Opacity(
        opacity: 1 - progress,
        child: Text(title, style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleLarge),
      ),
    );
  }

  @override
  bool shouldRebuild(SectionHeader old) => old.title != title || old.color != color;
}

// an EXPANDING one
class ExpandingHeader extends SliverPersistentHeaderDelegate {
  ExpandingHeader(this.title);

  final String title;

  @override
  double get minExtent => 56;      // pinned
  @override
  double get maxExtent => 200;     // fully expanded

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context, double shrinkOffset, bool overlaps) {
    final t = (shrinkOffset / (maxExtent - minExtent)).clamp(0.0, 1.0);
    return SizedBox(
      height: maxExtent,
      child: Stack(fit: StackFit.expand, children: [
        Opacity(opacity: 1 - t, child: Image.asset('header.jpg', fit: BoxFit.cover)),
        Positioned(
          left: 16,
          bottom: minExtent - 30,
          child: Transform.scale(scale: 1 - t * 0.3, child: Text(title)),
        ),
      ]),
    );
  }

  @override
  bool shouldRebuild(ExpandingHeader old) => old.title != title;
}

3.4 Pinned and floating headers

Why headers live outside the list, not inside it

The mechanism for a header that stays put while the list scrolls is a CustomScrollView with more than one sliver, and the reason it works is worth stating because the alternative — a header inside the list — fails in a specific, diagnosable way. A CustomScrollView stacks slivers and gives them all one shared viewport. Each sliver receives the same scroll offset and lays out as if it were the only thing, so a small sliver placed first becomes a fixed-height band at the top and a list placed second scrolls underneath it. There is no coordination between them beyond the shared offset, which is exactly why it is cheap. A header inside a list is a row, and a row scrolls away. To make it stay you must either make it sticky — which the list sliver supports for one header at a time, with real restrictions — or rebuild the layout to keep it pinned, which means either a nested scroll view (which breaks the shared scroll) or a Stack with a ListView offset by the header's height (which requires knowing the height and does not survive a text-scale change). All three are worse. So the structure is: SliverAppBar or a SliverPersistentHeader first, then your content slivers. SliverAppBar gives a toolbar that can collapse on scroll and reappear on upward scroll, driven by two properties: floating makes it detach and float over the content as you scroll up, and pinned keeps it in place. The two are independent and the combination — pinned and not floating — is the ordinary app bar. For a header whose height is content-driven, a SliverPersistentHeader with a delegate gives you two callbacks — build for the content and shouldRebuild to decide whether to re-run — plus the constraint to report a minimum and maximum extent, which is how a header can shrink from a tall expanded state to a compact one. Then the three gotchas, each of which costs an afternoon the first time. Nested scroll views break the shared offset, so a ListView inside a CustomScrollView needs its own controller or it throws. A RefreshIndicator does not work on a bare CustomScrollView without specifying which sliver is the trigger, and the common symptom is a spinner that never appears because the notification does not reach the viewport. And padding inside a SliverAppBar is not what you expect — the toolbar's own height comes from the safe-area inset, and adding padding inside it moves the title rather than making room for it.

/* The mechanism. */
const CUSTOM_SCROLL_VIEW = {
  does: 'STACKS SLIVERS and GIVES THEM ALL ONE SHARED VIEWPORT',
  fact: 'EACH SLIVER RECEIVES THE SAME SCROLL OFFSET and LAYS OUT AS IF IT WERE THE ONLY THING',
  so: 'a SMALL SLIVER PLACED FIRST BECOMES A FIXED-HEIGHT BAND AT THE TOP and a LIST PLACED SECOND SCROLLS UNDERNEATH IT',
  and: 'THERE IS NO COORDINATION BETWEEN THEM BEYOND THE SHARED OFFSET, which is EXACTLY WHY IT IS CHEAP',
};
const INSIDE_THE_LIST = {
  is: 'A ROW, and A ROW SCROLLS AWAY',
  alternatives: [
    { a: 'make it STICKY', reality: 'the list sliver SUPPORTS IT FOR ONE HEADER AT A TIME, WITH REAL RESTRICTIONS' },
    { a: 'REBUILD THE LAYOUT to KEEP IT PINNED',
      means: 'a NESTED SCROLL VIEW, which BREAKS THE SHARED SCROLL',
      or: 'a Stack WITH A ListView OFFSET BY THE HEADERS HEIGHT',
      problems: 'WHICH REQUIRES KNOWING THE HEIGHT and DOES NOT SURVIVE A TEXT-SCALE CHANGE' },
  ],
  verdict: 'ALL THREE ARE WORSE',
};
const STRUCTURE = ['SliverAppBar or a SliverPersistentHeader FIRST', 'then YOUR CONTENT SLIVERS'];
const APP_BAR = {
  gives: 'a TOOLBAR THAT CAN COLLAPSE ON SCROLL and REAPPEAR ON UPWARD SCROLL',
  drivenBy: ['floating - makes it DETACH and FLOAT OVER the content as YOU SCROLL UP', 'pinned - KEEPS IT IN PLACE'],
  independent: true,
  combination: 'pinned and not floating IS THE ORDINARY APP BAR',
};
const PERSISTENT = {
  useWhen: 'a HEADER WHOSE HEIGHT IS CONTENT-DRIVEN',
  gives: 'a DELEGATE WITH TWO CALLBACKS - build FOR THE CONTENT and shouldRebuild TO DECIDE WHETHER TO RE-RUN',
  plus: 'the CONSTRAINT TO REPORT A MINIMUM and MAXIMUM EXTENT',
  gain: 'which is HOW A HEADER CAN SHRINK FROM A TALL EXPANDED STATE to a COMPACT ONE',
};

/* Three gotchas. */
const GOTCHAS = [
  { g: 'NESTED SCROLL VIEWS BREAK THE SHARED OFFSET',
    fix: 'a ListView INSIDE A CustomScrollView NEEDS ITS OWN CONTROLLER or it THROWS' },
  { g: 'A RefreshIndicator DOES NOT WORK on a BARE CustomScrollView',
    requires: 'SPECIFYING WHICH SLIVER IS THE TRIGGER',
    symptom: 'a SPINNER THAT NEVER APPEARS because the NOTIFICATION DOES NOT REACH the viewport' },
  { g: 'PADDING INSIDE A SliverAppBar IS NOT WHAT YOU EXPECT',
    detail: 'the TOOLBARS OWN HEIGHT COMES FROM THE SAFE-AREA INSET',
    symptom: 'and ADDING PADDING INSIDE IT MOVES THE TITLE rather than MAKING ROOM FOR IT' },
];

The three header behaviours, and the parameters that control them.

// SLIVERAPPBAR PARAMETERS
SliverAppBar(
  // does it stay at the top when you scroll?
  pinned: true,                 // stays, shrinks to toolbarHeight
  floating: true,               // slides back in when you scroll up
  // snap: when you release mid-way, go to a hard stop
  snap: true,

  expandedHeight: 240,          // the full height
  collapsedHeight: kToolbarHeight,   // the pinned height

  // the title animation
  centerTitle: true,
  title: Text('Field Notes'),

  // show the title only when collapsed
  forceElevated: false,
  elevation: 0,

  // the flexible space
  flexibleSpace: FlexibleSpaceBar(
    title: Text('Field Notes'),      // this one is easier to animate
    titlePadding: EdgeInsetsDirectional.only(start: 56, bottom: 16, end: 16),
    background: Image(image: AssetImage('hero.jpg'), fit: BoxFit.cover),
    collapseMode: CollapseMode.parallax,   // the default
    stretchModes: const [StretchMode.zoomBackground],
  ),

  actions: [...],
  bottom: PreferredSize(
    preferredSize: const Size.fromHeight(56),
    child: TabBar(tabs: [Tab(text: 'All'), Tab(text: 'Photos')]),
  ),
);

// THE THREE COMBINATIONS
// pinned: false, floating: false  - scrolls away completely
// pinned: true                    - sticks, shrinks
// pinned: true, floating: true    - sticks, and reappears on scroll up
// add snap: true                  - no half-states
// A COLLAPSING TOOLBAR, done by hand, which teaches the mechanism
class CollapsingBar extends StatelessWidget {
  const CollapsingBar({required this.child, super.key});

  final Widget child;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return CustomScrollView(
      slivers: [
        SliverAppBar(
          pinned: true,
          title: const Text('Search'),
          actions: [IconButton(onPressed: filter, icon: const Icon(Icons.tune))],
          bottom: PreferredSize(
            preferredSize: const Size.fromHeight(60),
            child: Padding(
              padding: const EdgeInsets.fromLTRB(16, 0, 16, 12),
              child: TextField(
                decoration: InputDecoration(
                  hintText: 'Search notes',
                  prefixIcon: const Icon(Icons.search),
                  filled: true,
                  border: OutlineInputBorder(borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(28)),
                ),
              ),
            ),
          ),
        ),
        SliverToBoxAdapter(child: child),
      ],
    );
  }
}

// THE NESTED-SCROLL PROBLEM, and the fix
// a GridView inside a CustomScrollView: the grid has its own
// scroll physics and they fight
CustomScrollView(
  slivers: [
    SliverAppBar(...),
    SliverGrid(                          // this is fine
      gridDelegate: const SliverGridDelegateWithFixedCrossAxisCount(
        crossAxisCount: 2, mainAxisSpacing: 8, crossAxisSpacing: 8,
      ),
      delegate: SliverChildBuilderDelegate(...),
    ),
  ],
)

// but a scrollable INSIDE a sliver is not
SliverToBoxAdapter(
  child: ListView.builder(itemCount: 100, ...),   // WRONG: nested scrolling
)
// FIX 1: give it a fixed height
SliverToBoxAdapter(child: SizedBox(height: 400, child: ListView(...)))
// FIX 2: shrinkWrap (costs performance: builds everything)
SliverToBoxAdapter(child: ListView(shrinkWrap: true, ...))
// FIX 3: make it a sliver instead
SliverList.builder(itemCount: 100, ...)

3.5 Keys, item extent and reordering

Reordering in a sliver list, and why it is harder than it looks

Reordering a list inside a sliver has a specific failure mode that does not exist in an ordinary list, and knowing it prevents a bug that is very hard to find. With itemExtent, the sliver computes any row's position from the index alone — so it never has to build a row to know where it goes. That is what makes it fast, and it is also what makes it wrong after a reorder: the positions are stale because they were derived from an order that has changed, and the list will scroll to the wrong place or will show a row whose content belongs to a different item until the user scrolls far enough for a rebuild. Without itemExtent, the sliver must build rows to know the extent, so it discovers the reorder correctly but pays for it. This is the trade, and the way out of it is to give the reorder to a widget that handles it: the reorderable widgets own the list, the keys and the animation together, which is why ReorderableListView and ReorderableList exist rather than a ReorderableListTile you drop into an existing list. The reason is structural: a reorderable widget needs to know the item order to draw the gap where an item was removed, and it needs to know the keys to animate the item from its old position, and both require the list rather than the tile. Then the key discipline, which is the part that matters even if you do not use a reorderable widget. When a list reorders, the elements must follow their items rather than their positions, so every row needs a stable key derived from the item's identity — and "derived from the item's identity" is the whole requirement. An index is not an identity: an index key means that when the list reorders, row three keeps its element and therefore its state, and whatever moved into position three inherits it. That is the same bug the chapter-one keys section described, and it is the reason a list that supports reordering should never use an index as a key. And then the three questions to ask before building a reorderable list. How large is the list, really? A drag-and-drop reorder on a list of five thousand items is a different feature from one on a list of twenty, and the animation cost is not linear. Does the order mean something the backend cares about? A reordering UI that does not persist is a toy; one that persists optimistically needs a conflict story for two devices reordering at once, which is a distributed-systems problem wearing a drag-and-drop costume. And what happens to the scroll position, because inserting an item above the viewport moves everything below it, and the user will perceive the list as jumping; the fix is to anchor the scroll to the item the user is looking at, which the framework widgets do and a hand-rolled implementation does not.

/* The trade itemExtent creates. */
const WITH_ITEM_EXTENT = {
  fact: 'the SLIVER COMPUTES ANY ROWS POSITION FROM THE INDEX ALONE - so it NEVER HAS TO BUILD A ROW TO KNOW WHERE IT GOES',
  gain: 'that is WHAT MAKES IT FAST',
  and: 'it is ALSO WHAT MAKES IT WRONG AFTER A REORDER',
  why: 'the POSITIONS ARE STALE because THEY WERE DERIVED FROM AN ORDER THAT HAS CHANGED',
  symptoms: ['the LIST WILL SCROLL TO THE WRONG PLACE', 'or WILL SHOW A ROW WHOSE CONTENT BELONGS TO A DIFFERENT ITEM until the USER SCROLLS FAR ENOUGH for a REBUILD'],
};
const WITHOUT_ITEM_EXTENT = {
  fact: 'the SLIVER MUST BUILD ROWS TO KNOW THE EXTENT',
  so: 'it DISCOVERS THE REORDER CORRECTLY but PAYS FOR IT',
};
const WAY_OUT = 'give the REORDER to a WIDGET THAT HANDLES IT';
const WHY_THE_WIDGET_OWNS_IT = {
  reasons: ['it NEEDS TO KNOW the ITEM ORDER to DRAW THE GAP WHERE AN ITEM WAS REMOVED',
    'and it NEEDS TO KNOW THE KEYS to ANIMATE the item FROM ITS OLD POSITION',
    'and BOTH REQUIRE THE LIST rather than the TILE'],
  and: 'which is WHY ReorderableListView and ReorderableList EXIST rather than a ReorderableListTile YOU DROP INTO AN EXISTING LIST',
};

/* The key discipline. */
const KEYS = {
  rule: 'WHEN A LIST REORDERS, the ELEMENTS MUST FOLLOW THEIR ITEMS rather than THEIR POSITIONS',
  so: 'EVERY ROW NEEDS A STABLE KEY DERIVED FROM THE ITEMS IDENTITY',
  and: 'DERIVED FROM THE ITEMS IDENTITY IS THE WHOLE REQUIREMENT',
  anIndexIsNotAnIdentity: 'an INDEX KEY MEANS THAT WHEN THE LIST REORDERS, ROW THREE KEEPS ITS ELEMENT and THEREFORE ITS STATE, and WHATEVER MOVED INTO POSITION THREE INHERITS IT',
  connects: 'which is THE SAME BUG the chapter-one keys section DESCRIBED',
  and: 'which is THE REASON A LIST THAT SUPPORTS REORDERING SHOULD NEVER USE AN INDEX AS A KEY',
};

/* Three questions before building one. */
const QUESTIONS = [
  { q: 'HOW LARGE IS THE LIST, REALLY', why: 'a DRAG-AND-DROP REORDER on a LIST of FIVE THOUSAND ITEMS IS A DIFFERENT FEATURE from ONE on a LIST of TWENTY', and: 'the ANIMATION COST IS NOT LINEAR' },
  { q: 'DOES THE ORDER MEAN SOMETHING THE BACKEND CARES ABOUT',
    detail: 'a REORDERING UI THAT DOES NOT PERSIST IS A TOY',
    or: 'one that PERSISTS OPTIMISTICALLY NEEDS A CONFLICT STORY for TWO DEVICES REORDERING AT ONCE',
    reframe: 'which is A DISTRIBUTED-SYSTEMS PROBLEM WEARING A DRAG-AND-DROP COSTUME' },
  { q: 'WHAT HAPPENS TO THE SCROLL POSITION',
    detail: 'INSERTING AN ITEM ABOVE THE VIEWPORT MOVES EVERYTHING BELOW IT, and the USER WILL PERCEIVE THE LIST AS JUMPING',
    fix: 'ANCHOR THE SCROLL TO THE ITEM THE USER IS LOOKING AT',
    and: 'which THE FRAMEWORK WIDGETS DO and A HAND-ROLLED IMPLEMENTATION DOES NOT' },
];

An incorrect itemExtent does not crash. Flutter trusts it, so the rows silently overlap or leave gaps, and the bug only appears on the device with the longest title. If the height is not genuinely constant, do not set it - use itemExtentBuilder or nothing at all.

The three things that must be right for a list, and what breaks when they are not.

// 1. KEYS: without them, state attaches to the position
ReorderableListView.builder(
  itemCount: items.length,
  onReorder: (oldIndex, newIndex) {
    if (newIndex > oldIndex) newIndex -= 1;
    setState(() {
      final item = items.removeAt(oldIndex);
      items.insert(newIndex, item);
    });
  },
  proxyDecorator: (child, index, animation) =>   // the dragged item
    AnimatedBuilder(
      animation: animation,
      builder: (context, _) => Material(
        elevation: 8,
        borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(12),
        color: Theme.of(context).colorScheme.surface,
        child: child,
      ),
    ),
  itemBuilder: (context, index) {
    final item = items[index];
    return ListTile(
      key: ValueKey(item.id),      // REQUIRED for reordering to work
      title: Text(item.name),
      trailing: ReorderableDragStartListener(   // not the whole row
        index: index,
        child: const Icon(Icons.drag_handle),
      ),
    );
  },
);

// ReorderableDragStartListener vs ReorderableDelayedDragStartListener
// the first starts the drag on a normal touch: conflicts with
// vertical scrolling on touch devices
// the delayed one waits for a long press: better on mobile
// 2. ITEM EXTENT: the speed switch
ListView.builder(
  itemExtent: 80,                 // constant height: the big win
  itemCount: 10000,
  itemBuilder: (context, i) => SizedBox(height: 80, child: EntryRow(entries[i])),
)

// the wrong itemExtent breaks scrolling silently: Flutter trusts
// you, so an inaccurate value means items are skipped or overlap
ListView.builder(
  itemExtent: 80,
  itemBuilder: (context, i) => EntryRow(entries[i]),   // height is 96
  // -> rows visibly overlap or leave gaps. It does NOT crash.
)
// RULE: only set it if the height REALLY is constant.

// for a grid, the delegate already provides the geometry
GridView.builder(
  gridDelegate: const SliverGridDelegateWithFixedCrossAxisCount(
    crossAxisCount: 3,
    childAspectRatio: 0.75,       // width / height
    mainAxisSpacing: 8,
    crossAxisSpacing: 8,
  ),
  itemCount: 1000,
  itemBuilder: (context, i) => GridTile(items[i]),
)

// 3. SHRINKWRAP: the expensive default people reach for
ListView(
  shrinkWrap: true,               // builds EVERY child, always
  children: [...],                // and measures them all
)
// it is correct, and it is O(n) in time and memory regardless of
// the viewport. Never inside a scroll view. Use a sliver instead.
// THE ANIMATED LIST: inserting and removing without a glitch
// the problem: a ListView with a changing itemCount will jump,
// because the total extent changes abruptly

class AnimatedEntries extends StatelessWidget {
  const AnimatedEntries({required this.entries, super.key});

  final List<Entry> entries;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return AnimatedList(
      key: const Key('list'),
      initialItemCount: entries.length,
      itemBuilder: (context, index, animation) {
        // each item fades and slides in
        return SizeTransition(
          sizeFactor: CurvedAnimation(parent: animation, curve: Curves.easeOut),
          child: FadeTransition(
            opacity: animation,
            child: EntryCard(key: ValueKey(entries[index].id), entry: entries[index]),
          ),
        );
      },
    );
  }

  // call these to insert and remove
  static void insertAt(GlobalKey<AnimatedListState> key, int index, Entry e) {
    key.currentState!.insertItem(index, duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 250));
  }
}

// but a simpler solution, when you do not need per-item animation:
// AnimatedSwitcher or just a key change. Do not reach for
// AnimatedList unless the per-item animation is the point.

3.6 Infinite and paginated lists

Pagination, and the state machine that loading actually is

Infinite scroll is a state machine that has been described as "load more" and is actually four states with two edges each, and getting the machine right is most of the implementation. The four states are: initial, loading-initial, ready, and loading-more. The two loading states are distinct because the UI differs — the first shows a spinner in place of content, the second shows a spinner at the bottom — and because the failure handling differs: an initial load that fails has nothing to show and must offer a retry, while a pagination load that fails has content and should offer a retry at the bottom without destroying what is there. The two edges that people forget. The forward edge — scroll near the bottom triggers a fetch — is the easy one. The backward edge — the user scrolls back up and the app should not refetch — is the one that produces the bug where a user scrolls to the top, back down, and the list reloads. The trigger is a threshold, not an event, and it must be expressed in scroll position rather than in "the user reached the end", because the end is not observable until the content is built. In practice that means a scroll listener that compares the maximum scroll extent against the current offset and triggers at some fraction below it — and the fraction is a design decision, because too small means the last page loads visibly and too large means the user reaches a spinner before it arrives. Then the four correctness requirements, each of which is a bug if missed. Guard the trigger. A scroll listener fires many times during a fling, so without an in-flight flag a single flick dispatches five requests and appends five pages. Handle a page that arrives out of order. If a slow second page and a fast third page are both in flight, appending by completion appends them in the wrong order; the fix is to track the requested page index and insert by index, or to serialise the requests. Handle a page that arrives after the user has changed the query. A search that has been superseded must not append its results to the new result set, and the check is a request token compared against the current one. And handle the end. When a page returns fewer items than the page size — or an empty page — the list has reached the end and the trigger must stop, and if it does not, the app will request pages forever against an API that returns nothing, which is both a waste and a way to get rate-limited.

Then the three alternatives worth knowing, because for most data the right answer is not infinite scroll. Pagination with explicit controls. A "load more" button or a numbered pager is better whenever the user wants to find something rather than browse, and it is dramatically better for accessibility and for a list whose length the user should know — an infinite list gives no way to say "there are four thousand results". "Load more" with a known total, which is the compromise most search interfaces use: the user sees the count and can jump. And windowing over a known-length list, which is the same sliver mechanism with no fetching: if the data is already in memory, a sliver list of a hundred thousand items is fast and needs no state machine at all. Then the two things that make pagination feel bad regardless of implementation, and they are worth naming because they are not code problems. Scroll position is lost when the list is rebuilt, so appending a page must preserve the offset or the content jumps under the user's thumb — which on a list of images looks like the images reloading. And the last page is often short, so a fixed-height placeholder row either leaves a gap or requires a different loading indicator; the usual answer is a row whose height is realistic and whose content is a spinner, and accepting that it is wrong for short pages.

/* Four states, two edges. */
const STATES = [
  { s: 'INITIAL' },
  { s: 'LOADING-INITIAL', differs: ['the UI - it SHOWS A SPINNER IN PLACE OF CONTENT'],
    and: ['the FAILURE HANDLING - an INITIAL LOAD THAT FAILS has NOTHING TO SHOW and MUST OFFER A RETRY, where a PAGINATION LOAD THAT FAILS HAS CONTENT and SHOULD OFFER A RETRY AT THE BOTTOM without DESTROYING WHAT IS THERE'] },
  { s: 'READY' },
  { s: 'LOADING-MORE' },
];
const EDGES = [
  { e: 'FORWARD', is: 'the EASY ONE' },
  { e: 'BACKWARD', rule: 'the USER SCROLLS BACK UP and the APP SHOULD NOT REFETCH',
    bug: 'which produces THE BUG WHERE A USER SCROLLS TO THE TOP, BACK DOWN, and THE LIST RELOADS' },
];

  why: 'it MUST BE EXPRESSED IN SCROLL POSITION rather than in the user reached the end, BECAUSE THE END IS NOT OBSERVABLE UNTIL THE CONTENT IS BUILT',
  inPractice: 'a SCROLL LISTENER THAT COMPARES the MAXIMUM SCROLL EXTENT against the CURRENT OFFSET and TRIGGERS AT SOME FRACTION BELOW IT',
  theFraction: 'a DESIGN DECISION',

/* Four correctness requirements. */
const REQUIREMENTS = [
  { r: 'GUARD THE TRIGGER',
    bug: 'a SCROLL LISTENER FIRES MANY TIMES DURING A FLING, so WITHOUT AN IN-FLIGHT FLAG a SINGLE FLICK DISPATCHES FIVE REQUESTS and APPENDS FIVE PAGES' },

/* Three alternatives. */

Loading more, the footer trigger, and the states that matter.

// THE INFINITE SCROLL PATTERN, done properly
class EntryList extends StatefulWidget {
  const EntryList({super.key});
  @override
  State<EntryList> createState() => _EntryListState();
}

class _EntryListState extends State<EntryList> {
  final _controller = ScrollController();
  final _entries = <Entry>[];
  int _page = 0;
  bool _loading = false;
  bool _hasMore = true;
  Object? _error;

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _controller.addListener(_onScroll);
    _loadMore();
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _controller
      ..removeListener(_onScroll)
      ..dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  // trigger when the user is within 500px of the end
  void _onScroll() {
    if (!_controller.hasClients || _loading || !_hasMore) return;
    final position = _controller.position;
    if (position.pixels >= position.maxScrollExtent - 500) {
      _loadMore();
    }
  }

  Future<void> _loadMore() async {
    if (_loading) return;
    setState(() {
      _loading = true;
      _error = null;
    });

    try {
      final page = await api.entries(page: _page, limit: 30);
      if (!mounted) return;
      setState(() {
        _entries.addAll(page.items);
        _page++;
        _hasMore = page.items.length == 30;
        _loading = false;
      });
    } catch (e) {
      if (!mounted) return;
      setState(() {
        _error = e;
        _loading = false;
      });
    }
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return RefreshIndicator(
      onRefresh: () async {
        setState(() {
          _entries.clear();
          _page = 0;
          _hasMore = true;
        });
        await _loadMore();
      },
      child: CustomScrollView(
        controller: _controller,
        physics: const AlwaysScrollableScrollPhysics(),   // needed for
        slivers: [                                        // RefreshIndicator
          if (_error != null)
            SliverFillRemaining(
              hasScrollBody: false,
              child: ErrorView(
                error: _error!,
                onRetry: _loadMore,
              ),
            )
          else if (_entries.isEmpty && !_loading)
            const SliverFillRemaining(
              hasScrollBody: false,
              child: EmptyView(message: 'No notes yet'),
            )
          else ...[
            SliverList.builder(
              itemCount: _entries.length,
              itemBuilder: (context, i) => EntryCard(
                key: ValueKey(_entries[i].id),
                entry: _entries[i],
              ),
            ),
            // the footer: loading, or the retry button
            SliverToBoxAdapter(
              child: _loading
                  ? const Padding(
                      padding: EdgeInsets.all(24),
                      child: Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator()),
                    )
                  : _error != null
                      ? Padding(
                          padding: const EdgeInsets.all(24),
                          child: TextButton.icon(
                            onPressed: _loadMore,
                            icon: const Icon(Icons.refresh),
                            label: const Text('Tap to retry'),
                          ),
                        )
                      : const SizedBox(height: 24),
            ),
          ],
        ],
      ),
    );
  }
}
// THE THREE STATES EVERY LIST NEEDS, and the common bug of
// having only one
//
// 1. LOADING: the first page. A skeleton, not a spinner over a
//    blank screen. It tells the user what is coming.
// 2. EMPTY: no data at all. Different from loading, and it needs
//    a call to action.
// 3. ERROR: the request failed. Needs a retry, and a message
//    that says what to do.
// 4. PARTIAL: some data loaded, then a failure. The list is
//    usable; the error is at the bottom. This is the state most
//    implementations forget.

class SkeletonList extends StatelessWidget {
  const SkeletonList({required this.count, super.key});
  final int count;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // a shimmer effect
    return ListView.builder(
      physics: const NeverScrollableScrollPhysics(),
      itemCount: count,
      itemBuilder: (context, i) => const SkeletonRow(),
    );
  }
}

class SkeletonRow extends StatefulWidget {
  const SkeletonRow({super.key});
  @override
  State<SkeletonRow> createState() => _SkeletonRowState();
}

class _SkeletonRowState extends State<SkeletonRow>
    with SingleTickerProviderStateMixin {
  late final AnimationController _controller = AnimationController(
    vsync: this,
    duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 1200),
  )..repeat(reverse: true);

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _controller.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return AnimatedBuilder(
      animation: _controller,
      builder: (context, _) {
        return Container(
          height: 72,
          margin: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 16, vertical: 6),
          decoration: BoxDecoration(
            color: Color.lerp(
              Theme.of(context).colorScheme.surfaceContainerHighest,
              Theme.of(context).colorScheme.surfaceContainerLow,
              _controller.value,
            ),
            borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(12),
          ),
        );
      },
    );
  }
}

3.7 Images in a list

Images in a list, and the four things that actually go wrong

A list of images fails in four specific ways and each has a mechanism, so each has a fix that is different from the other three. Decoding at the wrong resolution is the most common and the most invisible. An image is decoded to a bitmap at the size it will be painted; a list row painting a thumbnail that displays a full-resolution photograph has caused the framework to decode a twelve-megapixel image and hold it in memory as forty-eight megabytes of pixels, of which it will use perhaps two thousand. The fix is cacheWidth and cacheHeight on the image widget, which tell the decoder what the painted size will be so it decodes only that; the trap is that they are in pixels and must account for the device pixel ratio, so a thumbnail painted at one hundred logical pixels needs a cacheWidth of three hundred on a three-times device. Cache eviction produces a flash. The image cache holds a fixed number of bytes, evicts when full, and evicts the least recently used; a list scrolled past a thousand rows comes back and finds its images evicted, so they decode again and appear blank for a frame. The fixes are to reduce the decoded size so more fits, and to accept the eviction for a long list. No size means no reservation means layout shift, which the metrics section of the performance chapter covers and which in a list is worse because every row shifts every other row. An image with explicit width and height, or inside an AspectRatio, reserves its space before it loads. And fade-in animations hide the flash and make it worse. An AnimatedOpacity or a fade-in image widget makes a cache miss visible as a fade rather than an instant appearance, which feels smoother and is measurably slower and looks worse on a fast scroll where dozens of images are fading at once.

Then the four things that are worth knowing and are not obvious. precacheImage and ImageProvider.resolve let you warm the cache deliberately — for the images you know the user is about to see, such as the first screen after a navigation or the next page of an infinite list, warming the first two pages removes the load-in you would otherwise see on arrival. The cache has two parts with different policies. Live images are held weakly and evicted under pressure; pending images are held strongly until they resolve; and the memory cache and the disk cache are separate, with the disk cache persisting across runs, so a warm disk cache plus a cold memory cache still costs a decode. Format selection is a build-time decision with a runtime effect. A WebP or AVIF asset decodes to fewer bytes and usually less time; the cost is that it is not supported everywhere and that it is more expensive to produce. And the framework's own diagnostics answer the question this section poses. debugDumpImageCache prints the live and pending sets with their sizes and keys, and an image cache report widget can show the hit rate over time; a list whose images flash on scroll back has a cache problem and the report says so in one line, which is a great deal better than the usual approach of guessing.

/* Four ways a list of images fails. */
const FAILURES = [
  { f: 'DECODING AT THE WRONG RESOLUTION', common: true, invisible: true,
    detail: 'an IMAGE IS DECODED TO A BITMAP AT THE SIZE IT WILL BE PAINTED',
    instance: 'a LIST ROW PAINTING A THUMBNAIL that DISPLAYS A FULL-RESOLUTION PHOTOGRAPH HAS CAUSED the framework TO DECODE A TWELVE-MEGAPIXEL IMAGE and HOLD IT IN MEMORY as FORTY-EIGHT MEGABYTES of pixels, OF WHICH IT WILL USE PERHAPS TWO THOUSAND',
    fix: 'cacheWidth and cacheHeight ON THE IMAGE WIDGET, WHICH TELL THE DECODER WHAT THE PAINTED SIZE WILL BE so IT DECODES ONLY THAT',
    trap: 'they ARE IN PIXELS and MUST ACCOUNT FOR THE DEVICE PIXEL RATIO, so a THUMBNAIL PAINTED AT ONE HUNDRED LOGICAL PIXELS NEEDS a cacheWidth OF THREE HUNDRED on a THREE-TIMES DEVICE' },
  { f: 'CACHE EVICTION PRODUCES A FLASH',
    mechanism: 'the IMAGE CACHE holds a FIXED NUMBER OF BYTES, EVICTS WHEN FULL, and EVICTS the LEAST RECENTLY USED',
    instance: 'a LIST SCROLLED PAST A THOUSAND ROWS COMES BACK and FINDS ITS IMAGES EVICTED, so THEY DECODE AGAIN and APPEAR BLANK FOR A FRAME',
    fixes: ['REDUCE THE DECODED SIZE so MORE FITS', 'and ACCEPT THE EVICTION for a LONG LIST'] },
  { f: 'NO SIZE MEANS NO RESERVATION MEANS LAYOUT SHIFT',
    worse: 'which in a LIST IS WORSE BECAUSE EVERY ROW SHIFTS EVERY OTHER ROW',
    fix: 'an IMAGE WITH EXPLICIT WIDTH and HEIGHT, or INSIDE an AspectRatio, RESERVES ITS SPACE BEFORE IT LOADS' },
  { f: 'FADE-IN ANIMATIONS HIDE THE FLASH and MAKE IT WORSE',
    detail: 'an AnimatedOpacity or a FADE-IN IMAGE WIDGET MAKES A CACHE MISS VISIBLE AS A FADE rather than an INSTANT APPEARANCE',
    and: 'which FEELS SMOOTHER and is MEASURABLY SLOWER and LOOKS WORSE ON A FAST SCROLL where DOZENS OF IMAGES ARE FADING AT ONCE' },

/* Four things worth knowing. */
const WORTH_KNOWING = [
  { t: 'precacheImage and ImageProvider.resolve LET YOU WARM THE CACHE DELIBERATELY',

    facts: ['LIVE IMAGES are HELD WEAKLY and EVICTED UNDER PRESSURE', 'PENDING IMAGES are HELD STRONGLY UNTIL THEY RESOLVE',
      'and the MEMORY CACHE and the DISK CACHE are SEPARATE, with the DISK CACHE PERSISTING ACROSS RUNS'],
    consequence: 'so a WARM DISK CACHE plus a COLD MEMORY CACHE STILL COSTS A DECODE' },

    cost: 'it is NOT SUPPORTED EVERYWHERE and it is MORE EXPENSIVE TO PRODUCE' },

      'an IMAGE CACHE REPORT WIDGET - SHOWS the HIT RATE OVER TIME'],

The three image rules that make a list scroll smoothly.

// THE THREE RULES
// 1. CACHE: never build the same image twice
// 2. SIZE: decode at the size you display, not the size you have
// 3. RESERVE: give the box a fixed size so nothing reflows

// RULE 1 AND 2: use a package that does both
Image.network(
  entry.imageUrl,
  // 2. request exactly what you display
  cacheWidth: (MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).width * devicePixelRatio).round(),
  // 1. in-memory cache, so scrolling back is instant
  frameBuilder: (context, child, frame, wasSyncLoaded) {
    if (wasSyncLoaded || frame != null) {
      return child;
    }
    return const SkeletonBox();      // a placeholder of the RIGHT size
  },
  errorBuilder: (context, error, stack) => const ErrorBox(),
)

// cached_network_image is simpler and better for most cases
CachedNetworkImage(
  imageUrl: entry.imageUrl,
  maxWidthDiskCache: 800,
  maxHeightDiskCache: 800,
  memCacheWidth: 400,                 // decode at this width
  placeholder: (_, __) => const SkeletonBox(),
  errorWidget: (_, __, ___) => const ErrorBox(),
)

// for local assets
Image.asset(
  'assets/photo.jpg',
  cacheWidth: 400,                    // decode at 400px
  fit: BoxFit.cover,
  gaplessPlayback: true,              // no flash when it re-decodes
)

// RULE 3: a fixed size for the container
SizedBox(
  width: 64,
  height: 64,
  child: ClipRRect(
    borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(8),
    child: Image.network(url, fit: BoxFit.cover),
  ),
)
// WITHOUT the SizedBox, the image is its natural size, and when
// it loads, everything below it moves
// THE DECODE COST, and why it matters
// a 4000x3000 photo decodes to 4000*3000*4 = 48MB of RAM
// a 64x64 avatar decodes to 16KB
// a list of 20 full-resolution photos is 960MB: the OS kills
// your app
//
// THE FLOW, and where to intervene
//   network bytes -> disk cache -> decode to a bitmap ->
//   upload to the GPU -> paint
//                        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
//                        this is the expensive step, and
//                        cacheWidth/cacheHeight control it
//
// MEASURE IT: DevTools -> Memory, or the image cache report
//   debugDumpImageCache()

3.8 Making a list fast

Making a list fast, in the order to try things

The performance advice for long lists is usually a list of techniques, and a list of techniques is less useful than an order, because most lists are slow for one reason and applying the wrong technique does nothing measurable. So: the order. First, is the list building more than it needs to? That is the cache extent question, and it is the first thing to check because a list with a large cache extent builds several times as many children as are visible and every one of them costs a build, a layout and a render object. If the profile shows build time dominating, this is the cause and shrinking the cache extent is the fix — accepting that flicks will show blank space, which is a visible trade rather than a free win. Second, is the sliver computing extents by building rows? That is the itemExtent question, and it is the second because it is usually the largest single win on a list with variable-height content: the sliver goes from building rows to discover their heights to knowing the geometry from arithmetic. Third, is anything in a row rebuilding that does not need to? A row that reads an inherited widget and a state object will rebuild when either changes, and a list of a thousand rows means a thousand rebuilds per state change; extracting the changing part into a small child widget, or using a selector, converts a thousand rebuilds into one plus a thousand cheap ones. Fourth, is anything expensive happening per item that could happen once? A date format, a colour computation from a string, a TextStyle allocation, a BoxDecoration allocation inside a builder is work repeated for every row on every build, and hoisting it out of the builder or memoising it is a straightforward win that is invisible in the source and visible in the profile. Then the two things that are not on the list, because they are almost always the wrong answer. Shrinking the widget tree per row is not worth it unless a row genuinely has thirty widgets; below that the per-widget cost is smaller than the cost of the indirection to reduce it. And converting a list to a grid does not make it faster — a grid is a different sliver, not a faster list, and the sliver's cost model is unchanged. Then the measurement discipline, which the chapter's own warning is about. Profile in profile mode with a real device and a realistic data volume, because a profile of a list of fifty rows on a desktop with a debug build tells you nothing about a list of five thousand rows on a mid-range phone in release. And look at build counts rather than frame times — a frame-time graph says a frame was slow and a build-count view says which widget was responsible, and the second is the actionable one.

/* The order to try things. */
const ORDER = [
  { n: 1, q: 'IS THE LIST BUILDING MORE THAN IT NEEDS', cause: 'the CACHE EXTENT question',
    why: 'a LIST WITH A LARGE CACHE EXTENT BUILDS SEVERAL TIMES AS MANY CHILDREN as ARE VISIBLE and EVERY ONE OF THEM COSTS A BUILD, A LAYOUT and a RENDER OBJECT',
    ifProfileShows: 'BUILD TIME DOMINATING',
    fix: 'SHRINKING THE CACHE EXTENT',
    trade: 'ACCEPTING that FLICKS WILL SHOW BLANK SPACE, which is A VISIBLE TRADE rather than A FREE WIN' },
  { n: 2, q: 'IS THE SLIVER COMPUTING EXTENTS BY BUILDING ROWS', cause: 'the itemExtent question',
    whySecond: 'it is USUALLY THE LARGEST SINGLE WIN on a LIST WITH VARIABLE-HEIGHT CONTENT',
    gain: 'the SLIVER GOES FROM BUILDING ROWS TO DISCOVER THEIR HEIGHTS to KNOWING THE GEOMETRY FROM ARITHMETIC' },
  { n: 3, q: 'IS ANYTHING IN A ROW REBUILDING THAT DOES NOT NEED TO',
    detail: 'a ROW THAT READS AN INHERITED WIDGET and a STATE OBJECT WILL REBUILD WHEN EITHER CHANGES, and a LIST OF A THOUSAND ROWS MEANS A THOUSAND REBUILDS PER STATE CHANGE',
    fix: ['EXTRACT the CHANGING PART into a SMALL CHILD WIDGET', 'or USE A SELECTOR'],
    gain: 'CONVERTS a THOUSAND REBUILDS into ONE PLUS A THOUSAND CHEAP ONES' },
  { n: 4, q: 'IS ANYTHING EXPENSIVE HAPPENING PER ITEM that COULD HAPPEN ONCE',
    instances: ['a DATE FORMAT', 'a COLOUR COMPUTATION from a string', 'a TextStyle ALLOCATION', 'a BoxDecoration ALLOCATION INSIDE A BUILDER'],
    why: 'it is WORK REPEATED FOR EVERY ROW ON EVERY BUILD',
    fix: 'HOISTING IT OUT of the BUILDER or MEMOISING IT',
    note: 'a STRAIGHTFORWARD WIN that is INVISIBLE IN THE SOURCE and VISIBLE IN THE PROFILE' },
];

/* Two things that are not on the list. */
const NOT = [
  { t: 'SHRINKING THE WIDGET TREE PER ROW', whenWorthIt: 'a ROW GENUINELY HAS THIRTY WIDGETS',
    whyNot: 'BELOW THAT the PER-WIDGET COST is SMALLER than the COST OF THE INDIRECTION TO REDUCE IT' },
  { t: 'CONVERTING A LIST TO A GRID DOES NOT MAKE IT FASTER',
    why: 'a GRID IS A DIFFERENT SLIVER, not a FASTER LIST, and the SLIVERS COST MODEL IS UNCHANGED' },
];

/* The measurement discipline. */
const MEASURE = [
  { m: 'PROFILE IN PROFILE MODE WITH A REAL DEVICE and a REALISTIC DATA VOLUME',
    why: 'a PROFILE of a LIST of FIFTY ROWS on a DESKTOP WITH A DEBUG BUILD TELLS YOU NOTHING about a LIST of FIVE THOUSAND ROWS on a MID-RANGE PHONE IN RELEASE' },
  { m: 'LOOK AT BUILD COUNTS rather than FRAME TIMES',
    why: 'a FRAME-TIME GRAPH SAYS A FRAME WAS SLOW and a BUILD-COUNT VIEW SAYS WHICH WIDGET WAS RESPONSIBLE',
    and: 'the SECOND IS THE ACTIONABLE ONE' },
];

Measured in order of how often they are the answer: a missing itemExtent, a missing const, a missing ValueKey, a MediaQuery.of in a large build method, and a provider watch per row. The last three are architecture problems and the first two are typos.

An ordered checklist, applied to a list that stutters.

// THE CHECKLIST, in the order that fixes the most per unit of work

// 1. const every row that can be const
//    this is free and it skips the rebuild entirely
SliverList.builder(
  itemBuilder: (context, i) => const DividerRow(),   // if the data is
)                                                    // not needed

// 2. itemExtent, if the height is constant
SliverFixedExtentList.builder(
  itemExtent: 80,
  itemCount: 10000,
  itemBuilder: (context, i) => SizedBox(height: 80, child: EntryRow(entries[i])),
)

// 3. ValueKey on every row
//    without it, a data change rebuilds and remounts everything

// 4. cacheWidth on every image

// 5. avoid build() work: no MediaQuery, no Theme lookups
//    in a deep subtree, pass the values down as parameters
//    (Theme.of(context) is a lookup, and there are 10,000 of them)

// 6. avoid Provider/Riverpod watches in every row
//    watch the LIST, not each item
//    BAD: 1000 rows each watching an entry provider
//    GOOD: one provider for the list, rows read their item
final entriesProvider = Provider<List<Entry>>((ref) => ref.watch(repo).entries);
// the row takes an Entry parameter, and does no watching

// 7. separate the "is this item visible" logic from the data
//    the row should be dumb: take data, render it

// 8. RepaintBoundary where rows repaint independently
ListView.builder(
  itemBuilder: (context, i) => RepaintBoundary(
    key: ValueKey('boundary-$i'),
    child: EntryRow(entries[i]),
  ),
)
// a RepaintBoundary costs memory, so add it where it helps:
// an animating row, a video, a chart, not on every row of a
// static list
// 9. MEASURE, with the DevTools Performance panel
//    flutter run --profile
//    record while you scroll
//
//    what to look for:
//    - a build count that scales with scroll position instead of
//      staying flat: something is rebuilding the whole list
//    - raster time high: a shader, a blur, an image
//    - long frames: any main-thread work over 16ms
//
// 10. THE PROFILE-MODE TRUTH
//     debug mode: build is ~10x slower, and a janky debug build
//     tells you very little. Everything above only works in
//     profile or release.

3.9 The list antipatterns

The six things that make a list slow, and what each costs.

// 1. shrinkWrap
ListView(shrinkWrap: true, children: [...])
// BUILDS EVERYTHING, ALWAYS. O(n) time and memory, no matter how
// far you scroll. Use a sliver.

// 2. Column of children
Column(children: list.map((e) => EntryRow(e)).toList())
// BUILDS EVERYTHING and defeats any virtualisation. Use ListView.

// 3. Column inside a SingleChildScrollView
SingleChildScrollView(
  child: Column(children: list.map(...).toList()),
)
// same problem. Use CustomScrollView with slivers.

// 4. Nested scroll views
ListView(
  children: [ListView(children: [...])],   // both scroll: broken
)
// use one scroll view with slivers

// 5. A provider watch per row
for (final e in entries) ProviderWidget(provider: entryProvider(e.id), ...)
// 1000 subscriptions, 1000 rebuild triggers. Watch the list once.

// 6. setState on the screen for a row's state
class _ListState extends State<List> {
  String? _selectedId;
  // tapping a row calls setState -> the WHOLE list rebuilds
}
// move the selection into a ValueNotifier, or a per-row stateful
// widget, or a provider scoped to the row

The antipatterns, and what each one is really a symptom of

Six antipatterns, and the useful thing about them is that each is a symptom of a decision made elsewhere rather than a mistake about slivers. Shrinking every widget and calling the sliver. A codebase that replaces ListView with CustomScrollView and several tiny slivers "for performance" has usually not measured anything: the sliver's advantage is not building off-screen children, which ListView already does, so the change costs the complexity and gains nothing. The symptom is a belief that slivers are an optimisation rather than a composition mechanism. shrinkWrap: true on a long list. This is the one that produces the severe case, and the mechanism is worth being precise about: shrink-wrap tells the sliver to build all its children so it can measure the total extent, which is precisely the thing a sliver exists to avoid, so a shrink-wrapped list of ten thousand rows builds ten thousand rows, allocates ten thousand render objects, and can take seconds to appear. The symptom is usually "we had to rewrite it as a Column with a fixed height". Putting an IntrinsicHeight around a sliver. Intrinsic sizing lays the subtree out twice, and a sliver's subtree is the list, so this is the double-layout problem applied to the largest possible subtree; the combination is slow in a way that is hard to attribute because the code looks reasonable. Not supplying itemExtent on a fixed-height row. Not a bug, an omission, and the cost is that the sliver builds a row to discover a height it could have been told, so the first paint is delayed and the scroll extent is estimated rather than known. Rebuilding the list from scratch on every filter change. A search screen that replaces the delegate's list rather than filtering in place produces a new sliver configuration, loses scroll position, and rebuilds every visible row; the symptom is a search box that feels like a page load. And mixing a sliver list with a Column in the same CustomScrollView without a bounded height, which is the unbounded-axis problem from the layout chapter arriving in a new place — a sliver that is not a sliver, such as a SliverToBoxAdapter containing a ListView, needs the list to be given a bounded height from somewhere or it will throw.

/* Six antipatterns, each a symptom of a decision made elsewhere. */
const ANTI_PATTERNS = [
  { a: 'SHRINKING EVERY WIDGET and CALLING THE SLIVER',
    detail: 'a CODEBASE THAT REPLACES ListView with CustomScrollView and SEVERAL TINY SLIVERS for performance',
    hasNotMeasured: true,
    whyItDoesNothing: 'the SLIVERS ADVANTAGE is NOT BUILDING OFF-SCREEN CHILDREN, which ListView ALREADY DOES',
    so: 'the CHANGE COSTS THE COMPLEXITY and GAINS NOTHING',
    symptom: 'a BELIEF THAT SLIVERS ARE AN OPTIMISATION rather than A COMPOSITION MECHANISM' },
  { a: 'shrinkWrap: true ON A LONG LIST',
    mechanism: 'shrink-wrap TELLS THE SLIVER TO BUILD ALL ITS CHILDREN so IT CAN MEASURE THE TOTAL EXTENT',
    andThatIs: 'PRECISELY THE THING A SLIVER EXISTS TO AVOID',
    consequence: 'a SHRINK-WRAPPED LIST of TEN THOUSAND ROWS BUILDS TEN THOUSAND ROWS, ALLOCATES TEN THOUSAND RENDER OBJECTS, and CAN TAKE SECONDS TO APPEAR',
    symptom: 'usually we had to REWRITE IT AS A Column WITH A FIXED HEIGHT' },
  { a: 'PUTTING AN IntrinsicHeight AROUND A SLIVER',
    detail: 'INTRINSIC SIZING LAYS THE SUBTREE OUT TWICE, and a SLIVERS SUBTREE IS THE LIST',
    so: 'this is THE DOUBLE-LAYOUT PROBLEM APPLIED TO THE LARGEST POSSIBLE SUBTREE',
    whyHard: 'the COMBINATION IS SLOW IN A WAY THAT IS HARD TO ATTRIBUTE because the CODE LOOKS REASONABLE' },
  { a: 'NOT SUPPLYING itemExtent ON A FIXED-HEIGHT ROW',
    notABug: 'a N O T A B U G, A N O M I S S I O N',
    cost: 'the SLIVER BUILDS A ROW TO DISCOVER A HEIGHT IT COULD HAVE BEEN TOLD',
    so: ['the FIRST PAINT IS DELAYED', 'the SCROLL EXTENT is ESTIMATED rather than KNOWN'] },
  { a: 'REBUILDING THE LIST FROM SCRATCH ON EVERY FILTER CHANGE',
    detail: 'a SEARCH SCREEN THAT REPLACES THE DELEGATES LIST rather than FILTERING IN PLACE PRODUCES A NEW SLIVER CONFIGURATION, LOSES SCROLL POSITION, and REBUILDS EVERY VISIBLE ROW',

  { a: 'MIXING A SLIVER LIST WITH A Column IN THE SAME CustomScrollView WITHOUT A BOUNDED HEIGHT',

    detail: 'a SLIVER THAT IS NOT A SLIVER - such as a SliverToBoxAdapter CONTAINING A ListView - NEEDS THE LIST TO BE GIVEN A BOUNDED HEIGHT FROM SOMEWHERE or it WILL THROW' },
];

4 · Painting, CustomPainter and Shaders

4.1 The rendering pipeline4.2 CustomPainter4.3 Canvas drawing4.4 Gradients, shadows and effects4.5 Fragment shaders4.6 Impeller and the backends4.7 Images: decode, cache, paint4.8 Repainting and RepaintBoundary

How Flutter turns your widgets into pixels, and how to draw things the widget set does not provide.

4.1 The rendering pipeline

The four phases, and which one your problem is in

The pipeline has four stages and the single most useful thing about it is that each stage has its own thread, so "the app is slow" resolves into one of four different problems with four different fixes. Rasterisation is the first phase: turning your description into pixels. The framework walks the layer tree and converts each layer into a texture — actually issuing the drawing commands to the graphics processor. If a layer's content changes, that layer is re-rastered. Paint is the second: recording the drawing commands. The framework walks the render objects that need repainting and records what they would draw into a display list, without drawing anything. Paint is done on a worker thread off the platform thread. Layout is the third: computing geometry. Top-down constraints then bottom-up sizes, as the layout chapter described, and it runs on the platform thread because it touches the widget tree. And composition is the fourth: assembling the layers. The compositor takes the rasterised textures and puts them on screen with their transforms, opacities and clips, and it runs on its own thread. Then the consequences, and they are the whole reason the pipeline is worth knowing. Because rasterisation is the expensive phase, an animation that changes only a transform is nearly free and an animation that changes pixels is expensive — moving a layer's offset does not require re-rastering it, only re-compositing, which is why the framework promotes a subtree to its own layer when it is animated. Because paint is off-thread, a paint-heavy frame does not block interaction, which is why a janky-looking animation can still respond to taps and why the frame chart shows a long raster row while the interaction stays responsive. Because layout is on the platform thread, a layout-heavy frame does block everything, which is why an expensive build or a wide intrinsic measure is felt immediately as input lag. And because the phases are independent, a single frame can be limited by any one of them, which is why the profile panel shows four separate rows and why you must read the panel before optimising: a fix aimed at the wrong phase does nothing and can make things worse by adding work to an already-saturated thread.

/* Four phases, four threads, four problems. */
const PHASES = [
  { n: 1, name: 'RASTERISATION', thread: 'the GRAPHICS PROCESSOR', does: 'TURNING YOUR DESCRIPTION INTO PIXELS',
    action: 'the framework WALKS the LAYER TREE and CONVERTS EACH LAYER INTO A TEXTURE - actually ISSUING THE DRAWING COMMANDS',
    rule: 'if a LAYERS CONTENT CHANGES, that LAYER IS RE-RASTERED', expensive: true },
  { n: 2, name: 'PAINT', thread: 'a WORKER THREAD, off the platform thread',
    does: 'RECORDING THE DRAWING COMMANDS',
    action: 'the framework WALKS the RENDER OBJECTS THAT NEED REPAINTING and RECORDS WHAT THEY WOULD DRAW into a DISPLAY LIST, WITHOUT DRAWING ANYTHING' },
  { n: 3, name: 'LAYOUT', thread: 'THE PLATFORM THREAD', does: 'COMPUTING GEOMETRY',
    action: 'TOP-DOWN CONSTRAINTS THEN BOTTOM-UP SIZES',
    whyThatThread: 'because it TOUCHES THE WIDGET TREE' },
  { n: 4, name: 'COMPOSITION', thread: 'ITS OWN THREAD', does: 'ASSEMBLING THE LAYERS',
    action: 'the compositor TAKES the RASTERISED TEXTURES and PUTS THEM ON SCREEN with their TRANSFORMS, OPACITIES and CLIPS' },
];

/* The consequences - why it is worth knowing. */
const CONSEQUENCES = [
  { because: 'RASTERISATION IS THE EXPENSIVE PHASE',
    then: 'an ANIMATION THAT CHANGES ONLY A TRANSFORM IS NEARLY FREE and an ANIMATION THAT CHANGES PIXELS IS EXPENSIVE',
    mechanism: 'MOVING A LAYERS OFFSET DOES NOT REQUIRE RE-RASTERING IT, only RE-COMPOSITING',
    and: 'which is WHY the framework PROMOTES A SUBTREE TO ITS OWN LAYER when it IS ANIMATED' },
  { because: 'PAINT IS OFF-THREAD',
    then: 'a PAINT-HEAVY FRAME DOES NOT BLOCK INTERACTION',
    symptom: 'which is WHY a JANKY-LOOKING ANIMATION CAN STILL RESPOND TO TAPS',
    and: 'WHY THE FRAME CHART SHOWS A LONG RASTER ROW while the INTERACTION STAYS RESPONSIVE' },
  { because: 'LAYOUT IS ON THE PLATFORM THREAD',
    then: 'a LAYOUT-HEAVY FRAME DOES BLOCK EVERYTHING',
    symptom: 'which is WHY an EXPENSIVE BUILD or a WIDE INTRINSIC MEASURE IS FELT IMMEDIATELY as INPUT LAG' },
  { because: 'THE PHASES ARE INDEPENDENT',
    then: 'a SINGLE FRAME CAN BE LIMITED BY ANY ONE OF THEM',
    practice: 'which is WHY the PROFILE PANEL SHOWS FOUR SEPARATE ROWS and WHY YOU MUST READ THE PANEL BEFORE OPTIMISING',
    warning: 'a FIX AIMED AT THE WRONG PHASE DOES NOTHING and CAN MAKE THINGS WORSE by ADDING WORK to an ALREADY-SATURATED THREAD' },
];

Reading the frame chart correctly is the single most useful skill in this chapter. The UI thread row and the RASTER row tell you entirely different stories, and the fix for one is useless for the other. A red bar in the UI row means a rebuild, a layout or a paint; a red bar in the RASTER row means a blur, an image or a shader.

The four stages, and which one your performance problem is in.

// THE FOUR STAGES, in order, once per frame
//
// 1. BUILD      (the UI thread, Dart)
//    widget.build() -> widget tree
//    how many widgets, and how expensive each build is
//
// 2. LAYOUT     (the UI thread, Dart)
//    RenderObject.performLayout(), top-down with constraints
//    sizes and positions
//
// 3. PAINT      (the UI thread, Dart, recorded)
//    RenderObject.paint() -> a DISPLAY LIST of drawing commands
//    the commands are RECORDED here, not executed
//    this is why paint is cheap to repeat: the list is cached
//
// 4. RASTER / COMPOSITE  (the RASTER thread, NOT the UI thread)
//    the display list is executed into pixels
//    then the layers are composited onto the screen
//
// THE KEY FACT: raster is on a SEPARATE thread from build,
// layout and paint. So raster work does not block your Dart, and
// Dart work does not block raster - they can overlap.
//
// WHICH STAGE IS YOUR PROBLEM IN
//   build count high      -> too many rebuilds (chapter 1)
//   layout time high      -> constraints and flex (chapter 2)
//   paint time high       -> complex custom painting, many layers
//   raster time high      -> blurs, shaders, large images
//
// DevTools -> Performance shows all four as separate rows in
// the frame chart. Read it before you optimise.

4.2 CustomPainter

CustomPainter, and how to make it cheap

CustomPainter is the right tool when you need to draw something no combination of the standard widgets draws, and it is the wrong tool whenever the thing you are drawing could have been a composition — which is more often than people expect. A painter draws in the coordinate space of the box it is painting into, with the origin at its top-left and the size given to paint as the canvas size, so a painter is always relative rather than absolute and must scale to whatever box it is given; a painter that assumes a fixed size works on one screen and clips on another. Two methods decide when work happens. shouldRepaint is asked whether a new painter instance should repaint, and it receives the old painter, so the correct implementation compares the fields that affect the drawing — and returning true unconditionally makes every painter repaint on every frame, which is the single most common reason a custom-painted animation drops frames on a device and not on the developer's machine. hitTest is asked whether a point is inside, and returning the default — "not me" — is correct for a painter that is decorative; a painter that must respond to touches must override it, and the subtlety is that it receives coordinates relative to the painter and must convert them if the painter has a transform. Then the four ways to make it cheap, in the order that pays. Hoist everything constant out of paint. A Paint object, a Path, a gradient — created inside paint, they are allocated on every frame and, for a Path, recomputed from scratch, which for a path of a few hundred points is the whole cost. Cache the path in the painter or in the state and rebuild it only when the input changes. Draw in as few operations as possible, because each drawPath, drawCircle and drawImage is a separate call and a separate potential state change; a chart drawn as one path is one operation and a chart drawn as three hundred circles is three hundred. And avoid saveLayer unless you need it, because it allocates an intermediate buffer of the size of the box and composites it, which on a full-screen box is a large allocation per frame. And then the two structural facts, which are the ones that decide whether a painter is viable at all. A painter inside a scrolling list is repainted on every scroll frame, because the scroll offset changes and the paint output changes, so a painter that is expensive to draw is expensive on every frame of the scroll — which is the mechanism behind the "my list stutters" report. And a painter that does not change does not need to repaint: with a correct shouldRepaint returning false for unchanged fields, a static chart in a scrolling list is rastered once and then merely composited as the list scrolls, which is the correct behaviour and the whole reason shouldRepaint exists.

/* When to use it. */
const CHOICE = {
  rightWhen: 'you NEED TO DRAW something NO COMBINATION of the standard widgets DRAWS',
  wrongWhen: 'the thing YOU ARE DRAWING COULD HAVE BEEN A COMPOSITION - which is MORE OFTEN THAN PEOPLE EXPECT',
};

    detail: 'the SIZE is GIVEN TO paint as the CANVAS SIZE, so A PAINTER IS ALWAYS RELATIVE rather than ABSOLUTE and MUST SCALE to WHATEVER BOX IT IS GIVEN',

  { m: 'shouldRepaint', asked: 'WHETHER A NEW PAINTER INSTANCE SHOULD REPAINT',

    correct: 'COMPARE THE FIELDS THAT AFFECT THE DRAWING',

const CHEAP = [

const STRUCTURAL = [
  { f: 'A PAINTER INSIDE A SCROLLING LIST IS REPAINTED ON EVERY SCROLL FRAME',
    why: 'the SCROLL OFFSET CHANGES and the PAINT OUTPUT CHANGES',
    so: 'a PAINTER THAT IS EXPENSIVE TO DRAW IS EXPENSIVE ON EVERY FRAME OF THE SCROLL',

A shouldRepaint that returns true unconditionally is the most common CustomPainter performance bug, and it is invisible in a static screen. It only shows up when the painter is inside something that repaints often - an animation, a list, a scrolling parent - and then every frame pays for a full re-raster of the whole widget.

The two methods, the shouldRepaint contract, and the mistakes that cost frames.

class SparklinePainter extends CustomPainter {
  SparklinePainter({
    required this.values,
    required this.color,
    required this.fillColor,
  });

  final List<double> values;
  final Color color;
  final Color fillColor;

  // THE CONTRACT: shouldRepaint says whether the new instance
  // would paint something different.
  //
  //   return false -> the output is CACHED and reused. Free.
  //   return true  -> paint() runs again, and a new layer is
  //                  rasterised. Costs a frame's worth of work.
  //
  // returning true unconditionally is the most common
  // CustomPainter performance bug.
  @override
  bool shouldRepaint(SparklinePainter old) {
    return old.values != values || old.color != color;
  }

  // THE OTHER CONTRACT: if you keep a mutable object and mutate
  // it, shouldRepaint cannot see the change, because it is
  // comparing the same instance to itself.
  //   old.values != values   -> false, because it is the SAME list
  // FIX: pass an immutable snapshot, or a new list each rebuild
  //      (List.of(values) if you mutated the original)

  @override
  void paint(Canvas canvas, Size size) {
    if (values.length < 2) return;

    // 1. build the path
    final path = Path();
    final dx = size.width / (values.length - 1);

    for (var i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
      final x = i * dx;
      final y = size.height - (values[i] * size.height).clamp(0.0, 1.0);
      if (i == 0) {
        path.moveTo(x, y);
      } else {
        path.lineTo(x, y);
      }
    }

    // 2. the fill, drawn first so the stroke is on top
    final fillPath = Path.from(path)
      ..lineTo(size.width, size.height)
      ..lineTo(0, size.height)
      ..close();

    canvas.drawPath(
      fillPath,
      Paint()
        ..shader = LinearGradient(
          begin: Alignment.topCenter,
          end: Alignment.bottomCenter,
          colors: [fillColor, fillColor.withValues(alpha: 0)],
        ).createShader(Offset.zero & size),
    );

    // 3. the line
    canvas.drawPath(
      path,
      Paint()
        ..color = color
        ..style = PaintingStyle.stroke
        ..strokeWidth = 2
        ..strokeCap = StrokeCap.round
        ..strokeJoin = StrokeJoin.round,
    );
  }
}

// usage
CustomPaint(
  size: const Size(120, 40),          // a SIZE, so it is not unbounded
  painter: SparklinePainter(
    values: List.of(series),           // a snapshot
    color: Colors.blue,
    fillColor: Colors.blue.withValues(alpha: 0.2),
  ),
  // isComplex: true if the object is opaque and clips its children
  // willChange: true if it will paint again anyway (an animation)
)
// THE THREE Paint PROPERTIES THAT MATTER
CustomPaint(
  painter: myPainter,
  // isComplex: the object is opaque, so Flutter can skip
  //   compositing what is behind it. Set it for any solid shape.
  isComplex: true,
  // willChange: the object will repaint on its own (an animation).
  // Flutter keeps it in a separate layer so it can be rasterised
  // without re-recording the display list.
  willChange: true,
)

// isComplex: true   -> fewer layers, faster compositing, correct
//                    for an opaque custom paint
// willChange: true  -> a cached layer that is re-rasterised; right
//                    for anything animated with a CustomPainter
// both false        -> the default; fine for a static sparse paint
// THE SIZE PROBLEM, which produces a confusing error
// "CustomPaint without a size would be infinite"
CustomPaint(painter: myPainter, child: myChild)
// -> the CustomPaint takes the child's size, which is fine

CustomPaint(painter: myPainter)                      // WRONG
// -> unbounded: the parent asks "how big are you?" and you
//    have no answer. Error.

// the fixes
CustomPaint(
  size: const Size(100, 40),                        // explicit
  painter: myPainter,
)
SizedBox(
  width: 100, height: 40,
  child: CustomPaint(painter: myPainter),           // a bounded box
)
// or let it fill
CustomPaint(
  painter: myPainter,
  child: const SizedBox.expand(),                   // needs a Stack
)

4.3 Canvas drawing

Canvas primitives, and the performance order they sit in

The drawing API is small — a dozen primitives plus transforms, clips and blending — and the useful thing about it is that the primitives are not equally expensive and the order is knowable in advance. drawRect, drawCircle and drawLine are the cheapest because they are single shapes with no path construction and usually no blending. drawPath is next, and its cost is dominated by path construction rather than by drawing, which is why the caching advice is about the path and not about the call: a path that is built once and drawn a hundred times costs a hundred draws; a path rebuilt a hundred times costs a hundred builds plus a hundred draws, and the build is usually the larger half. drawImage costs in proportion to the area painted, so drawing a small destination rectangle from a large source image is cheap and drawing a large destination is expensive — and drawing the same source into many small rectangles in a grid is cheap per rectangle but not free, because each is a separate textured quad. drawPicture records a sequence and replays it, which is a genuine optimisation for a shape drawn repeatedly: record once into a Picture, then replay; the recording is done on the raster thread and the replay is a single operation, and this is the mechanism behind the chart-in-a-list performance case. saveLayer is the expensive one and is worth a rule of its own, because it is the only primitive that allocates a full-size buffer: it renders everything drawn inside it into a separate surface and then composites that surface, and on a full-screen box that is a screen-sized allocation and a screen-sized composite, every frame, if it is inside an animation. Then the operations that change cost without changing what is drawn, which is the part that surprises people. A clip is a state change, not a free hint, and clipping to a non-rectangular path is more expensive than clipping to a rectangle. A blend mode forces the surface to be composited rather than drawn directly, and every blend mode other than the default one has a cost even when the colours happen not to blend differently, because the framework cannot know in advance. A non-axis-aligned transform prevents the fast path. Rotating or scaling by a value that is not a whole number of pixels, or by a non-zero angle, means the rasteriser cannot use a cheap blit and must sample with filtering. And an opacity between zero and one on a layer forces an intermediate surface for the same reason as a blend mode — which is why "animate opacity" is a common recommendation and "animate opacity on a large subtree" is a common cause of dropped frames, and why the right advice is to animate a transform where the visual result permits.

/* Primitives in performance order. */
const PRIMITIVES = [
  { p: 'drawRect, drawCircle, drawLine', cost: 'THE CHEAPEST',
    why: 'they are SINGLE SHAPES with NO PATH CONSTRUCTION and USUALLY NO BLENDING' },
  { p: 'drawPath', cost: 'NEXT',
    dominatedBy: 'PATH CONSTRUCTION rather than BY DRAWING',
    so: 'which is WHY THE CACHING ADVICE IS ABOUT THE PATH and NOT ABOUT THE CALL',
    arithmetic: 'a PATH THAT IS BUILT ONCE and DRAWN A HUNDRED TIMES COSTS A HUNDRED DRAWS; a PATH REBUILT A HUNDRED TIMES COSTS A HUNDRED BUILDS PLUS A HUNDRED DRAWS, and THE BUILD IS USUALLY THE LARGER HALF' },
  { p: 'drawImage', costsInProportionTo: 'the AREA PAINTED',
    instances: ['drawing a SMALL DESTINATION RECTANGLE from a LARGE SOURCE IMAGE IS CHEAP',
      'drawing a LARGE DESTINATION IS EXPENSIVE'],
    and: 'drawing the SAME SOURCE into MANY SMALL RECTANGLES in a GRID IS CHEAP PER RECTANGLE but NOT FREE, because EACH IS A SEPARATE TEXTURED QUAD' },
  { p: 'drawPicture', does: 'RECORDS A SEQUENCE and REPLAYS IT',
    optimisation: 'a GENUINE OPTIMISATION for a SHAPE DRAWN REPEATEDLY',

    details: ['the RECORDING is DONE ON THE RASTER THREAD and the REPLAY IS A SINGLE OPERATION',
      'and this is THE MECHANISM BEHIND the CHART-IN-A-LIST PERFORMANCE CASE'] },
  { p: 'saveLayer', cost: 'THE EXPENSIVE ONE', worthARuleOfItsOwn: true,

/* Operations that change cost without changing what is drawn. */
const HIDDEN_COSTS = [

The drawing primitives, the transforms, and the cost of each.

canvas.drawRect(Rect.fromLTWH(0, 0, 50, 50), paint);
canvas.drawRRect(RRect.fromRectAndRadius(rect, const Radius.circular(8)), paint);
canvas.drawCircle(Offset(50, 50), 20, paint);
canvas.drawOval(Rect.fromLTWH(0, 0, 100, 50), paint);
canvas.drawArc(rect, startAngle, sweepAngle, useCenter, paint);
canvas.drawPath(path, paint);
canvas.drawPoints(PointMode.points, [Offset(0, 0), Offset(10, 10)], paint);
canvas.drawVertices(vertices, ...);        // for a custom mesh
canvas.drawAtlas(image, transforms, rects, paints, ...);   // sprites

// Text

  text: const TextSpan(text: 'Hello', style: TextStyle(fontSize: 16)),
  textDirection: TextDirection.ltr,
)..layout();
canvas.drawParagraph(tp, const Offset(0, 0));
// the Flutter way, which lays out and paints in one step:

// IMAGES
canvas.drawImage(image, Offset.zero, paint);
canvas.drawImageRect(image, srcRect, dstRect, paint);
canvas.drawImageNine(image, srcRect, dstRect, paint);
canvas.drawRawAtlas(...);

// PAINT
final paint = Paint()
  ..color = Colors.red
  ..style = PaintingStyle.fill          // or .stroke
  ..strokeWidth = 2.0
  ..strokeCap = StrokeCap.round
  ..strokeJoin = StrokeJoin.round
  ..blendMode = BlendMode.srcOver
  ..isAntiAlias = true
  ..filterQuality = FilterQuality.medium
  ..colorFilter = const ColorFilter.mode(Colors.grey, BlendMode.saturation)
  ..maskFilter = const MaskFilter.blur(BlurStyle.normal, 4);
// TRANSFORMS: canvas.save() / canvas.restore()

canvas.translate(50, 50);
canvas.rotate(math.pi / 4);
canvas.scale(2, 2);

// draw in the transformed space
canvas.drawCircle(Offset.zero, 20, paint);

canvas.restore();      // MUST pair every save with a restore

// THE RULE: every save() needs a restore() on every path, including
// the error path
void paint(Canvas canvas, Size size) {
  canvas.save();
  try {
    canvas.translate(10, 10);
    canvas.drawRect(Rect.fromLTWH(0, 0, 50, 50), Paint());
  } finally {
    canvas.restore();
  }
}

// THE COST RANKING, for a paint-heavy animation
//   drawRect, drawLine, drawCircle     cheap
//   drawPath with many segments         medium
//   drawImage                          medium

//   drawShader, drawAtlas              medium, but shaders can be

//   saveLayer                          EXPENSIVE: it allocates a
//                                       new buffer

// it allocates and composites an offscreen buffer

                                             // the render object
// NOT: saveLayer + drawImage with alpha

// when you MUST use saveLayer

canvas.drawPath(complexPath, paint);
canvas.restore();

// for a text or an icon fade, use the widget
FadeTransition(
  opacity: animation,
  child: const Text('...'),
);

4.4 Gradients, shadows and effects

Shadows, effects, and the cost of transparency

Everything in this section is expensive for one reason: transparency requires an intermediate surface. Drawing an opaque shape is a direct write to the target; drawing a shape with partial opacity requires the framework to know what is behind it, which means either blending per pixel against what is already there — which the hardware may not accelerate — or rendering to a separate buffer and compositing, which it definitely allocates. Box shadows come in three varieties and the difference matters. An elevation shadow on Material surfaces is a property of the widget and is rastered once per layer; it costs nothing per frame after that. An ambient and directional pair is what Material elevation actually draws, and the number is a design token rather than a performance setting. A custom BoxShadow with a blur radius is drawn by the rasteriser every time the layer is rastered, and a large blur radius on a large box is a genuinely expensive operation — the blur is computed over the whole area. So a soft shadow on a card is fine and a soft shadow on a full-screen container, animating, is not. Blur, whether ImageFiltered or a backdrop filter, is the most expensive effect in the framework, because it reads the pixels already drawn behind the region, which means it cannot be fused into the current draw and requires a copy of the backdrop. A BackdropFilter inside a scrolling list is the canonical expensive case, because every scroll frame changes the backdrop and therefore re-reads and re-blurs it. Then the three effects that are cheaper than they look and three that are cheaper than they are not. Opacity on a small leaf widget is cheap, because the intermediate surface is small. A ShaderMask is cheap if the mask is a single solid colour, because there is nothing to sample. A gradient is cheap in absolute terms — it is a fill with a varying colour and both rasterisers handle it in hardware — but a gradient over a large area animating is a full-screen re-raster every frame. An Opacity widget on a large subtree is expensive, because the surface is the subtree's bounds. A BackdropFilter is expensive, always, whatever its size. And a large blur radius is expensive, because the cost is roughly proportional to the area times the radius. Then the practical rules that follow. Prefer a transform or a colour change to an opacity change where the design permits, because a transform composites and a colour change re-rasters a small layer. Give an animating subtree its own layer with a RepaintBoundary, so the animation does not force the parent to re-raster. Never put a backdrop filter inside a scrolling list; if the frosted-glass effect is required, apply it to a small fixed element. And measure, because the raster row in the performance panel tells you exactly which of these you are paying for and which you are not.

/* Why everything here is expensive. */
const ROOT_CAUSE = 'TRANSPARENCY REQUIRES AN INTERMEDIATE SURFACE';
const MECHANISM = {

  transparent: 'drawing a SHAPE WITH PARTIAL OPACITY REQUIRES the framework TO KNOW WHAT IS BEHIND IT',

};
