4.5 Fragment shaders

Fragment shaders, and why they are worth the complexity

A fragment shader runs on the graphics processor for every pixel of the shape it draws, and that is simultaneously why it is powerful and why it must be used carefully. The programming model is small: a fragment shader is a function from a pixel coordinate and a set of uniforms to a colour, and the framework supplies one for you to fill in. The uniforms are the interface, and they are the thing to design around: whatever varies over time — a position, a colour, a progress value, a set of points — should be a uniform rather than something baked into the shader, because a uniform change does not require recompiling the shader while changing the source does. Then the two costs, and they are different. Running the shader is per-pixel work on the graphics processor, so its cost is proportional to the area it covers; a full-screen shader is a full-screen graphics workload every frame, and whether that is affordable depends entirely on the device, which is why a shader that is smooth on a development machine and drops frames on a low-end phone is the normal outcome rather than a surprise. And compiling the shader is a one-time cost that is not one-time in practice, because the shader is compiled by the graphics driver at runtime, and a driver may compile the same source differently for different pipelines, and some drivers cache compiled shaders across runs while some do not, which is why the first appearance of a shader effect can be noticeably slower than subsequent ones. Then the four situations where a shader is the right tool, and they are characterised by the same property: the per-pixel computation is genuinely cheap and the operation is impossible to express as composition. A gradient that is not linear or radial, and any multi-stop or angle-based effect. A live effect driven by time or by input, which is the case no combination of widgets can express. A mask with structure — noise, a pattern, a dithered edge, a signed-distance field. And an effect over a live texture, such as tinting a video or an animated image. And then the four situations where it is not, which are the ones people reach for anyway. Anything with per-frame logic that depends on neighbouring pixels — a blur, a convolution — belongs in an image filter rather than a shader if a filter exists, because a filter is implemented by the driver and a shader doing the same work in a texture is not. Anything over a large area that does not need to change every frame, because a static effect should be rastered once. Anything that could be a CustomPainter, which is cheaper and easier to debug because a painter's operations are inspectable while a shader's are not. And anything where you need the result on the CPU — a shader produces pixels and nothing else, so a shader cannot compute a layout, a hit test or a value.

/* The model. */
const MODEL = {

};
const UNIFORMS = {

  why: 'a UNIFORM CHANGE DOES NOT REQUIRE RECOMPILING THE SHADER while CHANGING THE SOURCE DOES',
};

A fragment shader runs once per pixel, every frame. At 1920x1080 that is roughly two million invocations per frame, or a hundred and twenty million per second at 60fps. Any real work inside the shader - a loop, a texture fetch chain, a noise function - multiplies that by the number of iterations and will drop frames on any device that is not the newest hardware.

GPU shaders in Flutter, and the cost of a fullscreen fragment effect.

// A FRAGMENT SHADER: a small program that runs on the GPU for
// every pixel. This is where Flutter stops being a widget
// framework and starts being a graphics engine.

// pubspec.yaml
// flutter:
//   shaders:
//     - shaders/water.frag
//     - shaders/noise.frag

// a .frag file: a GLSL ES fragment shader
// shaders/water.frag
#include <flutter/runtime_effect.glsl>

uniform vec2 uSize;
uniform float uTime;
uniform sampler2D uTexture;      // 0: the child being filtered

out vec4 fragColor;

void main() {
  vec2 uv = FlutterFragCoord().xy / uSize;

  // a simple sine wave distortion
  float wave = sin(uv.y * 20.0 + uTime * 2.0) * 0.01;
  uv.x += wave;

  vec4 color = texture(uTexture, uv);

  // a colour tint
  color.rgb = mix(color.rgb, vec3(0.2, 0.5, 0.9), 0.3);

  fragColor = color;
}
// using it
class WaterShader extends StatelessWidget {
  const WaterShader({required this.child, super.key});

  final Widget child;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return ShaderMask(
      blendMode: BlendMode.srcIn,
      shaderCallback: (bounds) => FragmentProgram.fromAsset('shaders/water.frag')
          .fragmentShader()
        ..setFloat('uTime', animationValue)
        ..setFloat2('uSize', (bounds.bottom, bounds.right)),
      child: child,
    );
  }
}

// OR, for a full-screen effect, the right way
class RippleEffect extends StatelessWidget {
  const RippleEffect({required this.child, required this.tapPosition, super.key});

  final Widget child;
  final Offset tapPosition;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return AnimatedBuilder(
      animation: _controller,
      builder: (context, child) {
        return CustomPaint(
          painter: _RipplePainter(tapPosition, _controller.value),
          child: child,
        );
      },
      child: child,
    );
  }
}

// and via a fragment shader, per frame
// each frame: setFloat, and the fragment shader re-runs for
// every pixel of the affected area
// THE COST RULES FOR SHADERS
//
// a fragment shader runs ONCE PER PIXEL, EVERY FRAME.
// 1920x1080 = 2 million invocations per frame. At 60fps that is
// 124 million shader invocations per second, and every one of
// them costs you.
//
// SO:
// 1. the shader must be TRIVIAL. A texture fetch and a lerp is
//    fine. A loop with 20 iterations is 40 million operations
//    per frame.
// 2. SHADE THE SMALLEST POSSIBLE AREA. A ripple in a 200x200 box
//    is 1% of the cost of a fullscreen one.
// 3. skip work early: if a pixel is outside the effect radius,
//    return immediately
// 4. avoid dynamic loops and branches; GPUs execute both sides
//    of a branch when neighbouring pixels differ
// 5. precisions matter: use mediump where you can

// MEASURE IT: the raster row in the Performance panel. If a
// shader animation drops frames, the raster time is the reason.

4.6 Impeller and the backends

Impeller, Skia, and what the choice means for your code

Flutter changed its rendering backend and the change is worth understanding because it alters what is fast, not just what is used. The Skia backend draws the whole scene into a single texture. Every draw operation in a frame composites into one surface, which means effects that require reading what is behind them — blurs, backdrop filters, clipping to a path — force the framework to allocate an intermediate buffer and copy. That design is simple and it is why those effects were historically expensive on every platform. Impeller draws into multiple offscreen textures, one per layer, and a small pass tree that composites them. Because each layer is already its own texture, an effect that reads the layers behind it is reading a texture rather than copying a surface, which removes the allocation from the two most expensive effects in the framework. That is the entire architectural argument, and it is why the migration mattered: blurs and backdrop filters became cheap enough to use in a scroll view, which they were not before. Then what changed for ordinary code, which is less than people expect and worth being precise about. Nothing in the widget layer changed. The same widget tree produces the same output; there is no new API and no migration for application code. What changed is which operations are cheap, so a design decision made under Skia — "no backdrop filters in a list, it will drop frames" — may now be over-cautious, and a decision made under Impeller — "add a blur to the list header" — is now correct where it would not have been. And what is still expensive is genuinely expensive: a large-area shader, a wide blur radius, and a large subtree that re-rasters every frame are slow under either backend, because the cost is pixels and pixels do not get cheaper. So the practical guidance is: re-measure rather than carrying old assumptions forward, and treat any performance claim about Flutter rendering that predates Impeller as suspect rather than as established. Then the three things that are worth checking regardless of backend, because they are the ones that actually appear in profiles. Layer boundaries. Every layer is a texture, so a tree with many layers costs memory and costs the compositor; the layer tree view shows what you have. Shader compilation. A shader's first use compiles at runtime on the graphics processor, and on Impeller shader pipelines are compiled differently, so an effect that is smooth after the first frame can stutter on first appearance; pre-warming a shader by drawing it once during startup is a real technique for this. And texture size. A layer larger than the maximum texture size fails to allocate, which produces a blank or corrupted region rather than an exception, and it is the reason a full-screen layer at a high device pixel ratio on a large display is worth checking.

/* The two backends. */
const SKIA = {
  does: 'DRAWS THE WHOLE SCENE INTO A SINGLE TEXTURE',
  detail: 'EVERY DRAW OPERATION in a frame COMPOSITES INTO ONE SURFACE',
  consequence: 'EFFECTS THAT REQUIRE READING WHAT IS BEHIND THEM - BLURS, BACKDROP FILTERS, CLIPPING TO A PATH - FORCE the framework TO ALLOCATE AN INTERMEDIATE BUFFER and COPY',
  why: 'THAT DESIGN IS SIMPLE and it is WHY THOSE EFFECTS WERE HISTORICALLY EXPENSIVE on EVERY PLATFORM',
};
const IMPELLER = {
  does: 'DRAWS INTO MULTIPLE OFFSCREEN TEXTURES, ONE PER LAYER, and A SMALL PASS TREE THAT COMPOSITES THEM',
  gain: 'because EACH LAYER IS ALREADY ITS OWN TEXTURE, an EFFECT THAT READS THE LAYERS BEHIND IT IS READING A TEXTURE rather than COPYING A SURFACE',
  removed: 'the ALLOCATION from the TWO MOST EXPENSIVE EFFECTS in the framework',
  whyItMattered: 'BLURS and BACKDROP FILTERS BECAME CHEAP ENOUGH TO USE IN A SCROLL VIEW, which they WERE NOT BEFORE',
};

/* What changed for ordinary code. */
const FOR_CODE = [
  { c: 'NOTHING IN THE WIDGET LAYER CHANGED',
    detail: 'the SAME WIDGET TREE PRODUCES THE SAME OUTPUT; there is NO NEW API and NO MIGRATION for APPLICATION CODE' },
  { c: 'WHAT CHANGED IS WHICH OPERATIONS ARE CHEAP',
    consequences: ['a DESIGN DECISION MADE UNDER SKIA - no backdrop filters in a list, it will drop frames - MAY NOW BE OVER-CAUTIOUS',
      'a DECISION MADE UNDER IMPELLER - add a blur to the list header - IS NOW CORRECT where it WOULD NOT HAVE BEEN'] },
  { c: 'WHAT IS STILL EXPENSIVE IS GENUINELY EXPENSIVE',
    instances: ['a LARGE-AREA SHADER', 'a WIDE BLUR RADIUS', 'a LARGE SUBTREE THAT RE-RASTERS EVERY FRAME'],
    why: 'the COST IS PIXELS and PIXELS DO NOT GET CHEAPER' },
];
const GUIDANCE = 'RE-MEASURE rather than CARRYING OLD ASSUMPTIONS FORWARD';
const SCEPTICISM = 'treat ANY PERFORMANCE CLAIM about Flutter rendering THAT PREDATES Impeller as SUSPECT rather than as ESTABLISHED';

/* Three things worth checking regardless. */
const CHECK = [
  { t: 'LAYER BOUNDARIES', fact: 'EVERY LAYER IS A TEXTURE',
    cost: 'a TREE WITH MANY LAYERS COSTS MEMORY and COSTS the COMPOSITOR', how: 'the LAYER TREE VIEW shows WHAT YOU HAVE' },
  { t: 'SHADER COMPILATION', fact: 'a SHADERS FIRST USE COMPILES AT RUNTIME on the GRAPHICS PROCESSOR',
    and: 'on Impeller SHADER PIPELINES ARE COMPILED DIFFERENTLY, so AN EFFECT THAT IS SMOOTH AFTER THE FIRST FRAME CAN STUTTER ON FIRST APPEARANCE',
    technique: 'PRE-WARM A SHADER by DRAWING IT ONCE DURING STARTUP' },
  { t: 'TEXTURE SIZE', failure: 'a LAYER LARGER THAN THE MAXIMUM TEXTURE SIZE FAILS TO ALLOCATE',
    symptom: 'which PRODUCES A BLANK or CORRUPTED REGION rather than AN EXCEPTION',
    and: 'it is THE REASON a FULL-SCREEN LAYER AT A HIGH DEVICE PIXEL RATIO on a LARGE DISPLAY IS WORTH CHECKING' },
];

Impeller is the default now, and the practical consequence for your code is that shader compilation happens up front rather than on first use. If you had a "the first few seconds are stuttery" problem with custom shaders or complex blurs, that is the change that fixed it. If a plugin still assumes Skia-only behaviour, it will show up on a physical device with Impeller and nowhere else.

The two renderers, what changed, and what it means for your code.

// SKIA was the original backend. IMPELLER is the default now
// (iOS since Flutter 3.10, Android from 3.29, and the web with
// CanvasKit).
//
// WHAT CHANGED
//                    Skia                 Impeller
//   iOS              Metal via Skia       Metal directly
//   Android          OpenGL / Vulkan      Vulkan / OpenGL / Metal
//   shader compiles  at first use          all up front
//   frame submission 2-3 frames queued     1 frame
//   jank             shader compile hitch  none
//   RSH             supported             supported
//
// THE PRACTICAL EFFECTS
// 1. NO MORE FIRST-FRAME HITCH from shader compilation. If you
//    had a "the first few seconds are stuttery" bug, Impeller
//    fixes it.
// 2. Custom shaders are compiled for ALL uniform permutations at
//    build time, so the app is slightly bigger and startup is
//    slightly slower on web.
// 3. Some Skia-only features are gone or different:
//    - SkSL shaders no longer run on iOS with Impeller; use
//      FragmentProgram (.frag files)
//    - colour space handling differs slightly
//    - BackdropFilter has different edge behaviour
//
// HOW TO CHECK AND TOGGLE
// in your app
//   import 'package:flutter/rendering.dart';
//   debugPrint(ImpellerEnabled ? 'Impeller' : 'Skia');
//
// opt out (iOS, if you must):
//   // ios/Runner/Info.plist
//   <key>FLTEnableImpeller</key>
//   <false/>
//
// opt out (Android):
//   <meta-data
//       android:name="io.flutter.embedding.android.EnableImpeller"
//       android:value="false" />
//
// WHAT TO DO: test on a physical device with Impeller, and do
// not rely on Skia-only behaviour. If you need to support an old
// device, keep the Skia escape hatch for a release, not forever.
// RUNNING SHADERS IN A HEADLESS TEST
// a shader is compiled at runtime, so a shader error is a crash
// in production, not a compile error

// wrap the use in a debug check
void main() {
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

class MyApp extends StatelessWidget {
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    assert(() {
      // in debug, compile it eagerly and loudly
      try {
        FragmentProgram.fromAsset('shaders/water.frag').fragmentShader();
      } catch (e) {
        debugPrint('SHADER FAILED TO COMPILE: $e');
      }
      return true;
    }());
    return const MaterialApp(home: Home());
  }
}

// and run the app in profile mode at least once before release:
// shader compilation behaves differently there

4.7 Images: decode, cache, paint

Decode, cache, paint, and the four stages a frame goes through

An image widget on screen is the end of a four-stage pipeline and knowing the stages is what makes the advice actionable, because each stage has its own failure and its own fix. Load is getting the encoded bytes — from the asset bundle, the network, or memory. This is the only stage where the format matters for size, and the only one where caching the bytes helps. Decode is turning encoded bytes into a raw bitmap, and it is the expensive one: a compressed image is stored compressed and expanded to width times height times four bytes when decoded, so a twelve-megapixel photograph becomes forty-eight megabytes the moment it is decoded. This is why cacheWidth and cacheHeight exist and why they are the highest-leverage thing to set on any list of images. Cache is the framework holding decoded bitmaps, in a memory cache with a byte budget and a disk cache for the encoded bytes. The two are independent, so a warm disk cache still pays decode on first display. Paint is drawing the bitmap into the layer, and its cost is proportional to the destination area, not the source size. Then the four things that go wrong in practice, and the mechanism for each. Decoding at the wrong resolution — the forty-eight megabyte case — fixed by the cache dimensions, and the trap is that they are in physical pixels so they must be multiplied by the device pixel ratio. Cache thrash — a list of images larger than the cache budget, so scrolling evicts everything and scrolling back re-decodes everything; fixed by reducing decoded sizes so more fits, and by accepting that a very long list will not keep its images. Uploading the same image twice when the same asset is referenced from two widgets with different cache dimensions, because the cache key includes those dimensions; fixed by giving the images a common size or by using the same widget instance. And format mismatch with the platform's decoder — WebP or AVIF not supported on an older device, which produces a decode error rather than a fallback, so the answer is to ship a format every supported platform can decode or to bundle a fallback. Then the two behaviours that matter for a smooth list, because they are the difference between images appearing and images appearing late. Reserve the space. An image with no intrinsic size until it loads produces a layout shift and, worse in a list, a shift of every row below it. And decode off the first frame. An image that decodes during the first frame delays it; prefetching the first screen's images during startup, and decoding the rest as they scroll into the cache extent, keeps the frame budget for the frame.

/* Four stages. */
const STAGES = [
  { n: 1, name: 'LOAD', is: 'GETTING THE ENCODED BYTES', from: ['the ASSET BUNDLE', 'the NETWORK', 'MEMORY'],
    fact: 'this is THE ONLY STAGE WHERE THE FORMAT MATTERS FOR SIZE, and the ONLY ONE WHERE CACHING THE BYTES HELPS' },
  { n: 2, name: 'DECODE', is: 'TURNING ENCODED BYTES INTO A RAW BITMAP', expensive: true,
    detail: 'a COMPRESSED IMAGE IS STORED COMPRESSED and EXPANDED TO WIDTH TIMES HEIGHT TIMES FOUR BYTES WHEN DECODED',
    arithmetic: 'a TWELVE-MEGAPIXEL PHOTOGRAPH BECOMES FORTY-EIGHT MEGABYTES THE MOMENT IT IS DECODED',
    and: 'which is WHY cacheWidth and cacheHeight EXIST and WHY THEY ARE THE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE THING TO SET on any LIST OF IMAGES' },
  { n: 3, name: 'CACHE', is: 'the FRAMEWORK HOLDING DECODED BITMAPS',
    has: ['a MEMORY CACHE with a BYTE BUDGET', 'a DISK CACHE for the ENCODED BYTES'],
    independent: 'the TWO ARE INDEPENDENT, so a WARM DISK CACHE STILL PAYS DECODE on FIRST DISPLAY' },
  { n: 4, name: 'PAINT', is: 'DRAWING THE BITMAP INTO THE LAYER',
    costIs: 'PROPORTIONAL TO THE DESTINATION AREA, NOT the SOURCE SIZE' },
];

/* Four things that go wrong. */
const FAILURES = [
  { f: 'DECODING AT THE WRONG RESOLUTION', detail: 'the FORTY-EIGHT MEGABYTE CASE',
    fix: 'the CACHE DIMENSIONS', trap: 'they ARE IN PHYSICAL PIXELS so THEY MUST BE MULTIPLIED BY the DEVICE PIXEL RATIO' },
  { f: 'CACHE THRASH', detail: 'a LIST OF IMAGES LARGER than the CACHE BUDGET, so SCROLLING EVICTS EVERYTHING and SCROLLING BACK RE-DECODES EVERYTHING',
    fixes: ['REDUCING DECODED SIZES so MORE FITS', 'and ACCEPTING that a VERY LONG LIST WILL NOT KEEP ITS IMAGES'] },
  { f: 'UPLOADING THE SAME IMAGE TWICE',
    cause: 'the SAME ASSET IS REFERENCED FROM TWO WIDGETS WITH DIFFERENT CACHE DIMENSIONS',
    why: 'the CACHE KEY INCLUDES THOSE DIMENSIONS',
    fix: ['giving the IMAGES A COMMON SIZE', 'or USING THE SAME WIDGET INSTANCE'] },
  { f: 'FORMAT MISMATCH WITH THE PLATFORMS DECODER', instances: ['WEBP', 'AVIF NOT SUPPORTED ON AN OLDER DEVICE'],
    symptom: 'which PRODUCES A DECODE ERROR rather than A FALLBACK',
    fix: 'ship A FORMAT EVERY SUPPORTED PLATFORM CAN DECODE or BUNDLE A FALLBACK' },
];

/* Two behaviours that matter for a smooth list. */
const BEHAVIOURS = [
  { b: 'RESERVE THE SPACE',
    why: 'an IMAGE WITH NO INTRINSIC SIZE UNTIL IT LOADS PRODUCES A LAYOUT SHIFT',
    worse: 'and, WORSE IN A LIST, A SHIFT OF EVERY ROW BELOW IT' },
  { b: 'DECODE OFF THE FIRST FRAME',
    why: 'an IMAGE THAT DECODES DURING THE FIRST FRAME DELAYS IT',
    how: ['PREFETCHING the FIRST SCREENS IMAGES DURING STARTUP',
      'and DECODING THE REST AS THEY SCROLL INTO the CACHE EXTENT'],
    gain: 'which KEEPS THE FRAME BUDGET FOR THE FRAME' },
];

A decoded image costs width * height * 4 bytes. A twelve-megapixel photo is 48MB while it is decoded, and a list of twenty of them is close to a gigabyte - which is more than a phone has, and the operating system kills the app for it. cacheWidth is not an optimisation, it is the difference between working and being killed.

The image pipeline, the caches, and the numbers that matter.

// THE PIPELINE
//
//   bytes (compressed, in a file or a response)
//     -> DECODE to a bitmap        <- the expensive step
//       -> store in the image cache (in memory, in MB)
//         -> upload to the GPU as a texture
//           -> paint
//
// THE TWO CACHES
//   ImageCache: decoded bitmaps, keyed by (asset bundle, key,
//               scale). Default 1000 images / 100MB.
//   image cache on disk: only with a package like
//               cached_network_image. Flutter's Image.network
//               does NOT cache to disk by default.
//
// SIZING: the decoded size is width * height * 4 bytes.
//   4000x3000 = 48MB. A list of 20 = 960MB. The OS kills you.
//
// THE FIX: decode at the size you display
Image.network(
  url,
  cacheWidth: 400,      // decode to 400px wide
  cacheHeight: 300,
)
// or with a package
CachedNetworkImage(
  imageUrl: url,
  memCacheWidth: 400,               // in-memory, in PHYSICAL px
  maxWidthDiskCache: 800,           // on disk, in PHYSICAL px
)
// CONFIGURING THE CACHE, and measuring it
void main() {
  PaintingBinding.instance.imageCache.maximumSizeBytes = 200 << 20;  // 200MB
  PaintingBinding.instance.imageCache.maximumSize = 300;             // 300 images
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

// measure it
debugDumpImageCache();
// or programmatically
final cache = PaintingBinding.instance.imageCache;
debugPrint('${cache.currentSize} images, ${cache.currentSizeBytes ~/ 1024}KB');
cache.clear();
cache.clearLiveImages();

// a custom paint filter: resize at paint time
Image.network(
  url,
  frameBuilder: (context, child, frame, wasSyncLoaded) {
    if (wasSyncLoaded) return child;
    return AnimatedSwitcher(
      duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 200),
      child: frame == null
          ? const SizedBox.expand(child: ColoredBox(color: Colors.grey))
          : child,
    );
  },
)

// for a very large image, decode a region instead
// decodeImageFromList with a targetWidth, or a package that
// supports tiled decoding

4.8 Repainting and RepaintBoundary

The layer boundary, and when one helps and when it costs you.

// WHAT A LAYER IS
// when a RenderObject needs its own compositing layer, Flutter
// allocates a texture and composites it separately. That means
// it can be moved, faded or animated WITHOUT re-running paint
// on everything behind it.
//
// A RepaintBoundary forces that boundary.

// WHEN IT HELPS
// 1. an animating child inside a large static parent
Stack(children: [
  ComplexStaticContent(),                    // never repaints
  const RepaintBoundary(
    child: AnimatedThing(),                  // repaints every frame
  ),
])
// without the boundary, the animation invalidates the paint of
// everything behind it, every frame

// 2. a list row that repaints on its own
ListView.builder(
  itemBuilder: (context, i) => RepaintBoundary(
    child: EntryRow(entries[i]),
  ),
)

// 3. a complex subtree inside a frequently-rebuilt parent
RepaintBoundary(child: ExpensiveChart(data))

// WHEN IT COSTS YOU
// each boundary is a texture: memory, and one more compositing
// step. A RepaintBoundary on every row of a 1000-row list adds
// 1000 layers.
//
// THE RULE: add boundaries where you have measured a repaint
// problem, not preemptively. The DevTools "Layer Tree" view
// shows exactly what became a layer.
// THE HIERARCHY RULE, which is the subtle part
// if a RepaintBoundary is INSIDE another one, the inner one may
// share the outer's layer: the boundary is not guaranteed
//
// this WON'T work as you expect:
RepaintBoundary(              // outer: one big layer
  child: RepaintBoundary(      // inner: MERGED into the outer
    child: AnimatedThing(),
  ),
)
// the outer repaints everything, so the inner boundary is moot

// this works:
RepaintBoundary(              // the animated one is at the TOP
  child: AnimatedThing(),
)
// inside a larger scroll view, each row is its own boundary
ListView(children: [
  for (final item in items)
    RepaintBoundary(child: Row(item)),   // siblings, not nested
])

// the AnimatedBuilder boundary, which you get for free
AnimatedBuilder(
  animation: controller,
  builder: (context, child) => Opacity(
    opacity: controller.value,
    child: child,                        // the CHILD is passed
  ),
  child: const ExpensiveWidget(),        // so it is built ONCE
)
// without `child`, the builder rebuilds the widget every frame

Repaint boundaries, and where to put them

A repaint boundary is a subtree the framework may raster independently of its parent, and putting one in the wrong place is worse than putting none in at all, so the rule needs to be stated before the technique. When a widget marks itself needing paint, the framework finds the nearest enclosing repaint boundary and re-rasters that layer. Everything above it is untouched: only the compositor moves the new texture. That is the whole benefit and it is a large one for a small change. A boundary is a layer, and layers cost memory, because each is a texture the size of its bounds, so a boundary around a small animated widget inside a large static subtree is nearly free and a boundary around the whole screen is a full-screen texture allocated for nothing. And a boundary does not help if the content inside it changes shape, because a layer's texture is the size of its bounds and growing content either forces a new texture every frame or clips — which is why a boundary around a list that changes length is worse than no boundary. Then where the boundaries belong, and the rule is stated in terms of what changes. Put one around anything that animates — an animated icon, a spinner, a progress indicator, a caret, a video — because the animation is a per-frame change to a small area and that is exactly the case the mechanism is for. Put one around a frequently-updating widget inside a large static subtree, such as a clock or a live price inside a settings screen, for the same reason at larger scale. Do not put one around a subtree that animates and also covers a lot, unless it needs it, because you have just chosen to re-raster that much every frame. And do not scatter them without a reason: each boundary is a texture, and a widget tree with a hundred boundaries of random sizes costs more in memory than it saves in raster time. Then the difference from a rebuild, because the two are routinely confused. A repaint boundary says nothing about rebuilds: a widget inside a boundary still rebuilds when its parent rebuilds unless it is const or its state is lower down. And a boundary does not help with layout or build cost at all. The two mechanisms are independent and a problem that is a build problem needs a smaller widget, not a boundary — which is why the layer tree view and the widget inspector are different tools for different questions and why "add a repaint boundary" applied to a build problem produces no improvement and a new texture. And finally the two situations where the framework inserts boundaries for you, because knowing them explains a layer tree you did not design: a widget that repaints on its own schedule is promoted, and a route or a page in a navigator is separated so that one page's repaint does not re-raster the others.

/* The mechanism. */
const MECHANISM = {
  is: 'a SUBTREE the framework MAY RASTER INDEPENDENTLY of its parent',
  rule: 'WHEN A WIDGET MARKS ITSELF NEEDING PAINT, the framework FINDS THE NEAREST ENCLOSING REPAINT BOUNDARY and RE-RASTERS THAT LAYER',
  effect: 'EVERYTHING ABOVE IT IS UNTOUCHED - only the COMPOSITOR MOVES the NEW TEXTURE',
  benefit: 'which is THE WHOLE BENEFIT and IT IS A LARGE ONE FOR A SMALL CHANGE',
};

/* Three costs, stated before the technique. */
const COSTS = [
  { c: 'A BOUNDARY IS A LAYER, and LAYERS COST MEMORY',
    detail: 'EACH IS A TEXTURE THE SIZE OF ITS BOUNDS',
    so: 'a BOUNDARY AROUND A SMALL ANIMATED WIDGET inside a LARGE STATIC SUBTREE IS NEARLY FREE',
    and: 'a BOUNDARY AROUND THE WHOLE SCREEN IS A FULL-SCREEN TEXTURE ALLOCATED FOR NOTHING' },
  { c: 'A BOUNDARY DOES NOT HELP if the CONTENT INSIDE IT CHANGES SHAPE',
    detail: 'a LAYERS TEXTURE IS THE SIZE OF ITS BOUNDS and GROWING CONTENT EITHER FORCES A NEW TEXTURE EVERY FRAME or CLIPS',
    and: 'which is WHY A BOUNDARY AROUND A LIST THAT CHANGES LENGTH IS WORSE THAN NO BOUNDARY' },
];

/* Where the boundaries belong. */
const WHERE = [
  { w: 'PUT ONE AROUND ANYTHING THAT ANIMATES',
    instances: ['an ANIMATED ICON', 'a SPINNER', 'a PROGRESS INDICATOR', 'a CARET', 'a VIDEO'],
    why: 'the ANIMATION IS A PER-FRAME CHANGE TO A SMALL AREA and THAT IS EXACTLY THE CASE the mechanism IS FOR' },
  { w: 'PUT ONE AROUND A FREQUENTLY-UPDATING WIDGET inside a LARGE STATIC SUBTREE',
    instances: ['a CLOCK', 'a LIVE PRICE inside a SETTINGS SCREEN'], sameReason: 'at LARGER SCALE' },
  { w: 'do NOT PUT ONE AROUND A SUBTREE THAT ANIMATES and ALSO COVERS A LOT',
    unless: 'it NEEDS IT', because: 'you HAVE JUST CHOSEN to RE-RASTER THAT MUCH EVERY FRAME' },
  { w: 'do NOT SCATTER THEM WITHOUT A REASON',
    cost: 'EACH BOUNDARY IS A TEXTURE, and a WIDGET TREE WITH A HUNDRED BOUNDARIES OF RANDOM SIZES COSTS MORE in MEMORY than it SAVES in RASTER TIME' },
];

/* The difference from a rebuild. */
const NOT_A_REBUILD = {
  saysNothingAbout: 'REBUILDS',
  detail: ['a WIDGET INSIDE A BOUNDARY STILL REBUILDS WHEN ITS PARENT REBUILDS unless it is const OR ITS STATE IS LOWER DOWN',
    'and A BOUNDARY DOES NOT HELP WITH LAYOUT or BUILD COST AT ALL'],
  twoMechanisms: 'the TWO MECHANISMS ARE INDEPENDENT and A PROBLEM THAT IS A BUILD PROBLEM NEEDS A SMALLER WIDGET, NOT A BOUNDARY',
  consequence: 'which is WHY add a repaint boundary APPLIED TO A BUILD PROBLEM PRODUCES NO IMPROVEMENT and A NEW TEXTURE',
  tools: 'the LAYER TREE VIEW and the WIDGET INSPECTOR ARE DIFFERENT TOOLS FOR DIFFERENT QUESTIONS',
};

/* Two the framework inserts for you. */
const AUTOMATIC = [
  'a WIDGET THAT REPAINTS ON ITS OWN SCHEDULE IS PROMOTED',
  'a ROUTE or a PAGE in a NAVIGATOR is SEPARATED so THAT ONE PAGES REPAINT DOES NOT RE-RASTER the OTHERS',
];
const EXPLAINS = 'knowing them EXPLAINS a LAYER TREE YOU DID NOT DESIGN';

The single highest-leverage performance technique in this chapter is passing a child to AnimatedBuilder, AnimatedOpacity and friends. Without it, the expensive subtree is rebuilt on every animation frame. With it, the subtree is built once and only a property is recomposited - which is what makes a 60fps animation of a complex widget possible.

Exercises 5

  1. Write a CustomPainter sparkline with a fill gradient and a stroke. Test shouldRepaint with a mutable list and find the bug.
  2. Profile a screen and identify whether the cost is in build, layout, paint or raster. Optimise the stage that is actually slow.
  3. Build a save/restore transform animation and confirm every path restores, including the error path.
  4. Write a fragment shader (a colour tint) and use it with ShaderMask. Add a debug-time compile check.
  5. Compare blurRadius: 24 against a three-layer fake shadow, with and without an animation. Measure the raster time difference.
  6. Add cacheWidth to a list of 4K images and measure the memory with debugDumpImageCache before and after.
  7. Add a RepaintBoundary around an animating child inside a large static subtree, and measure with the layer tree view.

5 · Animation, Physics and Effects

5.1 The animation architecture5.2 Implicit animations5.3 Explicit animations5.4 Curves and physics5.5 Springs and Simulation5.6 Hero and page transitions5.7 Motion, staggered and shared axis5.8 Animation performance

Flutter's animation system is one of its strongest features, and the difference between a cheap animation and an expensive one is usually one mistake in how you drive it.

5.1 The animation architecture

The ticker, and why every animation is the same machine

Flutter has exactly one animation mechanism and everything else is a configuration of it, which is worth knowing because it means there is one thing to learn rather than eight. A Ticker is driven by the framework's frame callback and reports an elapsed time on every frame. It does not know what it is animating and it does not draw anything; it produces a time, and something else turns that time into a value. An Animation wraps a ticker and turns elapsed time into a value in some range. It can be running forward, reversed, or stopped; it has a value; and it notifies listeners when the value changes. An AnimationController is the Animation that also knows how to drive a ticker — it owns the ticker, exposes forward, reverse, repeat and stop, and is the thing you create in practice. An AnimatedWidget rebuilds itself when the animation's value changes, which is how the value reaches the tree; and an AnimationBuilder is the base class doing exactly that, with a builder that receives the animated value. Then the status listener, and the one piece of vocabulary that trips up everybody. A controller has a status — dismissed, running, forward, reverse, completed — and three callbacks: addStatusListener, which fires when the status changes, and addListener, which fires on every tick. The distinction matters because the completion of a forward animation is a status change, not the last tick, and code written as "do the thing on the last tick" runs one frame early or, worse, is skipped if the animation is interrupted; using addStatusListener and checking for completed or dismissed is the correct form and is the thing that makes a navigation call happen after the transition rather than during it. Then the two rules that follow from the architecture and that account for most animation bugs. An animation must be disposed. A controller holds a ticker, and an undisposed ticker is not merely a leak — it is a live frame callback that keeps asking for frames, so a screen that starts an animation and does not dispose it produces a continuously scheduling screen after it is gone. And a controller cannot be reused after disposal, so a controller stored in a state and disposed in dispose cannot be the same object on the next build of that state; in practice this means the controller is created in the state, disposed in dispose, and never shared between states. And the third, which is the one that separates smooth from janky: what runs on a tick is your build and paint code, so a tick that does more work than a frame budget is a dropped frame. That is the animation performance chapter's whole subject and it follows directly from there being one mechanism.

/* One mechanism, everything else is configuration. */
const TIICKER = { isNot: 'not an ANIMATION', is: 'DRIVEN BY THE FRAMEWORKS FRAME CALLBACK',
  reports: 'an ELAPSED TIME on EVERY FRAME', doesNot: 'it does NOT KNOW WHAT IT IS ANIMATING and it DOES NOT DRAW ANYTHING',
  produces: 'a TIME, and SOMETHING ELSE TURNS THAT TIME INTO A VALUE' };
const ANIMATION = { is: 'a WRAPPER around a ticker that TURNS ELAPSED TIME INTO A VALUE in SOME RANGE',
  canBe: ['RUNNING FORWARD', 'REVERSED', 'STOPPED'], has: 'a value', notifies: 'LISTENERS WHEN THE VALUE CHANGES' };
const CONTROLLER = { is: 'the ANIMATION THAT ALSO KNOWS HOW TO DRIVE A TICKER',
  owns: 'the TICKER', exposes: ['forward', 'reverse', 'repeat', 'stop'],
  whatYouCreate: 'IN PRACTICE' };
const ANIMATED_WIDGET = { does: 'REBUILDS ITSELF when the ANIMATIONS VALUE CHANGES',
  and: 'which is HOW THE VALUE REACHES THE TREE' };
const BUILDER = 'AnimationBuilder IS THE BASE CLASS DOING EXACTLY THAT, with a BUILDER THAT RECEIVES the animated value';

/* Status. */
const STATUS = { values: ['DISMISSED', 'RUNNING', 'FORWARD', 'REVERSE', 'COMPLETED'],
  callbacks: ['addStatusListener - FIRES WHEN THE STATUS CHANGES', 'addListener - FIRES ON EVERY TICK'],
  theTrap: 'THE COMPLETION OF A FORWARD ANIMATION IS A STATUS CHANGE, not the LAST TICK',
  wrongSymptom: ['a thing done ON THE LAST TICK RUNS ONE FRAME EARLY',
    'or, WORSE, IS SKIPPED if the ANIMATION IS INTERRUPTED'],
  right: 'USE addStatusListener AND CHECKING FOR completed OR dismissed IS THE CORRECT FORM',
  gain: 'and it is THE THING THAT MAKES A NAVIGATION CALL HAPPEN AFTER the TRANSITION rather than DURING IT' };

/* Two rules, plus the third. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'AN ANIMATION MUST BE DISPOSED',
    notJust: 'a LEAK', detail: 'a CONTROLLER HOLDS A TICKER, and an UNDISPOSED TICKER IS NOT MERELY A LEAK - IT IS A LIVE FRAME CALLBACK',
    consequence: 'so a SCREEN THAT STARTS AN ANIMATION and DOES NOT DISPOSE IT PRODUCES A CONTINUOUSLY SCHEDULING SCREEN AFTER IT IS GONE',
    and: 'a CONTROLLER CANNOT BE REUSED AFTER DISPOSAL' },
  { r: 'a CONTROLLER CANNOT BE REUSED AFTER DISPOSAL',
    practice: 'so a CONTROLLER STORED IN A STATE and DISPOSED IN dispose CANNOT BE THE SAME OBJECT on the NEXT BUILD of that STATE',
    inPractice: ['CREATE the CONTROLLER IN THE STATE', 'DISPOSE IT IN dispose', 'and NEVER SHARE IT BETWEEN STATES'] },
  { r: 'WHAT RUNS ON A TICK IS YOUR BUILD and PAINT CODE',
    consequence: 'so a TICK THAT DOES MORE WORK THAN A FRAME BUDGET IS A DROPPED FRAME',
    and: 'that is THE ANIMATION PERFORMANCE CHAPTERS WHOLE SUBJECT and IT FOLLOWS DIRECTLY from there BEING ONE MECHANISM' },
];

The three layers, and how the ticker drives them.

// THE THREE LAYERS
//
// 1. Ticker          the clock. Fires a callback on every frame,
//                    aligned with the display's refresh rate.
//                    One global ticker, shared.
//
// 2. AnimationController
//                    produces a value from 0.0 to 1.0 (or beyond,
//                    with a lowerBound/upperBound), driven by the
//                    ticker, over a duration.
//
// 3. CurvedAnimation  maps the controller's linear 0..1 through
//                    a Curve, to produce a shaped value.
//                    AnimatedWidget / ImplicitlyAnimatedWidget
//                    consume the value and rebuild.
//
// the frame loop, in one picture:
//   Ticker fires
//     -> AnimationController.forward() computes the new value
//       from elapsed time
//         -> CurvedAnimation applies the curve
//           -> AnimatedWidget builds with the new value
//             -> the render tree updates
//               -> layout/paint/raster
//                 -> frame on screen

5.2 Implicit animations

The eight, and which one is right

There are eight implicit animation widgets and the reason it feels like eight is that they differ along two independent axes: what property they animate, and how they resolve the end value. Knowing the axes makes the set navigable. Along the first axis: AnimatedContainer animates anything a Container can set — decoration, padding, alignment, size — and is the general-purpose one; AnimatedPadding, AnimatedAlign, AnimatedPositioned and AnimatedOpacity each animate one property and are cheaper because they rebuild less; AnimatedDefaultTextStyle animates the text style of a subtree. Along the second axis: Animated* takes the end value as a property and animates from whatever it currently is, while TweenAnimationBuilder takes a builder and a target value and is the general escape hatch. The distinctions that matter in practice are these. An implicit animation needs a state change to re-run. Because it does not own a controller, it starts when its target property changes — so an animation that should replay on a tap needs something to change, which means a value or a key; this is why an implicit animation inside a Row that must replay requires a Key change to force a rebuild from the old value. It does not animate "from nothing". On first build the widget appears at its final value with no animation, because there is no previous value to animate from; if you want an entrance animation you need a controller that starts at zero, or a key that forces a rebuild. And the cross-fade problem. When the widget itself changes — a different child in the same slot — an implicit animation animates the property but the old widget is gone, so you get an instant swap rather than a transition; the correct widget is AnimatedSwitcher, which holds both children and cross-fades them. That single distinction resolves a whole family of "why does my animation not work" reports, and it is worth memorising as a rule: an implicit widget animates a property of one widget; use AnimatedSwitcher or a route transition when the widget changes. Then the two parameters that control the feel, and their defaults are worth knowing. duration defaults to two hundred milliseconds, which is right for a small property change on an element already on screen and wrong for anything that covers the screen; and curve defaults to Curves.linear, which is almost never what anyone wants — a linear animation is mechanical, and the default that most applications should change immediately is Curves.easeOut, which decelerates into place. And then the three cases where implicit is the wrong tool. A sequence of two or more animations, because an implicit widget animates one change and a sequence needs a controller and a Interval per segment. An animation that must be interruptible and resumable from its current position, which is the argument for explicit. And anything inside a list row that animates on scroll, because an implicit animation has no notion of being cancelled and will happily complete after the row is off screen.

/* Two axes. */
const AXIS_1 = [

  { w: 'AnimatedPadding, AnimatedAlign, AnimatedPositioned, AnimatedOpacity', animates: 'ONE PROPERTY each',
    cheaper: 'because THEY REBUILD LESS' },
  { w: 'AnimatedDefaultTextStyle', animates: 'the TEXT STYLE of a SUBTREE' },
];
const AXIS_2 = [
  { w: 'the Animated* widgets', take: 'the END VALUE AS A PROPERTY and ANIMATE FROM whatever it CURRENTLY IS' },
  { w: 'TweenAnimationBuilder', take: 'A BUILDER and a TARGET VALUE', is: 'the GENERAL ESCAPE HATCH' },
];

/* Three distinctions that matter. */

The implicit versus explicit rule is a genuinely useful line to keep: a property change is implicit, anything else is explicit. Two widgets cross-fading is AnimatedSwitcher, not two AnimatedOpacity widgets, because the incoming widget is genuinely a different widget and the framework needs to know it.

The widgets that animate themselves when a property changes, and the implicit/explicit rule.

// AN IMPLICIT ANIMATION: you change a property, the widget
// animates from the old value to the new one
AnimatedContainer(
  duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 300),
  curve: Curves.easeInOut,
  width: _selected ? 200 : 100,
  height: 100,
  decoration: BoxDecoration(
    color: _selected ? Colors.blue : Colors.grey,
    borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(_selected ? 24 : 0),
  ),
  child: const Text('tap me'),
)

// the whole family
AnimatedContainer       colour, size, border, decoration
AnimatedOpacity         0.0 to 1.0
AnimatedPadding         padding
AnimatedAlign           alignment
AnimatedPositioned      position (must be in a Stack)
AnimatedDefaultTextStyle
AnimatedCrossFade       one child to another
AnimatedSwitcher        one WIDGET to another, with a transition
AnimatedRotation        turns
AnimatedScale           scale
AnimatedSlide           offset

// the pattern: a bool drives it
class Expandable extends StatefulWidget {
  const Expandable({super.key});
  @override
  State<Expandable> createState() => _ExpandableState();
}

class _ExpandableState extends State<Expandable> {
  bool _expanded = false;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return GestureDetector(
      onTap: () => setState(() => _expanded = !_expanded),
      child: AnimatedContainer(
        duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 250),
        curve: Curves.easeOutCubic,
        width: _expanded ? 300 : 150,
        alignment: Alignment.center,
        child: const Text('tap me'),
      ),
    );
  }
}
// AnimatedSwitcher: for a change of CONTENT, not of properties
AnimatedSwitcher(
  duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 200),
  transitionBuilder: (child, animation) => FadeTransition(
    opacity: animation,
    child: SlideTransition(
      position: Tween<Offset>(
        begin: const Offset(0, 0.1),
        end: Offset.zero,
      ).animate(CurvedAnimation(parent: animation, curve: Curves.easeOut)),
      child: child,
    ),
  ),
  child: _loading
      ? const CircularProgressIndicator(key: ValueKey('loading'))
      : Text(data, key: const ValueKey('data')),
)
// THE KEY IS ESSENTIAL. Without it, AnimatedSwitcher cannot tell
// the two children apart, so it sees "the same widget, still the
// same" and does not animate.

// THE RULE: implicit for a property change, explicit for anything
// else. Two widgets cross-fading is AnimatedSwitcher, not
// AnimatedOpacity, because the incoming widget is different.

5.3 Explicit animations

Status, interruption, and composing several animations

Explicit animation is more than the implicit version with more parameters; it changes what you can do, and the reason is the two capabilities implicit animation does not have. You can control the time dimension. A controller takes a duration you choose, and forward(from:) starts from a value you specify, which means "animate from 0.7 to 1.0 over two hundred milliseconds" is a single call. That is not expressible with an implicit widget, which only knows how to go from wherever it was to the new target. And you can compose. Because several controllers can drive one widget, a single animated property can be the product of two or three independent animations — a staggered entrance is several controllers with different intervals and one builder. Then the status and the interruption rules, which is where explicit animation actually gets tricky. forward() on a completed controller does nothing, because the controller is at its end value and the status is completed; the correct call to replay is forward(from: 0). This is the single most common confusion and the symptom is an animation that works once. An animation can be reversed from where it is, which is what makes a drag-to-dismiss gesture feel right: the gesture drives the controller's value directly, and if the user releases part way the controller animates either to the end or back to zero from the current value, and neither requires knowing how far the gesture got. And stop is not cancel. stop(canceled: true) stops the controller and stops the ticker, leaving the value where it is; stop(canceled: false) stops it but lets the animation complete to its target from where it is, which is the behaviour you want in a "settle back" gesture. Then the three composition patterns, because they cover most real cases. Sequential: one controller, and the second segment is a second controller whose animation begins when the first completes, driven by a status listener. Overlapping with intervals: one long controller whose value is mapped through an Interval so each property only responds during its own slice of the timeline, which is the elegant solution for a staggered entrance because it is one controller and one builder rather than several. And chained with a controller per property: simplest to read for two properties, and the right choice when the segments have different durations. Then the four mistakes that produce the reports. Forgetting dispose, which the architecture section covers. Calling setState inside a listener, which fights the framework — the builder is already called on every tick, so a setState adds a second rebuild per tick for no reason. Animating something that is expensive to rebuild, so a controller driving a subtree of hundreds of widgets drops frames regardless of how simple the animation is. And leaving the controller running after the widget leaves, which schedules frames for a screen that is gone and is the usual cause of "the app gets hot after I visit this page".

Driving an animation by hand, and the three required pieces.

class FadeIn extends StatefulWidget {
  const FadeIn({required this.child, super.key});
  final Widget child;

  @override
  State<FadeIn> createState() => _FadeInState();
}

class _FadeInState extends State<FadeIn> with SingleTickerProviderStateMixin {
  // 1. a controller. SingleTickerProviderStateMixin if there is
  //    one, TickerProviderStateMixin if there are several
  late final AnimationController _controller = AnimationController(
    vsync: this,                                  // REQUIRED
    duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 500),
  );

  // 2. a curve, if you want one
  late final Animation<double> _opacity = CurvedAnimation(
    parent: _controller,
    curve: Curves.easeOut,
  );

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _controller.forward();
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    // 3. ALWAYS dispose, or you leak the ticker
    _controller.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return FadeTransition(
      opacity: _opacity,
      child: widget.child,
    );
  }
}
// THE METHODS on AnimationController
_controller.forward(from: 0.0);      // play forward, optionally from a value
_controller.reverse();               // play backward
_controller.repeat(reverse: true);   // loop forever
_controller.stop();                  // pause where it is
_controller.reset();                 // jump to 0
_controller.value = 0.5;             // set directly (notifies listeners)
_controller.animateTo(1.0, duration: d, curve: c);
_controller.animateBack(0.0);
_controller.duration = ...;          // settable
_controller.value;                   // the current value
_controller.isAnimating;             // true while running
_controller.status;                   // forward, reverse, dismissed, completed

// MULTIPLE CONTROLLERS
class MultiAnim extends StatefulWidget {
  const MultiAnim({super.key});
  @override
  State<MultiAnim> createState() => _MultiAnimState();
}

class _MultiAnimState extends State<MultiAnim> with TickerProviderStateMixin {
  late final AnimationController _a = AnimationController(vsync: this, duration: const Duration(seconds: 1));
  late final AnimationController _b = AnimationController(vsync: this, duration: const Duration(seconds: 2));

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _a.dispose();
    _b.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }
  // ...
}

// the Tween classes
OpacityTransition(opacity: _controller, ...)          // double
SizeTransition(sizeFactor: _controller, ...)          // SizeFactor
PositionedTransition(position: _controller, ...)      // Offset
RotationTransition(turns: _controller, ...)           // double
ScaleTransition(scale: _controller, ...)              // Scale
SlideTransition(position: _controller, ...)           // Offset
DecoratedBoxTransition(decoration: _controller, ...)  // Decoration
DecoratedBoxTransition is the one for colour and shape

// AnimatedBuilder, for a value that drives something OTHER than
// a widget
AnimatedBuilder(
  animation: _controller,
  builder: (context, child) => CustomPaint(
    painter: _ProgressPainter(_controller.value),
    child: child,                     // the child is built ONCE
  ),
  child: const SizedBox(width: 200, height: 200),
)

5.4 Curves and physics

The curve catalogue, and how to choose

The named curves are a small, closed set and choosing between them is easier than it looks if you know what each one is for. Curves.linear is constant velocity and it is almost never right for a user interface: physical objects accelerate and decelerate, so a linear animation reads as mechanical because it does not. Curves.easeIn, easeOut and easeInOut are the three of a family, distinguished by which end the acceleration is at: easeIn starts slowly and ends fast, easeOut starts fast and ends slowly, and easeInOut does both. The convention is that easeOut is for something entering the screen and easeIn for something leaving it, which sounds arbitrary and is not: an element entering is decelerating into its final position, an element leaving is accelerating away from where it was, and matching the physics of arrival and departure is what makes motion read as physical. So if you change one default, change the implicit-animation default from linear to easeOut and most of your interface immediately feels better. Curves.fastOutSlowIn is the Material standard — a quick start, a long settle — and it is a good general-purpose choice because it spends few frames accelerating and many settling, which matches how attention moves: the eye tracks the start of a motion and then reads the destination. Curves.easeInOutCubic, easeOutCubic and the other *Cubic variants are polynomial curves with different rates, and the honest summary is that they differ in how abrupt they are and you can pick by trying; easeOutCubic is a good default for a large element because its deceleration is long enough to read. Curves.elasticOut and the bouncy curves are for a deliberate effect and are the ones to use least, because they are physically false — nothing the user interacts with overshoots and oscillates — and a screen full of them is tiring rather than playful. Then the two facts about curves that are not obvious and that matter. A curve shapes time, not distance, so a curve applied to a small movement looks almost linear while the same curve on a large movement is dramatic; if you want consistent perceived speed across sizes, animate a normalised value and scale it in the builder rather than hoping a curve will suit both. And the curve applies to the whole animation, including any delay before it, so a curve on a controller that waits before starting also bends the wait, which is occasionally what you want and is usually a surprise; the correct structure when you need both is an Interval on the timeline plus a curve applied inside the interval. Then the case where a curve is the wrong tool. When the motion should respond to input, a curve is a fixed time function and cannot respond to a finger; a drag gesture should be driven directly by the value and only settle with a curve after release, which is the explicit-animation section's material. And when the motion has a physical model — a fling, a spring, a card that should carry momentum — a time-based curve cannot express it at all, because the correct duration depends on the velocity at release.

/* The catalogue. */

The built-in curves, when to use which, and why physics usually looks better.

// THE BUILT-IN CURVES
Curves.linear
Curves.ease            // the CSS default. rarely what you want
Curves.easeIn          // slow start
Curves.easeOut         // slow end. the most natural for UI
Curves.easeInOut       // slow both ends
Curves.fastOutSlowIn   // Material 3 standard. the default look
Curves.easeOutCubic
Curves.easeInOutCubic
Curves.easeOutQuart
Curves.easeOutExpo     // very snappy
Curves.elasticOut      // overshoots and oscillates
Curves.elasticInOut
Curves.bounceOut       // bounces at the end
Curves.overshoot       // goes past, comes back
Curves.elasticIn
Curves.decelerate
Curves.anticipate      // pulls BACK before going

// THE CHOICE, in practice
// a colour or a size change:     Curves.easeOutCubic
// something entering the screen: Curves.easeOut
// something leaving:             Curves.easeIn
// a page transition:             Curves.easeInOutCubic
// Material components:           Curves.fastOutSlowIn
// a playful bounce:              Curves.elasticOut

// A CUSTOM CURVE
class BounceOut extends Curve {
  const BounceOut();

  @override
  double transformInternal(double t) {
    if (t < 1 / 2.75) return 7.5625 * t * t;
    if (t < 2 / 2.75) {
      t -= 1.5 / 2.75;
      return 7.5625 * t * t + 0.75;
    }
    if (t < 2.5 / 2.75) {
      t -= 2.25 / 2.75;
      return 7.5625 * t * t + 0.9375;
    }
    t -= 2.625 / 2.75;
    return 7.5625 * t * t + 0.984375;
  }
}

// or with a Cubic
class EaseOutBack extends Curve {
  const EaseOutBack();
  static const _c1 = 1.70158;
  static const _c3 = _c1 + 1;

  @override
  double transformInternal(double t) {
    return _c3 * t * t * t - _c1 * t * t;
  }
}
// THE PROBLEM WITH TIMED ANIMATIONS: they feel dead when the
// user interrupts them, and they do not respond to a drag
//
// a drag that moves a box, released with velocity, and the box
// carries on and settles - that needs PHYSICS, not a duration

// a crude physics animation with an AnimationController
class FlingSimulation extends Simulation {
  FlingSimulation({required this.position, required this.velocity, this.friction = 0.135});

  double position;
  double velocity;
  final double friction;

  @override
  double x(double time) {
    // an exponential decay, integrated
    return position +
        velocity * (1 - (1 - friction).pow(time * 60) / 60 / friction * friction) /
            1;
  }

  @override
  double dx(double time) {
    final double v = velocity * (1 - friction).pow(time * 60);
    return v;
  }

  @override
  bool isDone(double time) => velocity.abs() < 0.5;

  @override
  void advance(double dt) {
    position += dx(dt) * dt;
    velocity = dx(dt);
  }
}

// driving a Simulation with an AnimationController
_controller.animateWith(FlingSimulation(position: _x, velocity: _velocity));
// and reading the value:
AnimatedBuilder(
  animation: _controller,
  builder: (context, _) => Transform.translate(
    offset: Offset(_controller.value, 0),
    child: box,
  ),
)

5.5 Springs and Simulation

Springs, simulations, and reading the parameters

A spring is a physical model rather than a duration and a curve, and that difference shows up in every property of the API. A SpringDescription has two numbers that matter: stiffness and damping. The mass is normally one and rarely worth changing. Stiffness is how hard the spring pulls toward its target, and the practical reading is that higher stiffness means faster and more forceful: a low-stiffness spring takes noticeably longer to arrive and a high-stiffness one arrives almost immediately. Damping is how much the spring resists overshooting, and the ratio of the two is what determines the feel. Below a ratio of one the spring overshoots and oscillates — it arrives, passes the target, comes back — and the amount of visible bounce is the ratio's distance below one. At a ratio of one it is critically damped: it reaches the target as fast as possible without overshooting at all, which is the right default for almost everything. Above one it is overdamped and approaches the target slowly, feeling sluggish, which is the failure people describe as a spring that "feels like it is dragging". Then the practical consequences, which is the useful part. A spring's duration is not specified and cannot be, because the time it takes is an output of the parameters; this means a spring cannot be used where a known duration is needed, such as an animation that must complete before a navigation, and it means two springs tuned to arrive together will not if their parameters differ in stiffness. Retargeting a running spring keeps its velocity, which is the property that makes a gesture-driven spring feel right: interrupting a spring and changing its target does not restart it, it redirects it while carrying the momentum, so the motion is continuous. And a spring can overshoot past its target and come back, which is the effect people want from a playful interface and which is unphysical for a data visualisation — so a chart's value transition should be a critically damped spring or a curve, not a bouncy one. Then the two alternatives, and when each is right. A SpringSimulation driven directly gives full control and is what the framework's own physics-backed widgets use; you build the simulation, you own the ticker, and you are responsible for stopping it. And AnimationController.animateWith with a spring simulation is the same thing expressed through a controller, which is usually what you want because the controller gives you the status, the value range and the disposal for free. And then the two things to be careful of. Sizing matters: the framework provides spring descriptions tuned for small, medium and large movements, and using the large one for a two-pixel change produces a visibly sluggish animation while using the small one for a full-screen transition produces a violent one. And a spring driven by a slow frame rate is wrong: the simulation advances by elapsed time, so it is frame-rate independent, but a spring that is being stepped at ten frames per second has a much larger time step and will overshoot differently than the same spring at sixty — which is another reason to keep the animation cheap.

A spring is the right tool whenever the user can interrupt the animation. A timed animation that is interrupted mid-flight has no correct continuation, so it either snaps or restarts, and both feel wrong. A spring takes the current velocity as input, so it always continues from where the finger left off.

// THE SPRING: mass, stiffness, damping. It has no duration, and
// that is the point: it always feels physically right, whatever
// the starting velocity.

class SpringSimulation extends Simulation {
  SpringSimulation({
    required this.start,
    required this.end,
    required this.velocity,
    required this.spring,
    required this.damping,
    this.snapToEnd = false,
  });

  final double start;
  final double end;
  final double velocity;
  final SpringDescription spring;
  final double damping;
  final bool snapToEnd;

  // the description, which is what you tune
  //   stiffness: how hard it pulls toward the target
  //   mass: how heavy the thing is
  //   damping: how much the oscillation is damped
  //     low damping  -> it bounces
  //     high damping -> it crawls in
  //   the underdamped/critically-damped/overdamped boundary is
  //   damping / (2 * sqrt(stiffness * mass)) vs 1
  @override
  double x(double time) { ... }

  @override
  double dx(double time) { ... }

  @override
  bool isDone(double time) => snapToEnd;
}

// the convenience constructors
SpringDescription.withDampingRatio({
  required double mass,
  required double stiffness,
  required double ratio,      // <1 underdamped, 1 critical, >1 overdamped
}) : assert(mass > 0);

SpringDescription.withBouncing(mass: 1, stiffness: 500);  // a preset
// USING A SPRING, which is the good version of the above
class SpringyButton extends StatefulWidget {
  const SpringyButton({super.key});
  @override
  State<SpringyButton> createState() => _SpringyButtonState();
}

class _SpringyButtonState extends State<SpringyButton>
    with SingleTickerProviderStateMixin {
  late final AnimationController _controller = AnimationController(
    vsync: this,
    // a spring has no duration, so give it a long "duration"
    // that acts as a time limit
    duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 600),
  );
  double _scale = 1.0;
  Offset _velocity = Offset.zero;

  void _press(TapDownDetails details) {
    // press in, with the gesture VELOCITY
    _controller.animateWith(
      SpringSimulation(
        start: 0.9,
        end: 1.0,
        velocity: -3.0,
        spring: const SpringDescription(mass: 1, stiffness: 500, damping: 30),
      ),
    );
  }

  void _release(TapUpDetails details) {
    _controller.animateWith(
      SpringSimulation(
        start: _scale,
        end: 1.0,
        velocity: 0.0,
        spring: const SpringDescription(mass: 1, stiffness: 400, damping: 28),
      ),
    );
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return GestureDetector(
      onTapDown: _press,
      onTapUp: _release,
      child: AnimatedBuilder(
        animation: _controller,
        builder: (context, child) => Transform.scale(
          scale: _controller.value,
          child: child,
        ),
        child: const ElevatedButton(onPressed: null, child: Text('Press me')),
      ),
    );
  }
}

// the tuning table, from experience
//   a subtle UI press:      stiffness 400, damping 25
//   a playful pop:          stiffness 300, damping 15
//   a drawer sliding in:    stiffness 350, damping 30
//   a card snapping back:   stiffness 500, damping 30
//   a heavy, slow movement: stiffness 100, damping 25
//   too low damping:        it oscillates visibly
//   too high damping:       it feels sluggish

5.6 Hero and page transitions

Transitions, and why a route transition is not a widget animation

A route transition is a different mechanism from an animation widget and the distinction matters because they compose in ways that surprise people. A route transition is an Animation<double> from zero to one that the navigator drives, and it is the thing that produces the standard push, and the reason it is not a widget is that the two screens must both exist during the transition — the outgoing route is still on screen while the incoming one is arriving, and an ordinary animation can only animate one widget's properties. So a transition is built from the animation plus two subtrees: the previous route's page and the new route's page, each wrapped in whatever effect the transition describes. That is why a custom transition takes a builder receiving a BuildContext and an Animation<double> and returns a widget: it is being asked to compose two things that both exist. Then the built-in transitions and what each is for, because they are not variations. A slide moves the incoming route in from the edge, which is the correct convention for a hierarchical relationship — a detail screen belongs to a list — and the horizontal direction should reverse for a right-to-left locale, which the framework does if you use the platform-aware variant rather than hard-coding a direction. A fade cross-dissolves both routes, and it is the right choice when there is no spatial relationship — a modal, a tab switch, a search result — because sliding implies a hierarchy that is not there. A shared-axis transition moves both routes along the same axis in opposite directions, which reads as "these are siblings at the same level" and is the right choice for switching tabs or changing a filter. Scale grows or shrinks the incoming route and is used for a dialog-like presentation; fade through briefly fades to a solid colour before the new route appears and is the one to use when the two routes have nothing in common and a slide would look like a mistake. Then the two things that make a custom transition correct, and both are easy to get wrong. It must respect the animation's value, not time. The animation is driven by the navigator and its value may run backwards if the user presses back mid-transition, so a transition built on a timer or a one-shot forward animation breaks; building from the supplied value means a reversed transition plays in reverse, which is what the user expects. And the outgoing route must remain mounted for the duration, so the builder is given two subtrees rather than one and both must be used; a transition that returns only the incoming route produces a flash of background during the transition, which is the most common custom-transition bug. Then the composition cases. A hero animation moving an element from one route to another is a separate mechanism built on a shared Hero widget with the same key on both sides, and it works with any transition because it operates on the two subtrees independently of what the transition does with them. A fade through plus a hero is wrong on purpose — the fade hides the movement — and the choice of which to use is a design decision about whether the user should track the element or simply see the destination.

/* Why it is not a widget. */

Shared-element transitions, custom route transitions, and the animations that look wrong.

// HERO: the shared element animation. THE widget that makes an
// app feel native.
class EntryList extends StatelessWidget {
  const EntryList({required this.entries, super.key});
  final List<Entry> entries;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return ListView.builder(
      itemCount: entries.length,
      itemBuilder: (context, index) {
        final entry = entries[index];
        return GestureDetector(
          onTap: () => Navigator.of(context).push(
            MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => EntryDetail(entry: entry)),
          ),
          // the Hero. The tag must be UNIQUE and MATCH on both sides
          child: Hero(
            tag: 'entry-image-${entry.id}',
            child: ClipRRect(
              borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(12),
              child: Image.network(entry.imageUrl, fit: BoxFit.cover),
            ),
          ),
        );
      },
    );
  }
}

class EntryDetail extends StatelessWidget {
  const EntryDetail({required this.entry, super.key});
  final Entry entry;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(title: Text(entry.title)),
      body: Column(children: [
        // the SAME tag, so Flutter matches them
        Hero(
          tag: 'entry-image-${entry.id}',
          child: Image.network(entry.imageUrl, fit: BoxFit.cover),
        ),
        const SizedBox(height: 16),
        Text(entry.body),
      ]),
    );
  }
}

// HERO RULES
// 1. the tags must match exactly
// 2. BOTH sides must be in the tree when the route changes
// 3. do not put a Hero inside a scrolling list that unmounts
//    during the transition: the flight is interrupted
// 4. flightShuttleBuilder for a custom look
Hero(
  tag: tag,
  createRectTween: (begin, end) => MaterialRectArcTween(begin: begin, end: end),
  flightShuttleBuilder: (context, animation, direction, from, to) {
    return AnimatedBuilder(
      animation: animation,
      builder: (context, _) => to.widget,
    );
  },
  child: content,
);
// CUSTOM PAGE TRANSITIONS
class SlideRoute<T> extends PageRouteBuilder<T> {
  SlideRoute({required this.page, this.offset = const Offset(1, 0)})
      : super(
          transitionDuration: const Duration(milliseconds: 300),
          reverseTransitionDuration: const Duration(milliseconds: 250),
          pageBuilder: (context, animation, secondary) => page,
          transitionsBuilder: (context, animation, secondary, child) {
            final curved = CurvedAnimation(parent: animation, curve: Curves.easeOutCubic);
            return SlideTransition(
              position: Tween(begin: offset, end: Offset.zero).animate(curved),
              child: child,
            );
          },
        );

  final Widget page;
  final Offset offset;
}

// shared axis: the Material 3 pattern, which is what native apps
// use for a "deeper" or "sibling" relationship
class SharedAxisPageRoute<T> extends PageRouteBuilder<T> {
  SharedAxisPageRoute({required this.page, this.type = AxisTransitionType.horizontal})
      : super(
          transitionDuration: const Duration(milliseconds: 300),
          pageBuilder: (context, animation, secondary) => page,
          transitionsBuilder: (context, animation, secondary, child) {
            final fade = CurvedAnimation(parent: animation, curve: Curves.fastOutSlowIn);
            final slide = Tween<Offset>(begin: const Offset(0, 0.1), end: Offset.zero)
                .animate(fade);
            return FadeTransition(
              opacity: fade,
              child: SlideTransition(position: slide, child: child),
            );
          },
        );

  final Widget page;
  final AxisTransitionType type;
}

// with go_router, set it per route - see chapter 8
PageRouteBuilder(
  pageBuilder: (context, state) => DetailScreen(),
  transitionsBuilder: (context, state, animation, child) =>
      FadeTransition(opacity: animation, child: child),
);

5.7 Motion, staggered and shared axis

// STAGGERED: children appear one after another
class StaggeredList extends StatelessWidget {
  const StaggeredList({required this.items, super.key});
  final List<Widget> items;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Column(
      children: [
        for (var i = 0; i < items.length; i++)
          TweenAnimationBuilder<double>(
            // the KEY is what creates the stagger: each item
            // has its own delay
            key: ValueKey(i),
            tween: Tween(begin: 0.0, end: 1.0),
            duration: Duration(milliseconds: 300 + i * 80),
            curve: Curves.easeOutCubic,
            builder: (context, value, child) => Opacity(
              opacity: value,
              child: Transform.translate(
                offset: Offset(0, 20 * (1 - value)),
                child: child,
              ),
            ),
            child: items[i],         // built once
          ),
      ],
    );
  }
}

// THE ANIMATION PACKAGE, which is worth learning for real work:
//   https://pub.dev/packages/animation
// it has builders that handle the "run when it first appears"
// logic, which is what stagger and entrance animations actually
// need
AnimationLimiter(
  child: ListView.builder(
    itemCount: 20,
    itemBuilder: (context, index) => AnimationConfiguration.staggeredList(
      position: index,
      duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 375),
      child: SlideAnimation(
        verticalOffset: 30.0,
        child: FadeInAnimation(child: ListTile(title: Text('Item $index'))),
      ),
    ),
  ),
);

Staggering, and the rules for choreographing a group

When several things change at once, the order and the delay between them determine whether the change reads as one event or as several, and the difference is worth designing deliberately because it is the difference between an interface that feels considered and one that feels busy. A stagger is a delay derived from an item's index. The mechanism is simple — Interval on a single controller, so each item responds only during its own slice of the timeline — and the elegance is that one controller drives every item, which means one setState-free builder and no coordination. Three parameters decide the character, and each has a defensible default. How long the whole thing takes should be short: the total duration including all the staggering, because a stagger that takes a second to finish is a second during which the interface is in motion, and the eye reads a long cascade as slow rather than as graceful. How much delay between items should be small enough that the items read as related — a few tens of milliseconds, not a tenth of a second, which is long enough for each item to be perceived as a separate event. And how many items should be staggered at all, which is the rule that is usually violated: stagger a small, fixed number of items — five, six — and let the rest appear together. A list of forty items staggered by thirty milliseconds each takes over a second to settle and looks broken; the same list with the first six staggered and the remainder appearing at the six-item point looks deliberate. Then the shared-axis and shared-element cases, which are the two forms of choreography that carry meaning rather than decoration. A shared axis says "same level". When a tab changes, both the outgoing and incoming content move along one axis in opposite directions, and the eye reads them as peers being swapped rather than as a page turning. A shared element says "the same thing, moved". A hero animation carrying a card from a list into a detail view tells the user that the thing they tapped is the thing now on screen, which is why hero animations are used on exactly the transitions where the user needs that confirmation and skipped where they do not. And a hero that moves across a fade-through is wasted, because the fade removes the continuity the hero depends on — this is the composition rule from the previous section and it is the single most common way a well-intentioned motion design fails. Then the three rules about when to animate at all, which are worth as much as the technique. Animate the change the user caused, not the ones they did not. Keep the duration proportional to the distance travelled, because a full-screen slide at the same duration as a ten-pixel fade feels wrong in one direction or the other. And respect the reduced-motion setting, which is both an accessibility requirement and a performance win: wrap the application's motion so that when the preference is set, animations become instant, and every screen gets the correct behaviour without each one consulting the preference.

/* What a stagger is. */
const STAGGER = {
  is: 'A DELAY DERIVED FROM AN ITEMS INDEX',
  mechanism: 'Interval ON A SINGLE CONTROLLER, so EACH ITEM RESPONDS ONLY DURING ITS OWN SLICE of the TIMELINE',
  whyElegant: 'ONE CONTROLLER DRIVES EVERY ITEM, which MEANS ONE BUILDER and NO COORDINATION',
  readsAs: 'whether the CHANGE READS AS ONE EVENT or AS SEVERAL is THE DIFFERENCE between an INTERFACE THAT FEELS CONSIDERED and one THAT FEELS BUSY',
};

/* Three parameters. */
const PARAMETERS = [
  { p: 'HOW LONG the WHOLE THING TAKES', shouldBe: 'SHORT',
    why: 'the TOTAL DURATION INCLUDING ALL the STAGGERING',
    detail: 'a STAGGER THAT TAKES A SECOND TO FINISH IS A SECOND DURING WHICH the INTERFACE IS IN MOTION',
    symptom: 'and the EYE READS A LONG CASCADE AS SLOW rather than AS GRACEFUL' },
  { p: 'HOW MUCH DELAY BETWEEN ITEMS', shouldBe: 'A FEW TENS OF MILLISECONDS',
    why: 'small enough THAT THE ITEMS READ AS RELATED',
