5.8 Animation performance

Why animations drop frames, and finding which cause it is

A dropped frame during an animation is almost always one of four things, and the performance panel tells you which in one reading — the difficulty is that people guess instead of reading, and the guesses are usually wrong. The first cause is building too much per tick. An animation calls a builder on every frame; if that builder creates widgets, allocates objects, or triggers layout over a large subtree, the frame budget is gone before painting starts. The fix is to make the builder build as little as possible: pass the animated value down to a leaf that rebuilds cheaply rather than rebuilding a container that contains a hundred widgets. The second is painting too much. A builder that animates a property requiring a repaint — a colour, an opacity, a shadow — repaints on every frame, and if the repainted area is large the rasteriser is the bottleneck. The fix is the repaint boundary, and the diagnostic is the raster row in the panel. The third is layout. Anything whose size changes — an animated width, a growing text, a value that changes the number of digits — forces a layout pass on every frame, and layout is on the platform thread so it blocks interaction as well as costing frame time. The fix is to animate something that does not change layout: a transform, an opacity, or a fixed-size container whose content changes. And the fourth is the ticker itself, which is the case people forget: an animation whose controller is being driven more than once, or a controller driving several independent rebuilds, will schedule frames faster than they can be produced, and the frame chart shows a build or layout row that looks fine but a total frame time over budget — which means the time is somewhere the panel attributes elsewhere. Then the discipline, and it is the same discipline as every other performance work in this book. Measure in profile mode on a real device. A debug build on a desktop will show an animation as smooth when it is dropping every fourth frame on a phone, because debug builds have different timing characteristics and a desktop has an order of magnitude more headroom. Read the frame chart, not the jank percentage. The chart shows four rows per frame and the row that is long is the diagnosis; the jank percentage tells you only that something is wrong. And fix the largest row. A frame that is over budget because three rows are slightly over is a different problem from one that is over budget because one row is four times over, and treating the first as the second produces work that does not help.

/* Four causes. */
const CAUSES = [
  { c: 'BUILDING TOO MUCH PER TICK',
    why: 'AN ANIMATION CALLS A BUILDER ON EVERY FRAME',
    detail: 'if that BUILDER CREATES WIDGETS, ALLOCATES OBJECTS, or TRIGGERS LAYOUT over a LARGE SUBTREE, the FRAME BUDGET IS GONE BEFORE PAINTING STARTS',
    fix: 'MAKE the BUILDER BUILD AS LITTLE AS POSSIBLE',
    how: ['PASS the ANIMATED VALUE DOWN to a LEAF THAT REBUILDS CHEAPLY',
      'rather than REBUILDING A CONTAINER THAT CONTAINS A HUNDRED WIDGETS'] },
  { c: 'PAINTING TOO MUCH',
    detail: 'A BUILDER THAT ANIMATES A PROPERTY REQUIRING A REPAINT - A COLOUR, AN OPACITY, A SHADOW - REPAINTS ON EVERY FRAME',
    and: 'if the REPAINTED AREA IS LARGE the RASTERISER IS THE BOTTLENECK',
    fix: 'the REPAINT BOUNDARY', diagnostic: 'the RASTER ROW in the PANEL' },
  { c: 'LAYOUT',
    detail: 'ANYTHING WHOSE SIZE CHANGES - AN ANIMATED WIDTH, A GROWING TEXT, A VALUE THAT CHANGES THE NUMBER OF DIGITS - FORCES A LAYOUT PASS ON EVERY FRAME',
    and: 'LAYOUT IS ON THE PLATFORM THREAD so it BLOCKS INTERACTION as well as COSTING FRAME TIME',
    fix: 'ANIMATE SOMETHING THAT DOES NOT CHANGE LAYOUT - A TRANSFORM, AN OPACITY, or A FIXED-SIZE CONTAINER WHOSE CONTENT CHANGES' },

    detail: 'AN ANIMATION WHOSE CONTROLLER IS BEING DRIVEN MORE THAN ONCE, or a CONTROLLER DRIVING SEVERAL INDEPENDENT REBUILDS, WILL SCHEDULE FRAMES FASTER THAN THEY CAN BE PRODUCED',

/* The discipline. */
const DISCIPLINE = [
  { d: 'MEASURE IN PROFILE MODE ON A REAL DEVICE',

    consequence: 'and TREATING THE FIRST AS the SECOND PRODUCES WORK THAT DOES NOT HELP' },
];

Animating width, height, padding or a Positioned offset runs the layout pass on every frame. On a complex subtree that is 16ms of layout before anything is painted, and the animation drops frames no matter how small the change is. Transform.translate and Transform.scale are paint-only and cost essentially nothing.

// THE FOUR THINGS THAT MAKE AN ANIMATION DROP FRAMES
//
// 1. work in build(), every frame
//    the fix: AnimatedBuilder with a `child` parameter, so the
//    subtree is built once
// BAD
AnimatedBuilder(
  animation: controller,
  builder: (context, child) {
    return Opacity(opacity: controller.value, child: ExpensiveWidget());
  },
)
// GOOD
AnimatedBuilder(
  animation: controller,
  builder: (context, child) {
    return Opacity(opacity: controller.value, child: child);
  },
  child: const ExpensiveWidget(),       // built ONCE
)

// 2. animating a property that triggers LAYOUT
//    width, height, padding, margin: layout runs every frame
//    GOOD: Transform.translate / Transform.scale
//    GOOD: FractionalTranslation
//    BAD:   Positioned(left: animatedValue)
//    BAD:   Padding(left: animatedValue)
//    a Container(width: animatedValue) is a layout animation
//
// 3. animating opacity on a huge subtree with a Blur
//    Opacity with a value between 0 and 1 needs a saveLayer
//    fix: keep the opacity at 1.0 most of the time, or use a
//    simpler child
//
// 4. the build method doing real work
//    parsing JSON in build, calling a repository, sorting a list
//    every frame
// THE CHEAP-PROPERTY LIST
//
// layout (EXPENSIVE to animate):
//   width, height, padding, margin, alignment, constraints,
//   flex, position (in a Stack)
//
// paint (CHEAP, a render-object property):
//   opacity, color, borderRadius, borderColor, backgroundColor,
//   transform (all four), decoration, shadows, elevation
//
// So: animate opacity, colour, scale and translate. Almost
// everything looks good with those four.

// the golden rule
// "if it can be expressed as a transform or an opacity, animate it
//  that way. Everything else is a fallback."

// MEASURE IT
// flutter run --profile
// DevTools -> Performance -> record during the animation
// a red bar in the UI thread row = your build/layout/paint
// a red bar in the RASTER row = a blur, a shadow, an image

6 · Gestures and Input

6.1 The gesture arena6.2 The basic gesture detectors6.3 Drag and drop6.4 Scrollables and physics6.5 RawGestureDetector and recognisers6.6 Scale, rotate and pinch6.7 Semantics and accessibility hooks6.8 Text input and the keyboard

Gesture handling is where a Flutter app either feels native or feels like a web page. The gesture arena is the mechanism behind all of it.

6.1 The gesture arena

Why the arena exists, and the rules that come out of it

The gesture arena exists because a single physical event can be several gestures at once, and the framework must choose. When the user touches the screen, the framework walks down from the root to find every recogniser whose hit-test area contains the point, and every one of them is a candidate. Each recogniser is added to the arena, and the arena accepts a gesture only when a member declares victory. A recogniser can win by being the first to recognise and claiming the arena, or by winning outright — a vertical drag recogniser declares victory when it recognises because horizontal and vertical drags are mutually exclusive. Until one wins, everyone is waiting, which is the detail that explains the most common gesture bug: nothing happens on touch-down, and the first movement is what resolves it. That is deliberate — a tap must not be cancelled by a small amount of finger movement, so the tap recogniser holds out — but it means a recogniser that never declares victory can hold the arena open indefinitely, and if the user simply taps and holds, nothing fires until they move or lift.

Then the four practical consequences, each of which is a design decision rather than a bug. Declare victory as early as you legally can. The framework requires a recogniser that has won the arena to have won it by an acceptable margin, so "as early as you can" means the first moment the gesture is unambiguously one kind and not another; a recogniser that waits for the finger to lift before claiming will lose to a parent Scrollable every time. Add to the arena only when you are genuinely ambiguous. A custom recogniser that immediately rejects any pointer event it does not want is cheaper and more predictable than one that enters the arena and then withdraws, because entering and withdrawing costs a full arena pass each time. Never win by rejecting after another recogniser has already won. The arena has already been resolved and dependents are being notified; a late rejection produces an inconsistent state, and the framework asserts in debug mode. And recognisers higher in the tree win ties. The arena sweeps depth-first from the root, and the first member to declare victory wins, which is why a recogniser placed as an ancestor of a scroll view behaves differently from the same recogniser placed as a sibling of it — and why "my gesture works but only sometimes" is usually an arena-resolution issue rather than a hit-test issue. And then the two ways to take control, and the honest advice on which to use. RawGestureDetector gives you the arena directly — you can build recognisers, configure which are in the team, and set who wins — and it is the tool when you need a gesture that the framework's recognisers do not model at all. Overriding recogniser configuration on an existing detector is the tool for the far more common case of tuning: which pointer device kinds count, whether a drag starts immediately or after a threshold, whether a gesture is already accepted elsewhere. And the honest ranking is that restructuring beats both: if the gesture is wrong because the widget tree puts the wrong thing in the arena, moving or wrapping a widget solves it in a line, and reaching for RawGestureDetector to work around a tree problem produces recogniser code that is harder to reason about and interacts with scroll views in ways that are hard to predict.

/* Why it exists. */
const WHY = {

The arena explains every "my tap handler is not firing" bug and every "both handlers fire" bug. When one recogniser wins, the others are rejected for the rest of that pointer sequence - they will not fire later, even after the movement settles. That is why a tap recogniser that has already been rejected cannot recover.

Why two nested gesture detectors conflict, and how the arena resolves it.

// THE ARENA: every pointer event goes to a contest
//
// 1. a pointer goes down
// 2. every GestureDetector in the hit-test path adds a recogniser
//    to the ARENA
// 3. when one recogniser declares VICTORY (a tap, a drag start),
//    it wins, and the arena is closed: every other recogniser is
//    rejected and will not fire
// 4. if two try to win in the same frame, the FIRST in the hit
//    test order wins - which is the innermost, deepest widget
//
// THAT is why nesting conflicts:
GestureDetector(                    // outer: registered first
  onTap: () => print('outer'),
  child: GestureDetector(            // inner: registered second
    onTap: () => print('inner'),
    child: Container(color: Colors.red),
  ),
)
// TAPPING: the inner wins, because it registered first.
// 'outer' does NOT fire.

// SCROLLING: VerticalDragGestureRecognizer wins the arena against
// a TapGestureRecognizer on the same widget, because a drag
// requires movement and a tap requires stillness. The arena
// holds the tap in a state where it MIGHT win until the pointer
// is released without movement.
// THE FIXES FOR A CONFLICT
//
// 1. GestureArenaTeam: let two recognisers cooperate
//    (see 6.5, and the ReorderableList source for a real example)

// 2. put them on DIFFERENT widgets, so only one is in the path
GestureDetector(
  onTap: onCardTap,
  child: Row(children: [
    // the inner one only handles its own area
    GestureDetector(
      onTap: onAvatarTap,
      child: const Avatar(),
    ),
    Expanded(child: Text(title)),
  ]),
)

// 3. HitTestBehavior: control what is in the hit-test path
GestureDetector(
  behavior: HitTestBehavior.opaque,     // always claim the hit
  onTap: f,
  child: child,
)
//   deferToChild   (the default) only the child is hit-tested
//   opaque         this widget is hit even if the child is not
//   translucent    both this and the child, and siblings behind
//   passThrough    neither: the event goes to what is BEHIND

// 4. RawGestureDetector, to control the arena directly
// 5. restructure: the right answer more often than not

6.2 The basic gesture detectors

GestureDetector(
  // TAP
  onTap: () {},
  onTapDown: (d) {},           // a finger went down
  onTapUp: (d) {},             // and came up
  onTapCancel: () {},          // and was cancelled
  onDoubleTap: () {},
  onLongPress: () {},
  onLongPressStart: (d) {},    // after the long-press delay
  onLongPressMoveUpdate: (d) {},
  onLongPressEnd: (d) {},

  // DOUBLE TAP, with a delay that is too long for a single tap
  onDoubleTapDown: (d) {},

  // the FLING: a fast swipe, with velocity
  onHorizontalDragStart: (d) {},
  onHorizontalDragUpdate: (d) {
    // d.delta is the movement SINCE THE LAST EVENT
    // d.primaryDelta is the movement along the recogniser's axis
    // d.globalPosition is where the finger is NOW
    // d.localPosition is the same, in this widget's coordinates
  },
  onHorizontalDragEnd: (d) {
    d.primaryVelocity;          // signed, +right / -left
    d.velocity.pixelsPerSecond;  // a full Velocity object
  },
  onVerticalDragStart: (d) {},
  onVerticalDragUpdate: (d) {},
  onVerticalDragEnd: (d) {},

  // the two together, for a pan
  onPanStart: (d) {},
  onPanUpdate: (d) {},
  onPanEnd: (d) {},

  child: child,
)

// child: the target size. a GestureDetector with a small child
// only responds where the child is, unless you set behavior
GestureDetector(
  behavior: HitTestBehavior.opaque,   // the whole area responds
  onTap: onTap,
  child: const SizedBox(width: 200, height: 200),
)

// MouseRegion for a desktop/web hover and cursor
MouseRegion(
  onEnter: (_) => setState(() => _hovered = true),
  onExit: (_) => setState(() => _hovered = false),
  cursor: _hovered ? SystemMouseCursors.click : SystemMouseCursors.basic,
  child: ...,
);

// a clickable that is a BUTTON, and therefore has semantics,
// focus, and a Material ink splash for free
FilledButton(onPressed: onPressed, child: Text(label));

Choosing between the detectors, and what each is actually for

There are five gesture detectors and they are not variants of each other; they are different answers to different questions, and picking the wrong one is the most common reason a gesture does not behave as intended. GestureDetector is the general-purpose one, built from recognisers and configured with a handful of callbacks — onTap, onTapDown, onTapUp, onTapCancel, onLongPress, onPanStart, onPanUpdate, onPanEnd, onScaleStart, onHorizontalDragUpdate and the rest. Its strength is that one widget can express a compound gesture — tap-and-hold-then-drag is a state machine over its callbacks — and its weakness is exactly that: the callbacks are not arbitrated against each other, so a pan and a tap can both fire from one gesture unless you write the state machine. InkWell, GestureDetector and MouseRegion together form the Material trio, and the difference is what each contributes: InkWell adds the ink splash and the Material ripple and handles accessibility activation, GestureDetector adds the gesture recognition, and MouseRegion adds hover and enter/exit plus cursor shape. A Material button gives you all three; a custom tappable therefore needs all three or it will lack the splash, the hover state and the keyboard activation. RawGestureDetector is the underlying recogniser wiring with no widget-level conveniences. And Listener is not a gesture detector at all — it receives raw pointer events before any recognition, and it is the right tool only for things no recogniser models: a custom drawing canvas tracking the pointer, a hover effect that must not be interrupted by a gesture. Then the three properties that change recognition, and each has a specific consequence. behavior — the default for GestureDetector is to defer to the child, so a transparent or padding-only child means no gestures; setting it to opaque makes the detector itself the hit-test target. This is the single most common cause of "my onTap does nothing", and it is invisible because nothing is drawn there. onTapDown versus onTap — down fires on touch-down and tap fires after the recogniser has decided, which is after the arena resolves and possibly after a cancel; a highlight that appears on down and is removed on tap needs both, and removing it on cancel is the case people forget. And excludeFromSemantics, which is the accessibility lever: leaving it false means the detector publishes a semantic action for its callbacks, which is what makes the thing operable by a screen reader and by a keyboard, and setting it true on a purely decorative gesture detector prevents a meaningless announcement.

/* Five detectors, five different questions. */
const DETECTORS = [
  { d: 'GestureDetector', kind: 'GENERAL-PURPOSE',
    builtFrom: 'RECOGNISERS',
    callbacks: ['onTap', 'onTapDown', 'onTapUp', 'onTapCancel', 'onLongPress',
      'onPanStart', 'onPanUpdate', 'onPanEnd', 'onScaleStart', 'onHorizontalDragUpdate'],
    strength: 'ONE WIDGET CAN EXPRESS A COMPOUND GESTURE - tap-and-hold-then-drag IS A STATE MACHINE over ITS CALLBACKS',
    weakness: 'EXACTLY THAT - the CALLBACKS ARE NOT ARBITRATED AGAINST EACH OTHER',
    so: 'a PAN and a TAP CAN BOTH FIRE FROM ONE GESTURE UNLESS YOU WRITE the STATE MACHINE' },
  { d: 'the Material trio', parts: [
    { p: 'InkWell', adds: 'the INK SPLASH and the MATERIAL RIPPLE and HANDLES ACCESSIBILITY ACTIVATION' },
    { p: 'GestureDetector', adds: 'the GESTURE RECOGNITION' },
    { p: 'MouseRegion', adds: 'HOVER and ENTER/EXIT PLUS CURSOR SHAPE' },
  ],
    note: 'a MATERIAL BUTTON GIVES YOU ALL THREE',
    custom: 'a CUSTOM TAPPABLE THEREFORE NEEDS ALL THREE or it WILL LACK the SPLASH, the HOVER STATE and the KEYBOARD ACTIVATION' },
  { d: 'RawGestureDetector', is: 'the UNDERLYING RECOGNISER WIRING with NO WIDGET-LEVEL CONVENIENCES' },
  { d: 'Listener', isNot: 'A GESTURE DETECTOR AT ALL',
    receives: 'RAW POINTER EVENTS BEFORE ANY RECOGNITION',
    rightWhen: 'things NO RECOGNISER MODELS - a CUSTOM DRAWING CANVAS TRACKING the POINTER, a HOVER EFFECT THAT MUST NOT BE INTERRUPTED BY A GESTURE' },

/* Three properties. */
const PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'behavior', default: 'the DEFAULT for GestureDetector IS TO DEFER TO the CHILD',
    consequence: 'a TRANSPARENT or PADDING-ONLY CHILD MEANS NO GESTURES',
    fix: 'SETTING IT TO OPAQUE MAKES the DETECTOR ITSELF the HIT-TEST TARGET',
    whyItMatters: 'this is THE SINGLE MOST COMMON CAUSE OF my onTap does nothing',

  { p: 'excludeFromSemantics', isThe: 'ACCESSIBILITY LEVER',
    leavingFalse: 'LEAVING IT FALSE MEANS the DETECTOR PUBLISHES A SEMANTIC ACTION for ITS CALLBACKS',
    gain: 'which is WHAT MAKES the THING OPERABLE BY A SCREEN READER and BY A KEYBOARD',
    settingTrue: 'SETTING IT TRUE ON A PURELY DECORATIVE GESTURE DETECTOR PREVENTS A MEANINGLESS ANNOUNCEMENT' },
];

6.3 Drag and drop

// DRAGGING: the offset must be applied and accumulated, and
// the widget must not be in the way of its own hit test
class DraggableBox extends StatefulWidget {
  const DraggableBox({super.key});
  @override
  State<DraggableBox> createState() => _DraggableBoxState();
}

class _DraggableBoxState extends State<DraggableBox> {
  Offset _offset = Offset.zero;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return GestureDetector(
      onPanUpdate: (d) => setState(() => _offset += d.delta),
      onPanEnd: (d) {
        // a FLING: keep moving with the velocity, and stop on
        // the screen edge
        final size = MediaQuery.sizeOf(context);
        var target = _offset;
        target = Offset(
          target.dx + d.velocity.pixelsPerSecond.dx * 0.15,
          target.dy + d.velocity.pixelsPerSecond.dy * 0.15,
        );
        target = Offset(
          target.dx.clamp(0.0, size.width - 100),
          target.dy.clamp(0.0, size.height - 100),
        );
        setState(() => _offset = target);
      },
      child: Transform.translate(
        offset: _offset,          // a PAINT transform: cheap
        child: Container(
          width: 100, height: 100,
          color: Colors.blue,
          // without this, the box is only draggable where the
          // coloured area is, and a Transform does not change
          // the hit test area
          decoration: const BoxDecoration(color: Colors.blue),
          child: const Center(child: Text('drag me', style: TextStyle(color: Colors.white))),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

// DRAGGABLE + DRAGTARGET: the data transfer pattern
Draggable<Entry>(
  data: entry,
  feedback: Material(          // what you see while dragging
    elevation: 4,
    child: SizedBox(width: 200, child: EntryCard(entry: entry)),
  ),
  childWhenDragging: const SizedBox(height: 80),   // the placeholder
  child: EntryCard(entry: entry),                    // the normal state
)

DragTarget<Entry>(
  onWillAcceptWithDetails: (details) => acceptHere(details.data),
  onAcceptWithDetails: (details) => addToList(details.data),
  builder: (context, candidate, rejected) {
    return AnimatedContainer(
      duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 200),
      height: candidate.isEmpty ? 100 : 120,      // it grows when targeted
      color: candidate.isEmpty ? Colors.grey : Colors.blue.shade100,
      child: candidate.isEmpty
          ? const Text('drop here')
          : Text('release to add ${candidate.first.title}'),
    );
  },
)

Reorderable lists, and the drag target that has to exist

A drag-and-drop list is a gesture plus a data structure plus a rule about what happens to the space the dragged item came from, and the third is the part people get wrong. The gesture is easy: a LongPressDraggable with feedback showing what is being dragged and childWhenDragging showing what stays behind. The data structure is a reorderable list widget, which owns the order and performs the move — and the reason it owns both is that the drag needs to know the order and the move needs to animate the items between positions, which requires the list. The rule is about the gap. While an item is being dragged, its space must be reserved, or every item below it jumps when it is removed and jumps again when it is dropped. The framework's reorderable widgets do this: they keep the dragged item's index reserved and move a placeholder to the new index as the drag passes over other items. Then the three things that make a drag-and-drop feel wrong, and each is a specific omission. No haptic or visual feedback as items are displaced. Dragging past an item that does not move until you drop is the single most common complaint, and the fix is the reorderable widget rather than a manual onDragUpdate that only reports the position. No boundary, so the item can be dragged off the end of the list into nothing; a reorderable list needs either a maximum index or a rejection handler so a drop outside the valid range is refused. And no autoscroll — when the pointer nears the edge of a long list, the list must scroll to reach the rest, and that requires the drag to inform the scrollable rather than fighting it. And then the two rules about what may be dropped where, because these are the business rules and they belong in the code rather than in the gesture handler. A drop is a move only if the target accepts the item's type, so a reorderable list that mixes rows needs a validator that returns false for incompatible pairs, and the framework calls it for each candidate index. And persisting the new order is not the same as the move succeeding — the local list has changed and the backend has not, so a reorder that fails to persist leaves the interface showing an order the server does not have, which is the bug the previous chapter's consistency argument is about. The correct handling is to treat the local move as optimistic, persist it, and revert on failure with the failure visible.

/* Three parts. */
const PARTS = [
  { p: 'the GESTURE', is: 'EASY',
    shape: 'a LongPressDraggable WITH FEEDBACK SHOWING WHAT IS BEING DRAGGED and childWhenDragging SHOWING WHAT STAYS BEHIND' },
  { p: 'the DATA STRUCTURE', is: 'A REORDERABLE LIST WIDGET, WHICH OWNS THE ORDER and PERFORMS the MOVE',
    whyItOwnsBoth: 'the DRAG NEEDS TO KNOW the ORDER and the MOVE NEEDS TO ANIMATE the ITEMS BETWEEN POSITIONS, WHICH REQUIRES the LIST' },
  { p: 'the GAP RULE', is: 'WHILE AN ITEM IS BEING DRAGGED, ITS SPACE MUST BE RESERVED',
    otherwise: 'or EVERY ITEM BELOW IT JUMPS WHEN IT IS REMOVED and JUMPS AGAIN WHEN IT IS DROPPED',
    mechanism: 'the FRAMEWORKS REORDERABLE WIDGETS KEEP the DRAGGED ITEMS INDEX RESERVED and MOVE A PLACEHOLDER to the NEW INDEX as the DRAG PASSES OVER OTHER ITEMS' },
];

/* Three things that make it feel wrong. */
const WRONG = [
  { m: 'NO HAPTIC or VISUAL FEEDBACK AS ITEMS ARE DISPLACED',
    symptom: 'DRAGGING PAST AN ITEM THAT DOES NOT MOVE UNTIL YOU DROP is THE SINGLE MOST COMMON COMPLAINT',
    fix: 'the REORDERABLE WIDGET rather than A MANUAL onDragUpdate THAT ONLY REPORTS the POSITION' },
  { m: 'NO BOUNDARY', consequence: 'so the ITEM CAN BE DRAGGED OFF the END of the LIST INTO NOTHING',
    fix: 'a REORDERABLE LIST NEEDS EITHER A MAXIMUM INDEX or A REJECTION HANDLER so a DROP OUTSIDE the VALID RANGE IS REFUSED' },
  { m: 'NO AUTOSCROLL', detail: 'WHEN the POINTER NEARS the EDGE of a LONG LIST, the LIST MUST SCROLL to REACH the REST',
    and: 'which REQUIRES the DRAG to INFORM the SCROLLABLE rather than FIGHTING IT' },

    and: 'the FRAMEWORK CALLS IT for EACH CANDIDATE INDEX' },

    connects: 'which is THE BUG the PREVIOUS CHAPTERS CONSISTENCY ARGUMENT IS ABOUT',

6.4 Scrollables and physics

// EVERY SCROLLABLE takes a ScrollPhysics, which decides how it
// behaves at the edges and how it decelerates.

const _physics = BouncingScrollPhysics(
  parent: AlwaysScrollableScrollPhysics(),
);

// BouncingScrollPhysics    the iOS feel: rubber-bands at the edges
// ClampingScrollPhysics   the Android feel: a hard stop at the edge
// AlwaysScrollableScrollPhysics  lets a non-scrollable child still
//                                 scroll: REQUIRED for
//                                 RefreshIndicator to work
// NeverScrollableScrollPhysics   no scrolling at all

ListView(
  physics: const BouncingScrollPhysics(parent: AlwaysScrollableScrollPhysics()),
  controller: _controller,
  padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
  itemExtent: 80,
  itemCount: 1000,
  itemBuilder: (context, i) => ListTile(title: Text('Item $i')),
)

// THE CONTROLLER, for programmatic scrolling
final _controller = ScrollController();

_controller.animateTo(
  500,
  duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 300),
  curve: Curves.easeOut,
);
_controller.jumpTo(500);
_controller.animateTo(_controller.position.maxScrollExtent);
_controller.nextPage(duration: d, curve: c);
_controller.previousPage(...);

// READING THE POSITION, which drives a parallax header
_controller.addListener(() {
  final offset = _controller.offset;    // may be NEGATIVE when
  setState(() {});                      // overscrolled at the top
});

// THE LISTENING PITFALL: a listener that calls setState
// rebuilds on EVERY scroll event, 60 times a second
// THE FIX: only setState when a value you DISPLAY changes
double _lastOffset = 0;
_controller.addListener(() {
  final offset = _controller.offset;
  if ((offset - _lastOffset).abs() < 1.0) return;   // a 1px threshold
  _lastOffset = offset;
  setState(() {});
});
// or use AnimatedBuilder, which rebuilds only the part that needs it
AnimatedBuilder(
  animation: _controller,
  builder: (context, child) => Opacity(
    opacity: 1 - (_controller.offset / 200).clamp(0.0, 1.0),
    child: child,
  ),
  child: const AppBar(title: Text('Field Notes')),
);
// PROGRAMMATIC SCROLL, done with an index
class EntryList extends StatefulWidget {
  const EntryList({required this.entries, required this.onOpen, super.key});
  final List<Entry> entries;
  final void Function(Entry) onOpen;

  @override
  State<EntryList> createState() => _EntryListState();
}

class _EntryListState extends State<EntryList> {
  final Map<String, int> _index = {};

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    for (var i = 0; i < widget.entries.length; i++) {
      _index[widget.entries[i].id] = i;
    }
  }

  void _scrollTo(Entry e) {
    final i = _index[e.id];
    if (i == null) return;
    _controller.scrollToIndex(
      i,
      duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 400),
      curve: Curves.easeInOutCubic,
      // THIS IS REQUIRED if the list is not built yet: it forces
      // the framework to build items up to index i, which
      // would otherwise throw a "no item at index" error
      alignmentPolicy: ScrollPositionAlignmentPolicy.leading,
    );
  }

  final _controller = ScrollController();
  late final AutoDisposeScrollController _autoController;
}

Scroll physics, and the one thing that has to be chosen deliberately

Everything about a scroll view that feels wrong is almost always the physics, and the physics are a small number of named models with different personalities. The framework picks a platform default, and the override is a single property. Bouncing is the iOS and macOS behaviour: content moves past its edge and springs back with a decelerating curve, and it is the behaviour users of those platforms expect. Never scrollable physics is the Android behaviour: content stops at the edge. Always scrollable means the list never stops — the user can drag from anywhere and release back to the start — and it is the right choice for content that is paginated, because a user who has scrolled to the bottom must be able to trigger the next page without scrolling back up first. Clamping is similar, for the case where overscroll should be visible only from a content edge. Then the two scroll behaviours people expect but which do not exist by default. Nested scrollables must not be nested. A ListView inside a ListView without bounded heights, or with the inner one given a fixed height, fights: the inner consumes the drag and the outer never sees it, and the outer scrollbar stops moving. A SingleChildScrollView around a Column of widgets is not a list, and the difference is not aesthetic: a column builds every child whether or not it is visible, which is the problem the sliver chapter exists to solve, so a column inside a scroll view is the correct choice for a screen of static content and the wrong choice for anything unbounded. Then the two decisions that have to be made deliberately, because the defaults are wrong more often than not. The controller, and whether it is disposed. A ScrollController not attached to a view must be disposed explicitly; one attached to a view is disposed by the view. Attaching and detaching the same controller from different views requires care, and reusing one across screens produces a scroll position from the previous screen. And whether the initial scroll offset should come from the state. Restoring a scroll position requires either a controller with an initial pixel value or a page controller with an initial page, and it must be applied only once — a restored offset applied on every rebuild resets the user's position, which is the classic "my list jumps to the top" report when combined with a list whose content length changes as it loads.

/* The physics models. */
const PHYSICS = [
  { p: 'the DEFAULT', is: 'A PLATFORM DEFAULT', override: 'a SINGLE PROPERTY' },
  { p: 'BOUNCING', behaviour: 'CONTENT MOVES PAST ITS EDGE and SPRINGS BACK WITH A DECELERATING CURVE',
    expectation: 'which is THE BEHAVIOUR USERS OF iOS and macOS EXPECT' },
  { p: 'NEVER SCROLLABLE PHYSICS', behaviour: 'CONTENT STOPS AT THE EDGE', is: 'the ANDROID BEHAVIOUR' },
  { p: 'ALWAYS SCROLLABLE', means: 'the LIST NEVER STOPS - the USER CAN DRAG from ANYWHERE and RELEASE BACK to the START',
    rightWhen: 'CONTENT THAT IS PAGINATED',
    why: 'because a USER WHO HAS SCROLLED TO the BOTTOM MUST BE ABLE to TRIGGER the NEXT PAGE without SCROLLING BACK UP FIRST' },
  { p: 'CLAMPING', means: 'OVERSHOOTT IS VISIBLE ONLY FROM A CONTENT EDGE' },
];

/* Two things that do not exist by default. */
const NOT_THERE = [
  { t: 'NESTED SCROLLABLES MUST NOT BE NESTED',

    symptom: 'the INNER CONSUMES the DRAG and the OUTER NEVER SEES IT, and the OUTER SCROLLBAR STOPS MOVING' },

  { d: 'the CONTROLLER, and WHETHER IT IS DISPOSED',

      'one ATTACHED TO A VIEW IS DISPOSED BY the VIEW'],

6.5 RawGestureDetector and recognisers

// RawGestureDetector: when you need to control the arena, or add
// a gesture the built-in detectors do not cover
RawGestureDetector(
  gestures: {
    // a built-in recogniser
    TapGestureRecognizer: GestureRecognizerFactoryWithHandlers<TapGestureRecognizer>(
      () => TapGestureRecognizer(),
      (recogniser) {
        recogniser
          ..onTap = onTap
          ..onLongPress = onLongPress;
      },
    ),

    // a TEAM: several recognisers that cooperate
    // this is how a horizontal drag inside a vertical list works
    _MyCustomRecogniser: GestureRecognizerFactoryWithHandlers<MyRecogniser>(
      () => MyRecogniser(),
      (recogniser) => recogniser.onStart = _onStart,
    ),
  },
  child: child,
);

// A CUSTOM RECOGNISER, which is where the real power is
class MyRecogniser extends OneSequenceGestureRecognizer {
  @override
  void addAllowedPointer(PointerDownEvent event) {
    startTrackingPointer(event.pointer);
  }

  @override
  void handleEvent(PointerEvent event) {
    if (event is PointerMoveEvent) {
      if (event.delta.dx.abs() > event.delta.dy.abs()) {
        resolve(GestureDisposition.accepted);   // I want this gesture
      } else {
        resolve(GestureDisposition.rejected);   // vertical: not mine
      }
    }
  }

  @override
  void acceptGesture(int pointer) {
    onStart?.call();
  }

  @override
  void rejectGesture(int pointer) {
    // someone else won: clean up
  }

  @override
  void didStopTrackingLastPointer(int pointer) {}
}

// THE COMMON CASE THIS SOLVES: a horizontal drag inside a
// horizontally-scrolling list inside a vertically-scrolling page
GestureDetector(
  // without this, the page's vertical drag always wins
  behavior: HitTestBehavior.translucent,
  onHorizontalDragUpdate: (d) => setState(() => _pageOffset -= d.delta.dx),
  child: PageView.builder(...),
);

Building a recogniser, and the arena rules it must follow

A custom recogniser is a class extending one of the framework's recognisers and overriding a small set of methods, and the methods are the same across recogniser types so learning one is close to learning all. addAllowedPointer is called for every pointer event that passes the hit test, and it is where you decide whether to accept the pointer at all — returning false for a pointer you do not want is cheaper and simpler than entering the arena and withdrawing. handleEvent receives every subsequent event for a pointer you accepted, and it is where recognition happens: you accumulate the delta, and when the accumulated movement passes a threshold you call resolve. resolve is the only legal way to win, and it takes a disposition: accept, reject, or accept-and-reject-others. didStopTrackingLastPointer is where you clean up and is called for every accepted pointer whether the gesture was won, lost or cancelled, which means it is the only reliable place to reset accumulated state. Then the three rules, and violating any of them produces a gesture that works in isolation and misbehaves inside a real widget tree. Declare victory with a margin, not at the exact threshold. The framework compares the point at which you claim with the point at which the gesture is unambiguously decided, and if you claim at the same point you lose the sweep to a parent. Claiming a few pixels early is the fix and costs nothing. Never resolve after the arena is already resolved. If a sibling recogniser has already won, your resolve is too late and the framework asserts; checking that you have not already resolved before resolving is the discipline. And accept exactly the pointer kinds you intend. A recogniser that accepts mouse, touch, stylus and trackpad when it was written for one of them will fight scroll views on platforms where a trackpad produces a scroll gesture that looks like a pan. Then the four situations that justify a custom recogniser, because the list is short and worth knowing. A gesture with no framework equivalent — a two-finger rotate, a three-finger pinch, a long-press-then-drag with a threshold the framework's drag does not have. A gesture that must not be arbitrated, where the recogniser needs to win immediately and unconditionally because a parent would otherwise steal it. A gesture with custom physics — a drag with momentum and a rubber-band limit, which is a simulation rather than a recogniser but lives alongside one. And wrapping several framework gestures as one, so that a caller gets a single callback with a combined state rather than four independent ones. And then the honest advice, which is the same as the arena section's: prefer restructuring the tree. A gesture that does not work because a Scrollable is an ancestor and a sibling recogniser wins the arena is a layout problem, and moving the detector up a level, wrapping the scrollable, or setting gestureSettings on the scrollable solves it without a single line of recogniser code. Writing a recogniser is the right answer when there is no gesture to configure, not when there is one that is being out-competed.

/* The four methods, and which is which. */
const METHODS = [
  { m: 'addAllowedPointer', called: 'for EVERY POINTER EVENT THAT PASSES the HIT TEST',
    decision: 'it is WHERE YOU DECIDE WHETHER TO ACCEPT the POINTER AT ALL',
    advice: 'RETURNING FALSE for a POINTER YOU DO NOT WANT IS CHEAPER and SIMPLER than ENTERING the ARENA and WITHDRAWING' },
  { m: 'handleEvent', called: 'with EVERY SUBSEQUENT EVENT for a POINTER YOU ACCEPTED',
    does: 'RECOGNITION HAPPENS HERE - you ACCUMULATE the DELTA, and WHEN the ACCUMULATED MOVEMENT PASSES A THRESHOLD YOU CALL resolve' },
  { m: 'resolve', is: 'the ONLY LEGAL WAY TO WIN',
    takes: 'a DISPOSITION - ACCEPT, REJECT, or ACCEPT-AND-REJECT-OTHERS' },
  { m: 'didStopTrackingLastPointer', does: 'CLEANS UP',
    called: 'for EVERY ACCEPTED POINTER WHETHER the GESTURE WAS WON, LOST or CANCELLED',
    why: 'which MEANS IT IS the ONLY RELIABLE PLACE to RESET ACCUMULATED STATE' },
];

/* Three rules. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'DECLARE VICTORY WITH A MARGIN, not AT the EXACT THRESHOLD',
    why: 'the FRAMEWORK COMPARES the POINT AT WHICH YOU CLAIM with the POINT AT WHICH the GESTURE IS UNAMBIGUOUSLY DECIDED',
    failure: 'and if YOU CLAIM AT THE SAME POINT YOU LOSE the SWEEP to a PARENT',
    fix: 'CLAIMING A FEW PIXELS EARLY IS THE FIX and COSTS NOTHING' },
  { r: 'NEVER RESOLVE AFTER the ARENA IS ALREADY RESOLVED',
    detail: 'if a SIBLING RECOGNISER HAS ALREADY WON, YOUR resolve IS TOO LATE and the FRAMEWORK ASSERTS',
    discipline: 'CHECKING THAT YOU HAVE NOT ALREADY RESOLVED BEFORE RESOLVING IS the DISCIPLINE' },
  { r: 'ACCEPT EXACTLY the POINTER KINDS YOU INTEND',
    failure: 'a RECOGNISER THAT ACCEPTS MOUSE, TOUCH, STYLUS and TRACKPAD when it WAS WRITTEN FOR ONE of THEM WILL FIGHT SCROLL VIEWS on PLATFORMS WHERE A TRACKPAD PRODUCES A SCROLL GESTURE THAT LOOKS LIKE A PAN' },
];

/* Four situations that justify it. */
const RIGHT_WHEN = [
  { c: 'a GESTURE WITH NO FRAMEWORK EQUIVALENT', instances: ['a TWO-FINGER ROTATE', 'a THREE-FINGER PINCH', 'a LONG-PRESS-THEN-DRAG with a THRESHOLD the FRAMEWORKS DRAG DOES NOT HAVE'] },
  { c: 'a GESTURE THAT MUST NOT BE ARBITRATED', detail: 'where the RECOGNISER NEEDS TO WIN IMMEDIATELY and UNCONDITIONALLY BECAUSE A PARENT WOULD OTHERWISE STEAL IT' },
  { c: 'a GESTURE WITH CUSTOM PHYSICS', instances: ['a DRAG WITH MOMENTUM and a RUBBER-BAND LIMIT'], note: 'which is A SIMULATION RATHER THAN A RECOGNISER but LIVES ALONGSIDE ONE' },
  { c: 'WRAPPING SEVERAL FRAMEWORK GESTURES AS ONE', gain: 'so that a CALLER GETS A SINGLE CALLBACK WITH A COMBINED STATE rather than FOUR INDEPENDENT ONES' },
];

const ADVICE = 'PREFER RESTRUCTURING the TREE';
const ADVICE_WHY = 'a GESTURE THAT DOES NOT WORK BECAUSE A Scrollable IS AN ANCESTOR and a SIBLING RECOGNISER WINS the ARENA IS A LAYOUT PROBLEM';
const ADVICE_FIX = 'and MOVING the DETECTOR UP A LEVEL, WRAPPING the SCROLLABLE, or SETTING gestureSettings ON the SCROLLABLE SOLVES IT WITHOUT A SINGLE LINE OF RECOGNISER CODE';

6.6 Scale, rotate and pinch

class PhotoViewer extends StatefulWidget {
  const PhotoViewer({required this.imageUrl, super.key});
  final String imageUrl;

  @override
  State<PhotoViewer> createState() => _PhotoViewerState();
}

class _PhotoViewerState extends State<PhotoViewer> {
  // the TRANSFORM, not separate scale/rotation values
  final _transform = Matrix4.identity();
  TapDownDetails? _lastTap;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return GestureDetector(
      onDoubleTapDown: (d) => _lastTap = d,
      onDoubleTap: () => _zoomToFit(),
      onScaleStart: (d) {
        // remember the scale at the START, so the gesture is
        // relative to where it began
        _startScale = _transform.getMaxScaleOnAxis();
        _startFocal = d.localFocalPoint;
      },
      onScaleUpdate: (d) {
        setState(() {
          // CLAMP: an unbounded zoom is never what you want
          final scale = (_startScale * d.scale).clamp(0.5, 5.0);
          final clampedScale = scale / _transform.getMaxScaleOnAxis();
          _transform
            ..translateByDouble(d.localFocalPoint.dx - _startFocal.dx, d.localFocalPoint.dy - _startFocal.dy, 0, 1)
            ..scaleByDouble(clampedScale, clampedScale, clampedScale, 1);
        });
      },
      child: InteractiveViewer(
        // EITHER use InteractiveViewer...
        transformationController: _controller,
        minScale: 0.5,
        maxScale: 5.0,
        child: Image.network(widget.imageUrl),
      ),
      // ...or a plain Transform for a fixed-scale interaction
    );
  }

  double _startScale = 1.0;
  Offset _startFocal = Offset.zero;
  final _controller = TransformationController();
}

// THE RIGHT WIDGET IS InteractiveViewer. It handles:
//   pan, pinch, double-tap-to-zoom, rotation if you allow it,
//   and the boundary so the image cannot be dragged off-screen.
// Hand-rolling it is a day of work and always has a bug.

Two-finger gestures, and why the built-ins do not compose

Scale and rotate are the gestures that have no first-class widget, and the reason is worth stating because it determines what you write. onScaleStart, onScaleUpdate and onScaleEnd on a GestureDetector report both scale and rotation from a multi-touch gesture, and that is the whole API: there is no ScaleGestureDetector and no RotateGestureDetector because one recogniser produces both and separating them would double the cost of every pinch. The scale value is a linear factor — two means twice as large, relative to the starting size, not to the previous event — and getting that wrong is why a naive pinch implementation overshoots on the second move event. The rotation is in radians and is the total rotation since the gesture began, so the incremental rotation each event is the difference between consecutive values. The focal point is a local position, which is the part that makes multi-touch genuinely hard: you get the scale and rotation but you also need the point the fingers are centred on, in your coordinate space, in order to keep the thing under the fingers under the fingers. Then the three problems that follow, and each has a specific mechanism. Coordinate spaces. A gesture recogniser reports positions in the coordinate space of the widget it is attached to; if the thing you are transforming is deeper in the tree, its local position differs by the accumulated transform, and using the recogniser's coordinates directly makes a rotated child drift. The fix is a GlobalKey on the transformed widget to get its own render box, or converting through the matrix explicitly. Combining scale and rotation as one transform. They are not independent — a rotation followed by a scale and a scale followed by a rotation give different results — so they must be composed into a single matrix in a fixed order rather than applied as separate properties, and the order must be the same on every update or the object will shear. And competing with the parent scroll view and with the platform's own pinch-zoom. A InteractiveViewer handles pinch, pan and scale in one widget and is the answer whenever the transformation is a camera; writing your own is right only when you are transforming something that is not the whole viewport. Then the practical recommendation, and it is mostly a recommendation not to write this. Use InteractiveViewer when the gesture zooms the content, because it handles bounds, clamping, double-tap zoom, keyboard shortcuts and the platform's accessibility magnification, and reimplementing that is days of work with a boundary bug in it. Use the scale callbacks when you are transforming a sub-widget, and keep the transformation inside a Transform so the framework composes it with the rest of the tree. And if you must hand-roll it, keep the accumulated scale and rotation in state, apply them as one composed matrix, convert coordinates through the transformed widget's own render box, and decide up front what happens when the scale would take the object outside its container — the boundary is the thing hand-rolled implementations forget.

/* The API. */
const API = {

};

6.7 Semantics and accessibility hooks

Building a custom widget that a screen reader can read

A custom widget is invisible to assistive technology unless it publishes semantics, and the publishing is two-part: a description and an action. A Semantics widget annotates its subtree with properties — a label, a value, a hint, flags for button, checkbox, selected, disabled, and a live-region setting — and the framework merges these down the tree so a child's annotation can override a parent's. An onTap on a Semantics widget publishes a semantic action, which is what makes a screen reader announce "double tap to activate" and what makes the widget reachable by keyboard on platforms where the framework maps semantic actions to key presses. And the two ways to supply semantics for a widget that paints itself: overriding describeSemanticsConfiguration on a render object, or wrapping it. The wrap is nearly always right and the override is for a custom render object or a widget that needs to describe a large subtree efficiently. Then the four things that go wrong in real code, and each has a specific mechanism. A label that duplicates what the user already hears. If a Semantics wraps a Text and also sets a label, the screen reader announces the label and then the text; the fix is either to omit the text from semantics with excludeSemantics or to let the text be the label. State announced only visually. A custom checkbox drawn as two rectangles with no semantic flag is announced as an unlabelled image; the fix is the checked flag, which is a first-class property precisely so that a drawn checkbox behaves like one. A gesture with no semantic action. A widget that responds to a horizontal drag but has no onIncrease or onSetText is announced but not operable, which is worse than not being announced because the user is told it is there and then nothing happens; the custom-action properties exist for exactly this and they are announced as named actions. And a live region that is too chatty. Marking a subtree as live means every change inside it is announced, so a live region around a whole screen announces every rebuild; it belongs on the one line of text that changes. Then the two tools, because debugging semantics without them is close to impossible. debugDumpSemanticsTree prints the merged semantic tree exactly as the platform receives it, which is the only way to find out what your annotations actually became after merging — and merging is where the surprises are. And the accessibility features in the inspector, which shows the same tree alongside the visual tree so you can see which widgets are contributing and which are absorbing. The discipline worth adopting is to dump the tree after adding any annotation and read it, because the annotations you wrote and the semantics the platform sees are different things and only one of them is what the user hears.

/* Two parts. */
const PARTS = [
  { p: 'a Semantics WIDGET', does: 'ANNOTATES ITS SUBTREE WITH PROPERTIES',
    properties: ['a LABEL', 'a VALUE', 'a HINT', 'FLAGS for button, checkbox, selected, disabled', 'a LIVE-REGION SETTING'],
    merging: 'the FRAMEWORK MERGES THESE DOWN the TREE so a CHILDS ANNOTATION CAN OVERRIDE a PARENTS' },
  { p: 'an onTap ON a Semantics WIDGET', publishes: 'A SEMANTIC ACTION',
    gain: 'which is WHAT MAKES A SCREEN READER ANNOUNCE double tap to activate',
    and: 'and WHAT MAKES the WIDGET REACHABLE BY KEYBOARD on PLATFORMS WHERE the FRAMEWORK MAPS SEMANTIC ACTIONS to KEY PRESSES' },
];
const TWO_WAYS = [
  { w: 'OVERRIDING describeSemanticsConfiguration on a RENDER OBJECT' },
  { w: 'WRAPPING IT', almostAlways: 'RIGHT',

/* Two tools. */
const TOOLS = [
  { t: 'debugDumpSemanticsTree', does: 'PRINTS the MERGED SEMANTIC TREE EXACTLY AS the PLATFORM RECEIVES IT',
    whyOnlyWay: 'which is THE ONLY WAY to FIND OUT what YOUR ANNOTATIONS ACTUALLY BECAME AFTER MERGING',
    and: 'MERGING IS WHERE the SURPRISES ARE' },
  { t: 'the ACCESSIBILITY FEATURES IN the INSPECTOR', does: 'SHOWS the SAME TREE ALONGSIDE the VISUAL TREE',
    gain: 'so you can SEE WHICH WIDGETS ARE CONTRIBUTING and WHICH ARE ABSORBING' },
];
const DISCIPLINE = 'DUMP the TREE AFTER ADDING ANY ANNOTATION and READ IT';

Semantics are not an afterthought and they are not optional. A custom CustomPainter has no semantics at all by default, so a chart or a sparkline is invisible to a screen reader. Wrap it, and write a widget test that asserts the label exists - it is one line and it stops the regression.

// EVERY interactive widget must expose a label, or a screen reader
// announces nothing useful.
Semantics(
  label: 'Delete entry ${entry.title}',
  hint: 'Removes this note permanently',
  button: true,
  onTap: _delete,
  child: IconButton(
    onPressed: _delete,
    icon: const Icon(Icons.delete),
    // the icon alone has no label, so the Semantics wrapper
    // supplies it
  ),
)

// merging and excluding
MergeSemantics(
  child: Row(children: [
    Text('Total: '),
    Text('\$42', semanticsLabel: '42 dollars'),
  ]),
)

ExcludeSemantics(
  child: Container(               // decorative: hide it from AT
    decoration: const BoxDecoration(gradient: LinearGradient(colors: [Colors.blue, Colors.purple])),
    height: 200,
  ),
)

// the actions a screen reader can perform
Semantics(
  label: 'Slider',
  value: '60%',
  increasedValue: '70%',
  decreasedValue: '50%',
  onIncrease: () => setState(() => _value = 0.7),
  onDecrease: () => setState(() => _value = 0.5),
  child: ...,
);

// for a custom widget, override the semantics in the RenderObject
class _RenderChart extends RenderBox {
  @override
  void describeSemanticsConfiguration(SemanticsConfiguration config) {
    super.describeSemanticsConfiguration(config);
    config
      ..label = 'Sales chart, ${_data.length} points'
      ..textDirection = TextDirection.ltr;
  }
}

// TEST IT
// the semantics tree is inspectable at runtime
final handle = debugDumpSemanticsTree();
debugDumpSemanticsTreeDisposal = false;

6.8 Text input and the keyboard

// THE TEXT FIELD, with the attributes that matter
TextField(
  controller: _controller,
  focusNode: _focusNode,
  keyboardType: TextInputType.emailAddress,
  textInputAction: TextInputAction.next,
  textCapitalization: TextCapitalization.none,
  autocorrect: false,
  enableSuggestions: false,
  maxLines: 1,                      // 1 for single line, null for many
  minLines: 1,
  keyboardAppearance: Theme.of(context).brightness,
  inputFormatters: [LengthLimitingTextInputFormatter(280)],
  onChanged: _onChanged,
  onSubmitted: (_) => FocusScope.of(context).nextFocus(),
  onEditingComplete: () => print('done'),
  decoration: InputDecoration(
    labelText: 'Email',
    hintText: 'you@example.com',
    prefixIcon: const Icon(Icons.mail),
    suffixIcon: _valid ? const Icon(Icons.check, color: Colors.green) : null,
    errorText: _error,
    border: const OutlineInputBorder(),
  ),
)

// FOCUS MANAGEMENT, which is the part people get wrong
final _focusNode = FocusNode();
final _passwordFocus = FocusNode();

@override
void initState() {
  super.initState();
  _focusNode.addListener(_onFocusChange);
}

void _onFocusChange() {
  if (!_focusNode.hasFocus) {
    // unfocusing: hide the keyboard
    FocusScope.of(context).unfocus();
  }
}

@override
void dispose() {
  _focusNode
    ..removeListener(_onFocusChange)
    ..dispose();
  _passwordFocus.dispose();
  super.dispose();
}

// move between fields without a mouse
onFieldSubmitted: (_) => _passwordFocus.requestFocus(),
onEditingComplete: () => _controller.text.isEmpty ? null : _login(),

// the tab order
FocusTraversalGroup(
  order: const NumericFocusOrder(1),
  child: Column(children: [...]),
);

// a focus error helper
autofocus: true,   // use sparingly: it opens the keyboard on launch

// LISTEN TO THE KEYBOARD, for a bottom sheet
final keyboardHeight = MediaQuery.viewInsetsOf(context).bottom;
AnimatedPadding(
  duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 200),
  curve: Curves.easeOut,
  padding: EdgeInsets.only(bottom: keyboardHeight),
  child: child,
);

Focus, the keyboard, and the interaction between them

Text input is the one place where the framework, the platform keyboard, and the view geometry all have to agree, and most of the difficulty is in the third. Focus is a widget-level concept and there are two kinds. A node can take focus, which is what determines whether it can receive keyboard input, or it can be autofocused, which is what determines whether it takes focus when the route appears. Setting both is the correct thing for the first field on a screen. The focus traversal order is the order of the widget tree, and the traversal policy determines whether traversal wraps and whether it is directional or ordered; a form whose order does not match the visual order is a real defect, and the fix is to make the tree order match. And unfocusing is explicit. Nothing unfocuses a field just because the user tapped elsewhere — the keyboard stays up unless something dismisses it, which is why every screen with an input needs either a barrier that dismisses on tap or a submit action that does. Then the three properties that control what the keyboard shows, and each is one of the things that makes a form feel right. keyboardType sets the layout — text, email, phone, number, multiline, and the platform-specific equivalents for a date or a number pad. textInputAction sets the action button at the bottom-right, and setting it to next on every field but the last and done on the last is what makes the keyboard's return key walk the form. textCapitalization sets the automatic capitalisation, and getting it wrong on a name field is a small daily irritation. And the two geometry problems, which are the actual difficulty. The keyboard covers content, and there are two correct answers: a scrollable with enough padding that the focused field can be scrolled into view above the keyboard, or MediaQuery.viewInsets — the inset the keyboard reduces the viewport by — used to size a bottom sheet or to pad a column. And the focused field may be below the fold with nothing to scroll. The framework does scroll a focused field into view when there is a scrollable ancestor, but only within that ancestor, so a form split across two scrollables or a field inside a non-scrolling container will be covered and stay covered; the fix is to ensure the whole form is inside one scroll view with bottom padding equal to the view inset. Then the two rules that are worth stating because they are conventions rather than requirements. Never put a password field in a list that can be reordered or dismissed, because the field may lose focus with the value still in memory and the row recycled — which is why a form is usually a stateful screen rather than list rows. And handle submission explicitly: on a single-line field the action key submits, on a multiline field it inserts a newline, and if the intended behaviour is submission on a multiline field then the action must be set and the newline must be handled, which is the single most common reason a chat composer does not send.

Exercises 7

  1. Put two GestureDetectors nested and confirm which wins a tap. Then fix the conflict with behavior.
  2. Build a draggable box that flings and clamps to the screen edges, and add a drop target that accepts it.
  3. Add a collapsing app bar driven by a scroll listener, and fix the "setState on every scroll event" problem.
  4. Build a RawGestureDetector with a custom recogniser that only claims horizontal drags.
  5. Build a pinch-to-zoom image with InteractiveViewer, with a scale clamp and a double-tap to fit.

7 · State Management in Depth

7.1 The taxonomy of state7.2 setState and its limits7.3 InheritedWidget, the foundation7.4 Provider7.5 Riverpod7.6 Bloc and Cubit7.7 Signals7.8 Choosing, and migrating

Six approaches, what each is actually for, and the reasoning that picks between them. This is the chapter where most Flutter projects go wrong.

7.1 The taxonomy of state

Where state lives, and the four questions that decide

Every state-management discussion is really a discussion of two questions — where does this data live and who is told when it changes — and answering them separately is what makes the taxonomy navigable rather than a list of libraries. The first axis is where the data lives. Component state is a field on a State object and dies with the widget. Shared state is a value several widgets need and it must outlive any of them. Server state is data the backend owns, which arrives asynchronously, can be stale, and is cached. Derived state is a value computed from other state and should not be stored at all. That last category is the one people forget and it is the one that causes the most bugs: a field that is only ever the result of other fields is a second source of truth that can disagree with the first. The second axis is how a widget learns about a change. By rebuild means every widget in a scope is rebuilt when anything in that scope changes — the simplest and the most wasteful. By subscription means a widget registers for the specific slice it uses and is rebuilt only when that slice changes. By pull means nothing is notified and a widget reads what it needs where it needs it, which is only possible if reads are tracked. And by binding, which is the most local option: the value lives in a widget above and is pushed down. Then the four questions, asked in order, and they settle almost every case. Does the value arrive from outside the app? If yes it is server state and it needs caching, staleness handling, error and loading states, and revalidation — and no library that only holds a value will give you those. Does more than one widget need it? If no, it is component state and setState is the correct answer, and reaching for a library is a cost with no benefit. Does it need to survive a route change or be shared between routes? If yes it cannot live in a State object, because the widget holding it is disposed. And is it derived? If yes, do not store it — compute it in the build method or in a computed getter, and the class of bug where the two copies disagree disappears. Then the honest summary of the library choice, which is that the libraries differ less than the discussions suggest. Provider, Riverpod, Bloc, MobX and signals all solve the same problem — scoped, observable, disposable state with subscription — and differ in ergonomics, in how much boilerplate they require, and in how much machinery they bring. The three that matter for a choice are how much code a trivial feature takes, how the state is declared (a class, a record of providers, an event-and-reducer pair), and how a widget subscribes (a builder wrapping the subtree, a hook returning a value, a bloc builder). Everything else — performance characteristics, ecosystem size, test support — follows from those three plus the team's familiarity.

/* Two questions. */
const AXES = [
  { q: 'WHERE DOES THIS DATA LIVE', kinds: [
    { k: 'COMPONENT STATE', is: 'A FIELD on a State OBJECT', dies: 'and DIES WITH the WIDGET' },
    { k: 'SHARED STATE', is: 'A VALUE SEVERAL WIDGETS NEED', and: 'it MUST OUTLIVE ANY of THEM' },
    { k: 'SERVER STATE', is: 'DATA the BACKEND OWNS', traits: ['ARRIVES ASYNCHRONOUSLY', 'CAN BE STALE', 'and IS CACHED'] },
    { k: 'DERIVED STATE', is: 'A VALUE COMPUTED FROM OTHER STATE', shouldBe: 'and SHOULD NOT BE STORED AT ALL' },
  ] },
  { q: 'HOW DOES A WIDGET LEARN ABOUT A CHANGE', kinds: [
    { k: 'BY REBUILD', means: 'EVERY WIDGET IN A SCOPE IS REBUILT when ANYTHING IN that SCOPE CHANGES', traits: ['the SIMPLEST', 'the MOST WASTEFUL'] },
    { k: 'BY SUBSCRIPTION', means: 'a WIDGET REGISTERS FOR the SPECIFIC SLICE IT USES and IS REBUILT ONLY WHEN that SLICE CHANGES' },
    { k: 'BY PULL', means: 'NOTHING IS NOTIFIED and a WIDGET READS WHAT IT NEEDS WHERE IT NEEDS IT', possibleOnlyIf: 'READS ARE TRACKED' },
    { k: 'BY BINDING', isThe: 'MOST LOCAL OPTION', and: 'the VALUE LIVES IN A WIDGET ABOVE and IS PUSHED DOWN' },
  ] },
];
const FORGOTTEN = 'a FIELD THAT IS ONLY EVER the RESULT of OTHER FIELDS IS A SECOND SOURCE OF TRUTH THAT CAN DISAGREE WITH the FIRST';

/* Four questions, in order. */
const QUESTIONS = [
  { q: 'DOES the VALUE ARRIVE FROM OUTSIDE the APP?',
    yes: 'it is SERVER STATE',
    needs: ['CACHING', 'STALENESS HANDLING', 'ERROR and LOADING STATES', 'and REVALIDATION'],
    why: 'and NO LIBRARY THAT ONLY HOLDS A VALUE WILL GIVE YOU THOSE' },
  { q: 'DOES MORE THAN ONE WIDGET NEED IT?',

  { q: 'IS IT DERIVED?', yes: 'DO NOT STORE IT - COMPUTE IT in the BUILD METHOD or in a COMPUTED GETTER',
    gain: 'and the CLASS OF BUG WHERE the TWO COPIES DISAGREE DISAPPEARS' },
];

/* The honest summary. */
const LIBRARIES = {
  fact: 'Provider, Riverpod, Bloc, MobX and SIGNALS ALL SOLVE the SAME PROBLEM - SCOPED, OBSERVABLE, DISPOSABLE STATE WITH SUBSCRIPTION',
  and: 'they DIFFER in ERGONOMICS, in HOW MUCH BOILERPLATE they REQUIRE, and in HOW MUCH MACHINERY they BRING',
  threeThatMatter: ['HOW MUCH CODE a TRIVIAL FEATURE TAKES',
    'HOW the STATE IS DECLARED - a CLASS, a RECORD of PROVIDERS, an EVENT-AND-REDUCER PAIR',
    'and HOW a WIDGET SUBSCRIBES - a BUILDER WRAPPING the SUBTREE, a HOOK RETURNING A VALUE, a BLOC BUILDER'],
  everythingElse: 'PERFORMANCE CHARACTERISTICS, ECOSYSTEM SIZE, TEST SUPPORT - FOLLOWS FROM THOSE THREE plus the TEAMS FAMILIARITY',
};

Ask which of the four kinds a piece of state is before reaching for a library. Most "we need state management" is local UI state that belongs in a setState two levels down. Installing Riverpod for a checkbox is the most common over-engineering in Flutter.

Four kinds of state, and only two of them need a library.

// FOUR KINDS OF STATE, and they need different solutions
//
// 1. LOCAL UI STATE
//    "is this menu open", "which tab", "the text in this field"
//    SOLUTION: setState in a StatefulWidget. Nothing else.
//
// 2. SHARED UI STATE
//    "the current user", "the selected entry", "the theme mode"
//    SOLUTION: an InheritedWidget, or a light library
//               (Riverpod, Provider). This is what most people
//               call "state management" and it is often not
//               what they need.
//
// 3. REMOTE STATE
//    a list from an API, a cached profile, a websocket stream
//    SOLUTION: a data layer that owns loading, error, cache and
//               staleness. Riverpod and Bloc both do this well.
//               A hand-rolled setState version is a bug factory.
//
// 4. DERIVED STATE
//    "is the form valid", "the filtered list", "the total"
//    SOLUTION: compute it. Do NOT store it. Two sources of
//               truth for one fact will drift.

// THE MOST COMMON MISTAKE
// a project installs Riverpod AND Bloc AND Provider AND
// getx AND mobX, and then has four competing sources of truth.
//
// PICK ONE. For almost every app that is: setState for local,
// and ONE library for everything else.

7.2 setState and its limits

// setState: the right answer far more often than people think
class Counter extends StatefulWidget {
  const Counter({super.key});
  @override
  State<Counter> createState() => _CounterState();
}

class _CounterState extends State<Counter> {
  int _count = 0;
  bool _expanded = false;

  void _increment() => setState(() => _count++);

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Column(children: [
      Text('$_count', style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.headlineMedium),
      // push the state DOWN: only the counter rebuilds
      if (_expanded) const DetailSection(),
      TextButton(onPressed: _increment, child: const Text('+')),
    ]);
  }
}

// THE LIMITS, and they are real
// 1. the State is private to the widget: a sibling cannot read
//    or change it
// 2. setState rebuilds the WHOLE build method of that widget
// 3. the State dies when the widget leaves the tree
// 4. there is no way to test it without pumping a widget
// 5. you cannot call it from a non-UI class

// FIX 1: lifting the state UP
class Parent extends StatefulWidget {
  const Parent({super.key});
  @override
  State<Parent> createState() => _ParentState();
}

class _ParentState extends State<Parent> {
  int _count = 0;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Column(children: [
      Text('\$_count'),
      // the CHILD takes a value and a callback: it is dumb
      IncrementButton(onPressed: () => setState(() => _count++)),
    ]);
  }
}

class IncrementButton extends StatelessWidget {
  const IncrementButton({required this.onPressed, super.key});
  final VoidCallback onPressed;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return FilledButton(onPressed: onPressed, child: const Text('+'));
  }
}

// THE RULE: if a child needs a value from a parent, pass it as a
// parameter. If it needs to CHANGE something the parent owns, pass
// a callback. This is the whole "props down, events up" idea,
// and it does not need a library.

// when it becomes painful: three or more levels deep, or several
// siblings needing the same state. THEN reach for an InheritedWidget.

The limits, and the moment to move on

setState is the right answer far more often than the discourse suggests, and the reasons it stops being right are worth being precise about because "my state management is getting complicated" is usually one of four specific problems. Limit one: it cannot be read from outside the widget. A sibling cannot read another widget's state; it can only be told. That is the reason the inherited-widget pattern exists, and the reason a form cannot validate from a button that is not a descendant of the field. Limit two: it cannot survive the widget. A State object is created when a stateful widget is inserted and disposed when it is removed, so state in it does not survive a navigation, a tab switch, or a rebuild that changes the widget type at that position — which is the mechanism behind "my state resets when I come back". Limit three: it rebuilds the whole subtree. setState marks the element dirty, and everything below rebuilds; a widget at the top of a screen whose state changes rebuilds every row beneath it, which is the layout chapter's rebuild mechanism and the reason a narrow widget is a performance technique. And limit four: it has no notion of derived state, so a value computed in a build method is recomputed on every rebuild and a value stored in a field can disagree with the fields it was derived from. Then the three refactors that fix the symptoms without a library, in the order to try them, because they solve most of what a library is wanted for. Lift the state to the nearest common ancestor. If two siblings need a value, the parent owns it and passes it down; this is the plainest possible fix and it turns a cross-widget read into a parameter. Make the stateful widget as small as possible. A text field's state belongs in the field, not in the screen, and a screen holding a hundred text controllers is the cause of most "rebuild is slow" reports. And convert the fields to initial values. A widget that receives a value and holds it in a field is stale by construction the moment the parent passes a new one; a widget that treats its input as the input and keeps only genuinely local state cannot be stale. Then the three signs that it is time for something more, and they are all about the shape of the code rather than the size of it. The same value is needed in two places that are not in a parent-child relationship — two routes, a dialog and the screen behind it, a widget and its sibling's child. The state must outlive the widget that owns it, which is the navigation case and is the one that makes setState structurally unable rather than merely inconvenient. And a field must be set from a listener — a widget that is a source of truth for something else, which is the shape that most often indicates the state is in the wrong place. And the discipline that goes with them: when you move to a library, move because of one of those three signs, not because a file has more than two hundred lines. Code length is a symptom of several different problems and only one of them is state management.

/* Four limits. */
const LIMITS = [
  { n: 1, l: 'IT CANNOT BE READ FROM OUTSIDE the WIDGET',
    detail: 'a SIBLING CANNOT READ another WIDGETS STATE; it CAN ONLY BE TOLD',
    because: 'which is THE REASON the INHERITED-WIDGET PATTERN EXISTS',
    and: 'the REASON A FORM CANNOT VALIDATE from a BUTTON THAT IS NOT A DESCENDANT of the FIELD' },
  { n: 2, l: 'IT CANNOT SURVIVE the WIDGET',
    detail: 'a State OBJECT IS CREATED WHEN A STATEFUL WIDGET IS INSERTED and DISPOSED WHEN IT IS REMOVED',
    so: 'STATE IN IT DOES NOT SURVIVE A NAVIGATION, A TAB SWITCH, or a REBUILD THAT CHANGES the WIDGET TYPE at that POSITION',
    symptom: 'which is THE MECHANISM BEHIND my state resets when I come back' },
  { n: 3, l: 'IT REBUILDS the WHOLE SUBTREE',
    detail: 'setState MARKS the ELEMENT DIRTY, and EVERYTHING BELOW REBUILDS',
    consequence: 'a WIDGET AT the TOP of a SCREEN WHOSE STATE CHANGES REBUILDS EVERY ROW BENEATH IT',
    connects: 'which is the LAYOUT CHAPTERS REBUILD MECHANISM and the REASON A NARROW WIDGET IS A PERFORMANCE TECHNIQUE' },
  { n: 4, l: 'IT HAS NO NOTION of DERIVED STATE',

/* Three refactors, no library. */
const REFACTORS = [
  { r: 'LIFT the STATE to the NEAREST COMMON ANCESTOR',
    detail: 'if TWO SIBLINGS NEED A VALUE, the PARENT OWNS IT and PASSES IT DOWN',
    gain: 'this is THE PLAINEST POSSIBLE FIX and it TURNS A CROSS-WIDGET READ INTO A PARAMETER' },
  { r: 'MAKE the STATEFUL WIDGET AS SMALL AS POSSIBLE',

];

/* Three signs it is time for more. */
const SIGNS = [
  { s: 'the SAME VALUE IS NEEDED IN TWO PLACES THAT ARE NOT IN A PARENT-CHILD RELATIONSHIP',
    instances: ['two ROUTES', 'a DIALOG and the SCREEN BEHIND IT', 'a WIDGET and its SIBLINGS CHILD'] },
  { s: 'the STATE MUST OUTLIVE the WIDGET THAT OWNS IT',

    why: 'and IT IS THE ONE THAT MAKES setState STRUCTURALLY UNABLE rather than MERELY INCONVENIENT' },
  { s: 'a FIELD MUST BE SET FROM A LISTENER',

7.3 InheritedWidget, the foundation

// what Provider, Riverpod and Flutter's own Theme are all built on
class AppState extends InheritedNotifier<AppStateModel> {
  AppState({required AppStateModel model, required super.child})
      : super(notifier: model) {
    // rebuild anything that reads us when we change
  }

  static AppStateModel of(BuildContext context) {
    final state = context.dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType<AppState>();
    assert(state != null, 'AppState not found in the widget tree');
    return state!.notifier!;
  }

  // and the no-listen variant
  static AppStateModel read(BuildContext context) {
    final element =
        context.getElementForInheritedWidgetOfExactType<AppState>();
    return (element!.widget as AppState).notifier!;
  }
}

class AppStateModel extends ChangeNotifier {
  final List<Entry> _entries = [];
  bool _loading = false;

  List<Entry> get entries => List.unmodifiable(_entries);
  bool get loading => _loading;
  int get count => _entries.length;
  bool get isEmpty => _entries.isEmpty;

  Future<void> load() async {
    _set(() => _loading = true);
    try {
      final loaded = await api.entries();
      _set(() {
        _entries
          ..clear()
          ..addAll(loaded);
      });
    } catch (e, s) {
      _set(() => _error = e);
    } finally {
      _set(() => _loading = false);
    }
  }

  void _set(VoidCallback fn) {
    fn();
    notifyListeners();     // rebuild every listener
  }
}

// usage
void main() {
  runApp(
    AppState(
      model: AppStateModel()..load(),
      child: const MyApp(),
    ),
  );
}

class EntryCount extends StatelessWidget {
  const EntryCount({super.key});
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // of() = subscribe: rebuild when the model changes
    final state = AppState.of(context);
    return Text('${state.count} entries');
  }
}

// the PERFORMANCE TRAP with ChangeNotifier
// a Notifier rebuilds EVERY listener on notifyListeners(), even
// the ones that only read `count` when you also read `_entries`
// and a row 200 entries down changes.
//
// THE FIX: a selector, which rebuilds only when the value changes
// (Provider gives you select; Riverpod does it automatically)

What a plain InheritedWidget costs, and what the packages added

A hand-written InheritedWidget is about thirty lines and has three problems, and each problem is exactly what the packages exist to solve. Problem one: every dependent rebuilds on any change. An inherited widget notifies all of its dependents when it notifies, and a widget that reads one field from a wide state object is rebuilt whenever any field changes — which for a screen with a form, a filter and a selection is most of the screen, most of the time. Problem two: the read and the subscribe are the same call. There is no way to read a value without registering a dependency, so a one-off read in an event handler permanently couples that widget to changes it does not care about. And problem three: disposal is the application's problem. A provider that creates a network client or subscribes to a stream must be told when to tear it down, and a bare InheritedWidget has no lifecycle for that; the widget that created it must, and there is nothing in the type that says so. Then the three things the packages add, and they are additive rather than different. Change notification with comparison, so a provider only notifies when the value actually differs rather than on every rebuild. A separate subscribe call, so a one-off read does not create a dependency. And disposal, with the provider calling a dispose callback when the widget that provided it is removed, which is the difference between a state container that leaks and one that does not. Then the three patterns that resolve the first problem, because they are worth knowing even if you use a package that implements them. Narrow the inherited widget. One inherited widget per field means a change to the field notifies only the widgets that read it; the cost is a proliferation of providers and the ceremony of keeping them in step. Reconstruct the value in the dependency check. The idiomatic hand-written form overrides updateShouldNotify to compare a derived value rather than the object identity, so a parent passing a new list with the same contents does not notify — and this is a one-line fix that eliminates most unnecessary rebuilds in a hand-written implementation. And use two inherited widgets, one for the value and one for the callbacks. Widgets that only dispatch an action do not need to rebuild when the value changes, and splitting the two means they do not; this is the cheapest real improvement available and it requires no package. Then the two things that are worth saying about testing, because a state container that is awkward to test will not be tested. A provider can be overridden in a test, which means a widget test can supply a fake state and assert on what the widget renders without constructing the real one — and this is the strongest practical argument for using a provider-shaped abstraction rather than a global variable. And the inverse is the warning: a global mutable singleton cannot be replaced, cannot be reset between tests, and leaks state from one test into the next, so a codebase that reaches for one will have order-dependent tests whether or not anyone wanted that.

/* Thirty lines, three problems. */
const PROBLEMS = [
  { n: 1, p: 'EVERY DEPENDENT REBUILDS ON ANY CHANGE',

    scale: 'which FOR A SCREEN WITH A FORM, A FILTER and a SELECTION IS MOST of the SCREEN, MOST of the TIME' },
