7.4 Provider

// pubspec.yaml
//   provider: ^6.1.0

// the four Provider variants
//   Provider         a value, created once
//   ChangeNotifierProvider  a ChangeNotifier
//   FutureProvider   a Future, with AsyncValue handling
//   StreamProvider   a Stream
//   ProxyProvider    provider A that depends on provider B

// a service, provided once
class EntryRepository {
  EntryRepository(this._api);
  final ApiClient _api;

  Future<List<Entry>> all() => _api.get('/entries');
}

// wiring: the composition root
MultiProvider(
  providers: [
    Provider<ApiClient>(
      create: (_) => ApiClient(baseUrl: 'https://api.acme.com'),
    ),
    ProxyProvider<ApiClient, EntryRepository>(
      update: (_, api, __) => EntryRepository(api),
    ),
    ChangeNotifierProvider(
      create: (context) => EntryListModel(
        context.read<EntryRepository>(),
      )..load(),
    ),
  ],
  child: const MyApp(),
)

// consuming
final repo = context.read<EntryRepository>();          // once, no rebuild
final model = context.watch<EntryListModel>();         // rebuild on change
context.select<EntryListModel, int>((m) => m.count);  // only on count
final notifier = context.read<EntryListModel>();       // for actions:
notifier.add(entry);                                       // no rebuild

// the SELECTOR pattern, which is Provider's main advantage over a
// plain ChangeNotifier
class EntryRow extends StatelessWidget {
  const EntryRow({required this.entry, super.key});
  final Entry entry;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // rebuild ONLY when this entry's title changes, not when
    // anything else in the model changes
    final title = context.select<EntryListModel, String?>(
      (m) => m.byId(entry.id)?.title,
    );
    return ListTile(title: Text(title ?? ''));
  }
}

// the watch/read/select distinction
//   watch    - subscribe, rebuild on change
//   read     - one-off read, no subscription
//   select   - subscribe, rebuild only if the SELECTED value changes
//
// the PROBLEM with Context.read in build
final repo = context.read<EntryRepository>();
return FutureBuilder(
  future: repo.all(),     // a NEW future on every rebuild:
  builder: ...            // an infinite loading loop
);
// the fix: cache the future, or use FutureProvider

The three Provider variants, and the async one that has to be right

Three widgets cover most uses and the distinctions between them are about lifetime, not about capability. ChangeNotifierProvider owns a ChangeNotifier — a class with a value, a setter that notifies, and a dispose method — and it is the right default: the notifier is a plain Dart class, testable without the framework, and the provider handles creation and disposal. Provider is a plain value with no notification, and it is for immutable configuration injected once: a theme, a feature flag, a repository. FutureProvider owns a Future and exposes its state — pending, data, or error — which is the mechanism that turns "loading" into a first-class thing rather than a boolean you manage by hand. Then the async rules, and getting them wrong is the single most common Provider bug. Do not create the future inside the build method. A provider's create function runs once, but if a future is constructed in a widget's build method then every rebuild creates a new one and the loading state restarts; this is why the future must be created inside the provider and not fetched in the widget. Handle the error state, not just the data. A provider that is only read for its data and never for its error will render an empty screen forever when the request fails, because there is no data and no loading and no error being rendered. And dispose controllers and clients. A provider that creates a text controller or a stream subscription must dispose it, and the reason to care is that a provider disposed with its widget is the mechanism that makes navigation-and-back not leak — which is the same argument as the disposal section's. Then the three things that make a provider-shaped state layer pleasant, and they are all about the boundary between state and widgets. Put the notifier's methods on it, not the framework calls. A notifier that exposes void addItem(Item) and internally calls notifyListeners can be tested by calling the method and asserting the value; a notifier whose widgets call notifyListeners cannot be tested at all without a widget. Expose selectors for anything read often, so a widget rebuilds on one field rather than on the whole object — and the cost of forgetting this is a screen that rebuilds in full whenever anything changes, which is invisible until the screen is large enough to notice. And keep derived values derived. A notifier with a getter for the filtered list rebuilds nothing when the filter is unchanged, whereas a filtered list stored in a field must be recomputed and re-notified, and the two implementations diverge the first time a field is added without recomputing. Then the two situations where a different tool is right, because knowing when not to use it is part of using it well. Deeply nested, interdependent state — where a change to one value implies changes to several others and the notification graph becomes hard to follow — is better served by a reducer-style library where every change goes through one path. And state that is mostly server data, which needs caching, revalidation-on-focus, deduplication of identical in-flight requests and stale-while-revalidate, is not solved by any provider package and is worth a dedicated library even though that library is usually built on a provider.

/* Three variants: lifetime, not capability. */
const VARIANTS = [
  { v: 'ChangeNotifierProvider', owns: 'a ChangeNotifier',
    notifier: 'a CLASS WITH A VALUE, A SETTER THAT NOTIFIES, and a DISPOSE METHOD',
    rightWhen: 'IT IS THE RIGHT DEFAULT',
    why: 'the NOTIFIER IS A PLAIN DART CLASS, TESTABLE WITHOUT the FRAMEWORK, and the PROVIDER HANDLES CREATION and DISPOSAL' },
  { v: 'Provider', owns: 'A PLAIN VALUE with NO NOTIFICATION',
    rightFor: 'IMMUTABLE CONFIGURATION INJECTED ONCE', instances: ['a THEME', 'a FEATURE FLAG', 'a REPOSITORY'] },
  { v: 'FutureProvider', owns: 'A Future', exposes: 'ITS STATE - PENDING, DATA, or ERROR',
    gain: 'which IS THE MECHANISM THAT TURNS loading INTO A FIRST-CLASS THING rather than A BOOLEAN you MANAGE BY HAND' },
];

7.5 Riverpod

Providers as values, and why the container is explicit

Riverpod's structural difference from Provider is that the state container is not created implicitly by a widget and is not owned by the widget tree. A provider is a value that describes how to obtain some state — a function, a notifier class, a future, a computed derivation — and a ProviderScope holds them, normally at the root of the app. Three consequences follow and they are the whole difference. A provider can be overridden at any scope, and the override is a value rather than a widget. In a test you replace the provider with a fake by wrapping the widget under test in a scope with an override list — no notifier subclass, no mock framework, and the override applies to the subtree from that point down. That is a genuinely better testing story than any other option here. A provider exists independently of any widget, so it can be read outside the build method — in an event handler, in a service, in a test — by obtaining the container explicitly, which removes the pattern where a listener closure captures a BuildContext in order to reach a value. And providers are declared as a class with static members rather than as widgets, which means the set of state in an app is enumerable: you can list the providers, read any of them from anywhere, and see the dependency structure in the type system rather than by reading the widget tree. Then the three provider families, and choosing between them is most of the work. A plain provider exposes a value that never changes, or a function to call. A notifier provider exposes an object with state and methods — the equivalent of ChangeNotifierProvider — and is what most application state is. A future or stream provider exposes asynchronous state and gives you the loading, error and data states and the invalidation and caching machinery, which is the server-state answer the previous sections described. And a derived provider is a value computed from others, cached and recomputed only when its inputs change — the construct the signals section says does most of the work in a fine-grained model, available here without changing paradigms. Then the three practices that make it work, and each is a specific failure avoided. Keep providers at module level, never inside a build method. A provider declared inside a widget is recreated on every rebuild, which is both a performance problem and a correctness one because its identity changes and anything watching it rebuilds. Make the notifier's interface the only way to change state, so that reading a value and writing a value are asymmetric — many readers, one writer — which is the property that keeps a codebase's mutations findable. And override in tests at the narrowest scope that works, because an override applied at the root hides which dependency the widget under test actually needs, and a test that overrides three providers to test one of them will keep passing after the widget starts depending on a fourth.

/* The structural difference. */

The real advantage of Riverpod over Provider is not syntax. It is that a provider owns its own async lifecycle - loading, error, caching, invalidation, cancellation on disposal - which is several hundred lines of careful code if you write it by hand with a ChangeNotifier. That code is where the bugs live.

// pubspec.yaml
//   flutter_riverpod: ^2.5.0
//   riverpod_annotation: ^2.5.0
//   riverpod_generator: ^2.4.0
//   build_runner: ^2.4.0

// the three provider flavours
//   Provider        synchronous, a value
//   FutureProvider   asynchronous, with AsyncValue
//   StreamProvider   a stream
//   NotifierProvider a class with build() and methods
//   AsyncNotifierProvider  the async version

// 1. a plain provider
final apiProvider = Provider<ApiClient>((ref) {
  return ApiClient(baseUrl: 'https://api.acme.com');
});

// 2. a FutureProvider: Riverpod handles loading/error/data
final entriesProvider = FutureProvider<List<Entry>>((ref) async {
  final api = ref.watch(apiProvider);
  return api.get('/entries');
});

// in a widget
final entries = ref.watch(entriesProvider);
return entries.when(
  loading: () => const SkeletonList(),
  error: (err, stack) => ErrorView(error: err, onRetry: () => ref.invalidate(entriesProvider)),
  data: (list) => EntryListView(entries: list),
);
// THAT is the whole three-state handling, done correctly

// 3. an AsyncNotifier: for state you MUTATE
class EntryListModel extends AsyncNotifier<List<Entry>> {
  @override
  Future<List<Entry>> build() async {
    final api = ref.watch(apiProvider);
    return api.get('/entries');
  }

  Future<void> add(Entry entry) async {
    // 1. update optimistically
    final current = state.valueOrNull ?? [];
    state = AsyncData([...current, entry]);
    try {
      // 2. send it
      await ref.read(apiProvider).create(entry);
    } catch (e) {
      // 3. roll back
      state = AsyncData(current);
      rethrow;
    }
  }

  Future<void> refresh() async {
    state = const AsyncLoading();
    state = await AsyncValue.guard(() async {
      return ref.read(apiProvider).get('/entries');
    });
  }
}

final entriesModelProvider = AsyncNotifierProvider<EntryListModel, List<Entry>>(
  EntryListModel.new,
);

// in a widget
final model = ref.watch(entriesModelProvider);
final value = model.valueOrNull;

// 4. SELECT, the automatic dependency narrowing
class EntryRow extends StatelessWidget {
  const EntryRow({required this.entryId, super.key});
  final String entryId;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context, WidgetRef ref) {
    // this rebuilds ONLY when THIS entry's title changes
    final title = ref.watch(entryProvider(entryId).select((e) => e.title));
    return ListTile(title: Text(title));
  }
}

final entryProvider = Provider.family<Entry, String>((ref, id) {
  final list = ref.watch(entriesModelProvider).valueOrNull ?? const [];
  return list.firstWhere((e) => e.id == id);
});
// CODE GENERATION, which removes the ProviderScope boilerplate
// lib/src/entries.dart
import 'package:riverpod_annotation/riverpod_annotation.dart';
part 'entries.g.dart';

@riverpod
ApiClient api() => ApiClient(baseUrl: 'https://api.acme.com');

@riverpod
Future<List<Entry>> entries(ApiRef ref) async {
  return ref.watch(apiProvider).get('/entries');
}

@riverpod
class EntryListModel extends _$EntryListModel {
  @override
  Future<List<Entry>> build() async {
    return ref.watch(apiProvider).get('/entries');
  }

  Future<void> add(Entry e) async { ... }
}

// then: dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
// and in the widget
final entries = ref.watch(entriesProvider);
// no .g.dart import needed: it is a part of the file

// THE PROVIDER SCOPE, which contains everything
void main() {
  runApp(
    const ProviderScope(
      child: MyApp(),
    ),
    // ProviderScope is where the container lives. Everything
    // below it can read providers.
  );
}

// SCOPING: a nested ProviderScope overrides providers for its
// subtree. Useful for a logged-in vs logged-out app
ProviderScope(
  overrides: [
    apiProvider.overrideWithValue(mockApi),
  ],
  child: const TestWidget(),
);

7.6 Bloc and Cubit

// pubspec.yaml
//   flutter_bloc: ^8.1.0

// CUBIT: the simpler form. A class with methods that emit states.
class CounterCubit extends Cubit<int> {
  CounterCubit() : super(0);

  void increment() => emit(state + 1);
  void decrement() => emit(state - 1);
  void reset() => emit(0);
}

class CounterView extends StatelessWidget {
  const CounterView({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return BlocProvider(
      create: (_) => CounterCubit(),
      child: BlocBuilder<CounterCubit, int>(
        builder: (context, state) {
          return Column(children: [
            Text('$state'),
            IconButton(
              onPressed: () => context.read<CounterCubit>().increment(),
              icon: const Icon(Icons.add),
            ),
          ]);
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}

// BLOC: events in, states out. For complex, event-sourced state
sealed class EntryEvent {
  const EntryEvent();
}

class EntriesRequested extends EntryEvent {
  const EntriesRequested();
}

class EntryAdded extends EntryEvent {
  const EntryAdded(this.entry);
  final Entry entry;
}

class EntryDeleted extends EntryEvent {
  const EntryDeleted(this.id);
  final String id;
}

// THE STATE: immutable, with a sealed hierarchy
sealed class EntryState {
  const EntryState();
}

class EntryInitial extends EntryState {
  const EntryInitial();
}

class EntryLoading extends EntryState {
  const EntryLoading();
}

class EntryLoaded extends EntryState {
  const EntryLoaded(this.entries);
  final List<Entry> entries;
}

class EntryError extends EntryState {
  const EntryError(this.message);
  final String message;
}

class EntryBloc extends Bloc<EntryEvent, EntryState> {
  EntryBloc({required EntryRepository repository})
      : _repository = repository,
        super(const EntryInitial()) {
    // 1. register handlers. on<E>() is typed and checked
    on<EntriesRequested>(_onRequested);
    on<EntryAdded>(_onAdded);
    on<EntryDeleted>(_onDeleted);
  }

  final EntryRepository _repository;

  Future<void> _onRequested(EntriesRequested event, Emitter<EntryState> emit) async {
    emit(const EntryLoading());
    try {
      final entries = await _repository.all();
      emit(EntryLoaded(entries));
    } catch (e) {
      emit(EntryError(e.toString()));
    }
  }

  Future<void> _onAdded(EntryAdded event, Emitter<EntryState> emit) async {
    // the current state must be loaded for the optimistic update
    final current = state;
    if (current is! EntryLoaded) return;
    emit(EntryLoaded([...current.entries, event.entry]));
    try {
      await _repository.create(event.entry);
    } catch (e) {
      emit(EntryLoaded(current.entries));   // roll back
    }
  }

  Future<void> _onDeleted(EntryDeleted event, Emitter<EntryState> emit) async {
    final current = state;
    if (current is! EntryLoaded) return;
    emit(EntryLoaded(current.entries.where((e) => e.id != event.id).toList()));
    await _repository.delete(event.id);
  }
}

// THE WIDGETS
BlocProvider(
  create: (context) => EntryBloc(repository: context.read<EntryRepository>())
    ..add(const EntriesRequested()),
  child: BlocBuilder<EntryBloc, EntryState>(
    // buildWhen is the same idea as Riverpod's select: rebuild
    // only for the states you care about
    buildWhen: (previous, current) => current is EntryLoaded,
    builder: (context, state) {
      if (state is EntryLoading) return const SkeletonList();
      if (state is EntryError) return ErrorView(message: state.message);
      if (state is EntryLoaded) return EntryListView(entries: state.entries);
      return const SizedBox.shrink();
    },
  ),
);

// dispatch an event
context.read<EntryBloc>().add(const EntryAdded(entry));

// WHY BLOC
// + every state change is an EVENT: a log, replayable, testable
// + the event-to-state mapping is a pure function
// + no hidden side effects: everything goes through on<E>
// - more ceremony: three files for a counter
// - the boilerplate is the cost

Events, states, and why the ceremony is the design

Bloc is the outlier in this list and the reason is worth understanding, because a lot of the criticism of it is really criticism of a deliberate choice. The rule is that state changes only in response to an event, and every event goes through one reducer. A bloc receives events, folds them into a new state, and emits that state; nothing else may write the state. The consequence is that the current state plus the event sequence fully determines the next state — there is no hidden mutable input — and that is a property worth having in the places where a state machine is genuinely the right model: a checkout flow, a media player, a connection that reconnects, a form with server-side validation. The ceremony is not incidental to the design; it is the design. Then the three types, and the difference is about what is exposed. A bloc exposes events and states; a widget sends an event and rebuilds when a new state arrives. A cubit exposes methods and states, which is the same machinery without the event class, and it is the version to reach for unless you specifically need the event objects to be part of an interface. A hydrated bloc reconstructs its state from storage on start, which is the mechanism that makes a bloc survive being killed — the framework can kill and restore a bloc's state, and a cubit cannot be hydrated the same way, which is the real difference. Then the three costs, stated honestly, because they are the reason not every project should use it. Boilerplate. An event class, a state class, a bloc class and a builder for a counter is four files, and the count does not go down as the app grows because it scales with the number of things that can happen. Learning curve, which is mostly the consequence of the first: a new developer must learn the event-to-state convention before they can read a screen. And the reactivity is explicit, which is a benefit for a state machine and a cost everywhere else — you cannot read a value out of a bloc, you subscribe to it, and a widget that needs one field rebuilds on every state change unless you filter, which is the same cost every library has and here it is more visible. Then the four practices that make it work, and each addresses a specific failure. One bloc per feature, not per screen, so a feature's state outlives its screens and navigation within the feature does not reset it. Sealed state classes, so the set of possible states is exhaustive at compile time and a switch over them is checked — this is the single biggest quality win the design provides and the reason to prefer it where a state machine fits. Emit a new state only on a real change, using equality on the state, because emitting an equal state rebuilds every subscriber for nothing — and for a state class containing a list, that means value equality or a deliberate identity. And do not put side effects in the bloc. The bloc decides; a listener or an injected service performs the work, and keeping the decision separate is what makes the bloc testable without a network.

/* The rule. */
const RULE = {
  says: 'STATE CHANGES ONLY IN RESPONSE TO AN EVENT, and EVERY EVENT GOES THROUGH ONE REDUCER',
  mechanism: 'a BLOC RECEIVES EVENTS, FOLDS THEM INTO A NEW STATE, and EMITS that STATE',
  invariant: 'NOTHING ELSE MAY WRITE the STATE',

  ceremony: 'the CEREMONY IS NOT INCIDENTAL TO the DESIGN; it IS the DESIGN',
};

7.7 Signals

// SIGNALS: a reactive primitive with fine-grained tracking, and
// no rebuild of the widget tree. The model that made fine-grained
// reactivity mainstream on the web.

// pubspec.yaml
//   signals: ^2.0.0
//   (or: flutter_signals, which adds widget bindings)

import 'package:signals/signals.dart';

class EntryStore {
  // 1. a signal: a value that notifies only what READS it
  final count = signal(0);
  final name = signal('Field Notes');
  final entries = signal<List<Entry>>(<Entry>[]);

  // 2. a computed: derived, recomputed lazily, cached until a
  //    dependency changes
  final isEmpty = computed(() => entries.value.isEmpty);
  final countLabel = computed(() => count.value == 1 ? '1 entry' : '${count.value} entries');

  // 3. an effect: a side effect that runs when a dependency changes
  late final Effect _persistence = effect((_) {
    // runs immediately and again whenever `entries` changes
    _save(entries.value);
  });

  void increment() => count.value++;
  void add(Entry e) => entries.value = [...entries.value, e];

  void dispose() {
    _persistence.dispose();
  }
}

// in a widget: the widget rebuilds ONLY when the signal it
// watches changes
class CounterView extends StatelessWidget {
  const CounterView({required this.store, super.key});
  final EntryStore store;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Text('${store.count.value}');
  }
}

// or, with the flutter_signals package, track signals as widget
// state and rebuild automatically
final count = signal(0);

class Counter extends StatelessWidget {
  const Counter({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Watch((_) => Text('${count.value}'));
  }
}

// THE BIG ADVANTAGE: a signal that changes does NOT rebuild the
// widget. It re-runs only the computations that read it.
//
//  for (final entry in store.entries.value)     // <- this re-runs
//    Text('${store.count.value}')               // <- this does not
//
// A rebuild of the widget would re-run both. This is why signal
// libraries feel instant: the work is proportional to what
// actually changed.

// THE DRAWBACKS
// - a new mental model on top of Flutter's
// - debugging is harder: the value is not in the widget state
// - no automatic async states: you handle loading and error
//   yourself, in the store
// - less ecosystem: fewer tutorials, fewer packages integrate it

Fine-grained reactivity, and what has to be true for it to be fast

Signals take a different approach from every other option here and the difference is not ergonomics — it is what happens when a value changes. A signal is a value plus a set of dependents. Reading a signal inside a reactive context records a dependency between the reader and that signal; writing to it notifies exactly the recorded dependents. There is no subtree rebuild, because nothing rebuilds: the widgets that read the value are the things that change. That is a genuinely different mechanism and it means the cost of a change is proportional to the number of things that read the value, not to the size of a subtree — which is the property that makes a large screen cheap to update. Then the three things that have to be true for it to be fast, and each is a rule about where you read and write. Reads must be tracked, and they are tracked automatically inside the framework's reactive scope but not in an ordinary callback — a value read in a timer callback or an event handler is not a dependency, which is why the frameworks that offer this pair a "computed" construct for values derived from signals and a discipline about not reading signals in the wrong place. Writes must be batched, because notifying a thousand dependents one at a time within a single event handler is a thousand intermediate states; the frameworks batch to the end of the current microtask so a handler that sets three signals produces one rebuild rather than three. And derived values must be computed lazily and cached, so a value derived from a hundred signals is not recomputed a hundred times — this is the single biggest performance lever in the model and the reason "computed" exists rather than a getter. Then the three limitations, and they are the honest reason this is not the default choice for everyone. It is a different paradigm, and a codebase mixing signals with setState and a provider has two sources of truth with two invalidation models, which is worse than either alone. The ecosystem is smaller, which in practice means fewer tutorials, fewer packages that integrate with it, and a higher cost for a new developer. And the debugging story is worse, because there is no rebuild to inspect in the widget tree — when a value is wrong you are inspecting a dependency graph rather than a build method, and that is a different skill. Then the two cases where it is clearly the right answer, and both share the same property. High-frequency updates — a drag position, a scroll offset, a cursor position, a progress value — where a subtree rebuild per frame is untenable and only the things reading the value need to change. And very wide dependency graphs, where a screen has many independent pieces of state and a change to one should affect only what reads it; in that shape the fine-grained model is not an optimisation but the difference between workable and not. And the discipline for both: keep the reactive boundary small and keep domain logic outside it, so the graph contains presentation state and the business rules are ordinary testable functions — a signal holding a formatted string is a signal that has leaked logic into the graph, and the two are harder to reason about together than apart.

/* The mechanism. */
const MECHANISM = {
  is: 'A VALUE plus A SET of DEPENDENTS',
  reading: 'READING A SIGNAL INSIDE A REACTIVE CONTEXT RECORDS A DEPENDENCY BETWEEN the READER and that SIGNAL',
  writing: 'WRITING TO IT NOTIFIES EXACTLY the RECORDED DEPENDENTS',
  consequence: 'there is NO SUBTREE REBUILD, BECAUSE NOTHING REBUILDS - the WIDGETS THAT READ the VALUE ARE THE THINGS THAT CHANGE',
  property: 'the COST of A CHANGE IS PROPORTIONAL TO the NUMBER OF THINGS THAT READ the VALUE, NOT TO the SIZE of A SUBTREE',
  whyItMatters: 'which IS THE PROPERTY THAT MAKES A LARGE SCREEN CHEAP TO UPDATE',
};

/* Three things that must be true. */
const MUST_BE_TRUE = [
  { r: 'READS MUST BE TRACKED',
    tracked: 'AUTOMATICALLY INSIDE the FRAMEWORKS REACTIVE SCOPE',
    notTracked: 'NOT IN AN ORDINARY CALLBACK - a VALUE READ IN A TIMER CALLBACK or AN EVENT HANDLER IS NOT A DEPENDENCY',
    consequence: 'which IS WHY the FRAMEWORKS THAT OFFER this PAIR A COMPUTED CONSTRUCT for VALUES DERIVED FROM SIGNALS and a DISCIPLINE ABOUT NOT READING SIGNALS IN the WRONG PLACE' },
  { r: 'WRITES MUST BE BATCHED',
    why: 'because NOTIFYING A THOUSAND DEPENDENTS ONE AT A TIME WITHIN A SINGLE EVENT HANDLER IS A THOUSAND INTERMEDIATE STATES',
    mechanism: 'the FRAMEWORKS BATCH TO the END of the CURRENT MICROTASK',
    gain: 'so a HANDLER THAT SETS THREE SIGNALS PRODUCES ONE REBUILD rather than THREE' },
  { r: 'DERIVED VALUES MUST BE COMPUTED LAZILY and CACHED',
    why: 'so a VALUE DERIVED FROM A HUNDRED SIGNALS IS NOT RECOMPUTED A HUNDRED TIMES',
    and: 'this IS THE SINGLE BIGGEST PERFORMANCE LEVER IN the MODEL and the REASON computed EXISTS rather than A GETTER' },
];

/* Three limitations. */
const LIMITATIONS = [
  { l: 'IT IS A DIFFERENT PARADIGM',
    danger: 'a CODEBASE MIXING SIGNALS WITH setState and A PROVIDER HAS TWO SOURCES OF TRUTH WITH TWO INVALIDATION MODELS',
    consequence: 'which IS WORSE THAN EITHER ALONE' },
  { l: 'the ECOSYSTEM IS SMALLER',
    detail: ['FEWER TUTORIALS', 'FEWER PACKAGES THAT INTEGRATE WITH IT', 'and A HIGHER COST for a NEW DEVELOPER'] },
  { l: 'the DEBUGGING STORY IS WORSE',
    detail: 'BECAUSE THERE IS NO REBUILD TO INSPECT IN the WIDGET TREE',
    consequence: 'when A VALUE IS WRONG YOU ARE INSPECTING A DEPENDENCY GRAPH rather than A BUILD METHOD, and that IS A DIFFERENT SKILL' },
];

/* Two cases. */
const RIGHT_WHEN = [
  { c: 'HIGH-FREQUENCY UPDATES',
    instances: ['a DRAG POSITION', 'a SCROLL OFFSET', 'a CURSOR POSITION', 'a PROGRESS VALUE'],
    why: 'where A SUBTREE REBUILD PER FRAME IS UNTENABLE and ONLY the THINGS READING the VALUE NEED TO CHANGE' },
  { c: 'VERY WIDE DEPENDENCY GRAPHS',
    detail: 'where A SCREEN HAS MANY INDEPENDENT PIECES of STATE and A CHANGE TO ONE SHOULD AFFECT ONLY WHAT READS IT',
    and: 'in that SHAPE the FINE-GRAINED MODEL IS NOT AN OPTIMISATION but the DIFFERENCE BETWEEN WORKABLE and NOT' },
];
const DISCIPLINE = ['KEEP the REACTIVE BOUNDARY SMALL', 'and KEEP DOMAIN LOGIC OUTSIDE IT'];
const DISCIPLINE_WHY = 'so the GRAPH CONTAINS PRESENTATION STATE and the BUSINESS RULES ARE ORDINARY TESTABLE FUNCTIONS';
const DISCIPLINE_WARNING = 'a SIGNAL HOLDING A FORMATTED STRING IS A SIGNAL THAT HAS LEAKED LOGIC INTO the GRAPH, and the TWO ARE HARDER TO REASON ABOUT TOGETHER THAN APART';

7.8 Choosing, and migrating

Installing four state management libraries and then having four competing sources of truth is a real and common outcome of trying to pick the best one. Pick one. A codebase that is seventy percent Riverpod and thirty percent setState is fine, because setState for local state is correct rather than a compromise.

// THE DECISION, honestly
//
// A small app (under about 20 screens, one developer):
//   setState + InheritedWidget. Do not add a dependency.
//   Most "we need state management" is setState and lifting
//   state up one level.
//
// A medium app (one team, shared state across features):
//   Riverpod. The best default in 2026: async handled, automatic
//   disposal, compile-time safe with code generation, easy to
//   test, and a real cache/invalidation story.
//
// A large app (several teams, complex event flows, audit
// requirements):
//   Bloc. More ceremony, and the event log is worth it when you
//   need to answer "how did the app get into this state".
//
// A performance-critical app with heavy derived state:
//   Signals, or Riverpod's computed. Fine-grained tracking is a
//   real win on a complex screen.
//
// A codebase that already has one of these:
//   keep it. A mixed codebase is worse than any single choice.

// THE MIGRATION PATH, which is much easier than people fear
// 1. wrap the app in ProviderScope or BlocProvider
// 2. move ONE feature's state into a provider
// 3. leave every other feature with setState
// 4. repeat
// 5. remove the old patterns as you go
//
// You do not have to migrate in one commit. A codebase that is
// 70% Riverpod and 30% setState is perfectly fine: setState for
// local state is CORRECT, not a compromise.
// THE PATTERNS THAT MATTER, regardless of library

// 1. STATE AS LOW AS POSSIBLE
//    a checkbox does not need a global store
class CheckboxWithState extends StatefulWidget {
  const CheckboxWithState({super.key});
  @override
  State<CheckboxWithState> createState() => _CheckboxWithStateState();
}

class _CheckboxWithStateState extends State<CheckboxWithState> {
  bool _checked = false;
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return CheckboxListTile(
      value: _checked,
      onChanged: (v) => setState(() => _checked = v ?? false),
      title: const Text('Done'),
    );
  }
}

// 2. NEVER DERIVE STATE, COMPUTE IT
final count = entriesProvider.select((list) => list.length);
// not: a stored `count` updated in three places

// 3. NO WORK IN BUILD
Widget build(BuildContext context) {
  final list = ref.watch(entriesProvider).valueOrNull ?? [];
  return list.sortedByName().map(Card).toList();
  //          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ this runs on every rebuild
}
// FIX: sort in the provider, or in the model

// 4. UNIQUE KEYS ON EVERY LIST ITEM

// 5. THE PROVIDER OWNS THE ASYNC LIFECYCLE
//    loading, error, retry, cancellation, caching, disposal
//    a hand-rolled version of this is 200 lines and has bugs
// TESTING each approach, briefly
// setState: pumpWidget, tap, check
testWidgets('counter increments', (tester) async {
  await tester.pumpWidget(const MaterialApp(home: Counter()));
  await tester.tap(find.byIcon(Icons.add));
  await tester.pump();
  expect(find.text('1'), findsOneWidget);
});

// Riverpod: override the provider, no widget needed
test('adds an entry', () async {
  final container = ProviderContainer(
    overrides: [apiProvider.overrideWithValue(MockApi())],
  );
  addTearDown(container.dispose);
  final model = container.read(entryListModelProvider.notifier);
  await model.add(const Entry(id: '1', title: 'Test'));
  expect(container.read(entryListModelProvider).value!.first.title, 'Test');
});

// Bloc: pure Dart, no Flutter at all
test('adds an entry', () async {
  final bloc = EntryBloc(repository: MockRepository());
  final states = <EntryState>[];
  final sub = bloc.stream.listen(states.add);
  bloc.add(const EntryAdded(Entry(id: '1')));
  await Future.delayed(Duration.zero);
  expect((states.last as EntryLoaded).entries, hasLength(1));
});

// THE TESTING ARGUMENT is real: a library that makes state
// testable without a widget tree is worth a lot on a project
// with a lot of logic in it.

Exercises 8

  1. Classify every piece of state in an app you have: local, shared, remote, or derived. Count the derived ones you are wrongly storing.
  2. Refactor three levels of nested setState into lifted state with parameters and callbacks. Note the readability change.
  3. Build a ChangeNotifier by hand with an InheritedNotifier, then replace it with Provider and a select selector.
  4. Build the same list screen three ways: setState, Riverpod with a select, and Bloc with buildWhen. Measure the rebuild count for each.
  5. Write a Riverpod AsyncNotifier with an optimistic update and a rollback, and test both paths.
  6. Write a signal store with a computed and an effect, and prove that changing one signal does not rebuild a widget that reads another.
  7. Migrate one feature of a real app to Riverpod, leaving the rest with setState.

8 · Navigation and Routing

8.1 The Navigator 1.0 API8.2 go_router8.3 Deep links8.4 Nested navigation8.5 Dialogs, sheets and overlays8.6 Guards and authentication8.7 Navigation and state

Navigator 1.0 still works, go_router is the recommended default, and a few patterns - nested navigation, guards and deep links - are where routing gets interesting.

8.1 The Navigator 1.0 API

// THE OLD API: still perfectly good for a simple app
Navigator(
  onGenerateRoute: (settings) {
    switch (settings.name) {
      case '/':
        return MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => const HomeScreen());
      case '/entry':
        final id = settings.arguments as String;
        return MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => EntryScreen(id: id));
      default:
        return MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => const NotFoundScreen());
    }
  },
  onPopPage: (route, result) {
    // required since Flutter 3.16: you must pop it yourself
    if (!route.didPop(result)) return false;
    return true;
  },
);

// imperative, for a stack
Navigator.of(context).push(MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => const Detail()));
Navigator.of(context).pushReplacement(...);   // no back to this one
Navigator.of(context).pushAndRemoveUntil(..., (r) => false);   // clear the stack
Navigator.of(context).pop();
Navigator.of(context).popUntil((r) => r.isFirst);
Navigator.of(context).maybePop();     // respects a PopScope
Navigator.of(context).canPop();

// the DRAWER / TABS patterns
Scaffold(
  drawer: const Drawer(child: AppDrawer()),
  body: DefaultTabController(
    length: 3,
    child: Column(children: [
      const TabBar(tabs: [Tab(text: 'All'), Tab(text: 'Photos'), Tab(text: 'Notes')]),
      Expanded(
        child: TabBarView(children: [AllList(), PhotosGrid(), NotesList()]),
      ),
    ]),
  ),
);
// THE MODAL ROUTES
showDialog<T>(
  context: context,
  builder: (context) => AlertDialog(
    title: const Text('Delete entry?'),
    content: const Text('This cannot be undone.'),
    actions: [
      TextButton(onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context), child: const Text('Cancel')),
      FilledButton(
        onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context, true),   // the result
        child: const Text('Delete'),
      ),
    ],
  ),
).then((confirmed) {
  if (confirmed == true) _delete();
});

showModalBottomSheet<T>(
  context: context,
  isScrollControlled: true,      // REQUIRED for a tall sheet with a keyboard
  useSafeArea: true,             // above the notch and the home indicator
  showDragHandle: true,          // the grab handle, in Material 3
  builder: (context) => const EntryEditorSheet(),
);

showModalBottomSheet(
  context: context,
  isScrollControlled: true,
  builder: (context) => Padding(
    // 1. the keyboard, so the field is not covered
    padding: EdgeInsets.only(bottom: MediaQuery.viewInsetsOf(context).bottom),
    child: Padding(
      padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
      child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [
        const TextField(),
        const SizedBox(height: 16),
        FilledButton(onPressed: submit, child: const Text('Save')),
      ]),
    ),
  ),
);

The stack, and why it is the wrong shape for a tabbed app

Every navigation model is a decision about what the user can go back to, and the imperative navigator answers it as a stack: push adds, pop removes, and back pops. That model is correct for a hierarchy and wrong for most real applications, because a real application is a set of tabs each of which has its own stack, and the imperative navigator has no first-class notion of either. Then the four APIs, and the difference between them is which object holds the state. Navigator pushes Route objects that own a BuildContext, and a route is opaque: the pushing side cannot reach into the pushed screen's state except through a key or a callback. Navigator.pages is the page-based API, where navigation state is a list of page objects the application owns, so the back stack is a value you can inspect, serialise and restore — which is what makes browser URL integration and state restoration possible rather than bolted on. Navigator.onGenerateRoute turns a route name into a widget, which is a routing table rather than a stack of closures, and is the older declarative middle ground. And Router with a router delegate is the same idea moved to the application level, where a delegate owns the whole navigation state and the navigator is a pure renderer of it — which is what declarative routers are built on and why they can integrate with a URL. Then the three things that go wrong with the imperative API, and each has a specific fix. State is lost on process death, because the stack of closures cannot be rebuilt; the fix is the page API, where the stack is data. A nested navigator does not participate in the outer back button unless it is wired to the parent, so a tab's stack grows invisibly and back leaves the tab rather than the screen — the fix is a single root navigator and one stack. And push-and-then-immediately-decide produces a flash, because the new route animates in before its data arrives; the fix is to push a route whose content shows a loading state, or to fetch before pushing, and both are worse than deciding after the fetch. Then the practical recommendation, which is short. Use a declarative router for anything with more than about five routes, because the things you get — a URL for every screen, inspectable state, state restoration, and guards — are things you will otherwise build. Use the imperative navigator for a modal, a bottom sheet, or a single-screen flow, where a stack is the right model and the ceremony is not worth it. And do not mix them in one app without a rule about which is which, because two navigation models means two back buttons' behaviour and two places where a redirect can happen.

/* The stack model. */
const STACK = {
  does: 'EVERY NAVIGATION MODEL IS A DECISION about WHAT the USER CAN GO BACK TO',
  imperativeAnswers: 'A STACK - push ADDS, pop REMOVES, and back POPS',
  rightFor: 'A HIERARCHY',
  wrongFor: 'MOST REAL APPLICATIONS',
  why: 'because A REAL APPLICATION IS A SET of TABS EACH of WHICH HAS ITS OWN STACK, and the IMPERATIVE NAVIGATOR HAS NO FIRST-CLASS NOTION of EITHER',
};

/* Four APIs. */
const APIS = [
  { a: 'Navigator', pushes: 'Route OBJECTS',
    route: 'A Route IS OPAQUE - the PUSHING SIDE CANNOT REACH INTO the PUSHED SCREENS STATE except THROUGH A KEY or A CALLBACK' },
  { a: 'Navigator.pages', is: 'the PAGE-BASED API',
    ownership: 'NAVIGATION STATE IS A LIST of PAGE OBJECTS the APPLICATION OWNS',
    gain: 'so the BACK STACK IS A VALUE YOU CAN INSPECT, SERIALISE and RESTORE',
    and: 'which IS WHAT MAKES BROWSER URL INTEGRATION and STATE RESTORATION POSSIBLE rather than BOLTED ON' },
  { a: 'Navigator.onGenerateRoute', does: 'TURNS A ROUTE NAME INTO A WIDGET',
    is: 'A ROUTING TABLE rather than A STACK of CLOSURES', and: 'the OLDER DECLARATIVE MIDDLE GROUND' },
  { a: 'Router WITH A ROUTER DELEGATE', is: 'the SAME IDEA MOVED TO the APPLICATION LEVEL',
    mechanism: 'a DELEGATE OWNS the WHOLE NAVIGATION STATE and the NAVIGATOR IS A PURE RENDERER of IT',
    why: 'which IS WHAT DECLARATIVE ROUTERS ARE BUILT ON and WHY THEY CAN INTEGRATE WITH A URL' },
];

/* Three things that go wrong. */
const FAILURES = [
  { f: 'STATE IS LOST ON PROCESS DEATH', cause: 'the STACK of CLOSURES CANNOT BE REBUILT', fix: 'the PAGE API, WHERE the STACK IS DATA' },
  { f: 'A NESTED NAVIGATOR DOES NOT PARTICIPATE IN the OUTER BACK BUTTON unless IT IS WIRED TO the PARENT',
    symptom: 'so a TABS STACK GROWS INVISIBLY and back LEAVES the TAB rather than the SCREEN',
    fix: 'a SINGLE ROOT NAVIGATOR and ONE STACK' },
  { f: 'PUSH-AND-THEN-IMMEDIATELY-DECIDE PRODUCES A FLASH', cause: 'the NEW ROUTE ANIMATES IN BEFORE ITS DATA ARRIVES',
    fixes: ['push a ROUTE WHOSE CONTENT SHOWS A LOADING STATE', 'or FETCH BEFORE PUSHING'],
    and: 'both are WORSE THAN DECIDING AFTER the FETCH' },
];

/* The recommendation. */
const ADVICE = [
  { a: 'USE A DECLARATIVE ROUTER for ANYTHING with MORE THAN ABOUT FIVE ROUTES',
    gain: 'because the THINGS YOU GET - A URL for EVERY SCREEN, INSPECTABLE STATE, STATE RESTORATION, and GUARDS - ARE THINGS YOU WILL OTHERWISE BUILD' },
  { a: 'USE the IMPERATIVE NAVIGATOR for A MODAL, A BOTTOM SHEET, or a SINGLE-SCREEN FLOW',
    why: 'where A STACK IS the RIGHT MODEL and the CEREMONY IS NOT WORTH IT' },
  { a: 'DO NOT MIX THEM IN ONE APP WITHOUT A RULE about WHICH IS WHICH',
    consequence: 'because TWO NAVIGATION MODELS MEANS TWO BACK BUTTONS BEHAVIOUR and TWO PLACES WHERE A REDIRECT CAN HAPPEN' },
];

8.2 go_router

The single most useful thing about go_router is the redirect. It runs on every navigation and on every session change, so a token that expires mid-session logs the user out from one place, and a deep link that arrives before the session is known waits rather than redirecting on incomplete information.

// pubspec.yaml
//   go_router: ^14.2.0

// the router, declared once
final router = GoRouter(
  // 1. where to start, and whether to start at all
  initialLocation: '/',

  // 2. navigation events, for analytics
  onLogAnalytics: (route) => analytics.logScreenView(route.matchedLocation),

  // 3. error handling
  errorBuilder: (context, state) => Scaffold(
    body: ErrorScreen(error: state.error, path: state.uri.path),
  ),

  // 4. observers, for a route-change side effect
  observers: [AuthRefreshListenable(router)],

  // 5. the routes
  routes: [
    // a simple route
    GoRoute(
      path: '/',
      name: 'home',
      builder: (context, state) => const HomeScreen(),
    ),

    // a route with a path parameter
    GoRoute(
      path: '/entries/:id',
      name: 'entry',
      builder: (context, state) {
        final id = state.pathParameters['id']!;
        return EntryScreen(id: id);
      },
      routes: [
        // 6. NESTED: a sub-route, and a full-screen child
        GoRoute(
          path: 'comments',
          name: 'entryComments',
          builder: (context, state) => CommentsScreen(id: state.pathParameters['id']!),
        ),
        // a modal, on top of the parent
        GoRoute(
          path: 'edit',
          name: 'entryEdit',
          pageBuilder: (context, state) => CustomTransitionPage(
            key: state.pageKey,
            opaque: false,                    // the parent stays visible
            barrierColor: Colors.black54,
            transitionDuration: const Duration(milliseconds: 250),
            transitionsBuilder: (context, animation, secondary, child) {
              return SlideTransition(
                position: Tween(begin: const Offset(0, 1), end: Offset.zero)
                    .animate(CurvedAnimation(parent: animation, curve: Curves.easeOutCubic)),
                child: child,
              );
            },
            child: EntryEditScreen(id: state.pathParameters['id']!),
          ),
        ),
      ],
    ),

    // a query parameter
    GoRoute(
      path: '/search',
      builder: (context, state) {
        final query = state.uri.queryParameters['q'] ?? '';
        return SearchScreen(initialQuery: query);
      },
    ),

    // a shell: a bottom nav with independent stacks
    StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack(
      builder: (context, state, navigationShell) => ScaffoldWithNavBar(
        navigationShell: navigationShell,
      ),
      branches: [
        StatefulShellBranch(routes: [
          GoRoute(path: '/home', builder: (_, __) => const HomeTab()),
          GoRoute(path: '/home/search', builder: (_, __) => const SearchTab()),
        ]),
        StatefulShellBranch(routes: [
          GoRoute(path: '/library', builder: (_, __) => const LibraryTab()),
        ]),
        StatefulShellBranch(routes: [
          GoRoute(path: '/settings', builder: (_, __) => const SettingsTab()),
        ]),
      ],
    ),
  ],
);

// and the app
MaterialApp.router(
  routerConfig: router,
  title: 'Field Notes',
  theme: AppTheme.light,
  darkTheme: AppTheme.dark,
  themeMode: ThemeMode.system,
);

// navigating
context.go('/entries/123');                  // REPLACE the stack
context.push('/entries/123/comments');       // PUSH on top
context.pop();
context.canPop();
context.go('/library');
context.popUntil((route) => route.matchedLocation == '/home');
// the push vs go distinction, which people get wrong
//
// context.go()    REPLACES the current stack. Like a web
//                  navigation. The back button goes to wherever
//                  you came from, not to a history of pushes.
//
// context.push()  ADDS to the stack. The back button returns to
//                  the previous screen. Use for drill-down.
//
// THE WRONG CHOICE
context.push('/entry/1');
context.push('/entry/2');
// now the user has to press back twice to leave
context.go('/entry/1');
context.go('/entry/2');
// now the back button exits the app, because there is one screen
//
// THE RIGHT PATTERNS
// tab navigation: go()      - a tab switch replaces
// drill-down:     push()    - a detail screen stacks
// submit a form: pop() with a result
// "open a detail and replace": pushReplacement

// named routes: readable, and refactor-safe
context.pushNamed('entry', pathParameters: {'id': '123'});
context.goNamed('entry', pathParameters: {'id': '123'});

// extra: passing objects that are not in the URL
context.push('/entries/123', extra: entry);
// read it
final entry = state.extra as Entry?;

// the type-safe version, with go_router_builder
@TypedGoRoute<EntryRoute>(path: '/entries/:id')
class EntryRoute extends GoRouteData {
  const EntryRoute({required this.id, this.initialTab});

  final String id;
  final int? initialTab;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context, GoRouterState state) {
    return EntryScreen(id: id, initialTab: initialTab ?? 0);
  }
}

// then: context.push(EntryRoute(id: '123').location)
// and a generated Location class: EntryRouteLocation(id: '123')
// the path is defined ONCE, in the annotation

Redirects, guards and the parts of the configuration that matter

A declarative router's value is concentrated in its redirect and guard mechanisms, and the difference between them is the thing most people get wrong. A redirect runs before navigation and can change where you go. It is for facts about the session: not signed in, signed in but on the login screen, account deactivated. A guard runs before the destination's page is built and can only stop it. It is for conditions about the destination: does this record exist, is this feature enabled for this plan, has the user completed onboarding. The distinction matters because a redirect that tries to do a guard's job produces a redirect loop when the condition is never satisfied, and the fix is a guard. Then the four configuration pieces that carry most of the weight, and each solves a specific problem. initialLocation fixes where a cold start lands, and its absence is why an app opened from a link sometimes shows the home screen first. redirect is a function of the current match and is evaluated on every navigation, so it must be cheap and must be total — every path in the app has to be covered by one of its branches or a deep link to an unknown route will fall through. onException is the router's error page and its redirect, and it is what turns a malformed URL into a screen rather than a blank one; without it the router's default is an error widget in the console. And errorBuilder on a specific route handles a failure inside that route rather than in the navigation itself. Then the three things that make a declarative router feel slow, and each has a known cause. The transition is animated and there are many of them. A router that pushes a new page for every filter change animates each one; the fix is to change a parameter rather than push a page. The route rebuilds its subtree. A router widget rebuilds when its configuration changes, and if the configuration object is constructed inline every build then it changes every build — so the configuration must be a top-level final, not a value built in a build method. And the scroll position is restored on every rebuild in some configurations, which looks like the list jumping; the fix is explicit scroll behaviour on the page rather than the default. Then the two practices worth adopting from the start. Give every route a name and keep the names in one file, because a route referred to by string literal from a redirect and from a link is two places that must agree and a typo in either is a runtime failure. And keep the redirect pure, taking only the match and returning a location: a redirect that performs a side effect is a redirect whose behaviour depends on when it ran, and that is the class of bug that only reproduces in production.

/* Redirect versus guard. */
const REDIRECT = {
  runs: 'BEFORE NAVIGATION',
  can: 'CHANGE WHERE YOU GO',
  for: 'FACTS ABOUT the SESSION',
  instances: ['not SIGNED IN', 'SIGNED IN but ON the LOGIN SCREEN', 'ACCOUNT DEACTIVATED'],
};
const GUARD = {
  runs: 'BEFORE the DESTINATIONS PAGE IS BUILT',
  can: 'ONLY STOP IT',
  for: 'CONDITIONS ABOUT the DESTINATION',
  instances: ['DOES THIS RECORD EXIST', 'IS THIS FEATURE ENABLED for this PLAN', 'HAS the USER COMPLETED ONBOARDING'],
};
const DISTINCTION_MATTERS = 'because A REDIRECT THAT TRIES TO DO A GUARDS JOB PRODUCES A REDIRECT LOOP WHEN the CONDITION IS NEVER SATISFIED, and the FIX IS A GUARD';

/* Four pieces. */
const CONFIG = [
  { p: 'initialLocation', fixes: 'WHERE A COLD START LANDS',
    whyNeeded: 'its ABSENCE IS WHY an APP OPENED FROM A LINK SOMETIMES SHOWS the HOME SCREEN FIRST' },
  { p: 'redirect', is: 'A FUNCTION of the CURRENT MATCH',
    evaluated: 'ON EVERY NAVIGATION',
    rules: ['it MUST BE CHEAP', 'and it MUST BE TOTAL - EVERY PATH in the APP HAS TO BE COVERED by ONE of ITS BRANCHES or a DEEP LINK TO AN UNKNOWN ROUTE WILL FALL THROUGH'] },
  { p: 'onException', is: 'the ROUTERS ERROR PAGE and ITS REDIRECT',
    gain: 'and IT IS WHAT TURNS A MALFORMED URL INTO A SCREEN rather than A BLANK ONE',
    withoutIt: 'WITHOUT IT the ROUTERS DEFAULT IS AN ERROR WIDGET IN the CONSOLE' },
  { p: 'errorBuilder on a SPECIFIC ROUTE', handles: 'A FAILURE INSIDE that ROUTE rather than IN the NAVIGATION ITSELF' },
];

/* Three things that feel slow. */
const SLOW = [
  { c: 'the TRANSITION IS ANIMATED and THERE ARE MANY of THEM',
    detail: 'A ROUTER THAT PUSHES A NEW PAGE for EVERY FILTER CHANGE ANIMATES EACH ONE',
    fix: 'CHANGE A PARAMETER rather than PUSH A PAGE' },
  { c: 'the ROUTE REBUILDS ITS SUBTREE',
    detail: 'A ROUTER WIDGET REBUILDS WHEN ITS CONFIGURATION CHANGES, and if the CONFIGURATION OBJECT IS CONSTRUCTED INLINE EVERY BUILD then IT CHANGES EVERY BUILD',
    fix: 'the CONFIGURATION MUST BE A TOP-LEVEL FINAL, not A VALUE BUILT IN A BUILD METHOD' },
  { c: 'the SCROLL POSITION IS RESTORED ON EVERY REBUILD in SOME CONFIGURATIONS',
    symptom: 'which LOOKS LIKE the LIST JUMPING',
    fix: 'EXPLICIT SCROLL BEHAVIOUR ON the PAGE rather than the DEFAULT' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'GIVE EVERY ROUTE A NAME and KEEP the NAMES IN ONE FILE',
    why: 'because A ROUTE REFERRED TO BY STRING LITERAL FROM A REDIRECT and FROM A LINK IS TWO PLACES THAT MUST AGREE',
    and: 'a TYPO IN EITHER IS A RUNTIME FAILURE' },
  { p: 'KEEP the REDIRECT PURE',
    shape: 'TAKING ONLY the MATCH and RETURNING A LOCATION',
    why: 'a REDIRECT THAT PERFORMS A SIDE EFFECT IS A REDIRECT WHOSE BEHAVIOUR DEPENDS ON WHEN IT RAN',
    and: 'which IS THE CLASS OF BUG THAT ONLY REPRODUCES IN PRODUCTION' },
];

8.3 Deep links

The classic deep-link bug is a redirect that runs before the app has finished initialising, so it decides the user is not logged in and sends them to the login screen - discarding the link they tapped. Make the initialised state part of the redirect decision rather than assuming it.

// A DEEP LINK opens the app at a specific screen
//   acme://entries/123              a custom scheme
//   https://acme.com/entries/123    a universal link (iOS)
//   https://acme.com/entries/123    an app link (Android)

// THE PLATFORM SETUP
// Android: android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml
<activity
    android:name=".MainActivity"
    android:launchMode="singleTask">    <!-- REQUIRED -->
  <intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">
    <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
    <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
    <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" />
    <data android:scheme="https" android:host="acme.com"
          android:pathPrefix="/entries" />
  </intent-filter>
</activity>

// iOS: ios/Runner/Info.plist
<key>CFBundleURLTypes</key>
<array>
  <dict>
    <key>CFBundleURLSchemes</key><array><string>acme</string></array>
  </dict>
</array>
// and the Associated Domains capability for universal links,
// with the apple-app-site-association file on your domain

// THE FLUTTER SIDE: with go_router, it is automatic
// the router matches the incoming URI against its route table
// MaterialApp.router(routerConfig: router)   // and you are done

// handling it manually, for a notification
final link = await getInitialLink();          // a cold start
final link = GetPlatform.isWeb ? null : null;
await _router.routerInformationProvider.restoreLink(link);
// or, per navigation
Notifications.onSelect = (payload) {
  context.push(payload['deepLink'] ?? '/');
};

// the types go_router handles
//   /entries/123                  path parameter
//   /search?q=flutter              query parameter
//   /entries/123#comment-5        a fragment: a page section
//   /entries/123?tab=comments     both

// a GoRoute that uses all of them
GoRoute(
  path: '/entries/:id',
  builder: (context, state) {
    final id = state.pathParameters['id']!;
    final tab = int.tryParse(state.uri.queryParameters['tab'] ?? '0') ?? 0;
    return EntryScreen(id: id, initialTab: tab);
  },
);
// THE TYPICAL FAILURE: a deep link on a COLD start
// the route is available before the app has finished
// initialising: a token check, a database open, a config fetch
//
// the symptom: the link opens the app and it lands on the login
// screen, or on a blank screen, because the guard ran before the
// session was known.

// THE FIX: make the redirect a value that updates
class AuthListenable extends ChangeNotifier {
  AuthListenable(this._session);
  Session? _session;
  bool _initialised = false;

  Session? get session => _session;
  bool get isInitialised => _initialised;

  void setSession(Session? s) {
    _session = s;
    _initialised = true;
    notifyListeners();
  }
}

final authListenable = AuthListenable(null);

final router = GoRouter(
  refreshListenable: authListenable,        // re-evaluates on notify
  redirect: (context, state) {
    // WAIT for initialisation, or the redirect makes a decision
    // on incomplete information
    if (!authListenable.isInitialised) return null;

    final loggedIn = authListenable.session != null;
    final goingToLogin = state.matchedLocation == '/login';

    if (!loggedIn && !goingToLogin) {
      // preserve the deep link so the user lands where they meant to
      return Uri(path: '/login', queryParameters: {'from': state.uri.toString()}).toString();
    }
    if (loggedIn && goingToLogin) return '/';
    return null;                              // no redirect
  },
  routes: [...],
);

// in main: restore the session, THEN let the router decide
void main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  await Firebase.initializeApp();
  final session = await SessionStore.restore();
  authListenable.setSession(session);
  runApp(const ProviderScope(child: MyApp()));
}

Cold start, warm start, and the initialisation order that breaks links

A deep link that works when the app is already running and does nothing when it is launched from cold is the most common deep-link bug, and the reason is an ordering problem rather than a parsing problem. Three pieces of state have to exist before a link can be handled: the initial route, the authentication state, and any data the destination screen needs. On a warm start all three exist and the link works. On a cold start none do, and whichever piece is checked first wins — which is why the failure is intermittent and why it often only reproduces on a real device with the app not running. Then the order that works, and each step's reason. The platform delivers the link to the app before any Dart code runs, as an initial route on the platform's own channel mechanism. The app must restore the session before resolving any route, because a redirect that runs first sees no session and sends a signed-in user to the login screen — and the fix is a splash or loading state that awaits the restore rather than a flag on every screen. Only then does the router see both the initial route and the session and produce the correct destination. And only after that can the destination screen fetch its data, which means a deep link into a detail screen must handle the case where the record does not exist — a cold-started link to a deleted record has to resolve to a not-found state rather than an error or a spinner that never ends. Then the three link kinds and their differences, because they arrive by different routes and are easy to conflate. A universal link is verified by the operating system against a file on a domain you own, so a link only opens your app if that domain association is set up and the file is served over HTTPS; the user can always override it, and a misconfigured association means the link opens a browser. An app link on Android is the same idea with different verification and different failure modes. And a custom scheme is a private URL scheme your app registers — it requires no verification, it works immediately, and it is the wrong choice for anything public because a custom scheme can be claimed by another app, which is the security reason the platform-verified links exist. Then the three practices that make links work reliably, and each is a specific failure. Test from a cold start every time, because warm-start testing cannot find the ordering bug and the ordering bug is the whole problem. Log the initial route, the restored session and the resolved destination, in that order, because the log sequence tells you which step is wrong in one reading and guessing does not. And have a fallback for an unknown or unparseable link — a home screen, not an error — because a link will eventually be malformed and an app that cannot start because of a bad URL is a worse outcome than losing the deep link.

/* Three pieces of state. */

const BUG = 'A DEEP LINK THAT WORKS WHEN the APP IS ALREADY RUNNING and DOES NOTHING WHEN IT IS LAUNCHED FROM COLD IS THE MOST COMMON DEEP-LINK BUG';

8.4 Nested navigation

// THE PROBLEM: a bottom nav with three tabs. Pressing back on
// tab 2 should return to tab 1, NOT exit the app - but a naive
// single Navigator stack does not do that.

// STATEFUL SHELL: the answer. Each branch has its OWN stack.
StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack(
  builder: (context, state, navigationShell) {
    // navigationShell.goBranch(index, initialLocation: index == currentIndex)
    return Scaffold(
      body: navigationShell,          // the current branch's stack
      bottomNavigationBar: NavigationBar(
        selectedIndex: navigationShell.currentIndex,
        onDestinationSelected: (index) => navigationShell.goBranch(
          index,
          // initialLocation: index == navigationShell.currentIndex
          //   ? true     -> pop this branch to its root when
          //                 re-tapping the same tab
          //   : false    -> preserve this branch's stack
        ),
        destinations: const [
          NavigationDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.home), label: 'Home'),
          NavigationDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.library), label: 'Library'),
          NavigationDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.settings), label: 'Settings'),
        ],
      ),
    );
  },
  branches: [
    StatefulShellBranch(routes: [
      GoRoute(path: '/home', builder: (_, __) => const HomeTab()),
      GoRoute(path: '/home/detail/:id', builder: (_, s) => DetailScreen(id: s.pathParameters['id']!)),
    ]),
    StatefulShellBranch(routes: [
      GoRoute(path: '/library', builder: (_, __) => const LibraryTab()),
    ]),
    StatefulShellBranch(routes: [
      GoRoute(path: '/settings', builder: (_, __) => const SettingsTab()),
    ]),
  ],
)

// WHAT THIS GIVES YOU, which is what users expect
// - each tab keeps its own navigation history
// - switching back to a tab shows where you left it
// - back inside a tab pops that tab's stack
// - back at the root of a tab exits (or goes to the first tab)
// - the IndexedStack keeps the state of all three alive

// THE OTHER APPROACH: a manually managed stack per tab
class _TabShellState extends State<TabShell> with RestorationMixin {
  final _navKeys = List.generate(3, (_) => GlobalKey<NavigatorState>());
  int _index = 0;

  // REQUIRED for the state to survive a process death and restore
  @override
  String? get restorationId => 'tab_shell';

  @override
  void restoreState(RestorationBucket? oldBucket, bool initialRestore) {
    registerForRestoration(_index, 'index');
    if (bucket != null) {
      _index = bucket.read<int>('index') ?? 0;
    }
  }

  @override
  void saveState(RestorationBucket? bucket) {
    bucket?.write('index', _index);
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return PopScope(
      canPop: false,
      onPopInvokedWithResult: (didPop, _) async {
        if (didPop) return;
        // back inside the current tab first
        final nav = _navKeys[_index].currentState;
        if (nav != null && nav.canPop()) {
          nav.pop();
          return;
        }
        // then go to the first tab
        if (_index != 0) {
          setState(() => _index = 0);
          return;
        }
        // then let it exit
        SystemNavigator.pop();
      },
      child: Scaffold(
        body: IndexedStack(
          index: _index,
          children: [
            for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++)
              Navigator(
                key: _navKeys[i],
                onGenerateRoute: (settings) => MaterialPageRoute(
                  settings: settings,
                  builder: (_) => _screens[i],
                ),
              ),
          ],
        ),
        bottomNavigationBar: NavigationBar(
          selectedIndex: _index,
          onDestinationSelected: (i) => setState(() => _index = i),
          destinations: const [...],
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}
// RESTORATION: surviving a process death
// Android will kill your app in the background and restore it.
// without restoration, the user lands on the home screen.

// at the top
class MyApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const MyApp({super.key});
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return RestorationScope(
      restorationId: 'app',
      child: MaterialApp.router(
        routerConfig: router,
        restorationScopeId: 'router',      // REQUIRED for the router
        builder: (context, child) => MediaQuery.withClampedTextScaling(
          // respect the OS font size, but cap it so the layout
          // does not break at 200%
          minScaleFactor: 1.0,
          maxScaleFactor: 1.5,
          child: child!,
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

// in a stateful widget
class EntryListState extends State<EntryList> with RestorationMixin {
  final _controller = TextEditingController();
  late final RestorableInt _scrollOffset = RestorableInt(0);

  @override
  String? get restorationId => 'entry_list';

  @override
  void restoreState(RestorationBucket? oldBucket, bool initialRestore) {
    registerForRestoration(_scrollOffset, 'scroll');
    registerForRestoration(_controller, 'query');
    if (_scrollOffset.value != 0) {
      WidgetsBinding.instance.addPostFrameCallback((_) {
        _scrollController.jumpTo(_scrollOffset.value.toDouble());
      });
    }
  }

  @override
  void saveState(RestorationBucket? bucket) {
    bucket?.write('scroll', _controller.position.pixels.round());
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _scrollOffset.dispose();
    _controller.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }
}

One stack or many, and why the choice is a design decision

Nested navigation is the question of whether the back button pops one stack or many, and every option is defensible for some application shape, so the right answer is decided by what the back button should mean. Option one: a single stack for the whole app, with tab changes implemented as a route replacement rather than a separate navigator. Then back behaves exactly as a user expects — it returns through the history of where you have been, across tabs. The cost is that a tab change is a navigation, so it is animated and can be recorded in history, and a user who switches tabs and presses back lands in the other tab, which some find surprising and some find correct. Option two: one navigator per tab, each with its own stack, where the system back button pops the active tab's stack and switches to the previous tab when that stack is empty. This is the pattern users know from native apps and it is what most tabbed applications should do. The cost is that the back behaviour is a behaviour of the shell rather than of the navigator, which means it must be implemented, and implemented correctly — including the case where a nested navigator is pushed as a route inside a tab, which produces two stacks and requires deciding which one the button touches. Option three: the declarative routers, which implement the shell behaviour for you, because the router owns the state and can express "each tab has a stack" as data. Then the three failure modes, and each has a specific cause. Back does nothing on the root of a nested navigator. The stack is empty, and the shell does not know to switch tabs; the fix is to check whether the active navigator can pop before handling the back event yourself. Back pops the wrong stack. A dialog pushed on a root navigator while a tab has its own navigator means two candidates and the wrong one may be popped; the fix is one navigator at the top and dialogs as routes on it. And state is lost when switching tabs, because the tab's navigator was disposed with the tab's widget; the fix is an IndexedStack so every tab's subtree stays alive, or a state container that owns the tab's state rather than its widgets. Then the two practices that prevent most of it. Decide where dialogs and sheets are pushed — a root navigator, so they cover everything and the back button closes them predictably — and say so in a comment, because it is the single decision that most often conflicts with an implementation's assumption. And keep tab state in a state container, not in tab widgets, so that a tab which is unmounted, remounted or rebuilt by a configuration change gets its state back; the state chapter's argument about what survives a widget applies here exactly.

/* The question. */
const QUESTION = 'WHETHER the BACK BUTTON POPS ONE STACK or MANY';
const DECIDED_BY = 'WHAT the BACK BUTTON SHOULD MEAN';

/* Three options. */
const OPTIONS = [
  { o: 'A SINGLE STACK for the WHOLE APP', how: 'with TAB CHANGES IMPLEMENTED AS A ROUTE REPLACEMENT rather than A SEPARATE NAVIGATOR',
    back: 'BEHAVES EXACTLY AS A USER EXPECTS - it RETURNS THROUGH the HISTORY of WHERE YOU HAVE BEEN, ACROSS TABS',
    cost: 'a TAB CHANGE IS A NAVIGATION, so IT IS ANIMATED and CAN BE RECORDED IN HISTORY',
    surprise: 'a USER WHO SWITCHES TABS and PRESSES BACK LANDS IN the OTHER TAB, WHICH SOME FIND SURPRISING and SOME FIND CORRECT' },
  { o: 'ONE NAVIGATOR PER TAB, each with ITS OWN STACK',
    back: 'the SYSTEM BACK BUTTON POPS the ACTIVE TABS STACK and SWITCHES TO the PREVIOUS TAB WHEN THAT STACK IS EMPTY',
    known: 'this IS THE PATTERN USERS KNOW FROM NATIVE APPS and IT IS WHAT MOST TABBED APPLICATIONS SHOULD DO',
    cost: 'the BACK BEHAVIOUR IS A BEHAVIOUR of the SHELL rather than of the NAVIGATOR, WHICH MEANS IT MUST BE IMPLEMENTED',
    and: 'IMPLEMENTED CORRECTLY - INCLUDING the CASE WHERE A NESTED NAVIGATOR IS PUSHED AS A ROUTE INSIDE A TAB, WHICH PRODUCES TWO STACKS and REQUIRES DECIDING WHICH ONE the BUTTON TOUCHES' },
  { o: 'the DECLARATIVE ROUTERS', implementTheShellBehaviourForYou: true,
    because: 'the ROUTER OWNS the STATE and CAN EXPRESS each tab has a stack AS DATA' },

/* Three failure modes. */
const FAILURES = [
  { f: 'BACK DOES NOTHING ON the ROOT of A NESTED NAVIGATOR',
    cause: 'the STACK IS EMPTY, and the SHELL DOES NOT KNOW TO SWITCH TABS',
    fix: 'CHECK WHETHER the ACTIVE NAVIGATOR CAN POP BEFORE HANDLING the BACK EVENT YOURSELF' },
  { f: 'BACK POPS the WRONG STACK',
    cause: 'a DIALOG PUSHED ON A ROOT NAVIGATOR WHILE A TAB HAS ITS OWN NAVIGATOR MEANS TWO CANDIDATES',
    symptom: 'and the WRONG ONE MAY BE POPPED',

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'DECIDE WHERE DIALOGS and SHEETS ARE PUSHED - A ROOT NAVIGATOR, so THEY COVER EVERYTHING and the BACK BUTTON CLOSES THEM PREDICTABLY',
    and: 'SAY SO IN A COMMENT, because IT IS the SINGLE DECISION THAT MOST OFTEN CONFLICTS WITH an IMPLEMENTATIONS ASSUMPTION' },
  { p: 'KEEP TAB STATE IN A STATE CONTAINER, not IN TAB WIDGETS',
