8.5 Dialogs, sheets and overlays

// A DIALOG that returns a value, and is dismissed correctly
Future<bool?> _confirmDelete(BuildContext context, Entry entry) async {
  return showDialog<bool>(
    context: context,
    barrierDismissible: false,      // require an explicit choice
    builder: (context) => AlertDialog(
      title: const Text('Delete this note?'),
      content: Text('"${entry.title}" will be removed permanently.'),
      actions: [
        TextButton(
          onPressed: () => Navigator.of(context).pop(false),
          child: const Text('Cancel'),
        ),
        FilledButton(
          onPressed: () => Navigator.of(context).pop(true),
          child: const Text('Delete'),
        ),
      ],
    ),
  );
}

// THE DISMISS RULE: a dialog with a TextField needs this, or
// the keyboard pushes the dialog off screen
showDialog(
  context: context,
  builder: (context) => Padding(
    // the outer padding moves the dialog up by the keyboard height
    padding: EdgeInsets.only(
      bottom: MediaQuery.viewInsetsOf(context).bottom,
    ),
    child: Dialog(
      child: SingleChildScrollView(      // so it can shrink
        child: Padding(
          padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
          child: Column(mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, children: [
            const TextField(),
            const SizedBox(height: 16),
            Row(mainAxisAlignment: MainAxisAlignment.end, children: [
              TextButton(
                onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context),
                child: const Text('Cancel'),
              ),
              const SizedBox(width: 8),
              FilledButton(onPressed: submit, child: const Text('Save')),
            ]),
          ]),
        ),
      ),
    ),
  ),
);

// A FULL-SCREEN DIALOG: a route that looks like a screen
GoRoute(
  path: '/entry/:id/edit',
  pageBuilder: (context, state) => MaterialPage(
    fullscreenDialog: true,      // the iOS swipe-down-to-dismiss
    child: EntryEditScreen(id: state.pathParameters['id']!),
  ),
);

// A CUSTOM OVERLAY: a snackbar, and a floating action sheet
ScaffoldMessenger.of(context)
  ..hideCurrentSnackBar()
  ..showSnackBar(
    SnackBar(
      content: const Text('Saved'),
      action: SnackBarAction(
        label: 'Undo',
        onPressed: _undoDelete,
      ),
      behavior: SnackBarBehavior.floating,
      duration: const Duration(seconds: 4),
    ),
  );

showModalBottomSheet(
  context: context,
  showDragHandle: true,
  builder: (context) => ActionSheet(
    actions: [
      ActionSheetAction(onPressed: () {}, icon: Icon(Icons.share), label: 'Share'),
      ActionSheetAction(onPressed: () {}, icon: Icon(Icons.download), label: 'Download'),
    ],
  ),
);

Overlays, and why they are not widgets

Dialogs, sheets and overlays all use the same mechanism, and the mechanism is worth understanding because it explains a family of surprising behaviour. An overlay is inserted into a separate part of the widget tree — the navigator's overlay — not where you wrote it. It is a subtree that is laid out on top of everything else, which is why a dialog covers a screen regardless of what is in that screen's tree, and why a dialog pushed from a nested navigator still covers the whole screen. The consequences are three and each is a common report. It is not a descendant of the widget that opened it, so it cannot read an inherited widget from there — which is why a dialog that needs a theme, a localisation or a state provider must be given them explicitly or be pushed on a navigator that sits below those providers. It is not inside the layout of the screen, so it does not scroll with it, does not participate in its bounds and is not clipped by it, which is the correct behaviour and also why a dialog near the bottom of a long screen does not move with the content. And its lifecycle is the route's, which is what makes a barrier dismissible and makes a sheet swipe-to-dismiss work. Then the four widgets and which one to use, because the choice is close to mechanical. A dialog is a centred card that is meant to interrupt; it takes a title, content and actions, it is dismissible by default, and it should be used for a decision the user must make. A bottom sheet is a surface that rises from the bottom, non-modal by default, and is used for content the user may want to dismiss by tapping away; a modal variant exists for a decision. A full-screen dialog covers the whole screen and is for a task that must be completed before continuing, and it is a different thing from a route because it does not create a navigation entry. And a side sheet for desktop layouts where a bottom sheet is wrong. Then the two rules, and both are about the barrier. A barrier's dismissibility is a design decision, not a default to keep. A destructive action behind a barrier that dismisses on an accidental tap outside is a defect, and setting the barrier to non-dismissible is one property. And a barrier must be built into the overlay tree rather than placed as a sibling, so that it covers the whole screen including the app bar — placing a container with a colour as a sibling behind a dialog dims only the content area, which is the second most common dialog appearance bug after not specifying a barrier colour at all.

/* The mechanism. */
const MECHANISM = {
  is: 'AN OVERLAY IS INSERTED INTO A SEPARATE PART of the WIDGET TREE - the NAVIGATORS OVERLAY - NOT WHERE YOU WROTE IT',
  what: 'it IS A SUBTREE THAT IS LAID OUT ON TOP of EVERYTHING ELSE',
  why: 'which IS WHY A DIALOG COVERS A SCREEN REGARDLESS of WHAT IS IN that SCREENS TREE',
  and: 'and WHY A DIALOG PUSHED FROM A NESTED NAVIGATOR STILL COVERS the WHOLE SCREEN',
};
const CONSEQUENCES = [
  { c: 'IT IS NOT A DESCENDANT of the WIDGET THAT OPENED IT',
    consequence: 'so it CANNOT READ AN INHERITED WIDGET from THERE',
    fix: 'a DIALOG THAT NEEDS A THEME, A LOCALISATION or A STATE PROVIDER MUST BE GIVEN THEM EXPLICITLY or BE PUSHED ON A NAVIGATOR THAT SITS BELOW THOSE PROVIDERS' },
  { c: 'IT IS NOT INSIDE the LAYOUT of the SCREEN',
    detail: ['it DOES NOT SCROLL WITH IT', 'it DOES NOT PARTICIPATE IN ITS BOUNDS and IS NOT CLIPPED BY IT'],
    note: 'which IS THE CORRECT BEHAVIOUR and ALSO WHY A DIALOG NEAR the BOTTOM of a LONG SCREEN DOES NOT MOVE WITH the CONTENT' },
  { c: 'ITS LIFECYCLE IS the ROUTES',
    gain: 'which IS WHAT MAKES A BARRIER DISMISSIBLE and MAKES A SHEET SWIPE-TO-DISMISS WORK' },
];

/* Four widgets. */
const WIDGETS = [
  { w: 'a DIALOG', is: 'A CENTRED CARD THAT IS MEANT TO INTERRUPT',
    takes: ['a TITLE', 'CONTENT', 'ACTIONS'], dismissibleByDefault: true, usedFor: 'A DECISION the USER MUST MAKE' },
  { w: 'a BOTTOM SHEET', is: 'A SURFACE THAT RISES FROM the BOTTOM', modalByDefault: false,
    usedFor: 'CONTENT the USER MAY WANT TO DISMISS BY TAPPING AWAY', plus: 'a MODAL VARIANT EXISTS for A DECISION' },
  { w: 'a FULL-SCREEN DIALOG', covers: 'the WHOLE SCREEN', usedFor: 'A TASK THAT MUST BE COMPLETED BEFORE CONTINUING',
    difference: 'it IS A DIFFERENT THING FROM A ROUTE BECAUSE it DOES NOT CREATE A NAVIGATION ENTRY' },
  { w: 'a SIDE SHEET', rightFor: 'DESKTOP LAYOUTS WHERE A BOTTOM SHEET IS WRONG' },
];

/* Two rules. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'A BARRIERS DISMISSIBILITY IS A DESIGN DECISION, not A DEFAULT TO KEEP',
    defect: 'A DESTRUCTIVE ACTION BEHIND A BARRIER THAT DISMISSES ON AN ACCIDENTAL TAP OUTSIDE IS A DEFECT',
    fix: 'and SETTING the BARRIER TO NON-DISMISSIBLE IS ONE PROPERTY' },
  { r: 'A BARRIER MUST BE BUILT INTO the OVERLAY TREE rather than PLACED AS A SIBLING',
    why: 'so THAT IT COVERS the WHOLE SCREEN INCLUDING the APP BAR',
    bug: 'PLACING A CONTAINER WITH A COLOUR AS A SIBLING BEHIND A DIALOG DIMS ONLY the CONTENT AREA',

8.6 Guards and authentication

// THE REDIRECT, which is the whole auth mechanism with go_router
final authListenable = AuthListenable();

final router = GoRouter(
  refreshListenable: authListenable,
  redirect: (context, state) {
    // 1. not ready yet: make no decision
    if (!authListenable.isInitialised) return null;

    final loggedIn = authListenable.session != null;
    final location = state.matchedLocation;

    // 2. the routes that are reachable without a session
    const publicRoutes = {'/login', '/signup', '/forgot-password', '/terms'};
    final isPublic = publicRoutes.any(location.startsWith);

    if (!loggedIn && !isPublic) {
      // 3. remember where they were going
      return Uri(
        path: '/login',
        queryParameters: {'from': state.uri.toString()},
      ).toString();
    }
    if (loggedIn && location == '/login') {
      // 4. logged in and on the login screen: send them on
      return authListenable.session!.homeRoute;
    }
    return null;
  },
  routes: [...],
);

// the redirect runs on EVERY navigation, so a session expiring
// mid-session kicks the user out automatically: just call
// authListenable.setSession(null) from the 401 handler.

// ROLE-BASED, the same mechanism
redirect: (context, state) {
  final session = authListenable.session;
  final needsAdmin = state.matchedLocation.startsWith('/admin');
  if (needsAdmin && session?.role != Role.admin) {
    return '/forbidden';
  }
  return null;
},

// AN ARGUMENT GUARD, for a route with a required parameter
GoRoute(
  path: '/entries/:id',
  builder: (context, state) {
    final id = state.pathParameters['id'];
    if (id == null || !_isValidId(id)) {
      return const ErrorScreen(message: 'That link is not valid');
    }
    return EntryScreen(id: id);
  },
);

// A NAVIGATOR 1.0 GUARD, for comparison: you check in each screen
class AdminScreen extends StatefulWidget {
  const AdminScreen({super.key});
  @override
  State<AdminScreen> createState() => _AdminScreenState();
}

class _AdminScreenState extends State<AdminScreen> {
  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    if (!auth.session.isAdmin) {
      // next microtask, so the build is not interrupted
      WidgetsBinding.instance.addPostFrameCallback((_) {
        if (mounted) Navigator.of(context).replace(MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => const ForbiddenScreen()));
      });
    }
  }
}
// this is worse: it flashes the screen before redirecting, and you
// have to remember to do it in every protected screen

Guards, and the failure that is worse than no guard at all

A route guard is a check that runs before a route is entered, and its purpose is to stop a user reaching a screen they should not be on. The mechanism differs by router but the failure modes are the same everywhere. Wrong: redirecting in the build method. A widget that discovers it is unauthenticated and calls a navigation call during build produces a flash of the protected screen, a navigation call during build is an assertion in debug mode, and the same check has to be repeated in every protected screen because nothing in the tree knows the check already happened. Right: redirecting in the router. A redirect is declared in the routing configuration, evaluated before the destination is built, and therefore produces no flash — which is the entire argument, and it is why every router with a first-class redirect API exists. Then the three questions a guard has to answer, and each has a failure when it is answered naively. What counts as authenticated, and when is it known? Restoring a session from storage is asynchronous, and a guard that runs before the restore has completed sees "not authenticated" and redirects a signed-in user to the login screen — which is the single most common guard bug, and the fix is to make the router itself wait for the restore rather than to add a loading flag to every screen. What happens to the destination? A user who taps a deep link to a protected screen while signed out gets sent to login and, on signing in, lands on the home screen rather than where they were going, because the intent was lost. And what happens when the session expires while the user is on a protected screen? Nothing happens until the next navigation, so a screen that was authorised when it was built stays visible; the fix is not in the guard but in an interceptor that reacts to a 401 by clearing the session and navigating. Then the two things worth saying about authorisation, which is a different problem from authentication. Authentication is who; authorisation is what. A guard that only checks authentication lets any signed-in user reach any screen, which is a broken access control finding and the API chapter's first OWASP item. And authorisation must be enforced on the server. A client-side guard is a convenience that prevents accidental navigation; it is not a security control, because anything in the client is under the user's control, so the server must check the session and the permission on every request — and the correct statement is that a client guard is about user experience and a server check is about security, and conflating them produces a system that looks protected and is not.

/* Wrong: redirect in build. */
const WRONG = {
  does: 'A WIDGET THAT DISCOVERS IT IS UNAUTHENTICATED and CALLS A NAVIGATION CALL DURING BUILD',
  failures: ['a FLASH OF the PROTECTED SCREEN',
    'a NAVIGATION CALL DURING BUILD IS AN ASSERTION IN DEBUG MODE',
    'and the SAME CHECK HAS TO BE REPEATED IN EVERY PROTECTED SCREEN BECAUSE NOTHING IN the TREE KNOWS the CHECK ALREADY HAPPENED'],
};

/* Right: redirect in the router. */
const RIGHT = {
  does: 'A REDIRECT IS DECLARED IN the ROUTING CONFIGURATION, EVALUATED BEFORE the DESTINATION IS BUILT',
  gain: 'and THEREFORE PRODUCES NO FLASH',
  and: 'which IS THE ENTIRE ARGUMENT, and IT IS WHY EVERY ROUTER WITH A FIRST-CLASS REDIRECT API EXISTS',
};

/* Three questions. */

/* Authentication versus authorisation. */
const DISTINCTION = {

  authorisation: 'WHAT',

  so: 'the SERVER MUST CHECK the SESSION and the PERMISSION ON EVERY REQUEST',
  reframe: 'the CORRECT STATEMENT IS THAT A CLIENT GUARD IS about USER EXPERIENCE and A SERVER CHECK IS about SECURITY, and CONFLATING THEM PRODUCES A SYSTEM THAT LOOKS PROTECTED and IS NOT',

8.7 Navigation and state

Preserving what the user did, and where it belongs

A route's state has four distinguishable parts, and they have different owners and different lifetimes, which is why "restore my state" is four separate decisions rather than one. The route stack itself is owned by the router and, in the page API, is data — so it can be restored exactly, and its restoration is the only one of the four that a declarative router does for you. The scroll offset of each list is owned by the screen and is the one most often forgotten: a restored route that rebuilds its list from the top feels like the app forgot everything, and the fix is a scroll controller per list with an initial pixel offset restored from storage, keyed by route. The state a user typed — a half-completed form, a search term, a scroll position in a tab — is owned by whatever state container holds it, and its restoration policy is a product decision: a draft that survives process death is usually wanted, and a form that survives a week is not. And the data the screen fetched is owned by the server and should be revalidated rather than restored, because restoring a cached copy and presenting it as current is the stale-data failure the previous chapter's drift section describes. Then the three mechanisms, and which one to reach for. Route state restoration — a route can carry a restoration identifier, and the framework saves and restores its state on Android when the process is killed; it is the correct tool for a screen's own state and it requires nothing. Explicit persistence — writing to storage on change and reading on build — is correct for anything that must survive across sessions and for anything the user would be annoyed to lose, and it is also where the cost lives: a write per keystroke is a write per keystroke, so it must be debounced. And a state container above the router, which is the mechanism for anything shared between routes. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a specific mechanism. Over-restoring. Restoring a screen's state after a user has explicitly navigated away produces a list scrolled to a position from three navigations ago, and the fix is a restoration policy that decides what each screen restores rather than restoring everything. Saving on every frame. A scroll listener that persists the offset on every scroll event writes thousands of times and can affect scroll performance; debouncing to the end of the gesture or on idle fixes it. And restoring into the wrong route after a configuration change, which happens when the restoration identifier is not unique — two instances of the same screen in a stack will restore each other's state, and the fix is to make the identifier include something that distinguishes the instance.

/* Four parts, four owners. */
const PARTS = [
  { p: 'the ROUTE STACK ITSELF', owner: 'the ROUTER',
    inThePageApi: 'IS DATA', gain: 'so IT CAN BE RESTORED EXACTLY',
    and: 'ITS RESTORATION IS THE ONLY ONE of the FOUR THAT A DECLARATIVE ROUTER DOES FOR YOU' },
  { p: 'the SCROLL OFFSET of EACH LIST', owner: 'the SCREEN', mostOftenForgotten: true,
    symptom: 'A RESTORED ROUTE THAT REBUILDS ITS LIST FROM the TOP FEELS LIKE the APP FORGOT EVERYTHING',
    fix: 'A SCROLL CONTROLLER PER LIST WITH AN INITIAL PIXEL OFFSET RESTORED FROM STORAGE, KEYED BY ROUTE' },
  { p: 'the STATE the USER TYPED', owner: 'WHATEVER STATE CONTAINER HOLDS IT',
    isA: 'PRODUCT DECISION',
    instances: ['a HALF-COMPLETED FORM', 'a SEARCH TERM', 'a SCROLL POSITION in a TAB'],
    examples: ['a DRAFT THAT SURVIVES PROCESS DEATH IS USUALLY WANTED', 'a FORM THAT SURVIVES A WEEK IS NOT'] },
  { p: 'the DATA the SCREEN FETCHED', owner: 'the SERVER', should: 'BE REVALIDATED rather than RESTORED',

];

A global variable for selection state works until you have two users, or a restored process, or a parallel test. State that survives navigation belongs in a provider above the router, or in the state the router owns - not in a top-level variable.

// A common question: does state survive navigation?
//
// NO, by default. A pushed route builds a new subtree with a new
// State. The previous screen's State is still in the tree (it is
// still on the stack) but it is not visible.
//
// THREE WAYS TO KEEP STATE ACROSS A NAVIGATION

// 1. Lift it above the Navigator. Correct and simple.
class AppShell extends StatefulWidget {
  const AppShell({super.key});
  @override
  State<AppShell> createState() => _AppShellState();
}

class _AppShellState extends State<AppShell> {
  final _selectedId = ValueNotifier<String?>(null);

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _selectedId.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // both screens are under the SAME ValueNotifier
    return ValueListenableBuilder<String?>(
      valueListenable: _selectedId,
      builder: (context, selectedId, _) {
        return Stack(children: [
          ListScreen(
            selectedId: selectedId,
            onSelect: (id) {
              _selectedId.value = id;
              Navigator.push(context, MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => DetailScreen(id: id)));
            },
          ),
          if (selectedId != null) DetailScreen(id: selectedId),
        ]);
      },
    );
  }
}

// 2. A provider above the Navigator
Provider(
  create: (_) => SelectionModel(),
  child: MaterialApp(home: HomeScreen()),
)
// the state lives in the provider, which is above the router

// 3. Restoration, for surviving a process death (see 8.4)

// THE WRONG PATTERN: a global variable
String? selectedId;     // it works until there are two users
                        // or the app is restored, or two isolates
                        // exist, or a test runs in parallel

Exercises 9

  1. Build a login flow with a go_router redirect that preserves the original destination, and test a deep link to a protected page while logged out.
  2. Build a four-tab shell with StatefulShellRoute. Verify each tab keeps its own history and that back behaves correctly.
  3. Add restoration to a list with a scroll offset, force-quit the app, and confirm the position is restored.
  4. Write a dialog with a TextField that stays above the keyboard on a small phone.
  5. Implement a role guard: an /admin route that redirects a non-admin to a forbidden screen.

9 · Theming, Design Systems and Assets

9.1 Colour, and Material 39.2 Typography9.3 Building a theme properly9.4 Theming the components you did not write9.5 Building a component library9.6 Assets, fonts and icons9.7 Responsive and adaptive

A theme is not a colour palette. It is a contract between design and code, and a good one makes a whole app consistent for free.

9.1 Colour, and Material 3

Colour schemes, and why a palette is not a list of colours

A colour scheme is a set of named roles rather than a set of colours, and the distinction is the difference between a theme that works in dark mode and one that does not. Each role describes what a colour is for — the container a surface sits on, the text on that surface, the primary action's fill, the outline of a divider — and each has a light and a dark value. Because the role is the unit, a widget that reads surface and onSurface is correct in both themes without knowing either value; a widget that reads a literal Colors.white is correct in exactly one. The pairs are the contract. Every scheme has a set of on-colours — onPrimary, onSurface, onError — each of which is the foreground intended for its paired background, and a component that uses a role without its on-role is the most common theming defect there is, because the colour is drawn and the contrast is not checked. Then the three ways to get a scheme, and they answer different questions. A hand-written light and dark pair is the right answer when brand colour matters and the brand is not derived from a hue; it is also the most work and the one most often done badly because there is no check that the light and dark schemes are actually related. ColorScheme.fromSeed derives both schemes from one colour using a Material algorithm, and it is the right default for most applications: one decision produces a coherent pair, and the derivation guarantees the roles are related. And a ColorScheme copied from a design tool, which is what to do when a designer has specified exact values and the design does not correspond to a single seed. Then the three things about colour that are not in the scheme and have to be handled separately, and each is a real defect in real apps. Contrast is not guaranteed. The scheme gives you roles; it does not guarantee that the pair you chose passes WCAG, and a designer-specified pair frequently does not — so contrast must be measured, which the accessibility chapter covers. Colour is not a sufficient signal. A form field marked invalid by a red border communicates nothing to a colour-blind user or in a high-contrast mode; the error must be text, an icon, or both. And the colours that mean something in the domain — a status green, a warning amber, a chart series — are semantic colours rather than scheme roles, and putting them in the scheme as extensions is what makes them themeable. Then the two practices that pay off immediately. Never write a literal colour in a widget. Not a brand colour, not a grey, not a white — a widget with a literal colour is a widget that is wrong in one of the two themes, and the count of such widgets is the count of places a dark-mode audit will find. And add a semantic layer as a theme extension, so that the domain's own vocabulary is expressed once and both themes can define it, which is the mechanism the next section's component theming depends on.

/* Roles, not colours. */

Never write a literal colour in a widget. Use Theme.of(context).colorScheme.primary and similar role names. Dark mode then works for free, a brand change is one line, and the contrast you validated against WCAG still holds - because the role and the background were designed as a pair.

// MATERIAL 3: a seeded colour scheme
// give it one brand colour, it derives the whole scheme,
// including the dark variant, from it
final scheme = ColorScheme.fromSeed(
  seedColor: const Color(0xFF5B8CFF),
  brightness: Brightness.light,
);
// scheme.primary, .onPrimary, .primaryContainer, .surface,
// .surfaceContainerHighest, .error, .outline, ...
// these are ROLES, not colours: use the role, not a hex value

final darkScheme = ColorScheme.fromSeed(
  seedColor: const Color(0xFF5B8CFF),
  brightness: Brightness.dark,
);

// THE ROLES, and why you use them
//   primary          the main action colour
//   onPrimary        text or an icon ON primary
//   primaryContainer a low-contrast version, for a large fill
//   onPrimaryContainer  content on primaryContainer
//   surface          the background
//   surfaceContainerHighest  a raised surface: a card, a sheet
//   onSurface        text on surface
//   onSurfaceVariant   secondary text
//   outline          a border
//   error            a destructive action
//
// THE RULE: never write Color(0xFF...) in a widget. Use
// Theme.of(context).colorScheme.primary. Then dark mode works
// for free, and a brand change is one line.

// A HAND-BUILT SCHEME, for full control
const brandScheme = ColorScheme(
  brightness: Brightness.light,
  primary: Color(0xFF5B8CFF),
  onPrimary: Color(0xFFFFFFFF),
  primaryContainer: Color(0xFFDCE6FF),
  onPrimaryContainer: Color(0xFF001A41),
  secondary: Color(0xFF585E71),
  onSecondary: Color(0xFFFFFFFF),
  secondaryContainer: Color(0xFFDBE2F9),
  onSecondaryContainer: Color(0xFF151B2C),
  tertiary: Color(0xFF75546F),
  onTertiary: Color(0xFFFFFFFF),
  error: Color(0xFFBA1A1A),
  onError: Color(0xFFFFFFFF),

  onErrorContainer: Color(0xFF410002),

9.2 Typography

Text styles, and why the scale exists

The text styles are named roles with a scale, and the reason the scale is fixed rather than chosen per widget is that a coherent interface needs its text sizes to relate to each other. Each style is a role with a size, a weight, a height and a letter spacing, and the height is the part most often ignored: the line height controls how much vertical space a line of text occupies, and text with too small a line height overlaps its own descenders and looks broken at large sizes. There are two families and the distinction is between the roles a screen uses for structure — headline, title, body, label — and the display styles, which are for very large single pieces of text. Using a display style for a section title is the most common type-scale error and it produces a screen where everything competes. Then the four things that have to be true of any text style you add, and each is a real requirement rather than a preference. It must scale with the platform text-size setting, which the framework's styles do automatically and a hand-built TextStyle with a fixed size does not — and this is both an accessibility requirement and the single most common type bug, because the screen looks correct at the default size and clips at large sizes. It must use the correct height for its size, because the height is a ratio and a ratio that suits body text makes headline text crowded and label text loose. It must have an on-colour that pairs with its surface, which is the same on-role rule as colours. And it must not set a letter spacing unless it is intentional, because the platform's default letter spacing is tuned per size and overriding it with a fixed value makes large text cramped. Then the two things about fonts that are not style at all. A bundled font must declare the weights it actually ships, and a family declaring a weight with no file for it will be synthesised — the platform will bold or thin a different weight, which looks subtly wrong and is a common complaint about a custom font. And a custom font increases the app's size and slows first paint, because every glyph in every weight must be fetched before text can be laid out; subsetting to the characters the app uses is the standard mitigation, and the framework will tell you which characters it needs. Then the two practices that make typography maintainable. Use the named styles and do not compose them. A widget that reads theme.textTheme.titleMedium and applies a colour is themable; a widget that reads titleMedium and copies its size into a new style is a copy that will not follow a theme change. And test at the largest text size the platform allows, once, on the screen with the most text, because that screen is where a fixed height, an inflexible row and a truncated label all show up at the same time and none of them show up at the default size.

/* What a style is. */
const STYLE = {
  is: 'A NAMED ROLE WITH A SIZE, A WEIGHT, A HEIGHT and A LETTER SPACING',
  whyScaleIsFixed: 'a COHERENT INTERFACE NEEDS ITS TEXT SIZES TO RELATE TO EACH OTHER',
  theIgnoredPart: 'the HEIGHT',
  why: 'the HEIGHT CONTROLS HOW MUCH VERTICAL SPACE A LINE OF TEXT OCCUPIES',
  failure: 'and TEXT WITH TOO SMALL A LINE HEIGHT OVERLAPS ITS OWN DESCENDERS and LOOKS BROKEN AT LARGE SIZES',
};
const FAMILIES = [
  { f: 'the STRUCTURAL ROLES', instances: ['headline', 'title', 'body', 'label'], usedFor: 'WHAT A SCREEN USES FOR STRUCTURE' },
  { f: 'the DISPLAY STYLES', usedFor: 'VERY LARGE SINGLE PIECES of TEXT' },
  { commonError: 'USING A DISPLAY STYLE for A SECTION TITLE IS THE MOST COMMON TYPE-SCALE ERROR',
    consequence: 'and IT PRODUCES A SCREEN WHERE EVERYTHING COMPETES' },
];

/* Four requirements. */
const REQUIREMENTS = [
  { r: 'it MUST SCALE WITH the PLATFORM TEXT-SIZE SETTING',
    frameworkDoes: 'the FRAMEWORKS STYLES DO AUTOMATICALLY',
    handBuiltDoesNot: 'a HAND-BUILT TextStyle WITH A FIXED SIZE DOES NOT',
    why: 'this IS BOTH an ACCESSIBILITY REQUIREMENT and the SINGLE MOST COMMON TYPE BUG',
    symptom: 'because the SCREEN LOOKS CORRECT AT the DEFAULT SIZE and CLIPS AT LARGE SIZES' },
  { r: 'it MUST USE the CORRECT HEIGHT FOR ITS SIZE',
    why: 'because the HEIGHT IS A RATIO and A RATIO THAT SUITS BODY TEXT MAKES HEADLINE TEXT CROWDED and LABEL TEXT LOOSE' },
  { r: 'it MUST HAVE AN ON-COLOUR THAT PAIRS WITH ITS SURFACE', why: 'which IS the SAME ON-ROLE RULE as COLOURS' },
  { r: 'it MUST NOT SET A LETTER SPACING UNLESS IT IS INTENTIONAL',
    why: 'because the PLATFORMS DEFAULT LETTER SPACING IS TUNED PER SIZE and OVERRIDING IT WITH A FIXED VALUE MAKES LARGE TEXT CRAMPED' },
];

/* Two things about fonts. */
const FONTS = [
  { f: 'A BUNDLED FONT MUST DECLARE the WEIGHTS IT ACTUALLY SHIPS',
    failure: 'and A FAMILY DECLARING A WEIGHT with NO FILE FOR IT WILL BE SYNTHESISED - the PLATFORM WILL BOLD or THIN A DIFFERENT WEIGHT',
    symptom: 'which LOOKS SUBTLY WRONG and IS A COMMON COMPLAINT ABOUT A CUSTOM FONT' },
  { f: 'A CUSTOM FONT INCREASES the APPS SIZE and SLOWS FIRST PAINT',
    why: 'because EVERY GLYPH IN EVERY WEIGHT MUST BE FETCHED BEFORE TEXT CAN BE LAID OUT',
    mitigation: 'SUBSETTING TO the CHARACTERS the APP USES IS the STANDARD MITIGATION',
    and: 'the FRAMEWORK WILL TELL YOU WHICH CHARACTERS IT NEEDS' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'USE the NAMED STYLES and DO NOT COMPOSE THEM',
    good: 'a WIDGET THAT READS theme.textTheme.titleMedium and APPLIES A COLOUR IS THEMEABLE',
    bad: 'a WIDGET THAT READS titleMedium and COPIES ITS SIZE INTO A NEW STYLE IS A COPY THAT WILL NOT FOLLOW A THEME CHANGE' },
  { p: 'TEST AT the LARGEST TEXT SIZE the PLATFORM ALLOWS, ONCE, ON the SCREEN WITH the MOST TEXT',
    why: 'because THAT SCREEN IS WHERE A FIXED HEIGHT, AN INFLEXIBLE ROW and A TRUNCATED LABEL ALL SHOW UP AT the SAME TIME',
    and: 'and NONE of THEM SHOW UP AT the DEFAULT SIZE' },
];

Set the OS font size to its maximum and check every screen before you release. This is an accessibility requirement and it is the single most common break, because a fixed pixel height somewhere in the layout stops being enough and text clips or overflows. Scale with the system setting and cap the scale only where a multi-column row genuinely cannot survive it.

// THE TYPE SCALE, from ThemeData.textTheme
//   displayLarge / displayMedium / displaySmall      57 / 45 / 36
//   headlineLarge / headlineMedium / headlineSmall  32 / 28 / 24
//   titleLarge / titleMedium / titleSmall           22 / 16 / 14
//   bodyLarge / bodyMedium / bodySmall               16 / 14 / 12
//   labelLarge / labelMedium / labelSmall            14 / 12 / 11
//
// USE THE ROLE
Text('Title', style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleLarge)
// NOT: TextStyle(fontSize: 18, fontWeight: FontWeight.w600)
// the role is what makes it consistent AND what makes it
// respect the user's font-size setting

// A TYPE SCALE FROM A FONT FILE
final base = TextTheme();
final textTheme = base.copyWith(
  displayLarge: base.displayLarge?.copyWith(fontFamily: 'Inter', fontSize: 52),
  bodyMedium: base.bodyMedium?.copyWith(fontFamily: 'Inter', fontSize: 15, height: 1.5),
);

// THE TWO PROPERTIES people get wrong
Text(
  'A long paragraph of text that needs to be readable',
  style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.bodyMedium,
)
//   height: 1.5 or more for body text. Flutter's default is 1.0,
//   which is too tight to read. 1.4 to 1.6 is the usual range.
//   letterSpacing: negative for large display text (-0.5 to -1.0),
//   which is what the platform guidelines say

// READING THE OS FONT SIZE
MediaQuery.textScalerOf(context).scale(16)
// which is why you must NOT use a fixed font size for body text
// and why you may need to cap the scale
MediaQuery.withClampedTextScaling(
  minScaleFactor: 1.0,
  maxScaleFactor: 1.6,      // above this, a 3-column row breaks
  child: child,
);

// TEST IT: set the OS font size to the largest, and check every
// screen. This is a real accessibility requirement and a very
// common bug.

9.3 Building a theme properly

// A COMPLETE THEME, with a dark variant generated from one seed
class AppTheme {
  AppTheme._();

  static const _seed = Color(0xFF5B8CFF);

  static ThemeData get light => _build(Brightness.light);
  static ThemeData get dark => _build(Brightness.dark);

  static ThemeData _build(Brightness brightness) {
    final scheme = ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: _seed, brightness: brightness);
    final base = ThemeData(colorScheme: scheme, useMaterial3: true);

    return base.copyWith(
      // TEXT
      textTheme: base.textTheme.copyWith(
        bodyMedium: base.textTheme.bodyMedium?.copyWith(height: 1.5),
        titleLarge: base.textTheme.titleLarge?.copyWith(letterSpacing: -0.3),
      ),

      // COMPONENTS: the theme is where you set a default for
      // EVERY component your app uses, once
      appBarTheme: AppBarTheme(
        backgroundColor: scheme.surface,
        foregroundColor: scheme.onSurface,
        elevation: 0,
        scrolledUnderElevation: 2,
        centerTitle: false,
        titleTextStyle: base.textTheme.titleLarge?.copyWith(
          color: scheme.onSurface,
          fontWeight: FontWeight.w600,
        ),
      ),
      cardTheme: CardThemeData(
        elevation: 0,
        color: scheme.surfaceContainerLow,
        margin: EdgeInsets.zero,
        shape: RoundedRectangleBorder(borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(12)),
      ),
      elevatedButtonTheme: ElevatedButtonThemeData(
        style: ElevatedButton.styleFrom(
          elevation: 0,
          padding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 20, vertical: 14),
          shape: RoundedRectangleBorder(borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(8)),
          textStyle: base.textTheme.labelLarge,
        ),
      ),
      inputDecorationTheme: InputDecorationTheme(
        filled: true,
        fillColor: scheme.surfaceContainerHighest.withValues(alpha: 0.4),
        border: OutlineInputBorder(
          borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(8),
          borderSide: BorderSide.none,
        ),
        focusedBorder: OutlineInputBorder(
          borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(8),
          borderSide: BorderSide(color: scheme.primary, width: 2),
        ),
        contentPadding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 16, vertical: 14),
      ),
      chipTheme: base.chipTheme.copyWith(
        shape: RoundedRectangleBorder(borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(8)),
        side: BorderSide(color: scheme.outlineVariant),
      ),
      dividerTheme: DividerThemeData(
        color: scheme.outlineVariant,
        thickness: 1,
        space: 1,
      ),
      navigationBarTheme: NavigationBarThemeData(
        backgroundColor: scheme.surface,
        indicatorColor: scheme.primaryContainer,
        elevation: 0,
        height: 68,
      ),
      bottomSheetTheme: BottomSheetThemeData(
        backgroundColor: scheme.surface,
        surfaceTintColor: Colors.transparent,   // a M3 bug otherwise
        shape: const RoundedRectangleBorder(
          borderRadius: BorderRadius.vertical(top: Radius.circular(28)),
        ),
      ),
      dialogTheme: DialogThemeData(
        backgroundColor: scheme.surface,
        surfaceTintColor: Colors.transparent,
        shape: RoundedRectangleBorder(borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(28)),
      ),
      snackBarTheme: SnackBarThemeData(
        behavior: SnackBarBehavior.floating,
        shape: RoundedRectangleBorder(borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(8)),
      ),
      listTileTheme: const ListTileThemeData(
        contentPadding: EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 16, vertical: 4),
      ),
      // PAGE TRANSITIONS
      pageTransitionsTheme: const PageTransitionsTheme(builders: {
        TargetPlatform.android: PredictiveBackPageTransitionsBuilder(),
        TargetPlatform.iOS: CupertinoPageTransitionsBuilder(),
        TargetPlatform.macOS: CupertinoPageTransitionsBuilder(),
      }),
    );
  }
}

// the app
MaterialApp(
  theme: AppTheme.light,
  darkTheme: AppTheme.dark,
  themeMode: ThemeMode.system,     // follow the OS
  themeAnimationDuration: const Duration(milliseconds: 200),
  themeAnimationCurve: Curves.easeOut,
  // ...and a toggle in settings
  themeMode: ref.watch(themeModeProvider),
);

Building a theme that survives contact with a product team

A theme is three objects and knowing which is which prevents most of the argument about them. A ColorScheme is the colours. A TextTheme is the type. A ThemeData is the assembled thing that components read, and it also carries non-colour decisions: which component variants are the defaults, whether the density is compact or comfortable, the shape radii, and the platform-specific overrides for dialogs, cards and app bars. The reason the third exists separately from the first two is that most of what a product team wants to change is not a colour or a font size but a component default — this app's cards are flat and outlined, this app's buttons are filled and tonal, this app's density is compact — and expressing that as component themes rather than as per-widget overrides is what makes it stick. Then the three problems that appear once a theme is more than one screen, and each has a specific cause. Widgets that override the theme. A widget that sets its own colour or its own padding is a place the theme no longer applies, and the count of them is the count of places a brand change will miss; the discipline is that overrides go into component themes, not into widgets. A theme built in a build method. A theme assembled inside a build method is a new object every build, every widget that depends on it rebuilds, and any equality comparison fails — so the theme must be a top-level value or a cached provider. And light and dark drifting apart. Two hand-written schemes that were each correct separately will disagree about roles as the product grows, and nothing detects it; the fix is either a seed or an explicit test that the two schemes define the same roles. Then the three extension mechanisms, and the difference matters. ThemeExtension adds typed fields to the theme, so a domain colour set or a spacing scale can be part of the theme and be resolved for the current brightness — which is the correct home for semantic colours and the right answer to "where do our status colours go". Component themes restyle a whole component family, and the framework's ThemeData.copyWith is how you do it. And Theme with a builder applies a theme to a subtree, which is the mechanism for a screen that is deliberately off-theme — an onboarding flow with its own visual language, a preview mode — and which is also the easiest way to end up with three themes. Then the two practices, both about making changes safe. Have a golden test that renders one screen in both themes, because a theme regression is otherwise invisible until a person looks at the app. And define the theme once, at the root, and read it from context everywhere else, because a theme passed down through constructors is a theme that will be missing in one subtree, and the subtree without it is the bug you will spend an hour on.

/* Three objects. */
const OBJECTS = [
  { o: 'a ColorScheme', is: 'the COLOURS' },
  { o: 'a TextTheme', is: 'the TYPE' },
  { o: 'a ThemeData', is: 'the ASSEMBLED THING THAT COMPONENTS READ',
    alsoCarries: ['WHICH COMPONENT VARIANTS ARE the DEFAULTS',
      'WHETHER the DENSITY IS COMPACT or COMFORTABLE',
      'the SHAPE RADII',
      'and the PLATFORM-SPECIFIC OVERRIDES for DIALOGS, CARDS and APP BARS'],
    whySeparate: 'because MOST of WHAT A PRODUCT TEAM WANTS TO CHANGE IS NOT A COLOUR or A FONT SIZE BUT A COMPONENT DEFAULT',
    instances: ['this APPS CARDS ARE FLAT and OUTLINED', 'this APPS BUTTONS ARE FILLED and TONAL', 'this APPS DENSITY IS COMPACT'],
    gain: 'and EXPRESSING THAT AS COMPONENT THEMES rather than AS PER-WIDGET OVERRIDES IS WHAT MAKES IT STICK' },
];

/* Three problems. */
const PROBLEMS = [
  { p: 'WIDGETS THAT OVERRIDE the THEME',
    detail: 'a WIDGET THAT SETS ITS OWN COLOUR or ITS OWN PADDING IS A PLACE the THEME NO LONGER APPLIES',
    and: 'the COUNT of THEM IS the COUNT of PLACES A BRAND CHANGE WILL MISS',
    discipline: 'OVERRIDES GO INTO COMPONENT THEMES, not INTO WIDGETS' },
  { p: 'A THEME BUILT IN A BUILD METHOD',
    detail: 'A THEME ASSEMBLED INSIDE A BUILD METHOD IS A NEW OBJECT EVERY BUILD, EVERY WIDGET THAT DEPENDS ON IT REBUILDS, and ANY EQUALITY COMPARISON FAILS',
    fix: 'the THEME MUST BE A TOP-LEVEL VALUE or A CACHED PROVIDER' },
  { p: 'LIGHT and DARK DRIFTING APART',
    detail: 'TWO HAND-WRITTEN SCHEMES THAT WERE EACH CORRECT SEPARATELY WILL DISAGREE ABOUT ROLES AS the PRODUCT GROWS',
    and: 'NOTHING DETECTS IT',

/* Three extension mechanisms. */
const EXTENSIONS = [
  { m: 'ThemeExtension', adds: 'TYPED FIELDS TO the THEME',
    gain: 'so a DOMAIN COLOUR SET or A SPACING SCALE CAN BE PART of the THEME and BE RESOLVED FOR the CURRENT BRIGHTNESS',
    isThe: 'CORRECT HOME for SEMANTIC COLOURS',
    and: 'the RIGHT ANSWER TO where do our status colours go' },
  { m: 'COMPONENT THEMES', restyle: 'A WHOLE COMPONENT FAMILY',

  { m: 'Theme WITH A BUILDER', applies: 'A THEME TO A SUBTREE',
    usedFor: 'A SCREEN THAT IS DELIBERATELY OFF-THEME - an ONBOARDING FLOW with ITS OWN VISUAL LANGUAGE, A PREVIEW MODE',
    risk: 'and WHICH IS ALSO the EASIEST WAY TO END UP WITH THREE THEMES' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'HAVE A GOLDEN TEST THAT RENDERS ONE SCREEN IN BOTH THEMES',
    why: 'because A THEME REGRESSION IS OTHERWISE INVISIBLE UNTIL A PERSON LOOKS AT the APP' },
  { p: 'DEFINE the THEME ONCE, AT the ROOT, and READ IT FROM CONTEXT EVERYWHERE ELSE',

    and: 'and the SUBTREE WITHOUT IT IS the BUG YOU WILL SPEND AN HOUR ON' },

9.4 Theming the components you did not write

// A THEME EXTENSION, for values a ThemeData does not have
// this is the correct way to add your own design tokens
@immutable
class AppSpacing extends ThemeExtension<AppSpacing> {
  const AppSpacing({
    this.pagePadding = const EdgeInsets.all(16),
    this.cardGap = 12,
    this.listItemGap = 8,
  });

  final EdgeInsets pagePadding;
  final double cardGap;
  final double listItemGap;

  // required for lerp, so an animated theme change is smooth
  @override
  AppSpacing copyWith({
    EdgeInsets? pagePadding,
    double? cardGap,
    double? listItemGap,
  }) {
    return AppSpacing(
      pagePadding: pagePadding ?? this.pagePadding,
      cardGap: cardGap ?? this.cardGap,
      listItemGap: listItemGap ?? this.listItemGap,
    );
  }

  @override
  AppSpacing lerp(covariant AppSpacing? other, double t) {
    if (other == null) return this;
    return AppSpacing(
      pagePadding: EdgeInsets.lerp(pagePadding, other.pagePadding, t)!,
      cardGap: cardGap + (other.cardGap - cardGap) * t,
      listItemGap: listItemGap + (other.listItemGap - listItemGap) * t,
    );
  }
}

// in the theme
theme: base.copyWith(
  extensions: const [AppSpacing()],
);

// in a widget
final spacing = Theme.of(context).extension<AppSpacing>() ?? const AppSpacing();
Padding(
  padding: spacing.pagePadding,
  child: Column(children: [
    Card1(),
    SizedBox(height: spacing.cardGap),
  ]),
);

// WHY A ThemeExtension AND NOT A GLOBAL CONSTANT
// - it is scoped to the tree: a test can override it
// - it participates in the animated theme change
// - it travels with the context, so a widget deep in the tree
//   gets the right one even if a subtree has its own Theme
// A DENSE AND A COMFORTABLE VARIANT, for a tablet
ThemeData _build(Brightness brightness, {required bool dense}) {
  final base = _build(brightness);
  return base.copyWith(
    visualDensity: dense ? VisualDensity.compact : VisualDensity.standard,
    textTheme: dense
        ? base.textTheme.apply(fontSizeFactor: 0.95)
        : base.textTheme,
    extensions: [
      AppSpacing(
        cardGap: dense ? 6 : 12,
        listItemGap: dense ? 4 : 8,
      ),
    ],
  );
}

// and provide it at the right level
MaterialApp(
  theme: AppTheme.light,
  builder: (context, child) {
    final width = MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).width;
    final dense = width >= 900;   // a large window
    return Theme(
      data: dense ? AppTheme.denseLight : Theme.of(context),
      child: child!,
    );
  },
);

// A SEMANTIC COLOUR HELPER, so a widget is never hardcoded
class AppColors {
  AppColors._(this.scheme);
  final ColorScheme scheme;

  Color get success => scheme.brightness == Brightness.dark
      ? const Color(0xFF4ADE80)
      : const Color(0xFF17794A);
  Color get warning => scheme.brightness == Brightness.dark
      ? const Color(0xFFFFB84D)
      : const Color(0xFFB26A00);
  Color get onSurfaceMuted => scheme.onSurfaceVariant;
}

// usage: AppColors(scheme).success
// or, as a ThemeExtension, which is cleaner

Theming a component you did not write

A third-party component is themed through whatever extension points it offers, and the order to try them is worth knowing because using the wrong one produces a change that works in one place and nowhere else. First: the component theme, if there is one. A component family that has a theme object can be restyled globally — all cards, all dialogs — with one object, and this is the only mechanism that survives the component being used on a screen nobody looked at. Second: a component's own parameters, which apply to one instance and are the right choice when one card is genuinely different. Third: a theme extension that the component understands, which is how the framework's own components accept custom colours. And only last: wrapping it, which is the mechanism of last resort and the one that produces an interface where two visually identical cards are implemented differently. Then the four things that go wrong, and each is a specific mistake rather than a limitation. Restyling with an opacity or a colour overlay rather than with the component's real parameters, which produces a surface that looks right and computes contrast against the wrong colour — the same defect as painting over a background. Fighting the component's internal padding with negative margins or a transform, which breaks the moment the component's own theme changes its density. Reaching into the component's internals — a subclass overriding a private method, or depending on a field that is not part of its contract — which works until a patch version changes it. And forgetting the states: a component restyled for its default appearance and not for its disabled, error, pressed and selected states will look correct in a screenshot and wrong in the app, because those states are where a component is actually seen. Then the two practices that make it maintainable. Collect the overrides in one file, so that the app's deviation from the component library's defaults is a readable list rather than a scattering — this is the same "make the deviation visible" argument as the design-system section. And check the component in both themes and at the largest text size, because a third-party component's own defaults were designed for one density and one text scale and your app's theme will differ from both.

/* Four mechanisms, in the order to try them. */
const MECHANISMS = [
  { n: 1, m: 'the COMPONENT THEME, if there is one',
    how: 'A COMPONENT FAMILY THAT HAS A THEME OBJECT CAN BE RESTYLED GLOBALLY - all CARDS, all DIALOGS',
    and: 'this IS THE ONLY MECHANISM THAT SURVIVES the COMPONENT BEING USED ON A SCREEN NOBODY LOOKED AT' },
  { n: 2, m: 'a COMPONENTS OWN PARAMETERS',
    appliesTo: 'ONE INSTANCE',
    rightWhen: 'when ONE CARD IS GENUINELY DIFFERENT' },
  { n: 3, m: 'a THEME EXTENSION THAT the COMPONENT UNDERSTANDS',
    how: 'which IS HOW the FRAMEWORKS OWN COMPONENTS ACCEPT CUSTOM COLOURS' },
  { n: 4, m: 'WRAPPING IT', isThe: 'MECHANISM OF LAST RESORT',
    produces: 'an INTERFACE WHERE TWO VISUALLY IDENTICAL CARDS ARE IMPLEMENTED DIFFERENTLY' },
];

/* Four things that go wrong. */
const GO_WRONG = [
  { f: 'RESTYLING WITH AN OPACITY or A COLOUR OVERLAY rather than WITH the COMPONENTS REAL PARAMETERS',
    consequence: 'WHICH PRODUCES A SURFACE THAT LOOKS RIGHT and COMPUTES CONTRAST AGAINST the WRONG COLOUR',
    and: 'the SAME DEFECT as PAINTING OVER A BACKGROUND' },
  { f: 'FIGHTING the COMPONENTS INTERNAL PADDING with NEGATIVE MARGINS or a TRANSFORM',
    symptom: 'which BREAKS the MOMENT the COMPONENTS OWN THEME CHANGES ITS DENSITY' },
  { f: 'REACHING INTO the COMPONENTS INTERNALS', instances: ['A SUBCLASS OVERRIDING A PRIVATE METHOD', 'or DEPENDING ON A FIELD THAT IS NOT PART of ITS CONTRACT'],
    symptom: 'which WORKS UNTIL A PATCH VERSION CHANGES IT' },
  { f: 'FORGETTING the STATES',
    detail: 'A COMPONENT RESTYLED FOR ITS DEFAULT APPEARANCE and NOT FOR ITS DISABLED, ERROR, PRESSED and SELECTED STATES WILL LOOK CORRECT IN A SCREENSHOT and WRONG IN the APP',
    why: 'BECAUSE THOSE STATES ARE WHERE A COMPONENT IS ACTUALLY SEEN' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'COLLECT the OVERRIDES IN ONE FILE',
    gain: 'so THAT the APPS DEVIATION FROM the COMPONENT LIBRARYS DEFAULTS IS A READABLE LIST rather than A SCATTERING',
    and: 'this IS the SAME make the deviation visible ARGUMENT as the DESIGN-SYSTEM SECTION' },
  { p: 'CHECK the COMPONENT IN BOTH THEMES and AT the LARGEST TEXT SIZE',
    why: 'because A THIRD-PARTY COMPONENTS OWN DEFAULTS WERE DESIGNED FOR ONE DENSITY and ONE TEXT SCALE and YOUR APPS THEME WILL DIFFER FROM BOTH' },
];

9.5 Building a component library

Designing a component that others will use

A component in your own codebase is still a component, and the design question is the same one a design system asks: what does it own, and what does it expose. Own the appearance, expose the content. A component that accepts colours, paddings and text styles as parameters is a component every screen will reimplement differently; a component that accepts content and a few semantic parameters and owns everything else is a component that can be changed centrally. Then the five things a component must define before it is used, and each is a decision that is expensive to add later. Its states. Loading, empty, error, disabled, pressed, selected, focused — and the empty state is the one most often omitted and the one a user sees on the first run of every new screen. Its size variants and whether it is compact, regular or large, because a component used at three sizes by accident is three components. Whether it handles its own interaction — is it a button that is tappable, or a container that contains a button — because this determines whether it can be nested and whether it is reachable by keyboard. Whether it is a leaf or a container, and if a container, what its slot structure is: leading, content, trailing. And what it does with the text scale, which is the accessibility requirement: at the largest platform text size, does it grow, clip, or wrap into an unreadable shape. Then the three rules about where the boundary goes, and they are the difference between a component library and a pile of widgets. Take a value or a callback, not a widget, for anything the component needs to know about. A component that accepts a boolean and renders a spinner owns the spinner; a component that accepts a widget for the spinner has a caller writing the spinner, and every caller will write a slightly different one. Expose the whole surface or none of it. A component with twenty optional parameters is a component whose combinations nobody has tested, and the parameters that are rarely used are the ones that are broken; a component with three required parameters and two optional ones is testable. And keep the component file until it needs to be two files. The instinct to split a two-hundred-line widget into a folder of three files makes the code harder to read and no easier to change, and the split should happen when there is a real second thing in the file rather than because the line count is uncomfortable. Then the two practices that decide whether it survives. Write the usage before the widget, as a snippet of how it will be called, because a component whose intended usage is awkward will be worked around in the first screen that uses it. And give it a preview or a story with every state, because a component reviewed only in its default appearance will have three broken states that nobody discovers until a user reaches them.

/* The design question. */
const QUESTION = {
  is: 'WHAT DOES IT OWN, and WHAT DOES IT EXPOSE',
  rule: 'OWN the APPEARANCE, EXPOSE the CONTENT',
  manyParameters: 'A COMPONENT THAT ACCEPTS COLOURS, PADDINGS and TEXT STYLES AS PARAMETERS IS A COMPONENT EVERY SCREEN WILL REIMPLEMENT DIFFERENTLY',
  fewParameters: 'A COMPONENT THAT ACCEPTS CONTENT and A FEW SEMANTIC PARAMETERS and OWNS EVERYTHING ELSE IS A COMPONENT THAT CAN BE CHANGED CENTRALLY',

  { d: 'ITS STATES', list: ['LOADING', 'EMPTY', 'ERROR', 'DISABLED', 'PRESSED', 'SELECTED', 'FOCUSED'],

    isThe: 'ACCESSIBILITY REQUIREMENT',
    question: 'AT the LARGEST PLATFORM TEXT SIZE, DOES IT GROW, CLIP, or WRAP INTO AN UNREADABLE SHAPE' },

/* Three boundary rules. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'TAKE A VALUE or A CALLBACK, not A WIDGET, for ANYTHING the COMPONENT NEEDS TO KNOW ABOUT',
    good: 'A COMPONENT THAT ACCEPTS A BOOLEAN and RENDERS A SPINNER OWNS the SPINNER',
    bad: 'A COMPONENT THAT ACCEPTS A WIDGET for the SPINNER HAS A CALLER WRITING the SPINNER, and EVERY CALLER WILL WRITE A SLIGHTLY DIFFERENT ONE' },
  { r: 'EXPOSE the WHOLE SURFACE or NONE OF IT',
    detail: 'A COMPONENT WITH TWENTY OPTIONAL PARAMETERS IS A COMPONENT WHOSE COMBINATIONS NOBODY HAS TESTED',
    and: 'the PARAMETERS THAT ARE RARELY USED ARE the ONES THAT ARE BROKEN',
    good: 'A COMPONENT WITH THREE REQUIRED PARAMETERS and TWO OPTIONAL ONES IS TESTABLE' },
  { r: 'KEEP the COMPONENT FILE UNTIL IT NEEDS TO BE TWO FILES',
    cost: 'the INSTINCT TO SPLIT a TWO-HUNDRED-LINE WIDGET INTO A FOLDER of THREE FILES MAKES the CODE HARDER TO READ and NO EASIER TO CHANGE',
    rule: 'and the SPLIT SHOULD HAPPEN WHEN THERE IS A REAL SECOND THING IN the FILE rather than BECAUSE the LINE COUNT IS UNCOMFORTABLE' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'WRITE the USAGE BEFORE the WIDGET', as: 'A SNIPPET of HOW IT WILL BE CALLED',
    why: 'because A COMPONENT WHOSE INTENDED USAGE IS AWKWARD WILL BE WORKED AROUND IN the FIRST SCREEN THAT USES IT' },
  { p: 'GIVE IT A PREVIEW or A STORY WITH EVERY STATE',
    why: 'because A COMPONENT REVIEWED ONLY IN ITS DEFAULT APPEARANCE WILL HAVE THREE BROKEN STATES THAT NOBODY DISCOVERS UNTIL A USER REACHES THEM' },
];

A component with loading, empty, error, disabled and pressed states is a component that cannot be shipped in a week. Building them into the component rather than at each call site means the states exist once, look the same everywhere, and the call site stays one line.

// THE PATTERN for a reusable component
class PrimaryButton extends StatelessWidget {
  const PrimaryButton({
    required this.label,
    this.onPressed,
    this.icon,
    this.loading = false,
    this.expanded = false,
    super.key,
  });

  final String label;
  final VoidCallback? onPressed;
  final IconData? icon;
  final bool loading;
  final bool expanded;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final theme = Theme.of(context);

    // a busy state that is impossible to get wrong: the button is
    // disabled AND shows a spinner, and the label is hidden so
    // nothing reflows
    final isEnabled = onPressed != null && !loading;

    final child = loading
        ? SizedBox(
            width: 18, height: 18,
            child: CircularProgressIndicator(
              strokeWidth: 2,
              color: theme.colorScheme.onPrimary,
            ),
          )
        : Row(
            mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
            children: [
              if (icon != null) ...[
                Icon(icon, size: 18),
                const SizedBox(width: 8),
              ],
              Text(label),
            ],
          );

    return SizedBox(
      width: expanded ? double.infinity : null,
      child: FilledButton(
        onPressed: isEnabled ? onPressed : null,
        // do not use a fixed height: it breaks with a large font
        style: FilledButton.styleFrom(
          minimumSize: const Size(64, 48),   // 48 is the touch target
          padding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: 20),
        ),
        child: child,
      ),
    );
  }
}

// THE RULES for a component library
// 1. it takes no global state, and no Context.read of a store
// 2. everything visual comes from Theme.of(context)
// 3. it accepts a key, and it is const-constructible
// 4. it exposes callbacks, not state changes
// 5. it works at any size: test with a 200% font scale
// 6. it has states: loading, empty, error, disabled, pressed
// 7. it is a single file until it needs to be two

9.6 Assets, fonts and icons

// pubspec.yaml - the assets block
flutter:
  uses-material-design: true

  assets:
    - assets/images/
    - assets/icons/
    - assets/data/default_entries.json

  fonts:
    - family: Inter
      fonts:
        - asset: assets/fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf
          weight: 400
        - asset: assets/fonts/Inter-Medium.ttf
          weight: 500
        - asset: assets/fonts/Inter-SemiBold.ttf
          weight: 600
        - asset: assets/fonts/Inter-Bold.ttf
          weight: 700
    - family: InterDisplay
      fonts:
        - asset: assets/fonts/InterDisplay-Bold.ttf
          weight: 700

// then
Text('Hi', style: TextStyle(fontFamily: 'Inter'))
Text('Hi', style: TextStyle(fontFamily: 'InterDisplay', fontWeight: FontWeight.bold))
Image.asset('assets/images/logo.png')
// a JSON file
final data = jsonDecode(await rootBundle.loadString('assets/data/default_entries.json') as String);

// ICONS
Icon(Icons.favorite)                      // the Material set: free
Icon(CupertinoIcons.heart)                // the Cupertino set
IconButton(
  onPressed: f,
  icon: const Icon(Icons.delete_outline),  // 2px, the outlined set
)
// for a custom icon, an icon FONT: declare it as a font family,
// then use Icon with the font family and the codepoint
Icon(IconData(0xe900, fontFamily: 'MyIcons'))
// or an SVG, with flutter_svg
SvgPicture.asset('assets/icons/logo.svg', width: 24, height: 24)

// THE ASSET RULES
// 1. a directory in the list includes everything in it
// 2. pubspec.yaml changes need a hot restart, not a hot reload
// 3. assets are bundled in the binary: a 4MB image is a 4MB app
// 4. tree-shake icons: this is on by default, and it means an
//    IconData with a non-const value defeats it
// 5. never use a raw asset path string; make a typed helper
class Assets {
  Assets._();
  static const logo = 'assets/images/logo.png';
  static const emptyState = 'assets/images/empty.png';
}

// and the image sizes
// an app icon: 1024x1024, no alpha, no rounded corners
// a Play Store icon: 512x512
// a feature graphic: 1024x500
// a screenshot: the device resolution, and no status bar clutter

Bundling assets, and the three that are not bundled at all

Assets in a Flutter app are declared in the pubspec and resolved at build time, and the mechanism has three properties that matter. Assets are declared by directory or by file with a path prefix, and the prefix is how they are addressed at run time — the key in the asset bundle is the pubspec path relative to the package root, which is why an asset moved from assets/ to assets/images/ breaks every reference and the compiler finds none of them at build time. Assets declared with a directory are included recursively, and the platform's case-sensitivity rules differ, so an asset referenced with different capitalisation works on one platform and fails on another — which is the mechanism behind the "works on Android, blank on iOS" asset bug. And fonts are assets, declared with their weight and style in the pubspec, which is where the declaration becomes the source of the synthesis problem the typography section described. Then the three asset kinds that behave differently, and each has a different loading strategy. An image is loaded asynchronously and cached, so it is fetched at run time from the bundle, it can miss, and it should be precached if it is needed immediately — which is the rendering chapter's four stages. A font is loaded on first use and blocks the text that needs it, which means a screen rendered before the font has loaded shows a fallback and then swaps; the fix is to load the font during startup. And a JSON file or any other data file is loaded as bytes and must be parsed, which means it cannot be a const and cannot be accessed synchronously at the top level — which is why configuration files are usually bundled as a Dart constant instead, precisely so that they are available synchronously and cannot be missing. Then the three practices that prevent the asset problems, and each is specific. Access assets through a single helper rather than through the asset bundle directly, so the path convention is in one place and a rename is a one-line change. Keep assets out of the repository's source tree root and in one directory, because a project with assets in five places has no way to answer "how large is the bundle" or "what is in it". And check what is actually in the bundle, because a build includes every declared asset and the most common cause of a large download is one high-resolution image declared once and used everywhere at one size — which the rendering chapter's resize advice fixes and which is worth checking before anything else. Then the one thing to know about platform assets, and it saves a lot of confusion: some assets are not in the asset bundle at all — app icons, launch screens, the platform manifest, notification icons and sounds, store screenshots — and they are configured per platform in the platform directories, not in the pubspec, so a change to any of them does not appear in the Dart code and a developer looking only at the pubspec will not find them.

9.7 Responsive and adaptive

// BREAKPOINTS, which are conventions rather than framework
//   compact   < 600   a phone
//   medium    600-905  a large phone, a small tablet in portrait
//   expanded  >= 905 a tablet, a desktop window
// (the Material window size classes)

enum SizeClass { compact, medium, expanded }

extension SizeClassX on BuildContext {
  SizeClass get sizeClass {
    final width = MediaQuery.sizeOf(this).width;
    if (width < 600) return SizeClass.compact;
    if (width < 905) return SizeClass.medium;
    return SizeClass.expanded;
  }
}

// and the patterns per class
class EntryListScreen extends StatelessWidget {
  const EntryListScreen({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return switch (context.sizeClass) {
      // a phone: a list, full width
      SizeClass.compact => const EntryListView(),

      // a tablet in portrait: a list plus a FAB
      SizeClass.medium => Scaffold(
          body: const EntryListView(),
          floatingActionButton: FloatingActionButton(onPressed: _add, child: const Icon(Icons.add)),
        ),

      // a large screen: a list-detail LAYOUT
      SizeClass.expanded => const EntryListDetailView(),
    };
  }
}

// the list-detail pattern
class EntryListDetailView extends StatefulWidget {
  const EntryListDetailView({super.key});
  @override
  State<EntryListDetailView> createState() => _EntryListDetailViewState();
}

class _EntryListDetailViewState extends State<EntryListDetailView> {
  String? _selectedId;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Row(
      children: [
        SizedBox(
          width: 360,                       // the list pane
          child: EntryListView(
            selectedId: _selectedId,
            onSelect: (id) => setState(() => _selectedId = id),
          ),
        ),
        const VerticalDivider(width: 1),
        Expanded(
          child: _selectedId == null
              ? const EmptyDetailPane()      // an empty state, not a blank
              : EntryDetailPane(id: _selectedId!),
        ),
      ],
    );
  }
}

// ORIENTATION AND THE KEYBOARD
final keyboardOpen = MediaQuery.viewInsetsOf(context).bottom > 0;
final size = MediaQuery.sizeOf(context);       // never size.height: it
                                             // changes with the keyboard
final isLandscape = size.width > size.height;
// THE MASTER-DETAIL TEMPLATE that adapts, for real apps
class AdaptiveScaffold extends StatelessWidget {
  const AdaptiveScaffold({
    required this.list,
    required this.detail,
    required this.selectedId,
    required this.onSelect,
    required this.breakpoint,
    super.key,
  });

  final Widget list;
  final Widget Function(BuildContext, String) detail;
  final String? selectedId;
  final ValueChanged<String> onSelect;
  final double breakpoint;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final width = MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).width;
    final twoPane = width >= breakpoint;

    if (twoPane) {
      return Row(children: [
        NavigationRail(
          selectedIndex: 0,
          labelType: NavigationRailLabelType.all,
          onDestinationSelected: (_) {},
          destinations: const [
            NavigationRailDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.inbox), label: Text('Inbox')),
            NavigationRailDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.archive), label: Text('Archive')),
            NavigationRailDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.settings), label: Text('Settings')),
          ],
        ),
        const VerticalDivider(width: 1),
        SizedBox(width: 320, child: list),
        const VerticalDivider(width: 1),
        Expanded(
          child: selectedId == null
              ? const Center(child: Text('Select an item'))
              : detail(context, selectedId!),
        ),
      ]);
    }

    // one pane: show the list, or the detail, based on selection
    return selectedId == null
        ? list
        : Scaffold(
            appBar: AppBar(leading: const BackButton()),
            body: detail(context, selectedId!),
          );
  }
}

Adaptive layouts, and the four sizes that matter

Responsive design in Flutter is easier than on the web because there is one layout language and the framework computes the geometry, and harder because a phone application is expected to run on a phone, a foldable, a tablet and a desktop with the same code. The decision that drives everything is what varies: the size, or the input method. A layout that adapts only to size is a phone layout stretched; a layout that adapts to input method is a different interface per device class, and that is usually the right answer for an application rather than the wrong one. Then the four breakpoints that matter in practice, and the reason they are these four rather than a continuous scale. Compact — a phone in portrait. One column, a bottom navigation bar or a drawer, and content stacked vertically. Medium — a large phone in landscape or a small tablet. Still one column of content but the navigation moves to a side rail, because a bottom bar on a wide, short screen is under the user's thumbs and out of the way of the content. Expanded — a tablet or a desktop window. Two panes: a list and a detail, which is the layout that makes a list-of-things application genuinely usable on a large screen rather than a phone layout with a lot of whitespace. And the intermediate state that is not a breakpoint at all: a foldable that is half-open, where the fold is a physical obstruction and content must not be placed under it. Then the three mechanisms, and they compose. Breakpoints by widget width, not by screen width, because the widget's width is what its layout must fit into — a card in a two-pane layout on a tablet has a tablet's screen width and a phone's width, and using the screen width produces the wrong layout for the card. The layout builder, which is a widget that picks one of several child layouts by constraint, and is the right mechanism when the alternatives are genuinely different layouts rather than the same layout with different values. And constraints rather than media queries, which is the same argument as the first point: a widget that reads MediaQuery.of(context).size.width has made a decision about a space it is not filling. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a specific mistake. Using the screen size, which produces a two-pane layout inside a one-pane container and a one-pane layout that overflows on a wide screen. Hard-coding breakpoints in pixels, which does not account for the platform's text scale — a user who has increased the text size has a smaller effective layout in every sense that matters, and a layout that only adapts to pixels will overflow. And not testing the intermediate states, which is where a two-pane layout breaks: at the boundary between one pane and two, the detail pane appears at a width that was never designed, and the fix is to check the width where the transition happens and not only the widths either side. Then the two practices that keep it correct. Test at the smallest and the largest width and at the platform's largest text scale, because the two extremes find most of what is broken and the middle rarely does. And decide what a tablet version is before writing it — a full second application, a wider version of the phone one, or a phone application that refuses to run large — because the default outcome of not deciding is a phone layout stretched, and the cost of that is a product decision made by accident.

/* What varies. */
const QUESTION = 'WHAT VARIES - the SIZE, or the INPUT METHOD';
const SIZE_ONLY = 'A LAYOUT THAT ADAPTS ONLY TO SIZE IS A PHONE LAYOUT STRETCHED';
const INPUT = 'A LAYOUT THAT ADAPTS TO INPUT METHOD IS A DIFFERENT INTERFACE PER DEVICE CLASS, and THAT IS USUALLY the RIGHT ANSWER FOR AN APPLICATION rather than the WRONG ONE';

/* Four breakpoints. */
const BREAKPOINTS = [
  { b: 'COMPACT - a PHONE in PORTRAIT', layout: ['ONE COLUMN', 'A BOTTOM NAVIGATION BAR or A DRAWER', 'CONTENT STACKED VERTICALLY'] },
  { b: 'MEDIUM - a LARGE PHONE in LANDSCAPE or a SMALL TABLET',
    layout: 'STILL ONE COLUMN of CONTENT',
    change: 'but the NAVIGATION MOVES TO A SIDE RAIL',
    why: 'BECAUSE A BOTTOM BAR ON A WIDE, SHORT SCREEN IS UNDER the USERS THUMBS and OUT of the WAY of the CONTENT' },
  { b: 'EXPANDED - a TABLET or a DESKTOP WINDOW',
    layout: 'TWO PANES - A LIST and A DETAIL',
    gain: 'which IS the LAYOUT THAT MAKES A LIST-OF-THINGS APPLICATION GENUINELY USABLE ON A LARGE SCREEN rather than A PHONE LAYOUT WITH A LOT OF WHITESPACE' },
  { b: 'the INTERMEDIATE STATE THAT IS NOT A BREAKPOINT AT ALL',
    instance: 'A FOLDABLE THAT IS HALF-OPEN',
    rule: 'the FOLD IS A PHYSICAL OBSTRUCTION and CONTENT MUST NOT BE PLACED UNDER IT' },
];

/* Three mechanisms. */
const MECHANISMS = [
  { m: 'BREAKPOINTS BY WIDGET WIDTH, not BY SCREEN WIDTH',
    why: 'because the WIDGETS WIDTH IS WHAT ITS LAYOUT MUST FIT INTO',
    example: 'A CARD IN A TWO-PANE LAYOUT ON A TABLET HAS A TABLETS SCREEN WIDTH and a PHONES WIDTH',

  { m: 'the LAYOUT BUILDER', is: 'A WIDGET THAT PICKS ONE of SEVERAL CHILD LAYOUTS BY CONSTRAINT',

  { m: 'CONSTRAINTS rather than MEDIA QUERIES',
    why: 'which IS the SAME ARGUMENT as the FIRST POINT',

/* Three things that go wrong. */
const GO_WRONG = [
  { f: 'USING the SCREEN SIZE', consequence: 'WHICH PRODUCES A TWO-PANE LAYOUT INSIDE A ONE-PANE CONTAINER and a ONE-PANE LAYOUT THAT OVERFLOWS ON A WIDE SCREEN' },
  { f: 'HARD-CODING BREAKPOINTS IN PIXELS',
    problem: 'WHICH DOES NOT ACCOUNT FOR the PLATFORMS TEXT SCALE',
    detail: 'A USER WHO HAS INCREASED the TEXT SIZE HAS A SMALLER EFFECTIVE LAYOUT IN EVERY SENSE THAT MATTERS',
    consequence: 'and A LAYOUT THAT ONLY ADAPTS TO PIXELS WILL OVERFLOW' },
  { f: 'NOT TESTING the INTERMEDIATE STATES',
    where: 'WHICH IS WHERE A TWO-PANE LAYOUT BREAKS',

    fix: 'CHECK the WIDTH WHERE the TRANSITION HAPPENS and NOT ONLY the WIDTHS EITHER SIDE' },

/* Two practices. */

  { p: 'TEST AT the SMALLEST and the LARGEST WIDTH and AT the PLATFORMS LARGEST TEXT SCALE',
    why: 'because the TWO EXTREMES FIND MOST of WHAT IS BROKEN and the MIDDLE RARELY DOES' },
  { p: 'DECIDE WHAT A TABLET VERSION IS BEFORE WRITING IT',

    why: 'because the DEFAULT OUTCOME of NOT DECIDING IS A PHONE LAYOUT STRETCHED',
