];

Exercises 10

  1. Build a ThemeData from a single seed colour with a generated dark variant, and confirm both look right.
  2. Set height: 1.5 on body text and compare readability with the default. Then check it at a 200% OS font size.
  3. Write a ThemeExtension for your spacing scale, and confirm an animated theme change lerps it smoothly.
  4. Build a component with loading, empty, error, disabled and pressed states, and test each.
  5. Declare a custom font family with four weights, use it in the type scale, and verify it falls back gracefully when the file is missing.
  6. Build the list-detail layout with a NavigationRail on a large screen and a bottom bar on a phone, sharing one state model.
  7. Grep your codebase for hardcoded Color(0x values outside the theme file, and replace them with roles.

10 · Accessibility and Internationalisation

10.1 What a screen reader needs10.2 Semantics in detail10.3 Colour and contrast10.4 Touch, focus and keyboard10.5 Localisation setup10.6 Right-to-left and text direction10.7 Dates, numbers and plurals10.8 Platform conventions

Accessibility is a requirement, not a feature, and internationalisation is a constraint on every string and every layout decision from the first day.

10.1 What a screen reader needs

What "accessible" means as a test, and the four requirements

An accessible screen is one that a person can perceive, operate, understand and survive — and breaking that into words produces four requirements that can each be tested, which is what makes accessibility actionable rather than a virtue. Perceivable: everything meaningful must be available without sight or without hearing, which means text alternatives for images, captions for video, and sufficient contrast for text. Operable: everything must be reachable and usable without a pointer, which means keyboard operability, a visible focus indicator, a touch target large enough to hit, and no time limit the user cannot extend. Understandable: the content must be readable and the behaviour predictable — plain language, labelled fields, errors that say what to do, and consistent navigation. And robust: it must work with the assistive technology that exists, which today means the semantics tree, and which is the subject of the previous section. Then the four requirements that are WCAG's most-cited success criteria, because they are the ones that catch the largest fraction of real defects. 1.4.3 contrast: text at four-and-a-half to one against its background, and three to one for large text and for the boundaries of user-interface components — which is the accessibility chapter's rule and the one most often failed by a designer's exact brand colour. 2.1.1 keyboard: all functionality available from the keyboard, with no trap. 2.4.7 focus visible: a visible focus indicator, which is broken by the very common outline: none in a CSS reset — and in Flutter by removing the focus highlight, which the framework provides by default. And 4.1.2 name, role, value: every control must expose all three, which in Flutter is the semantics tree the previous section described. Then the three things that are requirements rather than good practice, and each is a legal obligation in several jurisdictions. Text must scale with the platform setting, and a fixed-height row containing text is a failure for a user who has increased it. Touch targets must be at least forty-eight logical pixels, with the target — not the visual size — counting, so a small icon inside a larger transparent tap area passes and a small icon in a small box does not. And there must be a way to dismiss anything that appears over the content, including a snackbar, a modal and an error banner. Then the two practices that make it sustainable, because an accessibility pass as a project is a pass that decays. Put an automated check in the pipeline, which catches the mechanically detectable third and — more importantly — prevents regressions, since the common failure is a new screen added six months after the audit. And test with the platform's own accessibility features switched on, which is free and finds more than people expect: turn on the screen reader and walk the flow, turn on the largest text size and walk it again, turn on high contrast and walk it a third time, and turn on reduced motion if the screen animates.

/* Four requirements, each testable. */
const REQUIREMENTS = [
  { r: 'PERCEIVABLE', means: 'EVERYTHING MEANINGFUL MUST BE AVAILABLE WITHOUT SIGHT or WITHOUT HEARING',
    requires: ['TEXT ALTERNATIVES for IMAGES', 'CAPTIONS for VIDEO', 'and SUFFICIENT CONTRAST for TEXT'] },
  { r: 'OPERABLE', means: 'EVERYTHING MUST BE REACHABLE and USABLE WITHOUT A POINTER',
    requires: ['KEYBOARD OPERABILITY', 'A VISIBLE FOCUS INDICATOR', 'A TOUCH TARGET LARGE ENOUGH TO HIT',
      'and NO TIME LIMIT the USER CANNOT EXTEND'] },
  { r: 'UNDERSTANDABLE', means: 'the CONTENT MUST BE READABLE and the BEHAVIOUR PREDICTABLE',
    requires: ['PLAIN LANGUAGE', 'LABELLED FIELDS', 'ERRORS THAT SAY WHAT TO DO', 'and CONSISTENT NAVIGATION'] },
  { r: 'ROBUST', means: 'it MUST WORK WITH the ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY THAT EXISTS',
    today: 'WHICH MEANS the SEMANTICS TREE',
    and: 'which IS the SUBJECT of the PREVIOUS SECTION' },
];

/* Four success criteria. */
const CRITERIA = [
  { c: '1.4.3 CONTRAST', detail: 'TEXT AT FOUR-AND-A-HALF TO ONE against ITS BACKGROUND, and THREE TO ONE for LARGE TEXT and for the BOUNDARIES OF USER-INTERFACE COMPONENTS',
    mostOftenFailedBy: 'A DESIGNERS EXACT BRAND COLOUR' },
  { c: '2.1.1 KEYBOARD', detail: 'ALL FUNCTIONALITY AVAILABLE FROM the KEYBOARD, WITH NO TRAP' },
  { c: '2.4.7 FOCUS VISIBLE', detail: 'A VISIBLE FOCUS INDICATOR',
    brokenBy: ['the VERY COMMON outline: none IN A CSS RESET',
      'and IN FLUTTER by REMOVING the FOCUS HIGHLIGHT, WHICH the FRAMEWORK PROVIDES BY DEFAULT'] },
  { c: '4.1.2 NAME, ROLE, VALUE', detail: 'EVERY CONTROL MUST EXPOSE ALL THREE', which: 'in FLUTTER IS the SEMANTICS TREE the PREVIOUS SECTION DESCRIBED' },
];

/* Three requirements rather than good practice. */
const REQUIREMENTS_LEGAL = [
  { r: 'TEXT MUST SCALE WITH the PLATFORM SETTING',
    failure: 'and A FIXED-HEIGHT ROW CONTAINING TEXT IS A FAILURE for A USER WHO HAS INCREASED IT' },
  { r: 'TOUCH TARGETS MUST BE AT LEAST FORTY-EIGHT LOGICAL PIXELS',
    counts: 'the TARGET - not the VISUAL SIZE -',
    passes: 'a SMALL ICON INSIDE A LARGER TRANSPARENT TAP AREA PASSES',
    fails: 'a SMALL ICON IN A SMALL BOX DOES NOT' },
  { r: 'THERE MUST BE A WAY TO DISMISS ANYTHING THAT APPEARS OVER the CONTENT',
    instances: ['a SNACKBAR', 'A MODAL', 'AN ERROR BANNER'] },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'PUT AN AUTOMATED CHECK IN the PIPELINE',
    catches: 'the MECHANICALLY DETECTABLE THIRD',
    moreValuable: 'and - MORE IMPORTANTLY - PREVENTS REGRESSIONS',
    why: 'since the COMMON FAILURE IS A NEW SCREEN ADDED SIX MONTHS AFTER the AUDIT' },
  { p: 'TEST WITH the PLATFORMS OWN ACCESSIBILITY FEATURES SWITCHED ON',
    cost: 'FREE', and: 'FINDS MORE THAN PEOPLE EXPECT',
    how: ['turn ON the SCREEN READER and WALK the FLOW',
      'turn ON the LARGEST TEXT SIZE and WALK IT AGAIN',
      'turn ON HIGH CONTRAST and WALK IT A THIRD TIME',
      'and turn ON REDUCED MOTION if the SCREEN ANIMATES'],

];

Everything in this chapter is a store review requirement, not a nice-to-have. A screen reader must be able to announce every interactive element, and a touch target must be at least 44 by 44 logical pixels. Both are cheap to do correctly at the start and expensive to retrofit.

// A SCREEN READER announces the semantics tree, not the visuals.
// It needs, for every interactive element:
//   1. a LABEL: what it is
//   2. a ROLE: it is a button, a link, a checkbox
//   3. a VALUE: the current state, for a slider or a field
//   4. a HINT: what happens when you activate it, if not obvious
//   5. proper GROUPING: a card should be one node, not eleven
//   6. ORDER: the focus order must follow the visual order

// THE FOUR THINGS THAT ARE USUALLY MISSING
// 1. an IconButton with no tooltip and no label
IconButton(onPressed: _delete, icon: const Icon(Icons.delete))
// -> announced as "button", with no purpose

// 2. an image with no alt text
Image.asset('assets/chart.png')
// -> announced as "image", with no content

// 3. a custom painted widget, which has NO semantics at all
CustomPaint(painter: _SparklinePainter(values: data))
// -> announced as nothing, or as a blank box

// 4. a tap target smaller than 44x44 logical pixels
GestureDetector(onTap: onTap, child: const Icon(Icons.close, size: 16))
// -> impossible to hit, and announced as a tiny target
// THE FIXES
IconButton(
  onPressed: _delete,
  icon: const Icon(Icons.delete),
  tooltip: 'Delete entry',        // the tooltip IS the semantic label
)
// or, when the tooltip is not appropriate
Semantics(
  button: true,
  label: 'Delete entry',
  onTap: _delete,
  child: ExcludeSemantics(child: IconButton(onPressed: _delete, icon: const Icon(Icons.delete))),
)

Image.asset(
  'assets/chart.png',
  semanticLabel: 'Sales chart, up 12% this quarter',
  excludeFromSemantics: true,     // if a caption already says it
)

Semantics(
  label: 'Weekly sales, trending up',
  value: '\$42,000 this week',
  child: CustomPaint(painter: _SparklinePainter(values: data)),
)

// a big enough target
SizedBox(
  width: 48, height: 48,
  child: IconButton(
    onPressed: _close,
    icon: const Icon(Icons.close),
    padding: EdgeInsets.zero,        // remove the default padding
    constraints: const BoxConstraints(),
  ),
)
// or IconButton.filled / .outlined, which have a 48x48 target by
// default in Material 3

10.2 Semantics in detail

// GROUPING, which is what makes a card usable
// a card with a title, two lines of text, an avatar and a menu is
// FOUR or FIVE separate nodes by default. A screen reader user
// swipes through them one at a time.
class EntryCard extends StatelessWidget {
  const EntryCard({required this.entry, super.key});
  final Entry entry;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MergeSemantics(
      child: Semantics(
        button: true,
        label: '${entry.title}. ${entry.preview}',
        onTap: () => _open(context),
        child: Card(
          child: ListTile(
            leading: CircleAvatar(child: Text(entry.title[0])),
            title: Text(entry.title),
            subtitle: Text(entry.preview, maxLines: 2, overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis),
            trailing: PopupMenuButton(
              itemBuilder: (_) => const [PopupMenuItem(value: 'delete', child: Text('Delete'))],
            ),
          ),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

// the OTHER direction: ExcludeSemantics, to hide a decorative child
Row(children: [
  // the icon is decorative: the label already says "delete"
  ExcludeSemantics(child: Icon(Icons.delete)),
  const SizedBox(width: 8),
  const Text('Delete'),
]);

// LABELS FOR FORM FIELDS
TextField(
  decoration: const InputDecoration(labelText: 'Email address'),
)
// labelText becomes the semantic label: free

// or, when the label is not visible
TextField(
  decoration: const InputDecoration(
    labelText: 'Search',
    // ...but it is a hint, not a label, if the field is empty
  ),
  // a visible label is better than a semantic one
)

// VALIDATION ERRORS, announced when they change
TextFormField(
  validator: (value) => value == null || !value.contains('@') ? 'Enter a valid email' : null,
  // the errorText is announced automatically
  autovalidateMode: AutovalidateMode.onUserInteraction,
);

// STATE, for a checkbox or a toggle
Semantics(
  checked: isDone,
  label: 'Mark as done',
  child: Checkbox(value: isDone, onChanged: (v) => setState(() => isDone = v!)),
);

// LIVE REGIONS, for something that changes without a gesture
Semantics(
  liveRegion: true,
  child: Text('${count} items remaining'),
);
// use sparingly: every live region is announced, so a chatty one
// makes a screen reader unusable

// INSPECT IT
debugDumpSemanticsTree();
// and in a widget test
final handle = tester.ensureSemantics();
expect(find.bySemanticsLabel('Delete entry'), findsOneWidget);
handle.dispose();
// TESTING ACCESSIBILITY, which is the only reliable way
testWidgets('every icon button has a semantic label', (tester) async {
  await tester.pumpWidget(const MyApp());

  final buttons = tester.widgetList<IconButton>(find.byType(IconButton));
  for (final button in buttons) {
    // an IconButton with a tooltip gets its label from it
    expect(
      button.tooltip ?? (button.icon is Icon ? (button.icon as Icon).semanticLabel : null),
      isNotNull,
      reason: 'an IconButton with no tooltip and no semanticLabel',
    );
  }
});

testWidgets('the card is a single semantics node', (tester) async {
  final handle = tester.ensureSemantics();
  await tester.pumpWidget(MaterialApp(home: Scaffold(body: EntryCard(entry: testEntry))));

  final node = tester.getSemantics(find.byType(EntryCard));
  expect(node.label, contains('Test entry'));

  handle.dispose();
});

testWidgets('meets the contrast requirements', (tester) async {
  // or check it manually with a contrast calculator
  // a screenshot test that diffs the text colour
});

Reading the semantics tree, and the five defects it exposes

The semantics tree is the only way to see what a screen reader will actually receive, and reading it is a skill because the tree is not the widget tree. Five defects are visible in it and none of them are visible on screen. A missing label. An icon button with no semantic label appears in the accessibility tree as an unlabelled button, and the screen reader announces "button" and nothing else — the user cannot tell forty such buttons apart. A duplicated announcement. A Semantics wrapping a Text and also setting a label produces two announcements of the same content, because the child text is still in the tree; the fix is to exclude the child's semantics or to let the text be the label. An unlabelled group. A card containing three fields has no name, so a screen reader announces the fields without saying what they belong to; the fix is a labelled container or a merged semantics node. A missing state. A drawn toggle with no semantic flag is announced as an image rather than as a checkbox that is on or off. And a scrollable that is not marked as one, so the user has no way to know there is more content. Then the two things to check that are not in the tree, and both are requirements. The reading order. The semantics tree is in the same order as the widget tree, so a visually-correct column whose widget order differs produces a screen that reads correctly and sounds wrong — and the only reliable test is the reading-order test in the platform's accessibility inspector, which is not the same as the tree order. And the focus order under keyboard navigation, which follows the traversal policy and is affected by widget order in a way that reading order does not. Then the three practices that keep it correct, and each is cheap. Check the tree in a widget test, by pumping the widget with a semantics handle and asserting that a label exists — this is the only way to make semantics a test rather than a review, and it catches a label removed by a refactor. Give every tappable thing a label, including the ones that look obvious, because the ones that look obvious are the ones a screen reader user encounters most often: a row of three icon buttons with no labels is the canonical unusable screen. And merge semantics where the visual grouping is the meaning, because a card read as "group, heading, body, button, button, button" is six announcements and "card, heading, body, button, button, button" is one — and merging is also what makes a row read as a single actionable item rather than three separate ones, which is the difference between usable and tedious.

/* The tree is not the widget tree. */
const NOTE = 'the SEMANTICS TREE IS the ONLY WAY to SEE WHAT A SCREEN READER WILL ACTUALLY RECEIVE';
const FIVE_DEFECTS = [
  { d: 'A MISSING LABEL',
    symptom: 'AN ICON BUTTON WITH NO SEMANTIC LABEL APPEARS IN the ACCESSIBILITY TREE AS AN UNLABELLED BUTTON',
    announcement: 'the SCREEN READER ANNOUNCES button and NOTHING ELSE',
    consequence: 'and the USER CANNOT TELL FORTY SUCH BUTTONS APART' },
  { d: 'A DUPLICATED ANNOUNCEMENT',
    cause: 'A Semantics WRAPPING A Text and ALSO SETTING A LABEL PRODUCES TWO ANNOUNCEMENTS of the SAME CONTENT',
    why: 'BECAUSE the CHILD TEXT IS STILL IN the TREE',
    fix: ['EXCLUDE the CHILDS SEMANTICS', 'or LET the TEXT BE the LABEL'] },
  { d: 'AN UNLABELLED GROUP',
    symptom: 'A CARD CONTAINING THREE FIELDS HAS NO NAME, so a SCREEN READER ANNOUNCES the FIELDS WITHOUT SAYING WHAT THEY BELONG TO',
    fix: ['A LABELLED CONTAINER', 'A MERGED SEMANTICS NODE'] },
  { d: 'A MISSING STATE',
    symptom: 'A DRAWN TOGGLE WITH NO SEMANTIC FLAG IS ANNOUNCED AS AN IMAGE rather than AS A CHECKBOX THAT IS ON or OFF' },
  { d: 'A SCROLLABLE THAT IS NOT MARKED AS ONE', consequence: 'so the USER HAS NO WAY to KNOW THERE IS MORE CONTENT' },
];

/* Two things not in the tree. */
const NOT_IN_THE_TREE = [
  { t: 'the READING ORDER',
    fact: 'the SEMANTICS TREE IS IN the SAME ORDER as the WIDGET TREE',
    symptom: 'so A VISUALLY-CORRECT COLUMN WHOSE WIDGET ORDER DIFFERS PRODUCES A SCREEN THAT READS CORRECTLY and SOUNDS WRONG',
    onlyReliableTest: 'the READING-ORDER TEST IN the PLATFORMS ACCESSIBILITY INSPECTOR',
    and: 'which IS NOT the SAME AS the TREE ORDER' },
  { t: 'the FOCUS ORDER UNDER KEYBOARD NAVIGATION',
    fact: 'WHICH FOLLOWS the TRAVERSAL POLICY and IS AFFECTED BY WIDGET ORDER IN A WAY that READING ORDER DOES NOT' },
];

/* Three practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'CHECK the TREE IN A WIDGET TEST',
    how: 'BY PUMPING the WIDGET WITH A SEMANTICS HANDLE and ASSERTING THAT A LABEL EXISTS',
    gain: 'this IS THE ONLY WAY to MAKE SEMANTICS A TEST rather than A REVIEW',
    and: 'and IT CATCHES A LABEL REMOVED BY A REFACTOR' },
  { p: 'GIVE EVERY TAPPABLE THING A LABEL, INCLUDING the ONES THAT LOOK OBVIOUS',
    why: 'because the ONES THAT LOOK OBVIOUS ARE the ONES A SCREEN READER USER ENCOUNTERS MOST OFTEN',
    worst: 'a ROW of THREE ICON BUTTONS WITH NO LABELS IS the CANONICAL UNUSABLE SCREEN' },
  { p: 'MERGE SEMANTICS WHERE the VISUAL GROUPING IS the MEANING',
    example: 'a CARD READ AS group, heading, body, button, button, button IS SIX ANNOUNCEMENTS and card, heading, body, button, button, button IS ONE',
    gain: 'and MERGING IS ALSO WHAT MAKES A ROW READ AS A SINGLE ACTIONABLE ITEM rather than THREE SEPARATE ONES',
    verdict: 'which IS the DIFFERENCE BETWEEN USABLE and TEDIOUS' },
];

10.3 Colour and contrast

Measuring contrast, and the four pairs that usually fail

Contrast is a ratio between two colours and the rule is a threshold, and the arithmetic is worth being able to do by eye for a common case. Contrast is computed from relative luminance, where each channel is normalised, a linearisation is applied — because perception is not linear in the channel value — and the three are combined with weights that approximate human sensitivity. The ratio is the lighter luminance over the darker, plus a point zero five, and it ranges from one to twenty-one. Two things follow that matter practically. A ratio of one means the colours are identical and nothing is visible; the maximum of twenty-one is black on white and nothing can exceed it. And the ratio is non-linear, so a change that looks like nothing can cross a threshold — going from a light grey to a slightly darker grey can move the ratio from 4.2 to 4.6 and cross the requirement, which is why the threshold must be measured rather than judged. Then the four pairs that fail most often, and each has a specific cause. Disabled text. Every design system has a disabled colour that is deliberately faint, and it is almost always below the threshold — which is a genuine tension, since a disabled control's low prominence is the point; the resolution is that disabled text is exempt from the requirement in WCAG, and the practical advice is to still keep it readable enough to identify, because a user who cannot read it cannot tell what it says. Placeholder text in a field. Conventionally lighter than the entered text and therefore usually below the threshold, and the accessibility chapter's point that a placeholder is not a label applies here too — the fix is a real label and a placeholder that meets the contrast. Text over an image or a gradient. The contrast depends on the pixel behind the text, which varies, so a ratio computed against one sample of the image is meaningless; the fix is an overlay or a scrim with enough opacity that the worst-case pixel still passes. And white text on a mid-tone brand colour. A brand colour chosen for its appearance rather than for its contrast fails against white at a ratio of about three, and fails against black at about seven, so the choice is which text colour the brand colour will carry — and for a mid-tone the answer is usually to darken the brand colour for the button fill rather than to change the text. Then the two practices that keep contrast correct, because it is the requirement most likely to regress. Compute the pairs in a test, from the theme, — assert the ratio for every foreground-background pair your theme defines, in both light and dark — and the test fails the moment a designer changes a colour to one that does not work, which is the moment it is cheapest to notice. And check the states, not just the default: hover, pressed, selected and disabled all change the foreground or the background and each needs its own measurement, which is why a colour that passes in a screenshot fails when the button is pressed.

/* The arithmetic. */
const CONTRAST = {
  is: 'A RATIO BETWEEN TWO COLOURS',
  computedFrom: 'RELATIVE LUMINANCE',
  how: ['each CHANNEL IS NORMALISED', 'a LINEARISATION IS APPLIED - BECAUSE PERCEPTION IS NOT LINEAR IN the CHANNEL VALUE',
    'and the THREE ARE COMBINED with WEIGHTS THAT APPROXIMATE HUMAN SENSITIVITY'],
  ratio: 'the LIGHTER LUMINANCE OVER the DARKER, PLUS A POINT ZERO FIVE',
  range: 'ONE TO TWENTY-ONE',
  follows: ['a RATIO OF ONE MEANS the COLOURS ARE IDENTICAL and NOTHING IS VISIBLE',
    'the MAXIMUM of TWENTY-ONE IS BLACK ON WHITE and NOTHING CAN EXCEED IT'],
  nonLinear: 'the RATIO IS NON-LINEAR, SO A CHANGE THAT LOOKS LIKE NOTHING can CROSS A THRESHOLD',
  example: 'going FROM A LIGHT GREY to A SLIGHTLY DARKER GREY CAN MOVE the RATIO FROM FOUR-POINT-TWO to FOUR-POINT-SIX and CROSS the REQUIREMENT',
  therefore: 'WHICH IS WHY the THRESHOLD MUST BE MEASURED rather than JUDGED',
};

/* Four pairs that fail. */
const FAILING = [
  { p: 'DISABLED TEXT', detail: 'EVERY DESIGN SYSTEM HAS A DISABLED COLOUR THAT IS DELIBERATELY FAINT, and IT IS ALMOST ALWAYS BELOW the THRESHOLD',
    tension: 'which IS A GENUINE TENSION, SINCE A DISABLED CONTROLS LOW PROMinence IS the POINT',
    resolution: 'DISABLED TEXT IS EXEMPT FROM the REQUIREMENT IN WCAG',
    advice: 'and the PRACTICAL ADVICE IS to STILL KEEP IT READABLE ENOUGH TO IDENTIFY, BECAUSE A USER WHO CANNOT READ IT CANNOT TELL WHAT IT SAYS' },
  { p: 'PLACEHOLDER TEXT IN A FIELD', detail: 'CONVENTIONALLY LIGHTER than the ENTERED TEXT and THEREFORE USUALLY BELOW the THRESHOLD',
    connects: 'and the ACCESSIBILITY CHAPTERS POINT THAT A PLACEHOLDER IS NOT A LABEL APPLIES HERE TOO',
    fix: ['A REAL LABEL', 'and a PLACEHOLDER THAT MEETS the CONTRAST'] },
  { p: 'TEXT OVER an IMAGE or A GRADIENT',
    why: 'the CONTRAST DEPENDS ON the PIXEL BEHIND the TEXT, WHICH VARIES',
    so: 'a RATIO COMPUTED AGAINST ONE SAMPLE of the IMAGE IS MEANINGLESS',
    fix: 'AN OVERLAY or A SCRIM WITH ENOUGH OPACITY THAT the WORST-CASE PIXEL STILL PASSES' },
  { p: 'WHITE TEXT ON A MID-TONE BRAND COLOUR',
    detail: 'A BRAND COLOUR CHOSEN FOR ITS APPEARANCE rather than FOR ITS CONTRAST FAILS AGAINST WHITE at A RATIO of ABOUT THREE, and FAILS AGAINST BLACK at ABOUT SEVEN',
    decision: 'so the CHOICE IS WHICH TEXT COLOUR the BRAND COLOUR WILL CARRY',
    answer: 'and for a MID-TONE the ANSWER IS USUALLY to DARKEN the BRAND COLOUR FOR the BUTTON FILL rather than to CHANGE the TEXT' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'COMPUTE the PAIRS IN A TEST, FROM the THEME',
    how: 'ASSERT the RATIO for EVERY FOREGROUND-BACKGROUND PAIR YOUR THEME DEFINES, IN BOTH LIGHT and DARK',
    gain: 'and the TEST FAILS the MOMENT A DESIGNER CHANGES A COLOUR to ONE THAT DOES NOT WORK',
    why: 'which IS the MOMENT IT IS CHEAPEST TO NOTICE' },
  { p: 'CHECK the STATES, not JUST the DEFAULT',
    states: ['HOVER', 'PRESSED', 'SELECTED', 'DISABLED'],
    why: 'ALL CHANGE the FOREGROUND or the BACKGROUND and EACH NEEDS ITS OWN MEASUREMENT',
    symptom: 'which IS WHY A COLOUR THAT PASSES IN A SCREENSHOT FAILS WHEN the BUTTON IS PRESSED' },
];

Write the contrast check as a test rather than checking it by eye. A Material 3 scheme from a seed colour is designed to meet the ratios, so the test should pass without any tuning - and it will catch the day someone adds a hand-picked colour that does not.

// THE REQUIREMENTS (WCAG 2.1 AA, which both stores reference)
//   4.5:1  normal text (< 18pt, or < 14pt bold)
//   3.0:1  large text (>= 18pt, or >= 14pt bold)
//   3.0:1  UI components and graphics: a button border, a
//          focus indicator, a chart line
// 3:1 is also required for the focus indicator against its
// background.

// MATERIAL 3 schemes are designed to meet these, so using the
// roles gets you most of the way there
final scheme = ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: brand);
// scheme.onSurface on scheme.surface: check it, do not assume

// a helper, so the check is a build failure rather than a review
// comment
double contrastRatio(Color a, Color b) {
  final l1 = a.computeLuminance();
  final l2 = b.computeLuminance();
  final lighter = l1 > l2 ? l1 : l2;
  final darker = l1 > l2 ? l2 : l1;
  return (lighter + 0.05) / (darker + 0.05);
}

@visibleForTesting
bool meetsContrast(Color fg, Color bg, {bool large = false}) {
  return contrastRatio(fg, bg) >= (large ? 3.0 : 4.5);
}

test('all text roles meet AA contrast in both themes', () {
  for (final brightness in Brightness.values) {
    final theme = AppTheme.lightOf(brightness);
    final scheme = theme.colorScheme;
    final text = theme.textTheme;

    expect(meetsContrast(text.bodyMedium!.color!, scheme.surface), isTrue,
        reason: 'bodyMedium on surface, $brightness');
    expect(meetsContrast(text.bodySmall!.color!, scheme.surfaceContainerHigh), isTrue,
        reason: 'bodySmall on a raised surface, $brightness');
    expect(meetsContrast(scheme.onPrimary, scheme.primary), isTrue,
        reason: 'a button label, $brightness');
  }
});

// DO NOT USE COLOUR ALONE
// this fails for a colour-blind user and for a screen reader
Row(children: [
  Icon(isValid ? Icons.check_circle : Icons.error, color: isValid ? green : red),
  Text(isValid ? 'Valid' : 'Invalid'),   // the TEXT is the point
]);

// and for a status dot
Semantics(
  label: isValid ? 'Valid' : 'Invalid',
  child: Container(
    width: 8, height: 8,
    decoration: BoxDecoration(
      color: isValid ? green : red,
      shape: BoxShape.circle,
    ),
  ),
);
// THE FOCUS INDICATOR, which is required and often missing
// Flutter's default is a 2px outline in the primary colour. If
// you remove it with a custom ButtonStyle, you must replace it.
FilledButton(
  style: FilledButton.styleFrom(
    // do NOT do: overlayColor: Colors.transparent
  ),
  onPressed: f,
  child: const Text('Save'),
)

// a custom one, for a design that has no visible focus
ButtonStyle(
  overlayColor: WidgetStateProperty.resolveWith(
    (states) => states.contains(WidgetState.focused) ? Colors.transparent : null,
  ),
)

// for a custom widget
class TappableBox extends StatelessWidget {
  const TappableBox({required this.onTap, required this.child, super.key});
  final VoidCallback onTap;
  final Widget child;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return FocusableActionDetector(
      onShowFocusHighlight: (value) {},
      enabled: true,
      actions: { ActivateIntent: CallbackAction(onInvoke: (_) => onTap())},
      child: MouseRegion(
        cursor: SystemMouseCursors.click,
        child: GestureDetector(onTap: onTap, child: child),
      ),
    );
  }
}

10.4 Touch, focus and keyboard

// TOUCH TARGETS: 44x44 minimum, 48x48 is the Material 3 default
// check it: an Icon with size: 16 in an IconButton has a 48x48
// target by default, but a bare GestureDetector does not
test('every tappable is at least 44x44', (tester) async {
  await tester.pumpWidget(const MyApp());

  final finder = find.byWidgetPredicate(
    (w) => w is GestureDetector && w.onTap != null,
  );

  for (final element in finder.evaluate()) {
    final size = element.size!;
    if (size.width < 44 || size.height < 44) {
      fail('a tappable GestureDetector is ${size.width}x${size.height}');
    }
  }
});

// FOCUS ORDER, for a keyboard user on desktop
// it follows the widget tree order by default, which usually
// matches the visual order. Two cases to fix:
// 1. a CustomPaint or a custom layout that is not a Column/Row
// 2. a reordered list

FocusTraversalGroup(
  order: const NumericFocusOrder(),
  child: Column(children: [
    FocusTraversalOrder(order: const NumericFocusOrder(1), child: First()),
    FocusTraversalOrder(order: const NumericFocusOrder(2), child: Second()),
  ]),
);

// and for a shell with several focusable regions
Shortcuts(
  shortcuts: {
    SingleActivator(LogicalKeyboardKey.keyN, control: true): NewEntryIntent(),
  },
  child: Actions(
    actions: {NewEntryIntent: CallbackAction(onInvoke: (_) => _newEntry())},
    child: child,
  ),
);

// SHORTCUTS, and a conflict: Flutter has built-in ones, and some
// will fire when you do not expect
Actions(
  actions: <Type, Action<Intent>>{
    DismissIntent: CallbackAction<DismissIntent>(onInvoke: _dismiss),
  },
  child: Focus(
    autofocus: true,
    child: child,
  ),
);

Keyboard and pointer, and the two systems that have to coexist

Touch, mouse and keyboard are three input systems and the framework's default behaviour is tuned for one of them, which is why a widget that works on a phone frequently has problems on a desktop or with a keyboard. A pointer is a thing with a position and a button state, and events arrive as down, move and up with a position on each. A touch is a pointer that arrives, does something, and goes away, and the framework's gesture recognisers are built on that. A key is a discrete event with no position, and Flutter routes it to whatever holds focus. The three differ in a way that produces four specific problems. Then the four problems, and each has a known mechanism. Hover does nothing because there is nothing to show it. On a desktop every interactive element has a hover state and on a phone none of them is ever seen, so a hover-only affordance is a desktop-only affordance — and a custom widget built for touch will look dead on a desktop unless it has a MouseRegion with an onHover. A control is not reachable by keyboard. The framework's Material and Cupertino components handle focus and activation; a custom tappable does not, and the fix is a Focus with an onKeyEvent handler that activates on both Enter and Space, because the convention differs and a control that responds to one of them is broken for the users who press the other. A tooltip or a menu opens on hover and traps the mouse, which is fine with a mouse and impossible with a keyboard or a switch device, so anything hover-revealed must also be reachable by focus. And the cursor is an arrow over everything, because a custom widget has no cursor, and on a desktop that reads as "not interactive" — the fix is a MouseRegion with an appropriate cursor, which is a one-line change and is the difference between a desktop build that feels native and one that feels like a webpage. Then the three things that are requirements on every platform, and each is a legal obligation rather than a nicety. Everything reachable by pointer must be reachable by keyboard, in the same order. Focus must be visible, and the focus highlight is provided by default and removed by custom styling. And the focus indicator must not be obscured — a widget that paints over the focused child hides the indicator, which is a real defect that only appears when someone tabs through the screen. Then the two practices that make multi-platform work. Write the keyboard path first, because a control that only works by mouse gets a keyboard treatment added later, and it will be added for the whole screen rather than for the control. And test with a mouse and with the keyboard on every platform, including the platforms where neither is primary — because a widget tested only with a mouse has no keyboard path, and one tested only with touch has no hover path, and both defects are invisible in the environment they were not tested in.

/* Three input systems. */
const SYSTEMS = [
  { s: 'a POINTER', is: 'A THING with A POSITION and A BUTTON STATE',
    events: 'DOWN, MOVE and UP WITH A POSITION ON EACH' },
  { s: 'a TOUCH', is: 'A POINTER THAT ARRIVES, DOES SOMETHING, and GOES AWAY',
    and: 'the FRAMEWORKS GESTURE RECOGNISERS ARE BUILT ON THAT' },
  { s: 'a KEY', is: 'A DISCRETE EVENT with NO POSITION',
    routed: 'and FLUTTER ROUTES IT to WHATEVER HOLDS FOCUS' },
];
const DIFFERS = 'THE THREE DIFFER IN A WAY THAT PRODUCES FOUR SPECIFIC PROBLEMS';

/* Four problems. */
const PROBLEMS = [
  { p: 'HOVER DOES NOTHING BECAUSE THERE IS NOTHING TO SHOW IT',
    fact: 'ON A DESKTOP EVERY INTERACTIVE ELEMENT HAS A HOVER STATE and ON A PHONE NONE of THEM IS EVER SEEN',
    consequence: 'so a HOVER-ONLY AFFORDANCE IS A DESKTOP-ONLY AFFORDANCE',
    fix: 'a CUSTOM WIDGET BUILT FOR TOUCH WILL LOOK DEAD ON A DESKTOP UNLESS IT HAS a MouseRegion WITH AN onHover' },
  { p: 'A CONTROL IS NOT REACHABLE BY KEYBOARD',
    fact: 'the FRAMEWORKS MATERIAL and CUPERTINO COMPONENTS HANDLE FOCUS and ACTIVATION; a CUSTOM TAPPABLE DOES NOT',
    fix: 'a Focus WITH AN onKeyEvent HANDLER THAT ACTIVATES ON BOTH ENTER and SPACE',
    whyBoth: 'BECAUSE the CONVENTION DIFFERS and A CONTROL THAT RESPONDS TO ONE of THEM IS BROKEN for the USERS WHO PRESS the OTHER' },
  { p: 'A TOOLTIP or A MENU OPENS ON HOVER and TRAPS the MOUSE',
    detail: 'which IS FINE WITH A MOUSE and IMPOSSIBLE WITH A KEYBOARD or A SWITCH DEVICE',
    fix: 'ANYTHING HOVER-REVEALED MUST ALSO BE REACHABLE BY FOCUS' },
  { p: 'the CURSOR IS AN ARROW OVER EVERYTHING',
    cause: 'BECAUSE A CUSTOM WIDGET HAS NO CURSOR',
    reads: 'and ON A DESKTOP THAT READS AS not interactive',
    fix: 'a MouseRegion WITH AN APPROPRIATE CURSOR',
    and: 'which IS A ONE-LINE CHANGE and IS the DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A DESKTOP BUILD THAT FEELS NATIVE and ONE THAT FEELS LIKE A WEBPAGE' },
];

/* Three requirements. */
const REQUIREMENTS = [
  { r: 'EVERYTHING REACHABLE BY POINTER MUST BE REACHABLE BY KEYBOARD', inTheSameOrder: true, isA: 'LEGAL OBLIGATION rather than A NICETY' },
  { r: 'FOCUS MUST BE VISIBLE', note: 'and the FOCUS HIGHLIGHT IS PROVIDED BY DEFAULT and REMOVED BY CUSTOM STYLING' },
  { r: 'the FOCUS INDICATOR MUST NOT BE OBSCURED',
    defect: 'A WIDGET THAT PAINTS OVER the FOCUSED CHILD HIDES the INDICATOR',
    detail: 'which IS A REAL DEFECT THAT ONLY APPEARS WHEN SOMEONE TABS THROUGH the SCREEN' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'WRITE the KEYBOARD PATH FIRST',
    why: 'because A CONTROL THAT ONLY WORKS BY MOUSE GETS A KEYBOARD TREATMENT ADDED LATER',
    consequence: 'and IT WILL BE ADDED FOR the WHOLE SCREEN rather than FOR the CONTROL' },
  { p: 'TEST WITH A MOUSE and WITH the KEYBOARD ON EVERY PLATFORM, INCLUDING the PLATFORMS WHERE NEITHER IS PRIMARY',
    why: 'because A WIDGET TESTED ONLY WITH A MOUSE HAS NO KEYBOARD PATH, and ONE TESTED ONLY WITH TOUCH HAS NO HOVER PATH',
    and: 'both DEFECTS ARE INVISIBLE IN the ENVIRONMENT THEY WERE NOT TESTED IN' },
];

10.5 Localisation setup

How localisation works, and the strings that are not strings

Flutter's localisation has two layers and confusing them causes most of the problems. The lower layer is the gen_l10n tool, which reads a set of ARB files — one per locale, containing the same message identifiers with translated text — and generates typed classes: one getter per message per locale, with the text inlined into the binary and the placeholders and plurals resolved at build time. The upper layer is the delegate machinery — a localisations delegate and a supported-locales list — that the framework uses to choose which generated class to load and to react to a locale change. The important consequence is that a missing translation is a compile error, not a runtime fallback, because the generated class has a getter for every message in every locale it was generated for — which means the tooling tells you at build time exactly which strings are untranslated in which language. Then the three things that are not strings, and each is a common defect. Text assembled by concatenation. A sentence built as "You have " + count + " items" cannot be translated, because languages reorder and some require the noun before the number; the fix is a message with a placeholder and a plural form. Text laid out assuming the source language. German is routinely thirty per cent longer than English, so a label that fits in English clips in German; the fix is to test with the longest locale rather than to shorten the English. And text in a custom painter or a chart, which never goes through the delegate because it is drawn directly and so is invisible to every mechanism above — the fix is to resolve the string from the generated class and to measure it with the correct text direction. Then the two features that are needed more often than people expect, and both have their own failure modes. Pluralisation is not a single alternative form: it is zero, one, two, few, many and other, and which applies depends on the language's rules — English has two, Arabic has six, Polish has four, Russian has three — so a message that handles only singular and plural will produce wrong text in several languages even though it works in English. And gender applies to nouns and articles in many languages and has no equivalent in English, so a string with a gender placeholder is not optional in a localised product. Then the two practices, and each prevents a class of bug that is expensive to find. Run the app in the longest locale and in a right-to-left locale, once, before every release, because those two tests find most of what is wrong and they take ten minutes. And never hard-code a locale-dependent format, — dates, numbers, currency and units all have locale-specific conventions, and using the formatting from the internationalisation library rather than string interpolation is what makes a price correct in a market where the decimal separator is a comma and the symbol comes after the number.

/* Two layers. */
const LAYERS = [
  { l: 'gen_l10n', reads: 'A SET of ARB FILES - ONE PER LOCALE, CONTAINING the SAME MESSAGE IDENTIFIERS with TRANSLATED TEXT',
    generates: 'TYPED CLASSES - ONE GETTER PER MESSAGE PER LOCALE',
    does: ['the TEXT IS INLINED INTO the BINARY', 'the PLACEHOLDERS and PLURALS ARE RESOLVED AT BUILD TIME'] },
  { l: 'the DELEGATE MACHINERY', is: ['a LOCALISATIONS DELEGATE', 'a SUPPORTED-LOCALES LIST'],
    usedFor: 'the FRAMEWORK USES IT to CHOOSE WHICH GENERATED CLASS TO LOAD and to REACT TO A LOCALE CHANGE' },
];
const CONSEQUENCE = 'a MISSING TRANSLATION IS A COMPILE ERROR, not A RUNTIME FALLBACK';
const WHY = 'BECAUSE the GENERATED CLASS HAS A GETTER FOR EVERY MESSAGE IN EVERY LOCALE IT WAS GENERATED FOR';
const GAIN = 'which MEANS the TOOLING TELLS YOU AT BUILD TIME EXACTLY WHICH STRINGS ARE UNTRANSLATED IN WHICH LANGUAGE';

/* Three things that are not strings. */
const NOT_STRINGS = [
  { t: 'TEXT ASSEMBLED BY CONCATENATION',
    example: 'A SENTENCE BUILT AS You have + count + items',
    why: 'CANNOT BE TRANSLATED, BECAUSE LANGUAGES REORDER and SOME REQUIRE the NOUN BEFORE the NUMBER',
    fix: 'A MESSAGE WITH A PLACEHOLDER and A PLURAL FORM' },
  { t: 'TEXT LAID OUT ASSUMING the SOURCE LANGUAGE',
    fact: 'GERMAN IS ROUTINELY THIRTY PER CENT LONGER than ENGLISH',
    consequence: 'so A LABEL THAT FITS IN ENGLISH CLIPS IN GERMAN',
    fix: 'TEST WITH the LONGEST LOCALE rather than SHORTENING the ENGLISH' },
  { t: 'TEXT IN A CUSTOM PAINTER or A CHART',
    why: 'WHICH NEVER GOES THROUGH the DELEGATE BECAUSE IT IS DRAWN DIRECTLY and so IS INVISIBLE to EVERY MECHANISM ABOVE',
    fix: ['RESOLVE the STRING FROM the GENERATED CLASS', 'and MEASURE IT WITH the CORRECT TEXT DIRECTION'] },
];

/* Two features. */
const FEATURES = [
  { f: 'PLURALISATION', isNot: 'A SINGLE ALTERNATIVE FORM',
    categories: ['ZERO', 'ONE', 'TWO', 'FEW', 'MANY', 'OTHER'],
    dependsOn: 'WHICH APPLIES DEPENDS ON the LANGUAGES RULES',
    counts: ['ENGLISH HAS TWO', 'ARABIC HAS SIX', 'POLISH HAS FOUR', 'RUSSIAN HAS THREE'],
    failure: 'so A MESSAGE THAT HANDLES ONLY SINGULAR and PLURAL WILL PRODUCE WRONG TEXT IN SEVERAL LANGUAGES EVEN THOUGH it WORKS IN ENGLISH' },
  { f: 'GENDER', applies: 'TO NOUNS and ARTICLES IN MANY LANGUAGES',
    noEquivalent: 'and HAS NO EQUIVALENT IN ENGLISH',
    so: 'A STRING WITH A GENDER PLACEHOLDER IS NOT OPTIONAL IN A LOCALISED PRODUCT' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'RUN the APP IN the LONGEST LOCALE and IN A RIGHT-TO-LEFT LOCALE, ONCE, BEFORE EVERY RELEASE',
    gain: 'because THOSE TWO TESTS FIND MOST of WHAT IS WRONG and THEY TAKE TEN MINUTES' },
  { p: 'NEVER HARD-CODE A LOCALE-DEPENDENT FORMAT',
    formats: ['DATES', 'NUMBERS', 'CURRENCY', 'UNITS'],
    why: 'ALL HAVE LOCALE-SPECIFIC CONVENTIONS',
    and: 'USING the FORMATTING FROM the INTERNATIONALISATION LIBRARY rather than STRING INTERPOLATION IS WHAT MAKES A PRICE CORRECT IN A MARKET WHERE the DECIMAL SEPARATOR IS A COMMA and the SYMBOL COMES AFTER the NUMBER' },
];

Never build a user-visible string by concatenating translated fragments. Word order changes between languages, and in some languages the plural form is a completely different sentence structure. Every string goes through the ARB file, including the ones that look like they have no variables in them.

// 1. ENABLE IT
// pubspec.yaml
flutter_localizations:
  sdk: flutter
intl: any            # or a pinned version, 0.19.0

// 2. GENERATE THE LOCALES
// l10n.yaml
arb-dir: lib/l10n
template-arb-file: app_en.arb
output-localization-file: app_localizations.dart
output-class: AppLocalizations
nullable-getter: false

// 3. THE ARB FILES
// lib/l10n/app_en.arb
{
  "@@locale": "en",
  "appTitle": "Field Notes",
  "entryCount": "{count, plural, =0{No entries} =1{1 entry} other{{count} entries}}",
  "@entryCount": {
    "placeholders": { "count": { "type": "int" } }
  },
  "greeting": "Welcome, {name}",
  "@greeting": {
    "placeholders": { "name": { "type": "String" } }
  },
  "deleteConfirm": "Delete {title}?",
  "todayLabel": "Today",
  "yesterdayLabel": "Yesterday",
  "searchHint": "Search notes",
  "errorNetwork": "Could not reach the server. Check your connection.",
  "retry": "Retry",
  "cancel": "Cancel",
  "save": "Save"
}

// lib/l10n/app_es.arb
{
  "@@locale": "es",
  "appTitle": "Notas de campo",
  "greeting": "Bienvenido, {name}",
  "deleteConfirm": "¿Eliminar {title}?",
  ...
}
// run: flutter gen-l10n

// 4. USE IT
MaterialApp(
  localizationsDelegates: AppLocalizations.localizationsDelegates,
  supportedLocales: AppLocalizations.supportedLocales,
  locale: null,       // null = follow the device
  // or override it
  locale: Locale('es'),
  // or let the user choose
  locale: ref.watch(localeProvider),
);

final l10n = AppLocalizations.of(context);
Text(l10n.appTitle);
Text(l10n.greeting('Ana'));
Text(l10n.entryCount(3));    // "3 entries"

// CHANGE IT AT RUNTIME
final locale = ref.watch(localeProvider);
MaterialApp(
  locale: locale,
  onGenerateTitle: (context) => AppLocalizations.of(context).appTitle,
);
// THE RULES, and the bugs each one prevents
//
// 1. NEVER CONCATENATE A TRANSLATED STRING
// BAD:  Text('You have ${count} entries')
// GOOD: Text(l10n.entryCount(count))
// in some languages the word order changes, and in some the
// plural form is completely different
//
// 2. NO GENDERED PLACEHOLDERS, without a choice
// BAD:  'Mr. Smith' / a hardcoded salutation
// GOOD: a form asking for a salutation, or a neutral phrasing
//
// 3. NO ASSUMED DATE OR NUMBER FORMAT
// BAD:  Text(entry.createdAt.toString())       // 2026-03-14 10:22
// GOOD: Text(formatDate(entry.createdAt))
// GOOD: Text(MaterialLocalizations.of(context).formatMediumDate(entry.createdAt))
//
// 4. LEAVE ROOM FOR EXPANSION
// German is ~30% longer than English. Russian can be longer
// still. Arabic and Hindi wrap differently. Design the layout
// so a longer string does not break it.
//
// 5. NO TEXT IN CODE BLOCKS OR LOGOS
// an English word baked into an image is untranslatable
//
// 6. THE RIGHT-TO-LEFT TEST: run the app in Arabic and check
// every screen, including the charts and the custom painters

10.6 Right-to-left and text direction

// DIRECTION-AWARE WIDGETS. These handle it for you:
Row, Column, ListView, GridView, Stack,   // and their properties
Padding, Align, Positioned, Center        // the directional ones
Text, RichText                            // the text direction

// Padding is direction-aware with EdgeInsetsDirectional
Padding(
  padding: const EdgeInsetsDirectional.only(start: 16, end: 16),
  child: child,
)
// vs EdgeInsets.only(left: 16, right: 16), which does NOT flip
// and is almost always a mistake

// PositionedDirectional, for a Stack
PositionedDirectional(
  top: 8,
  end: 8,               // flips to left: 8 in RTL
  child: closeButton,
)

// THE ONES THAT DO NOT, and need manual work
CustomPaint(
  painter: _ChartPainter(data: data, isRtl: direction == TextDirection.rtl),
)
CustomScrollView(       // a custom sliver
  slivers: [MySliver()],
)

class _ChartPainter extends CustomPainter {
  @override
  void paint(Canvas canvas, Size size) {
    final rtl = Directionality.of(context) == TextDirection.rtl;
    // the x axis: where is zero, where does it grow?
    final zeroX = rtl ? size.width : 0.0;
    // the text alignment
    final align = rtl ? TextAlign.left : TextAlign.right;
  }
}

// THE DIRECTION
// it comes from the locale, automatically, via Directionality
// which MaterialApp inserts
Directionality.of(context);           // TextDirection.ltr or .rtl

// forcing it, for testing
MaterialApp(
  locale: const Locale('ar'),
);
// or, per subtree
Directionality(
  textDirection: TextDirection.rtl,
  child: child,
);

// AN RTL APP, in practice, breaks in these places
// 1. hardcoded left/right in a chart or a map
// 2. a custom arrow icon that should mirror
//    Icon(Icons.arrow_forward)  <- this DOES mirror automatically
//    Icon(Icons.chevron_right)  <- so does this
//    your own drawn arrow      <- does not
// 3. a slider that should grow right-to-left
//    Slider(value: ..., )      <- handles it
//    a custom progress bar     <- does not
// 4. a swipe-to-dismiss that should go the other way
// MIRRORING AN ICON, for a custom one
Icon(
  icon,
  textDirection: TextDirection.ltr,   // force: the icon means "back"
)
Transform(
  alignment: Alignment.center,
  transform: Matrix4.identity()..scale(-1.0, 1.0),
  child: Icon(Icons.arrow_back_ios_new),   // mirror it
)

// ICONS THAT MEAN "BACK" AND ARE CORRECT IN BOTH DIRECTIONS
//   Icons.arrow_back       (a hard left arrow: WRONG in RTL)
//   Icons.arrow_back_ios_new  (a chevron: correct)
//   CupertinoIcons.back    (correct)
//   Icons.chevron_left     (WRONG in RTL)
//   Icons.chevron_right    (correct)
// use the _ios_new or the Cupertino one

Direction, and the four things that have to mirror

Right-to-left support is mostly a matter of the framework already doing the work and the application not fighting it, and the mechanism is one value that everything reads. The ambient direction comes from the locale and is available through the localisation delegate, and the framework uses it in the places that matter automatically: start and end resolve to left or right as appropriate, alignment defaults are direction-aware, and the row and flex layouts put their children in the reading order for the direction. So a widget written entirely in start and end works in both directions without a single change, which is the property to design for. Then the four things that must be mirrored, and each has a specific mechanism. Directional icons. A back arrow, a chevron, a "next" arrow, a send arrow, an indent — each of these points in a direction and must flip. The framework's icon set handles this: an icon whose name ends in an automatic-direction suffix is flipped for you when the direction is right-to-left, and an icon whose name does not is not — so the fix is either to use the automatic variants or to choose the variant by direction explicitly, and to check which icons in the app do not flip. Directional layout that was written with left and right. Padding written as a left margin, an alignment of Alignment.centerLeft, a Row with a hard-coded ordering — each of these is wrong in one direction, and each is invisible until the app runs in Arabic. Text alignment. Text aligns to the start of the reading direction by default, which is correct, but any explicit left alignment is not, and a text field with left-aligned content in a right-to-left app reads oddly even when the layout is correct. And the custom painters, which are invisible to everything above. A CustomPainter that draws text or a chart reads the direction only if it asks for it, and one that assumes left-to-right produces a chart that is mirrored in its data and not in its axes, or a label on the wrong side. Then the two things that are not about direction but are found by the same test, and a right-to-left pass finds them. Any fixed positioning. A Stack with a child positioned at a left offset is a direction-dependent layout, and it is the most common cause of a right-to-left screen that is mostly correct with one element in the wrong place. And any text drawn into a canvas with a hard-coded alignment, which is the same class of defect as the painters above and is invisible to the widget-level fix. Then the two practices that keep it correct, and both are cheap. Run the whole app in Arabic once per release, because the defects above are all visible and all take minutes to find when the direction is right-to-left and the app is running in it; and because the direction of a layout is a different code path from the direction of a string, so a localised build in a left-to-right language will not reveal them. And never write a directional literal without a comment, — where a left or a right appears in a layout, the comment should say whether it is physical or logical, because the two are indistinguishable in the source and only one of them is correct.

/* The one value. */
const MECHANISM = {
  ambient: 'the DIRECTION COMES FROM the LOCALE and IS AVAILABLE THROUGH the LOCALISATION DELEGATE',
  frameworkDoes: ['start and end RESOLVE to LEFT or RIGHT as APPROPRIATE',
    'ALIGNMENT DEFAULTS ARE DIRECTION-AWARE',
    'and the ROW and FLEX LAYOUTS PUT THEIR CHILDREN IN the READING ORDER for the DIRECTION'],
  consequence: 'a WIDGET WRITTEN ENTIRELY IN start and end WORKS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS WITHOUT A SINGLE CHANGE',
  designFor: 'which IS the PROPERTY TO DESIGN FOR',
};

/* Four things to mirror. */
const MIRROR = [
  { t: 'DIRECTIONAL ICONS', instances: ['A BACK ARROW', 'A CHEVRON', 'A next ARROW', 'A SEND ARROW', 'AN INDENT'],
    framework: 'AN ICON WHOSE NAME ENDS IN AN AUTOMATIC-DIRECTION SUFFIX IS FLIPPED FOR YOU WHEN the DIRECTION IS RIGHT-TO-LEFT',
    and: 'AN ICON WHOSE NAME DOES NOT IS NOT',
    fix: ['use the AUTOMATIC VARIANTS', 'or CHOOSE the VARIANT BY DIRECTION EXPLICITLY'],
    check: 'and CHECK WHICH ICONS IN the APP DO NOT FLIP' },
  { t: 'DIRECTIONAL LAYOUT THAT WAS WRITTEN WITH LEFT and RIGHT',
    instances: ['PADDING WRITTEN AS A LEFT MARGIN', 'AN ALIGNMENT of Alignment.centerLeft',
      'A Row WITH A HARD-CODED ORDERING'],
    detail: 'EACH of THESE IS WRONG IN ONE DIRECTION',
    symptom: 'and EACH IS INVISIBLE UNTIL the APP RUNS IN ARABIC' },
  { t: 'TEXT ALIGNMENT',
    default: 'TEXT ALIGNS TO the START of the READING DIRECTION BY DEFAULT, WHICH IS CORRECT',
    but: 'ANY EXPLICIT LEFT ALIGNMENT IS NOT',
    symptom: 'and A TEXT FIELD WITH LEFT-ALIGNED CONTENT IN A RIGHT-TO-LEFT APP READS ODDLY EVEN WHEN the LAYOUT IS CORRECT' },
  { t: 'the CUSTOM PAINTERS, WHICH ARE INVISIBLE to EVERYTHING ABOVE',
    detail: 'A CustomPainter THAT DRAWS TEXT or A CHART READS the DIRECTION ONLY IF IT ASKS FOR IT',
    symptom: 'and ONE THAT ASSUMES LEFT-TO-RIGHT PRODUCES A CHART THAT IS MIRRORED IN ITS DATA and NOT IN ITS AXES, or A LABEL ON the WRONG SIDE' },
];

/* Two more, found by the same test. */
const ALSO_FOUND = [
  { t: 'ANY FIXED POSITIONING',
    detail: 'A Stack WITH A CHILD POSITIONED AT A LEFT OFFSET IS A DIRECTION-DEPENDENT LAYOUT',
    rank: 'and IT IS THE MOST COMMON CAUSE of A RIGHT-TO-LEFT SCREEN THAT IS MOSTLY CORRECT with ONE ELEMENT IN the WRONG PLACE' },
  { t: 'ANY TEXT DRAWN INTO A CANVAS WITH A HARD-CODED ALIGNMENT',
    sameClass: 'as the PAINTERS ABOVE', and: 'IT IS INVISIBLE TO the WIDGET-LEVEL FIX' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'RUN the WHOLE APP IN ARABIC ONCE PER RELEASE',
    why: 'because the DEFECTS ABOVE ARE ALL VISIBLE and ALL TAKE MINUTES TO FIND WHEN the DIRECTION IS RIGHT-TO-LEFT and the APP IS RUNNING IN IT',
    and: 'because the DIRECTION of a LAYOUT IS A DIFFERENT CODE PATH from the DIRECTION of a STRING, so A LOCALISED BUILD IN A LEFT-TO-RIGHT LANGUAGE WILL NOT REVEAL THEM' },
  { p: 'NEVER WRITE A DIRECTIONAL LITERAL WITHOUT A COMMENT',
    what: 'WHERE A LEFT or A RIGHT APPEARS IN A LAYOUT, the COMMENT SHOULD SAY WHETHER IT IS PHYSICAL or LOGICAL',
    why: 'BECAUSE the TWO ARE INDISTINGUISHABLE IN the SOURCE and ONLY ONE of THEM IS CORRECT' },
];

10.7 Dates, numbers and plurals

// DATES, formatted for the locale
final localizations = MaterialLocalizations.of(context);
Text(localizations.formatFullDate(entry.createdAt));
Text(localizations.formatShortDate(entry.createdAt));
Text(localizations.formatTimeOfDay(entry.createdAt, alwaysUse24HourFormat: MediaQuery.alwaysUse24HourFormatOf(context)));
Text(localizations.formatCompactDate(entry.createdAt));
Text(localizations.formatDecimal(entry.weight));      // 1,234.5
Text(localizations.formatFullDuration(Duration(minutes: 90)));   // 1 h 30 min

// RELATIVE DATES, which need the locale
final l10n = AppLocalizations.of(context);
final now = DateTime.now();
final diff = now.difference(entry.createdAt);
if (diff.inMinutes < 1) return l10n.justNow;
if (diff.inHours < 1) return l10n.minutesAgo(diff.inMinutes);
if (diff.inDays == 1) return l10n.yesterday;
if (diff.inDays < 7) return l10n.daysAgo(diff.inDays);
return l10n.formatDate(entry.createdAt);

// PLURALS, which is where translation most often goes wrong
// the ARB form, which handles the CLDR rules per language
"itemCount": "{count, plural, =0{No items} =1{1 item} other{{count} items}}"

// why a plural is not just a count:
//   Polish has 4 plural forms: 1, 2-4, 5+, and a fraction form
//   Arabic has 6: zero, one, two, few, many, other
//   Russian has 3, and the "one" form applies to 1, 21, 31
//   ...not to 2, 22, 32
// A hand-written switch is wrong in all of them.

// GENDER, for languages that require it
// some languages mark the gender of nouns, so "Save" is a
// different string for a masculine and a feminine noun
// the ARB form:
//   "saveItem": "{gender, select, male{Save item} female{Save item} other{Save item}}"
"gender": "female"

// SELECT, for a choice with more than two options
"greeting": "{timeOfDay, select, morning{Good morning} afternoon{Good afternoon} evening{Good evening} other{Hello}}"
// NUMBERS AND CURRENCY
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

final format = NumberFormat.decimalPattern(locale);
Text(format.format(1234567));      // 1,234,567 or 1.234.567

final currency = NumberFormat.simpleCurrency(locale: locale.toLanguageTag(), name: 'USD');
Text(currency.format(42.5));        // \$42.50

// or, from the platform
Text(MaterialLocalizations.of(context).formatDecimal(1234.56));

// and the ARB number form, which respects the locale's grouping
"total": "{amount, number, ::currency/USD}"

Numbers, dates and units, and why formatting is not formatting

The reason number and date formatting has its own section is that a value that is correct in one locale is wrong in most others, and the failures are silent: the string is produced, it contains only digits and punctuation, and nothing looks broken. The four things that vary. The decimal and grouping separators — the period and comma in English, the comma and period in most of Europe, a decimal comma with a space for the grouping in French, and a period in some locales where the comma is the grouping separator, which means the same punctuation means different things. The symbol position and the symbol itself — a currency symbol before the number in English, after it in much of Europe, and a code or a spelled-out name in some locales, so $1,234.56 is simply wrong in several markets. The date order — month-day-year in the United States, day-month-year nearly everywhere else, and year-month-day in several East Asian locales, so a date rendered from its parts in the wrong order is not merely formatted differently but means a different day. And the numbering system — Arabic numerals are not universal, and some locales use their own digits, which means a hard-coded digit renders correctly and is unreadable. Then the three rules, and each is a specific requirement. Never build a number by concatenating strings. Interpolating "$" + amount produces a string that no formatter can correct and that no screen reader reads as a number; the value must stay a number until a formatter renders it. Never construct a date from a format string in application code. The format is a property of the locale, not of the application, and the framework's date formatting takes the locale and chooses it. And never assume a unit. Distance, weight, temperature and currency have per-locale units and per-user preferences, and a value expressed in the wrong unit is a wrong number presented confidently — which is the same failure shape as the software-engineering chapter's unit-consistency argument. Then the two features that exist because of this, and both are worth knowing by name. Number formatting with a locale takes the grouping, the decimal separator, the symbol and the position, and it produces a string a screen reader reads correctly. And relative date formatting — "3 days ago", "in 2 months" — which is not a substitution into a fixed string but a computation against the current date and the locale's plural rules, which is why a hand-written "yesterday" string is wrong in every locale whose word for yesterday is not yesterday. Then the two practices that prevent the whole class, and both are cheap. Assert the formatted output in a test for at least one locale that is not English, because a formatting bug is invisible in the developer's locale and is a one-line assertion to catch. And pass the locale explicitly whenever a value is formatted outside a widget, because code that runs outside the widget tree has no ambient locale and will silently fall back to the default, which is how a correctly-localised screen ends up with an unformatted date in one place.

/* Why it has its own section. */
const WHY = 'A VALUE THAT IS CORRECT IN ONE LOCALE IS WRONG IN MOST OTHERS';
const FAILURE = 'and the FAILURES ARE SILENT - the STRING IS PRODUCED, it CONTAINS ONLY DIGITS and PUNCTUATION, and NOTHING LOOKS BROKEN';

/* Four things that vary. */
const VARIES = [

10.8 Platform conventions

Platform conventions, and the three that are not cosmetic

Platform convention is the set of behaviours a user of a platform expects and would notice their absence of, and on a cross-platform application most of it is handled by the framework's platform-adaptive widgets. Adaptive widgets read the platform and render the platform's own design language — the framework's equivalents of a button, a switch, a back affordance, a share sheet and a date picker each have a Material and a Cupertino implementation, and using them is what makes an application feel native without writing any platform code. So the default is correct, and the failures come from overriding it. Then the three conventions that are not cosmetic, and each has a real consequence when ignored. The back gesture. On Android it is an edge swipe and on iOS it is an edge swipe from the other edge or a gesture at the top; the framework maps it to the navigator's back, and an application that intercepts it — to confirm a discard, say — must do so with the platform's own mechanism so the gesture, the button and the system back all behave the same. An application that handles back only in a button produces a system gesture that silently exits the app, which is the most-reported cross-platform defect there is. The keyboard and the safe area. The software keyboard reduces the usable height, and a screen that does not account for the inset will have its submit button behind the keyboard; the framework's view insets are the mechanism and the previous sections' text-input material is where this is detailed. And the text-selection and copy behaviour, which differs between platforms — selection handles are on one side on one platform and both sides on the other, and long-press to paste has platform-specific affordances — so a custom text field that reimplements selection will look wrong on one of them. Then the four conventions that are cosmetic but are noticed, and they are cheap. Scroll physics, which the gesture chapter covers. The dialog's confirm and cancel button order, which is reversed between platforms. The date and time pickers, which have different formats and different interactions — an iOS picker is a wheel and an Android one is a calendar, and they are not interchangeable. And the transition animation for a route, which slides horizontally on both platforms for a push but comes from the bottom for a modal on one and not the other. Then the two practices, and each is a specific defence. Do not reimplement anything the framework has a platform-adaptive version of, because the reimplementation is correct on one platform and subtly wrong on the other, and the defect appears only on the device you do not have. And check the three screens that are hardest to make native — the list, the form and the settings screen — on both platforms once per release, because they are where the conventions accumulate and a screen that is merely acceptable will be fine forever while one that is wrong will be reported by users rather than found by you.

/* Adaptive widgets. */
const ADAPTIVE = {

Adapt the navigation, the platform conventions and the accessibility settings. Do not adapt the information architecture, the visual identity or the data model. An app that is two different apps depending on the platform is worse than one that is slightly off-convention.

An app that feels native on each platform, without looking broken on the other.

// THE DIFFERENCES THAT MATTER
//
// 1. the BACK gesture
//    Android: the system back button or a predictive back gesture
//    iOS: a swipe from the left edge, and no back button
//    Flutter: PopScope for both, but a predictive back needs
//    canPop: false and onPopInvokedWithResult
PopScope(
  canPop: false,                        // handle it yourself
  onPopInvokedWithResult: (didPop, result) async {
    if (didPop) return;
    final confirmed = await _confirmDiscard();
    if (confirmed) {
      _controller.pop();                 // now allow it
    }
  },
  child: Scaffold(...),
)

// 2. the APP BAR
//    iOS: a large title that collapses, and a back chevron
//    Android: a small title, a hamburger, and a FAB
SliverAppBar.large(title: Text(l10n.appTitle))    // iOS style
SliverAppBar(title: Text(l10n.appTitle))          // Android style

// 3. DIALOGS
//    iOS: a sheet from the bottom, with a grab handle
//    Android: a centred dialog
showModalBottomSheet(...)   // iOS
AlertDialog(...)            // Android
// or CupertinoAlertDialog for iOS, which has different buttons

// 4. the TAB BAR
//    iOS: a translucent bar with a hairline
//    Android: a solid bar, often with a top border
CupertinoTabScaffold(...)   // iOS
NavigationBar(...)          // Material

// 5. ICONS
//    iOS: SF Symbols, if you use CupertinoIcons
//    Android: Material icons
//    using Icons.* on iOS is acceptable, but it looks Android-ish

// 6. PULL TO REFRESH
//    iOS: a rubber-band overscroll
//    Android: a spinner that appears at the top
RefreshIndicator(...)   // both, with the right physics

// 7. SHARING
Share.share(...)   // the platform share sheet on both

// WHEN TO ADAPT, and WHEN NOT TO
// ADAPT: the navigation, the platform conventions, the
//         accessibility settings, the input conventions
// DO NOT ADAPT: the information architecture, the visual
//         identity, or the data model. An app that is two
//         different apps is worse than one that is slightly
//         off-convention.
// DETECTING THE PLATFORM, for the cases you must
import 'dart:io' show Platform;

final isIOS = !kIsWeb && Platform.isIOS;
final isAndroid = !kIsWeb && Platform.isAndroid;

TargetPlatform get platform {
  if (kIsWeb) return TargetPlatform.android;    // the browser default
  return switch (defaultTargetPlatform) {
    TargetPlatform.iOS => TargetPlatform.iOS,
    TargetPlatform.android => TargetPlatform.android,
    TargetPlatform.macOS => TargetPlatform.macOS,
    _ => TargetPlatform.linux,
  };
}

// and for the adaptive widgets
LayoutBuilder(
  builder: (context, constraints) {
    return constraints.maxWidth > 600
        ? const WideLayout()
        : const NarrowLayout();
  },
);

// or, with the window size class
final width = MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).width;
final isTablet = width >= 600;

// the test override, so you can test both
testWidgets('the wide layout on a tablet', (tester) async {
  tester.view.physicalSize = const Size(1200, 800);
  tester.view.devicePixelRatio = 1.0;
  addTearDown(tester.view.reset);
  await tester.pumpWidget(const MyApp());
  expect(find.byType(WideLayout), findsOneWidget);
});

11 · Data, Storage and Sync

11.1 Choosing a store11.2 SharedPreferences and the small stuff11.3 Secure storage11.4 Drift, a real SQL database11.5 Hive and Isar11.6 Offline-first architecture11.7 Sync and conflict resolution11.8 Migrations

Storage is where a mobile app earns or loses user trust. The wrong choice here is expensive to change later, so this chapter is mostly about deciding correctly.

11.1 Choosing a store

The four questions that decide, and the honest answer

Choosing a local store is usually discussed as a feature comparison, and it is better decided by four questions that any store will answer differently. What is the shape of the data? A key-value store is right for preferences and wrong for anything relational; a relational store is right for anything you would query and wrong for a blob. How much of it? A key-value store backed by a file is fine for kilobytes and wrong for tens of megabytes, because reading it means reading the file. Does it need to be queried? A filter over a thousand items in memory is fine; a filter over a million requires an index, and an index requires a store that has one. And does it need to be shared between processes? A store opened by two processes needs locking, and that is a feature not every store has. Then the four categories, and each is right for a different question. Shared preferences is a key-value store for a handful of small values, and it is the right answer for a theme choice, a last-opened tab and a flag — and the wrong answer for anything that grows. A secure store is for values that must not be readable on a rooted device, which in practice means an access token and a refresh token, and nothing else. A relational store is a real database with a real query language, and it is the right answer the moment the data has relationships or a non-trivial query. And a document or object store — a serialised map, a box store — is right for data that is read as a whole and written as a whole, which is less common than people assume and is a real pattern for a cache. Then the honest answer for a serious application, which is that a relational store is the default and the alternatives are specialisations of it. The reason is that every application eventually has a query it cannot express as a filter over a map, and the moment it does, the migration is not incremental: it is a rewrite of the data layer, its queries and its tests. Adopting the relational store early costs a little ceremony; adopting it late costs the data layer. And the two exceptions worth naming, because they are the cases where a lighter store is genuinely correct. A cache of server data with a single key — a downloaded bundle, a prefetched catalogue — is not application state and does not belong in the same store as it. And an application with a small, fixed schema and no growth — a configuration, a set of flags, a watchlist of ten symbols — will never need a query language and should not pay for one.

/* Four questions. */
const QUESTIONS = [
  { q: 'WHAT IS the SHAPE of the DATA?',
    detail: 'A KEY-VALUE STORE IS RIGHT for PREFERENCES and WRONG for ANYTHING RELATIONAL',
    and: 'A RELATIONAL STORE IS RIGHT for ANYTHING YOU WOULD QUERY and WRONG for A BLOB' },
  { q: 'HOW MUCH of IT?',
    detail: 'A KEY-VALUE STORE BACKED BY A FILE IS FINE FOR KILOBYTES and WRONG FOR TENS OF MEGABYTES',
    because: 'READING IT MEANS READING the FILE' },
  { q: 'DOES IT NEED TO BE QUERIED?',
    detail: 'A FILTER OVER A THOUSAND ITEMS IN MEMORY IS FINE',
    and: 'A FILTER OVER A MILLION REQUIRES AN INDEX, and AN INDEX REQUIRES A STORE THAT HAS ONE' },
  { q: 'DOES IT NEED TO BE SHARED BETWEEN PROCESSES?',
    detail: 'A STORE OPENED BY TWO PROCESSES NEEDS LOCKING',
    and: 'which IS A FEATURE NOT EVERY STORE HAS' },
];

/* Four categories. */
const CATEGORIES = [
  { c: 'SHARED PREFERENCES', is: 'A KEY-VALUE STORE for A HANDFUL of SMALL VALUES',
    rightFor: ['a THEME CHOICE', 'A LAST-OPENED TAB', 'A FLAG'],
    wrongFor: 'ANYTHING THAT GROWS' },
  { c: 'A SECURE STORE', is: 'for VALUES THAT MUST NOT BE READABLE ON A ROOTED DEVICE',
    inPractice: ['an ACCESS TOKEN', 'A REFRESH TOKEN'],
    and: 'NOTHING ELSE' },
  { c: 'A RELATIONAL STORE', is: 'A REAL DATABASE with A REAL QUERY LANGUAGE',
    rightWhen: 'the MOMENT the DATA HAS RELATIONSHIPS or A NON-TRIVIAL QUERY' },
  { c: 'A DOCUMENT or OBJECT STORE', is: 'A SERIALISED MAP or A BOX STORE',
    rightFor: 'DATA THAT IS READ AS A WHOLE and WRITTEN AS A WHOLE',
    note: 'which IS LESS COMMON THAN PEOPLE ASSUME and IS A REAL PATTERN for A CACHE' },
];

/* The honest answer. */
const ANSWER = {
  is: 'A RELATIONAL STORE IS the DEFAULT and the ALTERNATIVES ARE SPECIALISATIONS of IT',
  why: 'EVERY APPLICATION EVENTUALLY HAS A QUERY IT CANNOT EXPRESS AS A FILTER OVER A MAP',
  migration: 'and the MOMENT IT DOES, the MIGRATION IS NOT INCREMENTAL - IT IS A REWRITE of the DATA LAYER, ITS QUERIES and ITS TESTS',
  cost: 'ADOPTING the RELATIONAL STORE EARLY COSTS A LITTLE CEREMONY; ADOPTING IT LATE COSTS the DATA LAYER',
};

/* Two exceptions. */
const EXCEPTIONS = [
  { e: 'A CACHE of SERVER DATA with A SINGLE KEY', instances: ['A DOWNLOADED BUNDLE', 'A PREFETCHED CATALOGUE'],
    why: 'it IS NOT APPLICATION STATE and DOES NOT BELONG IN the SAME STORE as IT' },
  { e: 'AN APPLICATION with A SMALL, FIXED SCHEMA and NO GROWTH', instances: ['A CONFIGURATION', 'A SET of FLAGS', 'A WATCHLIST of TEN SYMBOLS'],
    why: 'it WILL NEVER NEED A QUERY LANGUAGE and SHOULD NOT PAY FOR ONE' },
];

If you are not sure, choose drift. SQL is unfashionable and it works: the questions you will ask of a local database are SQL questions, and every one of them - a join, a filter, a sort, an aggregate - is answered by an index instead of by loading everything into memory and doing it in Dart.

// THE OPTIONS, and what each is actually for
//
// SharedPreferences        a key-value store, in a plist/XML file
//                         for: theme, locale, a small flag
//                         not for: anything large, or sensitive
//
// flutter_secure_storage  Keychain / EncryptedSharedPreferences
//                         for: tokens, keys, a biometric unlock key
//                         not for: general data
//
// Hive                     a binary document store, no schema
//                         for: cached API responses, a local doc store
//                         not for: anything relational
//
// Isar                    a fast document database, with queries
//                         for: a large object graph, offline-first
//
// Drift                    SQLite with a type-safe Dart API,
//                         migrations and reactive queries
//                         for: relational data, anything you query
//
// sqflite                  raw SQLite
//                         for: when you need full SQL control
//
// objectbox                a fast NoSQL store, sync built in
//                         for: performance-critical local data
//
// THE DECISION
//   a handful of settings        -> SharedPreferences
//   a token                      -> flutter_secure_storage
//   a list of API objects, offline  -> Hive, Isar or Drift
//   anything you JOIN, FILTER, SORT or AGGREGATE  -> Drift
//   a complex graph of objects    -> Isar
//
// The default for a serious app: Drift. SQL is boring, it works,
// and the questions you will ask of your data are SQL questions.

11.2 SharedPreferences and the small stuff

// pubspec.yaml
//   shared_preferences: ^2.3.0

final prefs = await SharedPreferences.getInstance();

await prefs.setString('theme_mode', 'dark');
await prefs.setBool('onboarding_complete', true);
await prefs.setInt('last_opened_tab', 2);
await prefs.setDouble('font_scale', 1.0);
await prefs.setStringList('recent_searches', ['flutter', 'dart']);

// reading
final theme = prefs.getString('theme_mode') ?? 'system';
final done = prefs.getBool('onboarding_complete') ?? false;
final scale = prefs.getDouble('font_scale') ?? 1.0;

// THE TWO TRAPS
// 1. everything is cached in memory after the first read: a
//    write from another isolate is NOT visible
// 2. it is not encrypted, and it is not transactional: a crash
//    mid-write can leave a corrupt file

// A LISTENER, for a change from anywhere
prefs.addListener(() {
  // fires on any change
});

// WRAPPING IT, because a raw string key everywhere is a bug
// waiting to happen
class SettingsStore {
  SettingsStore(this._prefs);

  final SharedPreferences _prefs;

  static const _kThemeMode = 'theme_mode';
  static const _kFontScale = 'font_scale';
  static const _kOnboarded = 'onboarding_complete';

  ThemeMode get themeMode {
    return switch (_prefs.getString(_kThemeMode)) {
      'light' => ThemeMode.light,
      'dark' => ThemeMode.dark,
      _ => ThemeMode.system,
    };
  }

  Future<void> setThemeMode(ThemeMode mode) async {
    await _prefs.setString(_kThemeMode, mode.name);
  }

  double get fontScale => _prefs.getDouble(_kFontScale) ?? 1.0;

  Future<void> setFontScale(double scale) async {
    // CLAMP: an unbounded value from a settings screen is a
    // user error, and it breaks the layout
    await _prefs.setDouble(_kFontScale, scale.clamp(0.8, 2.0));
  }

  bool get onboardingComplete => _prefs.getBool(_kOnboarded) ?? false;

  Future<void> completeOnboarding() async {
    await _prefs.setBool(_kOnboarded, true);
  }
}
// WHAT NOT TO PUT IN IT
// - a list of 10,000 records: the whole file is read into
//   memory on load, and rewritten on every save
// - anything sensitive: it is a plain file in the app sandbox
// - data you need to query
// - data that must be consistent with another piece of data:
//   two prefs can disagree, and there is no transaction

// WHEN IT IS EXACTLY RIGHT
//   "has the user seen the onboarding"
//   "the chosen theme"
//   "the last tab they were on"
//   "a feature flag from a remote config"
//   "a cached access token EXPIRY time" (not the token itself)

What belongs in preferences, and what the API will not tell you

Shared preferences is the store people reach for first and the one whose failure mode is quiet enough that it survives into production. It is a key-value store with an in-memory map and a write-through to a platform file. That structure produces three behaviours that are not in its documentation. Reads are asynchronous and the first read is a disk read, so a widget that reads a preference before it has loaded gets the default and rebuilds when the real value arrives — which produces a visible flash of the wrong content on every cold start, and the fix is a loading state at the application root rather than a null check in each widget. Writes are asynchronous and are not guaranteed before the process dies, so a write issued during a state change the user is about to leave may not persist; the fix is to await the write where the user is leaving. And getAll loads everything, so a store that has accumulated preferences grows a load time that is paid on every cold start regardless of how many keys the screen reads. Then what belongs here and what does not, and the dividing line is size and sensitivity. A preference is a small value the user set and will read again in the same session or the next — a boolean, an enum, a short string, a number, a list of identifiers. Anything larger belongs in a database and anything sensitive belongs in a secure store, and the two mistakes are common in opposite directions: an application storing a cached JSON response in preferences and discovering at scale that every cold start now reads a megabyte, and an application storing a token in preferences where a rooted device can read it. Then the three things worth knowing about the API, because each has cost somebody an afternoon. Only certain types are supported — booleans, numbers, strings and lists of those — and anything else must be serialised, usually as JSON, which means the stored value is opaque and a version bump on the stored shape requires handling both shapes. There is no transactional guarantee and no ordering guarantee, so two writes issued in sequence can land in either order; if order matters, store one value rather than two. And the listener fires for any change to the store, so a listener must compare the key it cares about, because a widget that rebuilds on every preference change anywhere rebuilds whenever anything anywhere changes. Then the two practices, and both are about the failure that is invisible. Give every preference a typed accessor — a function that reads one key with its type and its default in one place — so the default is written down once and a value that is missing or the wrong type is handled in one place rather than at each call site. And log the preference count and the file size in development, because the growth of this store is invisible until it is large, and the only way to notice is to look.

/* The structure. */
const STRUCTURE = 'A KEY-VALUE STORE with AN IN-MEMORY MAP and A WRITE-THROUGH TO A PLATFORM FILE';
const THREE_BEHAVIOURS = [
