11.3 Secure storage

What the platform gives you, and what it does not

Secure storage on a mobile platform is the Android keystore and the iOS keychain, and the framework's secure storage wraps them. Understanding what they actually provide is what makes the security decisions correct, because the answer is narrower than most people assume. An encrypted store backed by the platform keystore means the encryption key is held by the operating system, in hardware where the platform supports it, and not by your application. On Android that is a key held in a hardware-backed keystore where one exists; on iOS the keychain holds the item and the item's accessibility class controls when it can be read. What this protects against: extracting the file from the device — by backup, by a file-system dump, by an attacker with the file — and reading the contents. What it does not protect against: a rooted or jailbroken device with an application running, because the key is available to that application while it is running; a compromised operating system; and a user who is looking at their own screen. Then the four rules that follow, and each is a real requirement. Store the token, not the data it protects. An access token stored in the keystore means the rest of your application's data — a cache, a database, a preferences file — can be ordinary storage, because the thing that grants access is the protected thing; storing the token in a database and encrypting the database is a much larger problem with a much larger key. Keep the token lifetime short. A long-lived token in secure storage is still a long-lived token, and the secure-store section of the API chapter's argument about tokens applies: minutes for the access token, a refresh token that can be revoked. Exclude the platform's backup where the platform offers the choice, because a backup that contains the encrypted file is a backup whose keychain item may not travel with it, and the result is a token that has silently stopped working after a restore. And never log the value, which is the one that survives review because a log statement added during debugging is rarely removed. Then the two things that are not security but are the most common failures, and both produce an authentication problem that looks like a server problem. Clearing the store on sign-out is not enough — a token can also live in memory, in a header cache, in a log, and in a cookie, and signing out that only clears the store leaves a usable credential in the process. And a token stored per-install but a session on the server means a device that is wiped and restored from a backup may present a token the server has revoked, producing a sign-in loop whose cause is not visible from either side. Then the two practices, and each is specific. Have one function that reads the token and one that writes it, so the secure store is touched in exactly two places and every other part of the application receives the token as an argument — which makes the secure surface auditable by reading two functions. And test sign-in, sign-out and restore-from-backup, because the third is the one that is never tested and is the one that produces the support ticket.

/* What the platform provides. */
const PROVIDES = {
  is: 'the ANDROID KEYSTORE and the iOS KEYCHAIN',
  mechanism: 'AN ENCRYPTED STORE BACKED BY the PLATFORM KEYSTORE MEANS the ENCRYPTION KEY IS HELD BY the OPERATING SYSTEM, IN HARDWARE WHERE the PLATFORM SUPPORTS IT, and NOT BY YOUR APPLICATION',
  android: 'A KEY HELD IN A HARDWARE-BACKED KEYSTORE WHERE ONE EXISTS',
  ios: 'the KEYCHAIN HOLDS the ITEM and THE ITEMS ACCESSIBILITY CLASS CONTROLS WHEN IT CAN BE READ',
};
const PROTECTS = 'EXTRACTING the FILE FROM the DEVICE - BY BACKUP, BY A FILE-SYSTEM DUMP, BY AN ATTACKER WITH the FILE - and READING the CONTENTS';
const DOES_NOT_PROTECT = [
  'A ROOTED or JAILBROKEN DEVICE WITH AN APPLICATION RUNNING, BECAUSE the KEY IS AVAILABLE TO THAT APPLICATION WHILE IT IS RUNNING',
  'A COMPROMISED OPERATING SYSTEM',
  'A USER WHO IS LOOKING AT THEIR OWN SCREEN',
];

/* Four rules. */
const RULES = [

    detail: 'AN ACCESS TOKEN STORED IN the KEYSTORE MEANS the REST of YOUR APPLICATIONS DATA - A CACHE, A DATABASE, A PREFERENCES FILE - CAN BE ORDINARY STORAGE',
    because: 'the THING THAT GRANTS ACCESS IS the PROTECTED THING',

  { r: 'KEEP the TOKEN LIFETIME SHORT',

    consequence: 'and SIGNING OUT THAT ONLY CLEARS the STORE LEAVES A USABLE CREDENTIAL IN the PROCESS' },

/* Two practices. */

    and: 'which MAKES the SECURE SURFACE AUDITABLE BY READING TWO FUNCTIONS' },

Move every token to secure storage before you ship, not after a security review asks. A refresh token in SharedPreferences is plain text inside the app sandbox, readable from a rooted device or a backup, and it is the single most common way app credentials leak.

// pubspec.yaml
//   flutter_secure_storage: ^9.2.0

final storage = FlutterSecureStorage(
  aOptions: const AndroidOptions(encryptedSharedPreferences: true),
  iOptions: const IOSOptions(accessibility: KeychainAccessibility.first_unlock),
);

await storage.write(key: 'access_token', value: token);
await storage.read(key: 'access_token');
await storage.delete(key: 'access_token');
await storage.deleteAll();

// WRAPPING IT: a token store with a real API
class TokenStore {
  TokenStore(this._storage);

  final FlutterSecureStorage _storage;

  static const _accessKey = 'access_token';
  static const _refreshKey = 'refresh_token';

  Future<String?> get accessToken => _storage.read(key: _accessKey);
  Future<String?> get refreshToken => _storage.read(key: _refreshKey);

  Future<void> save({required String access, required String refresh}) async {
    await _storage.write(key: _accessKey, value: access);
    await _storage.write(key: _refreshKey, value: refresh);
  }

  Future<void> clear() async {
    await _storage.delete(key: _accessKey);
    await _storage.delete(key: _refreshKey);
  }

  // A REFRESH, with a lock so two 401s do not race
  Future<void> _refreshing = Future.value();

  Future<String?> getValidToken() async {
    final token = await accessToken;
    if (token == null) return null;
    if (!_isExpired(token)) return token;

    // serialize the refresh: a second 401 waits
    return _refreshing.then((_) => _doRefresh());
  }
}
// THE CAVEATS
// 1. on Android it is EncryptedSharedPreferences, which means a
//    known issue on some OEM builds where the keystore is reset
//    on app update. Test an upgrade on a low-end device.
// 2. reading the keychain prompts for Face ID on iOS if you set
//    accessibility to userPresence. first_unlock (the default)
//    reads it silently, which is what an app usually wants.
// 3. a BACKUP can restore the keychain WITHOUT the keystore
//    key, making the data unreadable. Disable the backup, or
//    handle the read failure gracefully.
// 4. it is SLOW on Android: a few milliseconds per read. Do not
//    read it in build.

// iOS: exclude from the backup for a token you can re-fetch
// (this requires a small platform channel, see chapter 13)

11.4 Drift, a real SQL database

// pubspec.yaml
//   drift: ^2.20.0
//   drift_dev: ^2.20.0
//   sqlite3_flutter_libs: ^0.5.0
//   path_provider: ^2.1.0
//   path: ^1.8.0

// THE TABLE, in Dart, with a real type system
import 'package:drift/drift.dart';

class Entries extends Table {
  IntColumn get id => integer().autoIncrement()();
  TextColumn get title => text().withLength(min: 1, max: 200)();
  TextColumn get body => text().withDefault(const Constant(''))();
  TextColumn get photoPath => text().nullable()();
  DateTimeColumn get createdAt => dateTime()();
  DateTimeColumn get updatedAt => dateTime()();
  DateTimeColumn get syncedAt => dateTime().nullable()();
  IntColumn get serverVersion => integer().withDefault(const Constant(0))();
  BoolColumn get archived => boolean().withDefault(const Constant(false))();
  BoolColumn get pinned => boolean().withDefault(const Constant(false))();

  // an INDEX on the column you filter by, or every query scans
  @override
  List<Set<Column>> get uniqueKeys => [{id}];
}

// a JOIN, as a typed class
class EntryWithMeta extends Entry {
  final int photoCount;
  final int commentCount;

  EntryWithMeta({
    required super.id,
    required super.title,
    // ...every Entry field
    required this.photoCount,
    required this.commentCount,
  });
}

// THE DATABASE
@DriftDatabase(tables: [Entries, Photos, Comments], daos: [EntriesDao])
class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {
  AppDatabase() : super(_openConnection());
  AppDatabase.forTesting(super.executor);

  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 3;

  @override
  MigrationStrategy get migration => MigrationStrategy(
    onCreate: (m) async => m.createAll(),
    onUpgrade: (m, from, to) async {
      if (from < 2) {
        await m.addColumn(entries, entries.archived);
      }
      if (from < 3) {
        // a data migration, not just a schema one
        await customStatement('UPDATE entries SET pinned = 0');
        await m.createIndex('idx_entries_updated', entries, ['updatedAt']);
      }
    },
  );
}

LazyDatabase _openConnection() {
  return LazyDatabase(() async {
    final dir = await getApplicationDocumentsDirectory();
    final file = File(p.join(dir.path, 'fieldnotes.sqlite'));
    return NativeDatabase.createInBackground(file);
  });
}

// run: dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
// QUERIES, which is why you chose SQL
@DriftAccessor(tables: [Entries, Photos])
class EntriesDao extends DatabaseAccessor<AppDatabase> with _$EntriesDaoMixin {
  EntriesDao(super.db);

  // a simple select
  Future<List<Entry>> activeEntries() {
    return (select(entries)..where((e) => e.archived.equals(false)))
        .orderBy([(e) => OrderingTerm.desc(e.updatedAt)])
        .get();
  }

  // a JOIN, typed
  Future<List<EntryWithMeta>> entriesWithCounts() {
    final photoCount = photos.id.count();
    final commentCount = comments.id.count();

    final query = select(entries).join([
      leftOuterJoin(photos, photos.entryId.equalsExp(entries.id)),
      leftOuterJoin(comments, comments.entryId.equalsExp(entries.id)),
    ]);

    query
      ..addColumns([photoCount, commentCount])
      ..groupBy([entries.id])
      ..orderBy([OrderingTerm.desc(entries.updatedAt)]);

    final rows = await query.get();
    return rows
        .map((row) => EntryWithMeta(
              id: row.readTable(entries).id,
              title: row.readTable(entries).title,
              // ...every field
              photoCount: row.read(photoCount) ?? 0,
              commentCount: row.read(commentCount) ?? 0,
            ))
        .toList();
  }

  // a transaction, for a multi-statement change
  Future<void> archiveWithDelete(int entryId) async {
    await transaction(() async {
      await (update(entries)..where((e) => e.id.equals(entryId))).write(
        const EntriesCompanion(archived: Value(true)),
      );
      await (delete(photos)..where((p) => p.entryId.equals(entryId))).go();
    });
  }

  // FTS, for search
  Future<List<Entry>> search(String query) {
    return customSelect(
      'SELECT * FROM entries WHERE body MATCH ?1 OR title MATCH ?1',
      variables: [Variable(query)],
      readsFrom: {entries},
    ).get();
  }
}
// REACTIVE QUERIES: the feature that justifies Drift
// a watch stream that emits whenever the underlying data changes,
// so a list updates after a write, from anywhere, with no manual
// refresh
Stream<List<Entry>> watchActiveEntries() {
  return (select(entries)..where((e) => e.archived.equals(false)))
      .watch();
}

// in a Riverpod provider
final entriesProvider = StreamProvider<List<Entry>>((ref) {
  final db = ref.watch(databaseProvider);
  return db.entriesDao.watchActiveEntries();
});

// in the widget: it updates automatically after any write
final entries = ref.watch(entriesProvider);
final list = entries.valueOrNull ?? const [];

// WRITES, which update every watcher automatically
Future<int> create(EntriesCompanion entry) => into(entries).insert(entry);
Future<bool> updateEntry(int id, EntriesCompanion data) {
  return (update(entries)..where((e) => e.id.equals(id))).write(data).then((n) => n > 0);
}
Future<int> deleteEntry(int id) {
  return (delete(entries)..where((e) => e.id.equals(id))).go();
}
Future<int> softDelete(int id) {
  return (update(entries)..where((e) => e.id.equals(id)))
      .write(const EntriesCompanion(archived: Value(true)));
}

// AND the isolate part: heavy queries run off the main thread
// by default with NativeDatabase.createInBackground
Future<List<Entry>> heavyQuery() => db.entriesDao.allWithRelations();

Why a real database, and what the abstraction actually costs

A relational store in a Flutter application means a real SQLite engine, a schema, migrations and a query API — and the reason to accept that cost is that it is the only option that keeps answering questions as the data grows. The three capabilities that make it different from a serialised map are the ones that matter as the application ages. It queries without loading. A query runs in the database, so a filter or an aggregate over a million rows returns the answer rather than a million rows to filter in Dart — and this is not an optimisation, it is the difference between the query working and not working. It enforces a schema. The store knows each table's columns and types, so a row written with a field the column does not have is an error rather than a silent key, and a value of the wrong type is an error rather than a wrong number. And it is transactional. Several writes either all land or none do, which is what makes a multi-table update correct without the compensation machinery the distributed-systems chapter described. Then the three costs, and each is a real thing you are choosing to accept. Asynchronous setup. The store must be opened before it can be used, and every repository that touches it must handle the not-yet-open case — which is why the opening is usually done once at startup and awaited rather than lazily per repository. Migrations are not optional and are not free. The schema is versioned, and each release that changes it must supply the migration, and a migration that has not been tested against the version it migrates from is the mechanism behind the "works on new installs" report — an application that has never had the older data cannot exercise the migration at all. And the query API is a layer to learn. A code-generated typed layer over the schema gives compile-time checking of query results, and it is worth the setup cost for a non-trivial schema, but it is a layer. Then the four practices that make it maintainable, and each addresses a specific failure. Put the schema in one place and never write SQL in a screen. Queries live in a data-access object next to the schema; a screen that contains SQL is a screen that will be rewritten when the schema changes, and there will be forty of them. Test the migrations, by creating a database at version n with representative data and running the migrations forward to the current version — a migration test is a few lines and it is the only thing standing between a schema change and a corrupt install. Never block the UI thread on a query, and the framework's default for opening a database is to do so in the background for exactly this reason; a query that runs on the UI thread will eventually run on a large table and freeze a frame. And index what you filter and sort by, because a full scan over a table that grows is the performance cliff the database-design chapter describes, and an index is cheap to add at the schema level and expensive to retrofit to a shipped schema. Then the two practices that are about the boundary. Have one store for the whole application, because two stores mean two transactions that cannot be joined and two places where the same data can diverge. And keep the store out of the widget tree, — open it at the root, hand repositories to the widgets, and let no widget know the database exists, which is the same dependency-direction argument as the project-structure section.

/* The three capabilities that matter as the application ages. */
const CAPABILITIES = [

  { p: 'HAVE ONE STORE FOR the WHOLE APPLICATION', why: 'BECAUSE TWO STORES MEAN TWO TRANSACTIONS THAT CANNOT BE JOINED and TWO PLACES WHERE the SAME DATA CAN DIVERGE' },
  { p: 'KEEP the STORE OUT of the WIDGET TREE',
    how: ['OPEN IT AT the ROOT', 'HAND REPOSITORIES TO the WIDGETS', 'and LET NO WIDGET KNOW the DATABASE EXISTS'],
    connects: 'which IS the SAME DEPENDENCY-DIRECTION ARGUMENT as the PROJECT-STRUCTURE SECTION' },
];

11.5 Hive and Isar

// HIVE: a binary key-value document store. No schema, no SQL.
// good for: cached API responses, a settings blob, offline drafts
// not for: anything you need to query

// pubspec.yaml
//   hive: ^2.2.3
//   hive_flutter: ^1.1.0
//   hive_generator: ^2.0.1

class EntryAdapter extends TypeAdapter<Entry> {
  @override
  final int typeId = 1;

  @override
  Entry read(BinaryReader reader) {
    return Entry(
      id: reader.readInt(),
      title: reader.readString(),
      body: reader.readString(),
      createdAt: DateTime.fromMillisecondsSinceEpoch(reader.readInt()),
    );
  }

  @override
  void write(BinaryWriter writer, Entry obj) {
    writer
      ..writeInt(obj.id)
      ..writeString(obj.title)
      ..writeString(obj.body)
      ..writeInt(obj.createdAt.millisecondsSinceEpoch);
  }
}

// usage
final box = await Hive.openBox<Entry>('entries');
await box.put(entry.id, entry);
final all = box.values.toList();
final one = box.get(123);
await box.delete(123);
await box.clear();
await box.compact();     // reclaim space after many deletes

// the reactive part
box.watch().listen((event) => print('changed at ${event.key}'));

// a TYPE ADAPTER that fails after a schema change is the main
// gotcha: version your typeIds, never reuse one, and plan for
// a migration
// ISAR: a fast document database with a query builder
// pubspec.yaml
//   isar: ^3.1.0+1
//   isar_flutter_libs: ^3.1.0+1
//   isar_generator: ^3.1.0+1

@collection
class Entry {
  Id id = Isar.autoIncrement;

  @Index(type: IndexType.value)
  late String title;

  late String body;
  late DateTime createdAt;
  late DateTime updatedAt;
  DateTime? syncedAt;
  bool archived = false;

  @Index(composite: [CompositeIndex('updatedAt')])
  late List<String> tags;
}

// queries, which is where Isar is better than Hive
final entries = isar.entries
    .filter()
    .archivedEqualTo(false)
    .sortByUpdatedAtDesc()
    .limit(50)
    .findAll();

// a reactive query
isar.entries.watchLazy().listen((_) => load());

// full-text search
final results = await isar.entries
    .filter()
    .bodyContains('flutter', caseSensitive: false)
    .findAll();

// WHEN TO CHOOSE ISAR OVER DRIFT
// + simpler setup, and it is faster for document workloads
// + less code for a flat object graph
// - a single-writer model: you cannot have two write
//   transactions at once, which complicates a sync engine
// - less mature migration story
// - the ecosystem is smaller

Object stores, and the question they answer

Document and object stores sit between preferences and a database, and the question they answer is narrow enough to state: do you read the data as a whole and write it as a whole? If yes, a serialised object store is the right tool and is simpler than a database by an order of magnitude. If no — if you filter, sort, join or query — it is the wrong tool, because every query becomes a read of everything followed by a filter in Dart. Then what the family actually is, and the difference between the members is the API surface rather than the storage. A key-value object store holds arbitrary serialisable values under string keys, with typed getters that do the cast for you, so a value written as a map and read as a model either works or throws a clear type error. A box store adds an index — you declare which fields are indexed and the store maintains them, so a query filters by an indexed field without reading everything. An Isar-style store adds a query builder, transactions and reactive queries, so a query can re-run automatically when the data changes, which is the capability that makes a store usable as application state rather than only as a cache. And all of them are single-file or single-directory stores with no separate server, which is the property that makes them easy to adopt and easy to abandon. Then the three costs, and each is the reason a project outgrows one. No cross-object constraints. Nothing stops two objects from disagreeing about a relationship, so an invariant that a foreign key would enforce must be enforced in code, and it will not always be. No transactions across objects, or only in the members that have them, so a multi-object update can leave a partially applied state — which is the compensating-transaction problem the distributed-systems chapter described, arriving locally. And the data is opaque to the store, which means there is no way to ask it "how many entries are there" without reading them, so any aggregate is computed in Dart over everything. Then the three questions that decide between an object store and a relational one, and the second is the decisive one. How many objects will there be? Tens or hundreds is fine in either; tens of thousands in an object store means every query reads everything and every read is a parse. Will you ever need a query the store cannot express? — a join, an aggregate, a filter across two fields. If the answer is probably, choose the database, because the migration is a rewrite. And does the data have a schema you control? An object store with untyped maps is convenient until the day you change a field's type and find three hundred stored objects with the old shape and no migration story. Then the two things worth knowing regardless of the choice, and both are about what happens when the shape changes. A serialised object has a version in it, written by the serialiser or by your code, and a reader that sees an unknown version must handle it rather than crash — because an application that has shipped and then changes a stored shape will meet objects written by the previous version on the same device. And the store is a cache of your code's expectations, which means a development build that writes fields a production build does not expect will fail on the user's device rather than in your test; wiping the store on a schema mismatch is the pragmatic answer and is better than a crash.

/* The question. */
const QUESTION = 'DO YOU READ the DATA AS A WHOLE and WRITE IT AS A WHOLE?';
const YES = 'IF YES, A SERIALISED OBJECT STORE IS the RIGHT TOOL and IS SIMPLER THAN A DATABASE BY AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE';
const NO = 'IF NO - IF YOU FILTER, SORT, JOIN or QUERY - it IS the WRONG TOOL, BECAUSE EVERY QUERY BECOMES A READ of EVERYTHING FOLLOWED BY A FILTER IN DART';

11.6 Offline-first architecture

The three states, and the discipline that makes it work

Offline-first is a claim about what the application does when the network is not there, and the claim is meaningless unless the application has three named states rather than a data field and a spinner. The three are: local data, a synchronisation status, and a pending-change queue. Most offline bugs are really one of the three being absent — an application with local data and a spinner has no queue and will lose writes; an application with a queue and no status will silently fail to synchronise. Then the four rules, and each is a decision rather than a technique. Local is the source of truth for the user, the server is the source of truth for the truth. A read comes from the local store and is shown immediately; a write goes to the local store and is shown immediately; both then attempt to reach the server. This is the reverse of the naive design and it is the only one that makes an application usable on a train. Every write carries a stable local identifier. Without one the server cannot tell a retried write from a new one, and a write that is retried after a response was lost becomes a duplicate — the idempotency requirement from the API chapter, arriving here because offline writes are retried by definition. Conflicts are resolved by a rule you chose in advance, and the three possibilities are last-write-wins by timestamp, server-wins, or a merge the application defines; the first is the default and it is wrong whenever two devices edit the same field, and choosing "the server wins" for a collaborative application means a user's offline edit disappears without telling them. And the queue is durable. A queue held in memory is a queue that loses every pending write when the process is killed, which on a phone happens constantly, so the queue must be in the same durable store as the data. Then the three things that make it hard, and each is a distinct problem. Reads become stale rather than wrong. An application that is offline-first will show data that is out of date and has no way to know how out of date, so the interface must be able to say "as of" — and an application that shows stale data with no indication is worse than one that fails visibly. Deletes are hard. A record deleted on one device and edited on another: the server has to decide, and a tombstone with a timestamp is the usual mechanism, because a delete that is only a missing row is indistinguishable from data that has not yet arrived. And the application has to work offline on first launch, which is the case that catches everything: a device that has never synced has no data, and an application whose entire state comes from the server has nothing to show and no way to authenticate. Then the two practices, and each is cheap and each has caught a real class of bug. Make the network failure a normal path in development, by actually switching the network off rather than by simulating an error response — the difference between the two is that one exercises the queue and the other does not. And log every synchronisation cycle with what it sent and what it received, because the failure of an offline-first application is nearly always a specific write that was never sent or was sent twice, and without the log the question "why did my change not appear" cannot be answered.

/* Three states. */
const STATES = ['LOCAL DATA', 'A SYNCHRONISATION STATUS', 'and A PENDING-CHANGE QUEUE'];
const CLAIM = 'OFFLINE-FIRST IS A CLAIM about WHAT the APPLICATION DOES WHEN the NETWORK IS NOT THERE';
const CLAIM_MEANINGLESS_WITHOUT = 'THE CLAIM IS MEANINGLESS UNLESS the APPLICATION HAS THREE NAMED STATES rather than A DATA FIELD and A SPINNER';
const BUGS = 'MOST OFFLINE BUGS ARE REALLY ONE of the THREE BEING ABSENT - AN APPLICATION WITH LOCAL DATA and A SPINNER HAS NO QUEUE and WILL LOSE WRITES; AN APPLICATION WITH A QUEUE and NO STATUS WILL SILENTLY FAIL to SYNCHRONISE';

Design the sync engine around the assumption that it will be interrupted. The outbox pattern exists because a write must not depend on the network being available at the moment the user makes it - and because a partially drained queue must be resumable after the process is killed.

// THREE LEVELS, and they are not all equal
//
// 1. OFFLINE-CAPABLE: read from the cache, write to the network
//    the simple case, and it is fine for most apps
//    the cache is a cache, and it may be stale
//
// 2. OFFLINE-FIRST: the local database is the source of truth,
//    and the network is a sync partner
//    correct for anything a user would be upset to lose
//
// 3. LOCAL-FIRST WITH FULL CONFLICT RESOLUTION: like 2, plus a
//    real answer for concurrent edits
//    needed for collaborative apps

// THE ARCHITECTURE, for level 2
//
//   UI
//    |  watches
//    v
//   Repository        the ONLY thing the UI talks to
//    |                 it owns the offline-first logic
//    +--> LocalDb     the source of truth
//    +--> RemoteApi   the sync partner
//
// the repository, which is where the policy lives
class EntryRepository {
  EntryRepository({required this._db, required this._api, required this._connectivity});

  final AppDatabase _db;
  final ApiClient _api;
  final Connectivity _connectivity;

  // 1. READ: always from the database
  Stream<List<Entry>> watchAll() => _db.entriesDao.watchActiveEntries();

  // 2. WRITE: local first, sync later
  Future<Entry> create(EntriesCompanion draft) async {
    // write locally and immediately
    final id = await _db.entriesDao.create(draft);
    // queue the sync
    await _db.outboxDao.enqueue(OutboxEntry(
      entity: 'entry',
      id: id,
      op: 'create',
      payload: jsonEncode(draft.toJson()),
      queuedAt: DateTime.now(),
    ));
    // try now, if we can
    unawaited(syncIfConnected());
    return (await _db.entriesDao.byId(id))!;
  }

  // 3. SYNC: the outbox, drained in order
  Future<SyncResult> syncIfConnected() async {
    if (!_connectivity.isOnline) return SyncResult.skipped('offline');
    return _drainOutbox().then((_) => _pullChanges()).then((_) => SyncResult.ok());
  }

  Future<void> _drainOutbox() async {
    final queue = await _db.outboxDao.pending();
    for (final job in queue) {
      try {
        switch (job.op) {
          case 'create':
            final remote = await _api.createEntry(jsonDecode(job.payload));
            await _db.entriesDao.markSynced(job.id, remote.serverVersion);
          case 'update':
            final remote = await _api.updateEntry(job.id, jsonDecode(job.payload));
            await _db.entriesDao.markSynced(job.id, remote.serverVersion);
          case 'delete':
            await _api.deleteEntry(job.id);
            await _db.entriesDao.hardDelete(job.id);
        }
        await _db.outboxDao.remove(job.opId);
      } on ConflictException catch (e) {
        await _resolveConflict(job, e.server);
      } on ClientException {
        // a 4xx: our request is wrong. retrying will not help
        await _db.outboxDao.quarantine(job);
        await _db.outboxDao.remove(job.opId);
      } catch (_) {
        // a network error or a 5xx: STOP, and keep the order
        return;
      }
    }
  }

  // 4. PULL: get what changed, incrementally
  Future<void> _pullChanges() async {
    final cursor = await _db.metaDao.getInt('sync_cursor') ?? 0;
    final page = await _api.changes(since: cursor, limit: 200);

    for (final remote in page.records) {
      // do not overwrite a local edit that has not synced yet
      final local = await _db.entriesDao.byId(remote.id);
      if (local != null && local.syncedAt == null) continue;

      await _db.entriesDao.upsert(remote.toCompanion());
    }
    await _db.metaDao.setInt('sync_cursor', page.nextCursor);
  }
}

11.7 Sync and conflict resolution

Conflicts, and why the shape of the data decides how bad they are

A conflict is two devices changing the same thing while disconnected, and the resolution mechanism matters far less than which kind of thing was changed — because the kind determines whether a conflict is a real problem or an artefact of the data model. Three kinds, in increasing order of difficulty. A counter or a set membership — an increment, a like, a tag — is commutative: adding one on both devices and taking the sum or the union gives the correct answer, and no user ever sees the conflict. A whole-value overwrite — a title, a quantity, a status — is last-write-wins, and it is acceptable when the field is small and independently meaningful and wrong when a user spent effort producing a value that is now discarded. And a shared document edited in several places — the fields of one record edited together by two people, or one record edited field by field — is the hard case, and it needs either a merge rule per field or a real merge algorithm. Then the four mechanisms, and each solves a different case. A server timestamp with last-write-wins is the default and requires nothing, and it is wrong exactly when a user is offline for a long time and their edit is overwritten by a newer edit they never saw — which is the case users describe as "the app lost my work". A field-level merge means each field carries its own timestamp and a sync merges field by field, so an edit to the title does not overwrite an edit to the quantity; this is much better and costs one extra column per field, which is why it is worth it for any field a user types. A tombstone for deletes, which the previous section described. And an operation log, where each device appends operations rather than states and the server folds them — which is the only mechanism that gets counters right and it is the mechanism behind collaborative editing, at a cost that is only worth paying when several people edit the same thing at once. Then the three things that go wrong in practice, and each is a specific mechanism. Comparing timestamps from different clocks. Device clocks are wrong, and the user can change them, so a last-write-wins on a client timestamp will apply a rule based on a clock the server cannot trust; the fix is a hybrid logical clock or a server-assigned sequence, both of which are cheap and neither of which most applications implement. Deleting a record that was edited elsewhere resurrects it, because the edit arrives after the tombstone; the fix is to include the tombstone in the merge rather than letting an edit clear it. And a queue that coalesces changes silently loses a field. If a record's local state is stored as a whole object and twenty edits become one queued write, the coalescing is only correct if the queue stores the operations; the symptom is an edit that appears on one device and never on another. Then the two practices. Make the conflict policy visible in the interface — a "changed on another device" state with a merge control — because the alternative is a silent loss of a user's work, which is the failure users report and never forgive. And test with two devices and two accounts, making the same change offline on each and reconnecting; it is the only test that exercises the merge path, and a sync implementation that has only ever been tested with one device has not been tested.

    and: 'NO USER EVER SEES the CONFLICT' },

    why: 'because the ALTERNATIVE IS A SILENT LOSS of A USERS WORK',
    and: 'which IS the FAILURE USERS REPORT and NEVER FORGIVE' },
  { p: 'TEST WITH TWO DEVICES and TWO ACCOUNTS',
    how: 'MAKING the SAME CHANGE OFFLINE ON EACH and RECONNECTING',
    why: 'IT IS THE ONLY TEST THAT EXERCISES the MERGE PATH',
    consequence: 'and A SYNC IMPLEMENTATION THAT HAS ONLY EVER BEEN TESTED WITH ONE DEVICE HAS NOT BEEN TESTED' },
];

Never use a client timestamp for conflict resolution. Phone clocks are wrong, they are not monotonic, and a device ten minutes fast makes every record look newer than it is. The server assigns the order, and the client sends the version it last saw.

// THE QUESTION: two devices edit the same record while both are
// offline. When they reconnect, whose edit wins?

// THE STRATEGIES, and each is right for a different field
//
// 1. LAST-WRITE-WINS, by timestamp
//    simple, and it is right for: a "starred" flag, a read
//    marker, anything with a single obvious owner
//    WRONG for: prose. It silently loses one user's work.
//    and it needs a trusted clock, which you do not have
//
// 2. FIELD-LEVEL MERGE
//    merge the fields that differ, flag the ones that do not
//    right for: a record with independent fields
//    Entry { title, body, tags, archived }
//    device A changed the title, device B changed the body:
//    merge both. Correct, and cheap.
//
// 3. KEEP-BOTH
//    duplicate the record, link them, let the user reconcile
//    right for: notes, comments, anything prose-shaped
//    and it is the only strategy that never loses work
//
// 4. OPERATIONAL TRANSFORMATION or CRDT
//    the correct answer for real-time collaboration
//    a very large amount of machinery for most apps

// THE IMPLEMENTATION, for field-level with keep-both for prose
class SyncMerger {
  static MergeResult merge({
    required Entry local,
    required EntryServer remote,
    required List<String> locallyChangedFields,
  }) {
    // 1. fields nobody touched locally: take the server's
    final merged = remote.toLocal();

    // 2. fields only we changed: keep ours
    for (final field in locallyChangedFields) {
      merged.setField(field, local.field(field));
    }

    // 3. fields BOTH changed: this is the conflict
    final conflicts = <String>[];
    for (final field in locallyChangedFields) {
      if (remote.field(field) != local.field(field) && remote.wasChangedBy(field)) {
        conflicts.add(field);
      }
    }

    if (conflicts.isEmpty) {
      return MergeResult(merged, conflicts: const []);
    }

    // 4. resolve per field type
    for (final field in conflicts) {
      if (PROSE_FIELDS.contains(field)) {
        // keep BOTH: a copy, and the original stays
        _createConflictCopy(local, conflicts);
        continue;
      }
      if (BOOLEAN_FIELDS.contains(field)) {
        // for a flag, OR is usually right: a starred item that
        // one device starred is starred
        merged.setField(field, true);
        continue;
      }
      // for anything else: keep the local one and flag it
      _reportConflict(local, field);
    }

    return MergeResult(merged, conflicts: conflicts);
  }

  static const _proseFields = {'body', 'title'};
  static const _booleanFields = {'archived', 'pinned'};
}

// THE SERVER CONTRACT that makes this work
// it needs to tell you WHAT it changed, and WHO changed it,
// per field, since a cursor
class EntryServer {
  final int id;
  final String title;
  final String body;
  final int serverVersion;
  final Map<String, int> fieldUpdatedAt;    // field -> timestamp
  final Map<String, String> fieldUpdatedBy;  // field -> deviceId
  final DateTime updatedAt;
}

// GET /entries/changes?since=<cursor>&limit=200
// {
//   "records": [ ... ],
//   "deleted": [123, 456],
//   "nextCursor": "1730000000:42"
// }
// the cursor must be a SERVER value, not a client timestamp:
// client clocks are wrong, and they are not monotonic
// WHEN TO SYNC
// 1. on app start
// 2. on app resume (from the background)
// 3. on connectivity regained
// 4. on a timer, as a floor: every 5 minutes when foregrounded
// 5. after a local write, if online
// 6. on a pull-to-refresh, always

// the trigger set, done properly
class SyncScheduler {
  SyncScheduler({required this._repository, required this._connectivity});

  final EntryRepository _repository;
  final Connectivity _connectivity;
  final List<StreamSubscription> _subs = [];
  Timer? _timer;

  void start() {
    // 1. connectivity
    _subs.add(_connectivity.onChange.listen((online) {
      if (online) unawaited(_repository.syncIfConnected());
    }));

    // 2. app lifecycle
    _subs.add(AppLifecycleListener(
      onResume: () => unawaited(_repository.syncIfConnected()),
    ).onDispose);

    // 3. a floor, so a device that stays online still syncs
    _timer = Timer.periodic(const Duration(minutes: 5), (_) {
      if (_connectivity.isOnline) unawaited(_repository.syncIfConnected());
    });

    // 4. once at start
    unawaited(_repository.syncIfConnected());
  }

  void dispose() {
    for (final sub in _subs) {
      sub.cancel();
    }
    _timer?.cancel();
  }
}

// BACKGROUND SYNC, for when the app is closed
// see chapter 14: workmanager on Android, BGTaskScheduler on iOS,
// and neither is reliable, so the source of truth is local
// THE BUGS THAT ACTUALLY HAPPEN
//
// 1. a lost update, from the outbox draining out of order
//    fix: sort by queuedAt, and STOP on a failure
//
// 2. an infinite sync loop: a sync writes, which triggers a
//    sync, which writes...
//    fix: the writes from a sync must not enqueue, and the cursor
//    must advance past what you just applied
//
// 3. a duplicate record: the create succeeded, the response was
//    lost, and the retry created a second one
//    fix: a client-generated idempotency key, sent on the create
//    POST /entries { "clientId": "uuid", ... }
//    and the server returns the existing record if it has seen it
//
// 4. a clock-skew disaster: a device's clock is 10 minutes fast,
//    so every "last modified" is in the future
//    fix: never use a client timestamp for conflict resolution.
//    the server assigns the order
//
// 5. a huge outbox after a long offline period
//    fix: coalesce. 20 queued updates to one record become ONE
//    that reflects the final state

11.8 Migrations

Migrations, and the four rules that make them safe

A migration is a transformation of a schema, and the reason it deserves its own discipline is that it is the one piece of code that runs on data you did not create and cannot see. A schema has a version, stored in the database itself, and on opening, the store compares the stored version with the version the code expects and applies every migration between them in order. That mechanism is simple; the four rules are what make it safe. A migration must be forward-only and must never be edited once shipped. A user who installed version three has already run migrations one and two; changing what migration two does means their database has been through something the new code does not expect. The corollary is that a mistake in a shipped migration cannot be fixed by editing it — it needs a new migration that corrects it, which is uncomfortable and correct. A migration must be written against the data that exists, not the data you expect. The dangerous cases are the nullable column that someone wrote a value into anyway, the column that was optional in version one and is required in version three, and the table that was renamed but whose old name exists on some devices because the rename shipped in a release that was withdrawn before reaching everyone. A migration must not lose data, and a rename must be a rename. Dropping and re-adding a column to change its type silently discards every value in it, which is the single most common destructive migration and the one most often written by someone who has never had to run it against a populated database. And a migration must be fast, because it runs on application start. A migration that rewrites a million rows blocks the first launch for the duration, and on a slow device that is a timeout, and the application appears broken rather than slow. Then the three things that make it testable, and each is a few lines. Test the migration from the previous version with representative data — create a database at the old version, insert a hundred realistic rows including the awkward ones, run the migration, assert both the schema and the data. The data assertion is the one that matters and the one everybody omits, because a migration that produces the right schema and the wrong data is the worst outcome: it looks correct until a user opens the record. Test the migration from every supported prior version, because the paths compose and a migration that works from two versions back may not work from four. And keep a golden fixture, — a small database file at a known version — so that adding a migration is a matter of running against the fixture and asserting, rather than constructing the historical state by hand each time. Then the two practices that are about operations rather than code. Never ship a migration that cannot be rolled back by re-installing, which in practice means never ship one that is slow enough that a user will force-quit mid-migration and be left with a half-migrated database — which is why the framework runs migrations in a transaction where it can, and why a migration that cannot run in a transaction (because it changes a table in a way that implicitly commits) is a migration to think about twice. And log the migration, — the version found, the version reached, and the duration — because the first question about any "the app is slow on launch" report is whether a migration ran, and the answer should be in the log rather than requiring a reproduction.

/* The mechanism. */
const MECHANISM = 'A SCHEMA HAS A VERSION, STORED IN the DATABASE ITSELF';
const FLOW = ['ON OPENING, the STORE COMPARES the STORED VERSION with the VERSION the CODE EXPECTS',
  'and APPLIES EVERY MIGRATION BETWEEN THEM IN ORDER'];
const WHY = 'IT IS THE ONE PIECE OF CODE THAT RUNS ON DATA YOU DID NOT CREATE and CANNOT SEE';

/* Four rules. */

Write the migration test before you need it. The version that breaks is always the one that shipped to users who cannot reinstall without losing work, and a test that starts from the old schema and checks the data survived takes twenty minutes to write.

// THE RULE: a released app can never drop its database. The
// user's data is in there. There is no "reinstall to fix it"
// for anyone who does not want to lose work.

@DriftDatabase(tables: [Entries, Photos, Comments])
class AppDatabase extends _$AppDatabase {
  @override
  int get schemaVersion => 4;

  @override
  MigrationStrategy get migration => MigrationStrategy(
    onCreate: (m) async {
      await m.createAll();
      // seed the default data
      await batch((b) => b.insertAll(entries, defaultEntries));
    },

    onUpgrade: (m, from, to) async {
      // v1 -> v2: add a column with a default
      if (from < 2) {
        await m.addColumn(entries, entries.archived);
      }

      // v2 -> v3: a data migration, not just a schema change
      if (from < 3) {
        await customStatement(
          'UPDATE entries SET pinned = 0 WHERE pinned IS NULL',
        );
      }

      // v3 -> v4: a table rename, a column split, a new index
      if (from < 4) {
        await customStatement('ALTER TABLE entries RENAME TO entries_old');
        await customStatement('''
          CREATE TABLE entries (
            id INTEGER NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
            title TEXT NOT NULL,
            body TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT \'\',
            photo_path TEXT,
            created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
            updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
            synced_at INTEGER,
            server_version INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
            archived INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
            pinned INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
          )
        ''');
        await customStatement('INSERT INTO entries SELECT * FROM entries_old');
        await customStatement('DROP TABLE entries_old');
        await m.createIndex('idx_entries_updated', entries, ['updated_at']);
      }
    },

    // 3. a failed migration: do not crash
    onDowngrade: (m, from, to) async {
      // an older app opened a newer database
      // usually: the user downgraded, or a beta build leaked
      // the SAFE answer for a released app: refuse to run
      throw StateError(
        'Cannot downgrade the database from v$from to v$to',
      );
    },

    // 4. BEFORE the first query after an upgrade
    beforeOpen: (details) async {
      if (details.wasCreated) return;
      // a good place for a data integrity check
      await customStatement('PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON');
      // and a repair, if you shipped a bug
      // await customStatement('UPDATE entries SET body = TRIM(body)');
    },
  );
}
// TESTING MIGRATIONS, which is the only way to be sure
// build_runner produces the schema snapshots:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
// -> test/.drift_schemas/v1.sql, v2.sql, v3.sql

test('migrates from v1 to the current version', () async {
  // 1. create a database at the OLD version
  final old = NativeDatabase.memory();
  // apply the v1 schema
  // (in a test, use the generated schema: SchemaVerifier)

  final verifier = SchemaVerifier(generatedSchema);

  // 2. migrate
  await verifier.startAt(1);
  await verifier.migrateAndValidate(
    database,
    // 3. verify the DATA survived, not just the schema
    onCreate: (db) async {
      await db.customStatement(
        "INSERT INTO entries (id, title, body, created_at, updated_at) "
        "VALUES (1, 'Old note', 'Content that must survive', 0, 0)",
      );
    },
    stepUp: true,
  );

  // 4. check the old row is still there, with the new defaults
  final row = await database.select(database.entries).get();
  expect(row.length, 1);
  expect(row.first.title, 'Old note');
  expect(row.first.archived, isFalse);   // the new column's default
});

test('a failed migration does not corrupt the data', () async {
  // simulate an error partway through, and check the old data
  // is still readable
});

Exercises 12

  1. Set up Drift with an entries table, a DAO, and a watch query. Wire it to a Riverpod StreamProvider and confirm the list updates after a write.
  2. Add a join for a photo count, and confirm the typed result class works.
  3. Move a token from SharedPreferences to flutter_secure_storage, and confirm it survives an app upgrade.
  4. Build the outbox pattern: a local write, a queued sync job, and a drain in order. Test the order and the stop-on-failure behaviour.
  5. Implement field-level merge with keep-both for prose, and test the case where both devices edit the same sentence.
  6. Add an idempotency key to the create request, and simulate a lost response to prove there is no duplicate.
  7. Write a migration test from a v1 schema to the current one, with a data check rather than only a schema check.

12 · Networking and Serialization

12.1 The HTTP client12.2 Interceptors12.3 Errors, timeouts and retries12.4 Cancellation and deduplication12.5 Serialization: json_serializable12.6 Value types with freezed12.7 Parsing defensively12.8 Uploads and downloads12.9 WebSockets

Networking on a phone is different from networking on a server, and serialization is where type safety is either gained or quietly abandoned.

12.1 The HTTP client

Timeouts, base URLs, and the three defaults that are wrong

A configured HTTP client is a small object with a handful of properties, and three of its defaults are wrong often enough to be worth changing on day one. There is no default timeout. A request with no timeout waits as long as the platform's own limits allow, which on a phone is long enough that the user has given up and left the screen while the request is still pending; the consequence is that a screen shows a spinner forever on a connection that is not dead but is not working either. Set a connect timeout and a receive timeout, and set them separately, because they fail differently: a connect timeout catches an address that is unreachable, and a receive timeout catches a connection that was established and then went quiet — which is the common case on a mobile network and the one a single timeout is usually tuned for the wrong failure. The base URL is not configurable in the client, because it belongs to the environment, and an application that hard-codes it will need a rebuild to point at staging; the standard arrangement is to construct the client from a configuration value, and to have exactly one place in the codebase that decides which environment is current. And there is no request logging by default, which is correct for production — a client that logs every request logs every token it sends — and which means development needs logging switched on explicitly rather than left on and remembered. Then the three things worth knowing about the client's behaviour, and each affects how the rest of the application is written. A response is not a status code — it is a status code, a body and headers, and any of the three can be the problem. A handler that reads response.statusCode and otherwise assumes success will treat a two hundred with an empty body as success and then fail on the parse, with an error message about deserialisation rather than about the server. An exception from the client is not an HTTP error, — it is a socket error, a timeout or a cancellation, and it must be distinguishable from a four hundred because the two have completely different handling: one is retried and the other is not. And the client is not thread-safe with respect to closing, so a client that is closed while requests are in flight fails them, and a client closed and then reused throws immediately — which is the mechanism behind the "works until hot restart" family of network bugs. Then the two practices, and each prevents a class of report. Have one client, created once, injected everywhere, rather than one per call site — because a client per call means no connection reuse, no shared interceptors, and no shared timeout policy, and all three are the reason the library exists. And wrap every call in one function that turns the response or the exception into a domain result type, so that the rest of the application never sees an HTTP concept; this is the error-handling section's argument in a new place, and it is what makes the calling code testable without a network.

/* Three wrong defaults. */
const DEFAULTS = [
  { d: 'there is NO DEFAULT TIMEOUT',
    detail: 'A REQUEST WITH NO TIMEOUT WAITS as LONG AS the PLATFORMS OWN LIMITS ALLOW',
    consequence: 'which ON A PHONE IS LONG ENOUGH THAT the USER HAS GIVEN UP and LEFT the SCREEN while the REQUEST IS STILL PENDING',
    symptom: 'so a SCREEN SHOWS A SPINNER FOREVER ON A CONNECTION THAT IS NOT DEAD but IS NOT WORKING EITHER',
    fix: 'SET A CONNECT TIMEOUT and A RECEIVE TIMEOUT, and SET THEM SEPARATELY' },
  { d: 'the BASE URL IS NOT CONFIGURABLE IN the CLIENT',
    why: 'BECAUSE IT BELONGS TO the ENVIRONMENT',
    detail: 'AN APPLICATION THAT HARD-CODES IT WILL NEED A REBUILD TO POINT AT STAGING',
    practice: 'CONSTRUCT the CLIENT FROM A CONFIGURATION VALUE, and HAVE EXACTLY ONE PLACE IN the CODEBASE THAT DECIDES WHICH ENVIRONMENT IS CURRENT' },
  { d: 'there is NO REQUEST LOGGING BY DEFAULT', correctForProduction: true,
    why: 'A CLIENT THAT LOGS EVERY REQUEST LOGS EVERY TOKEN IT SENDS',
    consequence: 'which MEANS DEVELOPMENT NEEDS LOGGING SWITCHED ON EXPLICITLY rather than LEFT ON and REMEMBERED' },
];

/* Why two timeouts. */
const TWO_TIMEOUTS = {
  connect: 'CATCHES AN ADDRESS THAT IS UNREACHABLE',
  receive: 'CATCHES A CONNECTION THAT WAS ESTABLISHED and THEN WENT QUIET',
  common: 'which IS the COMMON CASE ON A MOBILE NETWORK and the ONE A SINGLE TIMEOUT IS USUALLY TUNED FOR the WRONG FAILURE',
};

/* Three behaviours. */
const BEHAVIOURS = [
  { b: 'A RESPONSE IS NOT A STATUS CODE',
    detail: 'it IS A STATUS CODE, A BODY and HEADERS, and ANY of the THREE CAN BE the PROBLEM',
    bug: 'A HANDLER THAT READS THE STATUS CODE and OTHERWISE ASSUMES SUCCESS WILL TREAT A TWO HUNDRED WITH AN EMPTY BODY AS SUCCESS',
    consequence: 'and THEN FAIL ON the PARSE, WITH AN ERROR MESSAGE about DESERIALISATION rather than ABOUT the SERVER' },
  { b: 'AN EXCEPTION FROM the CLIENT IS NOT AN HTTP ERROR',
    detail: 'it IS A SOCKET ERROR, A TIMEOUT or A CANCELLATION',

  { b: 'the CLIENT IS NOT SAFE TO CLOSE WHILE REQUESTS ARE IN FLIGHT',

    symptom: 'which IS the MECHANISM BEHIND the works until hot restart FAMILY of NETWORK BUGS' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'HAVE ONE CLIENT, CREATED ONCE, INJECTED EVERYWHERE', not: 'ONE PER CALL SITE',
    why: ['A CLIENT PER CALL MEANS NO CONNECTION REUSE', 'NO SHARED INTERCEPTORS', 'and NO SHARED TIMEOUT POLICY'],
    and: 'all THREE ARE the REASON the LIBRARY EXISTS' },
  { p: 'WRAP EVERY CALL IN ONE FUNCTION THAT TURNS the RESPONSE or the EXCEPTION INTO A DOMAIN RESULT TYPE',
    gain: 'so THAT the REST of the APPLICATION NEVER SEES AN HTTP CONCEPT',
    connects: 'this IS the ERROR-HANDLING CHAPTERS ARGUMENT IN A NEW PLACE',
    and: 'and IT IS WHAT MAKES the CALLING CODE TESTABLE WITHOUT A NETWORK' },

Never disable certificate validation, in any build, for any reason. It appears in a startling number of tutorials because it makes a self-signed certificate work during development. Ship the default; use a debug-only network security config for a local server instead.

// pubspec.yaml
//   dio: ^5.6.0        (interceptors, better errors, cancellation)
//   or: http: ^1.2.0   (lighter, from the Dart team)

// WITH DIO
final dio = Dio(BaseOptions(
  baseUrl: 'https://api.acme.com/v1',
  connectTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 10),
  receiveTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 20),
  sendTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 20),
  headers: {
    'accept': 'application/json',
    'x-client': 'field-notes/1.4.0',
  },
  contentType: Headers.jsonContentType,
  responseType: ResponseType.json,

  // DO NOT disable certificate validation, ever
  // validateStatus: (status) => status != null && status < 500,

  // and DO NOT put a token here that never expires
  // authorization: 'Bearer ...',
));

// GET
final response = await dio.get<Map<String, dynamic>>('/entries');
final entries = (response.data!['items'] as List)
    .map((e) => Entry.fromJson(e as Map<String, dynamic>))
    .toList();

// POST
await dio.post('/entries', data: entry.toJson());

// PATCH, for a partial update
await dio.patch('/entries/${entry.id}', data: {'title': newTitle});

// DELETE
await dio.delete('/entries/${entry.id}');

// with query parameters
await dio.get('/entries', queryParameters: {
  'page': page,
  'limit': 50,
  'search': query.isEmpty ? null : query,   // null omits the key
  'sort': 'updatedAt:desc',
});

// FORM data, for a file upload
final form = FormData.fromMap({
  'title': title,
  'file': await MultipartFile.fromFile(path, filename: 'photo.jpg'),
});
await dio.post('/entries', data: form);
// A REPOSITORY, which is where the client belongs
class EntryApi {
  EntryApi(this._dio);

  final Dio _dio;

  Future<EntryPage> entries({
    int page = 1,
    int limit = 50,
    String? search,
    bool archived = false,
  }) async {
    final response = await _dio.get<Map<String, dynamic>>('/entries', queryParameters: {
      'page': page,
      'limit': limit,
      if (search != null && search.isNotEmpty) 'search': search,
      'archived': archived,
    });

    return EntryPage.fromJson(response.data!);
  }

  Future<Entry> byId(String id) async {
    final response = await _dio.get<Map<String, dynamic>>('/entries/$id');
    return Entry.fromJson(response.data!);
  }

  Future<Entry> create(EntryDraft draft) async {
    final response = await _dio.post<Map<String, dynamic>>(
      '/entries',
      data: draft.toJson(),
      // an idempotency key: a retry does not create a duplicate
      options: Options(headers: {'idempotency-key': draft.clientId}),
    );
    return Entry.fromJson(response.data!);
  }

  Future<Entry> update(String id, EntryDraft draft, {int? ifMatch}) async {
    final response = await _dio.patch<Map<String, dynamic>>(
      '/entries/$id',
      data: draft.toJson(),
      // optimistic concurrency: the version I last saw
      options: ifMatch == null ? null : Options(headers: {'if-match': '$ifMatch'}),
    );
    return Entry.fromJson(response.data!);
  }

  Future<void> delete(String id) async => dio.delete('/entries/$id');

  Future<ChangePage> changes({required int since, int limit = 200}) async {
    final response = await dio.get<Map<String, dynamic>>(
      '/entries/changes',
      queryParameters: {'since': since, 'limit': limit},
    );
    return ChangePage.fromJson(response.data!);
  }
}

12.2 Interceptors

// AN INTERCEPTOR is code that runs on every request. This is where
// the cross-cutting concerns go, and getting them out of the
// repository makes the repository readable.

// 1. AUTH: attach the token, and refresh it on a 401
class AuthInterceptor extends Interceptor {
  AuthInterceptor({required this._tokens, required this._onSessionExpired});

  final TokenStore _tokens;
  final void Function() _onSessionExpired;
  bool _refreshing = false;

  @override
  void onRequest(RequestOptions options, RequestInterceptorHandler handler) async {
    final token = await _tokens.accessToken;
    if (token != null) {
      options.headers['authorization'] = 'Bearer $token';
    }
    handler.next(options);
  }

  @override
  void onError(DioException err, ErrorInterceptorHandler handler) async {
    if (err.response?.statusCode != 401 || _refreshing) {
      return handler.next(err);
    }

    _refreshing = true;
    try {
      final refreshed = await _tokens.refresh();
      if (refreshed) {
        // RETRY, with the new token
        final options = err.requestOptions;
        options.headers['authorization'] = 'Bearer $refreshed';
        final response = await Dio().fetch(options);
        return handler.resolve(response);
      }
    } catch (_) {
      // the refresh failed
    } finally {
      _refreshing = false;
    }

    _onSessionExpired();
    handler.next(err);
  }
}

// 2. LOGGING, in debug only
class LoggingInterceptor extends Interceptor {
  @override
  void onRequest(RequestOptions options, RequestInterceptorHandler handler) {
    if (kDebugMode) {
      debugPrint('→ ${options.method} ${options.uri}');
      if (options.data != null) debugPrint('  ${options.data}');
    }
    handler.next(options);
  }

  @override
  void onResponse(Response response, ResponseInterceptorHandler handler) {
    if (kDebugMode) {
      debugPrint('← ${response.statusCode} (${response.requestOptions.duration}ms)');
    }
    handler.next(response);
  }

  @override
  void onError(DioException err, ErrorInterceptorHandler handler) {
    if (kDebugMode) {
      debugPrint('✗ ${err.response?.statusCode ?? 'network'} ${err.requestOptions.uri}');
      debugPrint('  ${err.message}');
    }
    handler.next(err);
  }
}

// 3. OFFLINE: fail fast when there is no connection, rather than
// waiting for a timeout
class OfflineInterceptor extends Interceptor {
  OfflineInterceptor(this._connectivity);
  final Connectivity _connectivity;

  @override
  void onRequest(RequestOptions options, RequestInterceptorHandler handler) async {
    if (!_connectivity.isOnline) {
      return handler.reject(
        DioException(
          requestOptions: options,
          type: DioExceptionType.connectionError,
          error: const OfflineException(),
          message: 'No network connection',
        ),
      );
    }
    handler.next(options);
  }
}

// 4. RETRY, for transient failures
class RetryInterceptor extends Interceptor {
  RetryInterceptor({this.maxAttempts = 3, this.baseDelay = const Duration(milliseconds: 400)});

  final int maxAttempts;
  final Duration baseDelay;

  @override
  Future<void> onError(DioException err, ErrorInterceptorHandler handler) async {
    final shouldRetry = err.type == DioExceptionType.connectionTimeout ||
        err.type == DioExceptionType.receiveTimeout ||
        (err.response?.statusCode != null &&
            err.response!.statusCode! >= 500 &&
            err.response!.statusCode! != 501);

    final attempt = (err.requestOptions.extra['retry_attempt'] as int?) ?? 0;

    if (!shouldRetry || attempt >= maxAttempts) {
      return handler.next(err);
    }

    // EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF WITH JITTER
    final delay = baseDelay * (1 << attempt);
    final jittered = Duration(
      milliseconds: (delay.inMilliseconds * (0.5 + Random().nextDouble() * 0.5)).round(),
    );
    await Future.delayed(jittered);

    err.requestOptions.extra['retry_attempt'] = attempt + 1;
    try {
      final response = await Dio().fetch(err.requestOptions);
      handler.resolve(response);
    } catch (e) {
      handler.next(err);
    }
  }
}

// WIRING
final dio = Dio(BaseOptions(baseUrl: 'https://api.acme.com/v1'))
  ..interceptors.addAll([
    LoggingInterceptor(),
    OfflineInterceptor(connectivity),
    AuthInterceptor(tokens: tokenStore, onSessionExpired: signOut),
    RetryInterceptor(),
  ]);

Interceptors, and the order that matters

An interceptor is a function that sees a request on its way out and a response on its way back, and the value of the mechanism is that it puts cross-cutting behaviour in one place instead of in every call site. The four things worth intercepting, and they are worth doing in a specific order because each depends on the previous one having run. Logging, which should be outermost so that it can see a request that a later interceptor rejects — a request that never leaves the process should still be logged, or a bug where an interceptor throws will be invisible. Authentication, which attaches the credential and must be inside logging so that the log records that an authenticated request was made without recording the credential; the mechanism is to log the method and URL and never the headers. Retry, which must be outside authentication so that a retried request re-runs the whole chain including re-attaching a credential that may have been refreshed between attempts. And error translation, which should be innermost so that it converts the transport-level failure into a domain error and everything outside it sees the domain error. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a specific mechanism. A retry interceptor that retries everything. A four hundred and a four-zero-one are not transient; retrying a four-zero-one ten times with backoff turns a single failure into a ten-second wait and a rate-limit, and retrying a four hundred can duplicate a write if the server processed it and the response was lost. The fix is to retry only idempotent methods and only five-zero-three-style and network-level failures — which means the interceptor needs to know the request's method, and a retry that cannot tell is a retry that will eventually duplicate something. An interceptor that throws. An exception from an interceptor is not a network error and will not be caught by the caller's error handling if the caller only handles network errors, so it surfaces as an unhandled exception and the screen shows nothing; every interceptor must either return a response or return a domain error, never throw. And an interceptor that reads a stream twice. A request body is a stream and can only be consumed once, so an interceptor that logs the body and then forwards it forwards nothing — and the symptom is a request that is logged correctly and then produces no result. Then the two practices, and each is cheap. Write the interceptor as a pure function of request and response, so it can be tested with two literal objects and no client, which is the only way to test a cross-cutting behaviour cheaply and the reason it should not reach into a service. And have exactly one place that decides the retry policy, because retry policy scattered across call sites is a set of policies that disagree, and a request that is retried three times by three layers has waited thirty-one seconds by the time it fails.

/* Four things, in order. */
const CHAIN = [
  { n: 1, w: 'LOGGING', outermost: true,
    why: 'SO THAT IT CAN SEE A REQUEST THAT A LATER INTERCEPTOR REJECTS',
    and: 'A REQUEST THAT NEVER LEAVES the PROCESS SHOULD STILL BE LOGGED, or A BUG WHERE AN INTERCEPTOR THROWS WILL BE INVISIBLE' },
  { n: 2, w: 'AUTHENTICATION', inside: 'LOGGING',
    why: 'SO THAT the LOG RECORDS THAT AN AUTHENTICATED REQUEST WAS MADE WITHOUT RECORDING the CREDENTIAL',
    mechanism: 'LOG the METHOD and URL and NEVER the HEADERS' },
  { n: 3, w: 'RETRY', outside: 'AUTHENTICATION',
    why: 'so THAT A RETRIED REQUEST RE-RUNS the WHOLE CHAIN INCLUDING RE-ATTACHING A CREDENTIAL THAT MAY HAVE BEEN REFRESHED BETWEEN ATTEMPTS' },
  { n: 4, w: 'ERROR TRANSLATION', innermost: true,
    why: 'so THAT IT CONVERTS the TRANSPORT-LEVEL FAILURE INTO A DOMAIN ERROR and EVERYTHING OUTSIDE IT SEES the DOMAIN ERROR' },
];

/* Three things that go wrong. */
const GO_WRONG = [
  { f: 'A RETRY INTERCEPTOR THAT RETRIES EVERYTHING',
    detail: 'A FOUR HUNDRED and A FOUR-ZERO-ONE ARE NOT TRANSIENT',
    consequences: ['RETRYING A FOUR-ZERO-ONE TEN TIMES WITH BACKOFF TURNS A SINGLE FAILURE INTO A TEN-SECOND WAIT and A RATE-LIMIT',
      'and RETRYING A FOUR HUNDRED CAN DUPLICATE A WRITE if the SERVER PROCESSED IT and the RESPONSE WAS LOST'],
    fix: 'RETRY ONLY IDEMPOTENT METHODS and ONLY FIVE-ZERO-THREE-STYLE and NETWORK-LEVEL FAILURES',
    requires: 'which MEANS the INTERCEPTOR NEEDS TO KNOW the REQUESTS METHOD',
    and: 'A RETRY THAT CANNOT TELL IS A RETRY THAT WILL EVENTUALLY DUPLICATE SOMETHING' },
  { f: 'AN INTERCEPTOR THAT THROWS',
    detail: 'AN EXCEPTION FROM AN INTERCEPTOR IS NOT A NETWORK ERROR',
    consequence: 'and WILL NOT BE CAUGHT BY the CALLERS ERROR HANDLING if the CALLER ONLY HANDLES NETWORK ERRORS',
    symptom: 'so it SURFACES AS AN UNHANDLED EXCEPTION and the SCREEN SHOWS NOTHING',
    rule: 'EVERY INTERCEPTOR MUST EITHER RETURN A RESPONSE or RETURN A DOMAIN ERROR, NEVER THROW' },
  { f: 'AN INTERCEPTOR THAT READS A STREAM TWICE',
    detail: 'A REQUEST BODY IS A STREAM and CAN ONLY BE CONSUMED ONCE',
    consequence: 'so AN INTERCEPTOR THAT LOGS the BODY and THEN FORWARDS IT FORWARDS NOTHING',
    symptom: 'AND the SYMPTOM IS A REQUEST THAT IS LOGGED CORRECTLY and THEN PRODUCES NO RESULT' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'WRITE the INTERCEPTOR AS A PURE FUNCTION of REQUEST and RESPONSE',
    gain: 'so IT CAN BE TESTED WITH TWO LITERAL OBJECTS and NO CLIENT',
    why: 'which IS the ONLY WAY TO TEST A CROSS-CUTTING BEHAVIOUR CHEAPLY',
    and: 'and the REASON IT SHOULD NOT REACH INTO A SERVICE' },
  { p: 'HAVE EXACTLY ONE PLACE THAT DECIDES the RETRY POLICY',
    why: 'BECAUSE RETRY POLICY SCATTERED ACROSS CALL SITES IS A SET of POLICIES THAT DISAGREE',
    and: 'A REQUEST THAT IS RETRIED THREE TIMES BY THREE LAYERS HAS WAITED THIRTY-ONE SECONDS BY the TIME IT FAILS' },
];

12.3 Errors, timeouts and retries

The five error kinds, and what each one means for the user

Retrying is the mechanism this section is about and the discipline is that retry policy is a decision per operation, not a policy applied uniformly. There are five kinds of failure and only two of them are retryable, and conflating them is the reason an application either hammers a failing server or gives up on a request that would have succeeded. A timeout is retryable if the operation is idempotent, because nothing has been proven to have happened — the request may not have arrived. A connection failure is always retryable for the same reason. A five hundred and a five-zero-three are retryable because the server is telling you it could not do the work, with the caveat that a five hundred can also mean it did the work and then failed to respond. A four hundred is never retryable, because the request is wrong and will be wrong again identically. A four-zero-one and a four-zero-three are never retryable, because the credential is the problem and a retry sends the same credential. Then the three rules for a retry implementation, and each is a specific requirement. Exponential backoff with jitter, and the jitter is not optional. A backoff of one, two, four seconds makes every client that failed at the same moment retry at the same moment, so the recovering server receives the same thundering herd it just survived; a full jitter — a random duration between zero and the current window — breaks the synchronisation and is the difference between a recovery and a second outage. A bound on attempts, and a bound on total time. An unbounded retry with backoff will eventually succeed, which sounds good and means a user stares at a spinner for four minutes; the bound should be chosen so that the total wait is shorter than the user's patience, which is usually two or three attempts. And retry only what is safe to retry, which means the method — a get is safe, a post is not unless it carries an idempotency key, which is the API chapter's requirement arriving here again. Then the three things that go wrong, and each has a specific mechanism. Retrying a non-idempotent write without a key, which is a duplicate charge, a duplicate order, or a duplicate anything. Retrying a request whose response was lost after the server processed it, which is the same failure with a longer fuse — and the reason the idempotency key exists is that the client cannot distinguish "the server did not get it" from "the server got it and the reply was lost". And a retry inside a retry, because an interceptor that retries and a repository that retries produces exponential attempts: three layers of three attempts is twenty-seven requests, and each layer's backoff is unaware of the others. Then the two practices, and each is cheap. Make retryability a property of the call, not of the endpoint, — declared on the method wrapper rather than inferred — so that the decision is visible at the call site where it matters. And surface retry state to the user, because a request that is being retried should say so and a request that has permanently failed should say that rather than continuing to spin, and the difference between the two is the whole user experience of a bad network.

/* Five kinds. */
const KINDS = [
  { k: 'a TIMEOUT', retryable: 'IF the OPERATION IS IDEMPOTENT', why: 'NOTHING HAS BEEN PROVEN TO HAVE HAPPENED - the REQUEST MAY NOT HAVE ARRIVED' },
  { k: 'a CONNECTION FAILURE', retryable: true, why: 'FOR the SAME REASON' },
  { k: 'a FIVE HUNDRED or FIVE-ZERO-THREE', retryable: true,
    why: 'BECAUSE the SERVER IS TELLING YOU IT COULD NOT DO the WORK',
    caveat: 'WITH the CAVEAT THAT A FIVE HUNDRED CAN ALSO MEAN IT DID the WORK and THEN FAILED to RESPOND' },
  { k: 'a FOUR HUNDRED', retryable: false, why: 'BECAUSE the REQUEST IS WRONG and WILL BE WRONG AGAIN IDENTICALLY' },
  { k: 'a FOUR-ZERO-ONE or FOUR-ZERO-THREE', retryable: false, why: 'BECAUSE the CREDENTIAL IS the PROBLEM and A RETRY SENDS the SAME CREDENTIAL' },
];
const WHY_DISTINGUISH = 'CONFLATING THEM IS the REASON an APPLICATION EITHER HAMMERS A FAILING SERVER or GIVES UP ON A REQUEST THAT WOULD HAVE SUCCEEDED';

/* Three rules. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF WITH JITTER, and the JITTER IS NOT OPTIONAL',
    detail: 'A BACKOFF OF ONE, TWO, FOUR SECONDS MAKES EVERY CLIENT THAT FAILED AT the SAME MOMENT RETRY AT the SAME MOMENT',
    consequence: 'so the RECOVERING SERVER RECEIVES the SAME THUNDERING HERD IT JUST SURVIVED',

  { f: 'RETRYING A REQUEST WHOSE RESPONSE WAS LOST AFTER the SERVER PROCESSED IT',
