Always set a timeout, even when the request has its own natural deadline. Without one, a request on a flaky mobile network hangs for the platform default - often two minutes - and the user cannot tell whether the app is broken or slow.

// A FAILURE HIERARCHY, so callers can act on the KIND of problem
// rather than on a status code
sealed class Failure {
  const Failure(this.message);
  final String message;
}

class NetworkFailure extends Failure {
  const NetworkFailure() : super('No connection. Check your network.');
}

class TimeoutFailure extends Failure {
  const TimeoutFailure() : super('The server took too long to respond.');
}

class UnauthorizedFailure extends Failure {
  const UnauthorizedFailure() : super('Your session has expired.');
}

class ForbiddenFailure extends Failure {
  const ForbiddenFailure(this.action) : super('You do not have access to $action.');
}

class NotFoundFailure extends Failure {
  const NotFoundFailure(this.resource) : super('$resource was not found.');
}

class ValidationFailure extends Failure {
  const ValidationFailure(this.errors) : super('Please check the form.');
  final Map<String, String> errors;
}

class ConflictFailure extends Failure {
  const ConflictFailure() : super('This was changed on another device.');
}

class ServerFailure extends Failure {
  const ServerFailure(this.statusCode) : super('The server had a problem ($statusCode).');
  final int statusCode;
}

class ParseFailure extends Failure {
  const ParseFailure() : super('The response could not be read.');
}

// THE MAPPER, in one place
Failure mapDioException(DioException e) {
  switch (e.type) {
    case DioExceptionType.connectionTimeout:
    case DioExceptionType.sendTimeout:
    case DioExceptionType.receiveTimeout:
      return const TimeoutFailure();
    case DioExceptionType.connectionError:
      return const NetworkFailure();
    case DioExceptionType.badCertificate:
      return const Failure('A security check failed.');
    case DioExceptionType.cancel:
      return const Failure('Cancelled.');
    case DioExceptionType.badResponse:
      final status = e.response!.statusCode!;
      final body = e.response!.data;
      if (status == 401) return const UnauthorizedFailure();
      if (status == 403) return const ForbiddenFailure('this resource');
      if (status == 404) return const NotFoundFailure('That item');
      if (status == 409) return const ConflictFailure();
      if (status == 422 && body is Map) {
        return ValidationFailure(
          (body['errors'] as Map).map((k, v) => MapEntry(k.toString(), v.toString())),
        );
      }
      if (status >= 500) return ServerFailure(status);
      return Failure('Unexpected response ($status).');
    case DioExceptionType.unknown:
      return const Failure('Something went wrong.');
  }
}

// USING IT: the UI switches on the type, exhaustively
sealed class Result<T> {}

class Ok<T> extends Result<T> {
  const Ok(this.value);
  final T value;
}

class Err<T> extends Result<T> {
  const Err(this.failure);
  final Failure failure;
}

class EntryRepository {
  Future<Result<Entry>> byId(String id) async {
    try {
      return Ok(await _api.byId(id));
    } on DioException catch (e) {
      return Err(mapDioException(e));
    } on FormatException {
      return const Err(ParseFailure());
    }
  }
}

// in the widget
final result = await ref.read(entryProvider(id).future);
return result.when(
  ok: (entry) => EntryView(entry: entry),
  err: (failure) => switch (failure) {
        NetworkFailure() => OfflineView(retry: load),
        UnauthorizedFailure() => const SessionExpiredView(),
        NotFoundFailure() => const NotFoundView(),
        ValidationFailure(:final errors) => FormView(errors: errors),
        _ => ErrorView(failure: failure, retry: load),
      },
);
// THE TIMEOUT RULES, which people set wrong
// connectTimeout   the TCP/TLS handshake: 5-10s
//                  on a mobile network, 30s is too long to wait
// receiveTimeout   the time between packets: 10-30s
//                  it is NOT the total time
// sendTimeout      uploading a large body: 60s+
//
// THE TRAP: a request with a long receiveTimeout holds a
// connection open, and the user sees nothing for the whole time.
// It is usually better to fail fast and let the user retry.

// THE OTHER TRAP: no timeout at all
// the request hangs for the platform default, often 2 minutes,
// and the user cannot tell whether the app is broken
// ALWAYS set a timeout.

// THE NETWORK TYPE PROBLEM
// a video upload on mobile data is a bad idea without asking
if (_connectivity.isMetered && fileSize > 5 * 1024 * 1024) {
  final proceed = await showDialog(
    context: context,
    builder: (context) => AlertDialog(
      title: const Text('Large upload'),
      content: Text('This file is ${formatBytes(fileSize)}. You are on mobile data. Continue?'),
      actions: [
        TextButton(onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context, false), child: const Text('Cancel')),
        FilledButton(onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context, true), child: const Text('Upload')),
      ],
    ),
  );
  if (!proceed) return;
}

12.4 Cancellation and deduplication

// CANCELLATION: the user typed another character, so the previous
// search is pointless. Cancel it.
class SearchController extends ChangeNotifier {
  final Dio _dio;
  CancelToken? _token;
  String? _lastQuery;

  SearchController(this._dio);

  List<Entry> _results = [];
  List<Entry> get results => _results;

  Future<void> search(String query) async {
    // 1. cancel the previous request
    _token?.cancel('superseded');

    // 2. do not re-request an identical query
    if (query == _lastQuery) return;
    _lastQuery = query;

    if (query.trim().isEmpty) {
      _results = [];
      notifyListeners();
      return;
    }

    final token = CancelToken();
    _token = token;

    try {
      final page = await _api.entries(search: query);
      if (token.isCancelled) return;   // a newer request won
      _results = page.items;
      notifyListeners();
    } on DioException catch (e) {
      if (CancelToken.isCancel(e)) return;   // expected, not an error
      _results = [];
      notifyListeners();
    }
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _token?.cancel('disposed');
    super.dispose();
  }
}

// WITH RIVERPOD, cancellation is automatic and free
final searchProvider = FutureProvider.autoDispose.family<List<Entry>, String>((ref, query) async {
  if (query.isEmpty) return [];
  // the http client cancels this request when the provider is
  // disposed, which happens when the widget unmounts or when
  // the family key changes
  return ref.watch(entryApiProvider).entries(search: query).then((p) => p.items);
});
// autoDispose + family = the request is cancelled when the
// argument changes or the listener goes away

// DEDUPLICATION: two widgets fetching the same thing
final entryProvider = FutureProvider.family<Entry, String>((ref, id) {
  // the SAME family instance for the same id: one request
  return ref.watch(entryApiProvider).byId(id);
});
// calling entryProvider(id) from three places makes ONE request

// and a cache you control, for something expensive
final expensiveProvider = FutureProvider.family<Report, DateTime, String>((ref, params, id) {
  // keep it for five minutes
  final link = ref.keepAlive();
  Timer(const Duration(minutes: 5), link.close);
  return generate(params);
});

Cancelling work, and the three things that get lost

Cancellation in a mobile application is not an optimisation, it is a correctness requirement, and there are three distinct kinds of work each of which fails differently when the user leaves. An in-flight request, which continues and may complete against a screen that no longer exists — harmless except for the response handler touching a disposed widget, which is the framework's "used after dispose" assertion. A subscription or a stream listener, which keeps the state object alive and delivers callbacks after disposal, and which in debug mode produces a leak-tracking message and in release produces a slow leak that nobody finds. And an animation controller, which is the animation chapter's disposal rule and the one most often forgotten. Then the three mechanisms, and each covers a different kind. Cancelling the request, which the client supports and which aborts the connection — it saves bandwidth and it also means the response handler will not run, so anything that must happen regardless must not be in that handler. Cancelling the token, where a long-running operation checks a flag at its own boundaries and stops; this is the mechanism for work that is not a single request — a batch, a sync, a polling loop — and the discipline is that the check must be inside the loop rather than outside it. And disposal, which is the framework's mechanism for anything tied to a widget's lifetime, and which is what catches the subscription and the controller. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a specific mechanism. Cancelling a request whose result is still needed, which happens when a screen is disposed during a configuration change and the request is cancelled with it, and the new screen re-requests — the classic double-fetch that makes a list flicker on rotation. A response handler that runs after disposal, which in debug mode asserts and in release writes into freed memory; the fix is to check a mounted flag in the handler, which the previous section's "don't setState after dispose" argument covers. And not cancelling a debounced or throttled callback, which fires after the widget is gone — and which is the mechanism behind the "setState called after dispose" report that appears only when the user navigates quickly. Then the two practices, and each is a habit rather than a rule. Make every asynchronous entry point return something the caller can cancel, so that cancellation is available by construction rather than by remembering — and so that the interface makes the leak visible at the call site. And store the subscription or controller in a field and cancel it in dispose, always, with no exceptions; the cases where it appears unnecessary are the cases where the widget's lifetime is longer than the developer assumed, which is exactly the case a leak depends on.

/* Three kinds of work, three failures. */
const KINDS = [
  { k: 'AN IN-FLIGHT REQUEST', continues: 'and MAY COMPLETE AGAINST A SCREEN THAT NO LONGER EXISTS',
    harmlessExcept: 'EXCEPT FOR the RESPONSE HANDLER TOUCHING A DISPOSED WIDGET',
    which: 'WHICH IS the FRAMEWORKS used after dispose ASSERTION' },
  { k: 'A SUBSCRIPTION or A STREAM LISTENER', consequence: 'WHICH KEEPS the STATE OBJECT ALIVE and DELIVERS CALLBACKS AFTER DISPOSAL',
    inDebug: 'IN DEBUG MODE PRODUCES A LEAK-TRACKING MESSAGE',
    inRelease: 'and IN RELEASE PRODUCES A SLOW LEAK that NOBODY FINDS' },
  { k: 'AN ANIMATION CONTROLLER', covered: 'the ANIMATION CHAPTERS DISPOSAL RULE',
    and: 'the ONE MOST OFTEN FORGOTTEN' },
];
const WHY = 'CANCELLATION IN A MOBILE APPLICATION IS NOT AN OPTIMISATION, it IS A CORRECTNESS REQUIREMENT';

/* Three mechanisms. */
const MECHANISMS = [
  { m: 'CANCELLING the REQUEST', what: 'the CLIENT SUPPORTS IT and IT ABORTS the CONNECTION',
    gain: ['it SAVES BANDWIDTH', 'and IT ALSO MEANS the RESPONSE HANDLER WILL NOT RUN'],
    constraint: 'so ANYTHING THAT MUST HAPPEN REGARDLESS MUST NOT BE IN that HANDLER' },
  { m: 'CANCELLING the TOKEN', detail: 'WHERE A LONG-RUNNING OPERATION CHECKS A FLAG AT ITS OWN BOUNDARIES and STOPS',
    for: 'WORK THAT IS NOT A SINGLE REQUEST - A BATCH, A SYNC, A POLLING LOOP',
    discipline: 'the CHECK MUST BE INSIDE the LOOP rather than OUTSIDE IT' },
  { m: 'DISPOSAL', catches: ['the SUBSCRIPTION', 'the CONTROLLER'], is: 'the FRAMEWORKS MECHANISM for ANYTHING TIED TO A WIDGETS LIFETIME' },
];

/* Three things that go wrong. */
const GO_WRONG = [
  { f: 'CANCELLING A REQUEST WHOSE RESULT IS STILL NEEDED',
    detail: 'which HAPPENS WHEN A SCREEN IS DISPOSED DURING A CONFIGURATION CHANGE and the REQUEST IS CANCELLED WITH IT',
    consequence: 'and the NEW SCREEN RE-REQUESTS',
    symptom: 'the CLASSIC DOUBLE-FETCH THAT MAKES A LIST FLICKER ON ROTATION' },
  { f: 'A RESPONSE HANDLER THAT RUNS AFTER DISPOSAL',
    detail: 'which IN DEBUG MODE ASSERTS and IN RELEASE WRITES INTO FREED MEMORY',
    fix: 'CHECK A MOUNTED FLAG IN the HANDLER',
    connects: 'which the PREVIOUS CHAPTERS do not setState after dispose ARGUMENT COVERS' },
  { f: 'NOT CANCELLING A DEBOUNCED or THROTTLED CALLBACK',
    consequence: 'WHICH FIRES AFTER the WIDGET IS GONE',
    symptom: 'and WHICH IS the MECHANISM BEHIND the setState called after dispose REPORT THAT APPEARS ONLY WHEN the USER NAVIGATES QUICKLY' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'MAKE EVERY ASYNCHRONOUS ENTRY POINT RETURN SOMETHING the CALLER CAN CANCEL',
    gain: ['so THAT CANCELLATION IS AVAILABLE BY CONSTRUCTION rather than BY REMEMBERING',
      'and SO THAT the INTERFACE MAKES the LEAK VISIBLE AT the CALL SITE'] },
  { p: 'STORE the SUBSCRIPTION or CONTROLLER IN A FIELD and CANCEL IT IN dispose, ALWAYS, WITH NO EXCEPTIONS',
    why: 'the CASES WHERE IT APPEARS UNNECESSARY ARE the CASES WHERE the WIDGETS LIFETIME IS LONGER than the DEVELOPER ASSUMED',
    and: 'which IS EXACTLY the CASE A LEAK DEPENDS ON' },
];

12.5 Serialization: json_serializable

// pubspec.yaml
//   json_annotation: ^4.9.0
//   json_serializable: ^6.8.0
//   build_runner: ^2.4.0
// dev_dependencies:
//   json_serializable: ^6.8.0

// THE MODEL
import 'package:json_annotation/json_annotation.dart';

part 'entry.g.dart';

@JsonSerializable()
class Entry {
  const Entry({
    required this.id,
    required this.title,
    this.body = '',
    this.photoUrl,
    this.tags = const [],
    required this.createdAt,
    required this.updatedAt,
    this.syncedAt,
    this.serverVersion = 0,
    this.archived = false,
  });

  factory Entry.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) =>
      _$EntryFromJson(json);

  final String id;
  final String title;
  final String body;
  final String? photoUrl;
  final List<String> tags;
  final DateTime createdAt;
  final DateTime updatedAt;
  final DateTime? syncedAt;
  final int serverVersion;
  final bool archived;

  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() => _$EntryToJson(this);

  // a computed field that is also serialised
  @JsonKey(includeFromJson: false, includeToJson: true)
  String get displayTitle => title.isEmpty ? 'Untitled' : title;

  // a value that must be sent as an int, not a double
  @JsonKey(fromJson: _intFromDouble, toJson: _intToJson)
  final double? rating;

  static int _intFromDouble(Object? v) => (v as num?)?.toInt() ?? 0;
  static int _intToJson(double? v) => v?.round() ?? 0;

  // a value with a custom name on the wire
  @JsonKey(name: 'created_at')
  final DateTime createdAtRenamed;
}

// run: dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
// THE OPTIONS that matter
@JsonSerializable(
  // call the constructor: use initializers and asserts
  createToJson: true,
  createFactory: true,

  // rename fields to snake_case, which is a common API style
  fieldRename: FieldRename.snake,

  // include nulls, or omit them (smaller payloads, and the
  // server usually treats a missing key as null)
  includeIfNull: false,

  // run the field initializers when a key is missing, so a
  // default applies rather than an error
  applyDefaultValues: true,

  // warn about a field in the class with no matching key
  checked: true,

  // convert Dates to ISO8601 strings, not epoch milliseconds
  // (epoch is smaller; ISO is readable in a log)
  explicitToJson: true,

  // disambiguate two fields with the same JsonKey name
  disallowUnrecognizedKeys: false,
)

// THE NAMED CONSTRUCTOR for a nested shape
@JsonSerializable()
class EntryPage {
  const EntryPage({required this.items, this.cursor});

  factory EntryPage.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) =>
      _$EntryPageFromJson(json);

  final List<Entry> items;
  final String? cursor;

  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() => _$EntryPageToJson(this);
}

// THE GENERIC ANNOTATION, for a reusable wrapper
class Paginated<T> {
  const Paginated({required this.items, this.nextCursor});
  final List<T> items;
  final String? nextCursor;
}

@JsonSerializable()
class PaginatedEntry extends _$PaginatedEntry {
  factory PaginatedEntry.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) =>
      _$PaginatedEntryFromJson(json);
  @override
  Paginated<Entry> get items =>
      (json['items'] as List).map((e) => Entry.fromJson(e as Map<String, dynamic>)).toList();
  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() => {'items': items.map((e) => e.toJson()).toList()};
}

Code generation, and why hand-written serialisation breaks in the ways it does

The question is whether to write serialisation by hand or generate it, and the reason to generate is not that hand-writing is more typing — it is that hand-written serialisation fails in a specific set of ways, and every one of those ways is a silent wrong value rather than a crash. A hand-written fromJson reads each key it knows and ignores the rest, which means a field added on the server is silently dropped until someone notices the missing value; a generated one produces a compile error when the field is required and absent from the model, which is the only version of this bug that is free. A hand-written one takes Map<String, dynamic> and casts, so a number arrives as a double where an int was expected, a nested object arrives as a map where a model was expected, and a null arrives where a value was expected — all of which produce a model that is the right shape and the wrong contents, and none of which throws. And a hand-written one cannot know which fields are required, because it has no separate declaration: a nullable field and a field the server forgot to send are indistinguishable in the same constructor, so there is nothing to assert against. Then the three things a generated model gives you, and each is a specific mechanism. Compile-time completeness in both directions. Add a required field on the server and every model that fails to parse it is a compile error; change a field's type and every call site that used the old type is a compile error. Value equality, because a generated model overrides equality and hashing by field value rather than by identity, which means a widget can compare two models from two parses and correctly decide they are the same — a comparison that is always false with hand-written identity equality, and which is the mechanism behind a state-management layer that rebuilds on every refresh. And copyWith, which produces a new model with one field changed and is both a testability tool and the mechanism that makes immutable update patterns possible at all. Then the three things to decide, and each has a defensible answer. Whether unknown keys are an error or ignored, and the answer is almost always ignored on a client, because a server adding a field should not break shipped clients; but strict parsing is the right choice for an internal service where the two deploy together. Whether numbers are typed as int or double, and this is a real decision: JSON has one number type, so a value of 3 arrives as 3.0 in a strict decoder, and choosing double for every number is the pragmatic answer while choosing int for identifiers and letting the generator cast is the answer that makes the model read correctly. And where the generated file lives. Generated code in source control is greppable and reviewable and needs no build step; generated code ignored by source control cannot be diffed in a pull request, which means a model change is invisible in review — and that is the argument that decides it for most teams. Then the two practices, and both are about the failure the generator cannot catch. Test the model against a captured real response, not a response you constructed from the model, because a fixture built from the model cannot catch a mismatch between the two. And do not pass the raw map further than the model boundary, — the moment a screen reads a map key, the type safety ends and every generation benefit is lost.

/* Why generate. */
const WHY_GENERATE = {
  not: 'THAT HAND-WRITING IS MORE TYPING',
  is: 'THAT HAND-WRITTEN SERIALISATION FAILS IN A SPECIFIC SET of WAYS',
  and: 'EVERY ONE of THOSE WAYS IS A SILENT WRONG VALUE rather than A CRASH',
};
const HAND_WRITTEN_FAILS = [
  { f: 'READS EACH KEY IT KNOWS and IGNORES the REST',
    symptom: 'A FIELD ADDED ON the SERVER IS SILENTLY DROPPED UNTIL SOMEONE NOTICES the MISSING VALUE',
    generated: 'a GENERATED ONE PRODUCES A COMPILE ERROR when the FIELD IS REQUIRED and ABSENT FROM the MODEL',
    and: 'WHICH IS the ONLY VERSION of this BUG THAT IS FREE' },
  { f: 'TAKES A MAP and CASTS',
    detail: ['so a NUMBER ARRIVES AS A DOUBLE where AN INT WAS EXPECTED',
      'A NESTED OBJECT ARRIVES AS A MAP where A MODEL WAS EXPECTED',
      'and A NULL ARRIVES WHERE A VALUE WAS EXPECTED'],
    consequence: 'ALL of WHICH PRODUCE A MODEL THAT IS the RIGHT SHAPE and the WRONG CONTENTS, and NONE of WHICH THROWS' },
  { f: 'CANNOT KNOW WHICH FIELDS ARE REQUIRED',
    why: 'BECAUSE IT HAS NO SEPARATE DECLARATION',
    so: 'A NULLABLE FIELD and A FIELD the SERVER FORGOT TO SEND ARE INDISTINGUISHABLE IN the SAME CONSTRUCTOR',
    consequence: 'SO THERE IS NOTHING to ASSERT AGAINST' },
];

/* What generation gives. */
const GIVES = [
  { g: 'COMPILE-TIME COMPLETENESS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS',
    detail: ['ADD A REQUIRED FIELD ON the SERVER and EVERY MODEL THAT FAILS TO PARSE IT IS A COMPILE ERROR',
      'CHANGE A FIELDS TYPE and EVERY CALL SITE THAT USED the OLD TYPE IS A COMPILE ERROR'] },
  { g: 'VALUE EQUALITY',
    detail: 'BECAUSE A GENERATED MODEL OVERRIDES EQUALITY and HASHING BY FIELD VALUE rather than BY IDENTITY',
    gain: 'so A WIDGET CAN COMPARE TWO MODELS FROM TWO PARSES and CORRECTLY DECIDE THEY ARE the SAME',
    comparison: 'A COMPARISON THAT IS ALWAYS FALSE WITH HAND-WRITTEN IDENTITY EQUALITY',
    symptom: 'and WHICH IS the MECHANISM BEHIND A STATE-MANAGEMENT LAYER THAT REBUILDS ON EVERY REFRESH' },
  { g: 'copyWith', produces: 'A NEW MODEL WITH ONE FIELD CHANGED',

];

/* Three decisions. */
const DECISIONS = [
  { d: 'WHETHER UNKNOWN KEYS ARE AN ERROR or IGNORED',
    answer: 'ALMOST ALWAYS IGNORED ON A CLIENT, BECAUSE A SERVER ADDING A FIELD SHOULD NOT BREAK SHIPPED CLIENTS',
    strictFor: 'AN INTERNAL SERVICE WHERE the TWO DEPLOY TOGETHER' },
  { d: 'WHETHER NUMBERS ARE TYPED AS INT or DOUBLE',

    pragmatic: 'CHOOSING DOUBLE for EVERY NUMBER',
    readable: 'CHOOSING INT for IDENTIFIERS and LETTING the GENERATOR CAST IS the ANSWER THAT MAKES the MODEL READ CORRECTLY' },
  { d: 'WHERE the GENERATED FILE LIVES',
    committed: ['GENERATED CODE IN SOURCE CONTROL IS GREPPABLE and REVIEWABLE and NEEDS NO BUILD STEP'],
    ignored: ['GENERATED CODE IGNORED BY SOURCE CONTROL CANNOT BE DIFFED IN A PULL REQUEST',

const PRACTICES = [

    why: 'BECAUSE A FIXTURE BUILT FROM the MODEL CANNOT CATCH A MISMATCH BETWEEN the TWO' },
  { p: 'do NOT PASS the RAW MAP FURTHER THAN the MODEL BOUNDARY',

12.6 Value types with freezed

// pubspec.yaml
//   freezed_annotation: ^2.4.0
//   json_annotation: ^4.9.0
// dev_dependencies:
//   freezed: ^2.4.0
//   json_serializable: ^6.8.0

// WHAT freezed GENERATES, from one annotation
import 'package:freezed_annotation/freezed_annotation.dart';

part 'entry.freezed.dart';
part 'entry.g.dart';

@freezed
abstract class Entry with _$Entry {
  const factory Entry({
    required String id,
    required String title,
    @Default('') String body,
    @Default(<String>[]) List<String> tags,
    @Default(0) int serverVersion,
    @Default(false) bool archived,
    DateTime? syncedAt,
  }) = _Entry;

  // COPYWITH, with correct nullable handling
  // entry.copyWith(photoUrl: null) CLEARS it, because freezed
  // uses a sentinel. This is the thing a hand-written copyWith
  // gets wrong.
  factory Entry.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) =>
      _$EntryFromJson(json);
}

extension type EntryList._(List<Entry> _) {
  // an extension type gives you methods on a List without
  // changing the type: list.entriesOverdue works, and it is
  // still a List<Entry>
  int get overdueCount => _.where((e) => e.isOverdue).length;
}

// THE GENERATED API
final a = Entry(id: '1', title: 'Note');
final b = a.copyWith(title: 'Changed');
final c = a.copyWith(photoUrl: null);   // CLEARS, which is the point

a == b;                       // false
a == Entry(id: '1', title: 'Note');   // TRUE: value equality
hashCode;                     // consistent with ==
toString();                   // 'Entry(id: 1, title: Note, ...)'
// and the STATE: it is genuinely immutable, and the compiler
// enforces it

// THE SEALED VARIANT, which is where freezed is at its best
@freezed
sealed class EntryResult with _$EntryResult {
  const factory EntryResult.success(Entry entry) = EntrySuccess;
  const factory EntryResult.failure(Failure failure) = EntryFailure;
}

// which gives you an exhaustive switch, like a hand-written
// sealed class, with none of the boilerplate
final label = switch (result) {
  EntrySuccess(:final entry) => entry.title,
  EntryFailure(:final failure) => failure.message,
};

// run
// dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
// THE WORKAROUND for a hand-written copyWith that must
// distinguish "not passed" from "passed null"
class Entry2 {
  const Entry2({required this.id, required this.title, this.photoUrl});

  final String id;
  final String title;
  final String? photoUrl;

  // the sentinel: a private object that means "not provided"
  static const _unset = Object();

  Entry2 copyWith({
    String? id,
    String? title,
    Object? photoUrl = _unset,     // not String?
  }) {
    return Entry2(
      id: id ?? this.id,
      title: title ?? this.title,
      // the check: only replace if it was actually passed
      photoUrl: identical(photoUrl, _unset) ? this.photoUrl : photoUrl as String?,
    );
  }
}

// this is exactly what freezed generates. If you are hand-writing
// it, use freezed.

Sealed types, unions, and what pattern matching buys

The freezed-style generator is a code generator for immutable value types that adds one thing the others do not: a sealed union of cases, with pattern matching that is checked at compile time. That is worth understanding on its own terms, because the benefit is not the boilerplate removal — it is that it makes an illegal state unrepresentable and makes a switch over a closed set of states exhaustive. A sealed union is a type with a finite set of permitted subclasses, known to the compiler, so a function that takes one and returns something depending on which case it is can be written as an exhaustive switch — and if a new case is added to the union without a case in the switch, the code does not compile. That is the whole mechanism and its value is entirely in the compile error. Then the three cases where it is worth it, and each is a state machine that already exists in the application. A network result. Loading, data, failure — three cases, and a screen that renders it with a switch rather than with three booleans cannot render an impossible combination such as loading-and-error. A form's validation state per field. Untouched, valid, invalid, with the reason attached to the case rather than stored separately, which is what removes the class of bug where a field shows an error with no error text. And A permission or a feature-flag outcome, which is a small union that appears in many places and where a boolean pair would allow an impossible third state. Then the three costs, and each is a real consideration. It is more code generated than the plain models. Freezing generates the class, the copy method, equality and, for a union, one class per case — so a five-case union is six classes, and the generated file is long. Pattern matching needs a language feature or a generated matcher, and the ergonomics differ; a project that is not already using pattern matching in Dart will find the switch statement verbose. And an exhaustive switch stops being exhaustive the moment a case is handled by a default branch, which is the common way the benefit is lost — a default that returns a placeholder converts a compile-time guarantee into a runtime one. Then the three rules for using it well, and each is a specific practice. Never put a default branch on a sealed union. That is the single rule, and the reason is that the default is exactly where the compile-time check disappears; a switch with no default over a sealed type is exhaustive by construction. Put the payload in the case, not beside it. An error case that carries the message means the message cannot be absent; an error flag beside an error message field means it can. And prefer exhaustive maps over switches for large unions, because a map from case to result is data and can be composed, whereas a switch with twenty arms is control flow that has to be read. Then the two things to weigh, because the decision is real. How many of these unions will the application actually have, — a project with two of them has added a dependency and a codegen step for two compile errors, and a project with thirty has removed a large amount of repetitive code and an entire class of impossible state. And whether the team's Dart version supports the pattern-matching syntax, because if it does not the ergonomic advantage largely evaporates and only the exhaustive-switch guarantee remains, which is still real but is a smaller prize than it looks in a feature description.

/* The mechanism. */
const MECHANISM = {
  adds: 'A SEALED UNION of CASES, WITH PATTERN MATCHING THAT IS CHECKED AT COMPILE TIME',
  benefitIsNot: 'the BOILERPLATE REMOVAL',
  benefitIs: 'THAT IT MAKES AN ILLEGAL STATE UNREPRESENTABLE and MAKES A SWITCH OVER A CLOSED SET of STATES EXHAUSTIVE',
  union: 'A TYPE with A FINITE SET of PERMITTED SUBCLASSES, KNOWN TO the COMPILER',
  therefore: 'a FUNCTION THAT TAKES ONE and RETURNS SOMETHING DEPENDING ON WHICH CASE IT IS CAN BE WRITTEN AS AN EXHAUSTIVE SWITCH',
  gain: 'and IF A NEW CASE IS ADDED TO the UNION WITHOUT A CASE IN the SWITCH, the CODE DOES NOT COMPILE',
  and: 'THAT IS the WHOLE MECHANISM and ITS VALUE IS ENTIRELY IN the COMPILE ERROR',
};

/* Three cases worth it. */
const WORTH_IT = [
  { c: 'A NETWORK RESULT', cases: ['LOADING', 'DATA', 'FAILURE'],
    gain: 'A SCREEN THAT RENDERS IT WITH A SWITCH rather than WITH THREE BOOLEANS CANNOT RENDER AN IMPOSSIBLE COMBINATION SUCH AS LOADING-AND-ERROR' },
  { c: 'A FORMS VALIDATION STATE PER FIELD', cases: ['UNTOUCHED', 'VALID', 'INVALID'],
    gain: 'WITH the REASON ATTACHED TO the CASE rather than STORED SEPARATELY',
    removes: 'which IS WHAT REMOVES the CLASS OF BUG WHERE A FIELD SHOWS AN ERROR WITH NO ERROR TEXT' },
  { c: 'A PERMISSION or A FEATURE-FLAG OUTCOME',
    detail: 'which IS A SMALL UNION THAT APPEARS IN MANY PLACES',
    and: 'WHERE A BOOLEAN PAIR WOULD ALLOW AN IMPOSSIBLE THIRD STATE' },
];

/* Three costs. */
const COSTS = [
  { c: 'IT IS MORE CODE GENERATED THAN the PLAIN MODELS',
    detail: 'FREEZING GENERATES the CLASS, the COPY METHOD, EQUALITY and, FOR A UNION, ONE CLASS PER CASE',
    arithmetic: 'so a FIVE-CASE UNION IS SIX CLASSES, and the GENERATED FILE IS LONG' },
  { c: 'PATTERN MATCHING NEEDS A LANGUAGE FEATURE or A GENERATED MATCHER',
    detail: 'and the ERGONOMICS DIFFER',
    symptom: 'A PROJECT THAT IS NOT ALREADY USING PATTERN MATCHING IN DART WILL FIND the SWITCH STATEMENT VERBOSE' },
  { c: 'AN EXHAUSTIVE SWITCH STOPS BEING EXHAUSTIVE the MOMENT A CASE IS HANDLED BY A DEFAULT BRANCH',
    detail: 'WHICH IS the COMMON WAY the BENEFIT IS LOST',
    consequence: 'A DEFAULT THAT RETURNS A PLACEHOLDER CONVERTS A COMPILE-TIME GUARANTEE INTO A RUNTIME ONE' },
];

/* Three rules. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'NEVER PUT A DEFAULT BRANCH ON A SEALED UNION',
    why: 'THAT IS the SINGLE RULE',
    reason: 'and the REASON IS THAT the DEFAULT IS EXACTLY WHERE the COMPILE-TIME CHECK DISAPPEARS',
    practice: 'A SWITCH WITH NO DEFAULT OVER A SEALED TYPE IS EXHAUSTIVE BY CONSTRUCTION' },
  { r: 'PUT the PAYLOAD IN the CASE, not BESIDE IT',
    good: 'AN ERROR CASE THAT CARRIES the MESSAGE MEANS the MESSAGE CANNOT BE ABSENT',
    bad: 'AN ERROR FLAG BESIDE AN ERROR MESSAGE FIELD MEANS IT CAN' },
  { r: 'PREFER EXHAUSTIVE MAPS OVER SWITCHES for LARGE UNIONS',
    why: 'BECAUSE A MAP FROM CASE TO RESULT IS DATA and CAN BE COMPOSED',
    whereas: 'A SWITCH WITH TWENTY ARMS IS CONTROL FLOW THAT HAS TO BE READ' },
];

/* Two things to weigh. */
const WEIGH = [
  { w: 'HOW MANY of THESE UNIONS WILL the APPLICATION ACTUALLY HAVE',
    few: 'A PROJECT with TWO of THEM HAS ADDED A DEPENDENCY and A CODEGEN STEP for TWO COMPILE ERRORS',
    many: 'A PROJECT with THIRTY HAS REMOVED A LARGE AMOUNT of REPETITIVE CODE and AN ENTIRE CLASS of IMPOSSIBLE STATE' },
  { w: 'WHETHER the TEAMS DART VERSION SUPPORTS the PATTERN-MATCHING SYNTAX',
    ifNot: 'IF IT DOES NOT the ERGONOMIC ADVANTAGE LARGELY EVAPORATES and ONLY the EXHAUSTIVE-SWITCH GUARANTEE REMAINS',
    verdict: 'WHICH IS STILL REAL but IS A SMALLER PRIZE THAN IT LOOKS IN A FEATURE DESCRIPTION' },
];

12.7 Parsing defensively

Validating on the client, and why it is not the security boundary

Client-side validation is worth doing and it is not a security control, and the reason is worth stating precisely because the two are constantly conflated. A client is under the user's control. The application ships a binary; a determined user can modify the request that the binary makes, intercept it, or call the API directly with a tool. So anything a client validates can be bypassed, and the only enforcement point is the server. What client validation is for is three things, and each is legitimate. It gives immediate feedback before a round trip, which is the difference between a form that feels instant and one that feels broken. It prevents obviously malformed requests, which reduces server load and makes logs readable. And it lets the interface express the rules in a way that is consistent with how the interface is built. Then the three rules for doing it well, and each has a specific failure behind it. Validate at the boundary, once, and keep the result. A form that validates in one place on submit and again in another place on change and a third time before sending has three implementations of the same rule and they will drift; a validator that runs once and produces a result object that the interface reads is one implementation. Do not validate in the widget. Validation logic inside a build method or a field's onChanged is untestable without a widget and unreachable from anywhere else; it belongs in a plain function that takes the value and returns a result. And keep the rules in one place per field. Required, minimum length, format and range are four rules with one source, and the interface should ask the validator rather than also asking itself. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a specific mechanism. Validating only on submit, so the user fills ten fields, submits, and receives ten errors at once — which is the correct behaviour for accessibility and exhausting for a person, and the fix is to validate on blur per field and re-validate on change once a field has been touched. Clearing an error while the user is still typing in the field, which produces the maddening case where the error disappears at the moment the user is fixing it and returns at the moment they leave. And validating a password with a rule the server does not have, or the reverse, which produces a form that accepts a password the server rejects with a message about a rule the user was never shown. Then the two practices, and both are about keeping the client and server in agreement. Derive the validation from the same source as the API contract — an OpenAPI document, a shared schema, generated types — so that a rule added on the server appears on the client rather than being reimplemented; this is the API chapter's contract-first argument in a new place. And have the server return field-level validation errors, keyed by field, so that a submit failure populates the same error map the client computed locally; a server that returns one message for a whole form forces the client to guess which field it belonged to, and guessing is wrong.

/* Not a security control. */
const NOT_SECURITY = {
  reason: 'A CLIENT IS UNDER the USERS CONTROL',
  detail: ['the APPLICATION SHIPS A BINARY', 'a DETERMINED USER CAN MODIFY the REQUEST THAT the BINARY MAKES, INTERCEPT IT, or CALL the API DIRECTLY WITH a TOOL'],
  so: 'ANYTHING A CLIENT VALIDATES CAN BE BYPASSED, and the ONLY ENFORCEMENT POINT IS the SERVER',
};

/* Three legitimate reasons. */
const FOR = [
  { r: 'IMMEDIATE FEEDBACK BEFORE A ROUND TRIP', gain: 'WHICH IS the DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A FORM THAT FEELS INSTANT and ONE THAT FEELS BROKEN' },
  { r: 'PREVENTING OBVIOUSLY MALFORMED REQUESTS', gain: 'WHICH REDUCES SERVER LOAD and MAKES LOGS READABLE' },
  { r: 'EXPRESSING the RULES IN A WAY THAT IS CONSISTENT with HOW the INTERFACE IS BUILT' },
];

/* Three rules. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'VALIDATE AT the BOUNDARY, ONCE, and KEEP the RESULT',
    bug: 'A FORM THAT VALIDATES IN ONE PLACE ON SUBMIT and AGAIN IN ANOTHER PLACE ON CHANGE and A THIRD TIME BEFORE SENDING HAS THREE IMPLEMENTATIONS of the SAME RULE',
    consequence: 'and THEY WILL DRIFT',
    fix: 'A VALIDATOR THAT RUNS ONCE and PRODUCES A RESULT OBJECT THAT the INTERFACE READS IS ONE IMPLEMENTATION' },

    why: ['VALIDATION LOGIC INSIDE A BUILD METHOD or a FIELDS onChanged IS UNTESTABLE WITHOUT A WIDGET',
      'and UNREACHABLE FROM ANYWHERE ELSE'],
    fix: 'it BELONGS IN A PLAIN FUNCTION THAT TAKES the VALUE and RETURNS A RESULT' },
  { r: 'KEEP the RULES IN ONE PLACE PER FIELD',
    list: ['REQUIRED', 'MINIMUM LENGTH', 'FORMAT', 'RANGE'],
    fact: 'WHICH ARE FOUR RULES WITH ONE SOURCE',
    and: 'the INTERFACE SHOULD ASK the VALIDATOR rather than ALSO ASKING ITSELF' },
];

/* Three things that go wrong. */
const GO_WRONG = [
  { f: 'VALIDATING ONLY ON SUBMIT',
    symptom: 'so the USER FILLS TEN FIELDS, SUBMITS, and RECEIVES TEN ERRORS AT ONCE',
    correct: 'WHICH IS the CORRECT BEHAVIOUR for ACCESSIBILITY',
    exhausting: 'and EXHAUSTING for A PERSON',
    fix: 'VALIDATE ON BLUR PER FIELD and RE-VALIDATE ON CHANGE ONCE A FIELD HAS BEEN TOUCHED' },
  { f: 'CLEARING AN ERROR WHILE the USER IS STILL TYPING IN the FIELD',
    symptom: 'WHICH PRODUCES the MADDENING CASE WHERE the ERROR DISAPPEARS AT the MOMENT the USER IS FIXING IT and RETURNS AT the MOMENT THEY LEAVE' },
  { f: 'VALIDATING A PASSWORD WITH A RULE the SERVER DOES NOT HAVE, OR the REVERSE',
    symptom: 'WHICH PRODUCES A FORM THAT ACCEPTS A PASSWORD the SERVER REJECTS with A MESSAGE about A RULE the USER WAS NEVER SHOWN' },

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'DERIVE the VALIDATION FROM the SAME SOURCE as the API CONTRACT',
    sources: ['AN OPENAPI DOCUMENT', 'A SHARED SCHEMA', 'GENERATED TYPES'],
    gain: 'so THAT A RULE ADDED ON the SERVER APPEARS ON the CLIENT rather than BEING REIMPLEMENTED',
    connects: 'which IS the API CHAPTERS CONTRACT-FIRST ARGUMENT IN A NEW PLACE' },
  { p: 'HAVE the SERVER RETURN FIELD-LEVEL VALIDATION ERRORS, KEYED BY FIELD',
    gain: 'so THAT A SUBMIT FAILURE POPULATES the SAME ERROR MAP the CLIENT COMPUTED LOCALLY',
    and: 'A SERVER THAT RETURNS ONE MESSAGE FOR A WHOLE FORM FORCES the CLIENT TO GUESS WHICH FIELD it BELONGED TO',
    verdict: 'and GUESSING IS WRONG' },
];

A strict parser turns a server deploy into a crash for every user at once, in production, with no way to recover. Parse leniently at the boundary, log the payload when it fails, and fall back to something usable - a stale cached record is far better than an error screen.

// THE PROBLEM: json_serializable throws if a field has the wrong
// type. A server deploy that changes a type breaks the app for
// everyone, at runtime, with a crash.

// 1. THE STRICT MODE: fail loudly, and handle it
try {
  final entry = Entry.fromJson(json);
} on FormatException catch (e) {
  // log it, with the payload, so you can see what changed
  log.warning('Entry parse failed', error: e, data: json);
  // and fall back to something usable
  return Entry.malformed(id: json['id'] as String? ?? 'unknown');
}

// 2. THE LENIENT MODE: tolerate what you can
class LenientEntry {
  const LenientEntry({
    required this.id,
    this.title = '',
    this.body = '',
    this.createdAt,
  });

  factory LenientEntry.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) {
    // every field is defensive, and defaults are sane
    return LenientEntry(
      id: json['id'] as String? ?? 'unknown',
      // a number that arrived as a string
      title: switch (json['title']) {
        final String s => s,
        final num n => n.toString(),
        _ => '',
      },
      // an ISO string, an epoch int, or missing
      createdAt: switch (json['createdAt']) {
        final String s => DateTime.tryParse(s),
        final int epoch => DateTime.fromMillisecondsSinceEpoch(epoch),
        _ => null,
      },
    );
  }
}

// 3. VALIDATE AT THE BOUNDARY, with a schema library
// pubspec.yaml
//   json_schema: ^5.0.1

final entrySchema = Schema.fromJson({
  r'type': 'object',
  r'required': ['id', 'title', 'createdAt'],
  r'properties': {
    'id': {r'type': 'string', r'minLength': 1},
    'title': {r'type': 'string', r'maxLength': 200},
    'body': {r'type': 'string'},
    'createdAt': {r'type': 'string', r'format': 'date-time'},
  },
  r'additionalProperties': true,   // or false, to be strict
});

final validation = entrySchema.validate(json);
if (!validation.isValid) {
  log.warning('schema violation', problems: validation.problems);
}

// 4. AND THE SERVER SHOULD VALIDATE TOO
// Dart-side validation is for your own robustness. The server
// is the authority, and it should reject a bad payload with a
// 422 and a field-level error, not crash
// THE PRODUCTION PATTERN: a boundary that cannot crash
class SafeApi {
  SafeApi(this._dio);
  final Dio _dio;

  Future<T> _get<T>(
    String path, {
    required T Function(Map<String, dynamic> json) parse,
    T Function()? fallback,
  }) async {
    try {
      final response = await _dio.get<Map<String, dynamic>>(path);

      // 1. the shape is right
      if (response.data == null) {
        return fallback?.call() ?? (throw const ParseFailure());
      }

      // 2. the parse succeeds
      return parse(response.data!);
    } on FormatException catch (e) {
      // 3. it did not, and we know exactly why
      CrashReporter.report(e, context: {'path': path, 'data': response.data});
      if (fallback != null) return fallback();
      rethrow;
    } on DioException catch (e) {
      throw mapDioException(e);
    }
  }

  Future<Entry> entry(String id, {Entry? cached}) {
    return _get(
      '/entries/$id',
      parse: Entry.fromJson,
      fallback: cached == null ? null : () => cached,   // stale is better than an error
    );
  }
}

12.8 Uploads and downloads

// AN UPLOAD WITH PROGRESS, and a cancellation
Future<String> uploadPhoto(File file) async {
  final token = CancelToken();
  final completer = Completer<String>();

  final form = FormData.fromMap({
    'file': await MultipartFile.fromFile(
      file.path,
      filename: file.uri.pathSegments.last,
    ),
  });

  try {
    final response = await dio.post<Map<String, dynamic>>(
      '/uploads',
      data: form,
      cancelToken: token,
      onSendProgress: (sent, total) {
        if (total > 0) {
          uploadProgress.value = sent / total;   // a ValueNotifier
        }
      },
    );
    completer.complete(response.data!['url'] as String);
  } on DioException catch (e) {
    if (CancelToken.isCancel(e)) {
      completer.completeError(const UploadCancelled());
    } else {
      completer.completeError(mapDioException(e));
    }
  }
  return completer.future;
}

// RESUMING A LARGE UPLOAD
// chunked, with a record of what has been sent, so a failure
// does not start from zero
class ChunkedUploader {
  Future<String> upload(File file) async {
    const chunkSize = 1024 * 1024 * 2;   // 2MB chunks
    final total = await file.length();
    final totalChunks = (total / chunkSize).ceil();

    // 1. tell the server we are starting
    final session = await dio.post<Map<String, dynamic>>('/uploads', data: {
      'filename': file.uri.pathSegments.last,
      'size': total,
      'chunks': totalChunks,
    });
    final uploadId = session.data!['id'] as String;
    final alreadySent = (session.data!['received'] as List).cast<int>().toSet();

    // 2. send the missing chunks
    for (var i = 0; i < totalChunks; i++) {
      if (alreadySent.contains(i)) continue;

      final start = i * chunkSize;
      final end = min(start + chunkSize, total);
      final handle = await file.open();
      final bytes = await handle.read(end - start);
      await handle.close();

      try {
        await dio.post('/uploads/$uploadId/chunks/$i', data: Stream.fromIterable([bytes]));
      } on DioException {
        // 3. a failure: STOP and report. the session record
        //    means a retry skips what already arrived
        rethrow;
      }
      uploadProgress.value = (i + 1) / totalChunks;
    }

    // 4. finalise
    await dio.post('/uploads/$uploadId/complete');
    return '/uploads/$uploadId';
  }
}

// A DOWNLOAD, written to a file so a large one does not sit in
// memory
await dio.download(
  url,
  filePath,
  onReceiveProgress: (received, total) => progress.value = received / total,
  deleteOnError: true,       // do not leave a partial file
  options: Options(retryEvaluator: (attempt, error) => attempt < 3),
);

Uploads, and why they are a different problem from downloads

A file upload is a different problem from a download in five ways, and each of them breaks the download pattern, which is why uploads are where mobile networking code goes wrong. The request body is a stream, not a value, so it cannot be retried by re-sending the same object — retrying means finding the body again, which for a file means re-opening it. It is large, so it takes time and so a timeout that was reasonable for a query is not reasonable here. It can fail partway through, so a failure at ninety per cent has already transferred ninety per cent and the naive retry starts from zero. It is often not idempotent, because a server that receives a file usually creates something. And it is often the user's only copy, which means the failure is not a failed request but a lost photograph, and that changes the engineering entirely. Then the three mechanisms, and they compose. Chunked or resumable upload is the answer to the size problem and the partway problem together: the client sends the file in chunks, the server records which chunks it has, and a retry sends only the missing ones — so the client must keep the file path and be able to re-open it, which is why a cancelled upload is not simply forgotten but resumable. Multipart requests, which is how a file and its metadata travel together, and which requires the boundary and the headers to be correct or the server cannot parse the parts — a hand-rolled multipart body is a common source of a server that responds with a generic four hundred and no detail. And the platform's file picker, which returns a path or a content URI and which on some platforms is a temporary copy that is deleted when the process ends, which means an upload that continues after the app is backgrounded must have copied the bytes somewhere the app owns. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a specific mechanism. Reading the whole file into memory, which on a modern phone with a forty-megapixel photograph is a hundred megabytes of decoded pixels or at minimum a large byte array, and the failure is an out-of-memory crash on exactly the devices least able to afford it. Uploading on the main isolate, which blocks the UI and produces the freeze the framework's own build system warns about for large computations. And losing the upload when the app is backgrounded, because the platform may suspend the process and an in-flight request dies with it; the mechanisms for surviving this are a foreground service on Android and a background transfer session, and both are real work rather than a flag. Then the two practices, and each is about the failure that loses data. Copy the file into your own storage before uploading, so that the bytes survive the picker's temporary copy and a process death, and so that the upload can be resumed rather than restarted. And record the upload's intent durably before starting it — the file, the destination, the state — so that an application killed mid-upload can show what happened and can resume, rather than presenting a spinner that will never move again.

12.9 WebSockets

// A WEBSOCKET, with reconnection, which is the part that matters
import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:convert';
import 'package:web_socket_channel/web_socket_channel.dart';

class RealtimeSync {
  RealtimeSync({required this.url, required this.onMessage, required this.onStatusChange});

  final String url;
  final void Function(Map<String, dynamic>) onMessage;
  final void Function(ConnectionStatus) onStatusChange;

  WebSocketChannel? _channel;
  StreamSubscription? _sub;
  Timer? _reconnectTimer;
  int _attempt = 0;
  bool _closedByUs = false;

  static const _maxBackoff = 30;

  void connect() {
    _closedByUs = false;
    onStatusChange(ConnectionStatus.connecting);

    try {
      final channel = WebSocketChannel.connect(Uri.parse(url));
      _channel = channel;

      _sub = channel.stream.listen(
        (data) {
          _attempt = 0;                    // a success resets the backoff
          onStatusChange(ConnectionStatus.connected);
          try {
            onMessage(jsonDecode(data as String) as Map<String, dynamic>);
          } on FormatException catch (e) {
            log.warning('bad websocket payload', error: e, data: data);
          }
        },
        onError: (Object error) {
          onStatusChange(ConnectionStatus.disconnected);
          _scheduleReconnect();
        },
        onDone: () {
          onStatusChange(ConnectionStatus.disconnected);
          _scheduleReconnect();
        },
        cancelOnError: false,
      );
    } catch (e) {
      onStatusChange(ConnectionStatus.disconnected);
      _scheduleReconnect();
    }
  }

  void _scheduleReconnect() {
    if (_closedByUs) return;
    _reconnectTimer?.cancel();

    // EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF WITH JITTER AND A CEILING
    final backoff = min(_maxBackoff, 1 << _attempt);
    final delay = Duration(
      seconds: (backoff * (0.5 + Random().nextDouble() * 0.5)).round(),
    );
    _attempt++;

    _reconnectTimer = Timer(delay, connect);
  }

  void send(Map<String, dynamic> message) {
    _channel?.sink.add(jsonEncode(message));
  }

  Future<void> close() async {
    _closedByUs = true;
    _reconnectTimer?.cancel();
    await _sub?.cancel();
    await _channel?.sink.close();
  }
}

// THE LIFECYCLE, which is mandatory: a socket left open in the
// background is a battery and a crash
final sync = RealtimeSync(url: 'wss://api.acme.com/ws', onMessage: handle, onStatusChange: setStatus);

class RealtimeManager with WidgetsBindingObserver {
  @override
  void didChangeAppLifecycleState(AppLifecycleState state) {
    switch (state) {
      case AppLifecycleState.resumed:
        sync.connect();
      case AppLifecycleState.paused:
      case AppLifecycleState.detached:
      case AppLifecycleState.hidden:
        sync.close();     // do not hold a socket in the background
      case AppLifecycleState.inactive:
        break;
    }
  }
}

// THE STATUS, shown to the user
// an app that silently stops syncing looks broken
if (status == ConnectionStatus.disconnected) {
  Row(children: [
    Icon(Icons.cloud_off, size: 16, color: Colors.orange),
    Text('Reconnecting…', style: TextStyle(color: Colors.orange)),
  ]);
}

WebSockets, and the four things that make them hard on a phone

A WebSocket is a long-lived bidirectional connection, and on a phone it is a genuinely different problem from an HTTP request because the network under the device is not the network the application thinks it is. The connection will drop, and not because the server closed it — because the user walked into a lift, the radio was handed off, or the platform suspended the application. A dropped connection must be detected and re-established, and the detection is the first difficulty because there is no event when the network is merely gone; the socket stays open at the operating-system level while packets go nowhere, and the failure only becomes visible when a write eventually times out. So the application needs a liveness check of its own — a heartbeat message in both directions with a deadline, so that a connection that has stopped delivering is declared dead and replaced rather than silently accumulating as an apparently-live connection that receives nothing. Then the four difficulties, and each has a specific mechanism. Reconnection is not free, and naive reconnection causes a thundering herd. Every client that was connected drops at the same moment — a server restart, a deploy, a network outage — and every one reconnects immediately; exponential backoff with jitter, the networking chapter's mechanism, is what turns that into a staggered recovery. Messages can be lost or reordered across a reconnect, so anything that matters needs a sequence number or an acknowledgement, and the client needs to know what it missed — which means the server has to be able to say "here is everything since this point", and a server that does not have that cannot offer a reconnect that preserves state. The battery cost is real. A socket that is open keeps the radio awake, and a radio kept awake drains a battery in hours; the mechanisms are to close the connection when the application is backgrounded unless the application genuinely needs to receive, and to use the platform's background transfer or push notification mechanisms rather than a persistent socket. And the lifecycle is coupled to the widget in every implementation that is not careful. A socket opened in a build method or held by a widget that is disposed leaves a connection the application no longer owns. Then the three practices, and each is a specific discipline. Own the connection in a service, not in a widget, so that navigation does not connect and disconnect it and so that there is exactly one place that decides when the connection should be open — which is the same ownership argument as the persistence chapter's repository. Model reconnection explicitly as a state machine — disconnected, connecting, connected, backing-off — because the alternative is a boolean that is wrong in the interesting case, and the states are what make the exponential backoff and the heartbeat expressible. And use the platform's push mechanism for anything the user must be told about, rather than a socket, because a push notification is delivered when the application is not running and a socket is not, and the battery and reliability arguments both point the same way.

/* The core difficulty. */
const WHY_HARD = {

Exercises 13

  1. Build an EntryApi with Dio and four interceptors: auth, logging, offline and retry. Verify the retry only fires for 5xx and timeouts.
  2. Write a sealed Failure hierarchy and a Dio-to-Failure mapper, then handle it with an exhaustive switch in the UI.
  3. Implement a search box with cancellation, and confirm a slow earlier response never overwrites a newer one.
  4. Convert a hand-written model to json_serializable, then to freezed, and confirm copyWith can clear a nullable field.
  5. Write a lenient parser that tolerates a number arriving as a string and a date as an epoch int, and test both.
  6. Build a chunked upload that resumes from a partial session, and prove it skips the chunks that already arrived.
  7. Add a WebSocket with exponential backoff, connect it on resume and close it on pause, and verify the battery does not drain.

13.1 Platform channels

What a channel actually is, and why the boundary leaks

A platform channel is a named pipe between Dart and a host language, and the single most important fact about it is that the two sides are not type-checked against each other. A method channel sends a method name and an argument map; the host side looks up the name in a handler map and calls a function. There is no shared type, no generated interface and no compile-time check that the name on the Dart side is the name the host registered. A method name that exists on one side and not the other fails at run time, with a missing-plugin or missing-implementation exception, and it fails on the device rather than in the build — which is the single most common defect in platform-channel code and the reason the first rule below exists. Then the four things the boundary leaks, and each has a specific consequence. Names must match exactly, including case, and a typo is a run-time failure in a place where the compiler is silent. The argument map is dynamic, so a host function that expects a string and receives an integer will either throw its own type error or coerce it, and Dart has no way to know. The return value is dynamic, so a host function that returns a map when Dart expects a list produces a cast error at the point of use rather than at the call. And errors cross the boundary as strings, so a host exception becomes a PlatformException with a code and a message and no stack, which means an error that is diagnosable in the host is nearly undiagnosable in Dart. Then the four practices, and each is a requirement rather than a preference. Use one constant for the channel name and one for each method name, defined once and imported by both sides. The host side cannot import the Dart constant, so the mechanism is a generated file or a maintained pair that a test asserts are identical; without that, the two lists drift and the failure appears on a device. Make every method return a typed Dart object at the boundary, by wrapping the raw dynamic in a parsing function that throws a named exception when the shape is wrong — which converts a cast error in a screen into a clear failure in one place. Catch platform exceptions where they can be acted on, and translate them into domain errors, so the rest of the application never sees a platform code. And test the channel against a fake host, which is easy because the channel is just a name and a codec: a test that drives the Dart side with a fake implementation catches every name mismatch and shape error without a device. Then the two things worth knowing about the cost, because they decide whether a channel is the right tool. A channel call is a message and a thread hop, so it is not free and a loop that calls a channel method a thousand times is a thousand message hops; if you are calling in a loop, the answer is usually to call once and return a list. And the codec is what determines what you can send, — the standard codec sends null, bool, int, double, string, byte arrays, lists and maps of those, and anything else needs either a custom codec or a serialisation step inside those types; this is why a native object cannot simply be passed and why the "pass a map" convention exists.

/* What a channel is. */

};

Keep the channel name in one constant and use it on both sides. A typo produces MissingPluginException at runtime with a message that does not mention the typo, and it is the single most common platform channel bug.

// THREE KINDS, and which to use
//
// MethodChannel        request/response: "take a photo", "get the
//                      battery level". The default choice.
//   invokeMethod('name', arguments) -> a Future
//
// EventChannel          native to Dart, a stream: a sensor
//                      reading, a barcode scan, an incoming call
//   receiveBroadcastStream() -> a Stream
//
// BasicMessageChannel   raw, for a high-frequency or custom
//                      protocol. Rarely the right choice.
//
// THE NAME MUST BE THE SAME ON BOTH SIDES
// a typo produces "MissingPluginException" at runtime, not at
// compile time. Use a constant shared by both sides.

13.2 MethodChannel in detail

// THE DART SIDE
import 'package:flutter/services.dart';

class Battery {
  // a single instance, not a new channel per call
  static const _channel = MethodChannel('com.acme.fieldnotes/battery');

  static Future<int> level() async {
    final level = await _channel.invokeMethod<int>('getBatteryLevel');
    if (level == null) throw const BatteryUnavailable();
    return level;
  }

  static Future<bool> isCharging() async {
    return await _channel.invokeMethod<bool>('isCharging') ?? false;
  }

  static Future<void> setLowPowerMode(bool enabled) async {
    await _channel.invokeMethod('setLowPowerMode', {'enabled': enabled});
  }
}

// error handling: an error on the native side arrives as a
// PlatformException here
try {
  await Battery.level();
} on PlatformException catch (e) {
  // e.code    a string you defined, e.g. 'UNAVAILABLE'
  // e.message a human-readable message
  // e.details  any extra data
  log.error('battery failed', code: e.code, message: e.message);
} on MissingPluginException {
  // the native side is not registered: a build problem
}

// THE KOTLIN SIDE
// android/app/src/main/kotlin/com/acme/fieldnotes/MainActivity.kt
package com.acme.fieldnotes

import android.content.Intent
import android.content.IntentFilter
import android.os.BatteryManager
import io.flutter.embedding.android.FlutterActivity
import io.flutter.embedding.engine.FlutterEngine
import io.flutter.plugin.common.MethodCall
import io.flutter.plugin.common.MethodChannel

class MainActivity : FlutterActivity() {
    private val CHANNEL = "com.acme.fieldnotes/battery"

    override fun configureFlutterEngine(flutterEngine: FlutterEngine) {
        super.configureFlutterEngine(flutterEngine)

        MethodChannel(flutterEngine.dartExecutor.binaryMessenger, CHANNEL)
            .setMethodCallHandler { call, result ->
                when (call.method) {
                    "getBatteryLevel" -> result.success(getBatteryLevel())
                    "isCharging" -> result.success(isCharging())
                    else -> result.notImplemented()
                    // THE ELSE IS REQUIRED: an unhandled method
                    // must be reported, or the Dart side hangs
                }
            }
    }

    private fun getBatteryLevel(): Int {
        val bm = getSystemService(BATTERY_SERVICE) as BatteryManager
        return bm.getIntProperty(BatteryManager.BATTERY_PROPERTY_CAPACITY)
    }

    private fun isCharging(): Boolean {
        val intent: Intent = registerReceiver(
            null, IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED)
        ) ?: return false
        val status = intent.getIntExtra(BatteryManager.EXTRA_STATUS, -1)
        return status == BatteryManager.BATTERY_STATUS_CHARGING
    }
}
// THE SWIFT SIDE
// ios/Runner/AppDelegate.swift
import Flutter
import UIKit

@main
@objc class AppDelegate: FlutterAppDelegate {
    private let batteryChannelName = "com.acme.fieldnotes/battery"

    override func application(
        _ application: UIApplication,
        didFinishLaunchingWithOptions launchOptions: [UIApplication.LaunchOptionsKey: Any]?
    ) -> Bool {
        // in Swift 5 / Flutter 3.x, the standard way:
        let controller = window?.rootViewController as! FlutterViewController
        let channel = FlutterMethodChannel(
            name: batteryChannelName,
            binaryMessenger: controller.binaryMessenger
        )

        channel.setMethodCallHandler { [weak self] call, result in
            guard let self = self else { return }

            UIDevice.current.isBatteryMonitoringEnabled = true

            switch call.method {
            case "getBatteryLevel":
                let level = UIDevice.current.batteryLevel   // -1 if unknown
                if level < 0 {
                    result(FlutterError(
                        code: "UNAVAILABLE",
                        message: "Battery monitoring is not available",
                        details: nil
                    ))
                } else {
                    result(Int(level * 100))
                }

            case "isCharging":
                let state = UIDevice.current.batteryState
                result(state == .charging || state == .full)

            case "setLowPowerMode":
                // iOS has no public API for this: the app cannot
                // change the system low-power mode
                result(FlutterError(
                    code: "UNSUPPORTED",
                    message: "Not available on iOS",
                    details: nil
                ))

            default:
                result(FlutterMethodNotImplemented)
                // REQUIRED, or the Dart Future never completes
            }
        }

        GeneratedPluginRegistrant.register(with: self)
        return super.application(application, didFinishLaunchingWithOptions: launchOptions)
    }
}
// SENDING AN ERROR, which is how you reject
// Kotlin
result.error(
    "PERMISSION_DENIED",
    "Camera permission is required",
    mapOf("code" to 401)
)

// Swift
result(FlutterError(
    code: "PERMISSION_DENIED",
    message: "Camera permission is required",
    details: ["code": 401]
))

// and Dart
try {
  await Camera.take();
} on PlatformException catch (e) {
  switch (e.code) {
    case 'PERMISSION_DENIED': showPermissionDialog();
    case 'UNAVAILABLE': showUnsupported();
    default: showError(e.message);
  }
}

// THE TYPES THAT CROSS THE CHANNEL
//   Dart            native
//   null            null / NSNull
//   bool            Boolean / bool
//   int             Int32 / Int64 / NSNumber / int
//   double          Double / NSNumber / double
//   String          String / NSString
//   Uint8List       ByteArray / FlutterStandardTypedData / Data
//   List            Array / NSArray
//   Map             HashMap / NSDictionary
//   <platform type>  the platform object, on the native side only
//
// A Dart class instance is NOT sendable. Send a Map and rebuild
// it on the other side.
// HANDLING A COLD START FROM A NOTIFICATION
// the platform channel handler is not registered when the app
// is launched cold, so a message sent at launch is lost
// the fix: buffer the initial message, and flush it in
// configureFlutterEngine / didFinishLaunching

// Kotlin
class MainActivity : FlutterActivity() {
    private var pendingIntent: Intent? = null
    private var channel: MethodChannel? = null

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        pendingIntent = intent    // hold it until the channel is ready
    }

    override fun configureFlutterEngine(flutterEngine: FlutterEngine) {
        super.configureFlutterEngine(flutterEngine)
        channel = MethodChannel(flutterEngine.dartExecutor.binaryMessenger, CHANNEL)
        channel!!.setMethodCallHandler { call, result ->
            // ...
        }

        // NOW flush whatever arrived before we were listening
        pendingIntent?.let {
            val deepLink = it.getStringExtra("deepLink")
            if (deepLink != null) {
                channel!!.invokeMethod("onColdStart", deepLink)
            }
            pendingIntent = null
        }
    }

    // a link that arrives while running
    override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
        super.onNewIntent(intent)
        val deepLink = intent.getStringExtra("deepLink")
        if (deepLink != null) {
            channel?.invokeMethod("onDeepLink", deepLink)
        }
    }
}

Host handlers, threading, and the two ways a call goes wrong

The host side of a method channel is where the real work happens and where the platform's own rules apply, and there are two of those rules that produce most of the bugs. The handler runs on the platform's main thread unless it says otherwise, so a handler that does a slow operation — a file read, a network call, a database query — blocks the interface and produces an unresponsive application that the platform may terminate. The second rule is that the reply must be sent exactly once. The framework waits for a reply with a timeout, and a handler that replies twice, or that returns a value and also calls the result callback, produces an error; and a handler that never replies produces a timeout that surfaces to Dart as a timeout rather than as an error in the handler, which is the worst possible diagnostic. Then the two ways a call goes wrong, and they need different handling. A wrong result, which means the handler succeeded and returned something the Dart side cannot use — the shape leak from the previous section — and which is caught by the parsing function at the boundary. A failed call, which means the handler could not do the work, and which on Android is reported by throwing a method-call exception with a code and a message and on iOS by returning a FlutterError with a code and a message. The code is the part that matters: it is the only machine-readable part of the failure, so it is what Dart should branch on and what should be a named constant rather than a literal. Then the three things to get right, and each is a specific mechanism. Do the slow work off the main thread and reply from there. The pattern is a handler that starts work, hands it to a background executor, and calls the result callback from the background thread when it finishes; the reply itself is thread-safe because the framework marshals it. Handle the activity and engine lifetimes explicitly. The host object has a lifetime tied to the engine, so a handler that registers a listener must unregister it, and an activity-scoped object must be released when the activity is destroyed or the plugin leaks an activity across a configuration change — the platform's own leak detector reports this, and it is a real and common defect. And keep the channel's work small. A handler that does one thing is a handler that can be tested on the host side without a device; a handler that reads a preference, formats a string and calls another native library is a handler that can only be tested in the application. Then the two practices, and both are cheap. Return a structured error, not a string, so the Dart side can distinguish "the file does not exist" from "permission denied" without parsing prose — which is what the error-code constant is for. And write the host-side test, because host code is testable without a device and the alternative is that every change to a plugin requires a device build, which is the reason plugin code rots.

/* Two platform rules. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'the HANDLER RUNS ON the PLATFORMS MAIN THREAD UNLESS IT SAYS OTHERWISE',
    consequence: 'so A HANDLER THAT DOES A SLOW OPERATION - A FILE READ, A NETWORK CALL, A DATABASE QUERY - BLOCKS the INTERFACE',
    symptom: 'and PRODUCES AN UNRESPONSIVE APPLICATION THAT the PLATFORM MAY TERMINATE' },
  { r: 'the REPLY MUST BE SENT EXACTLY ONCE',
    failures: ['A HANDLER THAT REPLIES TWICE, or THAT RETURNS A VALUE and ALSO CALLS the RESULT CALLBACK, PRODUCES AN ERROR',
      'and A HANDLER THAT NEVER REPLIES PRODUCES A TIMEOUT'],
    worst: 'WHICH SURFACES TO DART AS A TIMEOUT rather than AS AN ERROR IN the HANDLER, which IS the WORST POSSIBLE DIAGNOSTIC' },
];

/* Two ways a call goes wrong. */
const GOES_WRONG = [

    caughtBy: 'the PARSING FUNCTION AT the BOUNDARY' },
  { w: 'A FAILED CALL', means: 'the HANDLER COULD NOT DO the WORK',

13.3 EventChannel and BasicMessageChannel

// EventChannel: a native-to-Dart STREAM
// the right tool for: a sensor, a barcode scanner, an incoming
// call, a drag from a native view

// DART
class BarcodeScanner {
  static const _channel = EventChannel('com.acme.fieldnotes/barcode');

  static Stream<String> get scans {
    return _channel.receiveBroadcastStream().map((event) => event as String);
  }
}

// KOTLIN
class BarcodeChannel(private val context: Context) : EventChannel.StreamHandler {
    private var sink: EventChannel.EventSink? = null
    private var handler: Handler? = null

    override fun onListen(arguments: Any?, events: EventChannel.EventSink?) {
        sink = events
        handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
        // start the native loop
        handler?.postDelayed(scanRunnable, 0)
    }

    override fun onCancel(arguments: Any?) {
        // REQUIRED: without this the native side leaks
        handler?.removeCallbacks(scanRunnable)
        handler = null
        sink = null
    }

    private val scanRunnable = object : Runnable {
        override fun run() {
            val code = doScan()          // your native scan
            if (code != null) sink?.success(code)
            handler?.postDelayed(this, 100)   // 10 fps
        }
    }
}

// register it
class MainActivity : FlutterActivity() {
    private var barcode: BarcodeChannel? = null

    override fun configureFlutterEngine(flutterEngine: FlutterEngine) {
        super.configureFlutterEngine(flutterEngine)
        barcode = BarcodeChannel(applicationContext).also {
            EventChannel(flutterEngine.dartExecutor.binaryMessenger, CHANNEL_NAME)
                .setStreamHandler(it)
        }
    }

    override fun onDestroy() {
        barcode = null
        super.onDestroy()
    }
}

// SWIFT
class BarcodeStreamHandler: NSObject, FlutterStreamHandler {
    private var sink: FlutterEventSink?
    private var timer: Timer?

    func onListen(withArguments arguments: Any?, eventSink events: @escaping FlutterEventSink) -> FlutterError? {
        sink = events
        timer = Timer.scheduledTimer(withTimeInterval: 0.1, repeats: true) { [weak self] _ in
            self?.sink?("1234567890")
        }
        return nil
    }

    func onCancel(withArguments arguments: Any?) -> FlutterError? {
        timer?.invalidate()   // REQUIRED
        timer = nil
        sink = nil
        return nil
    }
}

// A BROADCAST STREAM, so several listeners can share
BarcodeScanner.scans.asBroadcastStream().listen(_onScan);
final _scanSub = BarcodeScanner.scans.listen(_onScan);   // the ORIGINAL
final _scanSub2 = BarcodeScanner.scans.listen(_onScan2);  // ERROR
// a receiveBroadcastStream from an EventChannel is single-
// subscription, so you need asBroadcastStream for two listeners
// BasicMessageChannel: when you need a custom codec or high
// frequency. The default StandardMessageCodec handles the
// standard types, so this is only for something special.

// DART
final _channel = BasicMessageChannel<Uint8List>(
  'com.acme.fieldnotes/stream',
  const StandardMessageCodec(),
);

_channel.setMessageHandler((Uint8List? message) async {
  // a raw frame, for a video or an audio stream
  return _onFrame(message);
});

final subscription = _channel.listen(
  (message) { render(message as Uint8List); },
  onError: (Object error) { log.error(error); },
);

// and a BINARY codec, for a custom payload
class BitstreamCodec extends StandardMessageCodec {
  @override
  Object? readValueOfType(int type, ByteData? value) {
    if (type == 42) {                 // your custom type id
      final buffer = value!.buffer.asUint8List();
      return Bitstream(buffer);
    }
    return super.readValueOfType(type, value);
  }

  @override
  void writeValue(WriteBuffer buffer, Object? value) {
    if (value is Bitstream) {
      buffer.putUint8(42);
      buffer.putUint32(value.data.length);
      buffer.putUint8List(value.data);
      return;
    }
    super.writeValue(buffer, value);
  }
}

// WHEN TO USE IT
// a video or audio frame stream: you cannot afford the
//   StandardMessageCodec's reflection on every frame
// a high-frequency sensor: 200+ messages a second
// a protocol you already have
//
// WHEN NOT TO
// anything occasional: the overhead of a BasicMessageChannel
//   is the same as a MethodChannel for a few messages a second

Streams, messages, and choosing between the three channel types

The three channel types exist because three different communication patterns exist, and confusing them produces either a stream used for a request or a request used for a stream. A method channel is request and reply: Dart asks, the host answers, one result per call. It is the right type for anything that produces a value. An event channel is a stream from the host to Dart, set up once by a listen call and cancelled by a cancel call, and it is the right type for something the host observes and Dart wants to hear about repeatedly — a sensor, a connection state, an incoming call. A basic message channel is a fire-and-forget message in either direction with no reply, and it is the right type for a notification with no result: a log line, a "cache invalidated" hint, a value pushed once. Then the three rules, and each has a specific failure behind it. An event channel must be balanced: one listen, one cancel. The host receives a listen call with arguments and registers a handler for those arguments; it receives a cancel when Dart cancels. A host that registers on every message rather than on the listen call accumulates handlers, and a Dart side that listens without ever cancelling leaves the handler running after the screen is gone. A basic message channel carries no reply, so anything expecting a result must not use one. And argument changes on an event channel require a new listen. Changing what you are listening to means cancelling and listening again, because the arguments are supplied once at listen time. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Registering an event handler without removing it, which leaks the handler and, in a plugin that holds an activity, leaks the activity — the platform leak detector reports this, so it is findable. Sending events faster than Dart can process them, which on the Dart side means events queue and memory grows, so a host that emits a hundred events a second needs a conflation policy: replace the pending event with the newer one rather than queueing all of them. And using an event channel for data that must not be missed, because a stream can be silently dropped when the sink is cancelled — a sensor reading is fine, a transaction confirmation is not, and the latter belongs on a method call where the reply is the guarantee. Then the two practices, and each is cheap. Keep the channel's event type simple, — a number, a string, a small map — because the codec is what you can send and a host that tries to send a native object is solving the codec problem at run time rather than at design time. And buffer or conflate deliberately at the boundary, so the rate at which the host produces events and the rate at which the interface consumes them are decoupled, which is the difference between a smooth interface and one that degrades under load.

/* Three patterns. */
const TYPES = [
  { t: 'a METHOD CHANNEL', pattern: 'REQUEST and REPLY - DART ASKS, the HOST ANSWERS, ONE RESULT PER CALL', rightFor: 'ANYTHING THAT PRODUCES A VALUE' },
  { t: 'an EVENT CHANNEL', pattern: 'A STREAM FROM the HOST TO DART, SET UP ONCE BY A LISTEN CALL and CANCELLED BY A CANCEL CALL',
    rightFor: 'SOMETHING the HOST OBSERVES and DART WANTS TO HEAR ABOUT REPEATEDLY',

];
const WHY_CONFUSION = 'CONFLATING THEM PRODUCES EITHER A STREAM USED FOR A REQUEST or A REQUEST USED FOR A STREAM';

/* Three rules. */
const RULES = [
