13.4 FFI

Calling C directly, and why the boundary is measured in ownership

The foreign function interface calls C functions directly rather than serialising through a channel, and the reason to use it is a specific performance requirement: a large binary operation per channel hop is unusable, while the same operation per call through the interface is free. If you need to process ten megabytes of pixels or ten million numbers, the channel's serialisation step dominates completely and the interface removes it. The reason not to use it is more important, and it is that the boundary has no type safety on either side beyond what C itself provides — which means the correctness of a call is a matter of argument order, argument type and ownership, and a mistake in any of them is a crash rather than an exception. Then the four things that must be true, and each has a specific failure. Argument and return types must match exactly. The declaration in Dart is a promise about the C signature, and nothing checks it, so a mismatch is undefined behaviour: a wrong integer width reads part of a pointer, a wrong return type interprets a returned void as a value. Ownership must be stated. Every allocation crossing the boundary is either owned by C and must be freed, or owned by Dart and must be kept alive while C holds a reference to it; getting this backwards is either a leak or a use-after-free, and the use-after-free is the one that produces a crash some time after the mistake. Lifetime must be pinned. A Dart object that is garbage-collected while C holds a pointer to it is a dangling pointer, so the object must be kept alive for as long as C might use it, which the interface expresses explicitly. And the callback must not throw across the boundary. A Dart exception propagating through a C frame is undefined behaviour; the pattern is to catch inside the callback and convert to an error code or a recorded result. Then the three things that make it safe in practice, and each is the mechanism that exists because the language cannot check it. Generate the bindings rather than writing them. A bindings generator reads the header files and produces declarations with correct types, and that removes the whole class of mismatch errors — the reason every project that uses the interface uses generated bindings. Do not pass pointers; pass handles. A library that allocates a structure and returns an integer handle, with functions to get and set fields, is safe from almost every use-after-free because Dart holds the only reference and the handle is meaningless once freed. And keep the interface surface small, because every function is an unchecked boundary and the cost of auditing grows with the number of them. Then the two practices, and each is cheap. Test the bindings with a small native function before testing the real one, — a function that returns a constant, a function that writes to an out-parameter — because a bindings error presents as a crash in whatever code happens to run first, and the constant-returning function tells you the declaration is right in one run. And never do heavy work on the platform thread, even through the interface, because the interface call is fast but the native work is not and it still runs where the interface says it runs unless you hand it to a background thread.

/* When. */
const WHEN = {
  reason: 'A SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE REQUIREMENT',
  detail: 'A LARGE BINARY OPERATION PER CHANNEL HOP IS UNUSABLE, while the SAME OPERATION PER CALL THROUGH the INTERFACE IS FREE',
  instance: 'IF YOU NEED TO PROCESS TEN MEGABYTES of PIXELS or TEN MILLION NUMBERS, the CHANNELS SERIALISATION STEP DOMINATES COMPLETELY and the INTERFACE REMOVES IT',
};

/* The cost. */
const COST = {
  fact: 'the BOUNDARY HAS NO TYPE SAFETY ON EITHER SIDE BEYOND WHAT C ITSELF PROVIDES',
  consequence: 'WHICH MEANS the CORRECTNESS OF A CALL IS A MATTER of ARGUMENT ORDER, ARGUMENT TYPE and OWNERSHIP',
  and: 'A MISTAKE IN ANY of THEM IS A CRASH rather than AN EXCEPTION',
};

/* Four things that must be true. */
const MUST = [
  { r: 'ARGUMENT and RETURN TYPES MUST MATCH EXACTLY',
    detail: 'the DECLARATION IN DART IS A PROMISE ABOUT the C SIGNATURE, and NOTHING CHECKS IT',
    so: 'A MISMATCH IS UNDEFINED BEHAVIOUR - A WRONG INTEGER WIDTH READS PART of A POINTER, A WRONG RETURN TYPE INTERPRETS A RETURNED void AS A VALUE' },
  { r: 'OWNERSHIP MUST BE STATED',
    detail: 'EVERY ALLOCATION CROSSING the BOUNDARY IS EITHER OWNED BY C and MUST BE FREED, OR OWNED BY DART and MUST BE KEPT ALIVE WHILE C HOLDS A REFERENCE TO IT',
    wrong: 'GETTING THIS BACKWARDS IS EITHER A LEAK or A USE-AFTER-FREE',
    and: 'and the USE-AFTER-FREE IS the ONE THAT PRODUCES A CRASH SOME TIME AFTER the MISTAKE' },
  { r: 'LIFETIME MUST BE PINNED',

    so: 'the OBJECT MUST BE KEPT ALIVE for AS LONG AS C MIGHT USE IT, WHICH the INTERFACE EXPRESSES EXPLICITLY' },

/* Three things that make it safe. */
const SAFE = [
  { s: 'GENERATE the BINDINGS rather than WRITING THEM',
    how: 'A BINDINGS GENERATOR READS the HEADER FILES and PRODUCES DECLARATIONS with CORRECT TYPES',
    gain: 'WHICH REMOVES the WHOLE CLASS of MISMATCH ERRORS',
    and: 'the REASON EVERY PROJECT THAT USES the INTERFACE USES GENERATED BINDINGS' },
  { s: 'do NOT PASS POINTERS; PASS HANDLES',
    detail: 'A LIBRARY THAT ALLOCATES A STRUCTURE and RETURNS AN INTEGER HANDLE, WITH FUNCTIONS TO GET and SET FIELDS, IS SAFE FROM ALMOST EVERY USE-AFTER-FREE',
    why: 'BECAUSE DART HOLDS the ONLY REFERENCE and the HANDLE IS MEANINGLESS ONCE FREED' },
  { s: 'KEEP the INTERFACE SURFACE SMALL',
    why: 'BECAUSE EVERY FUNCTION IS AN UNCHECKED BOUNDARY and the COST of AUDITING GROWS WITH the NUMBER of THEM' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'TEST the BINDINGS WITH A SMALL NATIVE FUNCTION BEFORE TESTING the REAL ONE',
    functions: ['A FUNCTION THAT RETURNS A CONSTANT', 'A FUNCTION THAT WRITES TO AN OUT-PARAMETER'],
    why: 'BECAUSE A BINDINGS ERROR PRESENTS AS A CRASH IN WHATEVER CODE HAPPENS TO RUN FIRST',
    gain: 'and the CONSTANT-RETURNING FUNCTION TELLS YOU the DECLARATION IS RIGHT IN ONE RUN' },
  { p: 'NEVER DO HEAVY WORK ON the PLATFORM THREAD, EVEN THROUGH the INTERFACE',
    detail: 'because the INTERFACE CALL IS FAST but the NATIVE WORK IS NOT',
    and: 'and IT STILL RUNS WHERE the INTERFACE SAYS IT RUNS UNLESS YOU HAND IT TO A BACKGROUND THREAD' },
];

Every rule in FFI exists because breaking it does not produce an error. A wrong signature, freeing with the wrong allocator, or letting a callback be collected are all silent until the process crashes. The try/finally discipline is not style; it is the only thing standing between you and a segfault in production.

// FFI: a DIRECT FUNCTION CALL into C or C++, with no serialisation
// use it for: a C library with no Dart equivalent, a
// performance-critical inner loop, a vendor SDK

// WHEN NOT TO USE IT
// - a plugin already exists: it is far less work
// - the work is CPU-bound but not hot: an ISOLATE handles it
//   and is portable to the web
// - you need the web: dart:ffi does not exist there
// - you are not prepared to debug a segfault

// THE ANNOTATION FORM
import 'dart:ffi';
import 'package:ffi/ffi.dart';

// pubspec.yaml
//   ffi: ^2.1.0

@Native<Int32 Function(Pointer<Utf8>)>(symbol: 'greet_length')
external int greetLength(Pointer<Utf8> text);

@Native<Uint8List Function(Uint8List, Int32, Int32)>(symbol: 'process')
external Uint8List processImage(Uint8List data, int width, int height);

// a library you load at runtime
final DynamicLibrary openLib() {
  if (Platform.isWindows) return DynamicLibrary.open('mylib.dll');
  if (Platform.isMacOS) return DynamicLibrary.open('libmylib.dylib');
  return DynamicLibrary.open('libmylib.so');
}

final _process = openLib().lookupFunction<
    Uint8List Function(Uint8List, Int32, Int32),
    Uint8List Function(Uint8List, int, int)
  >('process');

// A STRUCT, for a zero-copy layout
final class ImageInfo extends Struct {
  @Int32() external int width;
  @Int32() external int height;
  @Uint8Ptr() external Pointer<Uint8> data;
}

// AND THE BINDING LAYER, which is where you own the memory
class NativeImageProcessor {
  final _process = openLib().lookupFunction<...>('process');

  Uint8List process(Uint8List data, int width, int height) {
    final inputPtr = malloc<Uint8>(data.length);
    final outputPtr = malloc<Uint8>(width * height * 4);
    final infoPtr = malloc<ImageInfo>();

    try {
      inputPtr.asTypedList(data.length).setAll(0, data);

      final result = _process(inputPtr, width, height);
      if (result != 0) {
        throw NativeException('process_image failed: $result');
      }

      final size = infoPtr.ref.width * infoPtr.ref.height * 4;
      return outputPtr.asTypedList(size);
    } finally {
      // EVERY allocation is freed, in a finally
      malloc.free(inputPtr);
      malloc.free(outputPtr);
      malloc.free(infoPtr);
    }
  }
}

// AND IT RUNS IN AN ISOLATE, because FFI work is CPU-bound
Future<Uint8List> processInBackground(Uint8List data, int w, int h) {
  // TransferableTypedData moves the memory instead of copying it
  final transferable = TransferableTypedData.fromList([data]);
  return Isolate.run(() {
    final input = transferable.materialize().asUint8List();
    return NativeImageProcessor().process(input, w, h);
  });
}
// THE RULES, and violating them is a segfault, not an exception
// 1. every malloc has a matching free, in a finally
// 2. free with the SAME allocator that allocated
// 3. free exactly once: a double free crashes
// 4. a Uint8List from FFI is a VIEW into native memory: it is
//    only valid until you free it. Copy it if you need to keep it
// 5. do not free memory a pointer is still pointing at
// 6. run it in an isolate: FFI calls BLOCK the Dart thread

// THE COPY RULE, which is the subtle one
Uint8List unsafeView = _nativeGetBuffer();   // a view
// using it later, after the native side freed the buffer:
// a use-after-free, which is undefined behaviour and usually a
// crash or garbage
final safe = Uint8List.fromList(unsafeView);  // a COPY: safe

13.5 Writing a plugin

// THE STRUCTURE, from the official template:
// npx flutter create --template=plugin --platforms=android,ios,web \
//       --org com.acme field_notes_battery

field_notes_battery/
├── pubspec.yaml
├── lib/
│   ├── field_notes_battery.dart        the public API
│   └── src/
│       ├── field_notes_battery_platform_interface.dart
│       ├── field_notes_battery_method_channel.dart
│       ├── field_notes_battery_web.dart
│       └── field_notes_battery.dart    the facade
├── android/
│   ├── build.gradle
│   └── src/main/kotlin/com/acme/field_notes_battery/
│       ├── FieldNotesBatteryPlugin.kt
│       └── FieldNotesBatteryPlugin.java    the registrar
├── ios/
│   ├── field_notes_battery.podspec
│   └── Classes/
│       ├── FieldNotesBatteryPlugin.h
│       ├── FieldNotesBatteryPlugin.m       the registration
│       └── FieldNotesBatteryPlugin.swift
├── test/
├── example/                              a runnable example
└── README.md
// THE PUBSPEC
name: field_notes_battery
description: Read the device battery level and charging state on iOS, Android and web. A first-party example of a federated plugin.
version: 1.0.0
repository: https://github.com/acme/field_notes_battery
issue_tracker: https://github.com/acme/field_notes_battery/issues

environment:
  sdk: ">=3.0.0 <4.0.0"
  flutter: ">=3.10.0"

dependencies:
  flutter:
    sdk: flutter
  plugin_platform_interface: ^2.1.0

dev_dependencies:
  flutter_test:
    sdk: flutter
  flutter_lints: ^4.0.0

flutter:
  plugin:
    implements: field_notes_battery_platform_interface
    platforms:
      android:
        package: com.acme.field_notes_battery
        pluginClass: FieldNotesBatteryPlugin
      ios:
        pluginClass: FieldNotesBatteryPlugin
      web:
        pluginClass: FieldNotesBatteryWeb
        fileName: field_notes_battery_web.dart
// THE PLATFORM INTERFACE, so third parties can implement it
// lib/src/field_notes_battery_platform_interface.dart
abstract class FieldNotesBatteryPlatform extends PlatformInterface {
  FieldNotesBatteryPlatform() : super(token: _token);
  static final Object _token = Object();

  static FieldNotesBatteryPlatform _instance = MethodChannelFieldNotesBattery();
  static FieldNotesBatteryPlatform get instance => _instance;

  static set instance(FieldNotesBatteryPlatform value) {
    PlatformInterface.verifyToken(value, _token);
    _instance = value;
  }

  Future<BatteryStatus> status() {
    throw UnimplementedError('status() has not been implemented.');
  }
}

// THE METHOD CHANNEL IMPLEMENTATION
// lib/src/field_notes_battery_method_channel.dart
class MethodChannelFieldNotesBattery extends FieldNotesBatteryPlatform {
  final _channel = const MethodChannel('com.acme.fieldnotes/battery');

  @override
  Future<BatteryStatus> status() async {
    final data = await _channel.invokeMapMethod<String, dynamic>('getStatus');
    if (data == null) {
      throw const BatteryUnavailableException();
    }
    return BatteryStatus(
      level: (data['level'] as num).toInt(),
      isCharging: data['isCharging'] as bool? ?? false,
      // the web has no battery API, so it returns -1
      supported: (data['level'] as num).toInt() >= 0,
    );
  }
}

// THE FACADE: the only thing users import
// lib/field_notes_battery.dart
import 'package:field_notes_battery/src/field_notes_battery_platform_interface.dart';
import 'package:field_notes_battery/src/field_notes_battery_method_channel.dart';

export 'src/battery_status.dart';
export 'src/field_notes_battery_platform_interface.dart';
export 'src/field_notes_battery_method_channel.dart';

class FieldNotesBattery {
  FieldNotesBattery._();

  static BatteryStatus _cached = const BatteryStatus.unsupported();
  static DateTime? _cachedAt;

  static Future<BatteryStatus> status({Duration maxAge = const Duration(minutes: 5)}) async {
    // CACHE: the battery level does not change by the second,
    // and a platform channel call is 1-5ms
    final now = DateTime.now();
    if (_cachedAt != null && now.difference(_cachedAt!) < maxAge) {
      return _cached;
    }
    _cached = await FieldNotesBatteryPlatform.instance.status();
    _cachedAt = now;
    return _cached;
  }
}

The package shape, and the four things a plugin must get right

A plugin is a package with two implementations of the same interface, and the interface itself is a plain Dart class that the application depends on while the framework depends on nothing. That separation is the design and it is why a plugin can be replaced without touching the application. The Dart side is an implementation of an abstract class the plugin defines, so the application code talks to the interface and the platform-specific class is selected at registration time by the plugin itself. The host side is a registrant that installs a method-channel handler, and both iOS and Android registrants are declared in the platform packages. Then the four things that must be right, and each is a specific requirement rather than a preference. Register against the correct lifecycle object. On Android the handler must be attached to the activity or the application depending on what the plugin needs, and attaching to the activity means it must be detached when the activity is destroyed — the mechanism is the registry class the plugin framework provides, which handles both and which should always be used rather than a hand-written attach. Declare the platforms the plugin supports and implement all of them. A plugin that declares four platforms and implements two produces an application that builds on four and fails on two, and the failure is at run time on a device. Handle the no-implementation case gracefully. A plugin that is registered for a platform it does not implement should report a clear error rather than failing to register at all, because a missing plugin and a broken plugin present differently. And respect the main-thread rule, which is the previous section's rule: work that takes time must be handed to a background executor and the reply sent from there. Then the three things that go wrong in practice, and each is a mechanism. Registering the channel in the wrong lifecycle scope, which produces either a crash on rotation or a handler that is never called — and the second is much worse because it looks like a missing plugin. Depending on an application-provided value from the host side, which is impossible: the host has no access to the application's state, so anything the plugin needs must be passed through the channel as an argument or read from a platform configuration. And shipping a plugin with a hard dependency on a specific framework version, which makes it un-upgradeable; the plugin's own constraints should be the loosest that work. Then the two practices, and each is about the plugin being usable. Have the Dart-side interface be free of framework types, so it can be unit tested with no engine and no platform — which is what makes a plugin testable at all, and what lets somebody write a fake implementation for their own tests. And include a Dart-only implementation for every plugin, even a stub that throws, so that the application compiles and its tests run on a platform the plugin does not support, rather than failing to build.

/* The package shape. */
const SHAPE = {

  hostSide: 'A REGISTRANT THAT INSTALLS A METHOD-CHANNEL HANDLER',

};

13.6 Publishing and maintaining a plugin

The publishing surface, and the compatibility problem

Publishing a plugin is a contract with people who will build it in environments you do not control, and the contract has three parts: what it declares, what it documents, and what it continues to support. The declared surface is the manifest, the platform implementations, the minimum framework version and the platform version ranges. Each of these is a promise. A minimum framework version that is too high excludes users; too low and you cannot use APIs that are not present. A platform version range that is too narrow excludes devices you could have supported; too wide and your code uses an API that does not exist on the older versions and crashes. Both are compile-time-checkable on one platform and invisible on the others, which is why a plugin that declares a wide range and assumes a new API is the most common published defect. Then the three compatibility dimensions, and each breaks independently. The Dart API. Changing a method signature is a breaking change for every caller, and a semantic-version bump is the mechanism that communicates it — but only if the version is correct, and the discipline is that removing a method, changing a parameter type or changing a return type is always a major bump and adding an optional parameter is not. The platform API. The plugin's host code calls into the operating system, and a new operating-system version can deprecate or remove something the plugin uses, which means a plugin can break without the author changing anything. And the framework. Each release of the framework can change its own plugin APIs, and a plugin that used an internal rather than a public API will break on the next major release with no warning at build time. Then the three things that go wrong, and each has a mechanism. Using an internal framework API, which compiles today and fails after the next major release — and there is no compile-time warning because the internal API exists; the mitigation is to use only documented public API and to accept slightly more code. Not testing against the oldest supported version, so the plugin works on the maintainer's device and on the newest version and fails on the oldest, which is the version a user's old phone runs. And not testing against the newest, which is the version that changes the deprecation warnings into errors and where the platform's own behaviour changes. Then the two practices, and each is a specific discipline. Run continuous integration across every platform and every declared version range, on every push, because the compatibility matrix is the product and the only way to know it still holds is to build it. And publish a minimum version for the plugin and keep it moving, with a changelog that says what broke, because a plugin with an unstated breaking change is indistinguishable from a plugin that stopped working.

/* The declared surface. */
const DECLARED = ['the MANIFEST', 'the PLATFORM IMPLEMENTATIONS', 'the MINIMUM FRAMEWORK VERSION', 'the PLATFORM VERSION RANGES'];
const PROMISES = [
  { p: 'a MINIMUM FRAMEWORK VERSION THAT IS TOO HIGH', consequence: 'EXCLUDES USERS' },
  { p: 'a MINIMUM FRAMEWORK VERSION THAT IS TOO LOW', consequence: 'and YOU CANNOT USE APIS THAT ARE NOT PRESENT' },
  { p: 'a PLATFORM VERSION RANGE THAT IS TOO NARROW', consequence: 'EXCLUDES DEVICES YOU COULD HAVE SUPPORTED' },

const WORST = 'WHICH IS WHY A PLUGIN THAT DECLARES A WIDE RANGE and ASSUMES A NEW API IS the MOST COMMON PUBLISHED DEFECT';

The highest-value thing you can do for a plugin is a CI job that builds it for all six platforms on every push. A plugin that only builds on the machine of the person maintaining it is a plugin that will break the first time a Flutter version lands, and its users will find out before you do.

// THE NATIVE PLUGIN CLASS
// android/.../FieldNotesBatteryPlugin.kt
package com.acme.field_notes_battery

import android.content.Context
import android.content.Intent
import android.content.IntentFilter
import android.os.BatteryManager
import io.flutter.embedding.engine.plugins.FlutterPlugin
import io.flutter.plugin.common.EventChannel
import io.flutter.plugin.common.MethodCall
import io.flutter.plugin.common.MethodChannel.MethodCallHandler
import io.flutter.plugin.common.MethodChannel.Result

class FieldNotesBatteryPlugin : FlutterPlugin, MethodCallHandler {
    private lateinit var channel: MethodChannel
    private var eventChannel: EventChannel? = null
    private var context: Context? = null

    override fun onAttachedToEngine(binding: FlutterPlugin.FlutterPluginBinding) {
        context = binding.applicationContext
        channel = MethodChannel(binding.binaryMessenger, "com.acme.fieldnotes/battery")
        channel.setMethodCallHandler(this)
    }

    override fun onMethodCall(call: MethodCall, result: Result) {
        when (call.method) {
            "getStatus" -> {
                val bm = context?.getSystemService(Context.BATTERY_SERVICE) as? BatteryManager
                if (bm == null) {
                    result.error("UNAVAILABLE", "Battery service not found", null)
                    return
                }
                val level = bm.getIntProperty(BatteryManager.BATTERY_PROPERTY_CAPACITY)
                val intent = context?.registerReceiver(
                    null, IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED)
                )
                val status = intent?.getIntExtra(BatteryManager.EXTRA_STATUS, -1) ?: -1
                result.success(mapOf(
                    "level" to level,
                    "isCharging" to (status == BatteryManager.BATTERY_STATUS_CHARGING ||
                                     status == BatteryManager.BATTERY_STATUS_FULL),
                ))
            }
            else -> result.notImplemented()
        }
    }

    // THE CLEANUP, which is what most plugins get wrong
    override fun onDetachedFromEngine(binding: FlutterPlugin.FlutterPluginBinding) {
        channel.setMethodCallHandler(null)
        eventChannel?.setStreamHandler(null)
        eventChannel = null
        context = null
    }
}

// THE REGISTRAR, for the old embedding
// android/.../FieldNotesBatteryPlugin.java
public class FieldNotesBatteryPlugin {
    public static void registerWith(FlutterEngine engine) {
        new FieldNotesBatteryPlugin().onAttachedToEngine(
            new FlutterPluginBinding() { ... }
        );
    }
}

// needed for v1. Modern plugins can skip it.
// THE IOS PLUGIN
// ios/Classes/FieldNotesBatteryPlugin.m   (the registration)
#import <Flutter/Flutter.h>

@interface FieldNotesBatteryPlugin : NSObject<FlutterPlugin>
@end

// ios/Classes/FieldNotesBatteryPlugin.h
#import <Flutter/Flutter.h>
@interface FieldNotesBatteryPlugin : NSObject <FlutterPlugin>
@end

// ios/Classes/FieldNotesBatteryPlugin.swift
import Flutter
import UIKit

public class FieldNotesBatteryPlugin: NSObject, FlutterPlugin {
    private var channel: FlutterMethodChannel?
    private var eventSink: FlutterEventSink?

    public static func register(with registrar: FlutterPluginRegistrar) {
        let instance = FieldNotesBatteryPlugin()

        let channel = FlutterMethodChannel(
            name: "com.acme.fieldnotes/battery",
            binaryMessenger: registrar.messenger()
        )
        registrar.addMethodCallDelegate(instance, channel: channel)
        instance.channel = channel
    }

    public func handle(_ call: FlutterMethodCall, result: @escaping FlutterResult) {
        switch call.method {
        case "getStatus":
            UIDevice.current.isBatteryMonitoringEnabled = true
            let level = UIDevice.current.batteryLevel
            let state = UIDevice.current.batteryState

            if level < 0 {
                result(FlutterError(
                    code: "UNAVAILABLE",
                    message: "Battery state is unknown",
                    details: nil
                ))
                return
            }

            result([
                "level": Int(level * 100),
                "isCharging": state == .charging || state == .full,
            ])

        default:
            result(FlutterMethodNotImplemented)
        }
    }

    public func detachFromEngine(for registrar: FlutterPluginRegistrar) {
        channel?.setMethodCallHandler(nil)
        channel = nil
    }
}
// TESTING, which is where a plugin earns its keep
// 1. a Dart test with a mocked platform interface
test('returns the cached value within maxAge', () async {
  var callCount = 0;
  FieldNotesBatteryPlatform.instance = _FakePlatform(() {
    callCount++;
    return const BatteryStatus(level: 55, isCharging: true, supported: true);
  });

  await FieldNotesBattery.status();
  await FieldNotesBattery.status(maxAge: const Duration(minutes: 5));

  expect(callCount, 1, reason: 'the second call should be cached');
});

13.7 Native work in an isolate

// A PLATFORM CHANNEL FROM AN ISOLATE
// this works, and it is the pattern for anything heavy
// the channel uses the default BinaryMessenger, which works
// across isolates

class NativeImageProcessor {
  static const _channel = MethodChannel('com.acme.fieldnotes/image');

  static Future<Uint8List> process(Uint8List data, int width, int height) async {
    return Isolate.run(() async {
      final result = await _channel.invokeMethod<Uint8List>('process', {
        'data': data,
        'width': width,
        'height': height,
      });
      return result!;
    });
  }
}

// and on the native side, run the work on a background thread
// because a platform channel call arrives on the PLATFORM thread
class ImagePlugin : FlutterPlugin, MethodCallHandler {
    private val executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()
    private var channel: MethodChannel? = null

    override fun onMethodCall(call: MethodCall, result: Result) {
        if (call.method == "process") {
            // THIS MATTERS: without the executor, a heavy native
            // call BLOCKS the platform thread and janks the UI
            executor.execute {
                try {
                    val bytes = call.argument<ByteArray>("data")!!
                    val width = call.argument<Int>("width")!!
                    val height = call.argument<Int>("height")!!
                    val output = processImage(bytes, width, height)
                    result.success(output)
                } catch (e: Exception) {
                    result.error("PROCESS_FAILED", e.message, null)
                }
            }
        } else {
            result.notImplemented()
        }
    }

    override fun onDetachedFromEngine(binding: FlutterPlugin.FlutterPluginBinding) {
        channel?.setMethodCallHandler(null)
        channel = null
        executor.shutdown()   // the cleanup
    }
}

Exercises 14

  1. Write a MethodChannel for the device battery level, with a proper notImplemented default on both platforms, and a Dart-side PlatformException handler.
  2. Add a cold-start notification deep link to the Android side, buffer the intent, and verify the Dart side receives it on a cold start.
  3. Write an EventChannel for a native sensor at 10Hz, with onCancel that stops the loop, and verify no leak.
  4. Scaffold a federated plugin with flutter create --template=plugin, implement Android and iOS, and test it from the example app on both.
  5. Move a heavy platform channel call onto a background executor in Kotlin, and measure the jank before and after.
  6. Write a Dart test with a mocked platform interface that proves the caching logic, and one that proves the error mapping.
  7. Add CI that builds the plugin for Android, iOS, web, macOS, Windows and Linux on every push.

Isolates, and the three cases that justify one

An isolate is an independent execution context with its own memory and its own event loop, and the reason it exists is that Dart's single-threaded event loop cannot use more than one core — so a computation that takes a hundred milliseconds blocks everything, including the frame. An isolate is the answer, and the reason it is rarely needed in a Flutter application is worth understanding first. The image decoding, the layout, the painting and the networking are already off the main isolate, which is the framework's architecture, so the cases where an application needs its own isolate are narrow. Compression and encryption of large payloads, where the work is genuinely CPU-bound and genuinely large. Parsing a very large JSON or binary file that would otherwise block the interface for a visible fraction of a second. And image processing that the framework does not do for you — resizing, cropping, applying a filter — as opposed to decoding, which it already does. Then the three costs, and each is a real constraint. Isolates cannot share mutable memory, so the only way to get data in is to copy it and the only way to get a result out is to copy it back — which means a large payload is copied twice and an isolate is the wrong tool for a large payload. Message passing is asynchronous, so the result arrives as a later event and the calling code must be structured around a completion, which means a future rather than a return value. And an isolate has a startup cost — spawning one is not free and a long-lived isolate should be spawned once and reused rather than created per operation. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Spawning an isolate per operation, which pays the startup cost every time and, for short operations, spends more time spawning than working. Sending a huge object through the message port, which copies it and can exceed the limit on message size, producing an error that is easy to misread; the fix is to send an identifier and have the isolate read from storage itself, so only a small value crosses. And sharing a resource without synchronising, which the isolation makes impossible to do correctly by accident — and which is exactly why the isolation is the right tool for anything touching a file that another thread may also touch. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Move the work to a compute isolate rather than blocking, and only after measuring: a computation that takes five milliseconds does not need an isolate, and an isolate that does five milliseconds of work spends more time being started. And give the isolate a narrow, explicit interface — it receives identifiers, it returns identifiers, it never receives an object graph, because an interface that takes an object graph will eventually pass something that cannot be copied and the failure will be an obscure error rather than a design problem you can see.

14 · Background Work and Notifications

14.1 Local notifications14.2 Push notifications14.3 Scheduled and repeating14.4 Background execution14.5 Headless isolates14.6 Battery and the reality of it14.7 No connection, and telling the user

Background work is the least reliable thing on a mobile platform, and the whole design of your app should assume it will not happen when you want it to.

14.1 Local notifications

Permissions, channels, and the platform's rules about noise

A local notification is the simplest thing in this chapter and has the most platform-specific rules, because both operating systems regulate when an application may interrupt a person. Both platforms require an explicit runtime permission, requested at a moment the user will understand, and both treat a refusal as final for that install — so asking on first launch is asking at the worst moment and asking again is not permitted. Both require the notification to belong to an importance category, and on iOS those categories are user-controlled and on Android the highest one is reserved for alarms and calls, so an application that asks for the highest importance for a marketing message will be refused by review and distrusted by users. Then the three things the platforms require that are not about permission, and each has a specific consequence. An application icon that is not a silhouette on iOS, because the system masks it, so a notification showing a square icon looks broken — this is a hard requirement and the failure is purely visual and immediately noticed. A category on iOS, without which the notification is uncategorised and cannot be configured by the user, which means the user cannot silence it and will uninstall rather than do that. And a sound that is short and respectful, because a sound that plays in a meeting is the fastest route to an uninstall; the standard is to use the default sound and never a custom one for anything but the highest category. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Requesting permission on first launch, which is a permission prompt before the user has any reason to grant it, and the refusal rate for that is dramatically higher than for a request made after the user has seen the feature. Firing a notification for something the user is looking at, which is the failure that produces a reputation for spam: an application that notifies the user about an event they are currently watching has told them nothing and interrupted them for nothing. And creating a channel per notification type and then forgetting to keep them in sync with the code, so a channel that was renamed in code retains its old name and its old settings on the user's device — because the channel is created once and its settings are then the user's, which is why renaming one requires a new identifier. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Have a notifications section in settings, always present, with a working per-category switch that writes to the channel's own settings on Android and opens the system settings on iOS — because the only reliable way for a user to change notification behaviour is through the system, and an application that provides its own switch and does nothing with it is worse than providing none. And make every notification carry a route, so tapping it opens the right screen and the right record, and test that path from a cold start — which is the deep-link chapter's cold-start problem arriving in a different form, and the most common defect in notification handling is that the tap does nothing because the payload was parsed against the wrong route shape.

Ask for notification permission at the moment the feature needs it, with an in-context explanation of what the user gets. Asked at launch with no explanation, it is the permission most likely to be refused - and a refusal is much harder to recover from on iOS.

// pubspec.yaml
//   flutter_local_notifications: ^17.2.0
//   timezone: ^0.9.4        the tz database, for scheduling

final plugin = FlutterLocalNotificationsPlugin();

// 1. INITIALISE, per platform
Future<void> initNotifications() async {
  const androidSettings = AndroidInitializationSettings('@mipmap/ic_notification');

  const darwinSettings = DarwinInitializationSettings(
    // three levels, and you should ask for the right one
    //   provisional: show quietly, no prompt. the polite default.
    //   alert: show with sound and a banner
    //   badge: also update the app icon badge
    requestAlertPermission: false,      // ask LATER, in context
    requestBadgePermission: false,
    requestSoundPermission: false,
  );

  await plugin.initialize(
    const InitializationSettings(android: androidSettings, iOS: darwinSettings),
    onDidReceiveNotificationResponse: _onTap,
  );
}

// 2. ASK, at the moment the feature needs it
Future<bool> requestPermission() async {
  final android = await plugin.resolvePlatformSpecificImplementation<
      AndroidFlutterLocalNotificationsPlugin>()?.requestNotificationsPermission();
  if (android != null) return android;

  final ios = await plugin.resolvePlatformSpecificImplementation<
      IOSFlutterLocalNotificationsPlugin>()?.requestPermissions(
    alert: true, badge: true, sound: true, critical: false,
  );
  return ios ?? false;
}

// 3. SHOW
await plugin.show(
  id,
  'Your note needs a title',
  'You started one yesterday and left it empty.',
  NotificationDetails(
    android: AndroidNotificationDetails(
      'reminders',
      'Reminders',
      channelDescription: 'Nudges about unfinished notes',
      importance: Importance.defaultImportance,
      priority: Priority.defaultPriority,
      // A SMALL ICON, or a white square appears
      // android/app/src/main/res/drawable/ic_notification.png
      // it must be white-on-transparent, referenced by name
    ),
    iOS: const DarwinNotificationDetails(
      presentAlert: true,
      presentBadge: true,
      presentSound: true,
    ),
  ),
  payload: 'entry:123',      // a string, read on tap
);

// 4. HANDLE THE TAP
void _onTap(NotificationResponse response) {
  final payload = response.payload;
  if (payload == null) return;
  final (type, id) = payload.split(':');
  // navigate
}
// THE FOUR STYLES, and the one that is almost always right
//   DefaultStyle     a heads-up banner, briefly
//   BigTextStyle     expanded, with the whole body
//   InboxStyle       several lines, collapsed to "3 new messages"
//   MessagingStyle   a conversation, grouped by sender

final big = NotificationDetails(
  android: AndroidNotificationDetails(
    'reminders', 'Reminders',
    style: AndroidNotificationStyle.bigText,
  ),
  iOS: const DarwinNotificationDetails(),
);
await plugin.show(id, title, longBody, big);

// A THREAD, for a conversation
final threadId = 'thread-$id';
await plugin.show(
  id, senderName, message,
  NotificationDetails(
    threadId: threadId,
    groupKey: threadId,        // the GROUPING
  ),
);

// THE GROUP SUMMARY, which is REQUIRED for grouping to look right
await plugin.show(
  0,
  '3 new messages',
  null,
  NotificationDetails(
    android: AndroidNotificationDetails(
      'messages', 'Messages',
      groupKey: threadId,
      groupAlertBehavior: AndroidNotificationGroupAlertBehavior.summary,
    ),
  ),
);

// THE ACTIONS, which is what makes a notification useful
await plugin.show(
  id, 'New comment', 'Ana replied to your note',
  NotificationDetails(
    actions: <AndroidNotificationAction>[
      AndroidNotificationAction('reply', 'Reply'),
      AndroidNotificationAction('mute', 'Mute', showsUserInterface: false),
    ],
    iOS: const DarwinNotificationDetails(
      categoryIdentifier: 'comment',   // needs a category
    ),
  ),
);

14.2 Push notifications

// pubspec.yaml
//   firebase_messaging: ^15.1.0
//   flutter_local_notifications: ^17.2.0
//   firebase_core: ^3.0.0

class PushService {
  PushService({required this._local, required this._onToken, required this._onMessage});

  final FlutterLocalNotificationsPlugin _local;
  final void Function(String token) _onToken;
  final void Function(RemoteMessage message) _onMessage;

  Future<void> init() async {
    // 1. the BACKGROUND handler, which runs in its own isolate
    //    and MUST be a top-level function
    FirebaseMessaging.onBackgroundMessage(_backgroundHandler);

    // 2. foreground notifications: show them yourself, or the
    //    OS will not (by design)
    FirebaseMessaging.onMessage.listen(_onMessage);

    // 3. a notification that was tapped
    FirebaseMessaging.onMessageOpenedApp.listen(_onMessage);

    // 4. a notification that launched the app: COLD START
    final initial = await FirebaseMessaging.instance.getInitialMessage();
    if (initial != null) {
      // defer: the app may not be ready to navigate yet
      WidgetsBinding.instance.addPostFrameCallback((_) => _onMessage(initial));
    }

    // 5. PERMISSION
    final settings = await FirebaseMessaging.instance.requestPermission(
      alert: true,
      badge: true,
      sound: true,
      provisional: false,
      critical: false,
    );
    if (settings.authorizationStatus == AuthorizationStatus.denied) {
      // denied: offer the Settings deep link, because iOS will
      // never ask again
      await openAppSettings();
    }

    // 6. the token, and its lifecycle
    final token = await FirebaseMessaging.instance.getToken();
    if (token != null) _onToken(token);

    FirebaseMessaging.instance.onTokenRefresh.listen(_onToken);

    // 7. channels, before you send anything
    await _createAndroidChannels();
  }

  Future<void> _createAndroidChannels() async {
    final android = _local.resolvePlatformSpecificImplementation<
        AndroidFlutterLocalNotificationsPlugin>();

    await android?.createNotificationChannel(
      const AndroidNotificationChannel(
        'reminders', 'Reminders',
        description: 'Nudges about unfinished notes',
        importance: Importance.defaultImportance,
      ),
    );
    await android?.createNotificationChannel(
      const AndroidNotificationChannel(
        'sync', 'Background sync',
        description: 'Errors from a background sync',
        importance: Importance.low,   // silent: no sound
        playSound: false,
      ),
    );
  }
}

// THE BACKGROUND HANDLER: a top-level function, and it must
// complete quickly
@pragma('vm:entry-point')
Future<void> _backgroundHandler(RemoteMessage message) async {
  // this runs in a separate isolate, with its own Firebase
  // instance. Do the MINIMUM: maybe log it, maybe show a
  // notification. Anything slow is killed.
  final FirebaseMessaging.instance;
  // show a notification if the message says to
}
// THE PAYLOAD SHAPE, which you should design deliberately
// a notification payload is shown by the OS when the app is
// background or killed; a data payload is handled by your code
{
  "notification": {                  // shown by the OS
    "title": "Ana replied",
    "body": "Nice work on the migration",
    "sound": "default"
  },
  "data": {                          // YOUR structure: a string map
    "type": "comment",
    "entryId": "123",
    "deepLink": "/entries/123#comment-5",
    "title": "On the database migration"
  },
  "android": {
    "priority": "high",
    "notification": {
      "channel_id": "reminders",     // MUST exist, or it is dropped
      "click_action": "FLUTTER_NOTIFICATION_CLICK",
      "color": "#5B8CFF"
    }
  },
  "apns": {
    "payload": {
      "aps": {
        "alert": { "title": "Ana replied", "body": "Nice work" },
        "sound": "default",
        "badge": 1,
        "mutable-content": 1,        // for a notification service extension
        "content-available": 1       // a SILENT push, for background work
      }
    }
  }
}

// HANDLING IT, exhaustively
void _onMessage(RemoteMessage message) {
  final data = message.data;

  // 1. a silent push: no UI, just a signal
  if (data['type'] == 'sync_requested') {
    unawaited(syncNow());
    return;
  }

  // 2. a real notification, in the FOREGROUND: show it yourself
  if (data['type'] != null) {
    _local.show(
      message.hashCode,
      message.notification?.title ?? '',
      message.notification?.body ?? '',
      NotificationDetails(
        android: AndroidNotificationDetails(
          'reminders', 'Reminders',
          // the payload becomes the tap data
          icon: '@mipmap/ic_notification',
        ),
        iOS: const DarwinNotificationDetails(),
      ),
      payload: data['deepLink'],
    );
    return;
  }

  // 3. a data-only message while in the foreground:
  //    nothing is shown, and you must handle it
  if (data.containsKey('action')) {
    handleAction(data);
  }
}
// THE BADGE, which is fiddly and often expected
// iOS
await FirebaseMessaging.instance.setBadgeNumber(3);
// and clear it when the app is opened
FirebaseMessaging.instance.setBadgeNumber(0);

// Android: needs a channel with setShowBadge true (the default)
// and a launcher icon that is adaptive, or the badge is a white
// dot on a white background: invisible

// THE PERMISSION REFUSAL UX
// this is the flow that gets the most acceptance
if (status == AuthorizationStatus.denied) {
  // 1. explain WHY you want it, at the moment of value
  final understood = await showDialog(
    context: context,
    builder: (context) => AlertDialog(
      title: const Text('Stay up to date'),
      content: const Text(
        'Get notified when a teammate comments on a note, so you '
        'do not have to keep checking.',
      ),
      actions: [
        TextButton(
          onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context, false),
          child: const Text('Not now'),
        ),
        FilledButton(
          onPressed: () => Navigator.pop(context, true),
          child: const Text('Turn on'),
        ),
      ],
    ),
  );
  if (understood) {
    await FirebaseMessaging.instance.requestPermission();
  }
}

// and a SETTINGS entry, so the user can change their mind
// "Notifications" in your settings screen, always present

Push, tokens, and the four ways it fails silently

Push notification delivery is a three-party system — the device, the platform's service, and your server — and each party can fail in a way that looks like the other two are working. The device registers with the platform service and receives a token, which identifies the app installation on that device for that platform's service; the token is not stable, is invalidated when the application is reinstalled, and must be sent to your server. Your server sends a message to the platform's service, which delivers it to the device, which displays it — and each arrow can fail. Then the four ways it fails silently, and each has a specific mechanism. A token was invalidated and the server does not know. The platform's service reports an unregistration when a token stops being valid, and a server that ignores that report keeps sending to a token that will never be delivered — so the failure mode is a notification that worked yesterday and does not today with no error anywhere. A message was accepted but dropped. The platform's service accepts a message and may deliver it late or not at all when a device is offline or the application is force-quit, and it reports this through a feedback mechanism that most integrations do not consume. A payload was too large. There is a size limit and exceeding it is reported as a failure that is easy to miss because the error arrives asynchronously. And a user denied permission after registration, so the token is valid and the message is delivered and nothing appears — which looks identical to a server problem and is a configuration problem. Then the four practices, and each is a requirement. Treat the token as invalid until proven otherwise: send it with every registration, replace it when a new one arrives, and remove it when the platform reports unregistration. Keep the server's copy of which devices exist and when each token was last seen, because "which users can be reached" is a question with a real answer and most implementations cannot answer it. Never put anything sensitive in a payload — it is delivered to the device and stored by the platform, it is visible in some debugging tools, and on Android the payload of a message to a backgrounded application is delivered to the platform service before the application is running; so a payload is a channel to the device and must contain an identifier, not data. And handle the notification tap on a cold start, which is the deep-link chapter's ordering problem again — the payload arrives, the application launches, the session is not yet restored, and the tap handler that needs the session does nothing. Then the two things worth knowing about testing, because this is the area where testing is hardest. Test with the real transport — a real device, a real push, a real backgrounded application — because a test that calls the handler directly proves only that the handler works. And log the whole path — registration, token arrival at the server, send, delivery callback, tap — because the question "did they get the notification" has four answers and only a log across all four distinguishes them.

/* Three parties. */
const PATH = {
  parties: ['the DEVICE', 'the PLATFORMS SERVICE', 'YOUR SERVER'],

  server: 'SENDS A MESSAGE TO the PLATFORMS SERVICE, WHICH DELIVERS IT TO the DEVICE, WHICH DISPLAYS IT',
  fact: 'and EACH ARROW CAN FAIL',
};

14.3 Scheduled and repeating

// SCHEDULING, which needs the timezone database
final tz = await _configureTimeZone();

Future<void> scheduleReminder() async {
  await _local.zonedSchedule(
    _id,
    'Stand-up reminder',
    'You have been sitting for 50 minutes.',
    // a zoned DateTime, not a DateTime: a DST change moves it
    tz.TZDateTime.from(
      DateTime.now().add(const Duration(minutes: 50)),
      tz.local,
    ),
    NotificationDetails(
      android: AndroidNotificationDetails('reminders', 'Reminders'),
      iOS: const DarwinNotificationDetails(),
    ),

    // THE MATCHING RULES, and getting these wrong is why
    // notifications never fire
    androidScheduleMode: AndroidScheduleMode.inexactAllowWhileIdle,
    //   exactAllowWhileIdle: fires at an exact time, but it needs
    //     the SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM permission, and Android 13+
    //     requires the user to grant it in Settings
    //   inexactAllowWhileIdle: a window, no permission needed
    //   use inexact unless the exact time really matters
    uiLocalNotificationDateInterpretation:
        UILocalNotificationDateInterpretation.absoluteTime,

    matchDateTimeComponents: null,   // null: fire once
  );
}

// A DAILY REMINDER
final tomorrow = tz.TZDateTime.now(tz.local).add(const Duration(days: 1));
await _local.zonedSchedule(
  _id, 'Daily review', 'You logged 4 runs this week.',
  tomorrow,
  details,
  androidScheduleMode: AndroidScheduleMode.inexactAllowWhileIdle,
  matchDateTimeComponents: DateTimeComponents.time,   // repeats daily at
);                                                     // the same time

// EVERY WEEK
matchDateTimeComponents: DateTimeComponents.dayOfWeekAndTime;

// THE EXACT-ALARM PERMISSION, if you need an exact time
// android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.USE_EXACT_ALARM" />
// Android 14: USE_EXACT_ALARM is for ALARM CLOCK apps and is
// policy-restricted. For a reminder, ask for SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM
// and handle the user declining.
if (await _android.canScheduleExactNotifications() == false) {
  await _android.requestExactAlarmsPermission();
}

// MANAGE EXISTING SCHEDULES
final pending = await _local.pendingNotificationRequests();
await _local.cancel(_id);
await _local.cancelAll();
await _local.cancelAllPendingNotifications();   // iOS: clears delivered too

Scheduling, and why a scheduled notification is a promise you cannot keep exactly

A scheduled notification is one the platform will deliver at a future time without the application running, and both platforms implement it as a request stored in the operating system's own scheduler — which is the source of every surprising behaviour in this section. The system may deliver late. There is no guarantee of exact time on either platform; the platform batches delivery to save power, so a notification scheduled for nine in the morning can arrive at ten. And the system may not deliver at all if the application has been force-quit by the user, if the device has been restarted and the request was not restored, or if the platform's own optimisation classified it as low value. Then the three things that follow, and each is a design consequence. A scheduled notification cannot depend on anything computed at delivery time. The payload is fixed when the schedule is made, so anything dynamic must be computed then or fetched when the application next runs; a notification that says "you have 3 new messages" requires knowing there are three at scheduling time, which means the count goes stale. The schedule is stored in the operating system, so your application's state and the system's state can disagree, and on iOS the pending list can be read back — which is worth doing, because it is the only way to answer "what is scheduled" and a user asking that question cannot be answered from your database alone. And rescheduling is not idempotent in either platform. Cancelling and re-adding a schedule on iOS can produce a duplicate if the cancellation and the addition are not both applied, and on Android a notification identifier that is reused cancels the previous one — so the discipline is to use a stable identifier per schedule and to always cancel before adding. Then the three things that go wrong, and each has a mechanism. Duplicates on reschedule, which is the cancel-then-add race, and the fix is a stable identifier plus a single code path that does both. Time zones. A notification scheduled at eight in the morning local time and delivered after the user changes time zone fires at the wrong hour unless the schedule stores an absolute instant rather than a wall-clock time — and "nine in the morning" is a wall-clock time, so the correct handling is to reschedule when the zone changes. And a schedule that was never registered because the permission was requested after the scheduling call, which silently produces no notification at all. Then the two practices, and each is cheap. Keep your own record of what is scheduled, with the platform identifier, so you can cancel precisely, answer the user's question, and detect a schedule that was lost by comparing your record with the platform's pending list. And treat scheduling as best-effort and design the feature to work without it, because a reminder that arrives forty minutes late is worse than one that arrives on time every time and occasionally not at all — so if the notification is important, the application's own scheduling on next launch should be the mechanism and the platform schedule is the safety net.

14.4 Background execution

The declared background modes, and what each is for

Background execution is a set of separately-declared capabilities, and each is a promise to the platform about what your application does when it is not in front. Each capability is declared in the platform manifest, and declaring one you do not use is a review problem on iOS and a heuristic problem on Android, because the system uses the declarations to decide what to grant and reviewers use them to decide whether to approve. So the first discipline is to declare only what you use, and the second is to know what each one actually permits. Then the four modes, and each has a specific purpose and a specific limit. Periodic background refresh is a window the system grants at an interval it chooses, with no guarantee of frequency and no guarantee of any run at all; it is the right capability for "check for something that changes occasionally" and the wrong one for anything time-sensitive. Background fetch is the iOS equivalent and is the mechanism behind opportunistic refresh. A background task for a long transfer, which is what an upload uses, and which requires the registration to happen during launch so the system knows to grant it. And A foreground service, which is the only capability that lets an application run continuously with a visible notification, and which is the correct answer for a navigation screen, a media player or an active upload — and which the user can revoke at any time from the operating system's own settings, so it is not a capability you can rely on having. Then the three things that go wrong, and each has a mechanism. Registering too late, which is the launch-time requirement from the previous section and which produces a feature that works in debug and never in release. Doing unbounded work, which the system kills, and the fix is the idempotence discipline. And not declaring a foreground service for something that needs one, which produces a background task that is killed the moment the screen locks, and the symptom is a feature that works while the user watches and stops the moment they do not. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Pick one capability per feature, and pick the narrowest, because a feature that needs both a periodic refresh and a foreground service is usually a feature that has been designed around polling rather than around an event. And make every background entry point the same function as the foreground one, so that the code path is exercised in the foreground where it is testable and the background is a scheduler in front of it rather than a second implementation.

/* The discipline. */

  promise: 'a PROMISE TO the PLATFORM about WHAT YOUR APPLICATION DOES WHEN IT IS NOT IN FRONT',

};

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'PICK ONE CAPABILITY PER FEATURE, and PICK the NARROWEST',
    why: 'BECAUSE A FEATURE THAT NEEDS BOTH A PERIODIC REFRESH and A FOREGROUND SERVICE IS USUALLY A FEATURE THAT HAS BEEN DESIGNED AROUND POLLING rather than AROUND AN EVENT' },
  { p: 'MAKE EVERY BACKGROUND ENTRY POINT the SAME FUNCTION AS the FOREGROUND ONE',
    gain: 'so THAT the CODE PATH IS EXERCISED IN the FOREGROUND WHERE IT IS TESTABLE',
    and: 'the BACKGROUND IS A SCHEDULER IN FRONT of IT rather than A SECOND IMPLEMENTATION' },
];

Never make the correctness of the app depend on background work. The system may not run it, may run it hours late, and may batch it with other work; and on both platforms the OS terminates an app the user swiped away without telling you. The local database is the source of truth, and the app reconciles when it is next opened.

// THE HARD TRUTH, which you must design around
//
// when the user swipes your app away, the OS terminates it.
// the system may kill your app to reclaim memory at any time.
// background execution is throttled, delayed, and batched.
// the OS decides, not you, and it does not tell you.
//
// SO: the design rule is
//   "the local database is the source of truth, and the app
//    reconciles when it is next opened"
// not
//   "something syncs in the background so the data is fresh"

// THE HIERARCHY, from reliable to unreliable
//
// 1. WHILE THE APP IS FOREGROUNDED: full control
//    AppLifecycleState.resumed -> sync, listen, watch
//
// 2. A SCHEDULED NOTIFICATION: OS-owned, fires reliably
//    good for: a reminder, a deadline
//
// 3. ANDROID: WorkManager
//    periodic work, deferrable, survives a reboot
//    the right tool for a background sync on Android
//
// 4. iOS: BGTaskScheduler
//    BGAppRefreshTask, BGProcessingTask
//    the system decides when, and it may be days late
//
// 5. A FOREGROUND SERVICE: only with a user-visible notification
//    for continuous work the user has opted into
//
// 6. A HEADLESS ISOLATE via flutter_background_service
//    a plugin, because the framework does not support this
//
// 7. A DAEMON: impossible, and any app claiming otherwise
//    is either using a foreground service or being killed
// ANDROID: WorkManager, which is the correct tool
// android/app/build.gradle
//   implementation "androidx.work:work-runtime-ktx:2.9.1"

class SyncWorker(context: Context, params: WorkerParameters)
    : CoroutineWorker(context, params) {

    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        return try {
            // the constraints were checked before doWork ran
            val count = SyncEngine.pushPending()

            // a result the app can read
            setProgress(workDataOf("pushed" to count))
            Result.success(workDataOf("pushed" to count, "at" to System.currentTimeMillis()))

        } catch (e: IOException) {
            // a NETWORK failure: retry with backoff
            Result.retry()

        } catch (e: HttpException) {
            if (e.code in 500..599) return Result.retry()
            // a 4xx: our request is wrong, retrying will not help
            Result.failure(workDataOf("error" to e.message))

        } catch (e: Exception) {
            Result.failure()
        }
    }
}

// scheduling it, with constraints
class SyncScheduler(private val context: Context) {
    fun schedulePeriodic() {
        val constraints = Constraints.Builder()
            .setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED)
            .setRequiresBatteryNotLow(true)
            .setRequiresCharging(false)
            .setRequiresDeviceIdle(false)      // not during Doze
            .build()

        val request = PeriodicWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>(6, TimeUnit.HOURS)
            .setConstraints(constraints)
            .setBackoffCriteria(BackoffPolicy.EXPONENTIAL, 10, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
            .addTag("sync")
            .build()

        WorkManager.getInstance(context).enqueueUniquePeriodicWork(
            "sync",
            // KEEP: do not replace an existing schedule, or a
            // reschedule on every launch resets the interval
            ExistingPeriodicWorkPolicy.KEEP,
            request,
        )
    }

    fun scheduleNow() {
        val request = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>()
            .setConstraints(
                Constraints.Builder().setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED).build()
            )
            .build()
        WorkManager.getInstance(context).enqueueUniqueWork(
            "sync_now", ExistingWorkPolicy.REPLACE, request
        )
    }

    fun cancel() {
        WorkManager.getInstance(context).cancelUniqueWork("sync")
    }
}

// OBSERVING IT, so the app can show the state
WorkManager.getInstance(context)
    .getWorkInfosForUniqueWorkLiveData("sync")
    .observe(activity) { infos -> infos.forEach { info ->
        when (info.state) {
            WorkInfo.State.RUNNING -> setStatus('Syncing…'),
            WorkInfo.State.SUCCEEDED -> setStatus('Up to date'),
            WorkInfo.State.FAILED -> setStatus('Sync failed'),
            else -> {}
        }
    }}
// a LiveData, so the UI updates without a platform channel
// ANDROID MANIFEST: the components WorkManager needs
<!-- WorkManager initialises itself; do not disable it -->

// if you need a boot-time reschedule
<receiver
    android:name="androidx.work.impl.background.systemjob.RescheduleReceiver"
    android:enabled="true"
    android:exported="false">
  <intent-filter>
    <action android:name="android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED" />
    <action android:name="android.intent.action.MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED" />
  </intent-filter>
</receiver>

// and the permission
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED" />

// iOS: BGTaskScheduler
// Info.plist
<key>UIBackgroundModes</key>
<array><string>processing</string></array>
<key>BGTaskSchedulerPermittedIdentifiers</key>
<array>
  <string>com.acme.fieldnotes.sync</string>
  <string>com.acme.fieldnotes.refresh</string>
</array>

// AppDelegate.swift
import BackgroundTasks

func registerBackgroundTasks() {
    BGTaskScheduler.shared.register(
        forTaskWithIdentifier: "com.acme.fieldnotes.sync",
        using: nil
    ) { task in
        self.handleSyncTask(task as! BGProcessingTask)
    }
}

func scheduleSync() {
    let request = BGProcessingTaskRequest(identifier: "com.acme.fieldnotes.sync")
    request.requiresNetworkConnectivity = true
    request.requiresExternalPower = false
    request.earliestBeginDate = Date(timeIntervalSinceNow: 15 * 60)
    try? BGTaskScheduler.shared.submit(request)
}

func handleSyncTask(_ task: BGProcessingTask) {
    // ALWAYS queue the next one first: if this one is killed,
    // there is still a scheduled run
    scheduleSync()

    task.expirationHandler = {
        // the system is taking the memory back: clean up and stop
        task.setTaskCompleted(success: false)
    }

    SyncEngine.shared.pushPending { result in
        task.setTaskCompleted(success: result)
    }
}

// the AppDelegate must call registerBackgroundTasks() in
// didFinishLaunchingWithOptions, BEFORE the app finishes launching

14.5 Headless isolates

// A HEADLESS ISOLATE: Dart code that runs with no UI, for
// a plugin like flutter_background_service

// pubspec.yaml
//   flutter_background_service: ^5.0.0
//   flutter_background_service_android: ^5.0.0
//   flutter_background_service_ios: ^5.0.0

@pragma('vm:entry-point')
void onStart(ServiceInstance service) async {
    DartPluginRegistrant.ensureInitialized();

    if (service is AndroidServiceInstance) {
        // start as a FOREGROUND service, or Android kills it in
        // about 30 seconds. This is required, and it needs a
        // visible notification.
        service.setAsForegroundService();

        service.on('setAsForegroundServiceNotification').listen((args) {
            service.setForegroundNotification(
                const AndroidNotification(
                    channelId: 'sync',
                    id: 1001,
                    title: 'Syncing your notes',
                    priority: AndroidNotificationPriority.low,
                    ongoing: false,
                ),
            );
        });
    }

    service.on('sync').listen((args) async {
        try {
            final count = await SyncEngine.pushPending();
            service.invoke('syncComplete', {'count': count});
        } catch (e) {
            service.invoke('syncFailed', {'error': '$e'});
        }
    });
}

// and on the Dart side
final service = FlutterBackgroundService();

Future<void> startBackgroundSync() async {
  await service.configure(
    androidConfiguration: AndroidConfiguration(
      onStart: onStart,
      autoStart: false,
      isForegroundMode: true,
      notificationChannelId: 'sync',
      initialNotificationTitle: 'Syncing',
      initialNotificationContent: 'Preparing…',
    ),
    iosConfiguration: IosConfiguration(
      autoStart: false,
      onForeground: onStart,
      onBackground: onIosBackground,
    ),
  );
  await service.startService();
}

Future<void> requestSync() async {
  if (service.isRunning) {
    service.invoke('sync');
  } else {
    await startBackgroundSync();
    service.invoke('sync');
  }
}

// THE IOS LIMITATIONS, which are severe
// iOS gives an app about 30 seconds of background time per launch.
// A background service on iOS runs until the system kills it,
// which is usually within minutes. It is NOT a daemon.
// Anything long-running on iOS needs a foreground mode, and
// Apple rejects apps that abuse it.

Headless execution, and the three things you cannot do

A headless isolate is an isolate started by the operating system without the user opening the application — the mechanism behind a background fetch, a headless task, and a background notification action — and it runs Dart with no interface and with a limited time budget. On Android it is a headless task the system starts when it decides to, and it may not run at all; the scheduling is the operating system's power decision, not yours, and it will run sooner on a device that is charging and on a network than on one that is not. On iOS it is a background task with a short window that the system grants on specific triggers, and the application has to declare what it is doing before the system will grant it. Then the three things you cannot do, and each is a hard limit that shapes the design. You cannot run for an arbitrary time. There is a budget — on Android of the order of half a minute to a few minutes, on iOS seconds — and exceeding it gets the process killed, which is a worse outcome than being slow because work is interrupted rather than finished. You cannot touch the interface, so there is no widget, no context, no animation and no way to show progress; a background task that needs to tell the user something must schedule a notification rather than draw. And you cannot assume the network or the storage is available in the way you are used to, because the task runs under the system's conditions and a slow network is common, which means everything must be bounded and retryable. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a specific mechanism. Doing a long computation in a headless task, which is killed mid-way and leaves partial state, and the fix is to make the task idempotent so that being killed is not a corruption. Assuming the task will run. If the feature depends on it, the feature is broken on a device where the system decided not to run it, and the correct design is to have a second mechanism — a schedule, a push, or work done when the application next opens. And registering too late. The registration must happen during launch on iOS, and a registration performed after the launch has completed is not accepted, which is a failure that appears only in a release build. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Make every headless task idempotent and short, so that being killed and re-run is safe — which means the task should be able to stop at any point and be re-entered without duplicating work, and the standard mechanism is a durable record of what has been done. And instrument it, because a background task that silently stops running is invisible: log each invocation with its start, its duration and its outcome, and the log is the only way to discover that the feature stopped working a month after it was shipped.

14.6 Battery and the reality of it

The trade, stated honestly

Every background capability on a phone is a claim on the user's battery, and the operating system is the referee: it grants background work to applications that behave well and takes it away from those that do not, so the question is not what you can do but what you will be allowed to keep doing. The radio is the expensive part. A network connection that keeps the cellular or wifi radio awake costs far more than the computation it enables, because a radio that is awake cannot sleep, and sleep is where the battery goes. So an application that polls every minute is not paying for its request — it is paying for the radio being unable to sleep. Work batching is the platform's default answer, and both operating systems batch background work precisely because it saves power: they will run your task when it is convenient, delay it, and combine it with other applications' work. An exact schedule is expensive and will be refused. Then the four things that decide whether a background feature survives, and each is a policy rather than a technique. Use push rather than polling, always: the platform's delivery infrastructure batches across every application on the device, so a push is free for your application where a poll keeps the radio awake; and a WebSocket is worse than a poll because it keeps a connection rather than waking periodically. Ask for the narrowest capability. An exact alarm requires a permission and a justification and is reserved for alarms and calendars; a background refresh requires nothing; and the difference in user trust between an application that asked for one and one that asked for both is large. Do the work when the application is already open, because a task scheduled for immediately after launch costs nothing while a task that wakes the application costs a full wake. And be willing to do less. The most reliable background feature is one that tolerates running rarely, because the system will make it rare and an application that copes is not broken. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Polling on a timer, which is the classic and which the system will eventually throttle to the point of being useless — and which costs battery for a data freshness the user does not perceive. Holding a connection open for real-time updates, which is the previous chapter's socket problem and which drains a battery in hours. And registering for a capability that is not used, which the system notices — the heuristics that decide who gets background work are partly based on whether the application uses what it registered for — and which results in work being refused later. Then the two practices, and each is a habit. Measure battery, not features,: run the application for a realistic session with the feature enabled and disabled and compare, because the difference is the only argument that will survive a product discussion. And say in the interface what the feature costs — a setting that says "updates use a little battery" and defaults sensibly is both better design and better battery, because a user who has been told can make the choice and a user who has not will simply uninstall.
