Tell the user what the sync state is. "Saved on this device", "synced two minutes ago" and "offline, three changes waiting" are three short strings that convert an app which looks broken into one which looks reliable.

// WHAT YOU CAN AND CANNOT ASK FOR
//
// iOS:
//   background fetch: a user-visible switch, and it may be never
//   BGProcessingTask: needs a justification, and it is throttled
//   background modes: location, audio, voip - each is reviewed
//   anything continuous: a foreground mode, and App Review will
//     ask why
//
// Android:
//   WorkManager: the sanctioned way. Periodic, deferrable,
//     constrained, survives a reboot. Throttled in Doze.
//   a foreground service: a visible notification, and a type
//     (Android 14+ requires it), and Play reviews the reason
//   an exact alarm: a user-granted permission, for alarms
//
// BOTH: the system will not tell you when it stopped running.

// THE DESIGN CONSEQUENCE
// never make the app's correctness depend on background work.
// the pattern that works:
//
//   1. the local database is the source of truth
//   2. every write goes local-first
//   3. a sync is ATTEMPTED:
//      - on app start
//      - on app resume
//      - on connectivity regained
//      - on a local write, if online
//      - from WorkManager or BGTask, as a bonus
//   4. the UI shows the state, always:
//      "Saved on this device"
//      "Synced 2 minutes ago"
//      "Offline - 3 changes waiting"

// THE STATE, which is what the user actually needs to see
class SyncStatus {
  final SyncState state;         // idle, syncing, offline, error
  final DateTime? lastSyncedAt;
  final int pendingCount;
  final String? message;
}

class SyncBanner extends StatelessWidget {
  const SyncBanner({required this.status, super.key});
  final SyncStatus status;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final scheme = Theme.of(context).colorScheme;

    switch (status.state) {
      case SyncState.offline:
        return Banner(
          background: scheme.tertiaryContainer,
          child: Text(
            status.pendingCount > 0
                ? 'Offline · ${status.pendingCount} change${status.pendingCount == 1 ? '' : 's'} saved on this device'
                : 'Offline',
            style: TextStyle(color: scheme.onTertiaryContainer),
          ),
        );
      case SyncState.error:
        return Banner(
          background: scheme.errorContainer,
          child: TextButton(
            onPressed: () => ref.read(syncProvider.notifier).retry(),
            child: Text('Sync failed: ${status.message} · Tap to retry'),
          ),
        );
      default:
        return const SizedBox.shrink();
    }
  }
}

14.7 No connection, and telling the user

// CONNECTIVITY, and why you need a package
// pubspec.yaml
//   connectivity_plus: ^6.0.5

final connectivity = Connectivity();
final _online = ValueNotifier<bool>(true);

Future<void> initConnectivity() async {
  _online.value = await _check();
  // the STREAM, for changes
  connectivity.onConnectivityChanged.listen((results) {
    _online.value = !results.contains(ConnectivityResult.none);
    if (_online.value) {
      // connectivity does not mean the API is reachable, but it
      // is a good enough signal to try a sync
      unawaited(syncIfConnected());
    }
  });
}

Future<bool> _check() async {
  final results = await connectivity.checkConnectivity();
  return !results.contains(ConnectivityResult.none);
}

// THE CAVEATS
// 1. it reports the INTERFACE, not the internet. A captive
//    portal at a hotel wifi reports "wifi" and no internet.
// 2. on iOS it needs the location permission to distinguish
//    cellular from wifi on some versions
// 3. it is a hint. ALWAYS handle the request failing anyway.

// THE UI: three states, always
switch (state) {
  case 'empty':
    // nothing saved yet
  case 'loading':
    // the first load, with no cache
  case 'data':
    // real content
  case 'stale':
    // cached content, and a banner
  case 'error':
    // a failure, with a retry
}

// a PATTERN that handles it all
Future<void> load() async {
  // 1. paint the cache immediately
  state = cached == null ? 'loading' : 'data';

  // 2. then try the network
  try {
    final fresh = await api.fetch();
    await cache.write(fresh);
    state = 'data';
  } on NetworkFailure {
    if (cached != null) {
      state = 'stale';       // usable, and honest
    } else {
      state = 'error';       // nothing to show
    }
  }
}

Detecting it, and the three states the user needs to see

Every mobile application eventually meets a network that does not work, and the question is not whether to handle it but what to show. The framework gives you a connectivity value that reports whether a network interface exists — and that value answers a question the user does not care about. Having a network is not the same as being able to reach the server. A captive portal, a hotel wi-fi that requires a sign-in page, a tunnel with no route out, a server that is down: all of these report connectivity and all of them mean a request will fail. So connectivity is a hint, not a fact, and an application that disables a button when the value is false and enables it when true will enable a button that cannot work. Then the three states the user needs to distinguish, and conflating them is the reason the interface feels wrong. The request is in flight, which is not an error and should not look like one; a spinner is right and an error message is wrong. The request failed and can be retried, which is a transient condition and should offer a retry without asking the user to do anything else. And the request failed and retrying will not help, which is a permanent condition — the record does not exist, the input is invalid — and should say what happened rather than offering a retry that will fail identically. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Showing a full-screen error for a background refresh, which is the classic: the user is reading a screen, a background sync fails, and a dialog covers the content they were looking at; the fix is that a background failure updates a status indicator and a failed foreground action shows an error. Trusting the connectivity value, as above, which produces an enabled control that cannot work and the appearance of a bug rather than of a network problem. And not distinguishing empty from failed, which is the offline-first chapter's point in a different place: a list showing nothing because the request failed and a list showing nothing because there is nothing are different states and a user who cannot tell them will report the application as broken when it is empty. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Cache enough to render the last known good state, so that opening a screen offline shows something rather than an error — and label it as cached, because presenting stale data as current is the stale-data failure again. And make the offline case a designed state rather than an absence, because an application designed for offline looks deliberate and one that merely survives it looks broken, and the difference is entirely in whether somebody wrote the empty and failed states down.

/* What connectivity tells you. */
const VALUE = 'the FRAMEWORK GIVES YOU A CONNECTIVITY VALUE THAT REPORTS WHETHER A NETWORK INTERFACE EXISTS';
const WRONG_QUESTION = 'AND THAT VALUE ANSWERS A QUESTION the USER DOES NOT CARE ABOUT';
const DISTINCTION = {
  isNot: 'HAVING A NETWORK IS NOT the SAME AS BEING ABLE TO REACH the SERVER',
  examples: ['A CAPTIVE PORTAL', 'A HOTEL WI-FI THAT REQUIRES A SIGN-IN PAGE',
    'A TUNNEL with NO ROUTE OUT', 'A SERVER THAT IS DOWN'],
  all: 'ALL of THESE REPORT CONNECTIVITY and ALL of THEM MEAN A REQUEST WILL FAIL',
  therefore: 'CONNECTIVITY IS A HINT, NOT A FACT',
  bug: 'AN APPLICATION THAT DISABLES A BUTTON WHEN the VALUE IS FALSE and ENABLES IT WHEN TRUE WILL ENABLE A BUTTON THAT CANNOT WORK',
};

/* Three states. */
const STATES = [
  { s: 'the REQUEST IS IN FLIGHT', isNot: 'AN ERROR', should: 'A SPINNER',
    notShould: 'AN ERROR MESSAGE' },
  { s: 'the REQUEST FAILED and CAN BE RETRIED', kind: 'A TRANSIENT CONDITION',
    should: 'OFFER A RETRY WITHOUT ASKING the USER TO DO ANYTHING ELSE' },
  { s: 'the REQUEST FAILED and RETRYING WILL NOT HELP', kind: 'A PERMANENT CONDITION',
    instances: ['the RECORD DOES NOT EXIST', 'the INPUT IS INVALID'],
    should: 'SAY WHAT HAPPENED rather than OFFERING A RETRY THAT WILL FAIL IDENTICALLY' },
];
const WHY_STATES = 'CONFLATING THEM IS the REASON the INTERFACE FEELS WRONG';

/* Three things that go wrong. */
const GO_WRONG = [
  { f: 'SHOWING A FULL-SCREEN ERROR for A BACKGROUND REFRESH', rank: 'WHICH IS the CLASSIC',
    detail: 'the USER IS READING A SCREEN, A BACKGROUND SYNC FAILS, and A DIALOG COVERS the CONTENT THEY WERE LOOKING AT',
    fix: 'A BACKGROUND FAILURE UPDATES A STATUS INDICATOR and A FAILED FOREGROUND ACTION SHOWS AN ERROR' },
  { f: 'TRUSTING the CONNECTIVITY VALUE', consequence: 'WHICH PRODUCES AN ENABLED CONTROL THAT CANNOT WORK and the APPEARANCE of A BUG rather than of A NETWORK PROBLEM' },
  { f: 'NOT DISTINGUISHING EMPTY from FAILED',
    detail: 'WHICH IS the OFFLINE-FIRST CHAPTERS POINT IN A DIFFERENT PLACE',
    symptom: 'A LIST SHOWING NOTHING BECAUSE the REQUEST FAILED and A LIST SHOWING NOTHING BECAUSE THERE IS NOTHING ARE DIFFERENT STATES',
    and: 'A USER WHO CANNOT TELL THEM WILL REPORT the APPLICATION AS BROKEN WHEN IT IS EMPTY' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'CACHE ENOUGH TO RENDER the LAST KNOWN GOOD STATE',
    gain: 'SO THAT OPENING A SCREEN OFFLINE SHOWS SOMETHING rather than AN ERROR',
    but: 'and LABEL IT AS CACHED, BECAUSE PRESENTING STALE DATA AS CURRENT IS the STALE-DATA FAILURE AGAIN' },
  { p: 'MAKE the OFFLINE CASE A DESIGNED STATE rather than AN ABSENCE',
    why: 'BECAUSE AN APPLICATION DESIGNED FOR OFFLINE LOOKS DELIBERATE and ONE THAT MERELY SURVIVES IT LOOKS BROKEN',
    and: 'the DIFFERENCE IS ENTIRELY IN WHETHER SOMEBODY WROTE the EMPTY and FAILED STATES DOWN' },
];

Exercises 15

  1. Show a local notification, then handle a tap with a payload that navigates to a specific screen. Test a cold start from the notification.
  2. Add a daily scheduled reminder with a zonedSchedule, and verify it survives a reboot and a time-zone change.
  3. Register a FirebaseMessaging token, send a test message from the console, and handle the tap in all three states: foreground, background, killed.
  4. Implement the permission flow with an in-context rationale, a Settings deep link on refusal, and a settings-screen toggle.
  5. Add a WorkManager periodic sync with a network constraint and exponential backoff, and observe it in the WorkManager logs.
  6. Add a BGTaskScheduler task on iOS that always reschedules itself first, and confirm it runs at all on a real device.
  7. Build the four-state data loader from 14.7 - loading, empty, data, stale, error - and verify the stale state is reachable by killing the network.
  8. Measure the app's battery usage over an hour with a naive 5-minute background sync, then with a WorkManager periodic task, and compare.

15 · Testing and Golden Tests

15.1 The test pyramid for Flutter15.2 Widget tests in detail15.3 Finders and the interactions that matter15.4 Golden tests15.5 Making goldens reliable15.6 Unit testing the logic15.7 Mocking the platform15.8 Integration tests15.9 CI and coverage

Widget tests are unusually powerful in Flutter, and unusual things go wrong with them. This chapter is about both the power and the traps.

15.1 The test pyramid for Flutter

The three kinds, what each can and cannot catch

The pyramid's shape is a consequence of what each kind of test can reach, so it is worth stating what that is rather than memorising the ratio. A unit test runs a plain Dart object with no framework, in milliseconds, thousands of them in a second. It can therefore be exhaustive about logic — every branch, every boundary, every error path — and it is the only kind that can afford to be thorough. A widget test pumps one widget with a fake environment, in a second or two, and it can reach the rendered tree and simulate gestures and verify layout constraints; what it cannot reach is anything outside the widget, which is why a widget test needs fakes for every dependency the widget has. An integration test drives the whole application on a device or emulator, in tens of seconds, and it can reach the real network and the real platform — and it is the only kind that can catch a wiring mistake between two correct pieces, which is the class of bug the other two cannot see by construction. Then the three things that follow, and each is a practical consequence. Only an integration test finds a wiring bug. A repository and a screen can each be correct and the call between them can be wrong, and only something that runs both finds it — which is why "unit tests are at a hundred per cent and the application is broken" is a coherent state. Push the logic down so the unit tests can reach it, because a widget test that asserts on rendered text is asserting on the framework's rendering, and a text change is a false failure while a logic change may be a false pass. And have few integration tests that assert on journeys, not on screens. Sign in, add something, see it, delete it — four journeys, each running the real thing, catch the wiring and the platform and the packaging; twenty integration tests that assert on individual screens are twenty slow widget tests. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. A pyramid inverted by accident, where integration tests accumulate because they are easy to write and slow to fail usefully; the diagnostic is the ratio of test runtimes, and if the slowest tests outnumber the fastest by more than a few to one the shape is wrong. Widget tests that assert on nothing, which pass when the widget renders even though it renders the wrong thing — and the cause is almost always a fake that returns a default rather than a value that exercises the assertion. And unit tests of the framework rather than the logic, which is a test that passes when nothing is wrong and fails when the framework changes. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Follow the change, not the screen: when you change a rule, the test that should fail is the one that exercises the rule, and if none fails you did not test the change. And keep the fast suite under a few seconds, because a suite that takes a minute is a suite people run once a day rather than on every change, and a test suite's value is in frequency rather than in quantity.

/* What each kind can reach. */
const UNIT = {
  runs: 'A PLAIN DART OBJECT with NO FRAMEWORK, IN MILLISECONDS, THOUSANDS of THEM IN A SECOND',
  can: 'BE EXHAUSTIVE ABOUT LOGIC - EVERY BRANCH, EVERY BOUNDARY, EVERY ERROR PATH',
  and: 'it IS the ONLY KIND THAT CAN AFFORD TO BE THOROUGH',
};
const WIDGET = {
  runs: 'PUMPS ONE WIDGET with A FAKE ENVIRONMENT, IN A SECOND OR TWO',
  can: ['REACH the RENDERED TREE', 'SIMULATE GESTURES', 'VERIFY LAYOUT CONSTRAINTS'],
  cannot: 'ANYTHING OUTSIDE the WIDGET',
  consequence: 'WHICH IS WHY A WIDGET TEST NEEDS FAKES for EVERY DEPENDENCY the WIDGET HAS',
};
const INTEGRATION = {
  runs: 'DRIVES the WHOLE APPLICATION ON A DEVICE or EMULATOR, IN TENS OF SECONDS',
  can: ['REACH the REAL NETWORK', 'and the REAL PLATFORM'],
  unique: 'and IT IS the ONLY KIND THAT CAN CATCH A WIRING MISTAKE BETWEEN TWO CORRECT PIECES',
  classOfBug: 'WHICH IS the CLASS of BUG the OTHER TWO CANNOT SEE BY CONSTRUCTION',
};

/* Three consequences. */
const CONSEQUENCES = [
  { c: 'ONLY AN INTEGRATION TEST FINDS A WIRING BUG',
    detail: 'A REPOSITORY and A SCREEN CAN EACH BE CORRECT and the CALL BETWEEN THEM CAN BE WRONG',
    symptom: 'WHICH IS WHY unit tests are at a hundred per cent and the APPLICATION IS BROKEN IS A COHERENT STATE' },
  { c: 'PUSH the LOGIC DOWN so the UNIT TESTS CAN REACH IT',

    consequence: 'AND A TEXT CHANGE IS A FALSE FAILURE while A LOGIC CHANGE MAY BE A FALSE PASS' },
  { c: 'HAVE FEW INTEGRATION TESTS THAT ASSERT ON JOURNEYS, NOT ON SCREENS',

    gain: 'FOUR JOURNEYS, EACH RUNNING the REAL THING, CATCH the WIRING and the PLATFORM and the PACKAGING',
    bad: 'TWENTY INTEGRATION TESTS THAT ASSERT ON INDIVIDUAL SCREENS ARE TWENTY SLOW WIDGET TESTS' },
];

/* Three things that go wrong. */
const GO_WRONG = [
  { f: 'A PYRAMID INVERTED BY ACCIDENT',
    detail: 'WHERE INTEGRATION TESTS ACCUMULATE BECAUSE THEY ARE EASY TO WRITE and SLOW TO FAIL USEFULLY',
    diagnostic: 'the RATIO of TEST RUNTIMES',
    and: 'IF the SLOWEST TESTS OUTNUMBER the FASTEST BY MORE THAN A FEW TO ONE the SHAPE IS WRONG' },
  { f: 'WIDGET TESTS THAT ASSERT ON NOTHING',
    symptom: 'WHICH PASS WHEN the WIDGET RENDERS EVEN THOUGH IT RENDERS the WRONG THING',
    cause: 'and the CAUSE IS ALMOST ALWAYS A FAKE THAT RETURNS A DEFAULT rather than A VALUE THAT EXERCISES the ASSERTION' },
  { f: 'UNIT TESTS of the FRAMEWORK rather than of the LOGIC',
    symptom: 'WHICH IS A TEST THAT PASSES WHEN NOTHING IS WRONG and FAILS WHEN the FRAMEWORK CHANGES' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'FOLLOW the CHANGE, NOT the SCREEN',
    detail: 'WHEN YOU CHANGE A RULE, the TEST THAT SHOULD FAIL IS the ONE THAT EXERCISES the RULE',
    and: 'IF NONE FAILS YOU DID NOT TEST the CHANGE' },
  { p: 'KEEP the FAST SUITE UNDER A FEW SECONDS',
    why: 'BECAUSE A SUITE THAT TAKES A MINUTE IS A SUITE PEOPLE RUN ONCE A DAY rather than ON EVERY CHANGE',
    and: 'A TEST SUITES VALUE IS IN FREQUENCY rather than IN QUANTITY' },
];

Widget tests are unusually strong in Flutter because a widget tree is a pure function of its inputs. That makes UI logic testable without a device, which is why the widget level should hold most of your tests rather than the unit level alone.

// FOUR LEVELS, and what each is for
//
// 1. UNIT        plain Dart: a model, a repository, a mapper
//                fast, no Flutter, the majority of your tests
//
// 2. WIDGET      a widget in isolation, with a mocked repository
//                fast, and the highest-value level for UI logic
//
// 3. GOLDEN      a rendered screenshot, compared to a reference
//                catches visual regressions; slow and brittle if
//                you are not careful
//
// 4. INTEGRATION the whole app on a real device or emulator
//                slow, few, and for the flows that must not break
//
// A WORKABLE RATIO for a team of three
//   250 unit, 120 widget, 20 golden, 12 integration
//
// and the rule: if an integration test is slow, the thing it tests
// is not integrated. That is useful information.
// THE COMMANDS
flutter test                                everything
flutter test test/entry_card_test.dart        one file
flutter test --plain-name "renders the title"  by name
flutter test --coverage
flutter test --update-goldens                  accept new goldens
flutter test --concurrency=1                  serialised: for
                                              timers or a
                                              shared resource
flutter test --reporter expanded
flutter test --platform chrome                web
flutter test integration_test/               on a device
flutter drive --driver=test_driver/integration_test.dart \
              --target=integration_test/app_test.dart

15.2 Widget tests in detail

// THE ANATOMY
testWidgets('renders the entry title', (tester) async {
  // 1. pump a widget tree
  await tester.pumpWidget(
    MaterialApp(
      home: Scaffold(
        body: EntryCard(entry: testEntry),
      ),
    ),
  );

  // 2. assert on what is rendered
  expect(find.text('Test entry'), findsOneWidget);
  expect(find.byType(CircleAvatar), findsOneWidget);
  expect(find.byIcon(Icons.edit), findsNothing);
});

// THE PUMP FAMILY, and choosing the wrong one is the most
// common cause of a flaky test
//
// pump()           one frame. for a state change.
// pumpAndSettle()  until nothing is animating. for an
//                   animation that ends.
// pump(Duration)   advance the clock by that much, one frame.
//                   for a timer, a delay, an animation mid-way.
//
// WHY pumpAndSettle TIMES OUT
// if a CircularProgressIndicator or a shimmer is on screen, it
// animates forever, so pumpAndSettle never settles
await tester.pump();                 // do NOT settle
await tester.pump(const Duration(milliseconds: 400));

// and it times out at 10 minutes by default, which is a very
// long time to wait before finding out
await tester.pumpAndSettle(
  const Duration(milliseconds: 100),
  EnginePhase.sendSemanticsUpdate,
  const Duration(seconds: 5),       // an explicit timeout
);

// A GOLDEN OR SKELETON ON SCREEN: use pump, not pumpAndSettle
// SETUP AND TEARDOWN, inside a group
void main() {
  late Directory tempDir;
  late AppDatabase database;
  late EntryRepository repository;

  setUp(() async {
    tempDir = await Directory.systemTemp.createTemp('test');
    database = AppDatabase.forTesting(NativeDatabase.memory());
    repository = EntryRepository(
      db: database,
      api: MockEntryApi(entries: [testEntry]),
    );
  });

  tearDown(() async {
    await database.close();
    await tempDir.delete(recursive: true);
  });

  // in-memory SQLite: fast, and it tests the real SQL
  group('EntryRepository', () {
    test('returns the entries', () async {
      final entries = await repository.all();
      expect(entries, hasLength(1));
      expect(entries.first.title, 'Test entry');
    });

    test('throws for a missing entry', () async {
      expect(
        () => repository.byId('nope'),
        throwsA(isA<NotFoundException>()),
      );
    });
  });
}

// THE OVERRIDE, for a widget test with real data
await tester.pumpWidget(
  ProviderScope(
    overrides: [
      databaseProvider.overrideWithValue(database),
      entryRepositoryProvider.overrideWithValue(repository),
    ],
    child: const MyApp(),
  ),
);

Pumping, and why pump and settle is a trap

A widget test builds a widget tree, attaches it to a fake environment, and drives frames — and the mechanism has one rule that catches everybody, which is that frames are not time. Nothing happens until you ask for a frame. The fake clock does not advance on its own; a widget that calls setState marks itself dirty and the new state is not built until pump is called. This is deliberate — it is what makes a test deterministic — and it is the reason a widget test that pumps once and asserts will assert on the state before the update the test just triggered. pump advances time by a duration and builds one frame; pumpAndSettle repeats until nothing schedules another frame. Then the trap, which is the single most common widget-test defect. An animation that never ends means pumpAndSettle never returns. A spinner, an infinite animation, a repeating progress indicator — anything that schedules frames forever will make pumpAndSettle pump forever, and the test hangs with no error, which is worse than a failure because a hanging test blocks the suite. The fix is to pump a fixed duration instead of settling, so the test asserts at a known point in the animation, which is also more precise. And the second trap is the mirror image: pumpAndSettle on a screen with a loading state that resolves asynchronously pumps until the future completes, so a test that settles on a screen with a network call will either take as long as the network takes or hang. Then the three things to do properly, and each is a practice. Wrap the widget under test in the providers it needs, with fakes, so that the test does not depend on anything global — and the reason is that a widget test that reads a global is one test removed from being order-dependent. Assert on things that cannot change accidentally: that a specific text appears, that a specific key is present, that a specific callback fired with a specific argument — rather than on a widget's exact type or a render object's internals, both of which change with a refactor that broke nothing. And set the surface size explicitly when layout matters, because the default test surface is a fixed size and a test that asserts on a layout which only holds at a different size will pass in the test and fail on a device. Then the three things that go wrong, and each has a mechanism. A test that passes without pumping again, which asserts on the pre-update state and is a test that cannot fail when the feature is broken. A fake that returns a default, which makes the widget render its empty state and produces a passing test of nothing. And asserting on a scroll position or a text measurement, which depends on the test environment's font and size and fails on a machine with a different configuration — which is why the golden tests exist and why they have their own section. Then the two practices, and each is a habit. Write the test as the specification of one behaviour, so that a failure names the behaviour rather than a line number. And use a key on anything you need to find, because a finder by type finds every instance and a finder by key finds the one you meant — which is the difference between a test that survives a refactor and one that does not.

/* The rule. */
const RULE = {
  mechanism: 'A WIDGET TEST BUILDS A WIDGET TREE, ATTACHES IT TO A FAKE ENVIRONMENT, and DRIVES FRAMES',
  fact: 'FRAMES ARE NOT TIME',
  detail: 'NOTHING HAPPENS UNTIL YOU ASK FOR A FRAME',
  how: 'the FAKE CLOCK DOES NOT ADVANCE ON ITS OWN',
  consequence: 'A WIDGET THAT CALLS setState MARKS ITSELF DIRTY and the NEW STATE IS NOT BUILT UNTIL pump IS CALLED',
  deliberate: 'THIS IS DELIBERATE - IT IS WHAT MAKES A TEST DETERMINISTIC',
  so: 'and IT IS the REASON A WIDGET TEST THAT PUMPS ONCE and ASSERTS WILL ASSERT ON the STATE BEFORE the UPDATE the TEST JUST TRIGGERED',
};
const TWO = {
  pump: 'ADVANCES TIME BY A DURATION and BUILDS ONE FRAME',
  pumpAndSettle: 'REPEATS UNTIL NOTHING SCHEDULES ANOTHER FRAME',
};

/* The trap. */
const TRAP = {
  is: 'AN ANIMATION THAT NEVER ENDS MEANS pumpAndSettle NEVER RETURNS',
  instances: ['A SPINNER', 'AN INFINITE ANIMATION', 'A REPEATING PROGRESS INDICATOR'],
  effect: 'ANYTHING THAT SCHEDULES FRAMES FOREVER WILL MAKE pumpAndSettle PUMP FOREVER',
  symptom: 'and the TEST HANGS WITH NO ERROR',
  worse: 'WHICH IS WORSE THAN A FAILURE BECAUSE A HANGING TEST BLOCKS the SUITE',
  fix: 'PUMP A FIXED DURATION instead of SETTLING',
  gain: 'so the TEST ASSERTS AT A KNOWN POINT IN the ANIMATION, WHICH IS ALSO MORE PRECISE',
};
const TRAP2 = {
  is: 'the SECOND TRAP IS the MIRROR IMAGE',
  detail: 'pumpAndSettle ON A SCREEN with A LOADING STATE THAT RESOLVES ASYNCHRONOUSLY PUMPS UNTIL the FUTURE COMPLETES',
  consequence: 'so A TEST THAT SETTLES ON A SCREEN with A NETWORK CALL WILL EITHER TAKE AS LONG AS the NETWORK TAKES or HANG',
};

/* Three to do properly. */
const RIGHT = [
  { r: 'WRAP the WIDGET UNDER TEST IN the PROVIDERS IT NEEDS, WITH FAKES',
    so: 'the TEST DOES NOT DEPEND ON ANYTHING GLOBAL',
    why: 'and the REASON IS THAT A WIDGET TEST THAT READS A GLOBAL IS ONE TEST REMOVED from BEING ORDER-DEPENDENT' },
  { r: 'ASSERT ON THINGS THAT CANNOT CHANGE ACCIDENTALLY',
    good: ['THAT A SPECIFIC TEXT APPEARS', 'THAT A SPECIFIC KEY IS PRESENT', 'THAT A SPECIFIC CALLBACK FIRED with A SPECIFIC ARGUMENT'],
    bad: ['A WIDGETS EXACT TYPE', 'A RENDER OBJECTS INTERNALS'],
    why: 'BOTH of WHICH CHANGE WITH A REFACTOR THAT BROKE NOTHING' },
  { r: 'SET the SURFACE SIZE EXPLICITLY WHEN LAYOUT MATTERS',
    detail: 'BECAUSE the DEFAULT TEST SURFACE IS A FIXED SIZE',
    symptom: 'and A TEST THAT ASSERTS ON A LAYOUT WHICH ONLY HOLDS AT A DIFFERENT SIZE WILL PASS IN the TEST and FAIL ON A DEVICE' },
];

/* Three things that go wrong. */
const GO_WRONG = [
  { f: 'A TEST THAT PASSES WITHOUT PUMPING AGAIN', consequence: 'WHICH ASSERTS ON the PRE-UPDATE STATE and IS A TEST THAT CANNOT FAIL WHEN the FEATURE IS BROKEN' },
  { f: 'A FAKE THAT RETURNS A DEFAULT', consequence: 'WHICH MAKES the WIDGET RENDER ITS EMPTY STATE and PRODUCES A PASSING TEST of NOTHING' },
  { f: 'ASSERTING ON A SCROLL POSITION or A TEXT MEASUREMENT',
    detail: 'WHICH DEPENDS ON the TEST ENVIRONMENTS FONT and SIZE and FAILS ON A MACHINE with A DIFFERENT CONFIGURATION',
    and: 'WHICH IS WHY the GOLDEN TESTS EXIST and WHY THEY HAVE THEIR OWN SECTION' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'WRITE the TEST AS the SPECIFICATION of ONE BEHAVIOUR', gain: 'so THAT A FAILURE NAMES the BEHAVIOUR rather than A LINE NUMBER' },
  { p: 'USE A KEY on ANYTHING YOU NEED TO FIND',
    why: 'BECAUSE A FINDER BY TYPE FINDS EVERY INSTANCE and A FINDER BY KEY FINDS the ONE YOU MEANT',
    verdict: 'WHICH IS the DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A TEST THAT SURVIVES A REFACTOR and ONE THAT DOES NOT' },

15.3 Finders and the interactions that matter

// THE FINDERS
find.text('Save')                        exact text
find.textContaining('Save')              a substring
find.byType(TextField)                   by widget type
find.byIcon(Icons.save)                  by icon
find.byKey(const Key('submit'))          by key: the reliable one
find.bySemanticsLabel('Save entry')     by semantic label
find.bySemanticsLabel(RegExp('Save'))    a pattern
find.ancestor(of: find.text('x'), matching: find.byType(Card))
find.descendant(of: find.byType(ListView), matching: find.byType(EntryCard))
find.byWidgetPredicate((w) => w is EntryCard && w.entry.id == '1')
find.bySemanticsLabel('Save', skipOffstage: false)

// THE COUNTS
findsOneWidget      exactly one
findsNothing        zero
findsNWidgets(3)    exactly three
findsWidgets        one or more

// THE INTERACTIONS
await tester.tap(find.byKey(const Key('submit')));
await tester.longPress(find.byType(ListTile));
await tester.drag(find.byType(ListView), const Offset(0, -300));
await tester.fling(find.byType(ListView), const Offset(0, -500), 1000);
await tester.scrollUntilVisible(find.text('Bottom'), 200);
await tester.enterText(find.byType(TextField), 'hello');
await tester.testTextInput.receiveAction(TextInputAction.done);
await tester.dragUntilVisible(find.byType(Target), find.byType(ListView), const Offset(0, -100));
await tester.tapAt(tester.getCenter(find.byType(IconButton)));
await tester.pumpWidget(...)          // replace the tree
await tester.runAsync(() async { ... });  // REAL async: a real API call
// THE FIVE TRAPS

// 1. THE SCROLL TRAP: an off-screen widget is not found
// ERROR: "Finder could not find any matching widgets" for
//        a button below the fold
await tester.scrollUntilVisible(find.text('Delete'), 200);
await tester.tap(find.text('Delete'));
await tester.pumpAndSettle();

// 2. THE HIT TEST TRAP: a tap can miss
// a tap at the centre of a widget can land on something on top
await tester.tap(find.byType(IconButton).last, warnIfMissed: false);
// better: make it visible first, or use a key
await tester.ensureVisible(find.byType(IconButton));
await tester.tap(find.byType(IconButton));

// 3. THE SIZE TRAP: the default test surface is 800x600
// a widget that is off-screen at 800x600 is missing
tester.view.physicalSize = const Size(1080, 1920);
tester.view.devicePixelRatio = 1.0;
addTearDown(tester.view.reset);

// 4. THE ANIMATION TRAP
await tester.tap(find.byType(ElevatedButton));   // the ink splash starts
await tester.pump();                             // one frame
// the button is now DISABLED-looking during the splash, and a
// second tap in the same frame does nothing

// 5. THE ASYNC TRAP: a future that never completes
// a real API call in a test hangs, because the test framework's
// fake async does not advance
// the fix: mock it, or use tester.runAsync for the real thing
await tester.runAsync(() async {
  await repository.load();
});

Choosing a finder, and the interactions that actually assert

A finder locates something in the rendered tree and an interaction does something to it, and the quality of a widget test is almost entirely determined by which of each it uses. A finder can search by type, by key, by text, by semantic label, or by an ancestor or descendant of another finder. Type is the most obvious and the least good, because a type that appears three times in a row gives three results and a test written against it is a test against an implementation detail. Key is the reliable one, because a key is chosen by the developer for the purpose of being found, it can be unique in a whole subtree, and it survives a refactor that changes the widget's type. Then the four interactions, and what each asserts. Tap finds the widget's centre and sends a pointer down and up, and it therefore triggers whatever the gesture recogniser does with a tap — which is the right interaction for a button and wrong for a long-press target, because a tap does not trigger it. Long press sends a down and waits past the long-press threshold before lifting, and it is the interaction a long-press-only control requires; a test that taps a long-press target passes for the wrong reason if the target also handles tap. Enter text sets the field's text and is the right interaction for a form; but note that it does not go through the platform's input channel, so a bug in the input handling itself will not be found. Drag sends a pointer sequence and is how you test a gesture recogniser, and the important detail is that a drag must be moved in steps rather than teleported, because a recogniser that requires movement to accumulate will not see a single jump. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Using a type finder where a key finder is possible, which couples the test to the widget hierarchy and means a refactor that changes a container breaks a test that was asserting on a label. Testing a control through the wrong interaction, which is the long-press case and also the case of a control that requires a long press to activate being tested with a tap that activates something else in the same row. And performing an interaction on a widget that is not the one you mean, which happens with a type finder returning several and the test using the first — so the test passes while the second is the broken one. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Put a key on anything the tests need to interact with, and give it a name that says what it is rather than where it is, so that moving it does not require renaming it. And assert on the effect of the interaction, not on the interaction, — after tapping a button that submits a form, assert that the confirmation appeared, not that the button's callback fired, because the callback firing and the submission succeeding are different claims and only the second is what the user cares about.

/* Finders. */
const FINDERS = [
  { f: 'BY TYPE', best: 'NO', why: 'BECAUSE A TYPE THAT APPEARS THREE TIMES IN A ROW GIVES THREE RESULTS', consequence: 'and A TEST WRITTEN AGAINST IT IS A TEST AGAINST AN IMPLEMENTATION DETAIL' },
  { f: 'BY KEY', best: true,
    why: ['BECAUSE A KEY IS CHOSEN BY the DEVELOPER FOR the PURPOSE of BEING FOUND',
      'IT CAN BE UNIQUE IN A WHOLE SUBTREE',
      'and IT SURVIVES A REFACTOR THAT CHANGES the WIDGETS TYPE'] },
  { f: 'BY TEXT', note: 'READABLE, and TIED TO CONTENT - WHICH IS FINE FOR A LABEL and WRONG FOR A CONTROL WHOSE TEXT MAY CHANGE' },
  { f: 'BY SEMANTIC LABEL', note: 'THE RIGHT FINDER WHEN THE INTERACTION MATTERS TO THE USER RATHER than TO THE CODE' },
  { f: 'BY ANCESTOR or DESCENDANT', note: 'FOR A NESTED FINDER WHEN THE CHILD ALONE IS NOT UNIQUE' },
];

/* Four interactions. */
const INTERACTIONS = [
  { i: 'TAP', does: 'FINDS the WIDGETS CENTRE and SENDS A POINTER DOWN and UP',
    therefore: 'IT TRIGGERS WHATEVER the GESTURE RECOGNISER DOES with A TAP',
    right: 'FOR A BUTTON', wrong: 'FOR A LONG-PRESS TARGET, BECAUSE A TAP DOES NOT TRIGGER IT' },
  { i: 'LONG PRESS', does: 'SENDS A DOWN and WAITS PAST the LONG-PRESS THRESHOLD BEFORE LIFTING',
    rightFor: 'A CONTROL THAT REQUIRES A LONG PRESS',
    trap: 'A TEST THAT TAPS A LONG-PRESS TARGET PASSES FOR the WRONG REASON if the TARGET ALSO HANDLES TAP' },
  { i: 'ENTER TEXT', does: 'SETS the FIELDS TEXT', rightFor: 'A FORM',
    limitation: 'and IT DOES NOT GO THROUGH the PLATFORMS INPUT CHANNEL', consequence: 'SO A BUG IN the INPUT HANDLING ITSELF WILL NOT BE FOUND' },
  { i: 'DRAG', does: 'SENDS A POINTER SEQUENCE', rightFor: 'TESTING A GESTURE RECOGNISER',
    detail: 'and the IMPORTANT DETAIL IS THAT A DRAG MUST BE MOVED IN STEPS rather than TELEPORTED',
    why: 'BECAUSE A RECOGNISER THAT REQUIRES MOVEMENT TO ACCUMULATE WILL NOT SEE A SINGLE JUMP' },
];

/* Three things that go wrong. */
const GO_WRONG = [
  { f: 'USING A TYPE FINDER WHERE A KEY FINDER IS POSSIBLE',
    consequence: 'WHICH COUPLES the TEST TO the WIDGET HIERARCHY',
    symptom: 'and MEANS A REFACTOR THAT CHANGES A CONTAINER BREAKS A TEST THAT WAS ASSERTING ON A LABEL' },
  { f: 'TESTING A CONTROL THROUGH the WRONG INTERACTION',
    instances: ['the LONG-PRESS CASE',
      'and THE CASE of A CONTROL THAT REQUIRES A LONG PRESS TO ACTIVATE BEING TESTED with A TAP THAT ACTIVATES SOMETHING ELSE IN the SAME ROW'] },
  { f: 'PERFORMING AN INTERACTION ON A WIDGET THAT IS NOT the ONE YOU MEAN',
    detail: 'WHICH HAPPENS WITH A TYPE FINDER RETURNING SEVERAL and the TEST USING the FIRST',
    symptom: 'SO the TEST PASSES WHILE the SECOND IS the BROKEN ONE' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'PUT A KEY on ANYTHING the TESTS NEED TO INTERACT WITH',
    name: 'GIVE IT A NAME THAT SAYS WHAT IT IS rather than WHERE IT IS',
    gain: 'SO THAT MOVING IT DOES NOT REQUIRE RENAMING IT' },
  { p: 'ASSERT ON the EFFECT of the INTERACTION, NOT ON the INTERACTION',
    example: 'AFTER TAPPING A BUTTON THAT SUBMITS A FORM, ASSERT THAT the CONFIRMATION APPEARED, NOT THAT the BUTTONS CALLBACK FIRED',
    why: 'BECAUSE the CALLBACK FIRING and the SUBMISSION SUCCEEDING ARE DIFFERENT CLAIMS',
    and: 'ONLY the SECOND IS WHAT the USER CARES ABOUT' },
];

15.4 Golden tests

What a golden is, and why it is the only test of appearance

A golden test renders a widget and compares the resulting pixels against a stored image, and it is the only kind of test that can catch a change in appearance — which is why it is valuable and why it is dangerous in equal measure. The value is that no assertion you can write captures what the widget actually looks like. You can assert that a colour was used, that a text style was applied, that a widget exists — and every one of those can be true while the interface is wrong, because the wrongness is in the composition: an overlap, a clipping, a colour on a colour that meets no contrast requirement, a text that wraps where it did not. A golden catches all of that because it is a picture of the result. Then the three properties that make it dangerous, and each is a mechanism. It fails for reasons that have nothing to do with the code. Rendering differs between platforms, between operating-system versions, between graphics backends and between devices, and a golden that was generated on one machine will differ on another for reasons that are entirely in the renderer. It is a snapshot of everything at once, so a failure says "something changed" and not what; the developer must look at the diff, which is a step that gets skipped under time pressure and then a golden is regenerated without reading it. And it has a habit of becoming a rubber stamp, because the fix for a failing golden is to regenerate it, and if the answer is always to regenerate then the test never prevents anything. Then the four practices, and each is a specific requirement. Generate goldens per platform and per configuration, named by everything that changes the output: the platform, the theme, the text scale, the locale — so that a failure on one does not invalidate the others and so that a genuine change is not drowned by an environmental one. Review the diff, every time, and treat an unexpected diff as a defect until understood; the mechanical guard is to make regenerating require a deliberate act rather than a command anyone can type. Keep the goldens small, — a component, not a screen — because a small golden diff is readable and a screen-sized one is not. And assert on structure as well, so that a golden is not the only test of a screen: a widget test that asserts the labels and the layout is what actually prevents a regression, and the golden is the check that catches the visual residue. Then the two things worth knowing, because they decide where goldens are worth having. Goldens are for components whose appearance is a specification, which means design-system components, charts, and anything with a visual edge case; a screen that is mostly text and standard components does not need one because a widget test covers it. And the accessibility interaction is worth a golden of its own, because the largest text scale at the largest contrast is a visual state that no structural assertion will catch and that is a real user's screen.

/* What it is. */
const GOLDEN = 'RENDERS A WIDGET and COMPARES the RESULTING PIXELS AGAINST A STORED IMAGE';
const VALUE = {
  fact: 'it IS the ONLY KIND of TEST THAT CAN CATCH A CHANGE IN APPEARANCE',
  why: 'BECAUSE NO ASSERTION YOU CAN WRITE CAPTURES WHAT the WIDGET ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE',
  missedByAssertions: [
    'AN OVERLAP', 'A CLIPPING', 'A COLOUR ON A COLOUR THAT MEETS NO CONTRAST REQUIREMENT',
    'A TEXT THAT WRAPS WHERE IT DID NOT',
  ],
  missMechanism: 'BECAUSE the WRONGNESS IS IN the COMPOSITION, NOT IN ANY SINGLE PROPERTY',
  catch: 'A GOLDEN CATCHES ALL of THAT BECAUSE IT IS A PICTURE of the RESULT',
};

/* Three dangers. */
const DANGEROUS = [
  { d: 'it FAILS FOR REASONS THAT HAVE NOTHING to DO with the CODE',
    detail: ['RENDERING DIFFERS BETWEEN PLATFORMS', 'BETWEEN OPERATING-SYSTEM VERSIONS',
      'BETWEEN GRAPHICS BACKENDS', 'and BETWEEN DEVICES'],
    symptom: 'and A GOLDEN THAT WAS GENERATED ON ONE MACHINE WILL DIFFER ON ANOTHER for REASONS THAT ARE ENTIRELY IN the RENDERER' },
  { d: 'it IS A SNAPSHOT of EVERYTHING AT ONCE',
    symptom: 'SO A FAILURE SAYS something changed and NOT WHAT',
    consequence: 'the DEVELOPER MUST LOOK AT the DIFF',
    and: 'WHICH IS A STEP THAT GETS SKIPPED UNDER TIME PRESSURE and THEN A GOLDEN IS REGENERATED WITHOUT READING IT' },
  { d: 'it HAS A HABIT of BECOMING A RUBBER STAMP',
    why: 'BECAUSE the FIX FOR A FAILING GOLDEN IS to REGENERATE IT',
    and: 'IF the ANSWER IS ALWAYS to REGENERATE then the TEST NEVER PREVENTS ANYTHING' },
];

/* Four practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'GENERATE GOLDENS PER PLATFORM and PER CONFIGURATION',
    namedBy: ['the PLATFORM', 'the THEME', 'the TEXT SCALE', 'the LOCALE'],
    gain: ['SO THAT A FAILURE ON ONE DOES NOT INVALIDATE the OTHERS',
      'and SO THAT A GENUINE CHANGE IS NOT DROWNED BY AN ENVIRONMENTAL ONE'] },
  { p: 'REVIEW the DIFF, EVERY TIME', rule: 'TREAT AN UNEXPECTED DIFF AS A DEFECT UNTIL UNDERSTOOD',
    mechanical: 'the MECHANICAL GUARD IS to MAKE REGENERATING REQUIRE A DELIBERATE ACT rather than A COMMAND ANYONE CAN TYPE' },
  { p: 'KEEP the GOLDENS SMALL', detail: 'A COMPONENT, NOT A SCREEN', why: 'BECAUSE A SMALL GOLDEN DIFF IS READABLE and A SCREEN-SIZED ONE IS NOT' },
  { p: 'ASSERT ON STRUCTURE AS WELL',
    detail: 'SO THAT A GOLDEN IS NOT the ONLY TEST of A SCREEN',
    why: 'A WIDGET TEST THAT ASSERTS the LABELS and the LAYOUT IS WHAT ACTUALLY PREVENTS A REGRESSION',
    and: 'the GOLDEN IS the CHECK THAT CATCHES the VISUAL RESIDUE' },
];

/* Where they are worth having. */
const WHERE = [
  { w: 'GOLDENS ARE for COMPONENTS WHOSE APPEARANCE IS A SPECIFICATION', instances: ['DESIGN-SYSTEM COMPONENTS', 'CHARTS', 'ANYTHING with A VISUAL EDGE CASE'],
    notNeeded: 'A SCREEN THAT IS MOSTLY TEXT and STANDARD COMPONENTS DOES NOT NEED ONE BECAUSE A WIDGET TEST COVERS IT' },
  { w: 'the ACCESSIBILITY INTERACTION IS WORTH A GOLDEN of ITS OWN',
    state: 'the LARGEST TEXT SCALE AT the LARGEST CONTRAST',
    why: 'BECAUSE IT IS A VISUAL STATE THAT NO STRUCTURAL ASSERTION WILL CATCH and THAT IS A REAL USERS SCREEN' },
];

Never call pumpAndSettle with an infinite animation on screen. A CircularProgressIndicator, a shimmer or a looping repeat never settles, so the call runs until the ten-minute timeout and the failure message tells you nothing about the real problem.

// A GOLDEN TEST compares a rendered frame to a stored image.
// it catches a visual regression that no other test can.

testWidgets('the card renders as designed', (tester) async {
  // 1. a FIXED surface, or the golden is meaningless
  tester.view.physicalSize = const Size(800, 600);
  tester.view.devicePixelRatio = 1.0;
  addTearDown(tester.view.reset);

  // 2. a FIXED font, or the text renders differently per machine
  final fontLoader = FontLoader('Roboto')
    ..addFont(rootBundle.load('assets/fonts/Roboto-Regular.ttf'));
  await fontLoader.load();

  await tester.pumpWidget(
    MaterialApp(
      theme: AppTheme.light,
      home: Scaffold(body: EntryCard(entry: testEntry)),
    ),
  );

  // 3. settle, because a golden of a half-faded animation is
  //    useless
  await tester.pumpAndSettle();

  // 4. the comparison
  await expectLater(
    find.byType(EntryCard),
    matchesGoldenFile('goldens/entry_card.png'),
  );
});

// RUN IT
flutter test                                  compare
flutter test --update-goldens                 accept the new ones

// A GALLERY, which is what a golden suite really is
testGoldens('EntryCard', (tester) async {
  await goldenTest('default', tester, EntryCard(entry: testEntry));
  await goldenTest('long title', tester, EntryCard(entry: testEntry.copyWith(title: 'A very long title that wraps onto three lines')));
  await goldenTest('empty', tester, EntryCard(entry: testEntry.copyWith(body: '')));
  await goldenTest('dark mode', tester, EntryCard(entry: testEntry), theme: AppTheme.dark);
  await goldenTest('large text', tester, EntryCard(entry: testEntry), textScale: 2.0);
  await goldenTest('pinned', tester, EntryCard(entry: testEntry.copyWith(pinned: true)));
});

// a helper
Future<void> goldenTest(
  String name,
  WidgetTester tester,
  Widget widget, {
  ThemeData? theme,
  double textScale = 1.0,
  Size size = const Size(400, 200),
}) async {
  tester.view.physicalSize = size;
  tester.view.devicePixelRatio = 1.0;
  addTearDown(tester.view.reset);

  await tester.pumpWidget(
    MaterialApp(
      theme: theme ?? AppTheme.light,
      builder: (context, child) => MediaQuery(
        data: MediaQuery.of(context).copyWith(textScaler: TextScaler.linear(textScale)),
        child: child!,
      ),
      home: Scaffold(body: widget),
    ),
  );
  await tester.pumpAndSettle();
  await expectLater(find.byType(Scaffold), matchesGoldenFile('goldens/$name.png'));
}

15.5 Making goldens reliable

Making the diff trustworthy

A golden suite is trustworthy only if a failure means something, and there are four things that decide whether a failure means something. Render determinism is the first requirement and it is a property of the environment rather than of the test: the same widget rendered twice in the same process must produce identical pixels, and where it does not — text anti-aliasing on a subpixel position, an animation at a non-deterministic phase, a shadow blurred on a thread boundary — the golden will be flaky and a flaky golden gets ignored. The mitigations are to pin everything that varies: a fixed surface size, a fixed text scale, a fixed device pixel ratio, an explicit locale and theme, and a deterministic animation state, which usually means asserting on a widget that is not animating or is at a known point in its animation. Font determinism is the second. Text rendering differs between platforms and between platform versions, so a golden that contains text is a golden that cannot be compared across platforms — which is why the mechanism for cross-platform goldens is to load a bundled test font rather than the system font, so that the glyphs and their metrics are the same everywhere. Then the two practices around the workflow, and each is a discipline rather than a tool. Regenerate only deliberately, and in the same change as the code that changed the output. A regenerated golden whose code change is in a separate commit is a golden nobody reviewed, because the review of the image diff and the review of the code diff are separate events and only one of them is required. And review the image, not just the text of the diff. A golden that changes because a shadow got slightly softer is either a regression or a rendering difference and the diff cannot tell you; a reviewer who looks at the image catches both, and the habit is to make the image viewable — which is why a workflow that produces a side-by-side rather than a binary is worth the setup. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. A golden regenerated to make the suite green, which is the failure mode the previous section named and the only defence is the review requirement — there is no technical way to distinguish a justified regeneration from a lazy one. A golden that includes a clock or a random value, which makes it fail every run and which is fixed by injecting the value rather than reading it. And a golden for a whole screen, which produces a large unreadable diff and therefore an unread diff, which is a golden that is technically guarding and practically not. Then the two things worth knowing about scope, because both determine whether the suite is affordable. Goldens are slow, — rendering and comparing an image is far more expensive than asserting on a widget tree — so a suite with a thousand component goldens is a suite that runs in minutes and the cost is paid on every change; the discipline is to have goldens for the components that actually need them and structural tests for everything else. And a golden is a promise about a specific configuration, so a golden set is really a set of promises and each one has a cost; a project with forty goldens has made forty promises and must keep all of them, and a project with four goldens on its five most visual components has made four and can keep them.

/* Requirement one: determinism. */
const DETERMINISM = {
  first: 'it IS A PROPERTY of the ENVIRONMENT rather than OF the TEST',
  requirement: 'the SAME WIDGET RENDERED TWICE IN the SAME PROCESS MUST PRODUCE IDENTICAL PIXELS',
  flakyCauses: ['TEXT ANTI-ALIASING ON A SUBPIXEL POSITION', 'AN ANIMATION AT A NON-DETERMINISTIC PHASE', 'A SHADOW BLURRED ON A THREAD BOUNDARY'],
  symptom: 'and WHERE IT DOES NOT the GOLDEN WILL BE FLAKY and A FLAKY GOLDEN GETS IGNORED',
  mitigations: ['A FIXED SURFACE SIZE', 'A FIXED TEXT SCALE', 'A FIXED DEVICE PIXEL RATIO', 'AN EXPLICIT LOCALE and THEME',
    'and A DETERMINISTIC ANIMATION STATE'],
  usually: 'WHICH USUALLY MEANS ASSERTING ON A WIDGET THAT IS NOT ANIMATING or IS AT A KNOWN POINT IN ITS ANIMATION',
};

/* Requirement two: fonts. */
const FONTS = {
  fact: 'TEXT RENDERING DIFFERS BETWEEN PLATFORMS and BETWEEN PLATFORM VERSIONS',
  consequence: 'so A GOLDEN THAT CONTAINS TEXT IS A GOLDEN THAT CANNOT BE COMPARED ACROSS PLATFORMS',
  mechanism: 'WHICH IS WHY the MECHANISM for CROSS-PLATFORM GOLDENS IS to LOAD A BUNDLED TEST FONT rather than the SYSTEM FONT',
  gain: 'SO THAT the GLYPHS and THEIR METRICS ARE the SAME EVERYWHERE',
};

/* Two workflow practices. */
const WORKFLOW = [
  { p: 'REGENERATE ONLY DELIBERATELY, and IN the SAME CHANGE AS the CODE THAT CHANGED the OUTPUT',
    why: 'A REGENERATED GOLDEN WHOSE CODE CHANGE IS IN A SEPARATE COMMIT IS A GOLDEN NOBODY REVIEWED',
    detail: 'BECAUSE the REVIEW of the IMAGE DIFF and the REVIEW of the CODE DIFF ARE SEPARATE EVENTS and ONLY ONE of THEM IS REQUIRED' },
  { p: 'REVIEW the IMAGE, NOT JUST the TEXT of the DIFF',
    detail: 'A GOLDEN THAT CHANGES BECAUSE A SHADOW GOT SLIGHTLY SOFTER IS EITHER A REGRESSION or A RENDERING DIFFERENCE and the DIFF CANNOT TELL YOU',
    gain: 'A REVIEWER WHO LOOKS AT the IMAGE CATCHES BOTH',
    habit: 'and the HABIT IS to MAKE the IMAGE VIEWABLE - WHICH IS WHY A WORKFLOW THAT PRODUCES A SIDE-BY-SIDE rather than A BINARY IS WORTH the SETUP' },
];

/* Three things that go wrong. */
const GO_WRONG = [
  { f: 'A GOLDEN REGENERATED to MAKE the SUITE GREEN',
    detail: 'WHICH IS the FAILURE MODE the PREVIOUS SECTION NAMED',
    defence: 'and the ONLY DEFENCE IS the REVIEW REQUIREMENT',
    honest: 'THERE IS NO TECHNICAL WAY to DISTINGUISH A JUSTIFIED REGENERATION FROM A LAZY ONE' },
  { f: 'A GOLDEN THAT INCLUDES A CLOCK or A RANDOM VALUE',
    symptom: 'WHICH MAKES IT FAIL EVERY RUN',
    fix: 'and WHICH IS FIXED BY INJECTING the VALUE rather than READING IT' },
  { f: 'A GOLDEN for A WHOLE SCREEN',
    detail: 'WHICH PRODUCES A LARGE UNREADABLE DIFF and THEREFORE AN UNREAD DIFF',
    verdict: 'WHICH IS A GOLDEN THAT IS TECHNICALLY GUARDING and PRACTICALLY NOT' },
];

/* Two things about scope. */
const SCOPE = [
  { s: 'GOLDENS ARE SLOW', detail: 'RENDERING and COMPARING AN IMAGE IS FAR MORE EXPENSIVE than ASSERTING ON A WIDGET TREE',
    arithmetic: 'SO A SUITE with A THOUSAND COMPONENT GOLDENS IS A SUITE THAT RUNS IN MINUTES and the COST IS PAID ON EVERY CHANGE',
    discipline: 'THE DISCIPLINE IS to HAVE GOLDENS FOR the COMPONENTS THAT ACTUALLY NEED THEM and STRUCTURAL TESTS for EVERYTHING ELSE' },
  { s: 'A GOLDEN IS A PROMISE ABOUT A SPECIFIC CONFIGURATION',
    detail: 'SO A GOLDEN SET IS REALLY A SET of PROMISES and EACH ONE HAS A COST',
    many: 'A PROJECT with FORTY GOLDENS HAS MADE FORTY PROMISES and MUST KEEP ALL of THEM',
    few: 'A PROJECT with FOUR GOLDENS ON ITS FIVE MOST VISUAL COMPONENTS HAS MADE FOUR and CAN KEEP THEM' },
];

The point of a golden is not the comparison - it is the diff you read. A failure that shows you a picture of what changed is a visual regression caught for you before a user sees it. A golden suite nobody reviews is a suite that will pass on a broken screen.

// WHY GOLDENS ARE FLAKY, and the fix for each
//
// 1. THE FONT
//    the biggest source of flakiness. the same font renders
//    differently on macOS, Linux and Windows
//    FIX: bundle the font and load it with a FontLoader in
//         setUpAll, and set it in the theme
final fontLoader = FontLoader('Roboto')
  ..addFont(rootBundle.load('assets/fonts/Roboto-Regular.ttf'))
  ..addFont(rootBundle.load('assets/fonts/Roboto-Medium.ttf'));
setUpAll(() async => fontLoader.load());

// 2. THE PLATFORM
//    a Material widget looks different on iOS: the scrollbar,
//    the page transition, the text selection handles
//    FIX: set the platform explicitly
await tester.pumpWidget(
  MaterialApp(
    theme: AppTheme.light,
    home: Scaffold(body: child),
  ),
);
// or, in the theme
ThemeData(platform: TargetPlatform.android);
// and for Cupertino widgets
debugDefaultTargetPlatformOverride = TargetPlatform.iOS;
addTearDown(() => debugDefaultTargetPlatformOverride = null);

// 3. THE ANIMATION
//    a hero transition, a shimmer, an ink splash: the golden
//    captures a random frame
//    FIX: pumpAndSettle, or pump to an exact duration
await tester.pumpAndSettle();
await tester.pump(const Duration(milliseconds: 200));   // exact

// 4. THE SURFACE
//    a different default size produces a different image
//    FIX: always set it, in a helper, for every golden

// 5. THE IMAGE ENCODER
//    the PNG output differs between engine versions
//    FIX: pin the Flutter version in CI, and regenerate the
//         goldens when you upgrade, reviewing the diff

// 6. THE IMAGE CACHE
//    a cached image renders differently from a fresh one
//    FIX: precache the image in setUp, or use a placeholder
await precacheImage(AssetImage('assets/photo.jpg'), context);
// REVIEWING THE DIFF, which is the actual point
// the goldens are committed, and a change shows up in the diff
// as a binary file. Open it and LOOK at it. A change you did not
// intend is a visual regression your test just caught.
//
// the workflow
// 1. run the tests
// 2. a golden fails
// 3. open the ACTUAL output:
//    test/goldens/failures/entry_card.png     the new render
//    test/goldens/entry_card.png               the reference
// 4. if the change is intended:
//    flutter test --update-goldens
//    and review the diff before committing
// 5. if not: fix the code, which is the real value

// WHERE THE FILES LIVE
test/
├── goldens/
│   ├── entry_card.png          the reference
│   ├── card_dark.png
│   └── failures/               the output from the last failure
│                               (git-ignored, usually)

// and the .gitignore
//   test/**/failures/
//   test/**/goldenFiles/     the generated comparator html
// GOLDENS FOR A WHOLE SCREEN, which is the useful level
testWidgets('the home screen in both themes', (tester) async {
  for (final theme in [AppTheme.light, AppTheme.dark]) {
    await setSurface(tester, const Size(390, 844));   // an iPhone 14
    await tester.pumpWidget(
      ProviderScope(
        overrides: [entriesProvider.overrideWith((ref) async => testEntries)],
        child: MaterialApp(theme: theme, home: const HomeScreen()),
      ),
    );
    await tester.pumpAndSettle();

    final name = theme == AppTheme.light ? 'home_light' : 'home_dark';
    await expectLater(find.byType(MaterialApp), matchesGoldenFile('screens/$name.png'));
  }
});

// THE STATES, and a golden suite that only covers the happy
// state is nearly useless
for (final size in [const Size(390, 844), const Size(1280, 800)]) {
  for (final state in ['loading', 'empty', 'data', 'error']) {
    await goldenTest('$state-$size', ...);
  }
}

15.6 Unit testing the logic

// THE LOGIC WORTH TESTING: the branches
// these are the tests that catch real bugs
test('mergeEntry', () {
  test('keeps the local edit when the server is older', () {
    final result = mergeEntry(
      server: serverEntry(body: 'server', updatedAt: 100, version: 7),
      local: localEdit(body: 'local', basedOnVersion: 7),
    );
    expect(result.body, 'local');
    expect(result.conflictFields, isEmpty);
  });

  test('flags a conflict when both changed the same field', () {
    final result = mergeEntry(
      server: serverEntry(body: 'server', updatedAt: 200, version: 8),
      local: localEdit(body: 'local', basedOnVersion: 7),
    );
    expect(result.conflictFields, ['body']);
  });

  test('refuses to merge onto a stale base', () {
    final result = mergeEntry(
      server: serverEntry(version: 9),
      local: localEdit(basedOnVersion: 7),   // 2 versions behind
    );
    expect(result.needsFullReconcile, isTrue);
  });

  test('handles an empty changed set', () {
    final result = mergeEntry(server: serverEntry(), local: localEdit(changed: {}));
    expect(result.needsFullReconcile, isFalse);
  });
});

// THE EDGE CASES THAT ACTUALLY BREAK
test('parsing', () {
  test('a number that arrives as a string', () {
    expect(LenientEntry.fromJson({'id': '1', 'rating': '4.5'}).rating, 4.5);
  });
  test('a date as an epoch int', () {
    final e = LenientEntry.fromJson({'id': '1', 'createdAt': 1730000000000});
    expect(e.createdAt, DateTime.fromMillisecondsSinceEpoch(1730000000000));
  });
  test('a missing required field', () {
    expect(() => Entry.fromJson({'title': 'x'}), throwsA(isA<CheckedFromJsonException>()));
  });
  test('a null where a list is expected', () {
    expect(LenientEntry.fromJson({'id': '1', 'tags': null}).tags, isEmpty);
  });
  test('an unknown field is ignored, not fatal', () {
    expect(() => Entry.fromJson({...'valid', 'newField': 1}), returnsNormally);
  });
});

// THE REGRESSION TEST, which is the highest-value test there is
test('regression: does not crash on a malformed entry', () {
  // the input that caused the bug
  final entry = LenientEntry.fromJson({'id': '1', 'title': null});
  expect(entry.title, '');
});

Testing logic without the framework, and the shape of a good unit test

A unit test in a Flutter application is a plain Dart test with no framework at all — no widget tree, no bindings, no pumps — and the reason it is worth having at that scale is that it can be exhaustive. You can run four hundred cases in the time a widget test takes to construct a single widget, so the economics allow a different style: table-driven tests where one function is called with dozens of inputs and every combination of a boundary is covered, including the ones nobody would think to write by hand. And the framework is an obstacle to that, because anything that imports a widget cannot be constructed without a binding and pumped, which brings back the cost. So the practical consequence is a structural rule: logic that is worth testing exhaustively must not depend on the framework. A validator, a parser, a formatter, a reducer, a pricing calculation, a permission decision — all of these are plain Dart and all of them are the kind of thing that has an awkward boundary case that a test suite should enumerate. Then the four things to test in this layer, and each is a category that is commonly untested because it is not a "function". Boundary values. Every numeric rule has a boundary and the boundary is where the bug is: empty, one, the maximum, the maximum plus one, negative, zero. Invalid input. Every function that accepts a value from outside the program will be given something it did not expect, and the test suite should have a case for each way the input can be malformed, because the production caller is a JSON parser and not your type system. The failure path. A function that returns an error must have a test that asserts the error, because the code path that produces an error is the code path nobody exercises. And the interaction between two rules. Two validations that are each correct and contradict each other produce a case that neither test covers. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Testing the framework through the logic, — a test that constructs a widget to check a calculation, which is slower, harder to read and will break when the framework changes. Asserting on a message string, which couples the test to wording that a user reads and that a translator will change; assert on the error type or the code instead. And a test that constructs the thing being tested inside the test body, so that every case pays for construction; building once and asserting many times is both faster and clearer about what varies. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Name the case, not the function, — a failing test named "rejects an empty string" tells you what is broken, while one named "testValidate" tells you to look. And test the pure function and leave the impure wrapper alone, because a function that reads a clock, a random source or a service is hard to test precisely; extract the pure core, test it exhaustively, and test the wrapper once for the wiring — which is the same separation as the chapter-one argument about pure functions, applied to tests.

/* What a unit test is here. */
const UNIT = {

15.7 Mocking the platform

// THREE KINDS OF DOUBLE, and when each
//
// 1. A FAKE: a working implementation, simplified
class InMemoryEntryRepository implements EntryRepository {
  final Map<String, Entry> _entries = {};

  @override
  Future<List<Entry>> all() async => _entries.values.toList();

  @override
  Future<Entry> byId(String id) async {
    final e = _entries[id];
    if (e == null) throw NotFoundException(id);
    return e;
  }

  @override
  Future<Entry> create(EntryDraft d) async {
    final e = Entry.fromDraft(d);
    _entries[e.id] = e;
    return e;
  }

  @override
  Future<void> delete(String id) async => _entries.remove(id);
}
// USE IT FOR: testing a flow end to end, including the error path

// 2. A MOCK: records the calls, so you assert on them
class MockEntryRepository extends Mock implements EntryRepository {}

// pubspec.yaml
//   mockito: ^5.14.0
//   build_runner: ^2.4.0

// 3. A HAND-WRITTEN STUB: a class that returns a fixed value
class AlwaysEmptyRepository implements EntryRepository {
  @override
  Future<List<Entry>> all() async => [];
  @override
  Future<Entry> byId(String id) async => throw UnimplementedError();
  // ...every method
}
// USE IT FOR: nothing, really. Prefer a fake.
// MOCKITO, for verifying interactions
@GenerateNiceMocks([MockSpec<EntryRepository>()])
class Repositories extends Mock {}

void main() {
  late Repositories repos;
  late EntryListModel model;

  setUp(() {
    repos = Repositories();
    model = EntryListModel(repos);
  });

  test('loads the entries on start', () async {
    when(() => repos.all()).thenAnswer((_) async => [testEntry, otherEntry]);

    await model.load();

    expect(model.entries, hasLength(2));
    verify(() => repos.all()).called(1);
  });

  test('maps a not-found to a state', () async {
    when(() => repos.byId('nope')).thenThrow(NotFoundException('nope'));

    await model.loadOne('nope');

    expect(model.state, EntryState.notFound);
  });

  test('does not call the API twice', () async {
    when(() => repos.all()).thenAnswer((_) async => []);

    await model.load();
    await model.load();

    verify(() => repos.all()).called(2);   // or use a real fake and
  });                                        // assert on the fake
}

// MOCKING A PLATFORM CHANNEL, which is the Flutter-specific part
class PlatformChannelMock {
  static const _channel = MethodChannel('com.acme.fieldnotes/battery');

  // a binary messenger that records, and does not talk to native
  static final _log = <MethodCall>[];

  static void setUp() {
    TestDefaultBinaryMessengerBinding.instance.defaultBinaryMessenger
        .setMockMethodCallHandler(_channel, (call) async {
      _log.add(call);
      switch (call.method) {
        case 'getBatteryLevel': return 55;
        case 'isCharging': return false;
        default: throw MissingPluginException();
      }
    });
  }

  static void tearDown() {
    TestDefaultBinaryMessengerBinding.instance.defaultBinaryMessenger
        .setMockMethodCallHandler(_channel, null);
    _log.clear();
  }

  static List<MethodCall> get calls => List.unmodifiable(_log);
}

setUp(PlatformChannelMock.setUp);
tearDown(PlatformChannelMock.tearDown);

// MOCKING THE OTHER WAY: a platform interface, which is better
// when you have one
class FakeBatteryPlatform extends FieldNotesBatteryPlatform {
  int level = 55;
  @override
  Future<BatteryStatus> status() async =>
      BatteryStatus(level: level, isCharging: false, supported: true);
}

// in the test
FieldNotesBatteryPlatform.instance = FakeBatteryPlatform();

Fakes, and why a mock is the weakest of the three substitutes

When a unit of code depends on something you do not want in a test, there are three substitutes and they differ in how much they assume about the real thing. A fake is a working implementation with a simpler behaviour — an in-memory repository that stores objects in a list instead of on disk, a clock that returns a fixed value, a network client that returns a canned response. A stub returns predetermined answers and does nothing else, which is right when the answer is all that matters and wrong when the call's side effects matter. A mock records its calls and asserts on the calls — the collaborator is a spy — and it is the weakest of the three because it tests the interaction rather than the result. Then why the mock is weakest, and it is worth being precise because mocks are the most widely used. A mock asserts that your code called a dependency, which is a statement about implementation rather than about behaviour, and the two differ: a refactor that replaces two calls with one loop and calls the dependency once instead of twice has broken every mock and changed no behaviour. And a mock's assertion is only as good as the test author. A mock with no expectations is a spy that records nothing useful; a mock that expects a call with a specific argument encodes the current design into the test; and a mock that expects nothing at all is a stub with extra machinery. Then the three rules, and each is a requirement. Prefer a fake where a fake will do. A fake that actually implements the interface exercises more of the code than a stub, because it responds to every call rather than only the ones the test anticipated. The fake must be complete enough not to surprise. An in-memory repository that returns an empty list for a method the real one throws on is a fake that hides a bug, and the standard is to implement the interface honestly and let the test's setup decide what is in it. And put the fakes in the test code, not in the production code, so that no production assembly ever constructs one — because a fake that is wired into a debug build becomes a fake that ships. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. A mock that asserts the wrong thing, which is asserting that a repository's save was called rather than that the item appears in the list on the next read — and the first passes while the second fails, which is exactly the wiring bug this test layer cannot find. A fake that is shared between tests and therefore carries state, which is the mechanism behind order-dependent tests; a fake must be constructed inside the test. And over-mocking the framework, which produces a test that constructs a widget, pumps it, and then mocks the very thing being tested, so that the test passes while the widget cannot work. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Make dependencies explicit rather than global, so that a test can supply a fake by passing it in rather than by installing it into a global registry — and that is the state-management chapter's argument again: a global singleton cannot be replaced, which is why a test cannot fake it. And give the fake the same interface and no more, so that when the real dependency gains a method the fake fails to compile rather than silently returning a wrong default — which is the compile-time-check argument from the serialization chapter, applied to test doubles.

/* Three substitutes. */
const SUBSTITUTES = [

];

15.8 Integration tests

// THE SETUP
// integration_test/app_test.dart
import 'package:integration_test/integration_test.dart';

void main() {
  IntegrationTestWidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();

  // a REAL database, a REAL repository, a mock server
  setUpAll(() async {
    await TestServer.start();          // a local HTTP server
  });

  testWidgets('the critical flow: sign in, create, sync', (tester) async {
    app.main();

    // 1. sign in
    await tester.pumpAndSettle();
    await tester.enterText(find.byKey(const Key('login-email')), 'e2e@acme.test');
    await tester.enterText(find.byKey(const Key('login-password')), 'password');
    await tester.tap(find.byKey(const Key('login-submit')));
    await tester.pumpAndSettle();

    expect(find.text('Entries'), findsOneWidget);

    // 2. create an entry
    await tester.tap(find.byKey(const Key('new-entry')));
    await tester.pumpAndSettle();
    await tester.enterText(find.byKey(const Key('entry-body')), 'from the test');
    await tester.tap(find.byKey(const Key('entry-save')));
    await tester.pumpAndSettle();

    expect(find.text('from the test'), findsOneWidget);

    // 3. the local database has it
    final db = await openTestDatabase();
    final entries = await db.entriesDao.all();
    expect(entries.any((e) => e.body == 'from the test'), isTrue);
  });

  testWidgets('it survives a restart', (tester) async {
    // a REAL restart is not possible in an integration test, but
    // you can clear the in-memory state and re-pump
    restartApp(tester);
    expect(find.text('from the test'), findsOneWidget);
  });
}

What integration tests are for, and why they are slow

An integration test runs the real application on a device, with the real platform, the real plugins and usually the real network, and its entire value is that it is the only kind that can find a class of bug the others cannot: the wiring. A repository and a screen can each be correct and the call between them can name a field that does not exist; two screens can each navigate correctly and the route can be wrong; a plugin can be registered correctly and the channel name can differ on one platform. None of these is visible to a unit test, because a unit test does not run both halves, and none is visible to a widget test, because a widget test substitutes the other half. So the test is worth writing for the wiring, and not for the logic. Then why they are slow, because the reason determines what to do about it. The cost is application startup. Every test pays for launching the application, initialising the bindings, loading the Dart code and building the first screen, which is seconds — and this is why a suite of fifty integration tests is measured in minutes while a suite of fifty widget tests is measured in seconds. The cost is also per-test isolation, because a test that leaves the application in a modified state must reset it, and resetting is itself slow: clearing storage, signing in again, waiting for the first frame. And the cost of a failure is high, because a failure deep in an integration suite may be a race rather than a defect and a race does not reproduce on the next run, which is the property that destroys trust in the suite. Then the four practices, and each addresses one of those costs. Assert on journeys, not on screens. Four journeys of eight steps each catch more wiring than forty single-screen assertions, and take a fraction of the time because they share the startup. Make each test independent and make the setup cheap, by driving the application to a known state through a single entry point rather than by navigating there — a test-only route that puts the application into a known state with known data is the mechanism, and it is worth the cost because it turns a navigation sequence into one call. Use a real backend or none at all, and this is the point people get wrong: an integration test against a mock backend tests the mock. If the point is the wiring, the backend must be real — a local server, a seeded test environment — because the thing being tested is the code between the two. And do not put timing into assertions,: waiting a fixed number of milliseconds and then asserting is the mechanism behind every flaky integration test, and the discipline is to wait for a condition rather than for a duration. Then the two things worth knowing, and both are about what to leave out. Do not run integration tests on every change. Run the unit and widget suites on every change and the integration suite before a release; the integration suite is the one whose feedback loop does not fit inside an edit-and-save cycle, and forcing it into that cycle produces a suite people skip. And do not let the integration suite become the only suite. It is the slowest to write and the slowest to run and the least pleasant to debug, so a team that relies on it exclusively will write few tests and will find that a failure in a four-hundred-step journey is hard to diagnose — which is the pyramid's whole argument arriving at the layer people tend to over-use.
