    why: 'the INTEGRATION SUITE IS the ONE WHOSE FEEDBACK LOOP DOES NOT FIT INSIDE AN EDIT-AND-SAVE CYCLE',
    consequence: 'and FORCING IT INTO THAT CYCLE PRODUCES A SUITE PEOPLE SKIP' },
  { t: 'do NOT LET the INTEGRATION SUITE BECOME the ONLY SUITE',
    why: 'IT IS the SLOWEST TO WRITE and the SLOWEST TO RUN and the LEAST PLEASANT TO DEBUG',
    consequence: 'SO A TEAM THAT RELIES ON IT EXCLUSIVELY WILL WRITE FEW TESTS',
    and: 'A FAILURE IN A FOUR-HUNDRED-STEP JOURNEY IS HARD TO DIAGNOSE',
    connects: 'WHICH IS the PYRAMIDS WHOLE ARGUMENT ARRIVING AT the LAYER PEOPLE TEND TO OVER-USE' },
];

15.9 CI and coverage

// THE PIPELINE, ordered so the fast failures come first
name: flutter
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  analyze:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { channel: stable, cache: true }
      - run: flutter pub get
      - run: dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .
      - run: flutter analyze --fatal-infos
      - run: dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
      - name: fail if code generation is out of date
        run: git diff --exit-code

  test:
    needs: analyze
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { channel: stable, cache: true }
      - run: flutter pub get
      - run: dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
      - run: flutter test --coverage --reporter expanded
      - uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
        with: { files: ./coverage/lcov.info }

  # goldens need a pinned platform, or they are flaky
  golden:
    needs: analyze
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with:
          channel: stable
          cache: true
      - run: flutter pub get
      - run: dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
      - run: flutter test test/goldens --reporter expanded
      # to regenerate deliberately:
      #   flutter test --update-goldens
      #   commit the changes

  integration:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { channel: stable, cache: true }
      - uses: reactivecircus/android-emulator-runner@v2
        with:
          api-level: 34
          arch: x86_64
          script: |
            flutter pub get
            flutter test integration_test/ --reporter expanded
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with: { name: screenshots, path: build/test_screenshots }
// AND THE BUILDS, so no platform rots
build:
  needs: [test]
  runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
  strategy:
    matrix:
      include:
        - os: ubuntu-latest   target: apk
        - os: macos-latest    target: ios
        - os: macos-latest    target: macos
        - os: windows-latest  target: windows
        - os: ubuntu-latest   target: web
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
      with: { channel: stable, cache: true }
    - run: flutter pub get
    - run: dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
    - run: flutter build ${{ matrix.target }} --release
    - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
      with:
        name: app-${{ matrix.target }}
        path: |
          build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/*.apk
          build/ios/ipa/*.ipa
          build/macos/Build/Products/Release/*.app
          build/windows/x64/runner/Release/**
          build/web/**
// COVERAGE, and reading it honestly
// what it measures: lines executed, not behaviour verified
// what it misses: a test that calls a function and asserts
//   nothing gives 100% of that function and proves nothing

// the useful gate: the DIFF, not the total
test('new code is covered', () {
  final report = parseLcov('coverage/lcov.info');
  final changed = changedFilesFromThePr();   // from the diff

  final uncovered = changed.where((f) {
    final l = report[f];
    return l != null && l.found > l.hit;
  }).toList();

  if (uncovered.isNotEmpty) {
    fail('uncovered lines in changed files: $uncovered');
  }
});

// the metrics that are actually worth tracking
// 1. the ERROR PATHS: how many catch blocks are covered
// 2. the golden count: a regression in a visual is a regression
// 3. the integration flow count: how many critical paths are
//    protected
//
// and the ratchet: record the number, never let it go down,
// raise the floor as you improve

Coverage, and why the number is the least interesting thing about it

Test coverage is the proportion of executed lines a test suite touches, and it is the most widely reported and least widely useful number in this chapter, for a specific reason: it measures whether a line ran, not whether a behaviour is verified. A line that assigns a field runs when the object is constructed, whether or not any assertion depends on that field's value. So a suite can report a hundred per cent while asserting almost nothing, and it does this regularly, because the natural way to reach a hundred per cent is to write tests that execute the lines and the natural way to miss a behaviour is to write none. Coverage is a measure of untested code, which is genuinely useful, and it is not a measure of test quality. Then the three legitimate uses, and each is a different question. Finding dead code. A line that no test reaches is either dead or reachable only through a path nobody exercises, and both are worth knowing. Finding an untested file. A new file with zero coverage is a file nobody thought about, and a coverage diff in continuous integration is the mechanism that catches it — because the failure is not that the file exists but that it appeared with no tests. And comparing two changes, which is the most valuable use: a pull request that adds forty lines with no tests is visible as a coverage drop even though the absolute percentage barely moved. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Setting a percentage target, which produces tests written to raise the number — which means executing the line, not asserting on it. Excluding files from the count, which is legitimate for generated code and configuration and illegitimate for everything else, and the illegitimate case is usually not noticed because the number went up. And writing tests after the fact to raise coverage, which produces the worst tests in the codebase: they exercise a path without understanding it, so they pass, and they will keep passing after the behaviour breaks because they never checked the behaviour. Then the two practices, and both are disciplines rather than tools. Measure coverage on the domain layer and treat everything else as unmeasured, because the domain layer is where the branches are and where a missing branch is a wrong answer; a widget's coverage says whether a build method ran, which tells you nothing. And use a coverage diff as a gate on new code, not a percentage as a target, so that the requirement is that a change comes with tests for its behaviour rather than that the whole project reaches a number — because the second is a project-level goal that never ends and the first is a per-change rule that can be followed.

/* What it measures. */
const COVERAGE = {
  is: 'the PROPORTION of EXECUTED LINES A TEST SUITE TOUCHES',
  problem: 'IT MEASURES WHETHER A LINE RAN, NOT WHETHER A BEHAVIOUR IS VERIFIED',
  example: 'A LINE THAT ASSIGNS A FIELD RUNS WHEN the OBJECT IS CONSTRUCTED, WHETHER OR NOT ANY ASSERTION DEPENDS ON THAT FIELDS VALUE',
  consequence: 'SO A SUITE CAN REPORT A HUNDRED PER CENT WHILE ASSERTING ALMOST NOTHING',
  and: 'IT DOES THIS REGULARLY, BECAUSE the NATURAL WAY TO REACH A HUNDRED PER CENT IS to WRITE TESTS THAT EXECUTE the LINES and the NATURAL WAY TO MISS A BEHAVIOUR IS to WRITE NONE',
  correctReading: 'IT IS A MEASURE OF UNTESTED CODE, WHICH IS GENUINELY USEFUL, and IT IS NOT A MEASURE OF TEST QUALITY',
};

/* Three legitimate uses. */
const USES = [
  { u: 'FINDING DEAD CODE', detail: 'A LINE THAT NO TEST REACHES IS EITHER DEAD or REACHABLE ONLY THROUGH A PATH NOBODY EXERCISES', and: 'BOTH ARE WORTH KNOWING' },
  { u: 'FINDING AN UNTESTED FILE',
    detail: 'A NEW FILE with ZERO COVERAGE IS A FILE NOBODY THOUGHT ABOUT',
    mechanism: 'and A COVERAGE DIFF IN CONTINUOUS INTEGRATION IS the MECHANISM THAT CATCHES IT',
    why: 'BECAUSE the FAILURE IS NOT THAT the FILE EXISTS but THAT IT APPEARED with NO TESTS' },
  { u: 'COMPARING TWO CHANGES', rank: 'the MOST VALUABLE USE',
    detail: 'A PULL REQUEST THAT ADDS FORTY LINES with NO TESTS IS VISIBLE AS A COVERAGE DROP EVEN THOUGH the ABSOLUTE PERCENTAGE BARELY MOVED' },
];

/* Three things that go wrong. */
const GO_WRONG = [
  { f: 'SETTING A PERCENTAGE TARGET',
    consequence: 'WHICH PRODUCES TESTS WRITTEN TO RAISE the NUMBER - WHICH MEANS EXECUTING the LINE, NOT ASSERTING ON IT' },
  { f: 'EXCLUDING FILES FROM the COUNT',
    legitimate: 'FOR GENERATED CODE and CONFIGURATION',
    illegitimate: 'and FOR EVERYTHING ELSE',
    symptom: 'and the ILLEGITIMATE CASE IS USUALLY NOT NOTICED BECAUSE the NUMBER WENT UP' },
  { f: 'WRITING TESTS AFTER the FACT TO RAISE COVERAGE',
    detail: 'WHICH PRODUCES the WORST TESTS IN the CODEBASE - THEY EXERCISE A PATH WITHOUT UNDERSTANDING IT',
    symptom: 'SO THEY PASS, and THEY WILL KEEP PASSING AFTER the BEHAVIOUR BREAKS BECAUSE THEY NEVER CHECKED the BEHAVIOUR' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'MEASURE COVERAGE ON the DOMAIN LAYER and TREAT EVERYTHING ELSE AS UNMEASURED',
    why: 'BECAUSE the DOMAIN LAYER IS WHERE the BRANCHES ARE and WHERE A MISSING BRANCH IS A WRONG ANSWER',
    and: 'A WIDGETS COVERAGE SAYS WHETHER A BUILD METHOD RAN, WHICH TELLS YOU NOTHING' },
  { p: 'USE A COVERAGE DIFF AS A GATE ON NEW CODE, NOT A PERCENTAGE AS A TARGET',
    goal: 'so THAT the REQUIREMENT IS THAT A CHANGE COMES WITH TESTS FOR ITS BEHAVIOUR rather than THAT the WHOLE PROJECT REACHES A NUMBER',
    why: 'BECAUSE the SECOND IS A PROJECT-LEVEL GOAL THAT NEVER ENDS and the FIRST IS A PER-CHANGE RULE THAT CAN BE FOLLOWED' },
];

Exercises 16

  1. Write a widget test for a screen, and prove it catches a deliberate break by changing a string and watching it fail.
  2. Write a golden test for a component in light and dark mode, with a loaded font, and run it on two different machines. Confirm it is stable.
  3. Add a golden for each of the four loading states of a list screen, and verify the stale state is reachable.
  4. Write a Fake repository that works, and a Mock with Mockito, and use each where it is the right tool.
  5. Mock a platform channel with a binary messenger, and verify the Dart side receives the mocked value and the failure path.
  6. Write an integration test for the create-and-persist flow, with a real database and a local test server.
  7. Set up the CI pipeline with the code-generation freshness check, and prove it fails when the generated files are stale.
  8. Add a coverage diff gate to CI and verify it fails for an uncovered new file.

16 · Performance and Profiling

16.1 Profile mode, and why debug lies16.2 The DevTools performance panel16.3 A diagnostic order16.4 Build and rebuild cost16.5 Images and video16.6 Startup and first frame16.7 Memory16.8 Measuring in production

Everything in this chapter assumes one thing: measure first, in profile mode, on a real device. Every other rule follows from that.

16.1 Profile mode, and why debug lies

What each mode changes, and which one to believe

Flutter has several build modes and the reason the difference matters is that the mode changes what the framework itself does — not only whether your code is optimised. Debug mode disables optimisation in the Dart compiler, runs with the framework's assertions and error checking fully on, and connects to the development tooling. The assertions are the reason debug is slow, and they are also the reason debug finds real bugs: a setState after dispose, a layout constraint violation, an incorrect widget state in a list, a null required argument — all of these are caught in debug and none of them is caught in release. Profile mode optimises the Dart code and runs the framework's service extensions — the timeline, the widget inspector, the memory view, the performance panel — while leaving the assertions off. Release mode optimises everything and tree-shakes the unreachable code, and it is what ships. Then the four reasons debug misleads, and each has a mechanism. Debug runs an unoptimised compiler, so the code is several times slower and a cost that is invisible in release is visible in debug — which means a profile you took in debug shows problems you do not have. Debug disables tree shaking, so code that will not exist in the release binary is loaded and run, which changes startup time and memory in ways that have nothing to do with your code. Debug's assertions add checks that are not in release, so the frame timings you measure include work that does not happen for a user. And the development build connects to a debugger, which changes the scheduling and the timing of everything. Then the two rules, and both are requirements. Never diagnose a performance problem in debug. Not because debug is useless — it is the right place to find a layout error — but because a timing conclusion drawn in debug is not a conclusion about the application. Measure in profile mode, on the slowest device you support, which is the second half of the sentence everybody gets wrong: a profile on the newest phone is a profile of a machine with headroom, and the device that produces the support tickets is the one at the other end of the distribution. Then the two things worth knowing that are not about modes, and both catch people. A release build on a real device is the only true test, because release changes the compiler, the size, and the absence of assertions — so a crash that appears only in release is a real release-only bug and the first thing to check is an assertion that was masking it. And profile mode is not release mode, so a build that is fast in profile may not be fast in release because tree shaking removes code and changes what runs at startup; and a build can be slower in release because of code that only runs when assertions are off. Then the discipline: have one device designated as the slow device and profile on it every time, because a performance regression is a comparison and a comparison needs a fixed baseline — and the baseline that matters is the slowest supported device, because that is where the frame budget is actually at risk.

/* The modes. */
const DEBUG = {
  does: ['DISABLES OPTIMISATION IN the DART COMPILER', 'RUNS WITH the FRAMEWORKS ASSERTIONS and ERROR CHECKING FULLY ON',
    'and CONNECTS TO the DEVELOPMENT TOOLING'],
  slowBecause: 'the ASSERTIONS ARE the REASON DEBUG IS SLOW',
  valuableBecause: 'and THEY ARE ALSO the REASON DEBUG FINDS REAL BUGS',
  catches: ['A setState AFTER DISPOSE', 'A LAYOUT CONSTRAINT VIOLATION', 'AN INCORRECT WIDGET STATE IN A LIST', 'A NULL REQUIRED ARGUMENT'],
  fact: 'ALL of THESE ARE CAUGHT IN DEBUG and NONE of THEM IS CAUGHT IN RELEASE',
};
const PROFILE = {
  does: ['OPTIMISES the DART CODE', 'RUNS the FRAMEWORKS SERVICE EXTENSIONS'],
  extensions: ['the TIMELINE', 'the WIDGET INSPECTOR', 'the MEMORY VIEW', 'the PERFORMANCE PANEL'],
  and: 'WHILE LEAVING the ASSERTIONS OFF',
};
const RELEASE = { does: ['OPTIMISES EVERYTHING', 'TREE-SHAKES the UNREACHABLE CODE'], and: 'IT IS WHAT SHIPS' };

/* Four reasons debug misleads. */
const MISLEADS = [
  { r: 'DEBUG RUNS AN UNOPTIMISED COMPILER', consequence: 'SO the CODE IS SEVERAL TIMES SLOWER and A COST THAT IS INVISIBLE IN RELEASE IS VISIBLE IN DEBUG',
    and: 'WHICH MEANS A PROFILE YOU TOOK IN DEBUG SHOWS PROBLEMS YOU DO NOT HAVE' },
  { r: 'DEBUG DISABLES TREE SHAKING', detail: 'SO CODE THAT WILL NOT EXIST IN the RELEASE BINARY IS LOADED and RUN',
    consequence: 'WHICH CHANGES STARTUP TIME and MEMORY IN WAYS THAT HAVE NOTHING to DO WITH YOUR CODE' },
  { r: 'DEBUGS ASSERTIONS ADD CHECKS THAT ARE NOT IN RELEASE', consequence: 'SO the FRAME TIMINGS YOU MEASURE INCLUDE WORK THAT DOES NOT HAPPEN for A USER' },
  { r: 'the DEVELOPMENT BUILD CONNECTS TO A DEBUGGER', consequence: 'WHICH CHANGES the SCHEDULING and the TIMING of EVERYTHING' },
];

/* Two rules. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'NEVER DIAGNOSE A PERFORMANCE PROBLEM IN DEBUG',
    not: 'NOT BECAUSE DEBUG IS USELESS',
    but: 'IT IS the RIGHT PLACE TO FIND A LAYOUT ERROR',

    and: 'the DEVICE THAT PRODUCES the SUPPORT TICKETS IS the ONE AT the OTHER END of the DISTRIBUTION' },
];

/* Two things worth knowing. */
const ALSO = [
  { t: 'A RELEASE BUILD ON A REAL DEVICE IS the ONLY TRUE TEST',
    why: 'BECAUSE RELEASE CHANGES the COMPILER, the SIZE, and the ABSENCE OF ASSERTIONS',
    symptom: 'SO A CRASH THAT APPEARS ONLY IN RELEASE IS A REAL RELEASE-ONLY BUG and the FIRST THING TO CHECK IS AN ASSERTION THAT WAS MASKING IT' },
  { t: 'PROFILE MODE IS NOT RELEASE MODE',
    detail: 'SO A BUILD THAT IS FAST IN PROFILE MAY NOT BE FAST IN RELEASE BECAUSE TREE SHAKING REMOVES CODE and CHANGES WHAT RUNS AT STARTUP',
    and: 'and A BUILD CAN BE SLOWER IN RELEASE BECAUSE of CODE THAT ONLY RUNS WHEN ASSERTIONS ARE OFF' },

/* The discipline. */
const DISCIPLINE = 'HAVE ONE DEVICE DESIGNATED AS the SLOW DEVICE and PROFILE ON IT EVERY TIME';
const WHY_DISCIPLINE = 'BECAUSE A PERFORMANCE REGRESSION IS A COMPARISON and A COMPARISON NEEDS A FIXED BASELINE';
const WHICH_BASELINE = 'and the BASELINE THAT MATTERS IS the SLOWEST SUPPORTED DEVICE, BECAUSE THAT IS WHERE the FRAME BUDGET IS ACTUALLY AT RISK';

"It is janky in debug" tells you almost nothing. A debug build is five to ten times slower than a release build, so a frame that takes 4ms in debug may be perfectly fine in production and a frame that takes 12ms in debug may be unusable. All performance work happens in profile mode, on a physical device.

// THE THREE MODES, and what each is for
//
// DEBUG      JIT, asserts on, debug painting, every widget
//            instrumented. Roughly 5-10x slower than release.
//            USE IT FOR: development, and nothing else.
//
// PROFILE    AOT, asserts off, observability on, service
//            extension available. Close to release performance.
//            USE IT FOR: all performance work.
//
// RELEASE    AOT, fully optimised, tree-shaken, minified.
//            USE IT FOR: the final check, and for the numbers you
//            report.
dart compile exe main.dart -o app --profile   // a profile build
flutter run --profile
flutter run --release

// WHY DEBUG LIES
// - every build is instrumented and every assert is evaluated
// - the framework draws debug banners and a debug paint overlay
// - the code is not optimised, so a hot loop is 5-10x slower
// - GC and layout behave differently
//
// THE CONSEQUENCE
// "it is janky in debug" tells you almost nothing.
// "it is janky in profile on a Pixel 4a" tells you everything.

// BUILD MODES, and which to use for what
// debug    : development
// profile  : performance measurement, and a realistic demo
// release  : the store build, and the final performance check
// THE DEVICES THAT MATTER
// your laptop: irrelevant. it has more CPU and RAM than any
//   phone you will ship to, and no thermal throttling
// a simulator on a laptop: the same CPU as the laptop
// a physical device: the only useful measurement
//
// THE TEST MATRIX, and three devices is the minimum
//   a low-end Android:  the 90th percentile of your users
//   a mid-range Android: the median
//   a recent iPhone:    the iOS baseline
//
// and the DEVICE you should optimise for is the low-end one.
// a 10% gain on a slow device is a 2 second improvement; the
// same gain on a fast one is invisible.

16.2 The DevTools performance panel

// HOW TO CONNECT
flutter run --profile
# it prints: "The Dart VM service is listening on http://127.0.0.1:xxxx/"
# open that in a browser, or use the IDE, or:
//   dart pub global activate dev_tools
//   dart pub global run dev_tools

// THE FRAME CHART, which is the first thing to read
//
//   a bar = 16.7ms, one frame at 60fps
//   red   = the frame MISSED its budget
//   the UI thread row: build + layout + paint
//   the RASTER row:   the GPU work, on another thread
//
// WHAT TO LOOK FOR
// 1. red bars in the UI row
//      -> build, layout or paint is too slow
// 2. red bars in the RASTER row
//      -> a blur, a shadow, an image, a shader
// 3. a long yellow stripe at the start
//      -> a shader compile, or a first-use code path
// 4. jank only when scrolling
//      -> build cost per item, or a layout in the row
// 5. jank only when an animation runs
//      -> work in build, or a saveLayer

// THE WIDGET TIMELINE
// below the frame chart: which widgets rebuilt, and how long
// a long bar = a widget with an expensive build
// a "build" spike in a list = a state problem

// THE MEMORY PANEL
// the live object count by class, over time
// a rising floor = a LEAK
// one class growing without bound = an unbounded cache
// THE OTHER PANELS, and when each is the right tool
//
// TIMELINE  a custom trace: Flutter then Dart
//           traceFrame, traceAction, custom marks
//           USE IT FOR: one specific slow interaction
//
// CPU        a sampled profile
//           USE IT FOR: a slow screen, in a real interaction
//
// ALLOCATION a flame chart of every allocation
//           USE IT FOR: GC pressure, and for finding the
//           allocation that dominates a hot path
//
// RASTER     a GPU-side view
//           USE IT FOR: paint and compositing problems
//
// The DART TIMER, for a micro-measurement
final sw = Stopwatch()..start();
await heavyOperation();
debugPrint('took ${sw.elapsedMilliseconds}ms');
// but the JIT optimiser can remove the work if you discard the
// result, so USE the result

// A CUSTOM TRACE, which is what you want when investigating
void main() {
  WidgetsBinding.instance.addTimingsCallback((frameData) {
    // every frame, with the build and layout timings
    for (final buildTiming in frameData.buildTimestamps) {
      final total = buildTiming.end!.difference(buildTiming.start!).inMicroseconds;
      if (total > 8000) {   // 8ms is a lot for a build
        debugPrint('slow build: ${total}us  ${buildTiming.target}');
      }
    }
  });
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

Reading the four rows, and the panel's vocabulary

The performance panel is a frame chart and the whole skill is reading which of its four rows is long, because that is the diagnosis and nothing else in the panel is. Each row is one phase of the rendering pipeline, and the order is the order they happen: UI, raster and so on. The UI row is the platform thread — build, layout, and the framework's own work. A long UI row means your Dart code and the widget system are the cost. The raster row is the graphics thread, which records the paint commands and issues them; a long raster row means too many draw calls or an expensive paint. The other two rows are the compositor and, on some platforms, the GPU work submitted from it. The practical reading is short. If the UI row is long, the cost is in build or layout, and the fix is structural: make the widget smaller, remove an intrinsic measurement, stop rebuilding a subtree. If the raster row is long, the cost is in painting, and the fix is a repaint boundary, fewer draw calls, or a smaller painted area. If both are short and the frame is still late, the cost is elsewhere — it is in the application's own asynchronous work competing for the platform thread, or in a frame that was scheduled late rather than processed slowly, which is a different problem with a different fix. Then the four things to know about using it, and each is a specific discipline. Record, do not watch. The panel's live view is for orientation; the recording is for diagnosis, because a recording has a timeline you can step through and a live view does not. Record while performing the interaction, not before it. A recording of an idle screen tells you the cost of doing nothing, which is useful once and useless afterwards. Look for the frame that is late, not for the slow one — a slow frame is one that took too long; a late frame is one that was produced after its deadline, which is the same thing when the display is synchronised to the producer and a different thing when it is not, and the panel distinguishes them. And clear the recording between attempts, because a recording that accumulates frames from three different interactions has three baselines and you will compare the wrong ones. Then the two things worth knowing that are about interpretation, and both are traps. A long row is a symptom, not a cause, and the same long UI row can be caused by a build that rebuilds a whole list, by an intrinsic measurement, or by a synchronous network read on the platform thread — and the panel tells you which thread, not which line. And the numbers differ between devices, so a frame chart is comparable across recordings on the same device and meaningless across two, which is the same fixed-baseline discipline the previous section ended on.

/* The rows. */
const ROWS = [
  { r: 'the UI ROW', is: 'the PLATFORM THREAD - BUILD, LAYOUT, and the FRAMEWORKS OWN WORK', meaning: 'A LONG UI ROW MEANS YOUR DART CODE and the WIDGET SYSTEM ARE the COST' },
  { r: 'the RASTER ROW', is: 'the GRAPHICS THREAD, WHICH RECORDS the PAINT COMMANDS and ISSUES THEM', meaning: 'A LONG RASTER ROW MEANS TOO MANY DRAW CALLS or AN EXPENSIVE PAINT' },
  { r: 'the OTHER ROWS', is: 'the COMPOSITOR and, ON SOME PLATFORMS, the GPU WORK SUBMITTED FROM IT' },
];
const ORDER = 'the ORDER IS the ORDER THEY HAPPEN';

/* How to read it. */
const READ = [
  { if: 'the UI ROW IS LONG', then: 'the COST IS IN BUILD or LAYOUT', fix: ['MAKE the WIDGET SMALLER', 'REMOVE AN INTRINSIC MEASUREMENT', 'STOP REBUILDING A SUBTREE'] },
  { if: 'the RASTER ROW IS LONG', then: 'the COST IS IN PAINTING', fix: ['A REPAINT BOUNDARY', 'FEWER DRAW CALLS', 'A SMALLER PAINTED AREA'] },
  { if: 'BOTH ARE SHORT and the FRAME IS STILL LATE', then: 'the COST IS ELSEWHERE',
    detail: ['IT IS IN the APPLICATIONS OWN ASYNCHRONOUS WORK COMPETING FOR the PLATFORM THREAD',
      'or IN A FRAME THAT WAS SCHEDULED LATE rather than PROCESSED SLOWLY'],
    and: 'WHICH IS A DIFFERENT PROBLEM with A DIFFERENT FIX' },
];

/* Four disciplines. */
const USE = [
  { u: 'RECORD, DO NOT WATCH',
    why: 'the PANELS LIVE VIEW IS FOR ORIENTATION',
    gain: 'the RECORDING IS FOR DIAGNOSIS, BECAUSE A RECORDING HAS A TIMELINE YOU CAN STEP THROUGH and A LIVE VIEW DOES NOT' },
  { u: 'RECORD WHILE PERFORMING the INTERACTION, NOT BEFORE IT',
    why: 'A RECORDING of AN IDLE SCREEN TELLS YOU the COST of DOING NOTHING',
    and: 'WHICH IS USEFUL ONCE and USELESS AFTERWARDS' },
  { u: 'LOOK FOR the FRAME THAT IS LATE, NOT FOR the SLOW ONE',
    detail: ['A SLOW FRAME IS ONE THAT TOOK TOO LONG', 'A LATE FRAME IS ONE THAT WAS PRODUCED AFTER ITS DEADLINE'],
    same: 'WHICH IS the SAME THING WHEN the DISPLAY IS SYNCHRONISED TO the PRODUCER',
    and: 'A DIFFERENT THING WHEN IT IS NOT',
    andThePanel: 'and the PANEL DISTINGUISHES THEM' },
  { u: 'CLEAR the RECORDING BETWEEN ATTEMPTS',
    why: 'BECAUSE A RECORDING THAT ACCUMULATES FRAMES from THREE DIFFERENT INTERACTIONS HAS THREE BASELINES',
    consequence: 'and YOU WILL COMPARE the WRONG ONES' },
];

/* Two traps. */
const TRAPS = [
  { t: 'A LONG ROW IS A SYMPTOM, NOT A CAUSE',
    detail: 'and the SAME LONG UI ROW CAN BE CAUSED BY A BUILD THAT REBUILDS A WHOLE LIST, BY AN INTRINSIC MEASUREMENT, or BY A SYNCHRONOUS NETWORK READ ON the PLATFORM THREAD',
    and: 'the PANEL TELLS YOU WHICH THREAD, NOT WHICH LINE' },
  { t: 'the NUMBERS DIFFER BETWEEN DEVICES',
    detail: 'SO A FRAME CHART IS COMPARABLE ACROSS RECORDINGS ON the SAME DEVICE and MEANINGLESS ACROSS TWO',
    connects: 'WHICH IS the FIXED-BASELINE DISCIPLINE the PREVIOUS SECTION ENDED ON' },
];

16.3 A diagnostic order

An order that avoids wasted work

Performance work goes wrong in a predictable way: a developer notices something slow, guesses at the cause, applies a change, and sees no improvement, then guesses again. Each guess is cheap and each is usually wrong, and the reason they are wrong is that the observable symptom maps to several causes and the intuition picks the most familiar one rather than the most likely one. So the useful thing is an order that eliminates causes cheaply before eliminating them expensively. First: is the cost in your code at all? Profile in release on the slow device and read the row that is long; if no row is long, the application is not slow and the perception is something else — an animation that is technically within budget but feels wrong, or a latency the user experiences as slowness. Second: which row is long, and is the cost build or layout? That distinction decides the whole direction: build and layout are both solved by making the widget tree smaller, and they are solved by different changes. Third: is a subtree rebuilding that should not? This is the single most common cause of a long UI row and it is countable — the widget inspector's rebuild tracking shows which widgets rebuilt during a specific interaction, and the question is whether any of them needed to. Fourth: is something measuring intrinsically? An intrinsic measurement forces a double layout over whatever subtree it wraps, and it is invisible unless you look for it. Fifth: is the application doing synchronous work on the platform thread? Reading a large file, parsing a large payload, a synchronous network call — all of these appear as a long UI row with no obvious widget cause, and the timeline's track for the main isolate shows them. Then the three things that are not about your code, and each is a real diagnosis that a developer chasing their own code will miss. The frame was scheduled late rather than processed slowly, which means something else on the device was competing for the same resources — a background application, a thermal throttle, a device that has been running for a week. The application is doing too much work before the first frame, which is the startup section's subject and presents as a slow application that is actually a slow start. And the perception is the problem, because a motion that is technically within budget reads as slow if it does not respond immediately to a touch — the responsiveness chapter's subject, and a different problem with a different fix. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Change one thing at a time and measure after each, because two changes that each improve the number by five per cent together improve it by five per cent and you will conclude that both are necessary. And write down the measurement before the change, on the same device in the same mode — because the alternative is a comparison against a remembered number, and remembered numbers are systematically wrong in the direction of the last thing you tried.

/* Why order matters. */
const WHY_ORDER = {
  goesWrong: ['A DEVELOPER NOTICES SOMETHING SLOW', 'GUESSES AT the CAUSE', 'APPLIES A CHANGE', 'and SEES NO IMPROEMENT, THEN GUESSES AGAIN'],
  cost: 'EACH GUESS IS CHEAP and EACH IS USUALLY WRONG',
  reason: 'and the REASON THEY ARE WRONG IS THAT the OBSERVABLE SYMPTOM MAPS TO SEVERAL CAUSES',
  intuition: 'and the INTUITION PICKS the MOST FAMILIAR ONE rather than the MOST LIKELY ONE',
  therefore: 'SO the USEFUL THING IS AN ORDER THAT ELIMINATES CAUSES CHEAPLY BEFORE ELIMINATES THEM EXPENSIVELY',
};

/* The order. */
const ORDER = [
  { n: 1, q: 'IS the COST IN YOUR CODE AT ALL?',

const NOT_YOUR_CODE = [

const PRACTICES = [

Do the three five-minute checks in this section before anything else. Adding itemExtent to a list, counting the rebuilds in a row, and grepping the build methods for toList, sort and jsonDecode resolve the large majority of "the app is slow" reports on their own.

// THE ORDER, and it matters: fix the biggest thing first

// STEP 1: WHICH STAGE
// is it the UI thread or the raster thread?
//   UI    -> build, layout or paint
//   RASTER -> a shader, a blur, an image, a layer
// this ONE measurement decides everything that follows

// STEP 2, IF THE UI THREAD: WHICH STAGE
// the frame chart breaks it down:
//   BUILD time  -> too many rebuilds, or an expensive build
//   LAYOUT time -> constraints, flex, an intrinsic measurement
//   PAINT time  -> a complex CustomPainter, or many layers

// STEP 3, BY STAGE
//
// BUILD:
//   a. are you rebuilding everything for a local change?
//      -> move the state down, or use a ValueListenableBuilder
//      -> const wherever possible
//   b. is work happening in build?
//      -> a sort, a filter, a JSON parse, a repository call
//      -> move it to a provider, an init method, or an isolate
//   c. is a provider watching more than it needs?
//      -> .select, or a narrower provider
//   d. is MediaQuery.of(context) in build?
//      -> .sizeOf, .paddingOf, or pass the value down
//
// LAYOUT:
//   a. a flex widget in an unbounded cross axis
//      -> SizedBox, IntrinsicHeight, mainAxisSize.min
//   b. IntrinsicWidth/Height on a deep subtree
//      -> a fixed size, or a different layout approach
//   c. a shrinkWrap list
//      -> a sliver
//   d. too many layers of nesting
//      -> flatten, or use a LayoutBuilder
//
// PAINT / RASTER:
//   a. a large blurRadius
//      -> a layered fake shadow, or a smaller blur
//   b. BackdropFilter over a large area
//      -> a smaller area, or a static approximation
//   c. a large image decoded at full resolution
//      -> cacheWidth
//   d. a custom shader doing a loop
//      -> simplify, or shrink the area
//   e. too many RepaintBoundaries
//      -> remove the ones that do not help
// THE FOUR FIXES, in order of effort
//
// 1. MOVE THE WORK
//    out of build, into a provider, an init method, or an isolate
//    FIXES: build, and sometimes layout
//    EFFORT: low
//
// 2. SHRINK THE WORK
//    1000 rows to 20 visible, a 10MB image to 400KB, a 300ms
//    job to a 20ms one
//    FIXES: everything
//    EFFORT: low to medium
//
// 3. MAKE IT CHEAPER
//    const, shallowRef, a typed list, a transform instead of a
//    layout property
//    FIXES: build, layout
//    EFFORT: medium
//
// 4. MOVE IT OFF THE THREAD
//    an isolate, a compute() call, a platform channel on a
//    background executor
//    FIXES: everything, at the cost of complexity
//    EFFORT: high
//
// THE ORDER: do 1 and 2 before 3, and 3 before 4. Most
// "performance problems" are a 1000-item list where 20 are
// visible, and the fix is itemExtent and a builder, not an
// isolate.
// THE THREE FIVE-MINUTE CHECKS, before anything else
//
// 1. IS IT THE LIST?
//    add itemExtent, or switch a ListView(children:) to a
//    ListView.builder. 80% of "the app is slow" is this.
//
// 2. ARE YOU REBUILDING EVERYTHING?
//    add a debugPrint of the build count in a row's build method,
//    scroll, and watch the number. If it grows with the scroll
//    position, something is wrong above the list.
//
// 3. IS THERE WORK IN BUILD?
//    grep your build methods for: .toList(), .sort(), .where(),
//    jsonDecode, await, a repository call, DateFormat.format
//    any of those in build is a bug.

// A QUICK INSTRUMENTATION
class PerfProbe extends StatefulWidget {
  const PerfProbe({required this.child, super.key});
  final Widget child;

  @override
  State<PerfProbe> createState() => _PerfProbeState();
}

class _PerfProbeState extends State<PerfProbe> {
  int _builds = 0;
  static int totalBuilds = 0;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    _builds++;
    totalBuilds++;
    return Stack(children: [
      widget.child,
      if (const bool.fromEnvironment('DEBUG_PERF'))
        Positioned(
          top: 0, right: 0,
          child: Container(
            color: Colors.red,
            padding: const EdgeInsets.all(2),
            child: Text('$_builds', style: const TextStyle(color: Colors.white, fontSize: 10)),
          ),
        ),
    ]);
  }
}

16.4 Build and rebuild cost

// WHY BUILD IS EXPENSIVE, and it is not what people think
// building a widget is not the cost. the cost is:
// - creating the Element and the RenderObject
// - LAYOUT: the whole subtree is measured again
// - the widget tree walk itself, which is small

// SO: a build that is cheap can still be expensive if it LAYS OUT

// THE FIXES, in order
// 1. const: identical widget, framework skips the subtree
//    entirely - not even didUpdateWidget is called
final staticTitle = SizedBox(height: 8);     // a const, hoisted

// 2. move the state down, so the rebuild is local
// BAD: a screen-level setState rebuilds 1000 rows
// GOOD: each row is a StatefulWidget with its own state

// 3. a narrow provider, or a select
final title = ref.watch(entryProvider(id).select((e) => e.title));

// 4. ValueListenableBuilder for a leaf
ValueListenableBuilder<int>(
  valueListenable: counter,
  builder: (context, value, child) => Text('$value'),
  child: const ExpensiveWidget(),      // built ONCE
);

// 5. AnimatedBuilder, same idea
// 6. keys, so the framework reuses the element instead of
//    rebuilding it

// THE REBUILD COUNT, which is the number to watch
// add a counter, scroll a 1000-row list, and check
//  GOOD: roughly the viewport height plus the cache extent,
//        INDEPENDENT of the scroll position
//  BAD:  grows with the scroll position
// LAYOUT, which is the second most common cost
// layout runs top-down with constraints, and a subtree is
// re-laid-out whenever anything above it changes

// the expensive layout patterns
// 1. INTRINSIC on a deep subtree: 2-3x layout passes
IntrinsicWidth(child: Row(children: [Expensive1(), Expensive2()]));

// 2. OVERLAPPING CONSTRAINTS: a layout pass that does not
//    converge
//    Flutter throws "RenderBox was not laid out" in debug;
//    in release it can silently loop

// 3. EXPENSIVE in the build of a subtree you do not need to
//    re-lay-out

// THE FIX for 1: replace the intrinsic measurement with an
// explicit size
// a text button row that should be equal width:
// instead of IntrinsicWidth, compute the widest label once
class EqualWidthButtons extends StatelessWidget {
  const EqualWidthButtons({required this.labels, super.key});
  final List<String> labels;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // measure with a TextPainter, not with a layout pass
    final widths = labels
        .map((l) => (TextPainter(
              text: TextSpan(text: l, style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.labelLarge),
              textDirection: Directionality.of(context),
              maxLines: 1,
            )..layout())
            .width)
        .toList();
    final maxWidth = widths.reduce((a, b) => a > b ? a : b) + 32;

    return Row(
      children: [
        for (var i = 0; i < labels.length; i++)
          SizedBox(width: maxWidth, child: ElevatedButton(onPressed: () {}, child: Text(labels[i]))),
      ],
    );
  }
}

Making a build cheap, and knowing whether it is

Build cost is the most common performance complaint in a widget framework and the least often measured, because it is invisible in every tool and obvious to the user. A rebuild is the framework walking a subtree and calling build on every widget in it. The cost is per widget, not per tree: a thousand widgets is a thousand build calls, and each one allocates whatever it allocates. So the question is never "how deep is my tree" but "how many widgets rebuild when something changes" — and the second is countable with the widget inspector's rebuild tracking, which marks every widget that rebuilt during a specific interaction. Then the four levers, in the order to try them. Make the widget const. A const widget is a compile-time constant, so when a parent rebuilds and produces an equal widget the element's update short-circuits and nothing below is touched — and this is a compile-time guarantee, not an optimisation, so it costs one keyword and cannot regress. Move the state down. A state change marks the element and everything below it dirty, so a state object in a widget at the top of a screen rebuilds every row beneath it; the fix is structural and the discipline is that a widget should hold only the state it actually reads. Split the widget. A widget that receives everything and uses one field will rebuild when any of them changes; a child widget that receives only the one field it uses will not, and the parent rebuild is cheap because it does not rebuild the child. This is the most broadly applicable of the four and the one most often skipped, because splitting feels like noise in the source. And avoid rebuilding from a listener. A setState in a stream listener rebuilds the whole state object's subtree on every event, and a stream that fires often makes that continuous. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. A big widget used to hold related fields together, which is correct for readability and expensive for rebuilding, and the resolution is not to abandon the grouping but to pass a slice rather than the whole object. An expensive widget's build that is called more often than it changes, which is the mechanism behind "this screen is slow and I cannot see why" — the build is doing a format, an allocation or a map lookup on every frame of a rebuild cycle it did not need. And rebuilding because an unrelated field changed, which is the same problem as the first and is fixed by the same thing. Then the two things worth knowing, and both are about measuring. Build counts are the right metric, not frame time, because a frame that rebuilds three widgets and one that rebuilds three thousand can both miss sixteen milliseconds, and the count is the number that scales. And the cost of a const widget is not zero, — it is a comparison — so a tree of ten thousand const widgets is not free; the win from const is skipping the subtree, not the widget itself, which is why const on a leaf with a large const subtree is where the win is.

/* What a rebuild is. */
const REBUILD = 'the FRAMEWORK WALKING A SUBTREE and CALLING build ON EVERY WIDGET IN IT';
const COST = {
  is: 'PER WIDGET, NOT PER TREE',
  detail: 'A THOUSAND WIDGETS IS A THOUSAND BUILD CALLS, and EACH ONE ALLOCATES WHATEVER IT ALLOCATES',
  question: 'SO the QUESTION IS NEVER how deep is my tree BUT HOW MANY WIDGETS REBUILD WHEN SOMETHING CHANGES',
  countable: 'and the SECOND IS COUNTABLE WITH the WIDGET INSPECTORS REBUILD TRACKING, WHICH MARKS EVERY WIDGET THAT REBUILT DURING A SPECIFIC INTERACTION',
};

/* Four levers, in order. */
const LEVERS = [
  { n: 1, l: 'MAKE the WIDGET const',
    mechanism: ['A const WIDGET IS A COMPILE-TIME CONSTANT',
      'SO WHEN A PARENT REBUILDS and PRODUCES AN EQUAL WIDGET the ELEMENTS UPDATE SHORT-CIRCUITS and NOTHING BELOW IS TOUCHED'],

16.5 Images and video

// THE THREE IMAGE NUMBERS, and only the first is obvious
//   the FILE size: 2MB for a 4000x3000 photo
//   the DECODED size: 4000 * 3000 * 4 = 48MB of RAM
//   the GPU texture: usually the same as the decoded, plus
//     a mipmap chain, so up to 1.33x
//
// 20 photos in a list at full resolution is 960MB. The OS
// kills the app.

// THE RULES
// 1. DECODE AT THE SIZE YOU DISPLAY
Image.network(
  url,
  cacheWidth: 400,     // PHYSICAL pixels
  cacheHeight: 300,
)
// for a package
CachedNetworkImage(
  imageUrl: url,
  memCacheWidth: 400,
  maxWidthDiskCache: 800,
)

// 2. REQUEST THE SIZE FROM THE SERVER
String thumb(String url, int width) => '$url?w=$width&format=webp&q=75';

// 3. CACHE, so scrolling back is instant
//    ImageCache is memory only. For disk, use a package.

// 4. RESERVE THE SPACE, so nothing reflows
SizedBox(
  width: 64, height: 64,
  child: Image.network(url, fit: BoxFit.cover),
)

// 5. gaplessPlayback, for a fade-in
Image.network(url, gaplessPlayback: true)

// 6. LAZY LOAD below the fold
Image.network(url, frameBuilder: (c, child, frame, wasSync) {
  return frame == null ? const SkeletonBox() : AnimatedSwitcher(
    duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 200),
    child: child,
  );
})

// MEASURE IT
debugDumpImageCache();
// or
final cache = PaintingBinding.instance.imageCache;
debugPrint('${cache.currentSize} images, ${cache.currentSizeBytes ~/ (1024*1024)}MB');

// AND CONFIGURE IT
PaintingBinding.instance.imageCache.maximumSizeBytes = 200 << 20;
// VIDEO, which is worse than images
// a video player is a texture per frame. 1080p is 1920*1080*4
// = 8MB per frame, and the decoder holds several

// THE RULES
// 1. set the size, or the texture is the source resolution
AspectRatio(
  aspectRatio: 16 / 9,
  child: VideoPlayer(controller),
)

// 2. the package
//    video_player (the official one) uses ExoPlayer on Android
//    and AVPlayer on iOS, and handles most of this

// 3. PRELOAD the next item, and PAUSE the offscreen ones
final _controllers = <String, VideoPlayerController>{};

@override
void didUpdateWidget(ListView old) {
  super.didUpdateWidget(old);
  for (final (id, c) in _controllers.entries) {
    if (indexOf(id) > indexOf(currentId) + 2) {
      c.pause();
      c.dispose();
      _controllers.remove(id);
    }
  }
}

// 4. NEVER autoplay with sound: it is a policy rejection on both
//    stores, and it is obnoxious

// 5. MUTE when backgrounded
_lifecycleListener = AppLifecycleListener(
  onPause: () => _controller.pause(),
  onResume: () => _controller.play(),
);

Video and animation, and the cost that is not in the widget

A video or an animated image on a phone is the single most expensive thing most applications display, and the cost is not in the widget that shows it — it is in what has to be true for the frames to arrive on time. A video is decoded into frames and presented by the platform's own player, which means the cost is a decoder, a surface, and a texture, and the widget itself is nearly free. The costs that matter are elsewhere: whether the frames are decoded ahead of time or on demand, which is what determines whether playback stutters; whether the codec is supported on the device, which is a hardware question and a compatibility question at once; and whether the surface is composited with the rest of the interface, which is where a video over an animated background becomes far more expensive than either. Then the four things that go wrong, and each is a specific mechanism. A high-resolution video for a small view. A video encoded at full device resolution and scaled down decodes at full resolution, so the decoder produces far more pixels than are displayed — which is the image chapter's decode-size problem arriving with a moving picture, and the fix is to encode at or near the display size and to pick a resolution per device rather than shipping one. A controller playing while the application is backgrounded. A video or animation that keeps requesting frames while the application is not visible keeps the decoder and the surface alive and prevents the platform from sleeping; the lifecycle callbacks are the fix and their absence is the mechanism behind an application that drains a battery while idle. An animated image being decoded and discarded repeatedly, which happens when a widget rebuilds and re-resolves an animated asset, so the animation restarts from the first frame on every rebuild — the symptom is a spinner or a loading animation that appears frozen or that flickers. And an animation running at full frame rate for something that does not need it, which the platform's own power-saving advice addresses: a progress indicator that updates on a timer rather than on progress is burning frames to display a state that changes once a second. Then the four practices, and each is specific. Pause and resume on the lifecycle, always, for every video, every animation controller and every repeating timer, because the cost of not doing it is not visible in development and is the difference between a battery that lasts and one that does not. Pick the codec by what the device supports, not by what is newest, because a codec that is not hardware-accelerated on that device decodes in software and will drop frames regardless of how well the rest of the application is built. Load the video lazily and dispose the controller, so a screen that is not showing one is not holding a decoder. And respect the reduced-motion preference, which for video means not autoplaying, and which is both an accessibility requirement and a battery measure. Then the two things worth knowing, because they change what you build. Autoplay is not free and not allowed everywhere, — it is a policy decision by the platform and a battery decision by the user, and an application that autoplays a video in a list will be noticed. And the video is not part of the widget tree, which means a video cannot be laid out like a widget, cannot be found by a finder, and — this is the one that surprises — does not participate in the semantics tree unless you annotate it, so a video with no annotation is invisible to a screen reader.

/* What a video costs. */
const VIDEO = {
  widgetIsNearlyFree: 'A VIDEO IS DECODED INTO FRAMES and PRESENTED BY the PLATFORMS OWN PLAYER, WHICH MEANS the WIDGET ITSELF IS NEARLY FREE',
  costsThatMatter: [

16.6 Startup and first frame

What happens before the first frame, and what to move

Startup is the interval between the user tapping the icon and the first frame appearing, and on a phone the user experiences it as "did it work" — so it is one of the few performance numbers with a direct relationship to how the application is judged. There are two distinct costs and they have different causes. Load is the operating system bringing the process up, loading the binary, and starting the runtime; it is not yours to control except by making the binary smaller. Initialisation is your code running before the first frame: everything between process start and runApp, plus everything your first widget does in its build. Then the four things to look for, in the order that matters. Work before runApp. Anything in main before the first frame is invisible to the user and blocks it: opening a database, reading a large preference file, initialising an analytics SDK, a synchronous network call for a configuration. Defer everything that can be deferred to after the first frame, and the discipline is that main should do the minimum that is required to draw something and nothing else. The first widget's build is doing too much. The first frame builds the whole initial screen, and a screen that builds a list, resolves a theme and reads a store synchronously takes longer than one that draws a placeholder and fills in after. A large binary. Tree shaking removes unreachable code, but assets do not shrink themselves, and a debug build is dramatically larger than a release build, so a startup measurement taken in debug is meaningless — which is the mode chapter's argument again. And the first frame after a warm start is not the same, because the process is already alive and the work is only your initialisation, so the two numbers measure different things and the metric that matters to a user tapping an icon is the cold one. Then the three things that go wrong, and each has a mechanism. Waiting for a network call before the first frame, which turns a configuration fetch into startup time and makes startup proportional to network conditions — the fix is to draw with defaults and update when the configuration arrives. Initialising plugins in main, which is where every plugin's registration happens, and several of them do real work. And measuring on a fast device in debug, which is the combination that produces a startup number that is both optimistic and not the one a user experiences. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Draw something immediately, then fill it in — a splash or a placeholder, then the content — so the first frame is cheap and the perceived startup is the frame the user sees rather than the data being ready. And measure cold start on the slow device with the application genuinely killed, because a warm start measures something the user does not do, and the platform tooling that reports it distinguishes the two.

/* The definition and the two costs. */
const STARTUP = 'the INTERVAL BETWEEN the USER TAPPING the ICON and the FIRST FRAME APPEARING';
const WHY_IT_MATTERS = 'ON A PHONE the USER EXPERIENCES IT AS did it work';
const WHY = 'SO IT IS ONE of the FEW PERFORMANCE NUMBERS with A DIRECT RELATIONSHIP TO HOW the APPLICATION IS JUDGED';

Never await anything in main() before runApp. It is the difference between a white screen for two seconds and an app that appears immediately with a shell and fills in behind it - and the shell approach also makes the app usable offline from the first frame.

// THE PHASES, and the budget
//   0-300ms   the splash, before Flutter starts
//   300-700ms Flutter engine start, the first frame
//   700ms+    your async initialisation
//
// THE TARGETS
//   cold start to first frame:  under 2s on a low-end Android
//   time to interactive:        under 3s
//   the FIRST FRAME should not need the network. ever.

// WHAT MAKES IT SLOW
// 1. work in main() before runApp
//    await something;   // 2 seconds of a white screen
//    runApp(...)
//
// 2. a big synchronous build on the first screen
//    a 1000-row list, a huge theme
//
// 3. a synchronous plugin call
//    await SharedPreferences.getInstance()   // it is fast, but
//                                             it is not free
//
// 4. too much code to parse
//    a 5MB Dart kernel
//
// 5. font loading: a network font blocks the first frame
// THE PATTERN: shell first, then fill
void main() {
  // 1. runApp IMMEDIATELY, with a shell that paints
  runApp(const BootstrapApp());
}

class BootstrapApp extends StatefulWidget {
  const BootstrapApp({super.key});
  @override
  State<BootstrapApp> createState() => _BootstrapAppState();
}

class _BootstrapAppState extends State<BootstrapApp> {
  late final Future<void> _init = _bootstrap();

  Future<void> _bootstrap() async {
    // 2. do the slow things AFTER the first frame
    WidgetsBinding.instance.addPostFrameCallback((_) async {
      final prefs = await SharedPreferences.getInstance();
      final session = await SessionStore.restore(prefs);
      final db = await AppDatabase.open();

      if (!mounted) return;
      setState(() {
        _session = session;
        _db = db;
        _ready = true;
      });
    });
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      theme: AppTheme.light,
      darkTheme: AppTheme.dark,
      // a SPLASH while initialising, not a blank screen
      home: _ready
          ? RootScreen(session: _session!, db: _db!)
          : const SplashScreen(),
    );
  }
}

// FOR FONTS: declare them in pubspec.yaml so they are bundled,
// and NOT via a network fetch. a network font blocks the first
// frame, and it fails offline
// MEASURING STARTUP
// a plugin, or your own marks
final stopwatch = Stopwatch()..start();
runApp(const MyApp());
WidgetsBinding.instance.addPostFrameCallback((_) {
  stopwatch.stop();
  debugPrint('first frame: ${stopwatch.elapsedMilliseconds}ms');
});

// and a custom trace for a finer breakdown
Timeline.startSync('startup');
// ... the phases
Timeline.finishSync();

// Flutter also reports it: the Performance panel shows the
// "first frame" marker, and `SchedulerBinding.instance
// .firstFrameRasterized`

// AND the honest measure, which is what the store cares about
// a real device, a cold start, from a terminated state:
//   adb shell am force-stop com.acme.app
//   adb shell am start -W -n com.acme.app/.MainActivity
//   # TotalTime is the cold start time

16.7 Memory

What holds memory, and what leaks

Memory problems on a phone present in two distinct shapes and they need different investigations, so the first thing is to tell them apart. The size problem is that the application needs more memory than the device has, which on a modern phone is almost always the wrong diagnosis because modern devices have gigabytes; what actually happens is that the application holds something proportional to usage — a list of everything the user has ever loaded, an image cache that never evicts, a log buffer — and that grows until the system kills the application. The leak problem is that memory is held by things that should have been released, and the classic leak on a phone is an object that outlives the widget that owned it: a controller, a subscription, a stream listener, an isolate, a closure captured by a callback. Then the four things that hold memory, in rough order of how much they usually hold. The image cache, which is bounded by configuration and which evicts, but a list of decoded images larger than the budget will evict and re-decode repeatedly. A list of everything. A list that grows without bound is the most common cause of the size problem, and the fix is pagination, windowing, or capping the in-memory length. Isolates, each of which has its own memory and no sharing with the main one, so an isolate per operation rather than one long-lived isolate accumulates. And a retained reference graph, which is the leak: something holds a reference to something that holds a reference back, and neither is collected. Then the three things that go wrong, and each has a mechanism. A controller or subscription not disposed. Every one of these holds a native resource as well as a Dart object, so it is a memory leak and a resource leak; the framework asserts in debug for the ones it can detect, which is why a leak that reaches production usually got there by being created somewhere the debug assertion does not cover. An isolate per operation, which does not release until the operation's queue drains and can hold several at once. And a closure that captures a context, which keeps a whole widget subtree alive because a button's callback closes over the enclosing state object — the mechanism behind "the memory grows every time I visit this screen" and the reason the disposal discipline is about cancellation as much as about memory. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Make disposal complete by construction — every controller created in a state is disposed in dispose, every subscription cancelled, every listener removed — and the way to enforce it is a lint rule and a review convention rather than memory, because memory does not tell you. And measure memory while performing the operation that grows it, because a leak is a function of how many times you do something, and a single run shows nothing; the discipline is to repeat the operation fifty times and watch whether the number climbs, which distinguishes a leak from a cache that is simply working.

    actually: 'WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS IS THAT the APPLICATION HOLDS SOMETHING PROPORTIONAL TO USAGE - A LIST of EVERYTHING the USER HAS EVER LOADED, AN IMAGE CACHE THAT NEVER EVICTS, A LOG BUFFER',
    consequence: 'and THAT GROWS UNTIL the SYSTEM KILLS the APPLICATION' },
  { s: 'the LEAK PROBLEM', detail: 'MEMORY IS HELD BY THINGS THAT SHOULD HAVE BEEN RELEASED',

A leak and unbounded growth look identical from the outside - the app is killed after an hour - but they have different fixes. A leak is a listener, a controller, a timer or an object URL that was never released. Growth is a cache with no bound. The heap snapshot panel showing the paths to the garbage collection roots tells you which one you have.

// THE TWO KINDS
// 1. A LEAK: memory that should be freed and is not. The
//    cause is almost always a listener, a controller, a timer
//    or an object URL that was never released.
// 2. GROWTH: a cache with no bound. Not a leak, but it grows
//    until the OS kills the app.

// THE LEAKS, and all four are the same mistake
// 1. a listener with no handle
App.addListener('backButton', handler);           // LEAKS
final handle = await App.addListener(...);
onDispose(() => handle.remove());                // does not leak

// 2. a controller with no dispose
final _controller = TextEditingController();      // LEAKS
final _controller = TextEditingController();
@override void dispose() { _controller.dispose(); super.dispose(); }

// 3. a timer
Timer.periodic(const Duration(seconds: 1), tick);  // LEAKS
final _timer = Timer.periodic(...);
@override void dispose() { _timer.cancel(); super.dispose(); }

// 4. an object URL
final url = URL.createObjectURL(file);             // LEAKS
@override void dispose() { URL.revokeObjectURL(url); super.dispose(); }

// 5. a StreamSubscription from a native stream
final _sub = battery.stream.listen(...);           // LEAKS
onDispose(() => _sub.cancel());

// 6. a closure capturing `this` inside an animation
controller.addListener(() => setState(() => _v = controller.value));
// the listener holds the state, the controller outlives the state
controller.removeListener(...);
// FINDING A LEAK, in practice
// 1. use the app for 10 minutes, doing normal things
// 2. DevTools -> Memory
// 3. take a snapshot
// 4. do the thing that leaks, five times
// 5. take another snapshot, and click the heap snapshot
// 6. filter by "Detached" or "Retained Size"
// 7. a RISING count means something is retained
// 8. select a retained object, and the "Paths to GC Roots"
//    panel shows WHO holds it. That is the answer.

// THE GROWTH PATTERNS
// an unbounded cache
final _cache = <String, Uint8List>{};          // GROWS
final _cache = <String, Uint8List>LruCache(50);

// a list that only ever appends
_items.add(item);                                   // GROWS
_items = [..._items, item];   // the caller must bound it
_items = [..._items.take(500), item];

// a growing static set
static final _seen = <String>{};                // GROWS
// and static fields are never collected: a permanent leak

// THE CRASH SIGNATURE
// "FATAL EXCEPTION: ... OutOfMemoryError" on a low-end
// device after 20 minutes, but never on yours
// that is a growth problem, not a leak, and it is a memory
// size problem: your device has 3GB and the low-end one has
// 2GB, and something scales with usage

16.8 Measuring in production

// THE FRAME MONITOR, in an app you ship
class FrameMonitor {
  static const _slowFrameThreshold = Duration(milliseconds: 20);

  static void start() {
    SchedulerBinding.instance.addTimingsCallback((frameData) {
      for (final frame in frameData.frames) {
        final total = frame.buildDuration + frame.rasterDuration;
        if (total > _slowFrameThreshold) {
          // a SAMPLE, not every frame: this is a hot path
          _report(frame, total);
        }
      }
    });
  }

  static final _buffer = <Map<String, dynamic>>[];

  static void _report(FrameTiming frame, Duration total) {
    _buffer.add({
      'total_ms': total.inMicroseconds / 1000,
      'build_ms': frame.buildDuration.inMicroseconds / 1000,
      'raster_ms': frame.rasterDuration.inMicroseconds / 1000,
      'vsync_overhead': frame.vsyncOverhead.inMicroseconds / 1000,
    });

    if (_buffer.length >= 60) {
      unawaited(_flush());
    }
  }

  static Future<void> _flush() async {
    final batch = List.of(_buffer);
    _buffer.clear();
    try {
      await http.post('${ApiBase}/metrics/frames', body: jsonEncode(batch));
    } catch (_) {
      // never let telemetry break the app
    }
  }
}

// THE STARTUP MARK
final _startupStopwatch = Stopwatch()..start();

void main() {
  runApp(const MyApp());
  WidgetsBinding.instance.addPostFrameCallback((_) {
    _startupStopwatch.stop();
    track('startup_ms', {'value': _startupStopwatch.elapsedMicroseconds / 1000});
  });
}

// THE APP SIZE, which users notice
// flutter build appbundle --release
// then check the download size, not the AAB size: Play generates
// a per-device APK, and that is what the user downloads
// analyze: dart analyze --fatal-infos reports the tree-shaken size
// the sizes that matter:
//   download (the AAB, per device)   the store listing number
//   install (on disk)               the storage number
//   runtime RAM                     the crash number
// THE METRICS WORTH TRACKING
// 1. cold start to first frame, by device model
// 2. the percentage of frames that miss 16.7ms, per screen
// 3. the download and install size
// 4. the crash-free rate, by device model
// 5. the ANR rate on Android: the app did not respond for 5s
// 6. memory high-water-mark, by device model
//
// THE ONE THAT PREDICTS THE RATING
// the crash-free rate. a janky app gets a bad review. an app
// that crashes on 2% of sessions gets a bad review and no
// one telling you why.

What to measure in production, and what a number means

Everything in this chapter so far has been measured on a developer's machine against a known input, and there is a category of problem that only exists in production: the slow device, the real network, the session that lasted forty minutes, the operating system version nobody tested. The only way to find those is to measure in production, and the difficulty is that a production number has no context unless you know what it should be. Measure frame times as a distribution, not as an average. An average frame time hides everything interesting: a hundred frames at eight milliseconds and one at four hundred milliseconds average to twelve, which looks fine and contains the frame the user felt. What matters is the proportion of frames over budget, and the proportion of distinct interactions with at least one late frame — the second is the number that correlates with complaints, because a user remembers an interaction that stuttered rather than a frame they did not notice. Measure with the application's own instrumentation, not the framework's, because the framework's timeline exists only in a development build; the production mechanism is to record frame timings from a global callback and aggregate them. Then the three things to instrument, and each has a specific purpose. Frame timings, with the slow-frame ratio and the worst frame, per interaction if possible. Startup time, cold, per launch, because the distribution across launches is more informative than the median. And Crash-free sessions, which is the only number that is universally understood and which every release should move. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Sampling. You cannot record every frame in production — the overhead and the data volume make it impossible — so you sample, and a sampled slow-frame ratio is a biased estimate if the sampling is periodic, because slow frames cluster in the interactions you happen to sample. Averaging. As above; the mean is not the number and reporting it is how a real problem stays invisible. And measuring only on fast devices, because the developer population is not the user population and the population that does not update the application is precisely the population with the slow devices. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Pair every performance number with a version and a device class, so that a change in the number can be attributed to a release rather than to the season, and so that a regression introduced in one release is findable. And make the slow-frame budget a release gate rather than a dashboard, because a number nobody blocks on is a number that is allowed to regress indefinitely, and the gate is what makes the instrumentation a mechanism rather than a curiosity.

/* Why production. */
const WHY_PRODUCTION = [
  'the SLOW DEVICE', 'the REAL NETWORK', 'the SESSION THAT LASTED FORTY MINUTES', 'the OPERATING-SYSTEM VERSION NOBODY TESTED',
];
const ONLY_THERE = 'AND THE ONLY WAY TO FIND THOSE IS to MEASURE IN PRODUCTION';
const DIFFICULTY = 'the DIFFICULTY IS THAT A PRODUCTION NUMBER HAS NO CONTEXT UNLESS YOU KNOW WHAT IT SHOULD BE';

};

/* Three things to instrument. */
const INSTRUMENT = [

/* Three things that go wrong. */

  { p: 'MAKE the SLOW-FRAME BUDGET A RELEASE GATE rather than A DASHBOARD',

Exercises 17

  1. Profile a scrollable list on a low-end physical device in profile mode. Record the frame chart and identify whether the UI or raster thread is the problem.
  2. Add a build counter to a row widget, scroll a 1000-row list, and confirm the count stays flat as the scroll position changes.
  3. Set itemExtent on a list that did not have it, and measure the build count before and after.
  4. Replace an IntrinsicWidth with a TextPainter measurement and compare the layout time.
  5. Add cacheWidth to a list of large images and measure the memory with debugDumpImageCache before and after.
  6. Use the heap snapshot "Paths to GC Roots" to find a leak in a screen, fix it, and re-measure after five cycles.
  7. Move the initialisation out of main() into a post-frame callback and measure the cold start before and after.
  8. Add a frame monitor that reports the slow-frame ratio to your own API, and check the numbers from a real device.

17 · Desktop, Web and Adaptive Layout

17.1 Running on every platform17.2 Desktop specifics17.3 The web, and its constraints17.4 CanvasKit, HTML and the trade-offs17.5 PWA and installability17.6 SEO for a Flutter web app17.7 Adaptive and responsive patterns17.8 Input across platforms

One Flutter codebase, six targets, and the platform differences that are not about layout.

17.1 Running on every platform

// the commands
flutter devices                        what you can run on
flutter config --enable-web
flutter config --enable-desktop
flutter config --enable-linux-desktop
flutter config --enable-macos-desktop
flutter config --enable-windows-desktop

flutter run -d chrome              web, in Chrome
flutter run -d web-server          web, in any browser
flutter run -d macos               desktop
flutter run -d windows
flutter run -d linux

flutter build web
flutter build macos --release
flutter build windows --release
flutter build linux --release

// THE PLATFORM CHECK, for the code that must differ
import 'dart:io' show Platform;
import 'package:flutter/foundation.dart' show kIsWeb;

bool get isDesktop =>
    !kIsWeb && (Platform.isMacOS || Platform.isWindows || Platform.isLinux);

bool get isMobile =>
    !kIsWeb && (Platform.isAndroid || Platform.isIOS);

TargetPlatform get platform {
  if (kIsWeb) return TargetPlatform.android;   // the browser default
  return defaultTargetPlatform;
}

// AND the check that does NOT work on the web
// Platform.isAndroid THROWS on the web: dart:io is not there
// use kIsWeb first, always

What is portable, what is not, and the boundary that catches people

Flutter's promise is one codebase and several platforms, and the honest version of that promise is: one codebase with a set of platform-specific pieces, and the pieces are not optional. The Dart code is portable unless it imports something that is not. dart:io is the boundary that catches everybody: it is the standard library for files, sockets, processes and platform paths, and it does not exist on the web. So a single unguarded File or HttpClient anywhere in an application shared with the web will fail to compile for the web target, which is a build error rather than a runtime one — which is good, and the reason people are surprised by it is that they expected a runtime failure. The mechanism for avoiding it is a platform interface with two implementations — an abstract class with the operations you need, a real implementation for the platforms that have the facility, and an implementation for the platform that does not — and the persistence chapter's repository pattern is exactly this shape. Then the four things that differ, and each has a specific consequence. Input. A phone has a touchscreen and no cursor, no hover and no right-click; a desktop has all four. A control designed for touch has no hover state and no keyboard shortcut, and one designed for a mouse has a target that is too small to hit with a finger. Window size is known and fixed on desktop, so the responsive chapter's breakpoints apply to a resizable window rather than to a device, and the layout must survive being dragged narrower than the narrowest intended width. The text scale is chosen by the user on a phone and by the operating system on a desktop, and the desktop's scaling can be fractional, which means text that is fine at one scale can be clipped at the next. And the platform conventions are different, which is the platform chapter's material and applies with more force on desktop where the conventions are what a person uses for eight hours a day. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Guarding with a runtime check where a compile-time one exists. The right question at a platform boundary is "does this platform have this facility", not "which platform am I on", because a facility is not the same as a platform — a web browser has local storage and a desktop has multiple windows, and neither is implied by the platform name. Using a screen size as a proxy for a platform. A tablet and a desktop window can be the same size and have completely different expectations, and a phone application that checks the width to decide whether it is on desktop will behave differently on a small desktop window than on a large tablet. And assuming the absence of a facility is a bug. A hover affordance on a platform with no hover is correct as a no-op, and treating it as an error produces a warning on every touch interaction. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Keep every platform difference behind an interface, so that the number of places that know which platform they are on is countable and small — and that count is the real measure of how portable an application is. And test the awkward case, not the happy one,: a desktop window dragged to its narrowest, a phone with the largest text scale, a desktop with fractional scaling, a browser at an unusual size, because those are the configurations nobody develops in and all of them are configurations users are in.

/* The promise and its honest version. */
