17.2 Desktop specifics

// WHAT A DESKTOP APP NEEDS THAT A MOBILE ONE DOES NOT

// 1. A REAL WINDOW: resizable, and the size is not a device
final window = WindowListener.instance;

class WindowService with WindowListener {
  Size get size => view.size;
  double get scale => view.devicePixelRatio;

  void init() {
    WindowListener.instance.addListener(this);
  }

  @override
  void onWindowResize() {
    // the layout must handle every width, including 400px
    ref.read(layoutProvider.notifier).update(size);
  }

  @override
  void onWindowClose() {
    // SAVE BEFORE CLOSING: the user expects their work
    unawaited(saveAll());
    _confirmExit();
  }

  void _confirmExit() {
    dialogService.showConfirm(
      title: 'Quit?',
      message: 'You have unsaved changes.',
      actions: [Text('Save and quit'), Text('Discard'), Text('Cancel')],
    );
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    WindowListener.instance.removeListener(this);
    super.dispose();
  }
}

// 2. A MENU BAR: on macOS, an app with no menus feels broken
MenuBar(
  menus: [
    MacTextMenuBar(),
    MenuBarItem(
      label: 'File',
      children: [
        MacTextMenuItem(
          label: 'New Entry',
          shortcut: MacMetaKey + KeyCode.keyN,
          onSelected: _newEntry,
        ),
        MacTextMenuItem(
          label: 'Open…',
          shortcut: MacMetaKey + KeyCode.keyO,
          onSelected: _openFile,
        ),
        MacTextMenuItemGroup(
          label: 'Recent',
          children: [for (final f in _recent) MacTextMenuItem(label: f.name)],
        ),
        MacTextMenuItem(label: 'Save', shortcut: MacMetaKey + KeyCode.keyS, onSelected: _save),
      ],
    ),
    MenuBarItem(label: 'Edit', children: [MacTextMenuBarEdit()]),
    MenuBarItem(label: 'Window', children: [MacTextMenuBarWindow()]),
  ],
)

// 3. SHORTCUTS: Cmd or Ctrl
Actions(
  actions: <Type, Action<Intent>>{
    NewEntryIntent: CallbackAction(onInvoke: (_) => _newEntry()),
  },
  child: Shortcuts(
    shortcuts: <ShortcutActivator, Intent>{
      // the SINGLE_INSTANCE is what maps Cmd on macOS, Ctrl elsewhere
      const SingleActivator(LogicalKeyboardKey.keyN, meta: true): const NewEntryIntent(),
      const SingleActivator(LogicalKeyboardKey.keyN, control: true): const NewEntryIntent(),
      const SingleActivator(LogicalKeyboardKey.keyS, meta: true): const SaveIntent(),
      const SingleActivator(LogicalKeyboardKey.keyF, meta: true): const SearchIntent(),
    },
    child: Focus(autofocus: true, child: child),
  ),
)

// 4. HOVER and FOCUS, which mobile has
MouseRegion(
  onEnter: (_) => setState(() => _hovered = true),
  onExit: (_) => setState(() => _hovered = false),
  cursor: SystemMouseCursors.click,
  child: AnimatedContainer(
    color: _hovered ? theme.colorScheme.surfaceContainerHigh : null,
    child: child,
  ),
);

// 5. SCROLL with a trackpad: the scroll wheel is a wheel, and a
//    trackpad gives fine deltas
Scrollbar(
  controller: _controller,
  thumbVisibility: true,       // a desktop convention
  child: ListView.builder(...),
);

// 6. RIGHT-CLICK
Listener(
  onPointerDown: (event) {
    if (event.kind == PointerDeviceKind.mouse && event.buttons == kSecondaryMouseButton) {
      _showContextMenu(event.position);
    }
  },
  child: child,
);

// 7. TEXT SELECTION, and a keyboard tab order
SelectionArea(
  child: Column(children: [TextField(), TextField()]),
)

// 8. MULTIPLE WINDOWS
//    on macOS: WindowManager from a package
//    on Windows: a separate window via a plugin
//    and restoration, so the windows come back

Windowing, menus, and the conventions that are not optional

Desktop is not a phone with a bigger screen; it is a different environment with different expectations, and most of the work is in honouring conventions the platform already established rather than in adapting a mobile design. The window is a window. A desktop application opens in a window that can be resized, minimised, maximised, and restored, and — on the platforms that support it — several of them at once. That means a layout that assumes a fixed size, and a state model that assumes one screen, and a menu model that assumes one window's worth of actions. Menus and keyboard shortcuts are the desktop convention for the actions a phone puts in an overflow menu. A desktop user expects a menu bar or a context menu, and expects every action to have a shortcut; an application with neither is usable but feels like a web page. Then the four things that must be done, and each has a specific mechanism. Handle multiple windows or explicitly refuse them. The framework supports multiple windows on the desktop platforms, and an application that does not implement them will open the same state in two windows if the user duplicates it — which is either a feature nobody intended or a bug, depending on whether the state is per-window. Provide a menu with the actions. A menu is not a list of buttons; it is a place where actions are grouped by what they affect, and the convention includes separators, disabled items that show what is unavailable rather than hiding it, and a preferences item that is always in the same place. Provide keyboard shortcuts for the actions that matter, including the standard ones — quit, new, close, save, find, copy, paste — because the absence of the standard ones is the most noticeable gap on the platform. And support the standard lifecycle, meaning window state restoration so that reopening the application restores the windows that were open, because a desktop user closes the application expecting to come back to it. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. A dialog that is sized for a phone. A modal that is sized relative to the screen is fine on a phone and absurd on a large desktop window — where the correct behaviour is a fixed or content-sized dialog positioned near the parent window rather than centred on the screen. Text that is unreadably small because the design assumed a phone, which is the scaling failure in a different direction: a design that scales its whole interface up for a large desktop window produces buttons and text that are enormous, because a desktop user is not further from the screen. And a pointer-only interface, which is the input chapter's material and which on desktop means the application cannot be used at all without a mouse — because a desktop user with a keyboard and a trackpad is a first-class case, not an edge case. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Read the platform's own conventions before designing, for the platform you are adding, because the conventions are documented and the cost of reading them is an hour against the cost of guessing wrongly being a redesign. And test at the smallest window size you claim to support, on every platform, because a desktop layout that has only been seen maximised is a layout that has not been designed.

17.3 The web, and its constraints

The browser's constraints, and why the web is the hardest target

Flutter web compiles the same Dart to JavaScript and renders into the browser's canvas, which means it inherits every constraint the browser imposes and none of the integrations a native target has. There is no platform channel. The browser has no equivalent of the host-side mechanism the previous chapters described, so plugins on the web are implemented in JavaScript and called through a different channel; a plugin with only native implementations has no web support at all, and a plugin whose web implementation is a thin wrapper over a browser API has a different set of capabilities and a different set of failure modes. There is no filesystem in the same sense. There is local storage, which is a small key-value store with a quota, and there is the browser's own cache, and there is a file API that requires a user gesture; an application that opens a database on a phone has no direct equivalent, and the choices are a web-specific storage library or a server. There is no process model, so an isolate is a web worker and a background task is not available at all. And the initial payload is large, because the rendering engine is compiled or downloaded and the application's own code is on top of it, which is the web section's performance subject and is the reason the SEO and first-paint material exists. Then the four things that catch people, and each is a specific mechanism. A plugin that compiles for web but does not work there, which happens because the Dart side is platform-agnostic and the native side is simply absent, so the call fails at run time with a missing-plugin error rather than at build time. Storage that silently fails when the quota is exceeded, which is a quota of a few megabytes and an error the browser reports as an exception the application may not be handling; this is why the persistence chapter's database answer becomes a server answer on the web. A layout that assumes a device pixel ratio of one — or, more often, one that assumes a ratio it does not know, since the browser's ratio depends on the display and the zoom and changes as the user zooms. And an application that was tested only in a desktop browser, which is where a percentage-based layout, a hover affordance and a fixed minimum width all pass and a phone browser all fail. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Treat the web as its own target with its own test matrix, because a feature that works in a desktop browser and fails on a phone browser is the common case and it is invisible in desktop testing. And decide early whether the web is a full target or a companion, because the two require different architectures: a full target needs web storage, web plugins, a responsive layout and a first-paint budget, and a companion — a link into the same product for sharing a view — needs almost none of them and is much cheaper to build.

/* The compilation and the inheritance. */
const HOW = 'COMPILES the SAME DART to JAVASCRIPT and RENDERS INTO the BROWSERS CANVAS';
const INHERITS = 'WHICH MEANS IT INHERITS EVERY CONSTRAINT the BROWSER IMPOSES and NONE of the INTEGRATIONS A NATIVE TARGET HAS';

/* Four constraints. */
const CONSTRAINTS = [
  { c: 'there is NO PLATFORM CHANNEL',
    detail: 'the BROWSER HAS NO EQUIVALENT of the HOST-SIDE MECHANISM the PREVIOUS CHAPTERS DESCRIBED',
    consequence: 'SO PLUGINS ON the WEB ARE IMPLEMENTED IN JAVASCRIPT and CALLED THROUGH A DIFFERENT CHANNEL',
    detail2: 'A PLUGIN with ONLY NATIVE IMPLEMENTATIONS HAS NO WEB SUPPORT AT ALL',
    and: 'A PLUGINS WEB IMPLEMENTATION IS A THIN WRAPPER OVER A BROWSER API HAS A DIFFERENT SET of CAPABILITIES and A DIFFERENT SET of FAILURE MODES' },
  { c: 'there is NO FILESYSTEM IN the SAME SENSE',

The server configuration for a Flutter web app is not optional. Without the SPA fallback a reload on any route but / returns a 404, and without the correct MIME types the WebAssembly module silently fails to load. Both are one block of nginx configuration and both fail in ways that look like an application bug.

// WHAT IS DIFFERENT ON THE WEB
//
// 1. THE INITIAL DOWNLOAD, and it is the whole problem
//    a Flutter web app is 1.5-3MB with CanvasKit
//    a website visitor will not wait
//
// 2. SEO: the page is a canvas, so a crawler sees nothing
//
// 3. NO dart:io: no files, no sockets, no processes
//    the equivalents are IndexedDB, WebSocket, and nothing
//
// 4. THE URL BAR: a route change is a browser navigation, and
//    a reload must still work
//
// 5. THE BACK BUTTON: it is the browser's
//
// 6. NO NOTIFICATIONS WITHOUT PERMISSION, and it is a web
//    permission, not a store one
//
// 7. PERFORMANCE: the main thread is shared with the browser,
//    and a heavy frame blocks scrolling entirely

// THE BUILD
flutter build web --release
// build/web/
//   index.html
//   main.dart.js        (or the .wasm + .mjs pair)
//   flutter.js
//   canvaskit/
//   assets/
//   manifest.json
//   favicon.png

// THE SERVER CONFIGURATION, which is not optional
// 1. SPA ROUTING: every path must serve index.html, or a reload
//    on /entries/123 gives a 404
// nginx
location / {
  try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
}

// 2. THE MIME TYPES, or the modules fail to load
types {
  application/wasm  wasm;
  application/javascript  js  mjs;
}

// 3. GZIP OR BROTLI
gzip on;
gzip_types application/javascript application/wasm text/html application/json image/svg+xml;
brotli on;
brotli_types application/wasm application/javascript text/html;

// 4. CACHE HEADERS, and this is the tricky part
//    index.html: NO caching, or a deploy never reaches a user
location = /index.html {
  add_header Cache-Control "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate";
}
//    the hashed assets: cache forever
location /assets/ {
  add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable";
}
//    main.dart.js: NO caching, it is not hashed
location = /main.dart.js {
  add_header Cache-Control "no-cache";
}
// ROUTING ON THE WEB, and the one real difference
// a browser navigation is a page load, so the router must
// restore from the URL
GoRouter(
  initialLocation: '/',
  routes: [...],
)

// and hash-based routing, which avoids the server config
// entirely: URLs become /#/entries/123
MaterialApp.router(
  routerConfig: router,
  // or, for a server you cannot configure:
  backButtonDispatcher: RootBackButtonDispatcher(),
);
// the modern answer: use path routing and configure the server

// THE DEEP LINK, which works if the path is served
// https://yourdomain.com/entries/123  ->  the app opens there

// THE FILE SIZE PROBLEM, and the fix
flutter build web --release --wasm              // WebAssembly: smaller
flutter build web --release --web-renderer html   // no CanvasKit: the
                                                  // smallest download,
//                                                  // the worst
                                                  // rendering
// and the split: load a splash in HTML, then the app
// index.html
<div id="loading" style="...">Loading…</div>
<script>
  // remove the splash once the app is up
  window.addEventListener('flutter-first-frame', () => {
    document.getElementById('loading')?.remove();
  });
</script>

17.4 CanvasKit, HTML and the trade-offs

// THREE RENDERERS, and the choice is a download-size against
// a rendering-quality trade-off
//
// CANVASKIT     Skia compiled to WebAssembly. Renders exactly
//               like the mobile and desktop apps. The default
//               since Flutter 3.x.
//   download:  1.5MB (CanvasKit) + the app
//   quality:   perfect
//   cost:      a WebAssembly download and a JIT-like warmup
//
// HTML          Maps DOM elements. No WebAssembly.
//   download:  the app only, ~600KB
//   quality:   WORSE: no blurs, no shaders, different text
//               rendering, and it is a different look from mobile
//   cost:      a much smaller download
//
// SKWASM        the newest: Skia in Wasm, faster than CanvasKit
//   download:  comparable, but it renders faster
//
// HOW TO CHOOSE
//   a marketing site, a landing page:      HTML
//   a full app, where the look must match:  CanvasKit
//   a slow network audience:                HTML, or a hybrid
//
// flutter build web --web-renderer canvaskit   (the default)
// flutter build web --web-renderer html
// flutter build web --wasm                      (skwasm)

// RUNTIME SWITCHING, for an experiment
// main.dart
import 'package:flutter/renderer.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  final useHtml = Uri.base.queryParameters['renderer'] == 'html';
  if (useHtml) {
    await useHtmlRenderer();
  }
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

Two renderers, and what choosing one costs

Flutter web draws with a renderer, and the two renderers trade initial load size against rendering fidelity in a way that has no free choice. The HTML renderer draws the interface with the browser's own layout and painting, so text is the browser's text, images are the browser's images and the accessibility tree is the browser's — which means it is small, it starts fast, and screen readers work without any work from you. CanvasKit draws the whole interface into a canvas with the same renderer the native targets use, so pixels are identical to the phone, every effect is available, and text is the framework's rather than the browser's. The costs are that the renderer must be downloaded before anything can be drawn, and that nothing the framework draws is in the document, so the browser's accessibility tree contains a single canvas. Then the four consequences of choosing, and each is a mechanism. First paint is much later with CanvasKit, because a megabyte or more of renderer must arrive before the first frame — and on a slow connection that is a blank page, which is the single thing a web application must not do. Accessibility requires work with CanvasKit, because the semantics tree must be rendered into the document separately from the pixels, and the frameworks that do it produce a DOM element alongside the canvas — so the accessibility story is the same but the work is not free. Text selection and copy depend on the browser's own handling, and a canvas has none, so selecting text in an input requires the input to be a real DOM element rather than drawn, which is a constraint on what you can build. And the download is cached, which is what makes the second visit fast and means the first-visit cost is the number that matters and the one that is hardest to improve. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Choosing CanvasKit and then adding a loading state that is itself delayed by the same download, so the loading indicator cannot use the renderer it is waiting for. Assuming the canvas is invisible to a search engine, which is true of the content and false of the surrounding document — which is the SEO section's argument that the application must render meaningful content server-side or the page is a blank canvas to a crawler. And measuring performance in one and shipping the other, which is the mode chapter's argument in a new place: the two renderers have completely different performance characteristics and a measurement of one says nothing about the other. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Decide the renderer per deployment, not per project, because it is a build flag and a server choice, and the right answer differs between an internal application on a fast network and a public marketing page. And measure the first visit on a slow connection, not the average connection, because the first visit is where the renderer is downloaded and the average connection is not the connection of the user who will not come back.

/* The trade. */
const TRADE = 'THE TWO RENDERERS TRADE INITIAL LOAD SIZE against RENDERING FIDELITY IN A WAY THAT HAS NO FREE CHOICE';
const HTML = {
  draws: 'with the BROWSERS OWN LAYOUT and PAINTING',
  benefits: ['TEXT IS the BROWSERS TEXT', 'IMAGES ARE the BROWSERS IMAGES',
    'and the ACCESSIBILITY TREE IS the BROWSERS'],
  consequence: 'WHICH MEANS IT IS SMALL, IT STARTS FAST, and SCREEN READERS WORK WITHOUT ANY WORK FROM YOU',
};

17.5 PWA and installability

What installability actually requires

An installable progressive web application needs four things and all four are declarations rather than code, which is why they are usually missed: a manifest naming the application with its icons and its display mode, a service worker that can serve the application when the network is unavailable, an icon set at the sizes the platform expects, and the served-over-secure-origin requirement without which none of it works outside localhost. The display mode is the one that has a design consequence rather than a configuration one: "standalone" removes the browser's own chrome, so the application draws edge to edge and must handle the safe area itself, which is the same safe-area material as the platform chapter and is the reason an application installed from a browser behaves differently from one installed from a store unless it accounts for it. Then the four things that decide whether the service worker helps or hurts, and each is a mechanism. The first visit is not faster because of the service worker — nothing is cached until something has been fetched, so a first visit is a plain page load and the perceived slowness is unchanged. A cache-first strategy on the application shell is wrong for an application that ships updates, because the shell is what changed and a cached shell means users run an old version indefinitely until the cache is invalidated; the correct strategy is a network-first for the shell and a cache-first for immutable assets. An over-eager cache grows without bound, and a cache that has grown to a hundred megabytes is a cache that will be evicted at the worst moment. And the service worker can serve a stale application that talks to a changed API, which produces errors that only some users see because only some users have the stale cache. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Assuming the service worker makes the application offline-capable, which is only true if every request the application makes has a cache entry — and a request to an API has none, so the application launches offline and then fails on its first data fetch, which is worse than a clear offline message. Not versioning the cache, so an update cannot evict the old entries and every deploy leaves a megabyte of dead cache behind. And not having an update path, which is the point: a progressive web application that never asks the user to reload is an application that can never be updated for the users who need it. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Treat the service worker as a cache with an eviction policy, not as an offline mode, and name the version so that a deploy can evict the previous one — the mechanism is a cache name that changes with the build. And test the installed application, not only the browser tab, because the installed application has no browser chrome, may have a different display mode, has its own storage partition in some browsers, and is what the user will keep — so an application tested only in a browser tab is an application tested in the configuration most people will not use.

/* Four requirements, all declarations. */
const REQUIREMENTS = [
  'a MANIFEST NAMING the APPLICATION with ITS ICONS and ITS DISPLAY MODE',
  'a SERVICE WORKER THAT CAN SERVE the APPLICATION WHEN the NETWORK IS UNAVAILABLE',
  'an ICON SET AT the SIZES the PLATFORM EXPECTS',
  'and the SERVED-OVER-SECURE-ORIGIN REQUIREMENT WITHOUT WHICH NONE of IT WORKS OUTSIDE LOCALHOST',
};
const WHY_MISSED = 'WHICH IS WHY THEY ARE USUALLY MISSED';
const DISPLAY_MODE = {

Never let a service worker cache anything the user generated. A deleted note that reappears on the second load is the single most damaging PWA bug, and it happens because the cache was populated before the record was deleted and nothing ever told it to stop serving that entry.

// A PWA, so a user can install it and it works offline
// pubspec.yaml
//   flutter_launcher_icons: ^0.13.1
//   pwa_manifest: ^2.0.0

// web/manifest.json  (or generated)
{
  "name": "Field Notes",
  "short_name": "Notes",
  "start_url": "/",
  "display": "standalone",
  "background_color": "#0b1020",
  "theme_color": "#0b1020",
  "description": "Your notes, everywhere",
  "orientation": "portrait",
  "icons": [
    { "src": "icons/Icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "icons/Icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "icons/Icon-maskable-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png", "purpose": "maskable" }
  ]
}

// web/index.html: the theme colour, so the address bar matches
<meta name="theme-color" content="#0b1020">
<link rel="manifest" href="manifest.json">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="icons/Icon-192.png">
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-capable" content="yes">
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style" content="black-translucent">

// A SERVICE WORKER, for offline
// pubspec.yaml
//   pwa_service_worker: ^3.2.0
//
// THE CACHE STRATEGY
//   the app shell: cache-first (it is hashed, so it is immutable)
//   the API: network-first, with a cache fallback
//   images: stale-while-revalidate
//   NOTHING user-generated: never cache it, or a deleted note
//     comes back on a second load

// the install prompt
final deferredPrompt = Completer<BeforeInstallPromptEvent>();

void onBeforeInstallPrompt(BeforeInstallPromptEvent event) {
  deferredPrompt.complete(event);
}

// in the UI: an install button
Future<void> promptInstall() async {
  final event = await deferredPrompt.future;
  await event.prompt();
}

// and detect an installed app
final isStandalone = js_util
    .getProperty<bool>(window.navigator, 'standalone')
    .toDart;

17.6 SEO for a Flutter web app

Why a canvas is invisible, and what to do about it

A search engine crawler does not run your application. It fetches the HTML, reads the metadata, follows links, and indexes what it finds — and a Flutter web page is a document containing a script tag and a canvas, so to a crawler it is an empty page with a title. Nothing the framework draws is in the document, because the drawing happens at run time in a canvas element the crawler does not execute; this is true of the HTML renderer and the CanvasKit renderer equally, and it is the single structural reason a Flutter web application has an SEO problem. Then the four things that can be done, and they are in decreasing order of effectiveness. Server-render the content, or at least the first screen, so that the document contains meaningful text before any script runs; this is the only approach that works for content that must be indexed, and it means the content exists in a form that is not the application's widgets, which is a real cost and a real constraint on what you build. Render the application into the document's accessibility tree and read that as a proxy, which is what a crawler that executes scripts may do — this is uncertain, it is not a strategy, and it is the reason it is worth doing as a fallback rather than as a plan. Provide a separate server-rendered page for the indexable content and link to the application, which is the pragmatic answer for a marketing site that links into a product. And make sure the metadata is right — a title, a description, canonical, Open Graph — which costs nothing and is the baseline every other approach assumes. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Believing the metadata is enough, because a page with a perfect title and no content is indexed as a thin page and can be treated as low quality by every engine. Rendering the content only after the framework loads, which means the content is present for a crawler that executes scripts and absent for one that does not, and the ones that do not are the ones that matter for a fresh page. And duplicating the content in a way that disagrees, where the server-rendered version says one thing and the application says another, which is a worse outcome than neither. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Decide per page whether it needs to be indexable, because the answer is different for a product screen, a documentation page and a marketing page, and a product screen almost never needs to be — which means the constraint applies to a small number of pages and should be scoped to them rather than imposed everywhere. And keep the first paint independent of the framework's download, because a crawler and a user on a slow connection both wait for the same bytes and a page that is blank for two seconds is a page that is ranked and a page that is abandoned.

/* Why. */
const CRAWLER = 'A SEARCH ENGINE CRAWLER DOES NOT RUN YOUR APPLICATION';
const DOES = ['IT FETCHES the HTML', 'READS the METADATA', 'FOLLOWS LINKS', 'and INDEXES WHAT IT FINDS'];
const PAGE = 'and A FLUTTER WEB PAGE IS A DOCUMENT CONTAINING A SCRIPT TAG and A CANVAS';
const RESULT = 'SO TO A CRAWLER IT IS AN EMPTY PAGE with A TITLE';
const NOTHING_DRAWN = 'NOTHING the FRAMEWORK DRAWS IS IN the DOCUMENT';
const BECAUSE = 'BECAUSE the DRAWING HAPPENS AT RUN TIME IN A CANVAS ELEMENT the CRAWLER DOES NOT EXECUTE';
const EQUAL = 'THIS IS TRUE of the HTML RENDERER and the CANVASKIT RENDERER EQUALLY';
const STRUCTURAL = 'and IT IS the SINGLE STRUCTURAL REASON A FLUTTER WEB APPLICATION HAS AN SEO PROBLEM';

/* Four things that can be done. */
const OPTIONS = [
  { o: 'SERVER-RENDER the CONTENT, OR AT LEAST the FIRST SCREEN',
    how: 'SO THAT the DOCUMENT CONTAINS MEANINGFUL TEXT BEFORE ANY SCRIPT RUNS',
    onlyWorks: 'WHICH IS the ONLY APPROACH THAT WORKS for CONTENT THAT MUST BE INDEXED',
    cost: 'and IT MEANS the CONTENT EXISTS IN A FORM THAT IS NOT the APPLICATIONS WIDGETS, WHICH IS A REAL COST and A REAL CONSTRAINT ON WHAT YOU BUILD' },
  { o: 'RENDER the APPLICATION INTO THE DOCUMENTS ACCESSIBILITY TREE and READ THAT AS A PROXY',
    who: 'WHICH IS WHAT A CRAWLER THAT EXECUTES SCRIPTS MAY DO',
    verdict: ['THIS IS UNCERTAIN', 'IT IS NOT A STRATEGY', 'and IT IS the REASON IT IS WORTH DOING AS A FALLBACK rather than AS A PLAN'] },
  { o: 'PROVIDE A SEPARATE SERVER-RENDERED PAGE for the INDEXABLE CONTENT and LINK TO the APPLICATION',
    verdict: 'WHICH IS the PRAGMATIC ANSWER for A MARKETING SITE THAT LINKS INTO A PRODUCT' },
  { o: 'MAKE SURE the METADATA IS RIGHT',
    list: ['A TITLE', 'A DESCRIPTION', 'CANONICAL', 'OPEN GRAPH'],
    cost: 'WHICH COSTS NOTHING and IS the BASELINE EVERY OTHER APPROACH ASSUMES' },
];

/* Three things that go wrong. */
const GO_WRONG = [
  { f: 'BELIEVING the METADATA IS ENOUGH',
    why: 'BECAUSE A PAGE with A PERFECT TITLE and NO CONTENT IS INDEXED AS A THIN PAGE',
    consequence: 'and CAN BE TREATED AS LOW QUALITY BY EVERY ENGINE' },
  { f: 'RENDERING the CONTENT ONLY AFTER the FRAMEWORK LOADS',
    detail: 'WHICH MEANS the CONTENT IS PRESENT for A CRAWLER THAT EXECUTES SCRIPTS and ABSENT FOR ONE THAT DOES NOT',
    and: 'the ONES THAT DO NOT ARE the ONES THAT MATTER FOR A FRESH PAGE' },
  { f: 'DUPLICATING the CONTENT IN A WAY THAT DISAGREES',
    detail: 'WHERE the SERVER-RENDERED VERSION SAYS ONE THING and the APPLICATION SAYS ANOTHER',
    verdict: 'WHICH IS A WORSE OUTCOME than NEITHER' },
];

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'DECIDE PER PAGE WHETHER IT NEEDS TO BE INDEXABLE',
    differences: ['A PRODUCT SCREEN', 'A DOCUMENTATION PAGE', 'A MARKETING PAGE'],
    mostly: 'A PRODUCT SCREEN ALMOST NEVER NEEDS TO BE',
    consequence: 'WHICH MEANS the CONSTRAINT APPLIES TO A SMALL NUMBER of PAGES and SHOULD BE SCOPED TO THEM rather than IMPOSED EVERYWHERE' },
  { p: 'KEEP the FIRST PAINT INDEPENDENT of the FRAMEWORKS DOWNLOAD',
    why: 'BECAUSE A CRAWLER and A USER ON A SLOW CONNECTION BOTH WAIT FOR the SAME BYTES',
    consequence: 'and A PAGE THAT IS BLANK FOR TWO SECONDS IS A PAGE THAT IS RANKED and A PAGE THAT IS ABANDONED' },
];

A Flutter web page is a canvas, so a crawler sees a loading div and a script tag. If anything needs to be indexed - the marketing pages, the docs, anything with content - it has to be server-rendered HTML, with the app behind a login or at a separate route.

// THE HONEST ANSWER
// a Flutter web app is a canvas. a search engine crawler sees
// index.html, which contains a loading div and a script tag.
// it sees NO content.
//
// SO: a Flutter web app is a poor choice for anything that
// needs to be indexed. If SEO matters, the marketing pages and
// the content pages must be server-rendered HTML.

// THE PRACTICAL APPROACH: a hybrid
// 1. the marketing site, the docs, the blog: a static site
//    generator, in Astro or Next. Fully indexable.
// 2. the app: Flutter web, at /app, behind a login
// 3. the public content routes: prerendered HTML, with a link
//    into the app
//
// ANOTHER OPTION: prerender the shell
// index.html has real content in it, and the app replaces it
// on load. The crawler sees the content; the user gets the app.
<body>
  <div id="app">
    <!-- THE SEO CONTENT: what a crawler sees. It is replaced
         on load, and it is also what a user with JS disabled
         sees, which is a real case. -->
    <h1>Field Notes - your notes, everywhere</h1>
    <p>Capture, organise and sync your notes…</p>
    <noscript>
      <p>This app needs JavaScript. The content above is
         available in full in the <a href="/text">text version</a>.</p>
    </noscript>
  </div>
</body>
// THE OTHER WEB-ONLY ADJUSTMENTS

// 1. THE URL BAR, and the fragment
//    path routing needs server config; the hash does not
//    but the hash is uglier and breaks some analytics
//    RECOMMENDATION: path routing + server config

// 2. RIGHT-CLICK, which a mobile design often has no answer for
Listener(
  onPointerDown: (e) {
    if (e.kind == PointerDeviceKind.mouse && e.buttons == kSecondaryMouseButton) {
      _showContextMenu(e.position);
    }
  },
  child: child,
)

// 3. TEXT SELECTION: a canvas does not select text natively
SelectionArea(
  child: Text('long readable content'),
)

// 4. ACCESSIBILITY, which is a canvas too
//    the semantics tree exists, so a screen reader works, but
//    test it: the semantics tree is a DOM overlay
debugDumpSemanticsTree();

// 5. THE TAB ORDER, for a keyboard user
//    a canvas has no DOM order to follow

// 6. SCROLL: a Flutter web page does not scroll with the
//    browser, and the address bar does not hide
//    for a marketing site, this is a real problem
//    the fix: the content is not in Flutter

// 7. PRINTING: it does not work
//    a canvas cannot be printed

// 8. THE FIRST PAINT: the user sees a blank canvas for
//    1-2 seconds on a slow connection

17.7 Adaptive and responsive patterns

// THE THREE LEVELS OF ADAPTATION, and they are different jobs
//
// 1. RESPONSIVE: the layout responds to the available size
//    the same widget, arranged differently
//
// 2. ADAPTIVE: the LAYOUT responds to the size class
//    a navigation rail instead of a bottom bar
//
// 3. PLATFORM-NATIVE: the CONVENTIONS respond to the platform
//    a menu bar on macOS, a hamburger on Android

// THE WINDOW SIZE CLASSES
enum SizeClass { compact, medium, expanded }

extension SizeClassX on BuildContext {
  SizeClass get sizeClass {
    final width = MediaQuery.sizeOf(this).width;
    if (width < 600) return SizeClass.compact;
    if (width < 905) return SizeClass.medium;
    return SizeClass.expanded;
  }
}

// A SKELETON, one widget per size class, chosen with a switch
class HomeScreen extends StatelessWidget {
  const HomeScreen({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return switch (context.sizeClass) {
      SizeClass.compact => const HomeCompact(),
      SizeClass.medium => const HomeMedium(),
      SizeClass.expanded => const HomeExpanded(),
    };
  }
}

// LAYOUTBUILDER, for a decision that depends on a CONSTRAINT
// rather than the window
LayoutBuilder(
  builder: (context, constraints) {
    // the number of columns that FIT, not the window width
    final columns = (constraints.maxWidth / 200).floor().clamp(1, 6);
    return GridView.builder(
      gridDelegate: SliverGridDelegateWithFixedCrossAxisCount(crossAxisCount: columns),
      itemCount: items.length,
      itemBuilder: (context, i) => Card(child: Text(items[i].name)),
    );
  },
)

// A MASTER-DETAIL that works at every size
class MasterDetail extends StatelessWidget {
  const MasterDetail({
    required this.list,
    required this.detail,
    required this.selectedId,
    required this.onSelect,
    required this.breakpoint,
    super.key,
  });

  final Widget list;
  final Widget detail;
  final String? selectedId;
  final ValueChanged<String> onSelect;
  final double breakpoint;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return LayoutBuilder(builder: (context, constraints) {
      final wide = constraints.maxWidth >= breakpoint;

      if (wide) {
        return Row(children: [
          NavigationRail(
            extended: constraints.maxWidth >= 1100,
            selectedIndex: 0,
            onDestinationSelected: (_) {},
            labelType: NavigationRailLabelType.none,
            destinations: const [
              NavigationRailDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.inbox), label: Text('Inbox')),
              NavigationRailDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.archive), label: Text('Archive')),
              NavigationRailDestination(icon: Icon(Icons.settings), label: Text('Settings')),
            ],
          ),
          const VerticalDivider(width: 1),
          SizedBox(width: 320, child: list),
          const VerticalDivider(width: 1),
          Expanded(
            child: selectedId == null
                ? Center(
                    child: Text(
                      'Select an item',
                      style: Theme.of(context).textTheme.bodyLarge,
                    ),
                  )
                : detail,
          ),
        ]);
      }

      return selectedId == null
          ? list
          : Scaffold(
              appBar: AppBar(leading: const BackButton()),
              body: detail,
            );
    });
  }
}

// THE TEXT SCALE AND THE FONT, which change with the platform
final theme = Theme.of(context);
final textScale = MediaQuery.textScalerOf(context);

// and the system font, which is different on each platform
// never hard-code a font for a cross-platform app: the system
// font is right on each one

Fonts, cursors, and the things that are wrong in only one place

Running one interface on platforms whose conventions differ produces a category of defect that is neither a layout bug nor a logic bug: it looks correct everywhere except one place, and the place is determined by which platform's convention the implementation followed. Fonts are the clearest case. Each platform ships its own default family and its own metrics, so an interface designed with one platform's default will have different line breaks, different heights and different label widths on the others — and an interface that hard-codes a font to make one platform look right has made the other two look wrong. The correct answer is to use the platform's own font and to design for the metrics that result, testing the layout on all of them rather than fixing the difference. Cursors are the second. A desktop user expects a pointer over anything tappable and a text cursor over anything editable, and neither exists by default on a custom widget — so an interface that is correct on touch and has no pointer feedback on desktop reads as not interactive, which is the input chapter's argument. Selection is the third, because text selection is a browser or platform behaviour that a custom-painted text does not get. And hover is the fourth, because an affordance that appears only on hover is invisible on a platform that never hovers. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Fixing a one-platform difference in shared code, which changes every platform to accommodate the one with the problem; the fix belongs in a platform-specific branch or, better, in the design rather than in the code. Assuming a desktop-sized interface is a phone interface, which produces tiny text and tiny targets on a large screen because a phone's density assumption is a phone's density assumption; the desktop convention is a fixed physical size, not a scaled phone. And ignoring the platform's own text metrics when setting a fixed height, which works on the platform it was measured on and clips on the others — the same accessibility requirement as the typography section, arriving from a different direction. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Test one screen on all platforms every release, and pick a screen that has text, a fixed-size control and a gesture — a settings row is ideal — because the three together find the three defects above. And treat any platform-conditional code as a cost and keep the list short, because every conditional is a place the application behaves differently and the count is the number of places you have to reason about; a design that needed no conditionals on any platform is a design that understood the conventions rather than worked around them.

/* The category. */
const CATEGORY = 'Running ONE INTERFACE ON PLATFORMS WHOSE CONVENTIONS DIFFER PRODUCES A CATEGORY of DEFECT THAT IS NEITHER A LAYOUT BUG nor A LOGIC BUG';
const SHAPE = 'IT LOOKS CORRECT EVERYWHERE EXCEPT ONE PLACE, and the PLACE IS DETERMINED BY WHICH PLATFORMS CONVENTION the IMPLEMENTATION FOLLOWED';

/* Four cases. */
const CASES = [

    correct: ['USE the PLATFORMS OWN FONT', 'DESIGN FOR the METRICS THAT RESULT'],

    symptom: 'SO AN INTERFACE THAT IS CORRECT ON TOUCH and HAS NO POINTER FEEDBACK ON DESKTOP READS AS NOT INTERACTIVE',

17.8 Input across platforms

// THE INPUT DIFFERENCES
//
// 1. HOVER STATES: desktop only
MouseRegion(
  onHover: (event) => setState((_) {}),   // fires on a move
  onEnter: (_) => setState(() => _hovered = true),
  onExit: (_) => setState(() => _hovered = false),
  cursor: _hovered ? SystemMouseCursors.click : SystemMouseCursors.basic,
  child: AnimatedContainer(
    duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 120),
    color: _hovered ? theme.colorScheme.surfaceContainerHigh : Colors.transparent,
    child: widget.child,
  ),
)

// 2. KEYBOARD FOCUS, which must be visible
//    the default is fine; do not remove it with a custom style
//    without replacing it
Focus(
  onFocusChange: (hasFocus) => setState(() => _focused = hasFocus),
  child: AnimatedContainer(
    decoration: BoxDecoration(
      border: _focused
          ? Border.all(color: theme.colorScheme.primary, width: 2)
          : null,
    ),
    child: widget.child,
  ),
)

// 3. TEXT SELECTION, on desktop only
SelectionArea(child: Text(content))

// 4. SCROLL WHEEL vs TOUCH DRAG
Listener(
  onPointerSignal: (event) {
    if (event is PointerScrollEvent) {
      // a wheel event: handle it yourself if the widget is a
      // custom scroller
    }
  },
  child: child,
)

// 5. DRAG AND DROP, desktop only
Draggable<String>(
  data: item.id,
  feedback: Material(child: EntryCard(entry: item)),
  childWhenDragging: Opacity(opacity: 0.4, child: EntryCard(entry: item)),
  child: EntryCard(entry: item),
)

DragTarget<String>(
  onAcceptWithDetails: (details) => _move(details.data),
  builder: (context, candidate, rejected) {
    return Container(
      color: candidate.isNotEmpty ? theme.colorScheme.primaryContainer : null,
      child: const DropTarget(),
    );
  },
)

// 6. RIGHT-CLICK
GestureDetector(
  onSecondaryTapUp: (details) => _showContextMenu(details.globalPosition),
  child: child,
)

// 7. THE SHORTCUT MODIFIER, which is platform-correct automatically
//    SingleActivator with meta: true is Cmd on macOS, Ctrl elsewhere
//    do NOT hard-code 'control' or 'meta': you get the wrong
//    behaviour on one of the platforms

Input models that only exist somewhere

The input chapter's requirement is that everything reachable by a pointer is reachable by a keyboard, and on a cross-platform application that requirement has a second half: everything reachable by a pointer on one platform must have some other route on the platforms where that pointer does not exist. A hover-only affordance has no route on a touch platform, because there is no hover and no second pointer, so anything that appears on hover must also appear somewhere else — persistently, or on a gesture. A right-click action has no route on a touch platform, because there is no right button; the conventional translation is a long press, and it is not automatic, so it must be implemented deliberately. A double-click has no route, because there is no second click to be fast; the translation is a double tap, which the recognisers support and which has a different threshold, so a double-click action needs its own recogniser. Drag and drop has no route on a touch platform either, because there is no drag operation distinct from a scroll, and the translation is a long press followed by a drag, which is why the drag chapter's long-press-then-drag exists. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. An action reachable only by a gesture that only one platform has, which produces an application that is fully functional on a desktop and has a dead affordance on a phone — and the dead affordance is usually a long-press target the user never discovers. A hover state that is the only place something is described, which means the description is invisible on touch, so a control whose purpose is explained on hover has no explanation on a phone. And translating gestures by mapping them one to one without checking the recognisers, which produces a double-tap that is too slow because the threshold is tuned for a double click and a long press that fires before the user intends it because the duration is tuned for a keyboard modifier. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Give every action at least two routes, — a gesture and a visible control — so that no action depends on an input model that may not exist; the visible control is what makes the action discoverable and the gesture is what makes it fast, and an application that has only the gesture has an action some users cannot find. And test each action on each platform's primary input only, which is the discipline that catches the dead affordances: pick the actions rather than the screens, and try each one with a mouse, with a finger and with a keyboard, because an action that works in a screen you happened to test on all three may still fail in a screen where the only route was the one you did not test.

/* The requirement and its halves. */
const HALVES = [

};

Exercises 18

  1. Run the same app on all six platforms, and write down every place it looks or behaves wrong.
  2. Add a macOS menu bar with File, Edit and Window, and verify the shortcuts work.
  3. Add hover states, focus rings and a visible keyboard tab order, and test with only a keyboard.
  4. Build the web version, configure nginx with the SPA fallback, the MIME types and no-cache for index.html, and deploy it.
  5. Measure the web download size with CanvasKit and with the HTML renderer, and decide which you would ship.
  6. Add a web manifest and make the app installable. Verify it launches standalone and works offline.
  7. Build the master-detail layout with a navigation rail on a wide window and a bottom bar on a phone, sharing one state model.
  8. Add drag and drop and right-click, and confirm they are simply absent on a phone rather than broken.

18 · Security and Release Engineering

18.1 Secrets and what ships in the bundle18.2 Transport security18.3 On-device storage18.4 Authentication and authorisation18.5 Obfuscation and integrity18.6 Signing and store accounts18.7 The release build18.8 Surviving store review

Everything here is about the two weeks before a release, which is when a security or signing problem is most expensive to discover.

18.1 Secrets and what ships in the bundle

What is in the bundle, and why obfuscation is not the answer

A mobile binary is distributed to every device and is therefore readable by anyone who wants to read it: the application is a file on a device the user owns, and everything in it — code, strings, configuration, assets — can be extracted. That means a secret compiled into the application is a secret you have published. The distinction that matters is between a secret and a configuration value: an API key that identifies your application and a credential that lets you act as a user are different categories, and the first is arguably public while the second is not. An application identifier shipped in the bundle is not a secret — it is a name, it must be present in every request, and it can be extracted and used. A shared secret, a private key, an admin credential or a signing key is a secret, and if it is in the bundle it is disclosed to everyone who installs the application. Then the four things to do instead, and each is a requirement. Move the secret to the server and have the server call the third party. If a third party requires a key that cannot be on a device, the request must originate from your server; the device asks your server, your server calls the third party with the key, and the device never sees it. This is the only approach that works and it is why most third-party integrations are designed as server-side. Use per-user credentials rather than application credentials. A token the user obtained by signing in is scoped to that user, revocable, and not disclosed to other users; the difference between an application key and a user token is the difference between a shared password and a password per account. Restrict what the key can do, so that a disclosed key is a nuisance rather than a breach: per-service, per-method, with a quota, from known origins where the platform supports it. And rotate, and know how to rotate,, because a key that is in the bundle today will be in the bundle of every installed application forever, and rotation is the only remedy that reaches applications you cannot update. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Believing obfuscation protects a secret. Obfuscation makes the code harder to read; it does not make it unreadable, it does not encrypt a string constant, and it does nothing about a value that must be present in plaintext to be used — so a disclosed key stays disclosed. Hiding a key in the native layer instead of the Dart layer, which is harder to extract and still extractable, and which adds a platform-specific code path to maintain. And treating a key as safe because it is obfuscated or base64-encoded, which is the most common version of the first mistake and is not a defence against anything. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Have a list, written down, of every credential the application uses and where each one lives, and check the bundle against it before every release; the list is what makes the question answerable and it is the artifact that stops the next key from being added without thought. And scan the built artifact, not the source, because the key that ships is the one that survived tree shaking and ended up in a generated file or an asset — a source grep will find a deliberate constant and miss the one in a generated model.

/* Why. */
const READABLE = 'A MOBILE BINARY IS DISTRIBUTED TO EVERY DEVICE and IS THEREFORE READABLE BY ANYONE WHO WANTS TO READ IT';
const CONTENTS = ['CODE', 'STRINGS', 'CONFIGURATION', 'ASSETS'];
const RULE = 'SO A SECRET COMPILED INTO the APPLICATION IS A SECRET YOU HAVE PUBLISHED';

/* Two categories. */
const CATEGORIES = [
  { c: 'AN APPLICATION IDENTIFIER SHIPPED IN the BUNDLE', isNot: 'A SECRET', is: 'A NAME',
    facts: ['IT MUST BE PRESENT IN EVERY REQUEST', 'IT CAN BE EXTRACTED and USED'],
    note: 'ARGUABLY PUBLIC' },
  { c: 'A SHARED SECRET, A PRIVATE KEY, AN ADMIN CREDENTIAL or A SIGNING KEY', is: 'A SECRET',
    fact: 'and IF IT IS IN the BUNDLE it IS DISCLOSED TO EVERYONE WHO INSTALLS the APPLICATION' },
];

/* Four things to do instead. */
const INSTEAD = [

Everything in your Dart code is in the shipped binary. Unzip the AAB or the IPA and read it. Any API secret, private key or admin password that is in there is public, and the only correct response is to rotate it and redesign so there is nothing to leak.

// THE UNCOMFORTABLE FACT
// everything in your Dart code is in the shipped binary
//
//   Android: unzip app-release.aab and read the .so, or run
//     strings on the libapp.so
//   iOS: unzip the .ipa, and strings the Frameworks/App.framework/App
//   Web: it is literally the source, in a .js file
//
// so: no API secret, no private key, no admin password, ever

// pubspec.yaml - the assets you SHIP
flutter:
  assets:
    - assets/config/
    # NEVER:
    # - .env
    # - assets/private_key.pem
    # - a firebase service account json with an admin key
    # - a Google Maps API key with the "unrestricted" setting

// THE ONLY THING THAT GOES IN THE BUNDLE
// a PUBLIC config: an API base URL, a public client id,
// a feature flag set that is not sensitive
class AppConfig {
  const AppConfig({
    required this.apiBase,
    required this.publicClientId,
    required this.environment,
  });

  final String apiBase;
  final String publicClientId;
  final Environment environment;

  // BUILD-TIME, so a dev build and a prod build differ
  static const environment = Environment.production;
  static const apiBase = String.fromEnvironment(
    'API_BASE',
    defaultValue: 'https://api.acme.com',
  );
  // the map key: restrict it by package name and signing
  // certificate, which is a Google Cloud setting, not a code
  // change
  static const publicClientId = String.fromEnvironment('CLIENT_ID');
}

// and the SECRET config, fetched at runtime
class Secrets {
  static Future<Secrets> load() async {
    // from the backend, authenticated as the user
    final res = await http.get('$apiBase/v1/session/config');
    return Secrets.fromJson(jsonDecode(res.body));
  }
}
// AUDIT YOUR BINARY, before you ship
# Android
unzip -p build/app/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab \
  > /tmp/app.aab
# the Dart code is in base/assets/flutter_assets or the .so
strings /tmp/app.aab | grep -iE "secret|password|api[_-]?key|BEGIN.*PRIVATE|sk_live|AIza"
strings /tmp/app.aab | grep -oE "https?://[a-z0-9.-]+" | sort -u

# iOS
unzip -q build/ios/ipa/FieldNotes.ipa -d /tmp/ipa
strings /tmp/ipa/Payload/App.app/Frameworks/App.framework/App \
  | grep -iE "secret|password|BEGIN.*PRIVATE"

# Web: it is a .js file, so
grep -oE "https?://[a-z0-9.-]+" build/web/main.dart.js | sort -u
grep -iE "secret|api[_-]?key" build/web/main.dart.js

# A CI GATE, so it never happens by accident
- name: audit the binary for secrets
  run: |
    if strings app-release.aab | grep -qiE "BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY|sk_live_|AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}"; then
      echo "::error::a secret is in the binary"
      exit 1
    fi

18.2 Transport security

// TLS, and the things people get wrong

// 1. NO CLEARTEXT. Android blocks it by default from API 28,
//    and that is correct. iOS requires it.
//    the ONLY exception is a local dev server
// android/app/src/debug/res/xml/network_security_config.xml
<network-security-config>
  <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false" />
  <domain-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="true">
    <domain includeSubdomains="true">10.0.2.2</domain>
  </domain-config>
</network-security-config>
// and reference it ONLY in the debug manifest

// 2. CERTIFICATE PINNING, with a BACKUP pin
// android/app/src/main/res/xml/network_security_config.xml
<network-security-config>
  <domain-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false">
    <domain includeSubdomains="true">api.acme.com</domain>
    <pin-set>
      <pin digest="SHA-256">CURRENT_SPKI_HASH==</pin>
      <!-- THE BACKUP PIN. Without it, the day you rotate the
           key, every installed copy of your app stops working
           and users cannot fix it. -->
      <pin digest="SHA-256">BACKUP_SPKI_HASH==</pin>
    </pin-set>
  </domain-config>
</network-security-config>
// get the hash:
//   openssl s_client -connect api.acme.com:443 \
//     | openssl x509 -pubkey -noout \
//     | openssl pkey -pubin -outform der \
//     | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl enc -base64
//
// 3. DO NOT DISABLE VERIFICATION. This appears in almost every
//    tutorial and it is a man-in-the-middle waiting to happen.
// BAD: HttpOverrides.global = _badCertificateHttpOverrides();
//      on iOS:
//      let r = NSURLSession(... delegate: self, delegateQueue: nil)
//      and then in didReceiveChallenge: useCredential
//      with ServerTrust(...), for EVERY host
// GOOD: nothing. Ship the default.

// 4. iOS: ATS is on by default. You do not need an exception
//    for a real HTTPS API. If you add NSAllowsArbitraryLoads,
//    App Review will ask why.

// 5. HSTS on the server, and it is a server change
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload

What is guaranteed by TLS, and what is not

Transport security is a set of properties rather than one, and knowing which ones you have is what makes it a control rather than a setting. Confidentiality: the bytes between the two endpoints are encrypted, so an observer on the network cannot read them. Integrity: the bytes cannot be modified in transit without detection, so an observer cannot alter what you sent. Authentication: the server proves it is the server it claims to be, which is the property that stops an attacker from impersonating it — and this is the property that certificate pinning strengthens and that a user-installed root certificate undermines. Forward secrecy: the session keys are derived per session so that a captured recording cannot be decrypted later with the server's long-term key. And the negotiation: which version and which cipher, which determines whether any of the first four hold. Then the four things that go wrong, and each has a mechanism. Disabling certificate validation to make a request work in development, which is the single most common mobile security mistake and which ships — because the code that disables it is in the binary and the flag that guards it is usually a debug flag that is false in release, so it does not ship, and someone then keeps it because it makes a specific problem go away and the removal never gets prioritised. Accepting all certificates. The dangerous version is not "trust this one certificate", which is a pinning decision, but "accept any certificate whose subject matches", which accepts a self-signed certificate for the right hostname and is no protection at all. Not pinning, which means any certificate authority can issue a certificate for your domain and a device that trusts that authority will trust it — which is a design property of the web's trust model and is a genuine risk on a mobile device where a user may have installed a corporate or personal root. And cleartext traffic permitted somewhere, because a manifest that allows cleartext permits it for every request the application makes, and one forgotten endpoint is a plaintext request. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Make the development exception impossible to ship, by putting it behind a compile-time define rather than a runtime flag, so a release build does not contain the code path at all; then a release build physically cannot have validation disabled. And make the server's configuration part of the security posture, because most transport problems are server problems: certificate chain complete, modern protocol versions only, weak ciphers disabled, strict transport security sent with a long max-age and preload, and redirects from cleartext to secure rather than serving both. A mobile application cannot fix any of those and depends on all of them.

/* The properties. */
const PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'CONFIDENTIALITY', means: 'the BYTES BETWEEN the TWO ENDPOINTS ARE ENCRYPTED, so AN OBSERVER ON the NETWORK CANNOT READ THEM' },
  { p: 'INTEGRITY', means: 'the BYTES CANNOT BE MODIFIED IN TRANSIT WITHOUT DETECTION, so AN OBSERVER CANNOT ALTER WHAT YOU SENT' },
  { p: 'AUTHENTICATION', means: 'the SERVER PROVES IT IS the SERVER IT CLAIMS TO BE',
    stops: 'WHICH IS the PROPERTY THAT STOPS AN ATTACKER from IMPERSONATING IT',
    note: 'and WHICH IS the PROPERTY THAT CERTIFICATE PINNING STRENGTHENS and THAT A USER-INSTALLED ROOT CERTIFICATE UNDERMINES' },
  { p: 'FORWARD SECRECY', means: 'the SESSION KEYS ARE DERIVED PER SESSION so THAT A CAPTURED RECORDING CANNOT BE DECRYPTED LATER WITH the SERVERS LONG-TERM KEY' },
  { p: 'the NEGOTIATION', which: 'WHICH VERSION and WHICH CIPHER', determines: 'WHICH DETERMINES WHETHER ANY of the FIRST FOUR HOLD' },
];

/* Four things that go wrong. */
const GO_WRONG = [
  { f: 'DISABLING CERTIFICATE VALIDATION to MAKE A REQUEST WORK IN DEVELOPMENT',
    rank: 'the SINGLE MOST COMMON MOBILE SECURITY MISTAKE',
    and: 'WHICH SHIPS',
    why: 'BECAUSE the CODE THAT DISABLES IT IS IN the BINARY and the FLAG THAT GUARDS IT IS USUALLY A DEBUG FLAG THAT IS FALSE IN RELEASE',
    consequence: 'and THEN SOMEONE KEEPS IT BECAUSE IT MAKES A SPECIFIC PROBLEM GO AWAY and the REMOVAL NEVER GETS PRIORITISED' },

const PRACTICES = [

    how: 'BY PUTTING IT BEHIND A COMPILE-TIME DEFINE rather than A RUNTIME FLAG',
    gain: 'SO A RELEASE BUILD DOES NOT CONTAIN the CODE PATH AT ALL',

18.3 On-device storage

// THE THREE TIERS, and the rule for each
//
// SHARED PREFERENCES  settings, a feature flag, a theme
//                     NOT sensitive. It is a plain file.
//
// SECURE STORAGE      a token, an API key, a biometric
//                     unlock key. Keychain / EncryptedSharedPreferences.
//
// THE DATABASE        your records. Encrypted if they contain
//                     anything sensitive - see below.

// ENCRYPTING THE DATABASE, when it holds real data
// two options: a whole-file encryption, or column-level
//
// 1. SQLCIPHER, for a whole-file encryption
// sqlite3_flutter_libs ships SQLCipher support in some builds;
// the cleanest path is the sqlcipher_flutter_libs package
import 'package:sqlcipher_flutter_libs/sqlcipher_flutter_libs.dart';
import 'package:drift/native.dart';

LazyDatabase openEncrypted(String path, String key) {
  return LazyDatabase(() async {
    await sqfliteFfiInit();
    return databaseExecutorFfi.openDatabase(
      path,
      options: OpenDatabaseOptions(
        // the KEY, not the passphrase
        password: key,
        cipher: 'sqlcipher',
      ),
    );
  });
}

// 2. COLUMN ENCRYPTION, for the fields that are sensitive
//    the right choice when you need to query the other columns
class EncryptedField {
  static const _keyName = 'field_notes_db_key';

  static Future<Cipher> _cipher() async {
    // the key lives in the keychain, and is generated once
    final storage = FlutterSecureStorage();
    var key = await storage.read(key: _keyName);
    if (key == null) {
      key = base64Url.encode(List.generate(32, (_) => Random().nextInt(256)));
      await storage.write(key: _keyName, value: key);
    }
    return Cipher(Encrypter(AES(Key.fromBase64(key!))));
  }

  static Future<String> encrypt(String plaintext) async {
    final cipher = await _cipher();
    return cipher.encrypt(plaintext);
  }

  static Future<String> decrypt(String ciphertext) async {
    final cipher = await _cipher();
    return cipher.decrypt64(ciphertext);
  }
}

// THE BACKUP PROBLEM, which is the one people miss
// Android auto-backup includes the app's data directory, so a
// database and a shared_preferences file are in the backup.
// iOS backs up the Documents directory.
// android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml
<application
    android:allowBackup="false"
    android:fullBackupContent="@xml/backup_rules">
<!-- or, selectively -->
<!-- android/app/src/main/res/xml/backup_rules.xml -->
<full-backup-content>
  <exclude domain="database" path="fieldnotes.sqlite" />
  <exclude domain="sharedpref" path="flutter_secure_storage.xml" />
</full-backup-content>
// AND for Android 12+
// android/app/src/main/res/xml/data_extraction_rules.xml
//   with cloud-backup and device-transfer exclusions

// On iOS, exclude a file from the backup
// (a platform channel, see chapter 13)

What the platform protects, and what it does not

Mobile platform storage has three tiers with different protections, and using the wrong one for a value is either over-engineering or a disclosure. Application preferences are a plist or an XML file in the application's private directory, protected by the operating system's file permissions and by the device's encryption at rest; they are readable by the application, by anything with root or a backup, and by the platform's own backup. The keychain and keystore hold a small number of values with hardware-backed keys where the device supports it, and the item's accessibility class controls when it can be read — whether it is available while the device is locked, whether it requires the user to have authenticated, and whether it syncs to other devices. The database and the files are in the private directory with the same permissions as preferences, and on iOS the data-protection classes control when they can be read. The important consequence is that "in the private directory" is not encryption: it protects against other applications, and it does not protect against a backup, against a rooted device, or against an attacker who has the device unlocked and the application running. Then the four things to decide for every value, and each is a question with a defensible answer. Does it need to be secret from other applications? If yes it belongs in the private directory, which is the default and is sufficient for almost everything. Does it need to be secret from someone who extracts the file? If yes it belongs in the keychain or the keystore, and that is a short list of values — tokens, keys, a biometric template reference. Does it need to be available when the device is locked? If yes its accessibility class must permit that, which is a decision rather than a default because the more permissive the class the more available it is. And does it belong in a backup? If no — a token you can re-fetch, a cached database, a temporary file — it should be excluded, because a backup that contains a token whose server-side session has been revoked produces a confusing sign-in failure on restore. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Putting a token in preferences, which is readable from a backup and from a file dump, and which is the most common storage mistake in mobile applications. Storing everything in the keychain, which is slow, has size limits, and is the wrong home for a list of two hundred cached records. And encrypting the database with a key stored on the same device, which protects against file extraction and against nothing else, because an attacker with the running application has both the database and the key. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Classify every persisted value once, in a table, with its tier and its backup decision, because the classification is a one-off exercise and the failure is a value added later without a decision. And delete on sign-out, completely, including the caches and the files, because a token that is cleared while the cached database holding the user's data is not is a partial sign-out that looks like a successful one.

/* Three tiers. */
const TIERS = [
  { t: 'APPLICATION PREFERENCES', is: 'A PLIST or AN XML FILE IN the APPLICATIONS PRIVATE DIRECTORY',
    protectedBy: ['the OPERATING SYSTEMS FILE PERMISSIONS', 'and the DEVICES ENCRYPTION AT REST'],
    readableBy: ['the APPLICATION', 'ANYTHING with ROOT or A BACKUP', 'and the PLATFORMS OWN BACKUP'] },
  { t: 'the KEYCHAIN and KEYSTORE', holds: 'A SMALL NUMBER of VALUES with HARDWARE-BACKED KEYS WHERE the DEVICE SUPPORTS IT',
    accessibility: 'the ITEMS ACCESSIBILITY CLASS CONTROLS WHEN IT CAN BE READ',
    controls: ['WHETHER IT IS AVAILABLE WHILE the DEVICE IS LOCKED', 'WHETHER IT REQUIRES the USER TO HAVE AUTHENTICATED', 'and WHETHER IT SYNCS TO OTHER DEVICES'] },
  { t: 'the DATABASE and the FILES', is: 'IN the PRIVATE DIRECTORY with the SAME PERMISSIONS as PREFERENCES',

];

18.4 Authentication and authorisation

// THE TOKEN PATTERN, done properly
class AuthRepository {
  AuthRepository({required this._api, required this._tokens});

  final ApiClient _api;
  final TokenStore _tokens;

  // ACCESS: short-lived, sent on every request
  // REFRESH: long-lived, used only to get a new access token
  Future<Session> login(String email, String password) async {
    final res = await _api.post('/auth/login', {
      'email': email,
      'password': password,
      // a device identifier, so a refresh token can be revoked
      'deviceId': await deviceId(),
    });

    await _tokens.save(
      access: res.accessToken,
      refresh: res.refreshToken,
    );
    return Session.fromJson(res.user);
  }

  // the refresh, with a LOCK: two 401s must not both refresh
  Future<String?> _refreshing = Future.value();

  Future<String?> validAccessToken() async {
    final token = await _tokens.accessToken;
    if (token == null) return null;
    if (!_isExpired(token)) return token;

    return _refreshing.then((_) async {
      final refresh = await _tokens.refreshToken;
      if (refresh == null) return null;
      try {
        final res = await _api.post('/auth/refresh', {'refreshToken': refresh});
        await _tokens.set('access_token', res.accessToken);
        return res.accessToken;
      } on UnauthorizedFailure {
        await logout();
        return null;
      }
    });
  }

  Future<void> logout() async {
    // tell the server, so the refresh token is revoked
    unawaited(_api.post('/auth/logout', {}).catchError((_) {}));
    await _tokens.clear();
  }
}

// THE SERVER RULES, which the app cannot enforce
// 1. the refresh token is rotated on every use, and the old one
//    is invalidated. A stolen refresh token is then usable at
//    most once.
// 2. a refresh token is bound to a device, and can be revoked
//    from another session
// 3. access tokens are SHORT-lived: 15 minutes, not a day
// 4. there is an account revocation endpoint
// 5. authorisation is checked from the token, never from a
//    field the client sent

// BIOMETRICS, for a local unlock
// pubspec.yaml
//   local_auth: ^2.3.0
import 'package:local_auth/local_auth.dart';

class BiometricGate {
  final _auth = LocalAuthentication();

  Future<bool> canUseBiometrics() async {
    try {
      final supported = await _auth.isDeviceSupported();
      final canCheck = await _auth.canCheckBiometrics;
      return supported && canCheck;
    } catch (_) {
      return false;   // a device without a sensor
    }
  }

  Future<bool> authenticate() async {
    try {
      return await _auth.authenticate(
        localizedReason: 'Unlock your notes',
        options: const AuthenticationOptions(
          biometricOnly: false,     // allow the passcode as a fallback
          stickyAuth: true,          // keep the prompt after a background
          useErrorDialogs: true,
        ),
      );
    } catch (_) {
      return false;
    }
  }
}

// THE RULES
// 1. biometrics is a GATE, not an identity. It unlocks a key
//    that is already on the device. It does not replace a
//    server session.
// 2. the fallback is the device passcode, never a PIN in the app
// 3. handle a failure gracefully: no sensor, too many attempts,
//    a cancelled prompt
// 4. the local_auth plugin requires:
//    iOS: NSFaceIDUsageDescription in Info.plist
//    Android: USE_BIOMETRIC permission, and a FragmentActivity

Three mechanisms, and the difference between them

Mobile authentication has three mechanisms that are routinely confused, and the confusion produces both security bugs and user frustration. A passcode or device credential is a secret the user knows, stored hashed or derived by the platform, and it is the weakest of the three because it is the one a person can be made to surrender. A biometric is measured by the platform's own hardware in a secure element and matched locally; the application receives a yes or a no and never sees the biometric, which is a good property and which is the reason the mechanism is safe to use for a local gate. A device credential presented to the platform as a keystore operation, where the keystore requires a user presence check and the key is used without ever being extracted — this is the one that is genuinely strong, and it is the mechanism behind the secure storage chapter's advice. The distinction that matters in design is between a biometric used as a local unlock for stored data and a biometric used to authenticate to a server. The first is safe and easy. The second needs a server-side protocol, because the server cannot ask the user's phone for a fingerprint — it can only be told, by an already-authenticated device, that a user presence check succeeded. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Using a boolean from the platform directly as the application's session, which means the "session" is true until the process restarts, and a false positive is a device that unlocks for whoever holds it — which is why the correct pattern is a keystore key released by a presence check, not a boolean. Not handling the case where the biometric hardware is unavailable or the user has not enrolled, which is the case that produces the "this device cannot be used" report, and the correct behaviour is a documented alternative rather than a failure. And not understanding that a biometric on a device is not an identity, — it is a presence check on the device's owner, so a server that treats a biometric assertion as authentication is accepting a device's claim about its owner. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Keep the credential on the server and use the device as a factor, so that revoking a session is a server operation and a lost device is recoverable — which is the difference between a session that is a boolean and one that is a token the server can revoke. And always provide a fallback, because a mechanism that can refuse has to have a path for when it does; the fallback is what makes the feature usable rather than a gate that some users cannot pass.

/* Three mechanisms. */
const MECHANISMS = [
  { m: 'A PASSCODE or DEVICE CREDENTIAL', is: 'A SECRET the USER KNOWS, STORED HASHED or DERIVED BY the PLATFORM',
    rank: 'IT IS the WEAKEST of the THREE BECAUSE IT IS the ONE A PERSON CAN BE MADE TO SURRENDER' },
  { m: 'A BIOMETRIC', is: 'MEASURED BY the PLATFORMS OWN HARDWARE IN A SECURE ELEMENT and MATCHED LOCALLY',
    property: 'the APPLICATION RECEIVES A YES or A NO and NEVER SEES the BIOMETRIC',

const PRACTICES = [

    gain: ['SO THAT REVOKING A SESSION IS A SERVER OPERATION and A LOST DEVICE IS RECOVERABLE'],
    difference: 'WHICH IS the DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A SESSION THAT IS A BOOLEAN and ONE THAT IS A TOKEN the SERVER CAN REVOKE' },
  { p: 'ALWAYS PROVIDE A FALLBACK',
    why: 'BECAUSE A MECHANISM THAT CAN REFUSE HAS TO HAVE A PATH FOR WHEN IT DOES',

18.5 Obfuscation and integrity

What obfuscation gives, and what integrity is for

Two different things are often lumped together as "protecting the binary", and they have different purposes and different limits. Obfuscation makes the code harder to read. A symbol-level transformation renames symbols, removes debug information, and sometimes restructures control flow, so a person who extracts the binary and opens it in a decompiler sees structure without names. That is a real cost to an attacker and it is not a wall: a determined reverse engineer recovers names by inference, and control-flow obfuscation raises the cost of an attack rather than making it impossible. The useful consequence is that obfuscation raises the price of the cheapest attacks — the automated ones, the scripts that look for a string, and the mass-repackaging of an application's premium features — while doing nothing against a person with time. Integrity checking is a different property: it detects modification. A value computed from the binary's own content and checked at run time will not match if the binary has been patched, so a repackaged application can detect that it was repackaged. Then the three things to know, and each is a mechanism. Obfuscation does not encrypt. A string constant in the binary is present as data and obfuscating the code around it does nothing; if a value must not be readable it must not be in the binary, which is the secrets section's argument. Integrity checks can be removed. A check that exists in the same binary it protects is a check an attacker can delete, so the mechanism only works if failing the check has consequences an attacker cannot bypass, and that generally means the server refuses to serve rather than the application refusing to run. And obfuscation makes crashes undiagnosable, because a symbolicated stack trace from an obfuscated build has no symbols — so the practice is to obfuscate only for release, keep a mapping file per version, and upload it to the crash reporter so that a report from a shipped build can be symbolicated. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. Shipping an obfuscated build without the mapping files, which means every crash from production is uninterpretable and the mapping cannot be regenerated. Making a server-enforced decision from a client check, which means the check is advisory and the attacker removes it. And treating an integrity failure as a crash, which produces an application that refuses to start on the devices where it was most likely tampered with — a user with a rooted phone — and generates support traffic about a bug that is not one. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Move the valuable decision to the server, so that what the client protects is only the client's own behaviour and the server's enforcement is unaffected by anything done to the client — which is the same argument as the secrets section's and the authorisation section's, and it is the only one that survives a determined attacker. And keep the mapping files, versioned and archived, because they are the only thing that makes a production crash diagnosable and they are the one artifact nobody thinks to keep.

/* Two things, not one. */
const DISTINCT = 'TWO DIFFERENT THINGS ARE OFTEN LUMPED TOGETHER AS protecting the binary';
const OBFUSCATION = {
  does: 'MAKES the CODE HARDER TO READ',
  how: ['A SYMBOL-LEVEL TRANSFORMATION RENAMES SYMBOLS', 'REMOVES DEBUG INFORMATION', 'and SOMETIMES RESTRUCTURES CONTROL FLOW'],
