Obfuscation raises the cost of reverse engineering; it is not a security control. Its real operational value is that it forces you to keep the symbol file - and a production stack trace without symbols is a list of meaningless identifiers, which is the difference between finding a crash and not.

// OBFUSCATION, and what it is actually for
//
// it is NOT for security. it raises the cost of reverse
// engineering, nothing more. An attacker with the binary and
// time will get through.
//
// what it does: rename your Dart symbols, so a stack trace and
// a decompiled class name are meaningless
// dart compile exe main.dart -o app --obfuscate --save-debugging-info=app.debug
//
// the debugging info is ESSENTIAL: without it, a crash report
// from an obfuscated build is a stack trace of
//   #aBcDeF.gHiJkL.mNoPqR
// keep the .debug file, upload it to your crash reporter, and
// symbolicate there. Losing it makes production stack traces
// useless.

// symbolication, in Sentry
// dart symbolize app.debug -o app.symbols
// and upload app.symbols to Sentry

// what obfuscation does NOT protect
// - data in local storage
// - the network traffic
// - the API surface, which is visible in the traffic
// - a determined attacker with a debugger

// THE INTEGRITY CHECKS, which are more useful
// 1. refuse to run on a rooted or jailbroken device
// pubspec.yaml
//   flutter_jailbreak_detection: ^6.0.0
//   device_info_plus: ^10.1.0
final jailbroken = await JailbreakDetection.isJailbroken();
// then: refuse, or restrict, or warn. Apple and Google both
// allow this, and most security-conscious apps do it.

// 2. an attestation, which is the real answer
//    Play Integrity API on Android, DeviceCheck / App Attest
//    on iOS
//    it proves: this binary, from your store, on a real device,
//    not tampered with
//    it is server-side, and it is free at low volume
//    it is the correct defence against a repackaged app and
//    against a modified client

// 3. a tamper check, for a cheap extra signal
//    hash a file in your bundle and compare
//    weak, and it breaks on a legitimate update. Use it as one
//    signal among several, never alone.

18.6 Signing and store accounts

// THE ACCOUNTS, and the cost
// Google Play: $25 one-time
// Apple Developer: $99/year, and the App Store rules are stricter

// ANDROID: TWO KEYS
// 1. THE UPLOAD KEY: you generate it, and use it to upload
keytool -genkeypair -v \
  -keystore upload-keystore.jks \
  -alias upload \
  -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000

// 2. THE APP SIGNING KEY: Google generates and holds it, once
//    you enrol in Play App Signing. THIS IS THE DEFAULT AND THE
//    RIGHT CHOICE. You never hold it.
//
// Enrolment happens automatically on the first upload to a new
// app, and you can verify it in Play Console.
//
// STORE IT: the upload key in a password manager, and in CI
// secrets. Nowhere else. Ever. Not in a repo, not in a
// screenshot, not in a chat message.

// android/app/build.gradle
def keystoreProperties = new Properties()
def keystorePropertiesFile = rootProject.file('keystore.properties')
if (keystorePropertiesFile.exists()) {
    keystoreProperties.load(new FileInputStream(keystorePropertiesFile))
}

android {
    signingConfigs {
        release {
            storeFile file(keystoreProperties['storeFile'])
            storePassword keystoreProperties['storePassword']
            keyAlias keystoreProperties['keyAlias']
            keyPassword keystoreProperties['keyPassword']
        }
    }
    buildTypes {
        release {
            minifyEnabled true
            shrinkResources true
            proguardFiles getDefaultProguardFile('proguard-android-optimize.txt'),
                        'proguard-rules.pro'
            signingConfig signingConfigs.release
        }
    }
}

// android/keystore.properties   (GIT-IGNORED)
//   storeFile=../upload-keystore.jks
//   storePassword=…
//   keyAlias=upload
//   keyPassword=…
// ANDROID: THE TARGET SDK, which is a moving deadline
// android/app/build.gradle or variables.gradle
android {
    defaultConfig {
        minSdkVersion = 23          // Flutter 3.24+ requires 23
        targetSdkVersion = 35       // Play requires a recent level
        compileSdkVersion = 35
    }
}
// Google Play requires new submissions to target within a year
// of the latest release. Check the current requirement each
// quarter, and test on an emulator at that API level.

// ANDROID: A VECTOR DRAWABLE, or a build failure on API 21+
// the launcher icon must be a vector drawable for adaptive icons
<!-- android/app/src/main/res/mipmap-anydpi-v26/ic_launcher.xml -->
<adaptive-icon xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android">
  <background android:drawable="@color/ic_launcher_background" />
  <foreground android:drawable="@mipmap/ic_launcher_foreground" />
  <monochrome android:drawable="@mipmap/ic_launcher_foreground" />
</adaptive-icon>

// iOS: THE CERTIFICATE CHAIN
// in CI, with an App Store Connect API key, there is no
// interactive unlock and no .p12: the key signs directly
xcodebuild archive \
  -workspace Runner.xcworkspace \
  -scheme Runner \
  -configuration Release \
  -destination 'generic/platform=iOS' \
  -archivePath build/Runner.xcarchive \
  -allowProvisioningUpdates \
  DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=ABCDE12345 \
  CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Automatic \
  archive

xcodebuild -exportArchive \
  -archivePath build/Runner.xcarchive \
  -exportOptionsPlist ExportOptions.plist \
  -exportPath build/ipa

// ExportOptions.plist
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN"
  "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0"><dict>
  <key>method</key>         <string>app-store-connect</string>
  <key>teamID</key>         <string>ABCDE12345</string>
  <key>signingStyle</key>   <string>automatic</string>
  <key>uploadSymbols</key>  <true/>
  <key>destination</key>    <string>upload</string>
  <key>manageAppVersionAndBuildNumber</key> <false/>
</dict></plist>

// iOS: THE VERSION NUMBERS
// ios/Runner.xcodeproj: MARKETING_VERSION and
// CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION. Or with fastlane's increment_build_number
// CI, with the secrets in the environment
name: release
on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']

jobs:
  android:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { channel: stable, cache: true }
      - run: flutter pub get
      - run: dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs

      # the keystore, from base64 in a secret
      - name: restore the keystore
        run: |
          echo "${{ secrets.UPLOAD_KEYSTORE_BASE64 }}" | base64 -d > android/upload-keystore.jks
          cat > android/keystore.properties <<EOF
          storeFile=../upload-keystore.jks
          storePassword=${{ secrets.UPLOAD_STORE_PASSWORD }}
          keyAlias=upload
          keyPassword=${{ secrets.UPLOAD_KEY_PASSWORD }}
          EOF

      - run: flutter build appbundle --release

      # AUDIT before you upload
      - name: audit the binary
        run: |
          BUNDLE=$(ls build/app/outputs/bundle/release/*.aab)
          if strings "$BUNDLE" | grep -qiE "BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY|sk_live_|AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}"; then
            echo "::error::a secret is in the binary"
            exit 1
          fi

      # the version
      - name: sync the version
        run: flutter build appbundle --release --build-number=${{ github.run_number }}

      - uses: fastlane/fastlane@2
        with: { args: "supply --aab ... --track internal --api_key_path $PLAY_JSON" }

  ios:
    needs: android              # ship Android first
    runs-on: macos-latest
    environment:
      ASC_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.ASC_KEY_ID }}
      ASC_ISSUER_ID: ${{ secrets.ASC_ISSUER_ID }}
      ASC_KEY: ${{ secrets.ASC_KEY_P8_BASE64 }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { channel: stable, cache: true }
      - run: flutter pub get
      - run: flutter build ipa --release --no-codesign
      - run: |
          cd ios/Runner.xcworkspace
          xcodebuild -exportArchive \
            -archivePath build/ios/ipa/Runner.xcarchive \
            -exportOptionsPlist ExportOptions.plist \
            -exportPath build/ios/ipa/export
      - uses: fastlane/fastlane@2
        with: { args: "supply --ipa build/ios/ipa/export/Runner.ipa" }

The signing identity, and where it must not be

Every mobile application is signed, and the signature is what ties a binary to a publisher and to a continuity of updates. Understanding the parts prevents a specific class of release incident, and the parts are fewer than they look. A signing key — the upload key on Android, the distribution certificate on iOS — is the identity that the store trusts. A signing certificate is derived from that key and has an expiry. The signature is embedded in the artifact, and the store verifies it on installation and uses it to decide whether an upload is a genuine update from the same publisher. On iOS the certificate's expiry is the awkward part, because an expired certificate prevents signing, so a team that has not run an automated build for two years discovers this at release time; the modern mechanism is to have the signing action authorised by the store rather than by a local certificate, which removes the expiry from the critical path. On Android the key is what matters and losing it is unrecoverable for the application listing, because a different key is a different application to the store. Then the four things that go wrong, and each is a mechanism. The signing key stored in the repository. It is the credential that lets somebody publish as you, and a repository is the one place that is copied to every developer's machine and to every continuous-integration log; the correct home is the platform's own secrets store or the store's own authentication. Handled by a person. A release that requires a specific person's laptop, their keychain and their availability is a release that will slip, and it is also an unversioned process with no audit trail. Uploading with the wrong key, which on iOS is recoverable because the certificate can be replaced but the bundle identifier and the team must match, and on Android is not recoverable. And not knowing which key a given build was signed with, which makes an incident impossible to reason about; recording the key fingerprint with the release is the fix. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Sign in continuous integration, not on a laptop, so that every release is reproducible from the repository state and the log records what was built, signed and uploaded — which is also the only way to satisfy the store's own requirements for some release types. And keep the key's fingerprint and the certificate's expiry date in the repository as data, not as a secret: the fingerprint is public and identifying, the expiry is a date that should be monitored, and putting them somewhere somebody will look before a release is what prevents the discovery.

18.7 The release build

What a release build does that a debug build does not

A release build is not a debug build with optimisation switched on; it is a different artifact with different properties, and knowing them makes the release checklist a list of known requirements rather than a set of habits. The compiler is in AOT mode on Android and iOS, producing machine code rather than a kernel that interprets the Dart, so the runtime is not in the artifact and there is no run-time compilation cost. Tree shaking removes unreachable code, so a library that is imported but whose features are unused contributes little — which is why the package that "we include but barely use" is usually not the one inflating the build. The whole-program compilation of a mobile build means one compilation unit, so the compiler can optimise across the whole application rather than across a module, which is why a global function is genuinely faster than a method on a class in some cases and why an unclosed generic can matter. Asserts are removed, so every check the framework performs in debug costs nothing in release — and so a bug the assert was catching is now silent, which is why a release-only crash is usually a state that should have been impossible. Then the three things that surprise people, and each is a mechanism. Assets dominate the size, not code. Tree shaking does nothing to images, fonts and videos, so an application with a few megabytes of code and forty megabytes of assets is forty megabytes, and the analysis command that reports the breakdown names the contributors — which is the only way to find them. Debug symbols are large. Split debug info out of the artifact and upload it to the crash reporter, which is the platform's own mechanism and is what makes a production crash symbolicated without shipping symbols to users. And the per-architecture split. An Android package can contain several architectures and a store bundle can be split per device, and shipping all of them is a download cost paid by every user for the benefit of a small fraction — so the split is the mechanism that reduces the download without changing the application. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Measure the size breakdown every release, because size is a regression like any other and it grows one asset at a time; a number that is only measured when someone asks will grow unnoticed. And build a release artifact in continuous integration, not on a machine, so that what is tested is what ships and so the artifact, its signature and its size report are the record of the release rather than a claim about it.

/* What differs. */

Test the artefact you are about to upload, not the debug build. Install the release AAB or IPA on a real device, sign in, create something, sync, force-quit and reopen. The debug build has been lying to you about the release configuration the whole time.

// THE BUILD COMMANDS
flutter build appbundle --release            # Play Store, the AAB
flutter build apk --release --split-per-abi  # direct APK, per ABI
flutter build ipa --release                 # App Store
flutter build macos --release
flutter build windows --release
flutter build linux --release
flutter build web --release --wasm

// THE FLAGS THAT MATTER
--release                    AOT, optimised. Non-negotiable.
--split-per-abi              one APK per architecture
--obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/symbols
                             obfuscate, and KEEP the symbols
--tree-shake-icons           on by default; do not disable
--analyze-size               a size report, before you upload
--build-number=42            the Android version code
--build-name=1.4.0           the visible version
--dart-define=API_BASE=…     a compile-time constant
--obfuscate --split-debug-info
                             and a ProGuard mapping for R8

// THE PRE-FLIGHT CHECKLIST
# 1. the version
flutter pub version minor

# 2. the CHANGELOG
#    update CHANGELOG.md: added, fixed, changed, breaking

# 3. static analysis, with zero warnings
flutter analyze --fatal-infos

# 4. format
dart format --set-exit-if-changed .

# 5. code generation is current
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
git diff --exit-code          # fails if it changed anything

# 6. the tests, including goldens
flutter test

# 7. build and AUDIT
flutter build appbundle --release
strings build/app/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab \
  | grep -iE "secret|private key|AIza|sk_live"   # must be empty

# 8. install the exact artefact on a real device
flutter install --release

# 9. the size, which users notice
ls -la build/app/outputs/bundle/release/
flutter build appbundle --analyze-size

# 10. a smoke test on the artefact, not the debug build
#     sign in, create, sync, kill, reopen
// THE SIZE BUDGETS, and why they are worth setting
// a Flutter app's download size is dominated by:
//   the engine:  ~4MB native, and it is per-architecture in
//                the AAB, so a device downloads one
//   your Dart code: 0.5MB to 3MB
//   assets: whatever you bundled
//   the plugins' native libraries: per-architecture
//
// so the levers are
// 1. ASSETS. A 4MB video in your bundle is a 4MB app.
//    stream it, or exclude it with --dart-define.
// 2. THE PLUGIN SET. Each native plugin adds libraries for
//    every architecture. Audit with --analyze-size.
// 3. TREE SHAKING. Do not use dynamic, and do not use
//    dart:mirrors.
// 4. ONE ARCHITECTURE, if you do not need the others:
//    the AAB does this for you

// THE ANALYSE
flutter build appbundle --analyze-size
// a per-ABI breakdown, and it names the largest contributors

18.8 Surviving store review

What review actually catches, and how to pass it

Store review is a filter for a small number of specific things, and knowing which is the difference between a rejection you can fix and a rejection you cannot argue with. It checks that the application does what it says. The description, the screenshots, the privacy label and the permissions requested must agree with what the application does when a reviewer runs it — and the most common rejection is not a policy violation at all, it is a reviewer being unable to reach a feature because they could not sign in, which is a documentation problem about how to obtain a test account. It checks the privacy disclosures against the behaviour. If the application collects data, the label must say what is collected, whether it is linked to identity, whether it is used for tracking, and whether it is shared — and an application that collects more than it declares is a compliance problem, not a review problem. It checks the permission usage strings. Every permission the manifest requests needs a string explaining why, and that string is shown to the user at the moment of the request, so it must be specific rather than a category. And it checks the age rating, the content declarations and, in some categories, specific requirements — a health application, a financial application or one with user-generated content has additional obligations. Then the three things that cause a rejection, and each is a mechanism. A reviewer cannot sign in, or cannot reach the feature. This is the single most common cause and it is entirely in your control: provide test credentials in the review notes, or a build with a bypass, or make the feature reachable without an account — and the review notes field is where this belongs, because it is the only part of your submission that the reviewer is instructed to read. A permission declared but not used, which prompts the question during review and which the store can and does verify. And a privacy policy that disagrees with the behaviour, where the policy is a document you wrote and the behaviour is what the application does, and a reviewer who notices a data-collection behaviour that the policy does not mention will reject it. Then the two practices, and each is a discipline. Do a release-candidate pass against the store's own checklist before submitting, and treat the checklist as the specification rather than as guidance — it is a list of things that cause rejection and reading it costs an hour. And roll out in stages, to internal testing, then a small percentage, because a staged rollout is the only mechanism that limits the blast radius of a release, and it gives you the crash and the review data from real users before everyone has it.

/* What review checks. */
const CHECKS = [
  { c: 'THAT the APPLICATION DOES WHAT IT SAYS',
    detail: ['the DESCRIPTION', 'the SCREENSHOTS', 'the PRIVACY LABEL', 'and the PERMISSIONS REQUESTED MUST AGREE WITH WHAT the APPLICATION DOES WHEN A REVIEWER RUNS IT'],
    mostCommon: 'and the MOST COMMON REJECTION IS NOT A POLICY VIOLATION AT ALL, IT IS A REVIEWER BEING UNABLE TO REACH A FEATURE BECAUSE THEY COULD NOT SIGN IN' },
  { c: 'the PRIVACY DISCLOSURES AGAINST the BEHAVIOUR',
    must: ['WHAT IS COLLECTED', 'WHETHER IT IS LINKED TO IDENTITY', 'WHETHER IT IS USED for TRACKING', 'and WHETHER IT IS SHARED'],
    consequence: 'and AN APPLICATION THAT COLLECTS MORE THAN IT DECLARES IS A COMPLIANCE PROBLEM, NOT A REVIEW PROBLEM' },
  { c: 'the PERMISSION USAGE STRINGS',
    detail: 'EVERY PERMISSION the MANIFEST REQUESTS NEEDS A STRING EXPLAINING WHY',
    and: 'and THAT STRING IS SHOWN TO the USER AT the MOMENT of the REQUEST',
    so: 'IT MUST BE SPECIFIC rather than A CATEGORY' },
  { c: 'the AGE RATING, the CONTENT DECLARATIONS and, IN SOME CATEGORIES, SPECIFIC REQUIREMENTS',
    detail: 'A HEALTH APPLICATION, A FINANCIAL APPLICATION or ONE with USER-GENERATED CONTENT HAS ADDITIONAL OBLIGATIONS' },
];

/* Three things that cause a rejection. */
const REJECT = [
  { f: 'A REVIEWER CANNOT SIGN IN, OR CANNOT REACH the FEATURE',
    rank: 'the SINGLE MOST COMMON CAUSE',
    control: 'AND IT IS ENTIRELY IN YOUR CONTROL',
    fixes: ['PROVIDE TEST CREDENTIALS IN the REVIEW NOTES', 'or A BUILD with A BYPASS', 'or MAKE the FEATURE REACHABLE WITHOUT AN ACCOUNT'],
    where: 'and the REVIEW NOTES FIELD IS WHERE THIS BELONGS',
    why: 'BECAUSE IT IS the ONLY PART of YOUR SUBMISSION THAT the REVIEWER IS INSTRUCTED TO READ' },
  { f: 'A PERMISSION DECLARED BUT NOT USED', consequence: 'WHICH PROMPTS the QUESTION DURING REVIEW and WHICH the STORE CAN and DOES VERIFY' },
  { f: 'A PRIVACY POLICY THAT DISAGREES WITH the BEHAVIOUR',

    symptom: 'and A REVIEWER WHO NOTICES A DATA-COLLECTION BEHAVIOUR THAT the POLICY DOES NOT MENTION WILL REJECT IT' },

/* Two practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'DO A RELEASE-CANDIDATE PASS AGAINST the STORES OWN CHECKLIST BEFORE SUBMITTING',
    how: 'and TREAT the CHECKLIST AS the SPECIFICATION rather than AS GUIDANCE',
    why: 'IT IS A LIST of THINGS THAT CAUSE REJECTION and READING IT COSTS AN HOUR' },
  { p: 'ROLL OUT IN STAGES', stages: ['INTERNAL TESTING', 'THEN A SMALL PERCENTAGE'],
    why: 'BECAUSE A STAGED ROLLOUT IS the ONLY MECHANISM THAT LIMITS the BLAST RADIUS of A RELEASE',
    gain: 'and IT GIVES YOU the CRASH and the REVIEW DATA from REAL USERS BEFORE EVERYONE HAS IT' },
];

When you are rejected, the response names a specific claim. Answer it literally: change what it names, and say in the resolution notes what changed and exactly where to find it. A reviewer is testing one thing, and a reply that argues rather than addresses it gets a second rejection.

// THE COMMON REJECTIONS, and what actually triggers them
//
// GOOGLE PLAY
// 1. PERMISSIONS without a core-feature justification
//    "This app requires ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION" with no
//    in-app use is a rejection
//    FIX: request it at the moment of use, and explain it in
//         the listing
// 2. A TARGET SDK that is too old
// 3. BROKEN functionality: a crash on launch, a dead button
// 4. DATA SAFETY that does not match the app
// 5. A deceptive design: a button that does something else
// 6. REPEATED policy violations on a developer account
//
// APPLE
// 1. 2.1 App Completeness: placeholders, a dead demo account
// 2. 3.2.2: an OTA that changed functionality
// 3. 4.2 Minimum Functionality: a repackaged website
// 4. 5.1.1 Data Collection: a privacy questionnaire that does
//    not match what a plugin does
// 5. Sign in with Apple required alongside other social login
// 6. Account deletion required if there is account creation
// 7. 4.7: an app that is only a web view in a wrapper

// THE ITEMS THAT CATCH PEOPLE
// - the demo account for the reviewer expires or is rate
//   limited: keep it alive for at least two weeks after
//   submission
// - a reviewer device that is not your device: test on a small
//   old phone
// - a permission that works on API 34 but not 33
// - an account deletion flow that is hard to find
// THE SUBMISSION CHECKLIST
//
// STORE LISTING
// [ ] an app icon, 512x512, no alpha, no rounded corners
// [ ] a feature graphic, 1024x500
// [ ] at least two phone screenshots per form factor
// [ ] a short description (<= 80 chars) and a full one
// [ ] a privacy policy URL that resolves, on your own domain
// [ ] a support URL
//
// PRIVACY
// [ ] the data safety form matches what you actually transmit,
//     INCLUDING what a plugin does
// [ ] the App Privacy questionnaire lists every data type
// [ ] an account deletion endpoint, if there is sign-up
// [ ] a privacy policy that names the data, the purpose, the
//     retention and the deletion process
//
// TECHNICAL
// [ ] zero analyzer warnings
// [ ] the tests pass, including the goldens
// [ ] the release artefact installed on a real device and
//     smoke-tested: sign in, create, sync, kill, reopen
// [ ] the binary audited for secrets
// [ ] the target SDK is current
// [ ] the version number is higher than the last upload
//
// STORE-SPECIFIC
// [ ] the demo account works and will keep working
// [ ] content rating completed
// [ ] the ads declaration, if there are ads
// [ ] the target audience and content, which affects COPPA
// [ ] health apps: the health declarations
// [ ] a "news" app: the source disclosure
// [ ] the App Store age rating questionnaire
// A STAGED ROLLOUT, which is the best thing you can do
// 1. internal testing: your team, instant
// 2. closed testing: a list of testers, if you need one
// 3. open testing: anyone who opts in
// 4. production: staged at 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100%
//
// each stage: watch the crash-free rate for 24-48 hours
// before increasing. Play's pre-launch report catches roughly a
// third of crashes before users see them.
//
// reversing a rollout takes minutes. un-publishing does not.

// THE STAGES, in the command line
flutter build appbundle --release
fastlane supply --aab app-release.aab --track internal --rollout 1.0
# ...after review
fastlane supply --track beta --rollout 0.01
# ...later
fastlane supply --track beta --rollout 0.05

// THE VERSION CODE must increase on EVERY upload, including a
// staged rollout increase
flutter build appbundle --build-number=$(( $(cat version.txt) + 1 ))

Exercises 19

  1. Run the secret audit from 18.1 on your own release build, and remove everything it finds.
  2. Add a CI step that fails the build if a secret pattern appears in the binary. Prove it fails by planting one.
  3. Configure certificate pinning with two pins, and test what happens when the server certificate is replaced.
  4. Enable an Android backup exclusion for your database, and verify the file is absent from a backup.
  5. Implement biometric unlock as a gate on a locally-held key, and handle a device with no sensor.
  6. Build a release AAB with obfuscation, keep the debug symbols, and symbolicate a crash report by hand.
  7. Write the full pre-flight checklist as a script, and run it on a clean checkout.
  8. Ship to internal testing, then a 1% staged rollout, and write down what you monitored.

A.1 Widget referenceA.2 Layout and constraintsA.3 State managementA.4 Command referenceA.5 Package referenceA.6 Build configurationA.7 Platform configurationA.8 Performance checklist

Lookup tables to keep open while you build: the widget and layout reference, the state management comparison, every command, the packages this guide uses, and the platform configuration for each target.

A.1 Widget reference

How to read the table, and the three columns that matter

This table is a lookup, and a lookup is only useful if you know what the rows mean and what the alternatives are, so the useful part of it is not the list of names but the reasoning behind the groupings. The first column is the widget; the second is what it is for; the third is when to reach for it instead of something else. That third column is the one worth reading, because the majority of mistakes in this framework are not "I used the wrong widget" but "I did not know there was a widget for this", and a list without the alternative teaches the name without the judgement. Grouping by role rather than by hierarchy is deliberate: layout widgets are grouped together because the question when choosing one is "how do I place this relative to that", and grouping by inheritance would give a list in which the useful neighbours are scattered. Then the three things the table deliberately does not contain, and each omission is a decision. It does not contain every parameter of every widget, because that is the framework's own documentation and it is exhaustive; a table that tried to be exhaustive would be unusable in the way a telephone directory is unusable. It does not contain the composition widgets, because those are built from what it does contain and listing them separately would invite choosing a composition where a primitive would do. And it does not rank the widgets, because there is no ranking that holds across applications — the right widget for a dialog in a data-dense desktop application is not the right widget for a dialog on a phone. Then the three ways people misuse a table like this, and each is worth avoiding. Treating it as a menu and picking from it when building, rather than as a check when reviewing — the second finds the mistake and the first creates it. Assuming a row means a widget has only that use, which is what produces the common finding of a hundred rows built with Container where a ListTile would have given semantics, ink and accessibility for free. And memorising it instead of knowing the categories, which produces a developer who can list the widgets and cannot choose between them — and the categories are what survive, because new widgets appear and the categories do not change. Then the two things worth doing with it, and both are habits rather than tasks. Use it to check, after writing. Find the widget that would have given you the behaviour you implemented yourself, which is the highest-value use and the one that turns a table into a review tool. And use it to check the states, not just the appearance, because a widget chosen from this table has disabled, error, pressed and selected states that the table does not list and that the widget provides — and an application that used the wrong widget will not have them.

/* The columns. */
const COLUMNS = [
  { c: 'the WIDGET', is: 'the NAME' },
  { c: 'WHAT IT IS FOR', is: 'the ROLE' },
  { c: 'WHEN TO REACH FOR IT instead of SOMETHING ELSE', isTheWorthwhileColumn: true },
];
const WHY_THIRD = 'THAT THIRD COLUMN IS the ONE WORTH READING';
const MISTAKE = 'BECAUSE the MAJORITY of MISTAKES IN this FRAMEWORK ARE NOT I USED the WRONG WIDGET BUT I DID NOT KNOW THERE WAS A WIDGET for THIS';
const TEACHES = 'and A LIST WITHOUT the ALTERNATIVE TEACHES the NAME WITHOUT the JUDGEMENT';
const GROUPING = {
  by: 'ROLE rather than BY HIERARCHY',
  why: ['the QUESTION WHEN CHOOSING ONE IS how do I PLACE THIS RELATIVE TO THAT',
    'and GROUPING BY INHERITANCE WOULD GIVE A LIST IN WHICH the USEFUL NEIGHBOURS ARE SCATTERED'],
};

/* Three deliberate omissions. */
const OMITS = [
  { o: 'EVERY PARAMETER of EVERY WIDGET',
    why: 'BECAUSE THAT IS the FRAMEWORKS OWN DOCUMENTATION and IT IS EXHAUSTIVE',
    consequence: 'A TABLE THAT TRIED TO BE EXHAUSTIVE WOULD BE UNUSABLE IN the WAY A TELEPHONE DIRECTORY IS UNUSABLE' },
  { o: 'the COMPOSITION WIDGETS',
    why: 'BECAUSE THOSE ARE BUILT FROM WHAT IT DOES CONTAIN',
    consequence: 'and LISTING THEM SEPARATELY WOULD INVITE CHOOSING A COMPOSITION WHERE A PRIMITIVE WOULD DO' },

/* Three ways it gets misused. */

  { m: 'TREATING IT AS A MENU',
    when: 'PICKING FROM IT WHEN BUILDING, rather than AS A CHECK WHEN REVIEWING',
    which: 'the SECOND FINDS the MISTAKE and the FIRST CREATES IT' },
  { m: 'ASSUMING A ROW MEANS A WIDGET HAS ONLY THAT USE',

    why: 'and the CATEGORIES ARE WHAT SURVIVE, BECAUSE NEW WIDGETS APPEAR and the CATEGORIES DO NOT CHANGE' },
];

/* Two habits. */
const HABITS = [
  { h: 'USE IT TO CHECK, AFTER WRITING', what: 'FIND the WIDGET THAT WOULD HAVE GIVEN YOU the BEHAVIOUR YOU IMPLEMENTED YOURSELF',
    value: 'WHICH IS the HIGHEST-VALUE USE and THE ONE THAT TURNS A TABLE INTO A REVIEW TOOL' },
  { h: 'USE IT TO CHECK the STATES, NOT JUST the APPEARANCE',
    detail: 'BECAUSE A WIDGET CHOSEN FROM THIS TABLE HAS DISABLED, ERROR, PRESSED and SELECTED STATES THAT the TABLE DOES NOT LIST and THAT the WIDGET PROVIDES',

The three render object widget variants are worth learning even if you only ever use the first one. SingleChildRenderObjectWidget is for a layout behaviour on a single child, MultiChildRenderObjectWidget with LayoutId is for positioning several, and RenderObjectWidget gives you complete control - and it is the only way to do something the framework has no widget for.

A.2 Layout and constraints

// THE MODEL
//   constraints go DOWN from the parent
//   the child CHOOSES a size within them
//   sizes go UP
//
// BoxConstraints
//   .tight(w, h)          min == max: no choice
//   .loose(w, h)          a range: the child picks
//   .expand(w, h)         loose with max = the parent's max
//   .tightFor(width: 100) tight on one axis only
//   minWidth / maxWidth / minHeight / maxHeight
//   .constrain(size)       clamp a desired size to them
//
// THE FIVE LAYOUT FAILURES, and their fixes
// 1. "RenderFlex children have non-zero flex but incoming
//     height constraints are unbounded"
//    a flex widget on the cross axis of a scroll view
//    FIX: SizedBox, IntrinsicHeight, or mainAxisSize.min
// 2. "RenderFlex overflowed by N pixels"
//    the children want more than the parent offers
//    FIX: Expanded, Flexible, FittedBox, or a scroll view
// 3. "RenderBox was not laid out"
//    a layout pass that does not converge: usually an
//    unbounded parent with an unbounded child
//    FIX: bound one of them
// 4. "CustomPaint without a size would be infinite"
//    FIX: size, or a child, or SizedBox.expand in a Stack
// 5. a Column that expands and starves its siblings
//    FIX: mainAxisSize.min, or give it content
//
// THE FLEX FITS
//   Expanded(flex: 1)              = Flexible(flex:1, tight)
//   Flexible(fit: FlexFit.loose)   the default: a maximum
//   Flexible(fit: FlexFit.tight)   a minimum: it fills
//   flex is a WEIGHT, not a fraction: flex 2 and flex 1
//   split the free space in a 2:1 ratio
//
// THE COST OF INTRINSIC SIZING
//   it runs 2-3 extra layout passes
//   fine on a small subtree, terrible on a list
//   measure with TextPainter for a one-off calculation

How to read this table, and the trap in its second column

This table is a decision aid rather than a lookup, so it is organised the way a decision is made: by what you are trying to achieve, then by the mechanism, then by the thing that goes wrong. The first column is the goal — place these in a row, make this fill, keep this on screen, centre this in what remains — and the second is the widget that does it. That ordering matters because the common mistake is to start at the widget and look for a goal it might serve, which is how a Container ends up laying out something a Row should have laid out. The third column is the trap, and it is the reason the table exists. Every row has a way to get it wrong that produces a result which looks correct in a screenshot and is wrong in use — a widget that fills when it should have shrunk, a scroll view that throws on a nested one, an intrinsic measurement that costs a second layout. Then the three things the table deliberately groups, and each grouping is a decision. By goal rather than by widget type, so the same goal that has two answers shows both. By the mechanism that is actually at work, so a row is not repeated for every widget that happens to achieve it. And By what it costs, because a layout that is free for one child and quadratic for two hundred is a different decision, and the cost column is what tells you which. Then the three ways people misuse a table of this kind, and each is worth naming. Reading the widget column without the trap column, which is reading half the table and the less useful half, because the widget names are learnable in an afternoon and the traps are what cost an afternoon each. Applying a row without checking whether the container allows it, which is the layout chapter's point that a widget's behaviour depends on the constraints it is handed — a row that is right inside a column and wrong inside a Stack is not a contradiction. And copying the mechanism rather than the goal, so a fix for one problem becomes a pattern that is applied to the next problem where it does not apply. Then the two things worth doing with it, and both are habits. Use it as a checklist for the screens that are hard, not for all of them: the screen with a keyboard, the screen with a long list inside a scroll view, and the screen with a fixed-height control containing text are the three that this table exists for. And read the trap column out loud when reviewing, because a layout decision that has been stated as a risk is a decision, and one that has not is an accident that happened to work.

/* What kind of table this is. */
const KIND = 'A DECISION AID rather than A LOOKUP';
const ORGANISED = 'ORGANISED the WAY A DECISION IS MADE - BY WHAT YOU ARE TRYING TO ACHIEVE, THEN BY the MECHANISM, THEN BY the THING THAT GOES WRONG';
const COLUMNS = [
  { c: 'the GOAL', instances: ['PLACE THESE IN A ROW', 'MAKE THIS FILL', 'KEEP THIS ON SCREEN', 'CENTRE THIS IN WHAT REMAINS'] },
  { c: 'the WIDGET', and: 'THAT ORDERING MATTERS',
    why: 'BECAUSE the COMMON MISTAKE IS to START AT the WIDGET and LOOK FOR A GOAL IT MIGHT SERVE',
    symptom: 'WHICH IS HOW A Container ENDS UP LAYING OUT SOMETHING A Row SHOULD HAVE LAID OUT' },
  { c: 'the TRAP', whyTheTableExists: true,
    detail: 'EVERY ROW HAS A WAY TO GET IT WRONG THAT PRODUCES A RESULT WHICH LOOKS CORRECT IN A SCREENSHOT and IS WRONG IN USE',
    instances: ['A WIDGET THAT FILLS WHEN IT SHOULD HAVE SHRUNK',
      'A SCROLL VIEW THAT THROWS ON A NESTED ONE', 'AN INTRINSIC MEASUREMENT THAT COSTS A SECOND LAYOUT'] },
];

/* Three groupings, each a decision. */
const GROUPED = [
  { g: 'BY GOAL rather than BY WIDGET TYPE', why: 'SO the SAME GOAL THAT HAS TWO ANSWERS SHOWS BOTH' },
  { g: 'BY the MECHANISM THAT IS ACTUALLY AT WORK', why: 'SO A ROW IS NOT REPEATED for EVERY WIDGET THAT HAPPENS TO ACHIEVE IT' },
  { g: 'BY WHAT IT COSTS',
    detail: 'BECAUSE A LAYOUT THAT IS FREE for ONE CHILD and QUADRATIC for TWO HUNDRED IS A DIFFERENT DECISION',

];

/* Three ways it gets misused. */
const MISUSE = [

  { m: 'APPLYING A ROW WITHOUT CHECKING WHETHER the CONTAINER ALLOWS IT',

/* Two habits. */

A.3 State management

//             complexity   async      codegen  testability
// setState     none         manual     no       widget test
// Inherited    low          manual     no       widget test
// Provider     low          good       no       widget test
// Riverpod     medium       built in   yes      plain Dart
// Bloc         high         built in   no       plain Dart
// signals      medium       manual     no       plain Dart
//
// Riverpod provider flavours
//   Provider               a value
//   FutureProvider          async, gives AsyncValue
//   StreamProvider          a stream
//   NotifierProvider        a class with build() and methods
//   AsyncNotifierProvider   the async version
//   .family                 a parameter: provider(id)
//   .autoDispose            freed when unlistened
//   .select(x)              rebuild only when x changes
//   ref.invalidate(p)       force a refetch
//   ref.keepAlive()         do not dispose
//
// AsyncValue states
//   .isLoading  .hasValue  .hasError  .valueOrNull
//   .when(loading:, error:, data:)
//
// Bloc
//   events in, states out, on<E>(handler)
//   BlocBuilder with buildWhen: rebuild only for some states
//   BlocProvider for creation
//   Cubit: a class with methods that emit
//
// signals
//   signal(v)              a value
//   computed(() => ...)   derived, cached until a dep changes
//   effect((ref) => ...)  a side effect on change
//   .value                  read; .value = ... write
//
// THE RULES, whatever you choose
//   1. local state stays local: setState, not a store
//   2. derive, do not store derived data
//   3. no work in build
//   4. a ValueKey on every list item
//   5. state as low in the tree as possible
//   6. dispose every controller, subscription and timer

How to read this table, and what the order encodes

This table is a decision procedure rather than a catalogue, and its most important property is the order of the rows: they are in the order you should consider them, from the cheapest and most local answer to the most capable and most expensive. That ordering is the whole point of the table, because the failure mode in state management is not choosing badly — it is choosing expensively when cheaply would have worked, and a list ordered alphabetically makes that failure invisible while a list ordered by cost makes it obvious. Each row therefore carries three things: what it is, what it costs, and the sign that you have gone one level too far. That last column is the one worth reading first, because it converts the table from a menu into a checklist: if the sign in the "too far" column is true of your code, the answer is the row above. Then the four things the table deliberately leaves out, and each omission is a judgement. It does not rank the libraries against each other, because the choice between them is decided by the state chapter's criteria — what shape the data has, who needs it, whether it must survive a route change — and a table that said "use this one" would be wrong for the majority of the applications that read it. It does not include a "no state management at all" row, because that is the default and a row that says "none" reads as a recommendation rather than as a starting point. It does not cover derived state, because derived state is not a tool choice but a modelling error, and a table row about it would be in the wrong table. And it does not mention the performance of a rebuild, which is a property of how you used the thing rather than of the thing. Then the three ways people misuse a table like this, and each is common. Skipping to the bottom row because a tutorial used it, which is the most common single cause of an over-engineered application, and the table's ordering is designed to make the skip visible: if the sign in the third column is true for the row above, the tutorial's choice was made for a different problem. Treating the cost column as a price rather than as a direction, so a cheap option is chosen for a problem it cannot solve — setState cannot be made correct for a value two routes need, and picking it because it is cheap does not make the problem go away. And adopting a library without writing down which problem it solved, so a year later the problem has changed and the library remains. Then the two things worth doing with it, and both are habits. Use the third column as a review check on your own code, asking for each state-holding widget whether the sign in the row above it is true. And read the state chapter's four questions before choosing, and then find the row whose description matches the answer — the table is an index into a decision, not the decision itself.

How to read a command reference, and the four commands that matter most

A command reference is only useful in two situations: when you know what you want to do and need the exact spelling, and when something has gone wrong and you need the diagnostic. Those two situations want different things from the list, and the table is organised for both by grouping the commands by what situation they serve. The groups are: create and run, inspect and diagnose, code generation and analysis, dependency management, build and release, and cleaning. The grouping is the useful part, because a command remembered by name is a command that is forgotten when the name differs between versions, while a command remembered by purpose is not. Almost every command has a short and a long form, and the short form is an abbreviation rather than a distinct command — so knowing that both exist is what tells you that a flag you read somewhere belongs to the long form. Flags are per-command, which is why a command copied from a tutorial can fail with an unknown-option error on a different version; the honest practice is to check the command's own help rather than to trust a remembered flag. Then the four commands that matter more than the rest, and each is worth knowing by heart because it is the answer to a common situation. The diagnostic — the one that reports every tool the environment has and every problem with it — because almost every "it worked yesterday and not today" is an environment answer and this is the command that produces it. The dependency resolution command, which restores the packages the project declares and can be run when the build fails on a missing package after a branch switch, because the lock file and the configuration can disagree. The generator run, which is required after every change to an annotated class and whose omission produces a build error that looks like a code problem and is not. And the clean, which removes build output and cached state, and which is the correct response to a build that has become inexplicable — with the important caveat that it makes the next build slow, so it is a diagnostic rather than a habit. Then the three ways command references get misused, and each is common. Copying a command from a blog post written for an older version, which produces a flag that no longer exists or an option whose meaning changed, and which is indistinguishable from a corrupted installation until you read the help. Running a destructive command to fix a problem without reading what it does, and the cleaning group is where this bites: several of those commands remove state that takes a long time to rebuild, and one class of them removes state that cannot be rebuilt. Treating a diagnostic's output as a failure, when the tool reports everything it checked including the things it is merely warning about, so an output with warnings in it is not an error. Then the two things worth doing with it, and both are habits. Learn the four, and read the help for the rest, because the help is on the machine and is versioned with the tool, whereas anything written down ages. And put the commands you use into the project's own documentation, with the version they were correct for, because the person who needs them is not you and will be on a different version.

What each package is for, and how to choose without a list

A package table is a directory, and a directory is only useful if you can navigate it by question rather than by scrolling — so the useful property of this list is that every entry answers one of a small number of questions, and knowing the questions is what makes the list navigable. Does the framework already do this? That is the first question and it has a high hit rate, because a surprising number of third-party packages exist to do something the framework does and did not when they were written. Is this a problem with a standard answer? Routing, state, storage and networking all have conventional answers in the ecosystem, and choosing a second one is usually a mistake. Do I need this to be small? Because every package is code in the binary and every package with its own dependencies multiplies that. And Will this still be maintained? — a package with one maintainer and no release in a year is a liability in a codebase you intend to maintain. Then the four things the table deliberately omits, and each omission is deliberate. It does not rank the packages in a category against each other, because the ecosystem moves faster than a table and a stale ranking is worse than none; the state chapter's criteria are what decide between the state packages. It does not list packages for problems the framework solves, which is the highest-value omission on the table because most of the packages people add are ones they did not need. It does not include anything that requires native code on a platform you do not target, because a package that needs a native implementation on a platform you do not ship is a package that cannot be added later without a rewrite. And it does not include utility collections — a package of a hundred functions — because those are adopted wholesale or not at all, and a codebase that depends on one has acquired a large API surface it did not design. Then the three ways people misuse a package list, and each is common. Adding a package for a problem with a ten-line solution, which is how a codebase accumulates a dependency for something that is three lines and would have stayed three lines. Adding a package to solve a problem that is really an architecture problem, where the symptom is "this is hard to organise" and the package adds an organisation mechanism without deciding what the organisation is. And not reading what a package does to the build, which is the native-code case above and which appears only at build time on a platform you did not test. Then the two things worth doing with it, and both are habits. Read the dependency count before adding, because a package with forty transitive dependencies has replaced one dependency with forty and each one is a thing that can be abandoned. And write one line about why a package is in the project, in the project's own notes — because the question "why is this here" is unanswerable from the source and inevitable after two years.

/* How to navigate it. */
const QUESTIONS = [

A.6 Build configuration

// android/app/build.gradle
android {
    namespace "com.acme.fieldnotes"
    compileSdk = 35
    ndkVersion = flutter.ndkVersion

    defaultConfig {
        applicationId = "com.acme.fieldnotes"
        minSdk = 23              // Flutter 3.24+ requires 23
        targetSdk = 35           // Play requires a recent level
        versionCode = 42         // MUST increase on every upload
        versionName = "1.4.0"    // what the user sees
    }

    buildTypes {
        release {
            signingConfig = signingConfigs.release
            minifyEnabled true
            shrinkResources true
            proguardFiles getDefaultProguardFile(
                            'proguard-android-optimize.txt'),
                        'proguard-rules.pro'
        }
    }

    // the AAB splits per architecture automatically
    splits {
        abi {
            enable true
            reset()
            include 'arm64-v8a'      // 99% of devices
            // include 'armeabi-v7a'  // old 32-bit
            // include 'x86_64'      // emulators
        }
    }
}

// ios/Runner.xcodeproj
//   MARKETING_VERSION      = 1.4.0
//   CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION = 42
//   IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET = 14.0 or later

// THE FLAGS THAT MATTER
--release                    AOT, optimised
--split-per-abi              one APK per architecture
--split-debug-info=DIR       KEEP the symbols
--obfuscate                  rename Dart symbols
--tree-shake-icons           on by default
--analyze-size               a size report
--build-number=N             the Android version code
--build-name=X.Y.Z           the visible version
--dart-define=K=V            a compile-time constant
--no-shrink                  keep resources (bigger)
--flavor=NAME                 a build flavour
--target=lib/main_dev.dart    an entry point per environment

// pubspec.yaml
flutter:
  uses-material-design: true
  assets:
    - assets/images/
  fonts:
    - family: Inter
      fonts:
        - asset: assets/fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf
          weight: 400
  shaders:
    - shaders/water.frag

// THE SIZE NUMBERS, roughly
//   engine, per architecture   ~4MB
//   your Dart code             0.5 - 3MB
//   assets                     whatever you bundled
//   the AAB download           15 - 30MB typical
//   the install size           30 - 60MB

What a build configuration actually decides

Build configuration looks like a list of key-value pairs and is actually a set of decisions about what goes into the artifact and in what form, and the difference matters because most of the settings people copy without reading are ones they should decide. The three that decide most builds are: the Dart define values, which are compile-time constants the application reads; the target platforms; and the tree-shaking and icon behaviour. The defines are the ones with a security consequence and they are the reason this table exists at compile time: a value in a define is a value in the binary, so a define used for a base URL or a feature flag is a value anyone with the application can read, and a define used for anything secret is a disclosure. That is the same argument as the secrets section, arriving at build time rather than in source. The size table has three rows and they mean different things, and confusing them produces a wrong reaction to a size number: the download size is what the user transfers, the install size is what occupies the device after installation, and the size on disk after first run is what it occupies once the application's data exists. A large download with a small install is an asset problem; a large install is a code problem; a small install that grows is a data problem, and the three require different investigations. Then the three things the table deliberately leaves out, and each is a decision about scope. It does not list the release build flags for every platform, because those are the build command's own options and they change with the version. It does not list signing configuration, because it is a secret and belongs in a platform's own store rather than in a table in a document. And it does not recommend a size, because a reasonable size depends on what the application is and a number without that context produces either alarm or indifference. Then the three ways people misuse a configuration table, and each is common. Copying a configuration from a tutorial and shipping flags meant for a development environment, which is the mechanism behind an application that points at a staging server in production. Assuming a define is private, which is the same error as the secrets section's and which the binary makes obvious once you look for the string. And adding a platform to the targets without implementing it, which produces a build that succeeds and an application that does not work on the platform nobody tested. Then the two things worth doing with it, and both are habits. Make the defines come from the build system rather than from a file in the repository, so that the value for a given artifact is chosen by whoever produced the artifact and is visible in the build log. And check the size breakdown before every release, and treat an increase as a review item — because the size of an application is a regression like any other and it grows one asset at a time.

What a manifest declares, and what declaring it commits you to

Every mobile platform has a manifest — one file, read by the operating system before your code runs, that declares what the application is, what it may do, and what the system should do on its behalf — and the reason it exists is that everything on a phone is a permission decision made in advance. It declares the application's identity: its identifier, its name, its version, its icon. It declares the capabilities it requests, and each capability is both a question the user will be asked and a promise you are making. And it declares what the system may do without asking — which activities exist, which URLs are handled, which files are shared with other applications, and whether the application may run when it is not in front. Then the four commitments, and each is a real obligation rather than a technicality. A declared capability is a request the user sees, and a request the user cannot understand is a request they will refuse — so the capability list is also a copy exercise, and the permission strings are that copy. A declared background mode is a promise to the system about what you do when the application is not in front, and the system uses those promises to decide what to grant you, so declaring more than you use costs you capability later. A declared URL scheme or domain association is a claim about the whole domain, and it is verified by the operating system against a file you serve, so getting it wrong means links open a browser instead of the application. And a declared permission that the application does not use is a review question and a privacy-policy mismatch, because the disclosure describes what the application does. Then the three things the table deliberately leaves out, and each is a decision about who owns the knowledge. It does not list every permission, because there are hundreds and they vary by version; what it lists is the ones a mobile application actually asks for. It does not include permission constants or their numeric values, because those are the platform's own documentation and they change between versions. And it does not tell you which permissions you need, because that depends on what your application does, and a table that guessed would be wrong for most of the applications that read it. Then the three ways people misuse a manifest, and each is common. Adding every permission the platform offers, which is the mechanism behind the "why is my application asking for my contacts" report and which the review will catch. Declaring a background mode and not implementing it, which is a promise not kept and which the system discovers. And forgetting that a manifest change requires a rebuild rather than a restart, so a permission added to the file appears not to work and is "fixed" by adding it again. Then the two things worth doing with it, and both are habits. Read the merged manifest from the built artifact rather than the source, because a library's manifest contributes entries and the merged file is what the system reads — which is the mechanism behind "I removed the permission and it is still there". And keep the permission list and the privacy policy in the same place, and check them against each other before a release, because they describe the same thing and a mismatch between them is a compliance problem rather than a documentation one.

/* What a manifest is. */

  declares: ['WHAT the APPLICATION IS', 'WHAT IT MAY DO', 'and WHAT the SYSTEM SHOULD DO ON ITS BEHALF'],

};

A.8 Performance checklist

How to run this checklist, and why it is ordered

A performance checklist is worth having only if it is run in an order that finds the biggest problem first, and this one is ordered by cost-per-effort rather than by category — so the first items are the ones that produce a large improvement for a small change, and the last are the ones that are correct but expensive. The order encodes a claim: most Flutter performance problems are caused by one of four things — a subtree rebuilding that should not, something measuring intrinsically, an image decoded at the wrong size, and an effect that requires an intermediate surface — and finding which of the four it is takes minutes and eliminates the other three. So the first four items are diagnostic, not corrective, and running them in order means you are never guessing. Then the three things the checklist deliberately does not include, and each omission is a judgement about what a checklist should be. It does not include anything that requires rewriting an architecture, because a checklist that contains an item you will skip produces the sense of completion without the benefit. It does not include platform-specific tuning — no font sizes, no density overrides, no per-device configuration — because those are product decisions rather than performance work and they belong in a design system. And it does not include a target, because the target for a list of fifty is different from the target for a list of fifty thousand, and a fixed number produces either alarm or indifference. Then the three ways a checklist gets misused, and each is common. Running it once at the end of a project, when the cost of the items is highest and the benefit is lowest; the checklist's value is that the first item is cheap and the tenth is not, and a project that runs them in reverse order pays the expensive ones for the smallest return. Running it without recording the numbers, which turns it into a list of opinions — and the items here are measurable, so an unmeasured pass is a pass that cannot tell you whether the next change helped. And treating every item as mandatory, which produces a codebase optimised for a case that does not exist and is harder to read for it. Then the two things worth doing with it, and both are habits. Run the first four items on every screen before you write it, because all four are visible in the widget inspector and the DevTools panel and each takes under a minute to check on a screen that does not have the problem yet. And keep the record, because the only thing that makes a performance practice durable is a number that was written down before the change and after it.

/* Why the order. */
const ORDER_WHY = {
  claim: 'MOST FLUTTER PERFORMANCE PROBLEMS ARE CAUSED BY ONE of FOUR THINGS',
  four: ['A SUBTREE REBUILDING THAT SHOULD NOT', 'SOMETHING MEASURING INTRINSICALLY',
    'AN IMAGE DECODED AT the WRONG SIZE', 'and AN EFFECT THAT REQUIRES AN INTERMEDIATE SURFACE'],
  gain: 'and FINDING WHICH of the FOUR IT IS TAKES MINUTES and ELIMINATES the OTHER THREE',
  firstFourAre: 'DIAGNOSTIC, NOT CORRECTIVE',
  so: 'SO THE FIRST FOUR ITEMS ARE DIAGNOSTIC, NOT CORRECTIVE, and RUNNING THEM IN ORDER MEANS YOU ARE NEVER GUESSING',
};

/* Three omissions. */
const OMITS = [
  { o: 'ANYTHING THAT REQUIRES REWRITING AN ARCHITECTURE',
    why: 'BECAUSE A CHECKLIST THAT CONTAINS AN ITEM YOU WILL SKIP PRODUCES the SENSE OF COMPLETION WITHOUT the BENEFIT' },
  { o: 'PLATFORM-SPECIFIC TUNING', instances: ['NO FONT SIZES', 'NO DENSITY OVERRIDES', 'NO PER-DEVICE CONFIGURATION'],
    why: 'BECAUSE THOSE ARE PRODUCT DECISIONS rather than PERFORMANCE WORK and THEY BELONG IN A DESIGN SYSTEM' },
  { o: 'A TARGET',
    why: 'BECAUSE the TARGET FOR A LIST of FIFTY IS DIFFERENT from the TARGET FOR A LIST of FIFTY THOUSAND',
    symptom: 'and A FIXED NUMBER PRODUCES EITHER ALARM or INDIFFERENCE' },
];

/* Three ways a checklist gets misused. */
const MISUSE = [
  { m: 'RUNNING IT ONCE AT the END of A PROJECT',
    symptom: 'WHEN the COST of the ITEMS IS HIGHEST and the BENEFIT IS LOWEST',
    detail: 'the CHECKLISTS VALUE IS THAT the FIRST ITEM IS CHEAP and the TENTH IS NOT',
    consequence: 'and A PROJECT THAT RUNS THEM IN REVERSE ORDER PAYS the EXPENSIVE ONES for the SMALLEST RETURN' },
  { m: 'RUNNING IT WITHOUT RECORDING the NUMBERS',
    symptom: 'WHICH TURNS IT INTO A LIST of OPINIONS',
    and: 'the ITEMS HERE ARE MEASURABLE, SO AN UNMEASURED PASS IS A PASS THAT CANNOT TELL YOU WHETHER the NEXT CHANGE HELPED' },
  { m: 'TREATING EVERY ITEM AS MANDATORY',
    symptom: 'WHICH PRODUCES A CODEBASE OPTIMISED FOR A CASE THAT DOES NOT EXIST and IS HARDER TO READ FOR IT' },

/* Two habits. */
const HABITS = [
  { h: 'RUN the FIRST FOUR ITEMS ON EVERY SCREEN BEFORE YOU WRITE IT',
    why: 'BECAUSE ALL FOUR ARE VISIBLE IN the WIDGET INSPECTOR and the DEVTOOLS PANEL',
    gain: 'and EACH TAKES UNDER A MINUTE TO CHECK on A SCREEN THAT DOES NOT HAVE the PROBLEM YET' },
  { h: 'KEEP the RECORD',
    why: 'BECAUSE the ONLY THING THAT MAKES A PERFORMANCE PRACTICE DURABLE IS A NUMBER THAT WAS WRITTEN DOWN BEFORE the CHANGE and AFTER IT' },
];

Work the performance checklist in order. The first two entries - an itemExtent and const - fix the large majority of list performance problems and cost almost nothing. Reaching for isolates or custom layout before those is optimising the wrong thing at the wrong cost.

// IN ORDER OF IMPACT
//
// 1. ITEM EXTENT, or a builder instead of children
//    ListView.builder(itemExtent: 80, ...)
//    the single biggest win in any list
//
// 2. const ON EVERYTHING THAT CAN BE const
//    free, and it skips the entire subtree
//
// 3. A ValueKey ON EVERY LIST ITEM
//
// 4. MOVE THE WORK OUT OF build
//    grep build methods for: toList, sort, where, jsonDecode,
//    await, a repository call, DateFormat.format
//
// 5. STATE AS LOW AS POSSIBLE
//    a row's state in the row, not the screen
//
// 6. A NARROWER DEPENDENCY
//    MediaQuery.viewInsetsOf, not .of
//    ref.watch(p.select((x) => x.title))
//    pass values as parameters down
//
// 7. cacheWidth ON EVERY IMAGE
//    a 4000x3000 photo is 48MB decoded
//
// 8. AnimatedBuilder WITH A child
//    so the subtree is built once
//
// 9. A RepaintBoundary, where MEASURED
//    an animating child in a large static parent
//    each boundary costs memory
//
// 10. AN ISOLATE, for real CPU work
//     compute() for under about 16ms of work is overhead
//
// 11. A SLIVER instead of shrinkWrap
//     shrinkWrap builds everything, always
//
// THE MEASUREMENT
//   flutter run --profile          never debug
//   on a low-end physical device   never a simulator
//   DevTools -> Performance
//     the frame chart: UI thread vs RASTER thread
//     the widget rebuild timeline
//     the memory panel, for a rising floor
//
// THE NUMBERS
//   16.7ms per frame at 60fps
//   a red bar = a missed frame
//   under 2s to first content, on a low-end device
//   a flat memory profile after 10 minutes

Exercises 20

  1. Print the widget and layout references. They are the two tables you will consult most while building UI.
  2. Fill in the package reference with what your own project actually uses, and drop the rest.
  3. Work the performance checklist against a real screen of yours, in order, and measure after each change.
  4. Check your AndroidManifest.xml and Info.plist against the configuration reference. Most permission problems are a missing entry here.
  5. Run every command in the command reference once, so you know they all work on your machine.
